Since $f _ { s } ^ { - 1 } B = \{ t \in T ; ( s , t ) \in f ^ { - 1 } B \} = ( f ^ { - 1 } B ) _ { s }$ , we see from (i) that $( \mu _ { s } \circ f _ { s } ^ { - 1 } ) B = \mu _ { s } ( f ^ { - 1 } B ) _ { s }$ is measurable, which means that $\nu _ { s } = \mu _ { s } \circ f _ { s } ^ { - 1 }$ is a kernel. Since $\| \nu _ { s } \| = \| \mu _ { s } \| < \infty$ for all $s \in S$ , the kernel ν is again finite. 

(iii) Since $\mu$ is s -finite and $\mathsf { N } ^ { 2 }$ is countable, we may assume that $\mu$ is finite. Putting $k _ { s } = [ \| \mu _ { s } \| ] + 1$ , we note that $\begin{array} { r } { \mu _ { s } = \sum _ { n } k _ { s } ^ { - 1 } 1 \{ n \leq k _ { s } \} \mu _ { s } } \end{array}$ , where each term is clearly a sub-probability kernel. 

(iv) First let $\mu$ be σ-finite, so that $\mu _ { s } f _ { s } < \infty$ for some measurable function $f > 0$ on $S \times T$ . Then (i) shows that $\nu _ { s } = f _ { s } \cdot \mu _ { s }$ is a finite kernel from $S$ to $T$ , and so $\mu _ { s } = g _ { s } \cdot \nu _ { s }$ with $g = 1 / f$ . Then $\begin{array} { r } { f = \sum _ { n } 1 _ { B _ { n } } f _ { n } > 0 } \end{array}$ , and 

$$

$$

$$
\leq \sum_ {n} 2 ^ {- n} = 1,
$$

which shows that $\mu$ is σ-finite. 

(v) If $\mu$ is σ-finite, then $\mu _ { s } g _ { s } < \infty$ for some measurable function $g > 0$ on $S \times T$ . which implies $A _ { \mu \nu } f = ( A _ { \mu } A _ { \nu } ) f$ , and hence $A _ { \mu \nu } = A _ { \mu } A _ { \nu }$ 

We turn to the reverse problem of representing a given measure $\rho$ on $S \times T$ in the form $\nu \otimes \mu ,$ , for some measure $\nu$ on $S$ and kernel $\mu : S \to T$ . The resulting disintegration may be regarded as an infinitesimal decomposition of $\rho$ into measures $\delta _ { s } \otimes \mu _ { s }$ . Any σ-finite measure $\nu \sim \rho ( \cdot \times T )$ is called a supporting measure of $\rho ,$ and we refer to $\mu$ as the associated disintegration kernel. 

Theorem 3.4 (disintegration) Let $\rho$ be a σ-finite measure on $S \times T$ , where $T$ is Borel. Then 

(i) $\rho = \nu \otimes \mu$ for a σ-finite measure $\nu \sim \rho ( \cdot \times T ) \equiv \hat { \rho } _ { S }$ and a σ-finite kernel $\mu \colon S \to T$ 

(ii) the $\mu _ { s }$ are $\nu { - } a . e .$ . unique up to normalizations, and they are $a . e .$ . bounded if $\hat { \rho } _ { S }$ is $\sigma { - } f i n i t e ,$ 

(iii) when $\hat { \rho }$ is σ-finite and $\nu = \hat { \rho } _ { S }$ , we may choose the $\mu _ { s }$ to be probability measures on $T$ . 

Proof: (i) If $\rho$ is σ-finite and $\neq 0$ , we may choose $g \in ( S \times T ) _ { + }$ such that $\rho = g \cdot { \tilde { \rho } }$ for some probability measure $\tilde { \rho }$ on $S \times T$ . If $\widetilde { \rho } = \nu \otimes \widetilde { \mu }$ for some measure ν on $S$ and kernel ${ \tilde { \mu } } \colon S \times T$ , then Lemma 3.2 (i) shows that $\mu = g \cdot \tilde { \mu }$ is a σ-finite kernel from $S$ to $T ,$ and so for any $f \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (\nu \otimes \mu) f = \bigl \{\mu \otimes (g \cdot \tilde {\mu}) \bigr \} f \\ = (\mu \otimes \tilde {\mu}) (f g) \\ = \tilde {\rho} (f g) = \rho f, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\rho = \nu \otimes \mu$ . We may then assume that $\rho$ is a probability measure on $S \times T$ . Since $T$ is Borel, we may further take $T = { \mathsf { R } }$ 

Choosing $\nu = \hat { \rho }$ and putting $\nu _ { r } = \rho ( \cdot \times ( - \infty , r ] )$ , we get $\nu _ { r } \leq \nu$ for all $r \in \mathsf { R } .$ , and so Theorem 2.10 yields $\nu _ { r } = f _ { r } \cdot \nu$ for some measurable functions $f _ { r } \colon S \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Here $f _ { r }$ is non-decreasing in $r \in \mathsf Q$ with limits 0 and 1 at $\pm \infty$ outside a fixed ν -null set $N \subset S$ . Redefining $f _ { r } = 0$ on N, we can make those properties hold identically. For the right-continuous versions $F _ { s , t } = \operatorname* { i n f } _ { r > t } f _ { r }$ with $t \in { \mathsf { R } }$ , we see by monotone convergence that $F _ { r } = f _ { r }$ a.e. for all $r \in \mathsf { Q }$ 

Now Proposition 2.14 yields some probability measures $\mu ( s , \cdot )$ on R with distribution functions $F ( s , t )$ . Here $\mu ( s , B )$ is measurable in $s \in S$ for each $B \in \tau$ by a monotone-class argument, which means that $\mu$ is a kernel from $S$ to $T$ . Furthermore, we have for any $A \in S$ and $r \in \mathsf { Q }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \rho (A \times (- \infty , r ]) = \int_ {A} \nu (d s) F _ {r} (s) \\ = \int_ {A} \nu (d s) \mu_ {s} (- \infty , r ], \end{array}
$$

which extends by a monotone-class argument and monotone convergence to the general disintegration formula $\rho f = ( \nu \otimes \mu ) f$ , for arbitrary $f \in ( S \times \mathcal { T } ) _ { + }$ 

(ii) Suppose that $\rho = \nu \otimes \mu = \nu ^ { \prime } \otimes \mu ^ { \prime }$ with $\nu \sim \nu ^ { \prime } \sim \rho ( \cdot \times T )$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} g \cdot \rho = \nu \otimes (g \cdot \mu) \\ = \nu^ {\prime} \otimes (g \cdot \mu^ {\prime}), \quad g \geq 0, \end{array}
$$

which allows us to consider only bounded measures $\rho .$ . Since also $\left( h \cdot \nu \right) \otimes \mu =$ $\nu ^ { \prime } \otimes \left( h \cdot \mu ^ { \prime } \right)$ for any $h \in S _ { + }$ , we may further assume that $\nu = \nu ^ { \prime }$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {A} \nu (d s) \left(\mu_ {s} B - \mu_ {s} ^ {\prime} B\right) = 0, \quad A \in \mathcal {S},   B \in \mathcal {T},
$$

which implies $\mu _ { s } B = \mu _ { s } ^ { \prime } B$ a.e. ν. Since $T$ is Borel, a monotone-class argument yields $\mu _ { s } = \mu _ { s } ^ { \prime }$ a.e. ν. ✷ 

The following partial disintegration will be needed in Chapter 31. 

Corollary 3.5 (partial disintegration) Let $\nu , \rho$ be σ-finite measures on $S$ and $S \times T$ , respectively, where $T$ is Borel. Then there exists an a.e. unique maximal kernel Q √T 

$$
\mu \colon S \to T, \quad \nu \otimes \mu \leq \rho .
$$

Here the maximality of $\mu$ means that, whenever $\mu ^ { \prime }$ is a kernel satisfying $\nu \otimes \mu ^ { \prime } \leq \rho _ { ; }$ we have $\mu _ { s } ^ { \prime } \le \mu _ { s }$ for $s \in S { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } \nu$ 

Proof: Since $\rho$ is σ-finite, we may choose a σ-finite measure $\gamma$ on $S$ with $\gamma \sim \rho ( \cdot \times T )$ . Consider its Lebesgue decomposition $\gamma = \gamma _ { a } + \gamma _ { s }$ with respect to $\nu ,$ as in Theorem 2.10, so that $\gamma _ { a } ~ \ll ~ \nu$ and $\gamma _ { s } \perp \nu .$ Choose $A \in S$ with $\nu A ^ { c } = \gamma _ { s } A = 0$ , and let $\rho ^ { \prime }$ denote the restriction of $\rho$ to $A \times T$ . Then $\rho ^ { \prime } ( \cdot \times T ) \ll \nu ,$ and so Theorem 3.4 yields a σ-finite kerne $\mu : S  T$ with $\nu \otimes \mu = \rho ^ { \prime } \leq \rho .$ 

Now consider any kernel $\mu ^ { \prime } \colon S \to T$ with $\nu \otimes \mu ^ { \prime } \leq \rho .$ . Since $\nu A ^ { c } = 0$ , we have $\nu \otimes \mu ^ { \prime } \leq \rho ^ { \prime } = \nu \otimes \mu$ . Since $\mu$ and $\mu ^ { \prime }$ are σ-finite, there exists a measurable function $g > 0$ on $S \times T$ , such that the kernels ${ \tilde { \mu } } = g \cdot \mu$ and $\tilde { \mu } ^ { \prime } = g \cdot \mu ^ { \prime }$ satisfy $\| \tilde { \mu } _ { s } \| \vee \| \tilde { \mu } _ { s } ^ { \prime } \| \leq 1$ . Then $\nu \otimes \tilde { \mu } ^ { \prime } \leq \nu \otimes \tilde { \mu }$ , and so $\tilde { \mu } _ { s } ^ { \prime } B \le \tilde { \mu } _ { s } B , s \in S \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } \nu .$ , for every $B \in S$ . This extends by a monotone-class argument to $\mu _ { s } ^ { \prime } \le \mu _ { s } \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } \nu ,$ which shows that $\mu$ is maximal. In particular, $\mu$ is a.e. unique. ✷ 

We often need to disintegrate kernels. Here the previous construction still applies, except that now we need a product-measurable version of the Radon– Nikodym theorem, and we must check that the required measurability is preserved throughout the construction. Since the simplest approach is based on martingale methods, we postpone the proof until Theorem 9.27. 

Corollary 3.6 (disintegration of kernels) Consider some σ-finite kernels $\nu :$ $S  T$ and $\rho \colon S  T \times U$ with $\nu _ { s } \sim \rho _ { s } ( \cdot \times U )$ for all $s \in S$ , where T, U are Borel. Then there exists a σ-finite kernel

$$

$$

$$

Theorem 3.7 (iterated disintegration) Consider a projective set of $\sigma { - } f i n i t e$ measures $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \mu _ { 3 } , \mu _ { 1 2 } , \mu _ { 1 3 } , \mu _ { 2 3 } , \mu _ { 1 2 3 }$ on products of Borel spaces $S , T , U$ and form the associated disintegration kernels $\mu _ { 1 | 2 } , \mu _ { 2 | 1 } , \mu _ { 3 | 1 } , \mu _ { 3 | 1 2 }$ . (ii) By (i) and Theorem 3.6, we have a.e.

A group $G$ with associated σ-field $\mathcal { G }$ is said to be measurable, if the group operations $r \mapsto r ^ { - 1 }$ and $( r , s ) \mapsto r s$ on G are -measurable. Defining the left and right $s h i f t s \ \theta _ { r }$ and $\widetilde { \theta } _ { r }$ on G by ${ \theta _ { r } } s = { \tilde { \theta } } _ { s } r = r s , \ r , s \in G .$ , we say that a measure λ on $G$ is left-invariant if $\lambda \circ \theta _ { r } ^ { - 1 } = \lambda$ for all $r \in G$ . A σ-finite, leftinvariant measure $\lambda \neq 0$ is called a Haar measure on $G .$ . Writing $\tilde { f } ( r ) = f ( r ^ { - 1 } )$ , we may define a corresponding right-invariant measure $\tilde { \lambda }$ by $\tilde { \lambda } f = \lambda \tilde { f }$ 

We call G a topological group if it is endowed with a topology rendering the group operations continuous. When $G$ is $l c s c H ^ { 2 }$ , it becomes a measurable group when endowed with the Borel σ-field $\mathcal { G }$ . We state the basic existence and uniqueness theorem for Haar measures. 

Theorem 3.8 (Haar measure) For any lcscH group $G ,$ 

(i) there exists a left-invariant, locally finite measure $\lambda \neq 0$ on $G _ { i }$

$$
f (x) \leq \sum_ {k \leq n} c _ {k}   g (s _ {k} x), \quad x \in G,

From (6) and (7) we note that

\begin{array}{c} \lambda_ {g} (f + f ^ {\prime}) \leq \lambda_ {g} f + \lambda_ {g} f ^ {\prime}, \\ \lambda_ {g} (c f) = c \lambda_ {g} f, \\ | f _ {0} | _ {f} ^ {- 1} \leq \lambda_ {g} f \leq | f | _ {f _ {0}}. \end{array}\tag{8}

To see that λ is linear, fix any $f , f ^ { \prime } \in { \hat { C } } _ { + }$ and $a , b \geq 0$ , and choose some $g _ { 1 } , g _ { 2 } , . . . \in \hat { C } _ { + }$ with supp $g _ { n } \downarrow \{ \iota \}$ , such that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda_ {g _ {n}} f \to \lambda f, \quad \lambda_ {g _ {n}} f ^ {\prime} \to \lambda f ^ {\prime}, \\ \lambda_ {g _ {n}} (a f + b f ^ {\prime}) \to \lambda (a f + b f ^ {\prime}). \end{array}
$$

By (8) and Lemma 3.9 we obtain $\lambda ( a f + b f ^ { \prime } ) = a \lambda f + b \lambda f ^ { \prime }$ . Thus, λ is a nontrivial, positive linear functional on $\hat { C } _ { + }$ , and so by Theorem 2.25 it extends uniquely to a locally finite measure on S. The invariance of the functionals $\lambda _ { g }$ clearly carries over to λ. 

Now consider any left-invariant, locally finite measure $\lambda \neq 0$ on G. Fixing a right-invariant, locally finite measure $\mu \neq 0$ and a function $h \in \hat { C } _ { + } \backslash \{ 0 \}$ , we define 

$$
p (x) = \int h (y ^ {- 1} x) \mu (d y), \quad x \in G,
$$

and note that $p > 0$ on $G .$ . Using the invariance of λ and $\mu$ along with Fubini’s theorem, we get for any $f \in \hat { C } _ { + }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\lambda h) (\mu f) = \int h (x) \lambda (d x) \int f (y) \mu (d y) \\ \qquad = \int h (x) \lambda (d x) \int f (y x) \mu (d y) \\ \qquad = \int \mu (d y) \int h (x) f (y x) \lambda (d x) \\ \qquad = \int \mu (d y) \int h (y ^ {- 1} x) f (x) \lambda (d x) \\ \qquad = \int f (x) \lambda (d x) \int h (y ^ {- 1} x) \mu (d y) = \lambda (f p). \end{array}
$$

Since $f$ was arbitrary, we obtain $( \lambda h ) \mu = p \cdot \lambda$ or equivalently $\lambda / \lambda h = p ^ { - 1 } \cdot \mu$ The asserted uniqueness now follows, since the right-hand side is independent of λ. If S is compact, we may choose $h \equiv 1$ to obtain $\lambda / \lambda S = \mu / \mu S$ ✷ 

From now on, we make no topological or other assumptions on G, beyond the existence of a Haar measure. The uniqueness and basic properties of such measures are covered by the following result, which also provides a basic factorization property. For technical convenience we consider s-finite (rather than σ-finite) measures, defined as countable sums of bounded measures. Note that most of the basic computational rules, including Fubini’s theorem, remain valid for s -finite measures, and that s -finiteness has the advantage of being preserved by measurable maps. 

Theorem 3.10 (factorization and modularity) Consider a measurable space S and a measurable group G with Haar measure λ. Then 

(i) for any s -finite, G-invariant measure μ on $G \times S$ , there exists a unique, $s - \beta n i t e$ measure ν on S satisfing $\mu = \lambda \otimes \nu _ { ; }$ 

(ii) $\mu , \nu$ are simultaneously σ-finite, 

(iii) there exists a measurable homomorphism $\Delta \colon G \to ( 0 , \infty )$ with 

$$
\tilde {\lambda} = \Delta \cdot \lambda , \qquad \lambda \circ \tilde {\theta} _ {r} ^ {- 1} = \Delta_ {r} \lambda , \quad r \in G,
$$

(iv) when $\| \lambda \| < \infty$ we have $\Delta \equiv 1$ , and λ is also right-invariant with $\tilde { \lambda } = \lambda$ 

In particular, (i) shows that any s -finite, left-invariant measure on G is proportional to λ. The dual mapping $\tilde { \Delta }$ is known as the modular function of $G .$ The use of s -finite measures leads to some significant simplifications in subsequent proofs. 

Proof: (i) Since λ is σ-finite, we may choose a measurable function $h > 0$ on $G$ with $\lambda h = 1$ , and define 

$$
\Delta_ {r} = \lambda (h \circ \tilde {\theta} _ {r}) \in (0, \infty ], \quad r \in G.
$$

Using Fubini’s theorem (three times), the G -invariance of $\mu$ and λ, and the definitions of $\Delta$ and $\tilde { \lambda } .$ , we get for any $f \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu (f \Delta) = \iint \mu (d r d s) f (r, s) \int \lambda (d p) h (p r) \\ \qquad = \int \lambda (d p) \iint \mu (d r d s) f \left(p ^ {- 1} r, s\right) h (r) \\ \qquad = \iint \mu (d r d s) h (r) \int \lambda (d p) f (p ^ {- 1}, s) \\ \qquad = \int \tilde {\lambda} (d p) \iint \mu (d r d s) h (r) f (p, s). \end{array}
$$

Choosing $\mu = \lambda$ for a singleton $S _ { ; }$ , we get $\tilde { \lambda } f = \lambda ( f \Delta )$ , and so $\tilde { \lambda } = \Delta \cdot \lambda$ Therefore $\lambda = \tilde { \Delta } \cdot \tilde { \lambda } = \tilde { \Delta } \Delta \cdot \lambda$ , hence $\tilde { \Delta } \Delta = 1 \mathrm { a . e . } \lambda$ , and finally $\Delta \in ( 0 , \infty ) \mathrm { a . e }$ λ. Thus, for general S, 

$$
\mu (f \Delta) = \int \lambda (d p)   \Delta (p) \iint \mu (d r   d s)   h (r)   f (p, s).
$$

Since $\Delta > 0$ , we have $\mu ( \cdot \times S ) \ll \lambda$ , and so $\Delta \in ( 0 , \infty ) { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } \mu ( \cdot \times S )$ , which yields the simplified formula 

$$
\mu f = \int \lambda (d p) \iint \mu (d r d s) h (r) f (p, s),
$$

showing that $\mu = \lambda \otimes \nu$ with $\nu f = \mu ( h \otimes f )$ 

(ii) When $\mu$ is $\sigma \mathrm { - }$ -finite, we have $\mu f < \infty$ for some measurable function $f > 0 \ \mathrm { o n } \ G \times S$ , and so by Fubini’s theorem $\nu f ( r , \cdot ) < \infty$ for $r \in G { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } \lambda$ which shows that even ν is σ-finite. The reverse implication is obvious. 

(iii) For every $r \in G$ , the measure $\lambda \circ \tilde { \theta } _ { r } ^ { - 1 }$ is left-invariant since $\theta _ { p }$ and $\widetilde { \theta } _ { r }$ commute for all $p , r \in G$ . Hence, (i) yields $\lambda \circ \tilde { \theta } _ { r } ^ { - 1 } = c _ { r } \lambda$ for some constants $c _ { r } > 0$ . Applying both sides to h gives $c _ { r } = \Delta ( r )$ . The homomorphism relation $\Delta ( p q ) = \Delta ( p ) \Delta ( q )$ follows from the reverse semi-group property $\tilde { \theta } _ { p q } = \tilde { \theta } _ { q } \circ \tilde { \theta } _ { p } ,$ and the measurability holds by the measurability of the group operation and Fubini’s theorem. 

(iv) Statement (iii) yields $\| \lambda \| = \Delta _ { r } \| \lambda \|$ for all $r \in G$ , and so $\Delta \equiv 1$ when $\| \lambda \| < \infty$ . Then (iii) gives $\tilde { \lambda } = \lambda$ and $\lambda \circ \tilde { \theta } _ { r } ^ { - 1 } = \lambda$ for all $r \in G$ , which shows that λ is also right-invariant. ✷ 

Given a group $G$ and a space $S ,$ we define an action of $G$ on $S$ as a mapping $( r , s ) \mapsto r s$ from $G \times S$ to $S _ { i }$ , such that $p ( r s ) = ( p r ) s$ and $\iota s = s$ for all $p , r \in G$ and $s \in S$ , where ι denotes the identity element of G. If G and $S$ are measurable spaces, we say that $G$ acts measurably on S if the action map is product-measurable. The shifts $\theta _ { r }$ and projections $\pi _ { s }$ are defined by $r s = \theta _ { r } s = \pi _ { s } r$ , and the orbit containing s is given by $\pi _ { s } G = \{ r s ; r \in G \}$ The orbits form a partition of $S ,$ , and we say that the action is transitive if $\pi _ { s } G \equiv S$ . For $s , s ^ { \prime } \in S$ , we write $s \sim s ^ { \prime }$ if s and $s ^ { \prime }$ belong to the same orbit, so that $s = r s ^ { \prime }$ for some $r \in G$ . If $G$ acts on both $S$ and $T _ { \ast }$ , its joint action on $S \times T$ is given by $r ( s , t ) = ( r s , r t )$ 

For any group G acting on S, we say that a subset $B \subset S$ is G-invariant if $B \circ \theta _ { r } ^ { - 1 } = B$ for all $r \in G$ , and a function $f$ on $S$ is G-invariant if $f \circ \theta _ { r } = f$ When S is measurable with σ-field ${ \mathbf { } } S .$ , the class of G -invariant sets in $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ is again a σ-field, denoted by $\mathcal { T } _ { S }$ . For a transitive group action we have ${ \mathcal { T } } _ { S } = \{ \emptyset , S \}$ , and every invariant function is a constant. When the group action is measurable, a measure ν on $S$ is said to be G-invariant if $\nu \circ \theta _ { r } ^ { - 1 } = \nu$ for all $r \in G$ 

When G is a measurable group with Haar measure $\lambda ,$ acting measurably on $S _ { ; }$ , we say that G acts $p r o p e r l y ^ { 4 }$ on $S _ { ; }$ , if there exists a normalizing function $g > 0$ on S, such that $g$ is measurable and satisfies $\lambda ( g \circ \pi _ { s } ) < \infty$ for all $s \in S$ We may then define a kernel $\varphi$ on $S$ by 

$$
\varphi_ {s} = \frac {\lambda \circ \pi_ {s} ^ {- 1}}{\lambda (g \circ \pi_ {s})}, \quad s \in S.\tag{10}
$$

Lemma 3.11 (orbit measures) Let G be a measurable group with Haar measure $\lambda ,$ acting properly on S. Then the measures $\varphi _ { s }$ are σ-finite and satisfy 

(i) $\varphi _ { s } = \varphi _ { s ^ { \prime } } , \ s \sim s ^ { \prime } ,$ 

$$
\varphi_ {s} \perp \varphi_ {s ^ {\prime}}, s \not \sim s ^ {\prime},
$$

(ii) $\varphi _ { s } \circ \theta _ { r } ^ { - 1 } = \varphi _ { s } = \varphi _ { r s } , r \in G , s \in S .$ 

Proof: The $\varphi _ { s }$ are σ-finite since $\varphi _ { s } g \equiv 1$ . The first equality in (ii) holds by the left-invariance of λ, and the second holds since $\lambda \circ \pi _ { r s } ^ { - 1 } = \Delta _ { r } \lambda \circ \pi _ { s } ^ { - 1 }$ by Lemma 3.10 (ii). The latter equation yields $\varphi _ { s } = \varphi _ { s ^ { \prime } }$ when $s \sim s ^ { \prime }$ . The orthogonality holds for $s \not \sim s ^ { \prime }$ , since $\varphi _ { s }$ is confined to the orbit $\pi _ { s } ( G )$ , which is universally measurable by Theorem A1.2 (i). ✷ 

We show that any s -finite, G -invariant measure on $S$ is a unique mixture of orbit measures. An invariant measure ν on $S$ is said to be ergodic if $\nu I \wedge \nu I ^ { c } = 0$ for all $I \in \mathcal { T } _ { S }$ . It is further said to be extreme, if for any decomposition $\nu = \nu ^ { \prime } + \nu ^ { \prime \prime }$ with invariant $\nu ^ { \prime }$ and $\nu ^ { \prime \prime }$ , all three measures are proportional. 

Theorem 3.12 (invariant measures) Let G be a measurable group with Haar measure $\lambda _ { i }$ , acting properly on $S ,$ and define $\varphi$ by (10) in terms ofa normalizing function $g > 0$ on $S _ { ☉ }$ . For such $\mu , \nu ,$ we have 

(iii) $\mu ,$ ν are simultaneously σ-finite, 

(iv) ν is ergodic or extreme if μ is degenerate,

Proof, (i) (ii): Let $\nu$ be s -finite and G -invariant. Using (10), Fubini’s theorem, and Theorem 3.10 (iii), we get for any $f \in S _ { + }$

which proves the first relation in (i). The second relation follows with $\mu$ as in (ii), by the substitution rule for integrals. 

Conversely, let $\begin{array} { r } { \nu = \int m \mu ( d m ) } \end{array}$ for an s -finite measure $\mu$ on $\varphi ( S )$ . For measurable $M \subset \mathcal { M } _ { S }$ -<sub>we have</sub> $A \equiv \varphi ^ { - 1 } M \in \mathcal { T } _ { S }$ by Lemma 3.11, and so

(iii) Use $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i } )$ and the facts that $g > 0$ and $\varphi _ { s } \neq 0$

Hence, $\nu$ is ergodic if $\mu$ is degenerate. 

(v) Choose a bounded measure $\hat { \nu } \sim \nu$ , and define $\tilde { \nu } = \hat { \nu } \varphi$ . Then $\tilde { \nu }$ is invariant by Lemma 3.11, and $\tilde { \nu } \sim ( g \cdot \nu ) \varphi = \nu$ by (ii). It is also $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i n i t e } } .$ since $\tilde { \nu } g = \hat { \nu } \varphi g = \hat { \nu } S < \infty$ by (i). ✷ 

When G acts measurably on $S$ and $T$ , we say that a kernel $\mu \colon S \to T$ is invariant5 if 0-1

Lemma 3.13 (invariant kernels) Let the group G act measurably on the Borel spaces S, T, and consider a σ-finite, invariant measure ν on $S$ and a kernel $\mu \colon S \to T$ . Then these conditions are equivalent:

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\big \{(\nu \otimes \mu) \circ \theta_ {r} ^ {- 1} \big \} f = (\nu \otimes \mu) (f \circ \theta_ {r})} \\ & {\qquad = \int \nu (d s) \int \mu_ {s} (d t) f (r s, r t)} \\ & {\qquad = \int \nu (d s) \int \Big (\mu_ {s} \circ \theta_ {r} ^ {- 1} \Big) (d t) f (r s, t)} \end{array}

$$
\begin{array}{l} = \int \nu (d s) \int \mu_ {r s} (d t) f (r s, t) \\ = \int \nu (d s) \int \mu_ {s} (d t) f (s, t) \\ = (\nu \otimes \mu) f. \end{array}

which extends to (ii) since f is arbitrary. 

We turn to the reverse problem of invariant disintegration. 

Theorem 3.14 (invariant disintegration) Let G be a measurable group with Haar measure λ, acting properly on S and measurably on T, where $S , T$ are Borel, and consider a σ-finite, jointly G-invariant measure ρ on $S \times T$ . Then

$$

$$

We begin with part (ii), which may be proved by a simple skew factorization. 

Proof of (ii): On $G \times S$ we define the mappings 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \vartheta (r, s) = (r, r s), \\ \theta_ {r} (p, s) = (r p, r s), \\ \theta_ {r} ^ {\prime} (p, s) = (r p, s), \end{array}
$$

where $p , r \in G$ and $s \in S$ . Since clearly $\vartheta ^ { - 1 } \circ \theta _ { r } = \theta _ { r } ^ { \prime } \circ \vartheta ^ { - 1 }$ , the joint $G \mathrm { - }$ invariance of ρ gives 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\rho \circ \vartheta \circ \theta_ {r} ^ {- 1} = \rho \circ \theta_ {r} ^ {- 1} \circ \vartheta} \\ & {\qquad = \rho \circ \vartheta , r \in G,} \end{array}
$$

where $\vartheta = ( \vartheta ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { - 1 }$ . Hence, $\rho \circ \vartheta$ is invariant under shifts of G alone, and so $\rho \circ \vartheta = \lambda \otimes \nu$ by Theorem 3.10 for a σ-finite measure ν on S, which yields the stated formula for the invariant kernel $\mu _ { r } = \nu \circ \theta _ { r } ^ { - 1 }$ . $$
\begin{array}{c} (\lambda \otimes \mu) f = \int \lambda (d r) \int \nu \circ \theta_ {r} ^ {- 1} (d s)   f (r, s) \\ = \int \lambda (d r) \int \nu (d s)   f (r, r s) \\ = \Bigl \{(\lambda \otimes \nu) \circ \vartheta^ {- 1} \Bigr \} f = \rho f. \end{array}
$$

Proof: By Theorem 3.14 (ii) we have $\rho = ( \lambda \otimes \chi ) \circ \vartheta ^ { - }$ −<sup>1</sup> for a σ-finite measure $\chi$ on $S \times T$ , where $\vartheta ( r , s , t ) = ( r , r s , r t )$ for all $( r , s , t ) \in G \times S \times T$ . Let A be the set of all $s \in S$ satisfying

We turn to some notions of asymptotic and local invariance, of importance in Chapters 25, 27, and 30–31. The uniformly bounded measures $\mu _ { n }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ are said to be asymptotically invariant if 

$$
\left\| \mu_ {n} - \mu_ {n} * \delta_ {x} \right\|\rightarrow 0, \quad x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.\tag{12}
$$

Lemma 3.17 (asymptotic invariance) Let $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be uniformly bounded, asymptotically invariant measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Then 

(i) (12) holds uniformly for bounded $x ,$ 

(ii) $\| \mu _ { n } - \mu _ { n } * \nu \| \to 0$ for any distribution $\nu$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$

which tends to 0 for fixed $r ,$ as $n \to \infty$ and then $h  \infty$

Theorem 3.19 (local invariance) Let $\mu ^ { \prime } \ll \mu$ be locally finite measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Then

and so it sufices to verify (13) for the measures $\mu _ { n , t } ^ { \prime }$ . Thus, we may henceforth choose $\mu ^ { \prime } = f \cdot \mu$ for a continuous function $f$ with bounded support. 

To verify (13), let r and ν be such that the measures ν and $\nu * \delta _ { r }$ are both supported by the ball $B _ { 0 } ^ { a }$ . Writing 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mu_ {t} ^ {\prime} & = (f \cdot \mu) _ {t} \\ & = (f \cdot \mu) \circ S _ {t} ^ {- 1} \\ & = (f \circ S _ {t}) \cdot (\mu \circ S _ {t} ^ {- 1}) \\ & = f _ {t} \cdot \mu_ {t}, \\ \nu - \nu * \delta_ {r} & = g \cdot \lambda^ {d} - (g \circ \theta_ {- r}) \cdot \lambda^ {d} \\ & = \Delta g \cdot \lambda^ {d}, \end{array}

## Exercises

1. Let $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be kernels between two measurable spaces S, T. Show that the function $\textstyle \mu = \sum _ { n } \mu _ { n }$ is again a kernel. 

2. Fix a function f between two measurable spaces S, T, and define $\mu ( s , B ) =$ $1 _ { B } \circ f ( s )$ . Show that $\mu$ is a kernel if f is measurable. 

3. Prove the existence and uniqueness of Lebesgue measure on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ from the corresponding properties of Haar measures. 

4. Show that if the group $G$ is compact, then every measurable group action is proper. Then show how the formula for the orbit measures simplifies in this case, and give a corresponding version of Theorem 3.12. 

5. Use the previous exercise to find the general form of the invariant measures on a sphere and on a spherical cylinder. 

6. Extend Lemma 3.10 (i) to the context of general invariant measures. 

7. Extend the mean continuity in Lemma 2.7 to general invariant measures. 

8. Give an example of some measures $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . that are weakly but not strictly asymptotically invariant. 

9. Give an example of a bounded measure $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R }$ that is locally invariant but not absolutely continuous. 

## II. Some Classical Probability Theory

Armed with the basic measure-theoretic machinery from Part I, we proceed with the foundations of general probability theory. After giving precise definitions of processes, distributions, expectations, and independence, we introduce the various notions of probabilistic convergence, and prove some of the classical limit theorems for sums and averages, including the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. Finally, a general compound Poisson approximation will enable us to give a short, probabilistic proof of the classical limit theorem for general null arrays. The material in Chapter 4, along with at least the beginnings of Chapters 5 6, may be regarded as essential core material, constantly needed for the continued study, whereas a detailed reading of the remaining material might be postponed until a later stage. 

4. Processes, distributions, and independence. Here the probabilistic notions of processes, distributions, expected values, and independence are defined in terms of standard notions of measure theory from Chapter 1. We proceed with a detailed study of independence criteria, 0 1 laws, and regularity conditions for processes. Finally, we prove the existence of sequences of independent random variables, and show how distributions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ are induced by their distribution functions. 

5. Random sequences, series, and averages. Here we examine the relationship between convergence a.s., in probability, and in $L ^ { p } .$ , and give conditions for uniform integrability. Next, we develop convergence criteria for random series and averages, including the strong laws of large numbers. Finally, we study the basic properties of convergence in distribution, with special emphasis on the continuous mapping and approximation theorems as well as the Skorohod coupling. 

6. Gaussian and Poisson convergence. Here we prove the classical Poisson and Gaussian limit theorems for null arrays of random variables or vectors, including the celebrated central limit theorem. The theory of regular variation enables us to identify the domain of Gaussian attraction. The mentioned results also yield precise criteria for the weak law of large numbers. Finally, we study the relationship between weak compactness and tightness, in the special case of distributions on Euclidean spaces. 

7. Infinite divisibility and general null arrays. Here we establish the representation of infinitely divisible distributions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ , involving a Gaussian component and a compound Poisson integral, material needed for the theory of L´evy processes and essential for a good understanding of Feller processes and general semi-martingales. The associated convergence criteria, along with a basic compound Poisson approximation, yield a short, non-technical approach to the classical limit theorem for general null arrays. 

Chapter 4 

# Processes, Distributions, and Independence

Random elements and processes, finite-dimensional distributions, expectation and covariance, moments and tails, Jensen’s inequality, independence, pairwise independence and grouping, product measures and convolution, iterated expectation, Kolmogorov and Hewitt–Savage 0 1 laws, Borel–Cantelli lemma, replication and Bernoulli sequences, kernel representation, H¨older continuity, multi-variate distributions 

Armed with the basic notions and results of measure theory from previous chapters, we may now embark on our study of proper probability theory. The dual purposes of this chapter are to introduce some basic terminology and notation and to prove some fundamental results, many of which will be needed throughout the remainder of the book. 

In modern probability theory, it is customary to relate all objects of study to a basic probability space $( \Omega , A , P )$ , which is simply a normalized measure space. Random variables may then be defined as measurable functions ξ on Ω, and their expected values as integrals $\textstyle E \xi = \int \xi d P$ . Furthermore, independence -<sub>between random quantities reduces to a kind of orthogonality between the</sub> induced sub-σ-fields. The reference space Ω is introduced only for technical convenience, to provide a consistent mathematical framework, and its actual choice plays no role<sup>1</sup>. Instead, our interest focuses on the induced distributions $\mathcal { L } ( \xi ) = P \circ \xi ^ { - 1 }$ and their associated characteristics. 

The notion of independence is fundamental for all areas of probability theory. Despite its simplicity, it has some truly remarkable consequences. A particularly striking result is Kolmogorov’s 0 1 law, stating that every tail event associated with a sequence of independent random elements has probability 0 or 1. Thus, any random variable that depends only on the ‘tail’ of the sequence is a.s. a constant. This result and the related Hewitt–Savage 0 1 law convey much of the flavor of modern probability: though the individual elements of a random sequence are erratic and unpredictable, the long-term behavior may often conform to deterministic laws and patterns. A major objective is then to uncover the latter. Here the classical Borel–Cantelli lemma is one of the simplest but most powerful tools available. 

To justify our study, we need to ensure the existence<sup>2</sup> of the random objects under discussion. For most purposes it sufices to use the Lebesgue unit interval $( [ 0 , 1 ] , B , \lambda )$ as our basic probability space. In this chapter, the existence will be proved only for independent random variables with prescribed distributions, whereas a more general discussion is postponed until Chapter 8. As a key step, we may use the binary expansion of real numbers to construct a socalled Bernoulli sequence, consisting of independent random digits 1 or 0 with probabilities p and $1 - p ,$ respectively.<sup>3</sup> The latter may be regarded as a discretetime counterpart of the fundamental Poisson processes, to be introduced and studied in Chapter 15. 

The distribution of a random process X is determined by its finite-dimensional distributions, which are not afected by a change on a null set of each variable $X _ { t }$ . It is then natural to look for versions of X with suitable regularity properties. As another striking result, we provide a moment condition ensuring the existence of a H¨older continuous modification of the process. Regularizations of various kind are important throughout modern probability theory, as they may enable us to deal with events depending on the values of a process at uncountably many times. 

To begin our systematic exposition of the theory, we fix an arbitrary probability space $( \Omega , A , P )$ , where $P$ is a probability measure with total mass 1. In the probabilistic context, the sets $A \in { \mathcal { A } }$ are called events, and $P A = P ( A )$ is called the probability of A. In addition to results valid for all measures, there are properties requiring the boundedness or normalization of $P$ , such as the relation $P A ^ { c } = 1 - P A$ and the fact that $A _ { n } \downarrow A$ implies $P A _ { n } \to P A$ 

Some infinite set operations have a special probabilistic significance. Thus, for any sequence of events $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \dotsc \in { \mathcal { A } }$ , we may consider the sets $\left\{ A _ { n } \thinspace \mathrm { i . o . } \right\}$ where $A _ { n }$ happens infinitely often, and $\left\{ A _ { n } \right.$ ult. where $A _ { n }$ happens ultimately (for all but finitely many n). Those occurrences are events in their own right, formally expressible in terms of the $A _ { n }$ as 

$$
\left\{A _ {n} \text { i.o. } \right\} = \left\{\sum_ {n} 1 _ {A _ {n}} = \infty \right\} = \bigcap_ {n} \bigcup_ {k \geq n} A _ {k},\tag{1}
$$

$$
\left\{A _ {n} \text {ult.} \right\} = \left\{\sum_ {n} 1 _ {A _ {n} ^ {c}} <   \infty \right\} = \bigcup_ {n} \bigcap_ {k \geq n} A _ {k}.\tag{2}
$$

The argument $\omega \in \Omega$ is usually omitted from our notation, when there is no risk for confusion. Thus, for example, the expression $\textstyle \left\{ \sum _ { n } 1 _ { A _ { n } } \ = \infty \right\}$ is a convenient shorthand form of the unwieldy $\begin{array} { r } { \left\{ \omega \in \Omega ; \sum _ { n } 1 _ { A _ { n } } ( \omega ) = \infty \right\} } \end{array}$ 

The indicator functions<sup>4</sup> of the events in (1) and (2) may be expressed as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 1 \{A _ {n} \text {   ult. } \} = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} 1 _ {A _ {n}} \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} 1 _ {A _ {n}} = 1 \{A _ {n} \text {   i.o. } \}. \end{array}
$$

Applying Fatou’s lemma to the functions $1 _ { A _ { n } }$ and $1 _ { A _ { n } ^ { c } }$ yields 

$$
P \{A _ {n} \text {   ult. } \} \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} P A _ {n}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P A _ {n} \\ \leq P \{A _ {n} \text {   i.o. } \}. \end{array}
$$

Using the continuity and sub-additivity of $P ,$ we further see from (1) that 

$$
P \{A _ {n} \text { i.o. } \} = \lim _ {n \to \infty} P \bigcup_ {k \geq n} A _ {k} \leq \lim _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {k \geq n} P A _ {k}.
$$

When $\textstyle \sum _ { n } P A _ { n } < \infty$ , the right-hand side becomes 0, and we get $P \{ A _ { n } \ \mathrm { i . o . } \} =$ 0. The resulting implication constitutes the easy part of the Borel–Cantelli lemma, to be revisited in Theorem 4.18. 

Any measurable mapping $\xi$ of Ω into some measurable space $( S , S )$ is called a random element in $S .$ . If $B \in S$ , then $\{ \xi \in B \} = \xi ^ { - 1 } B \in \mathcal { A }$ , and we may consider the associated probabilities 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} P \{\xi \in B \} & = P (\xi^ {- 1} B) \\ & = (P \circ \xi^ {- 1}) B, \quad B \in \mathcal {S}. \end{array}
$$

The set function $\mathcal { L } ( \xi ) = P \circ \xi ^ { - 1 }$ is a probability measure on the range space $S$ of $\xi ,$ , called the distribution or law of $\xi .$ . We often use the term distribution as synonymous to probability measure, even when no generating random element has been introduced. 

Random elements are of interest in a wide variety of spaces. A random element in $S$ is called a random variable when $S = { \mathsf { R } } .$ , a random vector when $S = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , a random sequence when $S = { \sf R } ^ { \infty }$ , a random (or $s t o c h a s t i c ^ { 5 } )$ process when $S$ is a function space, and a random measure or set when S is a class of measures or sets, respectively. A metric or topological space S will be endowed with its Borel σ-field $B _ { S }$ , unless a σ-field is otherwise specified. For any separable metric space $S ,$ Lemma 1.2 shows that $\xi = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . . )$ is a random element in $S ^ { \infty }$ if $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ . are random elements in $S _ { ☉ }$ 

For any measurable space $( S , S )$ , a subset $A \subset S$ becomes a measurable space in its own right, when endowed with the σ-field $A \cap { \mathcal { S } } = \left\{ A \cap B ; B \in { \mathcal { S } } \right\}$ In particular, Lemma 1.6 shows that if S is a metric space with Borel σ-field ${ \mathbf { } } S _ { ; }$ , then $A \cap { S }$ is the Borel σ-field in A. Any random element in $( A , A \cap { S } )$ may be regarded, alternatively, as a random element in S. Conversely, if $\xi$ is a random element in S with $\xi \in A \mathrm { ~ a . s . } ^ { 6 }$ for some $A \in S$ , then $\xi = \eta \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . for some random element η in A.

A random vector $\boldsymbol { \xi } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { d } )$ or process $X = \left( X _ { t } \right)$ is said to be inte grable, if integrability holds for every component $\xi _ { k }$ or value $X _ { t } ,$ , in which case we may write $E \xi = ( E \xi _ { 1 } , \dots , E \xi _ { d } )$ or $E X = ( E X _ { t } )$ . Lemma 4.5 (convex maps, H¨older, Jensen) For any integrable random vector $\xi \ i n \ \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and convex function $f \colon { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d } \to { \mathsf { R } }$ , we have

From a suitable 0 1 law it is often easy to see that a given event has probability 0 or 1. To distinguish between the two cases is often much harder. The following classical result, known as the Borel–Cantelli lemma, is sometimes helpful, especially when the events are independent. A more general version appears in Corollary 9.21. 

Theorem 4.18 (Borel, Cantelli) For any $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \dotsc \in { \mathcal { A } }$ 

$$
\sum_ {n} P A _ {n} <   \infty \quad \Rightarrow \quad P \{A _ {n} \text {   i.o. } \} = 0,
$$

and equivalence holds when the $A _ { n }$ are independent. 

The first assertion was proved earlier as an application of Fatou’s lemma. Using expected values yields a more transparent argument. 

Proof: If $\textstyle \sum _ { n } P A _ { n } < \infty$ , we get by monotone convergence 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E \sum_ {n} 1 _ {A _ {n}} & = \sum_ {n} E 1 _ {A _ {n}} \\ & = \sum_ {n} P A _ {n} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } 1 _ { A _ { n } } < \infty \mathrm { a . s . } } \end{array}$ , which means that $P \{ A _ { n } \ \mathrm { i . o . } \} = 0$ 

Now let the $A _ { n }$ be independent with $\textstyle \sum _ { n } P A _ { n } = \infty$ . Since $1 - x \leq e ^ { - x }$ for all x, we get P ⊥ ⊥ 4 PO 49 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \bigcup_ {k \geq n} A _ {k} = 1 - P \bigcap_ {k \geq n} A _ {k} ^ {c} \\ \qquad = 1 - \prod_ {k \geq n} P A _ {k} ^ {c} \\ \qquad = 1 - \prod_ {k \geq n} (1 - P A _ {k}) \\ \qquad \geq 1 - \prod_ {k \geq n} \exp (- P A _ {k}) \\ \qquad = 1 - \exp \Bigl (- \sum_ {k \geq n} P A _ {k} \Bigr) = 1. \end{array}
$$

Hence, as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 1 = P \bigcup_ {k \geq n} A _ {k} \downarrow P \bigcap_ {n} \bigcup_ {k \geq n} A _ {k} \\ = P \{A _ {n} \text {   i.o. } \}, \end{array}
$$

and so the probability on the right equals 1. 

For many purposes, it sufices to use the Lebesgue unit interval ([0, 1], $B [ 0 , 1 ] , \lambda )$ as our basic probability space. In particular, the following result ensures the existence on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ of some independent random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ with arbitrarily prescribed distributions. The present statement is only preliminary. Thus, we will remove the independence assumption in Theorem 8.21, prove an extension to arbitrary index sets in Theorem 8.23, and eliminate the restriction on the spaces in Theorem 8.24. 

Theorem 4.19 (existence, Borel) For any probability measures $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , . . . . o n$ the Borel spaces $S _ { 1 } , S _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ there exist some independent random elements $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . on $( [ 0 , 1 ] , \lambda )$ with distributions $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ 

As a consequence, there exists a probability measure $\mu$ on $S _ { 1 } \times S _ { 2 } \times \cdots$ satisfying 

$$
\mu \circ (\pi_ {1}, \dots , \pi_ {n}) ^ {- 1} = \mu_ {1} \otimes \dots \otimes \mu_ {n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

For the proof, we begin with two special cases of independent interest. 

By a Bernoulli sequence with rate p we mean a sequence of i.i.d. random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . with $P \{ \xi _ { n } = 1 \} = p = 1 - P \{ \xi _ { n } = 0 \}$ . We further say that a random variable $\xi$ is uniformly distributed on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ , written as $U ( 0 , 1 )$ if its distribution $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ equals Lebesgue measure λ on [0, 1]. Every number $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ has a binary expansion $r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , \ldots \in \{ 0 , 1 \}$ satisfying $\begin{array} { r } { x = \sum _ { n } r _ { n } 2 ^ { - n } } \end{array}$ , where for uniqueness we require that $\textstyle \sum _ { n } r _ { n } = \infty$ when $x > 0$ . We give a simple construction of Bernoulli sequences on the Lebesgue unit interval. 

Lemma 4.20 (Bernoulli sequence) Let $\xi$ be a random variable in $[ 0 , 1 ]$ with binary expansion $\eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi \ i s \ U ( 0 , 1 )$ 

(ii) the $\eta _ { n }$ form a Bernoulli sequence with rate $\frac { 1 } { 2 }$ . 

Proof, $\mathrm { ( i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i i ) } \colon \mathrm { ~ I f ~ } \xi \ \mathrm { i s ~ } U ( 0 , 1 )$ , then $P \cap _ { j \leq n } \{ \eta _ { j } \ = \ k _ { j } \} \ = \ 2 ^ { - n }$ for all $k _ { 1 } , \ldots , k _ { n } \in \{ 0 , 1 \}$ . Summing over $k _ { 1 } , \ldots , k _ { n - 1 }$  ≤<sub>gives</sub> $P \{ \eta _ { n } = k \} = \frac { 1 } { 2 }$ for $k = 0$ or 1. A similar calculation yields the asserted independence. 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Assume (ii). Letting $\xi ^ { \prime }$ be $U ( 0 , 1 )$ with binary expansion $\eta _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \eta _ { 2 } ^ { \prime }$ . . . , we get $( \eta _ { n } ) \stackrel { d } { = } ( \eta _ { n } ^ { \prime } )$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \xi = \sum_ {n} \eta_ {n} 2 ^ {- n} \\ \stackrel {d} {=} \sum_ {n} \eta_ {n} ^ {\prime} 2 ^ {- n} = \xi^ {\prime}. \end{array}
$$

Next we show how a single $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random variable can be used to generate a whole sequence. 

Lemma 4.21 (replication) There exist some measurable functions $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots$ on [0, 1] such that $( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ , where 

(i) $\xi \ i s \ U ( 0 , 1 )$ 

(ii) $\xi _ { n } = f _ { n } ( \xi ) , n \in \mathsf { N } , \ a r e \ i . i . d . \ U ( 0 , 1 )$ 

Proof: Let $b _ { 1 } ( x ) , b _ { 2 } ( x ) , . . .$ . be the binary expansion of $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , and note that the $b _ { k }$ are measurable. Rearranging the $b _ { k }$ into a two-dimensional array $h _ { n j } , n , j \in \mathbb { N }$ , we define 

$$
f _ {n} (x) = \sum_ {j} 2 ^ {- j} h _ {n j} (x), \quad x \in [ 0, 1 ], n \in \mathsf {N}.
$$

By Lemma 4.20, the random variables $b _ { k } ( \xi )$ form a Bernoulli sequence with rate $\frac { 1 } { 2 }$ , and the same result shows that the variables $\xi _ { n } = f _ { n } ( \xi )$ are $U ( 0 , 1 )$ . They are further independent by Corollary 4.7. ✷ 

We finally need to construct a random element with specified distribution from a given randomization variable. The result is stated in an extended form for kernels, to meet our needs in Chapters 8, 11, 22, and 27–28. 

Lemma 4.22 (kernel representation) Consider a probability kernel $\mu \colon S \to T$ with T Borel, and let $\xi$ be $U ( 0 , 1 )$ . Then there exists a measurable function $f \colon S \times [ 0 , 1 ] \to T$ , such that

f (s, t) = \sup \left\{x \in [ 0, 1 ]; \mu (s, [ 0, x ]) <   t \right\}, \quad s \in S, t \in [ 0, 1 ],\tag{9}

We turn to some regularizations and path properties of random processes. Say that two processes $X , Y$ on a common index set $T$ are versions of one another if $X _ { t } = Y _ { t }$ a.s. for every $t \in T$ . When $T = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , two continuous or right-continuous versions $X , Y$ of a given process are clearly indistinguishable, in the sense that $X \equiv Y { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , so that the entire paths agree outside a fixed null set. 

For any mapping f between two metric spaces $( S , \rho )$ and $( S ^ { \prime } , \rho ^ { \prime } )$ , we define the modulus of continuity $w _ { f } = w ( f , \cdot )$ by 

$$
w _ {f} (r) = \sup \left\{\rho^ {\prime} \left(f _ {s}, f _ {t}\right); s, t \in S, \rho (s, t) \leq r \right\}, \quad r > 0,
$$

so that $f$ is uniformly continuous if $w _ { f } ( r ) \to 0 \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } r \to 0$ . Say that f is H¨older continuous of order p, $\mathrm { i f } ^ { 1 0 } \ w _ { f } ( r ) \ < r ^ { \bar { p } }$ as $r  0$ . The stated property is said to hold locally if it is valid on every bounded set. 

A simple moment condition ensures the existence of a H¨older-continuous version of a given process on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Important applications are given in Theorems 14.5, 29.4, and 32.3, and a related tightness criterion appears in Corollary 23.7. 

Theorem 4.23 (moments and H¨older continuity, Kolmogorov, Lo`eve, Chentsov) Let X be a process on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with values in a complete metric space $( S , \rho )$ ， such that <sup>a</sup> d+b t ∈ Rd (10) 

$$
E \Bigl \{\rho (X _ {s}, X _ {t}) \Bigr \} ^ {a} \lesssim | s - t | ^ {d + b}, \quad s, t \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d},\tag{10}
$$

for some constants $a , b > 0$ . Then a version of X is locally H¨older continuous of order $p ,$ for every $p \in ( 0 , b / a )$ 

Proof: It is clearly enough to consider the restriction of X to $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { d }$ . Define 

$$
D _ {n} = \Big \{2 ^ {- n} (k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {d}); k _ {1}, \ldots , k _ {n} \in \{1, \ldots , 2 ^ {n} \} \Big \}, \quad n \in \mathsf {N},
$$

and put 

$$
\xi_ {n} = \max \Bigl \{\rho (X _ {s}, X _ {t}); s, t \in D _ {n}, | s - t | = 2 ^ {- n} \Bigr \}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Since 

$$
\left| \left\{(s, t) \in D _ {n} ^ {2}; | s - t | = 2 ^ {- n} \right\} \right| \leq d 2 ^ {d n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

we get by (10) for any $p \in ( 0 , b / a )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \sum_ {n} (2 ^ {p n} \xi_ {n}) ^ {a} = \sum_ {n} 2 ^ {a p n} E \xi_ {n} ^ {a} \\ \lesssim \sum_ {n} 2 ^ {a p n} 2 ^ {d n} (2 ^ {- n}) ^ {d + b} \\ = \sum_ {n} 2 ^ {(a p - b) n} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

The sum on the left is then a.s. convergent, and so $\xi _ { n } ~ \lesssim ~ 2 ^ { - p n } ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . Now any points $s , t \in \cup _ { n } D _ { n }$ with $| s - t | \leq 2 ^ { - m }$ can be connected by a piecewise <sub>linear path, which for every</sub> $n \geq m$ involves at most 2d steps between nearest neighbors in $D _ { n }$ . Thus, for any $r \in [ 2 ^ { - m - 1 } , 2 ^ { - m } ]$ ], 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\sup \Big \{\rho (X _ {s}, X _ {t}); s, t \in \bigcup_ {n} D _ {n}, | s - t | \leq r \Big \}} \\ & {\quad \lesssim \sum_ {n \geq m} \xi_ {n} \lesssim \sum_ {n \geq m} 2 ^ {- p n}} \\ & {\quad \lesssim 2 ^ {- p m} \lesssim r ^ {p},} \end{array}
$$

showing that X is $\mathrm { a . s }$ . H¨older continuous on $\cup _ { n } D _ { n }$ of order $p .$ 

In particular, X agrees a.s. on $\cup _ { n } D _ { n }$ <sub>with a continuous process</sub> $Y$ on $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { d } ;$ <sub>and we note that the H¨older continuity of</sub> $Y$ on $\cup _ { n } D _ { n }$ extends with the same order $p$ to the entire cube $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { d }$ . To show that $Y$ is a version of $X$ , fix any $t \in [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { d }$ , and choose $t _ { 1 } , t _ { 2 } , . . . \in \bigcup _ { n } D _ { n }$ with $t _ { n } \to t$ . Then $X _ { t _ { n } } = Y _ { t _ { n } }$ a.s. for each n. Since also $X _ { t _ { n } } \ { \overset { P } { \to } } \ X _ { t }$ by (10) and $Y _ { t _ { n } }  Y _ { t }$ a.s. by continuity, we get $X _ { t } = Y _ { t } \ \mathrm { a . s }$ ✷ 

Path regularity can sometimes be established by comparison with a regular process: 

Lemma 4.24 (transfer of regularity) Let $X \ { \stackrel { d } { = } } \ Y$ be random processes on $T$ with values in a separable metric space $S$ , where the paths of $Y$ belong to a set $U \subset S ^ { T }$ that is Borel for the σ-field $\mathcal { U } = ( B _ { S } ) ^ { T } \cap U$ . Then X has a version with paths in $U$ . 

Proof: For clarity we may write $\tilde { Y }$ for the path of $Y$ , regarded as a random element in U. Then $\tilde { Y }$ is Y-measurable, and Lemma 1.14 yields a measurable mapping $f \colon S ^ { T } \to U$ with $\tilde { Y } = f ( Y )$ a.s. Define ${ \tilde { X } } = f ( X )$ , and note that $( \tilde { X } , X ) \stackrel { d } { = } ( \tilde { Y } , Y )$ . Since the diagonal in $S ^ { 2 }$ is measurable, we get in particular 

$$
P \{\tilde {X} _ {t} = X _ {t} \} = P \{\tilde {Y} _ {t} = Y _ {t} \} = 1, t \in T.
$$

We conclude with a characterization of distribution functions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } ,$ , required in Chapter 6. For any vectors $\boldsymbol { x } = ( x _ { 1 } , \dots , x _ { d } )$ and $y = ( y _ { 1 } , \dotsc , y _ { d } )$ , write $x \ \leq \ y$ for the component-wise inequality $x _ { k } \leq y _ { k } , k = 1 , \ldots , d .$ , and similarly for $x < y$ . In particular, the distribution function $F$ of a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is given by $F ( x ) = \mu \{ y ; y \leq x \}$ . Similarly, let x y denote the componentwise maximum. Put $\mathbf { 1 } = ( 1 , \ldots , 1 )$ and $\infty = ( \infty , \ldots , \infty )$ 

For any rectangular box 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (x, y ] = \{u; x <   u \leq y \} \\ = (x _ {1}, y _ {1} ] \times \dots \times (x _ {d}, y _ {d} ], \end{array}
$$

we note that $\begin{array} { r } { \mu ( x , y ] = \sum _ { u } s ( u ) F ( u ) } \end{array}$ , where $s ( u ) = ( - 1 ) ^ { p }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { p = \sum _ { k } 1 \{ u _ { k } = } \end{array}$ $y _ { k } \}$ , and the summation extends over all vertices u of $( x , y ]$ . Writing $F ( x , y ]$ for the stated sum, we say that $F$ has non-negative increments if $F ( x , y ] \ge 0$ for all pairs $x < y$ . We further say that $F$ is right-continuous if $F ( x _ { n } ) \to F ( x )$ as $x _ { n } \downarrow x$ , and proper if $F ( x )  1$ or 0 as min $x _ { k } \to \pm \infty$ , respectively. 

We show that any function with the stated properties determines a probability measure on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

Theorem 4.25 (distribution functions) For functions $F \colon \mathsf { R } ^ { d }  [ 0 , 1 ]$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $F$ is the distribution function of a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , 

(ii) F is right-continuous and proper with non-negative increments. 

Proof: For any $F$ as in (ii), the set function $F ( x , y ]$ is clearly finitely addi tive. Since $F$ is proper, we have also $F ( x , y ] \to 1$ as $x \to - \infty$ and $y  \infty , \mathrm { i . e . }$ , as $( x , y ] \uparrow ( - \infty , \infty ) = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Hence, for every $n \in \mathsf N$ there exists a probability measure $\mu _ { n }$ on $( 2 ^ { - n } Z ) ^ { d }$ with $Z = \{ \dots , - 1 , 0 , 1 , \dots \}$ , such that 

$$
\mu_ {n} \{2 ^ {- n} k \} = F \left(2 ^ {- n} (k - 1), 2 ^ {- n} k \right], \quad k \in \mathbb {Z} ^ {d}, n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

The finite additivity of $F ( x , y ]$ yields 

$$
\mu_ {m} \left\{2 ^ {- m} (k - 1, k ] \right\} = \mu_ {n} \left\{2 ^ {- m} (k - 1, k ] \right\}, \quad k \in \mathbb {Z} ^ {d}, m <   n \text { in } \mathbb {N}.\tag{11}
$$

By (11) we can split the Lebesgue unit interval $( [ 0 , 1 ] , B [ 0 , 1 ] , \lambda )$ recursively to construct some random vectors $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . with distributions $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ , satisfying 2−m < ξ < ξ 

$$
\xi_ {m} - 2 ^ {- m} <   \xi_ {n} \leq \xi_ {m}, \quad m <   n.
$$

In particular, $\xi _ { 1 } \ge \xi _ { 2 } \ge \dots \ge \xi _ { 1 } - 1$ , and so $\xi _ { n }$ converges pointwise to some random vector $\xi .$ . Define $\mu = \lambda \circ \xi ^ { - 1 }$ 

To see that $\mu$ has distribution function $F$ , we conclude from the properness of $F$ that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda \Bigl \{\xi_ {n} \leq 2 ^ {- n} k \Bigr \} = \mu_ {n} (- \infty ,   2 ^ {- n} k ] \\ = F (2 ^ {- n} k), \quad k \in \mathsf {Z} ^ {d},    n \in \mathsf {N}. \end{array}
$$

Since also $\xi _ { n } \downarrow \xi \ \mathrm { a . s . } ,$ Fatou’s lemma yields for dyadic $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda \{\xi <   x \} = \lambda \{\xi_ {n} <   x \text {   ult. } \} \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \lambda \{\xi_ {n} <   x \} \leq F (x) \\ \quad = \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \lambda \{\xi_ {n} \leq x \} \\ \quad \leq \lambda \{\xi_ {n} \leq x \text {   i.o. } \} \\ \quad \leq \lambda \{\xi \leq x \}, \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} F (x) \leq \lambda \{\xi \leq x \} \\ \quad \leq F (x + 2 ^ {- n} {\bf 1}), \quad n \in {\sf N}. \end{array}
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ and using the right-continuity of $F ,$ we get $\lambda \{ \xi \leq x \} = F ( x )$ , which extends to any $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , by the right-continuity of both sides. ✷ 

We also need a version for unbounded measures, extending the one-dimensional Theorem 2.14: 

Corollary 4.26 (unbounded measures) For any right-continuous function $F$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with non-negative increments, there exists a measure $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with 

$$
\mu (x, y ] = F (x, y ], \quad x \leq y i n \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.
$$

Proof: For any $a \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we may apply Theorem 4.25 to suitably normalized versions of the function $F _ { a } ( x ) = F ( a , a \vee x ]$ to obtain a measure $\mu _ { a }$ on $[ a , \infty )$ with $\mu _ { a } ( a , x ] = F ( a , x ]$ for all $x > a$ . Then clearly $\mu _ { a } = \mu _ { b }$ on $( a \lor b , \infty )$ for any a, b, and so the set function $\mu = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { a } \mu _ { a }$ is a measure with the required property. ✷
