Chapter 5 

# Random Sequences, Series, and Averages

Moments and tails, convergence a.s. and in probability, sub-sequence criterion, continuity and completeness, convergence in distribution, tightness and uniform integrability, convergence of means, L<sup>p</sup>-convergence, random series and averages, positive and symmetric terms, variance criteria, three-series criterion, strong laws of large numbers, empirical distributions, portmanteau theorem, continuous mapping and approximation, Skorohod coupling, representation and measurability of limits 

Here our first aim is to introduce and compare the basic modes of convergence of random quantities. For random elements $\xi$ and $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . in a metric or topological space $S ,$ the most commonly used notions are those of almost sure convergence $\left( \xi _ { n } \to \xi { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } } \right)$ and convergence in probability $( \xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi )$ , corresponding to the general notions of convergence a.e. and in measure, respectively. When $S = { \mathsf { R } }$ we also have the concept of L<sup>p</sup>-convergence, familiar from Chapter 1. Those three notions are used throughout this book. For a special purpose in Chapter 10, we also need the notion of weak L<sup>1</sup>-convergence. 

Our second major theme is to study the very diferent notion of convergence in distribution $( \xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi )$ , defined by the condition $E f ( \xi _ { n } ) \to E f ( \xi )$ for all bounded, continuous functions $f$ on S. This is clearly equivalent to weak convergence of the associated distributions $\mu _ { n } = \mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { n } )$ and $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( \boldsymbol { \xi } )$ , written as $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } {  } \mu$ and defined by the condition $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ for every f as above. In this chapter we will establish only the most basic results of weak convergence theory, such as the ‘portmanteau’ theorem, the continuous mapping and approximation theorems, and the Skorohod coupling. Our development of the general theory continues in Chapters 6 and 23, and further distributional limit theorems of various kind appear throughout the remainder of the book. 

Our third main theme is to characterize the convergence of series $\textstyle \sum _ { k } \xi _ { k }$ and averages $n ^ { - c } \sum _ { k \leq n } \xi _ { k }$ , where $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ are independent random variables and c is a positive constant. The two problems are related by the elementary Kronecker lemma, and the main results are the basic three-series criterion and the strong law of large numbers. The former result is extended in Chapter 9 to the powerful martingale convergence theorem, whereas extensions and refinements of the latter result are proved in Chapters 22 and 25. The mentioned theorems are further related to certain weak convergence results presented in Chapters 6–7. 

Before embarking on our systematic study of the various notions of convergence, we consider a couple of elementary but useful inequalities. 

Lemma 5.1 (moments and tails, Bienaym´e, Chebyshev, Paley & Zygmund) For any random variable $\xi \ge 0$ with $0 < E \xi < \infty$ , we have 

$$
(1 - r) _ {+} ^ {2} \frac {(E \xi) ^ {2}}{E \xi^ {2}} \leq P \left\{\xi > r E \xi \right\} \leq \frac {1}{r}, \quad r > 0.
$$

The upper bound is often referred to as the Chebyshev or Markov inequality. When $E \xi ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , we get in particular the classical estimate 

$$
P \left\{\left| \xi - E \xi \right| > \varepsilon \right\} \leq \varepsilon^ {- 2} \operatorname{Var} (\xi), \quad \varepsilon > 0.
$$

Proof: We may clearly assume that $E \xi = 1$ . The upper bound then follows as we take expectations in the inequality $r 1 \{ \xi > r \} \leq \xi$ . To get the lower bound, we note that for any $r , t > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} t ^ {2} 1 \{\xi > r \} \geq (\xi - r) (2 t + r - \xi) \\ = 2   \xi (r + t) - r (2   t + r) - \xi^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

Taking expected values, we get for $r \in ( 0 , 1 )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} t ^ {2} P \{\xi > r \} \geq 2 (r + t) - r (2 t + r) - E \xi^ {2} \\ \geq 2 t (1 - r) - E \xi^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

Now choose $t = E \xi ^ { 2 } / ( 1 - r )$ 

For any random elements $\xi$ and $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . in a separable metric space $( S , \rho )$ we say that $\xi _ { n }$ converges in probability to $\xi$ and write $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi$ if 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} P \Bigl \{\rho (\xi_ {n}, \xi) > \varepsilon \Bigr \} = 0, \quad \varepsilon > 0.
$$

Lemma 5.2 (convergence in probability) For any random elements $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 }$ . . . in a separable metric space $( S , \rho )$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } { \to } \xi ,$ 

(ii) $E \Big \{ \rho ( \xi _ { n } , \xi ) \wedge 1 \Big \}  0 ,$ 

(iii) for any sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , we have $\xi _ { n }  \xi ~ a . s$ . along a further subsequence $N ^ { \prime \prime } \subset N ^ { \prime }$ 

In particular, $\xi _ { n }  \xi ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . implies $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } { \to } \xi$ , and the notion of convergence in probability depends only on the topology, regardless of the metrization $\rho .$ 

Proof: The implication ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ is obvious, and the converse holds by Chebyshev’s inequality. Now assume (ii), and fix an arbitrary sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ . We may then choose a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime } \subset N ^ { \prime }$ such that 

$$
E \sum_ {n \in N ^ {\prime \prime}} \Bigl \{\rho (\xi_ {n}, \xi) \wedge 1 \Bigr \} = \sum_ {n \in N ^ {\prime \prime}} E \Bigl \{\rho (\xi_ {n}, \xi) \wedge 1 \Bigr \} <   \infty ,
$$

where the equality holds by monotone convergence. The series on the left then converges $\mathrm { a . s . }$ , which implies $\xi _ { n }  \xi ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . along $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ , proving (iii). 

Now assume (iii). If (ii) fails, there exists an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $E \{ \rho ( \xi _ { n } , \xi ) \wedge 1 \}$ $> \varepsilon$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ . Then (iii) yields $\xi _ { n } \to \xi$ a.s. along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime } \subset N ^ { \prime }$ , and so by dominated convergence $E \{ \rho ( \xi _ { n } , \xi ) \land 1 \}  0$ along $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ , a contradiction proving (ii). ✷ 

For a first application, we show that convergence in probability is preserved by continuous mappings. 

Lemma 5.3 (continuous mapping) For any separable metric spaces S, T, let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be random elements in S, and let the mapping $f : S  T$ be measurable and a.s. continuous at $\xi .$ . Then 

$$
\xi_ {n} \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} \xi \quad \Rightarrow \quad f (\xi_ {n}) \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} f (\xi).
$$

Proof: Fix any sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ . By Lemma 5.2 we have $\xi _ { n } \to \xi$ a.s. along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime } \subset N ^ { \prime }$ , and so by continuity $f ( \xi _ { n } ) \to f ( \xi )$ a.s. along $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ . Hence, $f ( \xi _ { n } ) \overset { P } { \to } f ( \xi )$ by Lemma 5.2. ✷ 

For any separable metric spaces $( S _ { k } , \rho _ { k } )$ , we may introduce the product space $S = S _ { 1 } \times S _ { 2 } \times \cdots$ endowed with the product topology, admitting the metrization 7 

$$
\rho (x, y) = \sum_ {k} 2 ^ {- k} \Bigl \{\rho_ {k} (x _ {k}, y _ {k}) \wedge 1 \Bigr \}, \quad x, y \in S.\tag{1}
$$

Since $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { B } _ { S } } = \otimes _ { k } \boldsymbol { \mathcal { B } _ { S _ { k } } }$ by Lemma 1.2, a random element in $S$ is simply a sequence <sub>of random elements in</sub> $S _ { k } , k \in \mathbb { N }$ 

Lemma 5.4 (random sequences) Let $\boldsymbol { \xi } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \dots )$ and $\xi ^ { n } = ( \xi _ { 1 } ^ { n } , \xi _ { 2 } ^ { n } , \dots )$ ， $n \in { \mathbb N }$ , be random elements in $S _ { 1 } \times S _ { 2 } \times \cdots$ , for some separable metric spaces $S _ { 1 } , S _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ Then 

$$
\xi^ {n} \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} \xi \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \xi_ {k} ^ {n} \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} \xi_ {k} i n S _ {k}, k \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Proof: With $\rho$ as in (1), we get for any $n \in { \mathbb N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \Big \{\rho (\xi^ {n}, \xi) \wedge 1 \Big \} = E   \rho (\xi^ {n}, \xi) \\ = \sum_ {k} 2 ^ {- k} E \Big \{\rho_ {k} (\xi_ {k} ^ {n}, \xi_ {k}) \wedge 1 \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Thus, by dominated convergence, 

$$
E \left\{\rho (\xi^ {n}, \xi) \wedge 1 \right\}\rightarrow 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad E \left\{\rho_ {k} \left(\xi_ {k} ^ {n}, \xi_ {k}\right) \wedge 1 \right\}\rightarrow 0, \quad k \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Combining the last two lemmas, we may show how convergence in probability is preserved by the basic arithmetic operations. 

Corollary 5.5 (elementary operations) For any random variables $\xi _ { n } \stackrel { P } {  } \xi$ and $\eta _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \eta$ , we have 

(i) $a \xi _ { n } + b \eta _ { n } \overset { P } {  } a \xi + b \eta , \ a , b \in \mathsf { R } ,$ 

(ii) $\xi _ { n } \eta _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi \eta ,$ 

(iii) $\xi _ { n } / \eta _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi / \eta$ when $\eta , \eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , . . . \neq 0$ a.s. 

Proof: By Lemma 5.4 we have $( \xi _ { n } , \eta _ { n } ) \overset { P } {  } ( \xi , \eta )$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { 2 }$ , and so (i) and (ii) follow by Lemma 5.3. To prove (iii), we may apply Lemma 5.3 to the function $f \colon ( x , y ) \mapsto ( x / y ) 1 \{ y \neq 0 \}$ , which is clearly a.s. continuous at $( \xi , \eta )$ ✷ 

We turn to some associated completeness properties. For any random elements $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ in a separable metric space $( S , \rho )$ , we say that $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is Cauchy (convergent) in probability if $\rho ( \xi _ { m } , \xi _ { n } ) \stackrel { P } {  } 0$ as $m , n \to \infty$ , in the sense that $E \{ \rho ( \xi _ { m } , \xi _ { n } ) \wedge 1 \}  0$ 

Lemma 5.6 (completeness) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be random elements in a separable, complete metric space $( S , \rho )$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is Cauchy in probability, 

(ii) $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi$ for a random element $\xi$ in $S$ . 

Similar results hold for a.s. convergence. 

Proof: The a.s. case is immediate from Lemma 1.11. Assuming (ii), we get 

$$
E \left\{\rho \left(\xi_ {m}, \xi_ {n}\right) \wedge 1 \right\} \leq E \left\{\rho \left(\xi_ {m}, \xi\right) \wedge 1 \right\} + E \left\{\rho \left(\xi_ {n}, \xi\right) \wedge 1 \right\}\rightarrow 0,
$$

proving (i). 

Now assume (i), and define 

$$
n _ {k} = \inf \Bigl \{n \geq k; \sup _ {m \geq n} E \bigl \{\rho (\xi_ {m}, \xi_ {n}) \wedge 1 \bigr \} \leq 2 ^ {- k} \Bigr \}, \quad k \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

The $n _ { k }$ are finite and satisfy 

$$
E \sum_ {k} \left\{\rho \left(\xi_ {n _ {k}}, \xi_ {n _ {k + 1}}\right) \wedge 1 \right\} \leq \sum_ {k} 2 ^ {- k} <   \infty ,
$$

and so $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k } \rho ( \xi _ { n _ { k } } , \xi _ { n _ { k + 1 } } ) < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s } } \end{array}$ . The sequence $\left( \xi _ { n _ { k } } \right)$ is then a.s. Cauchy and converges a.s. toward a measurable limit $\xi .$ . To prove (ii), write 

$$
E \left\{\rho \left(\xi_ {m}, \xi\right) \wedge 1 \right\} \leq E \left\{\rho \left(\xi_ {m}, \xi_ {n _ {k}}\right) \wedge 1 \right\} + E \left\{\rho \left(\xi_ {n _ {k}}, \xi\right) \wedge 1 \right\},
$$

and note that the right-hand side tends to zero as $m , k \to \infty$ , by the Cauchy convergence of $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ and dominated convergence. ✷ 

For any probability measures $\mu$ and $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . on a metric space $( S , \rho )$ with Borel $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i e l d ~ } } S ,$ we say that $\mu _ { n }$ converges weakly to $\mu$ and write $\mu _ { n } \ { \stackrel { w } { \to } } \ \mu ,$ , if $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ for every $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ , defined as the class of bounded, continuous functions $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ . For any random elements $\xi$ and $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . in S, we further say that $\xi _ { n }$ converges in distribution to $\xi$ and write $\xi _ { n } \ \overset { d } { \to } \ \xi \ \mathrm { i f } \ \mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { n } ) \ \overset { w } { \to } \ \mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ 

i.e., if $E f ( \xi _ { n } ) \to E f ( \xi )$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ . The latter mode of convergence clearly depends only on the distributions, and the $\xi _ { n }$ and $\xi$ need not even be defined on the same probability space. To motivate the definition, note that $x _ { n } \to x$ in a metric space S if $f ( x _ { n } ) \to f ( x )$ for all continuous functions $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ , and that $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ is determined by the integrals $E f ( \xi )$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ 

We give a connection between convergence in probability and distribution. 

Lemma 5.7 (convergence in probability and distribution) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be random elements in a separable metric space $( S , \rho )$ . Then 

$$
\xi_ {n} \stackrel {P} {\to} \xi \quad \Rightarrow \quad \xi_ {n} \stackrel {d} {\to} \xi ,
$$

with equivalence when $\xi$ is a.s. a constant. 

Proof: Let $\xi _ { n } \ \overset { P } {  } \ \xi .$ . For any $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ we need to show that $E f ( \xi _ { n } ) \to$ $E f ( \xi )$ . If the convergence fails, there exists a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { i n f } _ { n \in N ^ { \prime } } | E f ( \xi _ { n } ) - E f ( \xi ) | > 0 } \end{array}$ . Then Lemma 5.2 yields $\xi _ { n }  \xi \mathrm { ~ a . s ~ }$ . along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime } \subset N ^ { \prime }$ . By continuity and dominated convergence, we get $E f ( \xi _ { n } ) \to E f ( \xi )$ along $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ , a contradiction. 

Conversely, let $\xi _ { n } \ \overset { d } { \to } \ s \in \ S$ . Since $\rho ( x , s ) \wedge 1$ is a bounded and continuous function of x, we get $E \{ \rho ( \xi _ { n } , s ) \wedge 1 \}  E \{ \rho ( s , s ) \wedge 1 \} = 0$ , and so $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } { \to } s , \ \sqcup$ 

A T-indexed family of random vectors $\xi _ { t }$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is said to be tight, if 

$$
\lim _ {r \to \infty} \sup _ {t \in T} P \Bigl \{| \xi_ {t} | > r \Bigr \} = 0.
$$

For sequences $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ , this is clearly equivalent to 

$$
\lim _ {r \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \Big \{| \xi_ {n} | > r \Big \} = 0,\tag{2}
$$

which is often easier to verify. Tightness plays an important role for the compactness methods developed in Chapters 6 and 23. For the moment, we note only the following simple connection with weak convergence. 

Lemma 5.8 (weak convergence and tightness) For random vectors $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 }$ . . . in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we have ξ <sup>d</sup> ξ (ξ ) is tight. 

Proof: Fix any $r > 0$ , and define $f ( x ) = \{ 1 - ( r - | x | ) _ { + } \} _ { + }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \underset {n \to \infty} {\lim \sup} P \Bigl \{| \xi_ {n} | > r \Bigr \} \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\lim} E f (\xi_ {n}) = E f (\xi) \\ \leq P \Bigl \{| \xi | > r - 1 \Bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

Here the right-hand side tends to 0 as $r  \infty$ , and (2) follows. 

We further note the following simple relationship between tightness and convergence in probability. 

Lemma 5.9 (tightness and convergence in probability) For random vectors $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ . in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is tight, 

(ii) $c _ { n } \xi _ { n } \overset { P } { \to } 0$ for any constants $c _ { n } \geq 0$ with $c _ { n } \to 0$ 

Proof: Assume (i), and let $c _ { n } \to 0$ . Fixing any $r , \varepsilon > 0$ , and noting that $c _ { n } r \leq \varepsilon$ for all but finitely many $n \in \mathsf N$ , we get 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \Big \{| c _ {n}   \xi_ {n} | > \varepsilon \Big \} \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \Big \{| \xi_ {n} | > r \Big \}.
$$

Here the right-hand side tends to 0 as $r  \infty$ , and so $P \{ | c _ { n } \xi _ { n } | > \varepsilon \}  0$ Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, we get $c _ { n } \xi _ { n } \overset { P } { \to } 0$ , proving (ii). If instead (i) is false, we have in $\mathrm { f } _ { k } P \{ | \xi _ { n _ { k } } | > k \} > 0$ for a sub-sequence $( n _ { k } ) \subset \mathbb { N }$ . Putting $c _ { n } =$ sup $\{ k ^ { - 1 } ; n _ { k } \ge n \}$ , we note that $c _ { n } \to 0$ , and yet $P \{ | c _ { n _ { k } } \xi _ { n _ { k } } | > 1 \} \not  0$ . Thus, even (ii) fails. ✷ 

We turn to a related notion for expected values. The random variables $\xi _ { t } .$ $t \in T ,$ , are said to be uniformly integrable if 

$$
\lim _ {r \to \infty} \sup _ {t \in T} E \big (| \xi_ {t} |; | \xi_ {t} | > r \big) = 0,\tag{3}
$$

where $E ( \xi ; A ) = E ( 1 _ { A } \xi )$ . For sequences $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ in $L ^ { 1 }$ , this is clearly equivalent to 

$$
\lim _ {r \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} E \Big (| \xi_ {n} |;   | \xi_ {n} | > r \Big) = 0.\tag{4}
$$

Condition (3) holds in particular if the $\xi _ { t }$ are L<sup>p</sup>-bounded for some $p > 1$ , in the sense that $\mathrm { s u p } _ { t } E | \xi _ { t } | ^ { p } < \infty$ . To see this, it sufices to write 

$$
E \left(\left| \xi_ {t} \right|; \left| \xi_ {t} \right| > r\right) \leq r ^ {- p + 1} E \left| \xi_ {t} \right| ^ {p}, \quad r, p > 0.
$$

We give a useful criterion for uniform integrability. For motivation, we note that if $\xi$ is an integrable random variable, then $E ( | \xi | ; A ) \to 0$ as $P A  0$ , by Lemma 5.2 and dominated convergence, in the sense that 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \sup _ {P A <   \varepsilon} E (| \xi |; A) = 0.
$$

Lemma 5.10 (uniform integrability) For any family of random variables $\xi _ { t }$ , $t \in T$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) the $\xi _ { t }$ are uniformly integrable, 

(ii) $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { t \in T } E | \xi _ { t } | < \infty$ and $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { P A \to 0 } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { t \in T } E ( | \xi _ { t } | ; A ) = 0 .$ 

Proof: Assuming (i), we may write 

$$
E \left(\left| \xi_ {t} \right|; A\right) \leq r P A + E \left(\left| \xi_ {t} \right|; \left| \xi_ {t} \right| > r\right), \quad r > 0.
$$

Here the second part of (ii) follows as we let $P A  0$ and then $r  \infty$ . To prove the first part, we may take $A = \Omega$ and choose $r > 0$ large enough. 

Conversely, assume (ii). By Chebyshev’s inequality, we get as $r  \infty$ 

$$
\sup _ {t} P \{| \xi_ {t} | > r \} \leq r ^ {- 1} \sup _ {t} E | \xi_ {t} | \to 0,
$$

and (i) follows from the second part of (ii) with $A = \{ | \xi _ { t } | > r \}$ 

The relevance of uniform integrability for the convergence of moments is clear from the following result, which also provides a weak convergence version of Fatou’s lemma. 

Lemma 5.11 (convergence of means) For any random variables $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ $\geq 0$ with $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ , we have 

(i) $E \xi \leq \operatorname* { l i m } \operatorname* { i n f } _ { n } E \xi _ { n } ,$ 

(ii) $E \xi _ { n } \to E \xi < \infty \Leftrightarrow$ the $\xi _ { n }$ are uniformly integrable. 

Proof: For any $r > 0$ , the function $x \mapsto x \wedge r$ is bounded and continuous on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ . Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E   \xi_ {n} \geq \lim _ {n \to \infty} E (\xi_ {n} \wedge r) \\ = E (\xi \wedge r), \end{array}
$$

and the first assertion follows as we let $r  \infty$ . Next assume $( 4 )$ , and note in particular that $E \xi \leq$ lim in $\mathrm { f } _ { n } E \xi _ { n } < \infty$ . For any $r > 0$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left| E   \xi_ {n} - E   \xi \right| \leq \left| E   \xi_ {n} - E (\xi_ {n} \wedge r) \right| + \left| E (\xi_ {n} \wedge r) - E (\xi \wedge r) \right| \\ + \left| E (\xi \wedge r) - E   \xi \right|. \end{array}
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ and then $r  \infty$ , we obtain $E \xi _ { n } \to E \xi$ . Now assume instead that $E \xi _ { n } \to E \xi < \infty$ . Keeping $r > 0$ fixed, we get as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \big (\xi_ {n};   \xi_ {n} > r \big)   \leq   E \Big \{\xi_ {n} - \xi_ {n} \wedge (r - \xi_ {n}) _ {+} \Big \} \\ \to E \Big \{\xi - \xi \wedge (r - \xi) _ {+} \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Since $x \wedge ( r - x ) _ { + } \uparrow x \operatorname { a s } r \to \infty$ , the right-hand side tends to zero by dominated convergence, and (4) follows. ✷ 

We may now prove some useful criteria for convergence in $L ^ { p }$ 

Theorem 5.12 (L<sup>p</sup>-convergence) For a fixed $p > 0$ , let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots \in L ^ { p }$ with $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\| \xi _ { n } - \xi \| _ { p } \to 0 .$ 

(ii) $\| \xi _ { n } \| _ { p } \to \| \xi \| _ { p } < \infty _ { . }$ 

(iii) the variables $| \xi _ { n } | ^ { p }$ are uniformly integrable. 

Conversely, (i) implies $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi$ 

Proof: First let $\xi _ { n } \to \xi$ in $L ^ { p }$ . Then $\| \xi _ { n } \| _ { p } \to \| \xi \| _ { p }$ by Lemma 1.31, and Lemma 5.1 yields for any $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \Big \{| \xi_ {n} - \xi | > \varepsilon \Big \} = P \Big \{| \xi_ {n} - \xi | ^ {p} > \varepsilon^ {p} \Big \} \\ & \qquad \leq \varepsilon^ {- p} \| \xi_ {n} - \xi \| _ {p} ^ {p} \to 0, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi$ . We may henceforth assume that $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \xi$ . In particular, $| \xi _ { n } | ^ { p } \overset { d } { \to } | \xi | ^ { p }$ by Lemmas 5.3 and $5 . 7 ,$ and so $( \mathrm { i i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ by Lemma 5.11. Next assume (ii). If (i) fails, there exists a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ with in $\mathrm { f } _ { n \in N ^ { \prime } } \| \xi _ { n } - \xi \| _ { p } > 0$ . Then Lemma 5.2 yields $\xi _ { n }  \xi \mathrm { ~ a . s ~ }$ . along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime } \subset N ^ { \prime }$ , and so Lemma 1.34 gives $\| \xi _ { n } - \xi \| _ { p } \to 0$ along $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ , a contradiction. Thus, $( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ , and so all three conditions are equivalent. ✷ 

We consider yet another mode of convergence for random variables. Letting $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots \in L ^ { p }$ for a $p \in [ 1 , \infty )$ , we say that $\xi _ { n } \to \xi$ weakly in $L ^ { p }$ if $E \xi _ { n } \eta \to E \xi \eta$ for every $\eta \in L ^ { q }$ , where $p ^ { - 1 } + q ^ { - 1 } = 1$ . Taking $\eta = | \xi | ^ { p - 1 } \mathrm { s g n } \xi \mathrm { g i v e s } \ \| \eta \| _ { q } =$ $\| \xi \| _ { p } ^ { p - 1 }$ , and so by H¨older’s inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| \xi \| _ {p} ^ {p} = E   \xi \eta = \lim _ {n \to \infty} E   \xi_ {n} \eta \\ \leq \| \xi \| _ {p} ^ {p - 1} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \| \xi_ {n} \| _ {p}, \end{array}
$$

which implies $\| \xi \| _ { p } \leq$ lim in $\mathrm { f } _ { n } \| \xi _ { n } \| _ { p } .$ 

Now recall that any L<sup>2</sup>-bounded sequence has a sub-sequence converging weakly in $L ^ { 2 }$ . The following related criterion for weak compactness in $L ^ { 1 }$ will be needed in Chapter 10. 

Lemma 5.13 (weak $L ^ { 1 } - c o m p a c t n e s s ^ { 1 }$ , Dunford) Every uniformly integrable sequence of random variables has a sub-sequence converging weakly in $L ^ { 1 }$ 

Proof: Let $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ be uniformly integrable. Define $\xi _ { n } ^ { k } = \xi _ { n } 1 \{ | \xi _ { n } | \leq k \}$ , and note that $( \xi _ { n } ^ { k } )$ is $L ^ { 2 } .$ -bounded in n for fixed k. By the compactness in $L ^ { 2 }$ and a diagonal argument, there exist a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ and some random variables $\eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ such that $\xi _ { n } ^ { k } \to \eta _ { k }$ holds weakly in $L ^ { 2 }$ and then also in $L ^ { 1 }$ as $n \to \infty$ along $N ^ { \prime }$ for fixed k. 

Now $\| \eta _ { k } - \eta _ { l } \| _ { 1 } \le$ lim in $\mathrm { f } _ { n } \| \xi _ { n } ^ { k } - \xi _ { n } ^ { l } \| _ { 1 }$ , and by uniform integrability the righthand side tends to zero as $k , l  \infty$ . Thus, the sequence $( \eta _ { k } )$ is Cauchy in $L ^ { 1 }$ and so it converges in $L ^ { 1 }$ toward some $\xi ,$ . By approximation it follows easily that $\xi _ { n } \to \xi$ weakly in $L ^ { 1 }$ along $N ^ { \prime }$ ✷ 

We turn to some convergence criteria for random series, beginning with an important special case. 

Proposition 5.14 (series with positive terms) For any independent random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots \ge 0$ , 

$$
\sum_ {n} \xi_ {n} <   \infty a. s. \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \sum_ {n} E (\xi_ {n} \wedge 1) <   \infty .
$$

Proof: The right-hand condition yields $E \sum _ { n } ( \xi _ { n } \wedge 1 ) < \infty$ by Fubini’s theorem, and so $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } ( \xi _ { n } \wedge 1 ) < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s } } \end{array}$ . In particular, $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } 1 \{ \xi _ { n } > 1 \} < \infty \mathrm { a . s . } , } \end{array}$ and so the series $\textstyle \sum _ { n } ( \xi _ { n } \wedge 1 )$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n }$ difer by at most finitely many terms, which implies $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n } <$ a.s. 

Conversely, let $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n } < \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ . Then also $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } ( \xi _ { n } \wedge 1 ) < \infty \mathrm { ~ a . s . } } \end{array}$ ., and so we may assume that $\xi _ { n } \leq 1$ for all n. Since $1 - x \leq e ^ { - x } \leq 1 - a x$ for $x \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ with $a = 1 - e ^ { - 1 }$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 <   E \exp \Bigl (- \sum_ {n} \xi_ {n} \Bigr) \\ = \prod_ {n} E e ^ {- \xi_ {n}} \\ \leq \prod_ {n} (1 - a   E \xi_ {n}) \\ \leq \prod_ {n} \exp (- a   E \xi_ {n}) \\ = \exp \Bigl (- a \sum_ {n} E \xi_ {n} \Bigr), \end{array}
$$

and so $\textstyle \sum _ { n } E \xi _ { n } < \infty$ 

To deal with more general series, we need the following strengthened version of Chebyshev’s inequality. A further extension appears as Proposition 9.16. 

Lemma 5.15 (maximum inequality, Kolmogorov) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be independent random variables with mean 0, and put $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { k \le n } \xi _ { k } } \end{array}$ . Then 

$$
P \Bigl \{\sup _ {n} | S _ {n} | > r \Bigr \} \leq r ^ {- 2} \sum_ {n} \mathrm{Var} (\xi_ {n}), \quad r > 0.
$$

Proof: We may assume that $\textstyle \sum _ { n } E \xi _ { n } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Writing $\tau = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n ; | S _ { n } | > r \}$ and noting that $S _ { k } 1 \{ \tau = k \} \bot \bot ( S _ { n } - S _ { k } )$ for $k \leq n$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {k \leq n} E \xi_ {k} ^ {2} = E   S _ {n} ^ {2} \geq \sum_ {k \leq n} E \big (S _ {n} ^ {2};   \tau = k \big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \sum_ {k \leq n} \Big (E \big \{S _ {k} ^ {2};   \tau = k \big \} + 2 E \big \{S _ {k} (S _ {n} - S _ {k});   \tau = k \big \} \Big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = \sum_ {k \leq n} E \big (S _ {k} ^ {2};   \tau = k \big) \geq r ^ {2} P \{\tau \leq n \}. \end{array}
$$

As $n \to \infty$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {k} E   \xi_ {k} ^ {2} \geq r ^ {2} P \{\tau <   \infty \} \\ = r ^ {2} P \Bigl \{\sup _ {k} | S _ {k} | > r \Bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

The last result yields a suficient condition for a.s. convergence of random series with independent terms. Precise criteria will be given in Theorem 5.18. 

Lemma 5.16 (variance criterion for series, Khinchin & Kolmogorov) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be independent random variables with mean 0. Then 

$$
\sum_ {n} \operatorname{Var} (\xi_ {n}) <   \infty \Rightarrow \sum_ {n} \xi_ {n} \text { converges a.s. }
$$

Proof: Write $S _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ . By Lemma 5.15 we get for any $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
P \Bigl \{\sup _ {k \geq n} | S _ {n} - S _ {k} | > \varepsilon \Bigr \} \leq \varepsilon^ {- 2} \sum_ {k \geq n} E \xi_ {k} ^ {2}.
$$

Hence, as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\sup _ {h, k \geq n} | S _ {h} - S _ {k} | \leq 2 \sup _ {k \geq n} | S _ {n} - S _ {k} | \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} 0,
$$

and Lemma 5.2 yields the corresponding a.s. convergence along a sub-sequence. Since the supremum on the left is non-increasing in n, the a.s. convergence extends to the entire sequence, which means that $( S _ { n } )$ is a.s. Cauchy convergent. Thus, $S _ { n }$ converges a.s. by Lemma 5.6. ✷ 

We turn to a basic connection between series with positive and symmetric terms. By $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  }$ we mean that $P \{ \xi _ { n } > r \}  1$ for every $r > 0$ 

Theorem 5.17 (positive and symmetric terms) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be independent, symmetric random variables. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\sum _ { n } \xi _ { n }$ converges a.s., 

(ii) $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n } ^ { 2 } < \infty \ a . s .$ 

(iii) $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } E \big ( \xi _ { n } ^ { 2 } \wedge 1 \big ) < \infty } \end{array}$ 

If the conditions fail, then $\begin{array} { r } { \left| \sum _ { k \le n } \xi _ { k } \right| \overset { P } { \to } \infty } \end{array}$ 

Proof: The equivalence $( \mathrm { i i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ holds by Proposition 5.14. Next assume (iii), and conclude from Lemma 5.16 that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n } 1 \{ | \xi _ { n } | \le 1 \} } \end{array}$ converges a.s. From (iii) and Fubini’s theorem we have also $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } 1 \{ | \xi _ { n } | > 1 \} < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s . } } \end{array}$ . Hence, the series $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n } 1 \{ | \xi _ { n } | \le 1 \} } \end{array}$ and $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n }$ difer by at most finitely many terms, and so even the latter series converges a.s. This shows that ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Leftarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } } \Leftrightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i i ) } }$ ). It remains to show that $| S _ { n } | \stackrel { P } {  }$ when (ii) fails, since the former condition yields $| S _ { n } | \to \infty$ a.s. along a sub-sequence, contradicting (i). Here $S _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ as before. 

Thus, suppose that (ii) fails. Then Kolmogorov’s 0 1 law yields $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n } ^ { 2 } = \infty$ a.s. First let $| \xi _ { n } | = c _ { n }$ be non-random for every n. If the $c _ { n }$ are unbounded, then for every $r > 0$ we may choose a sub-sequence $n _ { 1 } , n _ { 2 } , \ldots \in \mathsf { N }$ such that $c _ { n _ { 1 } } \ > \ r$ and $c _ { n _ { k + 1 } } > 2 c _ { n _ { k } }$ for all k. Then clearly $\begin{array} { r } { P \big \{ \sum _ { j \leq k } \xi _ { n _ { j } } \in I \big \} \leq 2 ^ { - k } } \end{array}$ for every interval I of length $2 r$ , and so by convolution $P \{ | S _ { n } | \leq r \} \leq 2 ^ { - k }$ for all $n \geq n _ { k }$ , which implies $P \{ | S _ { n } | \leq r \}  0$ 

Next let $c _ { n } \leq c < \infty$ for all n. Choosing $a > 0$ so small that cos $x \leq e ^ { - a x ^ { 2 } }$ for $| x | \le 1$ , we get for $0 < | t | \leq c ^ { - 1 }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq E e ^ {i t S _ {n}} = \prod_ {k \leq n} \cos (t   c _ {k}) \\ \leq \prod_ {k \leq n} \exp \Bigl (- a   t ^ {2} c _ {k} ^ {2} \Bigr) \\ = \exp \Bigl (- a   t ^ {2} \sum_ {k \leq n} c _ {k} ^ {2} \Bigr) \to 0. \end{array}
$$

Anticipating the elementary Lemma 6.1 below, we get again $P \{ | S _ { n } | \leq r \}  0$ for each $r > 0$ 

For general $\xi _ { n } .$ , choose some independent i.i.d. random variables $\vartheta _ { n }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { P \{ \vartheta _ { n } = \pm 1 \} = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , and note that the sequences $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ and $( \vartheta _ { n } | \xi _ { n } | )$ have the same distribution. Letting $\mu$ be the distribution of the sequence $\left( \left| \xi _ { n } \right| \right)$ , we get by Lemma 4.11 

$$
P \left\{\left| S _ {n} \right| > r \right\} = \int P \left\{\left| \sum_ {k \leq n} \vartheta_ {k} x _ {k} \right| > r \right\} \mu (d x), \quad r > 0.
$$

Here the integrand tends to 0 for $\mu { \mathrm { - a l m o s t } }$ every sequence $x = \left( x _ { n } \right)$ , by the result for constant $\left| \xi _ { n } \right|$ , and so the integral tends to 0 by dominated convergence. ✷ 

We may now give precise criteria for convergence, a.s. or in distribution, of a series of independent random variables. Write Va $( \xi ; A ) = \operatorname { V a r } ( \xi 1 _ { A } )$ 

Theorem 5.18 (three-series criterion, Kolmogorov, L´evy) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be independent random variables. Then $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n }$ converges a.s. if it converges in distribution, which holds if 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } P \Big \{ | \xi _ { n } | > 1 \Big \} < \infty , } \end{array}$ 

(ii) $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } E \big ( \xi _ { n } ; | \xi _ { n } | \le 1 \big ) } \end{array}$ converges, 

(iii) $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \mathrm { V a r } \Big ( \xi _ { n } ; | \xi _ { n } | \le 1 \Big ) < \infty . } \end{array}$ 

Our proof requires some simple symmetrization inequalities. Say that m is a median of the random variable ξ if $P \{ \xi > m \} \lor P \{ \xi < m \} \leq \frac { 1 } { 2 }$ . A symmetrization of $\xi$ is defined as a random variable of the form $\tilde { \xi } = \xi - \xi ^ { \prime }$ , where $\xi ^ { \prime } \bot \bot \xi$ with $\xi ^ { \prime } \overset { d } { = } \xi$ . For symmetrizations of the random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ , we require the same properties for the whole sequences $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ and $\left( \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } \right)$ 

Lemma 5.19 (symmetrization) Let $\tilde { \xi }$ be a symmetrization of a random variable $\xi$ with median m. Then for any $r > 0$ , 

$$
\frac {1}{2} P \left\{| \xi - m | > r \right\} \leq P \left\{| \tilde {\xi} | > r \right\} \leq 2 P \left\{| \xi | > r / 2 \right\}.
$$

Proof: Let $\tilde { \xi } = \xi - \xi ^ { \prime }$ as above, and write 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left\{\xi - m > r, \xi^ {\prime} \leq m \right\} \cup \left\{\xi - m <   - r, \xi^ {\prime} \geq m \right\}} \\ & {\qquad \subset \left\{| \tilde {\xi} | > r \right\}} \\ & {\qquad \subset \left\{| \xi | > r / 2 \right\} \cup \left\{| \xi^ {\prime} | > r / 2 \right\}.} \end{array}
$$

We also need a simple centering lemma. 

Lemma 5.20 (centering) For any random variables $\xi , \eta , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . and constants $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ , we have 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{c} \xi_ {n} \xrightarrow {d} \xi \\ \xi_ {n} + c _ {n} \xrightarrow {d} \eta \end{array} \right\}   \Rightarrow   c _ {n} \to   s o m e    c.
$$

Proof: Let $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ . If $c _ { n } \to \pm \infty$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N } .$ , then clearly $\xi _ { n } + c _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \pm \infty$ along $N ^ { \prime }$ , which contradicts the tightness of $\xi _ { n } + c _ { n }$ . Thus, the $c _ { n }$ are bounded. Now assume that $c _ { n } \to a$ and $c _ { n } \to b$ along two sub-sequences $N _ { 1 } , N _ { 2 } \subset \mathsf { N }$ . Then $\xi _ { n } + c _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi + a$ along $N _ { 1 }$ , while $\xi _ { n } + c _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi + b$ along $N _ { 2 }$ and so $\xi + a \overset { d } { = } \xi + b$ . Iterating this yields $\xi + n ( b - a ) \overset { d } { = } \xi$ for every $n \in { \mathord { \mathbb { Z } } }$ which is only possible when $a = b$ . Thus, all limit points of $\left( c _ { n } \right)$ agree, and $c _ { n }$ converges. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 5.18: Assume $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ , and define $\xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } = \xi _ { n } 1 \{ | \xi _ { n } | \le 1 \}$ By (iii) and Lemma 5.16 the series $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } ( \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } - E \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } ) } \end{array}$ converges a.s., and so by (ii) the same thing is true for $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ . Finally, $P \{ \xi _ { n } \neq \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } \ \mathrm { i . o . } \} = 0$ by (i) and the Borel–Cantelli lemma, and so $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } ( \xi _ { n } - \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } ) } \end{array}$ has a.s. finitely many non-zero terms. Hence, even $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n }$ converges a.s. 

Conversely, suppose that $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n }$ converges in distribution. By Lemma 5.19 the sequence of symmetrized partial sums $\textstyle \sum _ { k \leq n } \tilde { \xi } _ { k }$ is tight, and so $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \tilde { \xi } _ { n }$ converges a.s. by Theorem 5.17. In particular, $\tilde { \xi } _ { n } \  \ 0$ a.s. For any $\varepsilon \_ \mathrm { ~ } >$ 0 we obtain $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } P \{ | \tilde { \xi } _ { n } | > \varepsilon \} < \infty } \end{array}$ by the Borel–Cantelli lemma. Hence, $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } P \{ | \xi _ { n } - m _ { n } | > \varepsilon \} < \infty } \end{array}$ by Lemma 5.19, where $m _ { 1 } , m _ { 2 } , . . . ,$ . are medians of $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ Using the Borel–Cantelli lemma again, we get $\xi _ { n } - m _ { n } \to 0$ a.s. 

Now let $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be arbitrary with $m _ { n } - c _ { n } \to 0$ . Then even $\xi _ { n } - c _ { n } \to 0$ a.s. Putting $\eta _ { n } = \xi _ { n } 1 \{ | \xi _ { n } - c _ { n } | \le 1 \}$ , we get a.s. $\xi _ { n } = \eta _ { n }$ for all but finitely many n, and similarly for the symmetrized variables $\tilde { \xi } _ { n }$ and $\tilde { \eta } _ { n }$ . Thus, even $\textstyle \sum _ { n } { \tilde { \eta } } _ { n }$ converges a.s. Since the $\tilde { \eta } _ { n }$ are bounded and symmetric, Theorem 5.17 yields $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \mathrm { V a r } ( \eta _ { n } ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sum _ { n } \mathrm { V a r } ( \tilde { \eta } _ { n } ) < \infty } \end{array}$ . Thus, $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \left( \eta _ { n } - E \eta _ { n } \right) } \end{array}$ converges a.s. by Lemma 5.16, as does the series $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \left( \xi _ { n } - E \eta _ { n } \right) } \end{array}$ . Comparing with the distributional convergence of $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \xi _ { n }$ , we conclude from Lemma 5.20 that $\Sigma _ { n } E \eta _ { n }$ converges. In particular, $E \eta _ { n } \to 0$ and $\eta _ { n } - E \eta _ { n } \to 0$ a.s., and so $\eta _ { n }  0 ~ \mathrm { a . s . }$ whence $\xi _ { n }  0 ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . Then $m _ { n }  0$ , and so we may take $c _ { n } = 0$ in the previous argument, and $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ follow. ✷ 

A sequence of random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . with partial sums $S _ { n }$ is said to obey the strong law of large numbers, if $S _ { n } / n$ converges a.s. to a constant. The weak law is the corresponding property with convergence in probability. The following elementary proposition enables us to convert convergence results for random series into laws of large numbers. 

Lemma 5.21 (series and averages, Kronecker) For any $a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , \dotsc \in { \textsf { R } }$ and $c > 0$ , 

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 1} n ^ {- c} a _ {n} \text { converges } \Rightarrow n ^ {- c} \sum_ {k \leq n} a _ {k} \to 0
$$

Proof: Let $\textstyle \sum _ { n } b _ { n } \ = \ b$ with $b _ { n } = n ^ { - c } a _ { n }$ . By dominated convergence as $n  \infty ,$ 

$$
\sum_ {k \leq n} b _ {k} - n ^ {- c} \sum_ {k \leq n} a _ {k} = \sum_ {k \leq n} \left\{1 - (k / n) ^ {c} \right\} b _ {k}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = c \sum_ {k \leq n} b _ {k} \int_ {k / n} ^ {1} x ^ {c - 1} d x \\ = c \int_ {0} ^ {1} x ^ {c - 1} d x \sum_ {k \leq n x} b _ {k} \\ \to b   c \int_ {0} ^ {1} x ^ {c - 1} d x = b, \end{array}
$$

and the assertion follows since the first term on the left tends to $b .$ □ 

The following simple result illustrates the method. 

Corollary 5.22 (variance criterion for averages, Kolmogorov) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be independent random variables with mean 0, and fix any $c > 0$ . Then 

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 1} n ^ {- 2 c} \operatorname{Var} (\xi_ {n}) <   \infty \quad \Rightarrow \quad n ^ {- c} \sum_ {k \leq n} \xi_ {k} \to 0 a. s.
$$

Proof: Since $\textstyle \sum _ { n } n ^ { - c } \xi _ { n }$ converges a.s. by Lemma 5.16, the assertion follows by Lemma 5.21. ✷ 

In particular, we see that if $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . are i.i.d. with $E \xi = 0$ and $E \xi ^ { 2 } < \infty ,$ then $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - c } \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } \to 0 } \end{array}$ a.s. for any $c > { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } .$ . The statement fails for $\begin{array} { r } { c = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \end{array}$ , as we see by taking $\xi$ to be $N ( 0 , 1 )$ . The best possible normalization will be given in Corollary 22.8. The next result characterizes the stated convergence for arbitrary $\begin{array} { r } { c > { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \end{array}$ . For $c = 1$ we recognize the strong law of large numbers. Corresponding criteria for the weak law are given in Theorem 6.17. 

Theorem 5.23 (strong laws of large numbers, Kolmogorov, Marcinkiewicz & Zygmund) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be i.i.d. random variables, put $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { k \le n } \xi _ { k } } \end{array}$ , and fix a $p \in ( 0 , 2 )$ . Then n− $^ { - 1 / p } S _ { n }$ converges a.s. if these conditions hold, depending on the value of $p .$ t 

$f o r p \in ( 0 , 1 ] \colon \xi \in L ^ { p } ,$ 

for $p \in ( 1 , 2 ) \colon \ \xi \in L ^ { p }$ and $E \xi = 0$ 

In that case, the limit equals E ξ when $p = 1$ and is otherwise equal to 0. 

Proof: Assume $E | \xi | ^ { p } < \infty$ and also, for $p \geq 1$ , that $E \xi = 0$ . Define $\xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } = \xi _ { n } \mathrm { i } \{ | \xi _ { n } | \leq n ^ { 1 / p } \}$ , and note that by Lemma 4.4 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {n} P \Bigl \{\xi_ {n} ^ {\prime} \neq \xi_ {n} \Bigr \} = \sum_ {n} P \Bigl \{| \xi | ^ {p} > n \Bigr \} \\ \qquad \leq \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Bigl \{| \xi | ^ {p} > t \Bigr \} d t \\ \qquad = E | \xi | ^ {p} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

Hence, the Borel–Cantelli lemma yields $P \{ \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } \neq \xi _ { n } \ \mathrm { i . o . } \} = 0$ , and so $\xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } = \xi _ { n }$ for all but finitely many $n ~ \in ~ \mathsf { N }$ a.s. It is then equivalent to show that $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 / p } \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } ^ { \prime } \to ~ 0 } \end{array}$ a.s. By Lemma 5.21 it sufices to prove instead that $\textstyle \sum _ { n } n ^ { - 1 / p } \bar { \xi } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ converges a.s. 

For $p < 1$ , this is clear if we write 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} E \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 1 / p} | \xi_ {n} ^ {\prime} | & = \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 1 / p} E \big (| \xi |; | \xi | \leq n ^ {1 / p} \big) \\ & \lesssim \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} t ^ {- 1 / p} E \big (| \xi |; | \xi | \leq t ^ {1 / p} \big) d t \\ & = E \big (| \xi | \int_ {| \xi | ^ {p}} ^ {\infty} t ^ {- 1 / p} d t \big) \\ & \lesssim E | \xi | ^ {p} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

If instead $p > 1$ , then by Theorem 5.18 it sufices to prove that $\textstyle \sum _ { n } n ^ { - 1 / p } E \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ converges and $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } n ^ { - 2 / p } \operatorname { V a r } ( \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } ) < \infty } \end{array}$ . Since $E \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } = - E ( \xi ; | \xi | > n ^ { 1 / \bar { p } } )$ , we have for the former series 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 1 / p} | E   \xi_ {n} ^ {\prime} | & \leq & \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 1 / p} E \Big (| \xi |;   | \xi | > n ^ {1 / p} \Big) \\ & \leq & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} t ^ {- 1 / p} E \Big (| \xi |;   | \xi | > t ^ {1 / p} \Big)   d t \\ & = & E \Big (| \xi | \int_ {0} ^ {| \xi | ^ {p}} t ^ {- 1 / p}   d t \Big) \\ & \lesssim & E   | \xi | ^ {p} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

For the latter series, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 2 / p} \operatorname{Var} (\xi_ {n} ^ {\prime}) & \leq \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 2 / p} E (\xi_ {n} ^ {\prime}) ^ {2} \\ & = \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 2 / p} E \Big (\xi^ {2}; | \xi | \leq n ^ {1 / p} \Big) \\ & \lesssim \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} t ^ {- 2 / p} E \Big (\xi^ {2}; | \xi | \leq t ^ {1 / p} \Big) d t \\ & = E \Big (\xi^ {2} \int_ {| \xi | ^ {p}} ^ {\infty} t ^ {- 2 / p} d t \Big) \\ & \lesssim E | \xi | ^ {p} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

When $p = 1$ , we have $E \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } = E ( \xi ; | \xi | \leq n ) \to 0$ by dominated convergence. Thus, $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { k < n } E \xi _ { k } ^ { \prime } \to 0 } \end{array}$ , and we may prove instead that $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } ^ { \prime \prime } \to 0 } \end{array}$ a.s., where $\xi _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime } \overset { - } { = } \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } - E \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ . By Lemma 5.21 and Theorem 5.18 it is then enough to show that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } n ^ { - 2 } \operatorname { V a r } ( \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } ) < \infty } \end{array}$ , which may be seen as before. 

Conversely, suppose that $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 / p } S _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 / p } \sum _ { k \le n } \xi _ { k } } \end{array}$ converges a.s. Then 

$$
\frac {\xi_ {n}}{n ^ {1 / p}} = \frac {S _ {n}}{n ^ {1 / p}} - \left(\frac {n - 1}{n}\right) ^ {1 / p} \frac {S _ {n - 1}}{(n - 1) ^ {1 / p}} \to 0 \text {a.s.},
$$

and in particular $P \Big \{ | \xi _ { n } | ^ { p } > n \mathrm { i . o . } \Big \} = 0$ . Hence, by Lemma 4.4 and the Borel– Cantelli lemma, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E | \xi | ^ {p} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Big \{| \xi | ^ {p} > t \Big \} d t \\ \qquad \leq 1 + \sum_ {n \geq 1} P \Big \{| \xi | ^ {p} > n \Big \} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

For $p > 1$ , the direct assertion yields $n ^ { - 1 / p } ( S _ { n } - n E \xi ) \to 0$ a.s., and so $n ^ { 1 - 1 / p } E \xi$ converges, which implies $E \xi = 0$ ✷ 

For a simple application of the law of large numbers, consider an arbitrary sequence of random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ , and define the associated empirical distributions as the random probability measures $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { \mu } _ { n } \ = \ n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { k \le n } \delta _ { \xi _ { k } } } \end{array}$ . The corresponding empirical distribution functions $\hat { F } _ { n }$ are given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {F} _ {n} (x) = \hat {\mu} _ {n} (- \infty , x ] \\ \qquad = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k \leq n} 1 \{\xi_ {k} \leq x \}, \quad x \in \mathsf {R}, n \in \mathsf {N}. \end{array}
$$

Proposition 5.24 (empirical distribution functions, Glivenko, Cantelli) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables with distribution function F and empirical distribution functions $\hat { F } _ { 1 } , \hat { F } _ { 2 } , \dots .$ . Then 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \sup _ {x} \left| \hat {F} _ {n} (x) - F (x) \right| = 0 a. s.\tag{5}
$$

Proof: The law of large numbers yields ${ \hat { F } } _ { n } ( x )  F ( x )$ a.s. for every $x \in \mathsf { R }$ Now fix any finite partition $- \infty = x _ { 1 } < x _ { 2 } < \cdots < x _ { m } = \infty$ . By the monotonicity of $F$ and $\hat { F } _ { n }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sup _ {x} \left| \hat {F} _ {n} (x) - F (x) \right| \leq \max _ {k} \left| \hat {F} _ {n} (x _ {k}) - F (x _ {k}) \right| \\ + \max _ {k} \left| F (x _ {k + 1}) - F (x _ {k}) \right|. \end{array}
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ and refining the partition indefinitely, we get in the limit 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} \sup _ {x} \left| \hat {F} _ {n} (x) - F (x) \right| \leq \sup _ {x} \Delta F (x) \text { a.s., }
$$

which proves (5) when F is continuous. 

For general $F _ { ; }$ , let $\vartheta _ { 1 } , \vartheta _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be $\mathrm { i . i . d . } ~ U ( 0 , 1 )$ , and define $\eta _ { n } ~ = ~ g ( \vartheta _ { n } )$ for each $n .$ , where $g ( t ) = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ x ; F ( x ) < t \}$ . Then $\eta _ { n } \leq x { \mathrm { ~ i f f ~ } } \vartheta _ { n } \leq F ( x )$ , and so $( \eta _ { n } ) \ { \stackrel { d } { = } } \ ( \xi _ { n } )$ . We may then assume that $\xi _ { n } \equiv \eta _ { n }$ . Writing $\hat { G } _ { 1 } , \hat { G } _ { 2 } , \dots .$ . for the empirical distribution functions of $\vartheta _ { 1 } , \vartheta _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ we see that also ${ \hat { F } } _ { n } = { \hat { G } } _ { n } \circ F$ Writing $A = F ( { \mathsf { R } } )$ and using the result for continuous $F _ { ; }$ , we get a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sup _ {x} \left| \hat {F} _ {n} (x) - F (x) \right| = \sup _ {t \in A} \left| \hat {G} _ {n} (t) - t \right| \\ \leq \sup _ {t \in [ 0, 1 ]} \left| \hat {G} _ {n} (t) - t \right| \to 0. \end{array}
$$

We turn to a more systematic study of convergence in distribution. Though for the moment we are mostly interested in distributions on Euclidean spaces, it is crucial for future applications to consider the more general setting of an abstract metric space. In particular, the theory is applied in Chapter 23 to random elements in various function spaces. For a random elements $\xi$ in a metric space $S$ with Borel σ-field $S _ { ; }$ , let $S _ { \xi }$ denote the class of sets $B \in S$ with $\xi \notin \partial B$ a.s., called the $\xi - c o n t i n u i t y$ sets. 

Theorem 5.25 (portmanteau<sup>2</sup> theorem, Alexandrov) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be random elements in a metric space $( S , S )$ with classes $\mathcal { G } , \mathcal { F }$ of open and closed sets. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi ,$ 

(ii) $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \operatorname* { i n f } P \{ \xi _ { n } \in G \} \geq P \{ \xi \in G \} , \quad G \in \mathcal { G } ,$ 

(iii) lim sup $P \{ \xi _ { n } \in F \} \leq P \{ \xi \in F \} , \quad F \in \mathcal { F } ,$ n→∞ 

(iv) $P \{ \xi _ { n } \in B \}  P \{ \xi \in B \} , \quad B \in \mathcal { S } _ { \xi } .$ 

Proof: Assume (i), and fix any $G \in \mathcal G$ . Letting $f$ be continuous with $0 \leq f \leq 1 _ { G }$ , we get $E f ( \xi _ { n } ) \leq P \{ \xi _ { n } \in G \}$ , and (ii) follows as we let $n  \infty$ and then $f \uparrow 1 _ { G }$ . The equivalence $( \mathrm { i i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ is clear from taking complements. Now assume $( \mathrm { i i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ . For any $B \in S$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} P \{\xi \in B ^ {o} \} & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} P \{\xi_ {n} \in B \} \\ & \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \{\xi_ {n} \in B \} \\ & \leq P \{\xi \in \bar {B} \}. \end{array}
$$

Here the extreme members agree when $\xi \not \in \partial B { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , and (iv) follows. 

Conversely, assume (iv), and fix any $F \in { \mathcal { F } }$ . Write $F ^ { \varepsilon } = \{ s \in S ; \rho ( s , F ) \leq$ $\varepsilon \}$ . Then the sets $\partial F ^ { \varepsilon } \subset \{ s ; \rho ( s , F ) = \varepsilon \}$ are disjoint, and so $\xi \notin \partial F ^ { \varepsilon }$ for almost every $\varepsilon > 0$ . For such an $\varepsilon _ { i }$ , we may write $P \{ \xi _ { n } \in F \} \leq P \{ \xi _ { n } \in F ^ { \varepsilon } \}$ and (iii) follows as we let $n \to \infty$ and then $\varepsilon \to 0$ . Finally, assume (ii), and let $f \geq 0$ be continuous. By Lemma 4.4 and Fatou’s lemma, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E f (\xi) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Big \{f (\xi) > t \Big \} d t \\ \leq \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} P \Big \{f (\xi_ {n}) > t \Big \} d t \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Big \{f (\xi_ {n}) > t \Big \} d t \\ = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E f (\xi_ {n}). \end{array}\tag{6}
$$

Now let f be continuous with $| f | \le c < \infty$ . Applying (6) to the functions $c \pm f$ yields $E f ( \xi _ { n } ) \to E f ( \xi )$ , which proves (i). ✷ 

We insert an easy application to subspaces, needed in Chapter 23. 

Corollary 5.26 (sub-spaces) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be random elements in a subspace A of a metric space $( S , \rho )$ . Then 

$$
\xi_ {n} \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} \xi i n (A, \rho) \Leftrightarrow \xi_ {n} \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} \xi i n (S, \rho)
$$

Proof: Since $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots \in A$ , condition (ii) of Theorem 5.25 is equivalent to 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} P \Big \{\xi_ {n} \in A \cap G \Big \} \geq P \Big \{\xi \in A \cap G \Big \}, \quad G \subset S \text { open. }
$$

By Lemma 1.6, this agrees with condition (ii) of Theorem 5.25 for the subspace $A .$ ✷ 

Directly from the definitions, it is clear that convergence in distribution is preserved by continuous mappings. The following more general statement is a key result of weak convergence theory. 

Theorem 5.27 (continuous mapping, Mann & Wald, Prohorov, Rubin) For any metric spaces $S , T$ and set $C \in S$ , consider some measurable functions $f , f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots \ldots S  T$ satisfying 

$$
s _ {n} \to s \in C \quad \Rightarrow \quad f _ {n} (s _ {n}) \to f (s).
$$

Then for any random elements $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots i n \ S$ 

$$
\xi_ {n} \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} \xi \in C a. s. \quad \Rightarrow \quad f _ {n} (\xi_ {n}) \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} f (\xi).
$$

In particular, we see that if $f \colon S  T$ is a.s. continuous at $\xi ,$ then 

$$
\xi_ {n} \stackrel {d} {\to} \xi \quad \Rightarrow \quad f (\xi_ {n}) \stackrel {d} {\to} f (\xi).
$$

Proof: Fix any open set $G \subset T$ , and let $s \in f ^ { - 1 } G \cap C$ . By hypothesis there exist an integer $m \in \mathsf N$ and a neighborhood B of $s ,$ such that $f _ { k } ( s ^ { \prime } ) \in G$ for all $k \geq m$ and $s ^ { \prime } \in B$ . Thus, $B \subset \cap _ { k \geq m } f _ { k } ^ { - 1 } G$ , and so 

$$
f ^ {- 1} G \cap C \subset \bigcup_ {m} \left(\bigcap_ {k \geq m} f _ {k} ^ {- 1} G\right) ^ {o}.
$$

Writing $\mu , \mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . for the distributions of $\xi , \xi _ { 2 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ , we get by Theorem 5.25 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu (f ^ {- 1} G) \leq \mu \bigcup_ {m} \Big (\bigcap_ {k \geq m} f _ {k} ^ {- 1} G \Big) ^ {o} \\ = \sup _ {m} \mu \Big (\bigcap_ {k \geq m} f _ {k} ^ {- 1} G \Big) ^ {o} \\ \leq \sup _ {m} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} \Big (\bigcap_ {k \geq m} f _ {k} ^ {- 1} G \Big) ^ {o} \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} (f _ {n} ^ {- 1} G). \end{array}
$$

Then the same theorem yields $\mu _ { n } \circ f _ { n } ^ { - 1 } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu \circ f ^ { - 1 }$ , which means that $f _ { n } ( \xi _ { n } ) \xrightarrow [ \square ] { d }$ $f ( \xi )$ 

For a simple consequence, we note a useful randomization principle: 

Corollary 5.28 (randomization) For any metric spaces $S , T$ , consider some probability kernels $\mu , \mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , . . . . \nonumber$ satisfying 

$$
s _ {n} \rightarrow s i n S \Rightarrow \mu_ {n} (s _ {n}, \cdot) \stackrel {w} {\rightarrow} \mu (s, \cdot) i n \mathcal {M} _ {T}.
$$

Then for any random elements $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots i n \ S$ , 

$$
\xi_ {n} \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} \xi \quad \Rightarrow \quad E   \mu_ {n} (\xi_ {n}, \cdot) \stackrel {{w}} {{\to}} E   \mu (\xi , \cdot) i n \mathcal {M} _ {T}.
$$

Proof: For any bounded, continuous function $f$ on $T ,$ the integrals $\mu f$ and $\mu _ { n } f$ are bounded, measurable functions on $S _ { ; }$ , such that $s _ { n } \to s$ implies $\mu _ { n } f ( s _ { n } ) \to \mu f ( s )$ . Hence, Theorem 5.27 yields $\mu _ { n } f ( \xi _ { n } ) \ \overset { d } { \to } \ \mu f ( \xi )$ , and so $E \mu _ { n } f ( \xi _ { n } ) \to E \mu f ( \xi )$ . The assertion follows since f was arbitrary. ✷ 

We turn to an equally important approximation theorem. Here the idea is to prove $\xi _ { n } \ \overset { d } { \to } \ \xi$ by approximating $\xi _ { n } \approx \eta _ { n }$ and $\xi \approx \eta$ , where $\eta _ { n } \stackrel { d } {  } \eta$ . The required convergence will then follow, provided the former approximations hold uniformly in n. 

Theorem 5.29 (approximation) Let $\xi , \xi _ { n }$ and $\eta ^ { k } , \eta _ { n } ^ { k }$ be random elements in a separable metric space $( S , \rho )$ . Then $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ , whenever 

(i) $\eta ^ { k } \stackrel { d } { \to } \xi .$ 

(ii) $\eta _ { n } ^ { k } \xrightarrow [ ] { d } \eta ^ { k }$ as $n \to \infty$ , $k \in { \mathsf N }$ 

(iii) lim lim sup $E \Big \{ \rho ( \eta _ { n } ^ { k } , \xi _ { n } ) \wedge 1 \Big \} = 0$ k n 

Proof: For any closed set $F \subset S$ and constant $\varepsilon > 0$ , we have 

$$
P \{\xi_ {n} \in F \} \leq P \left\{\eta_ {n} ^ {k} \in F ^ {\varepsilon} \right\} + P \left\{\rho \left(\eta_ {n} ^ {k}, \xi_ {n}\right) > \varepsilon \right\},
$$

where $F ^ { \varepsilon } = \{ s \in S ; \rho ( s , F ) \leq \varepsilon \}$ . By Theorem 5.25, we get as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \{\xi_ {n} \in F \} \leq P \{\eta^ {k} \in F ^ {\varepsilon} \} + \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \Big \{\rho (\eta_ {n} ^ {k}, \xi_ {n}) > \varepsilon \Big \}.
$$

Letting $k  \infty$ , we conclude from Theorem 5.25 and (iii) that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \{\xi_ {n} \in F \} \leq P \{\xi \in F ^ {\varepsilon} \}.
$$

Here the right-hand side tends to $P \{ \xi \in F \} \ { \mathrm { a s } } \ \varepsilon  0$ . Since $F$ was arbitrary, Theorem 5.25 yields $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ ✷ 

We may now consider convergence in distribution of random sequences. 

Theorem 5.30 (random sequences) Let $\xi = ( \xi ^ { 1 } , \xi ^ { 2 } , \dots )$ and $\xi _ { n } ~ = ~ ( \xi _ { n } ^ { 1 } , \xi _ { n } ^ { 2 } .$ $\dots { } ) , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , be random elements in $S _ { 1 } \times S _ { 2 } \times \cdots$ , for some separable metric spaces $S _ { 1 } , S _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ . Then $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi \overset { . } { i } f f$ for any functions $f _ { k } \in \hat { C } _ { S _ { k } }$ , 

$$
E \left\{f _ {1} \left(\xi_ {n} ^ {1}\right) \dots f _ {m} \left(\xi_ {n} ^ {m}\right)\right\}\rightarrow E \left\{f _ {1} \left(\xi^ {1}\right) \dots f _ {m} \left(\xi^ {m}\right)\right\}, \quad m \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{7}
$$

In particular, $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ follows from the finite-dimensional convergence 

$$
\left(\xi_ {n} ^ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n} ^ {m}\right) \xrightarrow {d} \left(\xi^ {1}, \dots , \xi^ {m}\right), \quad m \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{8}
$$

If the sequences $\xi$ and $\xi _ { n }$ have independent components, it sufices that $\xi _ { n } ^ { k } \overset { d } { \to } \xi ^ { k }$ for each $k .$ 

Proof: The necessity is clear from the continuity of the projections $s \mapsto s _ { k }$ To prove the suficiency, we first assume that (7) holds for a fixed m. Writing ${ \cal S } _ { k } ^ { \prime } = \{ B \in { \mathcal { B } } _ { S _ { k } } ; \xi ^ { k } \notin \partial B \mathrm { ~ a . s . } \}$ and applying Theorem 5.25 m times, we obtain 

$$
P \Bigl \{(\xi_ {n} ^ {1}, \ldots , \xi_ {n} ^ {m}) \in B \Bigr \} \to P \Bigl \{(\xi^ {1}, \ldots , \xi^ {m}) \in B \Bigr \},\tag{9}
$$

for any set $B = B ^ { 1 } \times \cdot \cdot \cdot \times B ^ { m }$ with $B ^ { k } \in S _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ for all k. Since the $S _ { k }$ are separable, we may choose some countable bases $\mathcal { C } _ { k } \subset S _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ , so that $\mathcal { C } _ { 1 } \times \cdots \times \mathcal { C } _ { m }$ becomes a countable base in $S _ { 1 } \times \cdots \times S _ { m }$ . Hence, any open set $G \subset S _ { 1 } \times \cdots \times S _ { m }$ is a countable union of measurable rectangles $B _ { j } = B _ { j } ^ { 1 } \times \cdot \cdot \cdot \times B _ { j } ^ { m }$ with $B _ { j } ^ { k } \in S _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ for all k. Since the $ { \boldsymbol { S } } _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ are fields, we may easily reduce to the case of disjoint sets $B _ { j }$ . By Fatou’s lemma and (9), 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} P \Big \{(\xi_ {n} ^ {1}, \ldots , \xi_ {n} ^ {m}) \in G \Big \} & = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {j} P \Big \{(\xi_ {n} ^ {1}, \ldots , \xi_ {n} ^ {m}) \in B _ {j} \Big \} \\ & \geq \sum_ {j} P \Big \{(\xi^ {1}, \ldots , \xi^ {m}) \in B _ {j} \Big \} \\ & = P \Big \{(\xi^ {1}, \ldots , \xi^ {m}) \in G \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

and so (8) holds by Theorem 5.25. 

To see that (8) implies $\xi _ { n } \ \overset { d } { \to } \ \xi .$ , fix any $a _ { k } \in S _ { k } , k \in \mathsf { N }$ , and note that the mapping $( s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { m } ) \mapsto ( s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { m } , a _ { m + 1 } , a _ { m + 2 } , \ldots )$ is continuous on $S _ { 1 } \times$ $\cdots \times S _ { m }$ for each $m \in \mathbb { N }$ . By (8) it follows that 

$$
\left(\xi_ {n} ^ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n} ^ {m}, a _ {m + 1}, \dots\right) \xrightarrow {d} \left(\xi^ {1}, \dots , \xi^ {m}, a _ {m + 1}, \dots\right), \quad m \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{10}
$$

Writing $\eta _ { n } ^ { m }$ and $\eta ^ { m }$ for the sequences in (10) and letting ρ be the metric in (1), we also note that $\rho ( \xi , \eta ^ { m } ) \le 2 ^ { - m }$ and $\rho ( \xi _ { n } , \eta _ { n } ^ { m } ) \leq 2 ^ { - m }$ for all m and n. The convergence $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ now follows by Theorem 5.29. ✷ 

For distributional convergence of some random objects $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ the joint distribution of the elements $\xi _ { n }$ is clearly irrelevant. This suggests that we look for a more useful dependence, which may lead to simpler and more transparent proofs. 

Theorem 5.31 (coupling, Skorohod, Dudley) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be random elements in a separable metric space $( S , \rho )$ , such that $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ . Then there exist some random elements $\tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \xi } _ { 1 } , \tilde { \xi } _ { 2 } , \dots$ . in S with 

$$
\tilde {\xi} \stackrel {d} {=} \xi , \quad \tilde {\xi} _ {n} \stackrel {d} {=} \xi_ {n}; \qquad \tilde {\xi} _ {n} \to \tilde {\xi} a. s.
$$

Our proof involves families of independent random elements with specified distributions, whose existence is ensured in general by Corollary 8.25 below. When $S$ is complete, we may rely on the more elementary Theorem 4.19. 

Proof: First take $S = \{ 1 , \dots , m \}$ , and put $p _ { k } = P \{ \xi = k \}$ and $p _ { k } ^ { n } = { \cal P } \{ \xi _ { n } =$ $k \}$ . Letting $\vartheta \bot \bot \xi$ be $U ( 0 , 1 )$ , we may construct some random elements $\tilde { \xi } _ { n } \overset { d } { = } \xi _ { n } .$ 

such that $\tilde { \xi } _ { n } = k$ whenever $\xi = k$ and $\vartheta \leq p _ { k } ^ { n } / p _ { k }$ . Since $p _ { k } ^ { n } \to p _ { k }$ for each $k ,$ , we get $\tilde { \xi } _ { n }  \xi ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ 

For general S, fix any $p \in \mathsf { N }$ , and choose a partition of S into sets $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } , \ldots$ $\in { \cal S } _ { \xi }$ of diameter $< 2 ^ { - p }$ . Next choose m so large that $P \{ \xi \notin \cup _ { k \le m } B _ { k } \} < 2 ^ { - p } .$ and put $B _ { 0 } = \textstyle \bigcap _ { k \leq m } B _ { k } ^ { c }$ . For $k = 0 , \ldots , m$ , define $\kappa = k$ <sub>when</sub> $\xi \in B _ { k }$ and $\kappa _ { n } = k$ when $\xi _ { n } \in B _ { k } , \ n \in \mathbb { N }$ . Then $\kappa _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \kappa .$ , and the result for finite $S$ yields some $\tilde { \kappa } _ { n } \stackrel { d } { = } \kappa _ { n }$ with $\tilde { \kappa } _ { n }  \kappa \mathrm { a . s }$ . We further introduce some independent random elements $\zeta _ { n } ^ { k }$ in $S$ with distributions $\mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { n } | \xi _ { n } \in B _ { k } )$ , and define $\tilde { \xi } _ { n } ^ { p } =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { k } \zeta _ { n } ^ { k } 1 \{ { \tilde { \kappa } } _ { n } = k \} } \end{array}$ , so that $\tilde { \xi } _ { n } ^ { p } \overset { d } { = } \xi _ { n }$ for each $n .$ 

By construction, we have 

$$
\left\{\rho \left(\tilde {\xi} _ {n} ^ {p}, \xi\right) > 2 ^ {- p} \right\} \subset \left\{\tilde {\kappa} _ {n} \neq \kappa \right\} \cup \left\{\xi \in B _ {0} \right\}, \quad n, p \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Since $\tilde { \kappa } _ { n }  \kappa \mathrm { ~ a . s ~ }$ . and $P \{ \xi \in B _ { 0 } \} < 2 ^ { - p }$ , there exists for every p some $n _ { p } \in \mathsf { N }$ with 

$$
P \bigcup_ {n \geq n _ {p}} \left\{\rho (\tilde {\xi} _ {n} ^ {p}, \xi) > 2 ^ {- p} \right\} <   2 ^ {- p}, \quad p \in \mathsf {N},
$$

and we may further assume that $n _ { 1 } < n _ { 2 } < \cdots$ . Then the Borel–Cantelli lemma yields a.s. $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n \geq n _ { p } } \rho ( \tilde { \xi } _ { n } ^ { p } , \xi ) \leq 2 ^ { - p } } \end{array}$ for all but finitely many $p .$ . Defining $\eta _ { n } = \tilde { \xi } _ { n } ^ { p }$ for $n _ { p } \leq n < n _ { p + 1 }$ , we note that $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { = } \eta _ { n }  \xi \mathrm { a . s . }$ ✷ 

We conclude with a result on the functional representation of limits, needed in Chapters 18 and 32. To motivate the problem, recall from Lemma 5.6 that, if $\xi _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \eta$ for some random elements in a complete metric space $S _ { i }$ then $\eta = f ( \xi )$ a.s. for some measurable function $f : S ^ { \infty } \to S$ , where $\xi ~ = ~ ( \xi _ { n } )$ . Since f depends on the distribution $\mu$ of $\xi ,$ a universal representation would be of the form $\eta = f ( \xi , \mu )$ . For certain purposes, we need to choose a measurable version of the latter function. To allow constructions by repeated approximation in probability, we consider the more general case where $\eta _ { n } \overset { P } {  } \eta$ for some random elements $\eta _ { n } = f _ { n } ( \xi , \mu )$ 

For a precise statement, let $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ be the space of probability measures $\mu$ on S, endowed with the σ-field induced by the evaluation maps $\mu \mapsto \mu B , B \in \mathcal { B } _ { S }$ 

Proposition 5.32 (representation oflimits) Consider a complete metric space $( S , \rho )$ , a measurable space $U ,$ , and some measurable functions $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots \colon U \times$ $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { U } ~ \to ~ S$ Then there exist a measurable set $A \subset \hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { U }$ and a function $f \colon U \times A \to S$ such that, for any random element $\xi$ in U with ${ \mathcal { L } } ( \xi ) = \mu$ 

$$
f _ {n} (\xi , \mu) \xrightarrow {P} \text { some } \eta \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \mu \in A,
$$

in which case we can choose $\eta = f ( \xi , \mu )$ 

Proof: For sequences $\boldsymbol { s } ~ = ~ ( s _ { 1 } , s _ { 2 } , \ldots )$ in $S _ { i }$ , define $l ( s ) \ : = \ : \operatorname* { l i m } _ { k } s _ { k }$ when the limit exists and put $l ( s ) = s _ { \infty }$ otherwise, where $s _ { \infty } \in \ S$ is arbitrary. By Lemma 1.11, l is a measurable mapping from $S ^ { \infty }$ to $S .$ . Next consider a sequence $\eta = ( \eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , . . . )$ of random elements in $S ,$ and put $\nu = \mathcal { L } ( \eta )$ . Define $n _ { 1 } , n _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . as in the proof of Lemma 5.6, and note that each $n _ { k } = n _ { k } ( \nu )$ is a measurable function of $\nu .$ Let $C$ be the set of measures ν with $n _ { k } ( \nu ) < \infty$ for all $k ,$ and note that $\eta _ { n }$ converges in probability if $\nu \in C$ . Introduce the measurable function 

$$
g (s, \nu) = l \left\{s _ {n _ {1} (\nu)}, s _ {n _ {2} (\nu)}, \dots \right\}, \quad s = (s _ {1}, s _ {2}, \dots) \in S ^ {\infty}, \nu \in \hat {\mathcal {M}} _ {S ^ {\infty}}.
$$

If $\nu \in C$ , the proof of Lemma 5.6 shows that $\eta _ { n _ { k } ( \nu ) }$ converges a.s., and so $\eta _ { n } \stackrel { P } {  } g ( \eta , \nu )$ 

Now let $\eta _ { n } = f _ { n } ( \xi , \mu )$ for a random element $\xi$ in U with distribution $\mu$ and some measurable functions $f _ { n }$ . We need to show that ν is a measurable function of $\mu .$ . But this is clear from Lemma 3.2 (ii), applied to the kernel $\kappa ( \mu , \cdot ) = \mu$ from $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { U }$ to $U$ and the function $F = ( f _ { 1 } , { f } _ { 2 } , \ldots ) \colon U \times \hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { U }  S ^ { \infty }$ ✷ 

For a simple consequence, we consider limits in probability of measurable processes. The resulting statement will be needed in Chapter 18. 

Corollary 5.33 (measurability of limits, Stricker & Yor) Let $X ^ { 1 } , X ^ { 2 } , . . .$ . be S-valued, measurable processes on $T ,$ , for a complete metric space $S$ and a measurable space T. Then there exists a measurable set $A \subset T _ { i }$ , such that 

$$
X _ {t} ^ {n} \stackrel {P} {\to} s o m e X _ {t} \Leftrightarrow t \in A,
$$

Proof: Define $\xi _ { t } = ( X _ { t } ^ { 1 } , X _ { t } ^ { 2 } , \ldots )$ and $\mu _ { t } = \mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { t } )$ . By Proposition 5.32 there exist a measurable set $C \subset { \mathcal { P } } _ { S ^ { \infty } }$ and a measurable function $f \colon S ^ { \infty } \times C \to S$ 2 such that $X _ { t } ^ { n }$ converges in probability if $\mu _ { t } \in C$ , in which case $X _ { t } ^ { n } \overset { P } {  } f ( \xi _ { t } , \mu _ { t } )$ It remains to note that the mapping $t \mapsto \mu _ { t }$ is measurable, which is clear from Lemmas 1.4 and 1.28. □
