Chapter 6 

# Gaussian and Poisson Convergence

Characteristic functions and Laplace transforms, equi-continuity and tightness, linear projections, null arrays, Poisson convergence, positive and symmetric terms, central limit theorem, local CLT, Lindeberg condition, Gaussian convergence, weak laws of large numbers, domain of Gaussian attraction, slow variation, Helly’s selection theorem, vague and weak convergence, tightness and weak compactness, extended continuity theorem 

This is yet another key chapter, dealing with issues of fundamental importance throughout modern probability. Our main focus will be on the Poisson and Gaussian distributions, along with associated limit theorems, extending the classical central limit theorem and related Poisson approximation. 

The importance of the mentioned distributions extends far beyond the present context, as will gradually become clear throughout later chapters. Indeed, the Gaussian distributions underlie the construction of Brownian motion, arguably the most important process of the entire subject, whose study leads in turn into stochastic calculus. They also form a basis for the multiple Wiener– Itˆo integrals, of crucial importance in Malliavin calculus and other subjects. Similarly, the Poisson distributions underlie the construction of Poisson processes, which appear as limit laws for a wide variety of particle systems. 

Throughout this chapter, we will use the powerful machinery of characteristic functions and Laplace transforms, which leads to short and transparent proofs of all the main results. Methods based on such functions also extend far beyond the present context. Thus, characteristic functions are used to derive the basic time-change theorems for continuous martingales, and they underlie the use of exponential martingales, which are basic for the Girsanov theorems and related applications of stochastic calculus. Likewise, Laplace transforms play a basic role throughout random-measure theory, and underlie the notion of potentials, of utmost importance in advanced Markov-process theory. 

To begin with the basic definitions, consider a random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with distribution $\mu .$ The associated characteristic function $\hat { \mu }$ is given by 

$$
\hat {\mu} (t) = \int e ^ {i t x} \mu (d x) = E e ^ {i t \xi}, \quad t \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d},
$$

where $t x$ denotes the inner product $t _ { 1 } x _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + t _ { d } x _ { d }$ . For distributions $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ , it is often more convenient to consider the Laplace transform $\tilde { \mu }$ , given by 

$$
\tilde {\mu} (u) = \int e ^ {- u x} \mu (d x) = E e ^ {- u \xi}, \quad u \in \mathsf {R} _ {+} ^ {d}.
$$

Finally, for distributions $\mu$ on $Z _ { + }$ , it may be preferable to use the (probability) generating function $\psi$ , given by 

$$
\psi (s) = \sum_ {n \geq 0} s ^ {n} P \{\xi = n \} = E s ^ {\xi}, \quad s \in [ 0, 1 ].
$$

Formally, $\tilde { \mu } ( u ) ~ = ~ \hat { \mu } ( i u )$ and $\hat { \mu } ( t ) ~ = ~ \tilde { \mu } ( - i t )$ , and so the functions $\hat { \mu }$ and $\tilde { \mu }$ essentially agree apart from domain. Furthermore, the generating function $\psi$ is related to the Laplace transform $\tilde { \mu }$ by $\tilde { \mu } ( u ) = \psi ( e ^ { - u } )$ or $\psi ( s ) = \tilde { \mu } ( - \log { s } )$ Though the characteristic function always exists, it can’t always be extended to an analytic function on the complex plane. 

For any distribution $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , the characteristic function $\varphi = \hat { \mu }$ is clearly uniformly continuous with $| \varphi ( t ) | \leq \varphi ( 0 ) = 1$ . It is also Hermitian in the sense that $\varphi ( - t ) = \bar { \varphi } ( t )$ , where the bar denotes complex conjugation. If ξ has characteristic function $\varphi _ { ; }$ , then the linear combination $a \xi = a _ { 1 } \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + a _ { d } \xi _ { d }$ has characteristic function $t \mapsto \varphi ( t a )$ . Also note that, if $\xi$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with characteristic functions $\varphi$ and $\psi$ , then the characteristic function of the pair $( \xi , \eta )$ equals the tensor product $\varphi \otimes \psi \colon ( s , t ) \mapsto \varphi ( s ) \psi ( t )$ In particular, $\xi + \eta$ has characteristic function $\varphi \psi$ , and for the symmetrized variable $\xi - \xi ^ { \prime }$ it equals $| \varphi | ^ { 2 }$ 

Whenever applicable, the quoted statements carry over to Laplace transforms and generating functions. The latter functions have the further advantage of being positive, monotone, convex, and analytic—properties that simplify many arguments. 

We list some simple but useful estimates involving characteristic functions. The second inequality was used already in the proof of Theorem 5.17, and the remaining relations will be useful in the sequel to establish tightness. 

Lemma 6.1 (tail estimates) For probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { \ast }$ , 

(i) 

$$
\mu \bigl \{x; | x | \geq r \bigr \} \leq \frac {r}{2} \int_ {- 2 / r} ^ {2 / r} (1 - \hat {\mu} _ {t}) d t, \quad r > 0,\tag{ii}
$$

$$
\mu [ - r, r ] \leq 2 r \int_ {- 1 / r} ^ {1 / r} | \hat {\mu} _ {t} | d t, \quad r > 0.
$$

If $\mu$ is supported by $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , then also 

$$
\mu [ r, \infty) \leq 2 \left\{1 - \tilde {\mu} (r ^ {- 1}) \right\}, \quad r > 0.\tag{iii}
$$

Proof: (i) Using Fubini’s theorem and noting that sin $x \leq x / 2$ for $x \ge 2$ , we get for any $c > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {- c} ^ {c} (1 - \hat {\mu} _ {t})   d t = \int \mu (d x) \int_ {- c} ^ {c} (1 - e ^ {i t x})   d t \\ \qquad = 2 c \int \left(1 - \frac {\sin c x}{c x}\right) \mu (d x) \\ \qquad \geq c   \mu \bigl \{x; | c x | \geq 2 \bigr \}, \end{array}
$$

and it remains to take $c = 2 / r$ 

(ii) Write 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{2}   \mu [ - r, r ] \leq 2 \int \frac {1 - \cos (x / r)}{(x / r) ^ {2}} \mu (d x) \\ \quad = r \int \mu (d x) \int (1 - r | t |) _ {+} e ^ {i x t} d t \\ \quad = r \int (1 - r | t |) _ {+} \hat {\mu} _ {t}   d t \\ \quad \leq r \int_ {- 1 / r} ^ {1 / r} | \hat {\mu} _ {t} |   d t. \end{array}
$$

(iii) Noting that $\begin{array} { r } { e ^ { - x } < \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ when $x \geq 1$ , we get for any $t > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} 1 - \tilde {\mu} _ {t} = \int (1 - e ^ {- t x})   \mu (d x) \\ \geq \frac {1}{2}   \mu \bigl \{x; t x \geq 1 \bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

Recall that a family of probability measures $\mu _ { a }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is said to be tight if 

$$
\lim _ {r \to \infty} \sup _ {a} \mu_ {a} \Bigl \{x; | x | > r \Bigr \} = 0.
$$

We may characterize tightness in terms of characteristic functions. 

Lemma 6.2 (equi-continuity and tightness) For a family of probability measures $\mu _ { a }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ with characteristics functions $\hat { \mu } _ { a }$ or Laplace transforms $\tilde { \mu } _ { a }$ , we have 

(i) $\left( \mu _ { a } \right)$ is tight in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } \ \Leftrightarrow \ \left( \hat { \mu } _ { a } \right)$ is equi-continuous at $0 ,$ 

(ii) $\left( \mu _ { a } \right)$ is tight in ${ \sf R } _ { + } ^ { d } \ \Leftrightarrow \ \left( \tilde { \mu } _ { a } \right)$ is equi-continuous at 0. 

In that case, $\left( \hat { \mu } _ { a } \right) o r \left( \tilde { \mu } _ { a } \right)$ is uniformly equi-continuous on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ 

Proof: The suficiency is immediate from Lemma 6.1, applied separately in each coordinate. To prove the necessity, let $\xi _ { a }$ denote a random vector with distribution $\mu _ { a }$ , and write for any s, $t \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} | \hat {\mu} _ {a} (s) - \hat {\mu} _ {a} (t) | \leq E \Big | e ^ {i s \xi_ {a}} - e ^ {i t \xi_ {a}} \Big | \\ = E \Big | 1 - e ^ {i (t - s) \xi_ {a}} \Big | \\ \leq 2   E \Big (\big | (t - s)   \xi_ {a} \big | \wedge 1 \Big). \end{array}
$$

If $\{ \xi _ { a } \}$ is tight, then by Lemma 5.9 the right-hand side tends to 0 as $t - s  0$ 1 uniformly in $^ { a , }$ and the asserted uniform equi-continuity follows. The proof for Laplace transforms is similar. ✷ 

For any probability measures $\mu , \mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , recall that the weak convergence $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu$ is defined by $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ for any bounded, continuous function $f$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , where $\mu f$ denotes the integral $\textstyle int f d \mu$ . The usefulness of characteristic -<sub>functions is mainly due to the following basic result.</sub> 

Theorem 6.3 (characteristic functions, L´evy) Let $\mu , \mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be probability measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ with characteristic functions $\hat { \mu } , \hat { \mu } _ { 1 } , \hat { \mu } _ { 2 } , \dots .$ or Laplace transforms $\tilde { \mu } , \tilde { \mu } _ { 1 } , \tilde { \mu } _ { 2 } , \dots .$ . Then 

(i) $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu \ o n \ \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \ \Leftrightarrow \ \hat { \mu } _ { n } ( t ) \to \hat { \mu } ( t ) , \ t \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } ,$ 

(ii) $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } {  } \mu \ o n \ \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } \ \Leftrightarrow \ \tilde { \mu } _ { n } ( u )  \tilde { \mu } ( u ) , \ u \in \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } ;$ 

in which case $\hat { \mu } _ { n }  \hat { \mu } \ o r \ \tilde { \mu } _ { n }  \tilde { \mu }$ uniformly on every bounded set. 

In particular, a probability measure on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ is uniquely determined by its characteristic function or Laplace transform, respectively. For the proof of Theorem 6.3, we need some special cases of the Stone–Weierstrass approximation theorem. Here $[ 0 , \infty ]$ denotes the compactification of $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

Lemma 6.4 (uniform approximation, Weierstrass) 

(i) Any continuous function $f : { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d } \to { \mathsf { R } }$ with period $2 \pi$ in each coordinate admits a uniform approximation by linear combinations of cos kx and sin kx with $k \in Z _ { + } ^ { d }$ 

(ii) Any continuous function $g \colon [ 0 , \infty ] ^ { d } \to { \mathsf { R } } _ { + }$ admits a uniform approximation by linear combinations of functions $e ^ { - k x }$ with $k \in \mathsf { Z } _ { + } ^ { d }$ 

Proof of Theorem 6.3: We consider only (i), the proof of (ii) being similar. If $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu$ , then ${ \hat { \mu } } _ { n } ( t ) \to { \hat { \mu } } ( t )$ for every t, by the definition of weak convergence. By Lemmas 5.8 and 6.2, the latter convergence is uniform on every bounded set. 

Conversely, let ${ \hat { \mu } } _ { n } ( t ) \to { \hat { \mu } } ( t )$ for every t. By Lemma 6.1 and dominated convergence, we get for any $a \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and $r > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} \mu_ {n} \Bigl \{x; | a x | > r \Bigr \} \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\lim} \frac {r}{2} \int_ {- 2 / r} ^ {2 / r} \Bigl \{1 - \hat {\mu} _ {n} (t a) \Bigr \} d t \\ = \frac {r}{2} \int_ {- 2 / r} ^ {2 / r} \Bigl \{1 - \hat {\mu} (t a) \Bigr \} d t. \end{array}
$$

Since $\hat { \mu }$ is continuous at 0, the right-hand side tends to 0 as $r  \infty$ , which shows that the sequence $\left( \mu _ { n } \right)$ is tight. Given any $\varepsilon > 0$ , we may then choose $r > 0$ so large that $\mu _ { n } \{ | x | > r \} \leq \varepsilon$ for all n and $\mu \{ | x | > r \} \leq \varepsilon .$ 

Now fix any bounded, continuous function $f : \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \to \mathsf { R } .$ , say with $| f | \le c <$ $\infty$ . Let $f _ { r }$ denote the restriction of f to the ball $\{ | x | \leq r \}$ , and extend $f _ { r }$ to a continuous function $\tilde { f }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $| \tilde { f } | \le c$ and period 2πr in each coordinate. By Lemma 6.4 there exists a linear combination $g$ of the functions $\cos ( k x / r )$ and sin $( k x / r ) , k \in Z _ { + } ^ { d }$ , such that $| \tilde { f } - g | \leq \varepsilon$ . Writing $\| \cdot \|$ for the supremum norm, we get for any $n \in { \mathbb N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \left| \mu_ {n} f - \mu_ {n} g \right| & \leq \mu_ {n} \{| x | > r \} \| f - \tilde {f} \| + \| \tilde {f} - g \| \\ & \leq (2 c + 1) \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and similarly for $\mu .$ . Thus, 

$$
\left| \mu_ {n} f - \mu f \right| \leq \left| \mu_ {n} g - \mu g \right| + 2 (2 c + 1) \varepsilon , \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ and then $\varepsilon \to 0$ , we obtain $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ . Since $f$ was arbitrary, this proves that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } {  } \mu$ ✷ 

The next result often enables us to reduce the d -dimensional case to that of dimension 1. 

Corollary 6.5 (one-dimensional projections, Cram´er $\beta \ W o l d )$ For any random vectors $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ , we have 

(i) $\xi _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \xi \ i n \ \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \ \Leftrightarrow \ t \xi _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } t \xi , t \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

(ii) $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi \ i n \ \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } \ \Leftrightarrow \ u \xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } u \xi , u \in \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } .$ 

In particular, the distribution of a random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ is uniquely determined by those of all linear combinations $t \xi$ with $t \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ , respectively. 

Proof: If $t \xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } t \xi$ for all $t \in { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d } .$ , then $E e ^ { i t \xi n } \to E e ^ { i t \xi }$ by the definition of weak convergence, and so $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ by Theorem 6.3, proving (i). The proof of (ii) is similar. ✷ 

We now apply the continuity Theorem 6.3 to prove some classical limit theorems, beginning with the case of Poisson convergence. To motivate the introduction of the associated distribution, consider for each $n \in { \mathbb N }$ some i.i.d. random variables $\xi _ { n 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n n }$ with distribution 

$$
P \{\xi_ {n j} = 1 \} = 1 - P \{\xi_ {n j} = 0 \} = c _ {n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

and assume that n $c _ { n } \to c < \infty$ . Then the sums $S _ { n } = \xi _ { n 1 } + . . . + \xi _ { n n }$ have generating functions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \psi_ {n} (s) = \left\{1 - (1 - s)   c _ {n} \right\} ^ {n} \\ \to e ^ {- c   (1 - s)} \\ = e ^ {- c} \sum_ {n \geq 0} \frac {c ^ {n} s ^ {n}}{n !}, \quad s \in [ 0, 1 ]. \end{array}
$$

The limit $\psi ( s ) = e ^ { - c ( 1 - s ) }$ is the generating function of the Poisson distribution with parameter $c ,$ the distribution of a random variable $\eta$ with probabilities $P \{ \eta = n \} = e ^ { - c } c ^ { n } / n !$ for $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ . Note that $\eta$ has expected value ${ \boldsymbol { E } } { \boldsymbol { \eta } } =$ $\psi ^ { \prime } ( 1 ) = c .$ . Since $\psi _ { n }  \psi$ , Theorem 6.3 yields $S _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \eta .$ 

To state some more general instances of Poisson convergence, we need to introduce the notion of a null $a r r a y ^ { 1 }$ . By this we mean a triangular array of random variables or vectors $\xi _ { n j } , 1 \le j \le m _ { n } , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , that are independent for each n and satisfy

Informally, this means that $\xi _ { n j } \overset { P } {  } 0$ as $n \to \infty$ , uniformly in $j$ . When $\xi _ { n j } \ge 0$ for all n and $j ,$ , we may allow the $m _ { n }$ to be infinite. 

The ‘null’ property can be described as follows in terms of characteristic functions or Laplace transforms: 

Lemma 6.6 (null arrays) Let $\left( \xi _ { n j } \right)$ be a triangular array in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ with characteristic functions $\hat { \mu } _ { n j }$ or Laplace transforms $\widetilde { \mu } _ { n j }$ . Then 

(i) $\left( \xi _ { n j } \right)$ is null in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } \Leftrightarrow \mathsf { s u p } _ { j } | 1 - \hat { \mu } _ { n j } ( t ) |  0 , t \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ 

(ii) $( \xi _ { n j } )$ is null in $\begin{array} { r } { \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } \ \Leftrightarrow \ \operatorname* { i n f } _ { j } \tilde { \mu } _ { n j } ( u )  1 , \ u \in \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } } \end{array}$ 

Proof: Relation (1) holds if $\xi _ { n , j _ { n } } \overset { P } { \to } 0$ for all sequences $( j _ { n } )$ . By Theorem 6.3 this is equivalent to $\hat { \mu } _ { n , j _ { n } } ( t )  1$ for all t and $( j _ { n } )$ , which is in turn equivalent to the condition in (i). The proof of (ii) is similar. ✷

Theorem 6.7 (Poisson convergence) Let $( \xi _ { n j } )$ be a null array of $Z _ { + }$ -valued random variables, and let $\xi$ be a Poisson variable with mean c. Then $\textstyle \sum _ { j } \xi _ { n j }$ $\xrightarrow { d } \xi \mathrm { ~ } i f f$ 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } P \{ \xi _ { n j } > 1 \}  0 , } \end{array}$

Here (i) is equivalent to 

(i) su $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { l p } _ { j } \xi _ { n j } \vee 1 \stackrel { P } {  } 1 } \end{array}$ 4 

and when $\textstyle \sum _ { j } \xi _ { n j }$ is tight, (i) holds if every limit is Poisson. 

We need an elementary lemma. Related approximations will also be used in Chapters 7 and 30. 

Lemma 6.8 (sums and products) Consider a null array of constants $c _ { n j } \geq 0$ and fix any $c \in [ 0 , \infty ]$ . Then 

$$
\prod_ {j} (1 - c _ {n j}) \to e ^ {- c} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \sum_ {j} c _ {n j} \to c.

Proof of Theorem 6.7: Let $\psi _ { n j }$ be the generating function of $\xi _ { n j }$ . By Theorem 6.3, the convergence $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } \xi _ { n j } \overset { d } { \to } \xi } \end{array}$ is equivalent to $\prod _ { i } \psi _ { n j } ( s ) \to e ^ { - c ( 1 - s ) }$ for arbitrary $s \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , which holds by Lemmas 6.6 and 6.8 if

By an easy computation, the sum on the left equals

$$

$$
s (1 - s) \sum_ {j} P \{\xi_ {n j} > 1 \} \leq T _ {2} \leq s \sum_ {j} P \{\xi_ {n j} > 1 \}.\tag{4}

Assuming $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i } )$ , we note that (2) follows from (3) and (4). Now assume (2). Then for $s = 0$ we get $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i } P \{ \xi _ { n j } > 0 \}  c . } \end{array}$ , and so in general $T _ { 1 } \to c ( 1 - s )$ But then (2) implies $T _ { 2 }  \bar { 0 }$ , and (i) follows by (4). Finally, (ii) follows by subtraction. 

To see that $( \mathrm { i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i } ^ { \prime } )$ , we note that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Bigl \{\sup _ {j} \xi_ {n j} \leq 1 \Bigr \} = \prod_ {j} P \{\xi_ {n j} \leq 1 \} \\ = \prod_ {j} \Bigl (1 - P \{\xi_ {n j} > 1 \} \Bigr). \end{array}

To prove the last assertion, put $c _ { n j } = P \{ \xi _ { n j } > 0 \}$ , and write

\begin{array}{l} E \exp \Bigl (- \sum_ {j} \xi_ {n j} \Bigr) - P \Bigl \{\sup _ {j} \xi_ {n j} > 1 \Bigr \} \leq E \exp \Bigl \{- \sum_ {j} (\xi_ {n j} \wedge 1) \Bigr \} \\ \qquad = \prod_ {j} E \exp \Bigl \{- (\xi_ {n j} \wedge 1) \Bigr \} \\ \qquad = \prod_ {j} \Bigl \{1 - (1 - e ^ {- 1})   c _ {n j} \Bigr \} \\ \qquad \leq \prod_ {j} \exp \Bigl \{- (1 - e ^ {- 1})   c _ {n j} \Bigr \} \\ \qquad = \exp \Bigl \{- (1 - e ^ {- 1}) \sum_ {j} c _ {n j} \Bigr \}. \end{array}

If (i) holds and $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } \xi _ { n j } \overset { d } { \to } \eta } \end{array}$ , then the left-hand side tends to $E e ^ { - \eta } > 0$ , and so the sums $\begin{array} { r } { c _ { n } = \sum _ { j } \dot { c } _ { n j } } \end{array}$ are bounded. Hence, $c _ { n }$ converges along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ toward a constant c. But then $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i } )$ hold along $N ^ { \prime }$ , and the first assertion shows that $\eta$ is Poisson with mean c. ✷ 

Next we consider some i.i.d. random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . with $P \{ \xi _ { k } = \pm 1 \} =$ $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ , and write $S _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ . Then $n ^ { - 1 / 2 } S _ { n }$ has characteristic function 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \varphi_ {n} (t) & = \cos^ {n} (n ^ {- 1 / 2} t) \\ & = \left\{1 - \frac {1}{2} t ^ {2} n ^ {- 1} + O (n ^ {- 2}) \right\} ^ {n} \\ & \to e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2} = \varphi (t). \end{array}
$$

By a classical computation, the function $e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } / 2 }$ has Fourier transform 

$$
\int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} e ^ {i t x} e ^ {- x ^ {2} / 2} d x = (2 \pi) ^ {1 / 2} e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2}, \quad t \in \mathsf {R}.
$$

Hence, $\varphi$ is the characteristic function of a probability measure on R with density $( 2 \pi ) ^ { - 1 / 2 } e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } / 2 }$ . This is the standard normal or Gaussian distribution $N ( 0 , 1 )$ , and Theorem 6.3 shows that $n ^ { - 1 / 2 } S _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \zeta$ , where $\zeta \ \mathrm { i s } \ N ( 0 , 1 )$ . The notation is motivated by the facts that $E \zeta = 0$ and $\mathrm { V a r } ( \zeta ) = 1$ , where the former relation is obvious by symmetry and latter follows from Lemma 6.9 below. The general Gaussian law $N ( m , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ is defined as the distribution of the random variable $\eta = m + \sigma \zeta$ , which has clearly mean m and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ . From the form of the characteristic functions together with the uniqueness property, we see that any linear combination of independent Gaussian random variables is again Gaussian. 

More general limit theorems may be derived from the following technical result. 

Lemma 6.9 (Taylor expansion) Let $\varphi$ be the characteristic function of a random variable $\xi$ with $E | \xi | ^ { n } < \infty$ . Then 

$$
\varphi (t) = \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {n} \frac {(i t) ^ {k} E \xi^ {k}}{k !} + o (t ^ {n}), \quad t \to 0.
$$

Proof: Noting that $| e ^ { i t } - 1 | \leq | t |$ for all $t \in { \mathsf { R } }$ , we get recursively by dominated convergence 

$$
\varphi^ {(k)} (t) = E (i \xi) ^ {k} e ^ {i t \xi}, \quad t \in \mathsf {R}, 0 \leq k \leq n.
$$

In particular, $\varphi ^ { ( k ) } ( 0 ) = E ( i \xi ) ^ { k }$ for $k \leq n$ , and the result follows from Taylor’s formula. ✷ 

The following classical result, known as the central limit theorem, explains the importance of the normal distributions. The present statement is only preliminary, and more general versions will be obtained by diferent methods in Theorems 6.13, 6.16, and 6.18. 

Theorem 6.10 (central limit theorem, Lindeberg, L´evy) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . . .$ . be i.i.d. random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, and let $\zeta$ be $N ( 0 , 1 )$ . Then 

$$
n ^ {- 1 / 2} \sum_ {k \leq n} \xi_ {k} \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} \zeta .
$$

Proof: Let the $\xi _ { k }$ have characteristic function $\varphi .$ . By Lemma 6.9, the characteristic function of $n ^ { - 1 / 2 } S _ { n }$ equals 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \varphi_ {n} (t) & = \left\{\varphi (n ^ {- 1 / 2} t) \right\} ^ {n} \\ & = \left\{1 - \frac {1}{2} t ^ {2} n ^ {- 1} + o (n ^ {- 1}) \right\} ^ {n} \\ & \to e ^ {- t ^ {2} / 2}, \end{array}
$$

where the convergence holds as $n \to \infty$ for fixed t. 

We will also establish a stronger density version, needed in Chapter 30. Here we introduce the smoothing densities 

$$
p _ {h} (x) = (\pi h) ^ {- d} \prod_ {i \leq d} \left(1 - \cos h x _ {i}\right) / x _ {i} ^ {2}, \quad x = (x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {d}) \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d},
$$

with characteristic functions 

$$
\hat {p} _ {h} (t) = \prod_ {i \leq d} \left(1 - | t _ {i} | / h\right) _ {+}, \quad t = \left(t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {d}\right) \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.
$$

Say that a distribution on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is non-lattice if it is not supported by any shifted, proper sub-group of $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . 

Theorem 6.11 (density convergence, Stone) Let μ be a non-lattice distribution on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with mean 0 and covariances $\delta _ { i j }$ , and write $\varphi$ for the standard normal density on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Then 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {d / 2} \left\| \mu^ {* n} * p _ {h} - \varphi^ {* n} \right\| = 0, \quad h > 0.
$$

Proof: Since $| \partial _ { i } \varphi ^ { * n } | \lesssim n ^ { - 1 - d / 2 }$ for all $i \leq d ,$ , the assertion is trivially fulfilled for the standard normal distribution. It is then enough to prove that, for any measures $\mu$ and ν as stated, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {d / 2} \left\| (\mu^ {* n} - \nu^ {* n}) * p _ {h} \right\| = 0, \quad h > 0.
$$

By Fourier inversion, 

$$

For a further extension of the central limit theorem in Proposition 6.10, we characterize convergence toward a Gaussian limit of suitably normalized partial sums from a single i.i.d. sequence. Here a non-decreasing function $L \geq 0$ is said to vary slowly at $\infty ,$ , if $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { x } L ( x ) > 0$ and $L ( c x ) \sim L ( x )$ as $x \to \infty$ for each $c > 0$ . Theorem 6.18 (domain of Gaussian attraction, L´evy, Feller, Khinchin) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be i.i.d., non-degenerate random variables, and let $\zeta$ be $N ( 0 , 1 )$ Then these conditions are equivalent:

$$

We may then take $m _ { n } \equiv E \xi$ . Finally, (i) holds with $a _ { n } \equiv n ^ { - 1 / 2 }$ and $m _ { n } \equiv 0$ if $E \xi = 0$ and $E \xi ^ { 2 } = 1$

\begin{array}{l} x ^ {2 - p} E \big (| \xi | ^ {p};   | \xi | > x \big) = x ^ {2 - p}   \sum_ {n} E \Big \{| \xi | ^ {p};   | \xi | / x \in (2 ^ {n}, 2 ^ {n + 1} ] \Big \} \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {n} 2 ^ {(p - 2) n} E \Big \{\xi^ {2};   | \xi | / x \in (2 ^ {n}, 2 ^ {n + 1} ] \Big \} \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {n} 2 ^ {(p - 2) n} (r - 1)   r ^ {n} L _ {0} (x) \\ \qquad = \frac {(r - 1) L _ {0} (x)}{1 - 2 ^ {p - 2}   r}. \end{array}

In particular, $E | \xi | ^ { p } < \infty$ for all $p < 2$ . If even $E \xi ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , then $E ( \xi - m ) ^ { 2 } <$ $\infty ,$ , and the first assertion is obvious. If instead $E \xi ^ { 2 } = \infty$ , we may write

Here the last term is bounded, and the first term lies between the bounds $L _ { 0 } ( x \pm m ) \sim L _ { 0 } ( x )$ . Thus, $L _ { m } ( x ) \sim L _ { 0 } ( x )$ , and the slow variation of $L _ { m }$ follows from that of $L _ { 0 }$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 6.18: Let L vary slowly at $\infty .$ . Then so does $L _ { m }$ with $m = E \xi$ by Lemma 6.19, and so we may take $E \xi = 0$ . Now define

Then a corresponding result holds for the symmetrized variables $\tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \xi } _ { 1 } , \tilde { \xi } _ { 2 } , \dots .$ , with constants $a _ { n } / \sqrt { 2 }$ and $0 ,$ and so we may assume that $\begin{array} { r } { c _ { n } ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { k < n } \tilde { \xi } _ { k } \overset { d } { \to } \zeta . } \end{array}$ . Here clearly $c _ { n }  \infty$ , and moreover $c _ { n + 1 } \ \sim \ c _ { n } ,$ , since even $\begin{array} { r } { c _ { n + 1 } ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { k \leq n } \tilde { \xi } _ { k } \overset { d } { \to } \zeta } \end{array}$ by Theorem 5.29. which shows that L is slowly varying.

We return to the general problem of characterizing weak convergence of probability measures $\mu _ { n }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ in terms of the associated characteristic functions $\hat { \mu } _ { n }$ or Laplace transforms ${ \tilde { \mu } } _ { n }$ . Suppose that $\hat { \mu } _ { n }$ or ${ \tilde { \mu } } _ { n }$ converges toward a continuous limit $\varphi _ { i }$ , which is not known in advance to be a characteristic function or Laplace transform. To conclude that $\mu _ { n }$ tends weakly toward some measure $\mu ,$ , we need an extended version of Theorem 6.3, whose proof requires a compactness argument. 

Here let $\mathcal { M } _ { d }$ be the space of locally finite measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , endowed with the vague topology generated by the evaluation maps $\textstyle \pi _ { f } \colon \mu \mapsto \mu f = \int$ fdμ for all $f \in \hat { C } _ { + }$ , where $\hat { C } _ { + }$ is the class of continuous functions $f \geq 0$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with bounded support. Thus, $\mu _ { n }$ converges vaguely to $\mu _ { : }$ , written as $\mu _ { n } \ { \stackrel { v } { \to } } \ \mu .$ , if $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ for all $f \in \hat { C } _ { + }$ . If the $\mu _ { n }$ are probability measures, then clearly $\| \mu \| = \mu \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \leq 1$ . We prove a version of $H e l l y \prime s$ selection theorem, showing that the set of probability measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is vaguely relatively sequentially compact. 

Theorem 6.20 (vague compactness, Helly) Every sequence ofprobability measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ has a vaguely convergent sub-sequence. 

Proof: Fix some probability measures $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ . on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and let $F _ { 1 } , F _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be the corresponding distribution functions. Write Q for the set of rational numbers. By a diagonal argument, $F _ { n }$ converges on $\mathsf { Q } ^ { d }$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ toward a limit G, and we may define 

$$
F (x) = \inf \left\{G (r); r \in \mathbb {Q} ^ {d}, r > x \right\}, \quad x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}.\tag{8}
$$

Since each $F _ { n }$ has non-negative increments, so has G and hence also $F$ . We further see from (8) and the monotonicity of G that $F$ is right-continuous. Hence, Corollary 4.26 yields a measure $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\mu ( x , y ] = F ( x , y ]$ for any bounded rectangular box $( x , y ] \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and we need to show that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { v } { \to } \mu$ along $N ^ { \prime }$ 

Then note that $F _ { n } ( x ) \to F ( x )$ at every continuity point x of F. By the monotonicity of $F$ , there exists a countable, dense set $D \subset \mathsf { R }$ , such that F is continuous on $C = ( D ^ { c } ) ^ { d }$ . Then $\mu _ { n } U \to \mu U$ for every finite union U of rectangular boxes with corners in $C$ , and for any bounded Borel set $B \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , a simple approximation yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mu B ^ {o} & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} B \\ & \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \mu_ {n} B \leq \mu \bar {B}. \end{array}\tag{9}
$$

For any bounded μ-continuity set B, we may consider functions $f \in \hat { C } _ { + }$ supported by B, and show as in Theorem 5.25 that $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ , proving that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { v } { \to } \mu$ ✷ 

If $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { v } {  } \mu$ for some probability measures $\mu _ { n }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we may still have $\| \mu \| < 1$ , due to an escape of mass to infinity. To exclude this possibility, we need to assume that $\left( \mu _ { n } \right)$ is tight. 

Lemma 6.21 (vague and weak convergence) Let $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be probability measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , such that $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { v } { \to } \mu$ for a measure $\mu$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $( \mu _ { n } ) \ i s \ t i g h t ,$ 

(ii) $\| \mu \| = 1$ 

(iii) $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu$ 

Proof, $( \mathrm { i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ : By a simple approximation, the vague convergence yields (9) for every bounded Borel set $B _ { i }$ , and in particular for the balls $B _ { r } = \{ x \in$ $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } ; | x | < r \} , ~ r > 0$ . If (ii) holds, then $\mu B _ { r } \to 1$ as $r  \infty$ , and the first inequality gives (i). Conversely, (i) implies lim $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } \mu _ { n } B _ { r } \to 1$ , and the last inequality yields (ii). 

$( \mathrm { i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ : Assume (i), and fix any bounded continuous function f : $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } \to \mathsf { R }$ For any $r > 0$ , we may choose a $g _ { r } \in \hat { C } _ { + }$ with $1 _ { B _ { r } } \leq g _ { r } \leq 1$ , and note that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left| \mu_ {n} f - \mu f \right| \leq \left| \mu_ {n} f - \mu_ {n} f g _ {r} \right| + \left| \mu_ {n} f g _ {r} - \mu f g _ {r} \right| + \left| \mu f g _ {r} - \mu f \right| \\ \leq \left| \mu_ {n} f g _ {r} - \mu f g _ {r} \right| + \| f \| (\mu_ {n} + \mu) B _ {0} ^ {c}. \end{array}
$$

Here the right-hand side tends to zero as $n  \infty$ and then $r  \infty$ , and so $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ , proving (iii). The converse was proved in Lemma 5.8. ✷ 

Combining the last two results, we may prove the equivalence of tightness and weak sequential compactness. A more general version appears in Theorem 23.2, which forms the starting point for a theory of weak convergence on function spaces. 

Corollary 6.22 (tightness and weak compactness) For any probability measures $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\left( \mu _ { n } \right)$ is tight, 

(ii) every sub-sequence of $\left( \mu _ { n } \right)$ has a weakly convergent further sub-sequence. 

Proof, $( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ : By Theorem 6.20, every sub-sequence has a vaguely convergent further sub-sequence. If $\left( \mu _ { n } \right)$ is tight, then by Lemma 6.21 the convergence holds even in the weak sense. 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Assume (ii). If (i) fails, we may choose some $n _ { k } \to \infty$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $\mu _ { n _ { k } } B _ { k } ^ { c } > \varepsilon$ for all $k \in \mathsf { N }$ . By (ii) we have $\mu _ { n _ { k } } \ \xrightarrow { w } \ \mu$ along a subsequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , for a probability measure $\mu .$ . Then $( \mu _ { n _ { k } } ; k \in N ^ { \prime } )$ is tight by Lemma 5.8, and in particular there exists an $r > 0$ with $\mu _ { n _ { k } } B _ { r } ^ { c } \leq \varepsilon$ for all $k \in N ^ { \prime }$ . For $k > r$ this is a contradiction, and (i) follows. ✷ 

We may now prove the desired extension of Theorem 6.3. 

Theorem 6.23 (extended continuity theorem, L´evy, Bochner) Let $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be probability measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with characteristics functions $\hat { \mu } _ { n }$ . Then these conditions are equivalent:

(ii) $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu$ for a probability measure μ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

In that case, μ has characteristic function $\varphi .$ Similar statements hold for distributions $\mu _ { n }$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ with Laplace transforms ${ \tilde { \mu } } _ { n }$ 

Proof, $\mathrm { ( i i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i ) }$ : Clear by Theorem 6.3. 

$( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ : Assuming (i), we see from the proof of Theorem 6.3 that $\left( \mu _ { n } \right)$ is tight. Then Corollary 6.22 yields $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , for a probability measure $\mu .$ The convergence extends to N by Theorem 6.3, proving (ii). The proof for Laplace transforms is similar. ✷

# Infinite Divisibility and General Null Arrays

Compound Poisson distributions and approximation, i.i.d. and null arrays, infinitely divisible distributions, L´evy measure, characteristics, L´evy– Khinchin formula, convergence and closure, one-dimensional criteria, positive and symmetric terms, general null arrays, limit laws and convergence criteria, sums and extremes, difuse distributions 

The fundamental roles of Gaussian and Poisson distributions should be clear from Chapter 6. Here we consider the more general and equally basic family of infinitely divisible distributions, which may be defined as distributional limits of linear combinations of independent Poisson and Gaussian random variables. Such distributions constitute the most general limit laws appearing in the classical limit theorems for null arrays. They further appear as finite-dimensional distributions of L´evy processes—the fundamental processes with stationary, independent increments, treated in Chapter 16—which may be regarded as prototypes of general Markov processes. 

The special criteria for convergence toward Poisson and Gaussian distributions, derived by simple analytic methods in Chapter 6, will now be extended to the case of general infinitely divisible limits. Though the use of some analytic tools is still unavoidable, the present treatment is more probabilistic in flavor, and involves as crucial steps a centering at truncated means followed by a compound Poisson approximation. This approach has the advantage of providing some better insight into even the Gaussian and Poisson results, previously obtained by elementary but more technical estimates. 

Since the entire theory is based on approximations by compound Poisson distributions, we begin with some characterizations of the latter. Here the basic representation is in terms of Poisson processes, discussed more extensively in Chapter 15. Here we need only the basic definition in terms of independent, Poisson distributed increments. 

Lemma 7.1 (compound Poisson distributions) Let $\xi$ be a random vector in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , fix any bounded measure $\nu \neq 0$ on ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { d } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ , and put $c = \| \nu \|$ and $\hat { \nu } = \nu / c$ Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi \stackrel { d } { = } X _ { \kappa }$ for a random walk $X = \left( X _ { n } \right)$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ based on $\hat { \nu } _ { ; }$ , where $\kappa \bot \bot X$ is Poisson distributed with $E \kappa = c ,$ 

(ii) $\begin{array} { r } { \xi \overset { d } { = } \int x \eta ( d x ) } \end{array}$ for a Poisson process η on ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { d } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ with $E \eta = \nu _ { ; }$ 

(iii) log $E e ^ { i u \xi } = \int ( e ^ { i u x } - 1 ) \nu ( d x ) , \quad u \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ 

The measure ν is then uniquely determined by $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ 

Proof, ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i i i ) } }$ : Writing $E e ^ { i u X _ { 1 } } = \varphi ( u )$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E e ^ {i u X _ {\kappa}} = \sum_ {n \geq 0} e ^ {- c} \frac {c ^ {n}}{n !} \{\varphi (u) \} ^ {n} \\ = e ^ {- c} e ^ {c \varphi (u)} \\ = e ^ {c \{\varphi (u) - 1 \}}, \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \log E e ^ {i u X _ {\kappa}} & = c \Bigl \{\varphi (u) - 1 \Bigr \} \\ & = c \left\{\int e ^ {i u x} \hat {\nu} (d x) - 1 \right\} \\ & = \int (e ^ {i u x} - 1)   \nu (d x). \end{array}
$$

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ : To avoid repetitions, we defer the proof until Lemma 15.2 (ii), which remains valid with f replaced by the function $f ( x ) = i x$ 

$\mathrm { ( i i i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i ) } - \mathrm { ( i i ) }$ : Clear by the uniqueness in Theorem 6.3. 

The distributions in Lemma 7.1 are said to be compound Poisson, and the underlying measure $\nu$ is called the characteristic measure of $\xi .$ . We will use the compound Poisson distributions to approximate the row sums in triangular arrays $( \xi _ { n j } )$ , where the $\xi _ { n j }$ are understood to be independent in $j$ for fixed $n .$ Recall that $\left( \xi _ { n j } \right)$ is called a null array if $\xi _ { n j } \overset { P } {  } 0$ as $n  \infty$ , uniformly in $j .$ . It is further called an i.i.d. array if the $\xi _ { n j }$ are i.i.d. in $j$ for fixed $n ,$ and the successive rows have lengths $m _ { n } \to \infty$ 

For any random vector $\xi$ with distribution $\mu _ { : }$ we introduce an associated compound Poisson random vector $\tilde { \xi }$ with characteristic measure $\mu .$ . For a triangular array $\xi _ { n j }$ , the corresponding compound Poisson vectors $\xi _ { i j }$ are again assumed to have row-wise independent entries. By $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \sim } \eta _ { n }$ we mean that, if either side converges in distribution along a sub-sequence, then so does the other along the same sequence, and the two limits agree. 

Proposition 7.2 (compound Poisson approximation) Let $( \xi _ { \stackrel { n j } { \sim } } )$ be a triangular array in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with associated compound Poisson array $\left( \xi _ { n j } \right)$ . Then the equivalence $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } \xi _ { n j } \overset { d } { \sim } \sum _ { j } \tilde { \xi } _ { n j } } \end{array}$ holds under each of these conditions: 

(i) $\left( \xi _ { n j } \right)$ is a null array in $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ 

(ii) $\left( \xi _ { n j } \right)$ is a null array with $\xi _ { n j } \overset { d } { = } - \xi _ { n j }$ 

(iii) $( \xi _ { n j } )$ is an i.i.d. array.

A random vector $\xi$ or its distribution $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ is said to be infinitely divisible, if for every $n \in \mathsf N$ we have $\xi \stackrel { d } { = } \textstyle \sum _ { j } \xi _ { n j }$ for some i.i.d. random vectors $\xi _ { n 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n n } .$ Obvious examples of infinitely divisible distributions include the Gaussian and Poisson laws, which is clear by elementary calculations. More generally, we see from Lemma 7.1 that any compound Poisson distribution is infinitely divisible. The following approximation is fundamental: 

Corollary 7.4 (compound Poisson limits) For a random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi$ is infinitely divisible, 

(ii) $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \xi$ for some compound Poisson random vectors $\xi _ { n }$ 

Proof, $( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ : Under (i) we have $\xi \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ \sum _ { j } \xi _ { n j }$ for an i.i.d. array $( \xi _ { n j } )$ Choosing an associated compound Poisson array $( \tilde { \xi } _ { n j } )$ , we get $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } \tilde { \xi } _ { n j } \overset { d } { \to } \xi } \end{array}$ by Lemma 7.2 (iii), and we note that $\begin{array} { r } { \xi _ { n } = \sum _ { j } \tilde { \xi } _ { n j } } \end{array}$ is again compound Poisson. 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Assume (ii) for some $\xi _ { n }$ with characteristic measures $\nu _ { n }$ . For every $m \in \mathbb { N }$ , we may write $\begin{array} { r } { \xi _ { n } \overset { d } { = } \sum _ { j \leq m } \xi _ { n j } } \end{array}$ for some i.i.d. compound Poisson vectors $\xi _ { n j }$ with characteristic measures $\nu _ { n } / m$ . Then the sequence $\left( \xi _ { n 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n m } \right)$ is tight by Lemma 6.2, and so $( \xi _ { n 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n m } ) \overset { d } { \to } \left( \zeta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \zeta _ { m } \right)$ as $n $ along a sub-sequence, where the $\zeta _ { j }$ are again i.i.d. with sum $\Sigma _ { j } \zeta _ { j } \overset { d } { = } \xi$ . Since m was arbitrary, (i) follows. ✷ 

We proceed to characterize the general infinitely divisible distributions. For a special case, we may combine the Gaussian and compound Poisson distributions and use Lemma 7.1 (ii) to form a variable $\xi \triangleq b + \zeta +  { \boldsymbol { \mathscr { f } } } x  { \boldsymbol { \eta } } ( d x )$ , involving a constant vector $b ,$ a centered Gaussian random vector $\zeta ,$ -<sub>, and an independent</sub> Poisson process $\eta$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . For extensions to unbounded $\nu = E \eta$ , we need to apply a suitable centering, to ensure convergence of the Poisson integral. This suggests the more general representation: 

Theorem 7.5 (infinitely divisible distributions, L´evy, Itˆo) 

(i) A random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is infinitely divisible $i f f$ 

$$
\xi \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} b + \zeta + \int_ {| x | \leq 1} x (\eta - E \eta) (d x) + \int_ {| x | > 1} x \eta (d x),
$$

for a constant vector $b \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , a centered Gaussian random vector $\zeta$ with ${ \mathrm { C o v } } ( \zeta ) = a$ , and an independent Poisson process η on ${ \sf R } ^ { d } \ \backslash \ \{ \mathrm { 0 } \}$ with intensity ν satisfying $\textstyle \int ( | x | ^ { 2 } \wedge 1 ) \nu ( d x ) < \infty$ 

(ii) A random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ is infinitely divisible $i f$ 

$$
\xi \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} a + \int x   \eta (d x),
$$

for a constant vector $a \in \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ and a Poisson process η on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ with intensity ν satisfying $\int ( | x | \wedge 1 ) \nu ( d x ) < \infty$ 

The triple $( a , b , \nu )$ or pair $( a , \nu )$ is then unique, and any choice with the stated properties may occur. 

This shows that an infinitely divisible distribution on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ is uniquely characterized by the triple $( a , b , \nu )$ or pair $( a , \nu )$ , referred to as the characteristics of $\xi$ or $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ . The intensity measure ν of the Poisson component is called the L´evy measure of $\xi$ or $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ . The representations of Theorem 7.5 can also be expressed analytically in terms of characteristic functions or Laplace transforms, which leads to some celebrated formulas: 

Corollary 7.6 (L´evy–Khinchin representations, Kolmogorov, L´evy) Let $\xi$ be an infinitely divisible random vector in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ or $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ with characteristics $( a , b , \nu )$ or $( a , \nu )$ . Then 

(i) for $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ -valued $\xi$ we have $E e ^ { i u \xi } = e ^ { \psi ( u ) } , u \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , where 

$$
\psi (u) = i u ^ {\prime} b - \frac {1}{2}   u ^ {\prime} a u + \int \left(e ^ {i u ^ {\prime} x} - 1 - i u ^ {\prime} x   1 \{| x | \leq 1 \}\right) \nu (d x),
$$

(ii) for ${ \sf R } _ { + } ^ { d } - v a l u e d \xi$ we have $E e ^ { - u \xi } = e ^ { - \varphi ( u ) } , u \in \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ , where 

$$
\varphi (u) = u a + \int (1 - e ^ {- u x}) \nu (d x).
$$

The stated representations will be proved together with the associated convergence criteria, stated below. Given a characteristic triple $( a , b , \nu )$ , as above, we define for any $h > 0$ the truncated versions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} a ^ {h} = a + \int_ {| x | \leq h} x x ^ {\prime} \nu (d x), \\ b ^ {h} = b - \int_ {h <   | x | \leq 1} x   \nu (d x), \end{array}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { h < | x | \le 1 } = - \int _ { 1 < | x | \le h } } \end{array}$ when $h > 1$ . In the positive case, we put instead $\begin{array} { r } { a ^ { h } = a + \int _ { x \leq h } x \nu ( d x ) } \end{array}$ . Let $\overline { { \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } }$ denote the one-point compactification of $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

## Theorem 7.7 (convergence and closure)

(i) The class of infinitely divisible distributions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is closed under weak convergence. 

(ii) Let $\xi _ { n }$ and $\xi$ be infinitely divisible in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with characteristics $( a _ { n } , b _ { n } , \nu _ { n } )$ and $( a , b , \nu )$ , and fix any $h > 0$ with $\nu \partial B _ { 0 } ^ { h } = 0$ . $$

(iii) Let $\xi _ { n }$ and $\xi$ be infinitely divisible in $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ with characteristics $( a _ { n } , \nu _ { n } )$ and $( a , \nu )$ , and fix any $h > 0$ with $\nu \partial B _ { 0 } ^ { h } = 0$ . $$

$$

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {j} \int_ {f (x) \leq \varepsilon} f (x)   \mu_ {n j} (d x) = 0.\tag{10}
$$

Now (9) follows immediately from (i). To deduce (10), it sufices to note that the sum on the left is bounded by $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } \mu _ { n j } ( f \wedge \varepsilon ) \to \nu ( f \wedge \varepsilon ) } \end{array}$ 

Finally, assume (ii). By a simple approximation, $\eta _ { n } ( x , \infty ) \stackrel { d } { \to } \eta ( x , \infty )$ for any $x > 0$ with $\nu \{ x \} = 0$ . In particular, for such an x, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} P \{\alpha_ {n} ^ {+} \leq x \} & = P \Bigl \{\eta_ {n} (x, \infty) = 0 \Bigr \} \\ & \to P \Bigl \{\eta (x, \infty) = 0 \Bigr \} \\ & = P \{\alpha^ {+} \leq x \}, \end{array}
$$

and so $\alpha _ { n } ^ { + } \stackrel { d } { \to } \alpha ^ { + }$ . Similarly $\alpha _ { n } ^ { - } \stackrel { d } { \to } \alpha ^ { - }$ , which proves (iii). 

The characteristic pair or triple clearly contains important information about an infinitely divisible distribution. In particular, we have the following classical result: 

Proposition 7.16 $( d i f f u s e$ distributions, Doeblin) Let $\xi$ be an infinitely divisible random vector in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with characteristics $( a , b , \nu )$ . Then 

$$
\mathcal {L} (\xi) \text {   diffuse   } \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad a \neq 0 \text {   or   } \| \nu \| = \infty .
$$

Proof: If $a = 0$ and $\| \nu \| < \infty$ , then $\xi$ is compound Poisson apart from a shift, and so $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( \boldsymbol { \xi } )$ is not difuse. When either condition fails, it does so for at least one coordinate projection, and we may take $d = 1$ . If $a > 0$ the difuseness is obvious by Lemma 1.30. Next let $\nu$ be unbounded, say with $\nu ( 0 , \infty ) = \infty$ . For every $n \in \mathsf N$ we may then write $\nu = \nu _ { n } + \nu _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ , where $\nu _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ is supported by $( 0 , n ^ { - 1 } )$ and has total mass log 2. For $\mu$ we get a corresponding decomposition $\mu _ { n } * \mu _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ , where $\mu _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ is compound Poisson with L´evy measure $\nu _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \mu _ { n } ^ { \prime } \{ 0 \} = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ . For any $x \in \mathsf { R }$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu \{x \} \leq \mu_ {n} \{x \} \mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} \{0 \} + \mu_ {n} [ x - \varepsilon , x)   \mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} (0, \varepsilon ] + \mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} (\varepsilon , \infty) \\ \quad \leq \frac {1}{2}   \mu_ {n} [ x - \varepsilon , x ] + \mu_ {n} ^ {\prime} (\varepsilon , \infty). \end{array}
$$

Letting $n $ and then $\varepsilon \to 0$ , and noting that $\mu _ { n } ^ { \prime } \stackrel { w } {  } \delta _ { 0 }$ and $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } {  } \mu .$ , we get $\mu \{ x \} \leq { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \mu \{ x \}$ by Theorem 5.25, and so $\mu \{ x \} = 0$ ✷
