B _ {k} = \left\{\left(x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {n}\right) \in S ^ {n}; \left(x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {k - 1}, x _ {k + 1}, \dots , x _ {n}\right) \in B \right\}.
$$

Then (4) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \nu_ {t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n}} B _ {k} = \Big (\nu \mu_ {t _ {0}, t _ {1}} \otimes \dots \otimes \mu_ {t _ {k - 1}, t _ {k + 1}} \otimes \dots \otimes \mu_ {t _ {n - 1}, t _ {n}} \Big) B \\ = \nu_ {t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {k - 1}, t _ {k + 1}, \ldots , t _ {n}} B, \end{array}
$$

as desired. By Theorem 8.23 there exists an S-valued process X on T with 

$$
\mathcal {L} (X _ {t _ {1}}, \dots , X _ {t _ {n}}) = \nu_ {t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}}, \quad t _ {1} \leq \dots \leq t _ {n}, n \in \mathbb {N},\tag{5}
$$

and in particular $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { L } ( X _ { 0 } ) = \nu _ { 0 } = \nu . } \end{array}$ 

To see that X is Markov with transition kernels $\mu _ { s , t }$ , fix any times $s _ { 1 } \ \leq$ $\cdots \leq s _ { n } = s \leq t$ and sets $B \in S ^ { n }$ and $C \in S$ , and conclude from (5) that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{(X _ {s _ {1}}, \ldots , X _ {s _ {n}}, X _ {t}) \in B \times C \Big \} \\ \qquad = \nu_ {s _ {1}, \ldots , s _ {n}, t} (B \times C) \\ \qquad = E \Big \{\mu_ {s, t} (X _ {s}, C); (X _ {s _ {1}}, \ldots , X _ {s _ {n}}) \in B \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Letting $\mathcal { F }$ be the filtration induced by X, we get by a monotone-class argument 

$$
P \left\{X _ {t} \in C; A \right\} = E \left\{\mu_ {s, t} \left(X _ {s}, C\right); A \right\}, \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {s},
$$

and so $P \{ X _ { t } \in C | \mathcal { F } _ { s } \} = \mu _ { s , t } ( X _ { s } , C )$ a.s. 

Now let $( G , { \mathcal { G } } )$ be a measurable group with identity element ι. Recall that a kernel $\mu$ on G is said to be invariant if $\mu _ { r } = \mu _ { \iota } \circ \theta _ { r } ^ { - 1 } \equiv \theta _ { r } \mu _ { \iota }$ , meaning that 

$$
\mu (r, B) = \mu (\iota , r ^ {- 1} B), \quad r \in G, B \in \mathcal {G}.
$$

An G-valued Markov process is said to be space-homogeneous if its transition kernels $\mu _ { s , t }$ are invariant. We further say that a process X in G has independent increments, if for any times $t _ { 0 } \leq \cdots \leq t _ { n }$ the increments $X _ { t _ { k - 1 } } ^ { - 1 } X _ { t _ { k } }$ are mutually independent and independent of $X _ { 0 }$ . More generally, given a filtration $\mathcal { F }$ on $T _ { : }$ , we say that X has -independent increments, if X is adapted to $\mathcal { F }$ and such that $X _ { s } ^ { - 1 } X _ { t }$ Ⅱ $\mathcal { F } _ { s }$ for all $s \leq t$ in $T .$ . Note that the elementary notion of independence corresponds to the case where $\mathcal { F }$ is induced by $X$ . For Abelian groups $G$ , we may use an additive notation and write the increments in the usual way as $X _ { t } - X _ { s }$ 

Theorem 11.5 (space homogeneity and independence) Let X be an -adapted process on $T$ with values in a measurable group G. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) X is a G-homogeneous -Markov process, 

(ii) X has -independent increments. 

In that case, X has transition kernels 

$$
\mu_ {s, t} (r, B) = P \left\{X _ {s} ^ {- 1} X _ {t} \in r ^ {- 1} B \right\}, \quad r \in G, B \in \mathcal {G}, s \leq t \text { in } T.\tag{6}
$$

Proof, (i) (ii): Let X be -Markov with transition kernels 

$$
\mu_ {s, t} (r, B) = \mu_ {s, t} (r ^ {- 1} B), \quad r \in G, B \in \mathcal {G}, s \leq t \text {in} T.\tag{7}
$$

Then Theorem 8.5 yields for any $s \leq t$ in $T$ and $B \in { \mathcal { G } }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \Big \{X _ {s} ^ {- 1} X _ {t} \in B \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {s} \Big \} = P \Big \{X _ {t} \in X _ {s} B \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {s} \Big \} \\ & \qquad = \mu_ {s, t} (X _ {s}, X _ {s} B) \\ & \qquad = \mu_ {s, t} B. \end{array}
$$

Thus, $X _ { s } ^ { - 1 } X _ { t }$ is independent of $\mathcal { F } _ { s }$ with distribution $\mu _ { s , t }$ , and (6) follows by means of (7). 

(ii) (i): Let $X _ { s } ^ { - 1 } X _ { t }$ be independent of $\mathcal { F } _ { s }$ with distribution $\mu _ { s , t }$ . Defining the associated kernel $\mu _ { s , t }$ by (7), we get by Theorem 8.5 for any s, t, and B as before 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Bigl \{X _ {t} \in B   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {s} \Bigr \} = P \Bigl \{X _ {s} ^ {- 1} X _ {t} \in X _ {s} ^ {- 1} B   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {s} \Bigr \} \\ = \mu_ {s, t} (X _ {s} ^ {- 1} B) \\ = \mu_ {s, t} (X _ {s}, B), \end{array}
$$

and so X is Markov with the invariant transition kernels in (7). 

We now specialize to the time-homogeneous case, where $T = \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ or $Z _ { + }$ , and the transition kernels are of the form $\mu _ { s , t } = \mu _ { t - s } ,$ , so that 

$$
P \left\{X _ {t} \in B \mid \mathcal {F} _ {s} \right\} = \mu_ {t - s} (X _ {s}, B) \text { a.s., } B \in \mathcal {S}, s \leq t \text { in } T.
$$

Introducing the initial distribution $\nu = \mathcal { L } ( X _ { 0 } )$ , we get by Proposition 11.2 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {L} (X _ {t _ {0}}, \ldots , X _ {t _ {n}}) = \nu \mu_ {t _ {0}} \otimes \mu_ {t _ {1} - t _ {0}} \otimes \dots \otimes \mu_ {t _ {n} - t _ {n - 1}}, \\ \mathcal {L} \Big (X _ {t _ {1}}, \ldots , X _ {t _ {n}} \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {t _ {0}} \Big) = \Big (\mu_ {t _ {1} - t _ {0}} \otimes \dots \otimes \mu_ {t _ {n} - t _ {n - 1}} \Big) (X _ {t _ {0}}, \cdot). \end{array}
$$

The Chapman–Kolmogorov relation now reduces to the semi-group property 

$$
\mu_ {s + t} = \mu_ {s} \mu_ {t}, s, t \in T,
$$

which is again assumed to hold identically. 

The following result suggests that we think of a discrete-time Markov process as a stochastic dynamical system. Let $\vartheta$ be a generic $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random variable. 

Proposition 11.6 (random dynamical system) Let X be a process on $Z _ { + }$ with values in a Borel space S. Then these conditions are equivalent:

$$

$( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ : Assume (i). By Lemma 4.22 we may choose the associated functions $f _ { n }$ as above. Let $\tilde { \vartheta } _ { 1 } , \tilde { \vartheta } _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ and independent of ${ \tilde { X } } _ { 0 } \cong X _ { 0 }$ 2 and define recursively $\tilde { X } _ { n } = f _ { n } ( \tilde { X } _ { n - 1 } , \tilde { \vartheta } _ { n } )$ for $n \in \mathsf N$ . Now fix a transition semi-group $\left( \mu _ { t } \right)$ on a Borel space $S .$ . For any prob ability measure $\nu$ on $S ,$ Theorem 11.4 yields an associated Markov process $X _ { \nu } ,$ and Proposition 4.2 shows that the associated distribution $P _ { \nu }$ is uniquely determined by ν. Note that $P _ { \nu }$ is a probability measure on the path space $( S ^ { T } , S ^ { T } )$ . For $\nu = \delta _ { x } ,$ , we write $P _ { x }$ instead of $P _ { \delta _ { x } }$ . Integration with respect to $P _ { \nu }$ or $P _ { x }$ is denoted by $E _ { \nu }$ or $E _ { x }$ , respectively. 

Lemma 11.7 (mixtures) The measures $P _ { x }$ form a probability kernel from $S$ to $S ^ { T }$ , and for any initial distribution $\nu ,$ 

$$
P _ {\nu} A = \int_ {S} P _ {x} (A) \nu (d x), \quad A \in \mathcal {S} ^ {T}.

Proof: The measurability of $P _ { x } A$ and the stated formula are obvious for cylinder sets of the form $A = ( \pi _ { t _ { 1 } } , \ldots , \pi _ { t _ { n } } ) ^ { - 1 } B$ . The general case follows easily by a monotone-class argument. ✷ 

Rather than considering one Markov process $X _ { \nu }$ for every initial distribution $\nu ,$ , we may introduce a single canonical process $X$ , defined as the identity mapping on the path space $( S ^ { T } , S ^ { T } )$ , equipped with the diferent probability measures $P _ { \nu }$ . For our present purposes, it sufices to endow the path space $S ^ { T }$ with the canonical filtration $\mathcal { F }$ induced by $X$ . Optional times with respect to a Markov process are often constructed recursively in terms of shifts on the underlying path space. Thus, for any pair of optional times $\sigma$ and $\tau$ on the canonical space, we may consider the random time $\gamma = \sigma + \tau \circ \theta _ { \sigma }$ , which is understood to be infinite when $\sigma = \infty$ . Here $C _ { S }$ and $D _ { S }$ denote the spaces of continuous or rcll functions, respectively, from $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ to $S _ { ☉ }$ . 

Proposition 11.8 (iterated optional times) For a metric space $S ,$ , let $\sigma , \tau$ be optional times on the canonical space $S ^ { \infty } , \ C _ { S }$ , or $D _ { S }$ , endowed with the right-continuous, induced filtration. Then we may form an optional time 

$$
\gamma = \sigma + \tau \circ \theta_ {\sigma}.

$$

Now fix any $t \geq 0$ , and note that 

$$
\{\gamma <   t \} = \bigcup_ {r \in \mathbb {Q} \cap (0, t)} \Bigl \{\sigma <   r, \tau \circ \theta_ {\sigma} <   t - r \Bigr \}.\tag{9}
$$

For every $r \in ( 0 , t )$ we have $\{ \tau < t - r \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { t - r }$ , and so $\theta _ { \sigma } ^ { - 1 } \{ \tau < t - r \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { \sigma + t - r } ^ { + }$ by (8), and Lemma 9.2 gives 

$$
\left\{\sigma <   r, \tau \circ \theta_ {\sigma} <   t - r \right\} = \left\{\sigma + t - r <   t \right\} \cap \theta_ {\sigma} ^ {- 1} \left\{\tau <   t - r \right\} \in \mathcal {F} _ {t}.

Thus, (9) yields $\{ \gamma < t \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { t }$ , and so $\gamma$ is ${ \mathcal { F } } ^ { + }$ -optional by Lemma 9.2. ✷ 

We may now extend the Markov property to suitable optional times. The present statement is only preliminary, and stronger versions will be established, under appropriate conditions, in Theorems 13.1, 14.11, and 17.17. 

Proposition 11.9 (strong Markov property) Let X be a time-homogeneous Markov process on $T = { \mathsf { R } } _ { + } \ o r \ Z _ { + }$ , and let τ be an optional time taking countably many values. Then in the general and canonical cases, we have respectively

for any set $A \in S ^ { T }$ , distribution ν on $S$ , and bounded or non-negative random variable $\xi$ .

Proof: By Lemmas 8.3 and 9.1, we may take $\tau = t$ to be finite and nonrandom. For sets of the form

A = \left(\pi_ {t _ {1}}, \dots , \pi_ {t _ {n}}\right) ^ {- 1} B, \quad t _ {1} \leq \dots \leq t _ {n}, B \in \mathcal {S} ^ {n}, n \in \mathbb {N},\tag{10}

For canonical X, (i) is equivalent to (ii) with $\xi = 1 _ { A }$ , since in that case $\xi \circ \theta _ { \tau } = 1 \{ \theta _ { \tau } X \in A \}$ . The result extends to general ξ by linearity and monotone convergence. ✷ 

When X is both space- and time-homogeneous, we can state the strong Markov property without reference to the family $( P _ { x } )$ . For notational clarity, we consider only processes in Abelian groups, the general case being similar. 

Theorem 11.10 (space and time homogeneity) Let X be a space- and timehomogeneous Markov process in a measurable Abelian group S. Then 

(i) $P _ { x } A = P _ { 0 } ( A - x ) , x \in S , A \in { \mathcal { S } } ^ { T } ,$

$$
X - X _ {0} \stackrel {d} {=} \theta_ {\tau} X - X _ {\tau} \perp \mathcal {F} _ {\tau}.
$$

Proof: (i) By Proposition 11.2, we get for sets A as in (10) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P _ {x} A = P _ {x} \circ (\pi_ {t _ {1}}, \ldots , \pi_ {t _ {n}}) ^ {- 1} B \\ \qquad = \Big (\mu_ {t _ {1}} \otimes \mu_ {t _ {2} - t _ {1}} \otimes \dots \otimes \mu_ {t _ {n} - t _ {n - 1}} \Big) (x, B) \\ \qquad = \Big (\mu_ {t _ {1}} \otimes \mu_ {t _ {2} - t _ {1}} \otimes \dots \otimes \mu_ {t _ {n} - t _ {n - 1}} \Big) (0, B - x) \\ \qquad = P _ {0} \circ (\pi_ {t _ {1}}, \ldots , \pi_ {t _ {n}}) ^ {- 1} (B - x) \\ \qquad = P _ {0} (A - x), \end{array}
$$

which extends to general A by a monotone-class argument. 

(ii) Assume the strong Markov property at $\tau .$ . Letting $A = \pi _ { 0 } ^ { - 1 } B$ with $B \in S$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} 1 _ {B} (X _ {\tau}) = P _ {X _ {\tau}} \{\pi_ {0} \in B \} \\ = P \Bigl \{X _ {\tau} \in B   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Bigr \} \text {a.s.}, \end{array}
$$

and so $X _ { \tau }$ is a.s. $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau }$ <sub>-measurable. By (i) and Theorem 8.5,</sub> 

$$
P \Bigl \{\theta_ {\tau} X - X _ {\tau} \in A   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Bigr \} = P _ {X _ {\tau}} (A + X _ {\tau}) = P _ {0} A, \quad A \in \mathcal {S} ^ {T},\tag{11}

which shows that $\theta _ { \tau } X - X _ { \tau } \bot \bot \mathcal { F } _ { \tau }$ with distribution $P _ { 0 }$ . Taking $\tau = 0$ , we get in particular $\mathcal { L } ( X - X _ { 0 } ) = P _ { 0 }$ , and the asserted properties follow. 

Now assume the stated conditions. To deduce the strong Markov property at $\tau ,$ let $A \in S ^ { T }$ be arbitrary, and conclude from (i) and Theorem 8.5 that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} P \Big \{\theta_ {\tau} X \in A   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Big \} & = P \Big \{\theta_ {\tau} X - X _ {\tau} \in A - X _ {\tau}   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Big \} \\ & = P _ {0} (A - X _ {\tau}) \\ & = P _ {X _ {\tau}} A. \end{array}
$$

If a time-homogeneous Markov process X has initial distribution $\nu ,$ the distribution at time $t \in T$ equals $\nu _ { t } = \nu \mu _ { t }$ , or 

$$
\nu_ {t} B = \int \nu (d x) \mu_ {t} (x, B), \quad B \in \mathcal {S}, t \in T.
$$

A distribution ν is said to be invariant for the semi-group $\left( \mu _ { t } \right)$ if $\nu _ { t }$ is independent of t, so that $\nu \mu _ { t } = \nu$ for all $t \in T$ . We also say that a process $X$ on $T$ is stationary, if $\theta _ { t } X \stackrel { d } { = } X$ for all $t \in T$ . The two notions<sup>2</sup> are related as follows. 

Lemma 11.11 (stationarity and invariance) Let X be a time-homogeneous Markov process on T with transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ and initial distribution ν. Then 

X is stationary $\Leftrightarrow \nu$ is invariant for $\left( \mu _ { t } \right)$ 

Proof: If ν is invariant, then Proposition 11.2 yields 

$$
(X _ {t + t _ {1}}, \ldots , X _ {t + t _ {n}}) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (X _ {t _ {1}}, \ldots , X _ {t _ {n}}), \quad t, t _ {1} \leq \dots \leq t _ {n} \text {in} T,
$$

and so X is stationary by Proposition 4.2. The converse is obvious. 

The strong Markov property has many applications. We begin with a classical maximum inequality for random walks, which will be useful in Chapter 23. 

Proposition 11.12 (maximum inequality, Ottaviani) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be i.i.d. random variables with $E \xi _ { i } = 0$ and $E \xi _ { i } ^ { 2 } = 1$ , and put $\textstyle X _ { n } = \sum _ { i \leq n } \xi _ { i }$ . Then 

$$
P \left\{X _ {n} ^ {*} \geq 2 r \sqrt {n} \right\} \leq \frac {P \left\{| X _ {n} | \geq r \sqrt {n} \right\}}{1 - r ^ {- 2}}, \quad r > 1, n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Proof: Put $c = r { \sqrt { n } }$ , and define $\tau = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ k \in \mathsf { N } ; | X _ { k } | \geq 2 c \}$ . By the strong Markov property at τ and Theorem 8.5, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \{| X _ {n} | \geq c \} \geq P \Big \{| X _ {n} | \geq c,   X _ {n} ^ {*} \geq 2 c \Big \} \\ \geq P \Big \{\tau \leq n,   | X _ {n} - X _ {\tau} | \leq c \Big \} \\ \geq P \Big \{X _ {n} ^ {*} \geq 2   c \Big \} \min _ {k \leq n} P \Big \{| X _ {k} | \leq c \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

and Chebyshev’s inequality yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \min _ {k \leq n} P \Bigl \{| X _ {k} | \leq c \Bigr \} \geq \min _ {k \leq n} \left(1 - k   c ^ {- 2}\right) \\ \geq \left(1 - n   c ^ {- 2}\right) \\ = 1 - r ^ {- 2}. \end{array}
$$

Similar ideas can be used to prove the following more sophisticated result, which will find important applications in Chapters 16 and $2 7$ 

Corollary 11.13 (uniform convergence) For $r \in \mathsf { Q } _ { + }$ , let $X ^ { r }$ be rcll processes in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } { } _ { : }$ , such that the increments in r are independent and satisfy $( X ^ { r } - X ^ { s } ) _ { t } ^ { * } \overset { P } { \to } 0$ as $r , s  \infty$ for fixed $t > 0$ . Then there exists an rcll process X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , such that 

$$
(X ^ {r} - X) _ {t} ^ {*} \rightarrow 0 a. s., t > 0.

\left(X ^ {r _ {m}} - X ^ {r _ {n}}\right) _ {t} ^ {*} \rightarrow 0 \text { a   .   s   . }, \quad m, n \rightarrow \infty .

Fixing any $\varepsilon , r > 0$ and a finite set $A \subset [ r , \infty ) \cap \mathsf { Q }$ , and putting $\sigma = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ s \in A ; ( Y ^ { s } ) _ { t } ^ { * } > 2 \varepsilon \}$ , we get as in Proposition 11.12

\begin{array}{r c l} P \{(Y ^ {r}) _ {t} ^ {*} > \varepsilon \} & \geq & P \Big \{(Y ^ {r}) _ {t} ^ {*} > \varepsilon , \max _ {s \in A} (Y ^ {s}) _ {t} ^ {*} > 2 \varepsilon \Big \} \\ & \geq & P \Big \{\sigma <   \infty , (Y ^ {r} - Y ^ {s}) _ {t} ^ {*} \leq \varepsilon \Big \} \\ & \geq & P \Big \{\max _ {s \in A} (Y ^ {s}) _ {t} ^ {*} > 2 \varepsilon \Big \} \min _ {s \in A} P \Big \{(Y ^ {r} - Y ^ {s}) _ {t} ^ {*} \leq \varepsilon \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

P \Bigl \{\sup _ {s \geq r} (Y ^ {s}) _ {t} ^ {*} > 2 \varepsilon \Bigr \} \leq \frac {P \{(Y ^ {r}) _ {t} ^ {*} > \varepsilon \}}{1 - \sup _ {s \geq r} P \bigl \{(Y ^ {r} - Y ^ {s}) _ {t} ^ {*} > \varepsilon \bigr \}},

The assertion now follows since $t > 0$ was arbitrary. ✷ 

We proceed to clarify the nature of the strong Markov property of a process $X$ at a finite optional time $\tau$ . The condition is clearly a combination of the properties 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \underset {X _ {\tau}} {\coprod} \theta_ {\tau} X, \quad \mathcal {L} (\theta_ {\tau} X | X _ {\tau}) = P _ {X _ {\tau}} \text { a.s. }
$$

Though the latter relation—here referred to as strong homogeneity—appears to be weaker than the strong Markov property, the two conditions are in fact essentially equivalent. Here we fix any right-continuous filtration $\mathcal { F }$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

Theorem 11.14 (strong homogeneity) Let X be an ${ \mathcal { F } } .$ -adapted, rcll process in a separable metric space $( S , \rho )$ , and consider a probability kernel $( P _ { x } ) \colon S \to$ $D _ { S }$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) X is strongly homogeneous at every bounded, optional time $\tau ,$ 

(ii) X satisfies the strong Markov property at every optional time $\tau < \infty$ 

Our proof is based on a 0 1 law for absorption, involving the sets 

$$
I = \left\{x \in D; x _ {t} \equiv x _ {0} \right\}, \quad A = \left\{s \in S; P _ {s} I = 1 \right\}.\tag{12}
$$

Lemma 11.15 (absorption) For any X as in Theorem 11.14 (i) and optional times $\tau < \infty$ , we have 

$$
P _ {X _ {\tau}} I = 1 _ {I} (\theta_ {\tau} X) = 1 _ {A} (X _ {\tau}) a. s.
$$

Proof: We may clearly take $\tau$ to be bounded, say by $n \in { \mathbb N }$ . Fix any $h > 0 .$ and partition $S$ into disjoint Borel sets $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . of diameter $< h$ . For each $k \in \mathsf N$ , define 

$$
\tau_ {k} = n \wedge \inf \left\{t > \tau ; \rho (X _ {\tau}, X _ {t}) > h \right\} \text {on} \{X _ {\tau} \in B _ {k} \},\tag{13}
$$

and put $\tau _ { k } = \tau$ otherwise. The times $\tau _ { k }$ are again bounded and optional, and clearly 

$$
\big \{X _ {\tau_ {k}} \in B _ {k} \big \} \subset \Big \{X _ {\tau} \in B _ {k}, \sup _ {t \in [ \tau , n ]} \rho (X _ {\tau}, X _ {t}) \leq h \Big \}.\tag{14}
$$

Using property (i) and (14), we get as $n \to \infty$ and $h  0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \Big (P _ {X _ {\tau}} I ^ {c};   \theta_ {\tau} X \in I \Big) = \sum_ {k} E \Big (P _ {X _ {\tau}} I ^ {c};   \theta_ {\tau} X \in I,   X _ {\tau} \in B _ {k} \Big) \\ \leq \sum_ {k} E \Big (P _ {X _ {\tau_ {k}}} I ^ {c};   X _ {\tau_ {k}} \in B _ {k} \Big) \\ = \sum_ {k} P \Big \{\theta_ {\tau_ {k}} X \notin I,   X _ {\tau_ {k}} \in B _ {k} \Big \} \\ \leq \sum_ {k} P \Big \{\theta_ {\tau} X \notin I,   X _ {\tau} \in B _ {k},   \sup _ {t \in [ \tau , n ]} \rho (X _ {\tau}, X _ {t}) \leq h \Big \} \\ \to P \Big \{\theta_ {\tau} X \notin I,   \sup _ {t \geq \tau} \rho (X _ {\tau}, X _ {t}) = 0 \Big \} = 0, \end{array}
$$

and so $P _ { X _ { \tau } } I = 1 ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . on $\{ \theta _ { \tau } X \in I \}$ . Since also $E P _ { X _ { \tau } } I = P \{ \theta _ { \tau } X \in I \}$ by (i), we obtain the first of the displayed equalities. The second one follows by the definition of A. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 11.14: Assume (i), and define I and $A$ as in (12). To prove (ii) on $\{ X _ { \tau } \in A \}$ , fix any times $t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n }$ and Borel sets $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n }$ write $\textstyle B = \bigcap _ { k } B _ { k }$ , and conclude from (i) and Lemma 11.15 that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \left(\bigcap_ {k} \{X _ {\tau + t _ {k}} \in B _ {k} \}   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau}\right) = P \{X _ {\tau} \in B   |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \} \\ = 1 \{X _ {\tau} \in B \} \\ = P \{X _ {\tau} \in B   |   X _ {\tau} \} \\ = P _ {X _ {\tau}} \{x _ {0} \in B \} \\ = P _ {X _ {\tau}} \bigcap_ {k} \{x _ {t _ {k}} \in B _ {k} \}, \end{array}
$$

which extends to (ii) by a monotone-class argument. 

To prove (ii) on $\{ X _ { \tau } \notin A \}$ , we may take $\tau \leq n \mathrm { ~ a . s . ~ }$ , and divide $A ^ { c }$ into disjoint Borel sets $B _ { k }$ of diameter $< h$ . Fix any $F \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { \tau }$ with $F \subset \{ X _ { \tau } \not \in A \}$ For each $k \in { \mathsf N }$ , define $\tau _ { k }$ as in (13) on the set $F ^ { c } \cap \{ X _ { \tau } \in B _ { k } \}$ , and let $\tau _ { k } = \tau$ otherwise. Note that (14) remains true on $F ^ { c }$ . Using (i), (14), and Lemma 11.15, we get as $n \to \infty$ and $h  0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Big | \mathcal {L} (\theta_ {\tau} X; F) - E (P _ {X _ {\tau}}; F) \Big | \\ \qquad = \Big | \sum_ {k} E \Big (1 \{\theta_ {\tau} X \in \cdot \} - P _ {X _ {\tau}};   X _ {\tau} \in B _ {k},   F \Big) \Big | \\ \qquad = \Big | \sum_ {k} E \Big (1 \{\theta_ {\tau_ {k}} X \in \cdot \} - P _ {X _ {\tau_ {k}}};   X _ {\tau_ {k}} \in B _ {k},   F \Big) \Big | \\ \qquad = \Big | \sum_ {k} E \Big (1 \{\theta_ {\tau_ {k}} X \in \cdot \} - P _ {X _ {\tau_ {k}}};   X _ {\tau_ {k}} \in B _ {k},   F ^ {c} \Big) \Big | \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {k} P \Big \{X _ {\tau_ {k}} \in B _ {k};   F ^ {c} \Big \} \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {k} P \Big \{X _ {\tau} \in B _ {k},   \sup _ {t \in [ \tau , n ]} \rho (X _ {\tau}, X _ {t}) \leq h \Big \} \\ \qquad \to P \Big \{X _ {\tau} \notin A,   \sup _ {t \geq \tau} \rho (X _ {\tau}, X _ {t}) = 0 \Big \} = 0, \end{array}
$$

which shows that the left-hand side is zero. 

We conclude with some asymptotic and invariance properties for discretetime Markov chains. First we consider the successive visits to a fixed state $y \in S$ . Assuming the process to be canonical, we introduce the hitting time $\tau _ { y } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n \in \mathsf { N } ; X _ { n } = y \}$ , and define recursively 

$$
\tau_ {y} ^ {k + 1} = \tau_ {y} ^ {k} + \tau_ {y} \circ \theta_ {\tau_ {y} ^ {k}}, \quad k \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+},
$$

starting with $\tau _ { y } ^ { 0 } = 0$ . We further introduce the occupation times 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \kappa_ {y} = \sup \left\{k; \tau_ {y} ^ {k} <   \infty \right\} \\ = \sum_ {n \geq 1} 1 \{X _ {n} = y \}, \quad y \in S, \end{array}
$$

and show how the distribution of $\kappa _ { y }$ can be expressed in terms of the hitting probabilities 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} r _ {x y} & = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {y} <   \infty \} \\ & = P _ {x} \{\kappa_ {y} > 0 \}, \quad x, y \in S. \end{array}
$$

Lemma 11.16 (occupation times) For any $x , y \in S$ and $k \in { \mathsf N }$ 

(i) $P _ { x } \{ \kappa _ { y } \ge k \} = P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { y } ^ { k } < \infty \} = r _ { x y } r _ { y y } ^ { k - 1 } ,$ 

(ii) $E _ { x } \kappa _ { y } = { \frac { r _ { x y } } { 1 - r _ { y y } } }$ 

Proof: (i) By the strong Markov property, we have for any $k \in \mathsf { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P _ {x} \Big \{\tau_ {y} ^ {k + 1} <   \infty \Big \} = P _ {x} \Big \{\tau_ {y} ^ {k} <   \infty , \tau_ {y} \circ \theta_ {\tau_ {y} ^ {k}} <   \infty \Big \} \\ & \qquad = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {y} ^ {k} <   \infty \} P _ {y} \{\tau_ {y} <   \infty \} \\ & \qquad = r _ {y y} P _ {x} \{\tau_ {y} ^ {k} <   \infty \}, \end{array}
$$

and the second relation follows by induction on k. The first relation holds since $\kappa _ { y } \geq k$ if $\tau _ { y } ^ { k } < \infty$ 

(ii) By (i) and Lemma 4.4, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {x} \kappa_ {y} = \sum_ {k \geq 1} P _ {x} \{\kappa_ {y} \geq k \} \\ = \sum_ {k \geq 1} r _ {x y} r _ {y y} ^ {k - 1} = \frac {r _ {x y}}{1 - r _ {y y}}. \end{array}
$$

In particular, we get for $x = y$ 

$$
P _ {x} \{\kappa_ {x} \geq k \} = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {x} ^ {k} <   \infty \} = r _ {x x} ^ {k}, \quad k \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Thus, under $P _ { x }$ , the number of visits to x is either a.s. infinite or geometri cally distributed with mean $E _ { x } \kappa _ { x } + 1 = ( 1 - r _ { x x } ) ^ { - 1 } < \infty$ . This leads to a corresponding division of S into recurrent and transient states. 

Recurrence can often be deduced from the existence of an invariant distribution. Here and below we write $p _ { x y } ^ { n } = \mu _ { n } ( x , \{ y \} )$ 

Lemma 11.17 (invariant distributions and recurrence) Let ν be an invariant distribution on S. Then for any $x \in S$ 

$$
\nu \{x \} > 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x \text {   is   recurrent. }
$$

Proof: By the invariance of $\nu ,$ 

$$
0 <   \nu \{x \} = \int \nu (d y) p _ {y x} ^ {n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{15}
$$

Thus, by Lemma 11.16 and Fubini’s theorem, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \infty = \sum_ {n \geq 1} \int \nu (d y) p _ {y x} ^ {n} \\ = \int \nu (d y) \sum_ {n \geq 1} p _ {y x} ^ {n} \\ = \int \nu (d y) \frac {r _ {y x}}{1 - r _ {x x}} \leq \frac {1}{1 - r _ {x x}}. \end{array}
$$

Hence, $r _ { x x } = 1$ , and so x is recurrent. 

The period $d _ { x }$ of a state x is defined as the greatest common divisor of the set $\{ n \in \mathsf { N } ; p _ { x x } ^ { n } > 0 \}$ , and we say that x is aperiodic if $d _ { x } = 1$ 

Lemma 11.18 (periodicity) If a state $x \in S$ has period $d < \infty$ , we have $p _ { x x } ^ { n d } > 0$ for all but finitely many n. 

Proof: Put $C = \{ n \in \mathsf { N } ; p _ { x x } ^ { n d } > 0 \}$ , and conclude from the Chapman– Kolmogorov relation that C is closed under addition. Since C has greatest common divisor 1, the generated additive group equals Z. In particular, there exist some $n _ { 1 } , \dots , n _ { k } \ \in \ C$ and $z _ { 1 } , \dotsc , z _ { k } \in { \cal Z }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } z _ { j } n _ { j } \ = \ 1 } \end{array}$ . Writing $m = n _ { 1 } \sum _ { j } | z _ { j } | n _ { j }$ , we note that any number $n \geq m$ can be represented, for suitable $h \in Z _ { + }$ and $r \in \{ 0 , \ldots , n _ { 1 } - 1 \}$ , as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} n = m + h   n _ {1} + r \\ \qquad = h   n _ {1} + \sum_ {j \leq k} \left(n _ {1} | z _ {j} | + r z _ {j}\right) n _ {j} \in C. \end{array}
$$

For every $x \in S$ , we define the excursions of X from x by 

$$
Y _ {n} = X ^ {\tau_ {x}} \circ \theta_ {\tau_ {x} ^ {n}}, \quad n \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+},
$$

as long as $\tau _ { x } ^ { n } < \infty$ . To allow infinite excursions, we may introduce an extraneous element $\Delta \not \in S$ , and define $Y _ { n } = \bar { \Delta } \equiv ( \Delta , \Delta , . . . )$ whenever $\tau _ { x } ^ { n } = \infty$ Conversely, X may be recovered from the $Y _ { n }$ through the formulas 

$$
\tau_ {n} = \sum_ {k <   n} \inf \left\{t > 0; Y _ {k} (t) = x \right\},\tag{16}
$$

$$
X _ {t} = Y _ {n} (t - \tau_ {n}), \quad t \in [ \tau_ {n}, \tau_ {n + 1}), \qquad n \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+}.\tag{17}
$$

The distribution $\nu _ { x } = P _ { x } \circ Y _ { 0 } ^ { - 1 }$ is called the excursion law at $x$ . When x is recurrent and $r _ { y x } = 1$ , Proposition 11.9 shows that $Y _ { 1 } , Y _ { 2 } , \dots$ . are i.i.d. $\nu _ { x }$ under $P _ { y }$ . The result extends to the general case, as follows. 

Lemma 11.19 (excursions) Let X be a discrete-time Markov process in a Borel space $S ,$ and fix any $x \in S$ . Then there exist some independent processes $Y _ { 0 } , Y _ { 1 } , \dots$ . in S, all but $Y _ { 0 }$ with distribution $\nu _ { x }$ , such that X is a.s. given by (16) and (17). 

Proof: Put ${ \tilde { Y } } _ { 0 } \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ Y _ { 0 } .$ , and let $\tilde { Y } _ { 1 } , \tilde { Y } _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be independent of $\tilde { Y } _ { 0 }$ and i.i.d. $\nu _ { x }$ Construct associated random times $\tilde { \tau } _ { 0 } , \tilde { \tau } _ { 1 } , \ldots$ . as in (16), and define a process $\tilde { X }$ as in (17). By Corollary 8.18, it is enough to show that $X \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ { \tilde { X } }$ . Writing 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \kappa = \sup \Bigl \{n \geq 0;   \tau_ {n} <   \infty \Bigr \}, \\ \tilde {\kappa} = \sup \Bigl \{n \geq 0;   \tilde {\tau} _ {n} <   \infty \Bigr \}, \end{array}
$$

it is equivalent to show that 

$$
\left(Y _ {0}, \dots , Y _ {\kappa}, \bar {\Delta}, \bar {\Delta}, \dots\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left(\tilde {Y} _ {0}, \dots , \tilde {Y} _ {\tilde {\kappa}}, \bar {\Delta}, \bar {\Delta}, \dots\right).\tag{18}
$$

Using the strong Markov property on the left and the independence of the $\tilde { Y } _ { n }$ on the right, it is easy to check that both sides are Markov processes in $S ^ { Z + } \cup \left\{ \bar { \Delta } \right\}$ with the same initial distribution and transition kernel. Hence, (18) holds by Proposition 11.2. ✷ 

We now consider discrete-time Markov chains X on the time scale $Z _ { + } ,$ taking values in a countable state space S. Here the Chapman–Kolmogorov relation becomes 

$$
p _ {i k} ^ {m + n} = \sum_ {j} p _ {i j} ^ {m} p _ {j k} ^ {n}, i, k \in S, m, n \in \mathbb {N},\tag{19}
$$

where $p _ { i j } ^ { n } = \mu _ { n } ( i , \{ j \} ) , i , j \in S$ . This may be written in matrix form as $p ^ { m + n } =$ $p ^ { m } p ^ { n }$ , which shows that the matrix $p ^ { n }$ of n -step transition probabilities is simply the n-th power of the matrix $p = p ^ { 1 }$ , justifying our notation. Regarding the initial distribution ν as a row vector $\left( \nu _ { i } \right)$ , we may write the distribution at time n as $\nu p ^ { n }$ 

Now define $r _ { i j } = P _ { i } \{ \tau _ { j } < \infty \}$ as before, where $\tau _ { j } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n > 0 ; X _ { n } = j \}$ . A Markov chain in S is said to be irreducible if $r _ { i j } > 0$ for all $i , j \in S$ , so that every state can be reached from any other state. For irreducible chains, all states have the same recurrence and periodicity properties: 

Proposition 11.20 (irreducible chains) For an irreducible Markov chain, 

(i) either all states are recurrent or all are transient, 

(ii) all states have the same period, 

(iii) if ν is invariant, then $\nu _ { i } > 0$ for all i. 

For the proof of (i) we need the following lemma. 

Lemma 11.21 (recurrence classes) For a recurrent $i \in S$ , define $S _ { i } = \{ j \in S \}$ $r _ { i j } > 0 \}$ . Then 

(i) $r _ { j k } = 1$ for all $j , k \in S _ { i }$ 

(ii) all states in $S _ { i }$ are recurrent. 

Proof: By the recurrence of i and the strong Markov property, we get for any $j \in S _ { i }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {0 = P _ {i} \Big \{\tau_ {j} <   \infty , \tau_ {i} \circ \theta_ {\tau_ {j}} = \infty \Big \}} \\ & {\quad = P _ {i} \{\tau_ {j} <   \infty \} P _ {j} \{\tau_ {i} = \infty \}} \\ & {\quad = r _ {i j} (1 - r _ {j i}).} \end{array}
$$

Since $r _ { i j } > 0$ by hypothesis, we obtain $r _ { j i } = 1$ . Fixing any m, $n \in \mathsf N$ with $p _ { i j } ^ { m } , p _ { j i } ^ { n } > 0$ , we get by (19) 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E _ {j} \kappa_ {j} \geq \sum_ {s > 0} p _ {j j} ^ {m + n + s} \\ & \quad \geq \sum_ {s > 0} p _ {j i} ^ {n} p _ {i i} ^ {s} p _ {i j} ^ {m} \\ & \quad = p _ {j i} ^ {n} p _ {i j} ^ {m} E _ {i} \kappa_ {i} = \infty , \end{array}
$$

and so $j$ is recurrent by Lemma 11.16. Reversing the roles of i and $j$ gives $r _ { i j } = 1$ . Finally, we get for any $j , k \in S _ { i }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r _ {j k} \geq P _ {j} \Bigl \{\tau_ {i} <   \infty ,   \tau_ {k} \circ \theta_ {\tau_ {i}} <   \infty \Bigr \} \\ = r _ {j i} r _ {i k} = 1. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Proposition 11.20: (i) Use Lemma 11.21. 

(ii) Fix any $i , j \in S$ , and choose m, $n \in { \mathbb N }$ with $p _ { i j } ^ { m } , p _ { j i } ^ { n } > 0$ . By (19), 

$$
p _ {j j} ^ {m + h + n} \geq p _ {j i} ^ {n} p _ {i i} ^ {h} p _ {i j} ^ {m}, \quad h \geq 0.
$$

For $h = 0$ we get $p _ { j j } ^ { m + n } > 0$ , and $\mathrm { s o } ^ { 3 } \ d _ { j } \vert ( m + n )$ . Hence, in general $p _ { i i } ^ { h } > 0$ implies $d _ { j } | h$ , and we get $d _ { j } \ \leq \ d _ { i }$ . Reversing the roles of i and j yields the opposite inequality. 

(iii) Fix any $i \in S$ . Choosing $j \in S$ with $\nu _ { j } > 0$ , and then $n \in \mathsf N$ with $p _ { j i } ^ { n } > 0$ , we see from (15) that even $\nu _ { i } > 0$ ✷ 

We turn to the basic limit theorem for irreducible Markov chains. Related results appear in Chapters 13, 17, and 33. Write $\xrightarrow { u }$ for convergence in the total variation norm $\| \cdot \|$ , and let $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ be the class of probability measures on S. 

Theorem 11.22 (convergence dichotomy, Markov, Kolmogorov, Orey) For an irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain in S, one of these cases occurs: 

(i) There exists a unique invariant distribution ν, the latter satisfies $\nu _ { i } > 0$ for all $i \in S$ , and as $n \to \infty$ , 

$$
P _ {\mu} \circ \theta_ {n} ^ {- 1} \stackrel {u} {\to} P _ {\nu}, \quad \mu \in \hat {\mathcal {M}} _ {S}.\tag{20}
$$

(ii) No invariant distribution exists, and as $n \to \infty$ 2 

$$
p _ {i j} ^ {n} \to 0, i, j \in S.\tag{21}
$$

Markov chains satisfying (i) are clearly recurrent, whereas those in (ii) may be either recurrent or transient. This suggests a further division of the irreducible, aperiodic, and recurrent Markov chains into positive-recurrent and null-recurrent ones, depending on whether (i) or (ii) occurs. 

We shall prove Theorem 11.22 by a simple coupling<sup>4</sup> argument. For our present purposes, an elementary coupling by independence is suficient. 

Lemma 11.23 (coupling) Let X, Y be independent Markov chains in S, T with transition matrices $\left( { { p } _ { i i ^ { \prime } } } \right)$ and $( q _ { j j ^ { \prime } } )$ , respectively. Then 

(i) $( X , Y )$ is a Markov chain in $S \times T$ with transition matrix $r _ { i j , i ^ { \prime } j ^ { \prime } } = p _ { i i ^ { \prime } } q _ { j j ^ { \prime } }$ 

(ii) if X and Y are irreducible, aperiodic, then so is (X, Y), 

(iii) for X, Y as in (ii) with invariant distributions $\mu , \nu _ { ; }$ , the chain $( X , Y )$ is recurrent. 

Proof: (i) Using Proposition 11.2, we may compute the finite-dimensional distributions of (X, Y) for an arbitrary initial distribution $\mu \otimes \nu \ \mathrm { o n } \ S \times T$ 

(ii) For $X , Y$ as stated, fix any $i , i ^ { \prime } \in S$ and $j , j ^ { \prime } \in T$ . Then Proposition 11.18 yields $r _ { i j , i ^ { \prime } j ^ { \prime } } ^ { n } = p _ { i i ^ { \prime } } ^ { n } q _ { j j ^ { \prime } } ^ { n } > 0$ for all but finitely many $n \in { \mathbb N }$ , and so $( X , Y )$ has again the stated properties. 

(iii) Since the product measure $\mu \otimes \nu$ is clearly invariant for $( X , Y )$ , the assertion follows by Proposition 11.17. ✷ 

The point of the construction is that, if the coupled processes eventually meet, their distributions are asymptotically the same. 

Lemma 11.24 (strong ergodicity) For an irreducible, recurrent Markov chain in $S ^ { 2 }$ with transition matrix $p _ { i i ^ { \prime } } p _ { j j ^ { \prime } }$ , we have as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\left\| P _ {\mu} \circ \theta_ {n} ^ {- 1} - P _ {\nu} \circ \theta_ {n} ^ {- 1} \right\|\rightarrow 0, \quad \mu , \nu \in \hat {\mathcal {M}} _ {S}.\tag{22}
$$

Proof (Doeblin): Let X, Y be independent with distributions $P _ { \mu } , P _ { \nu }$ . By Lemma 11.23 the pair (X, Y) is again Markov with respect to the induced filtration ${ \mathcal F } .$ , and by Proposition 11.9 it satisfies the strong Markov property at every finite optional time $\tau$ . Choosing $\tau = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n \geq 0 ; X _ { n } = Y _ { n } \}$ , we get for any measurable set $A \subset S ^ { \infty }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Big \{\theta_ {\tau} X \in A   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Big \} = P _ {X _ {\tau}} A = P _ {Y _ {\tau}} A \\ = P \Big \{\theta_ {\tau} Y \in A   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

In particular, $( \tau , X ^ { \tau } , \theta _ { \tau } X ) \stackrel { d } { = } ( \tau , X ^ { \tau } , \theta _ { \tau } Y )$ . Putting ${ \tilde { X } } _ { n } = X _ { n }$ for $n \leq \tau$ and ${ \tilde { X } } _ { n } = Y _ { n }$ otherwise, we obtain ${ \tilde { X } } { \stackrel { d } { = } } X$ , and so for any A as above, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| P \{\theta_ {n} X \in A \} - P \{\theta_ {n} Y \in A \} \right| \\ \qquad = \left| P \{\theta_ {n} \tilde {X} \in A \} - P \{\theta_ {n} Y \in A \} \right| \\ \qquad = \left| P \Bigl \{\theta_ {n} \tilde {X} \in A,   \tau > n \Bigr \} - P \Bigl \{\theta_ {n} Y \in A,   \tau > n \Bigr \} \right| \\ \qquad \leq P \{\tau > n \} \to 0. \end{array}
$$

The next result ensures the existence of an invariant distribution. Here a coupling argument is again useful. 

Lemma 11.25 (existence) If (21) fails, then an invariant distribution exists. 

Proof: Suppose that (21) fails, so that lim su $\mathrm { l p } _ { n } p _ { i _ { 0 } , j _ { 0 } } ^ { n } > 0$ for some $i _ { 0 } , j _ { 0 } \in S$ By a diagonal argument, we have $p _ { i _ { 0 } , j } ^ { n }  c _ { j }$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ for some constants $c _ { j }$ with $c _ { j 0 } > 0$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < \sum _ { j } c _ { j } \le 1 } \end{array}$ by Fatou’s lemma. 

To extend the convergence to arbitrary i, let X, Y be independent processes with the same transition matrix $( p _ { i j } )$ , and conclude from Lemma 11.23 that $( X , Y )$ is an irreducible Markov chain on $S ^ { 2 }$ with transition probabilities $q _ { i j , i ^ { \prime } j ^ { \prime } } = p _ { i i ^ { \prime } } p _ { j j ^ { \prime } }$ . If (X, Y) is transient, then Proposition 11.16 yields 

$$
\sum_ {n} (p _ {i j} ^ {n}) ^ {2} = \sum_ {n} q _ {i i, j j} ^ {n} <   \infty , \quad i, j \in S,
$$

and (21) follows. The pair $( X , Y )$ is then recurrent, and Lemma 11.24 gives $p _ { i j } ^ { n } - p _ { i _ { 0 } , j } ^ { n } \to 0$ for all $i , j \in I$ . Hence, $p _ { i j } ^ { n } \to c _ { j }$ along $N ^ { \prime }$ for all $i , j$ 

Next conclude from the Chapman–Kolmogorov relation that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} p _ {i k} ^ {n + 1} = \sum_ {j} p _ {i j} ^ {n} p _ {j k} \\ = \sum_ {j} p _ {i j} p _ {j k} ^ {n}, \quad i, k \in S. \end{array}
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ along $N ^ { \prime }$ , and using Fatou’s lemma on the left and dominated convergence on the right, we get 

$$
\sum_ {j} c _ {j} p _ {j k} \leq \sum_ {j} p _ {i j} c _ {k} = c _ {k}, \quad k \in S.\tag{23}
$$

Summing over k gives $\textstyle \sum _ { j } c _ { j } \ \leq \ 1$ on both sides, and so (23) holds with equality. Thus, $\left( c _ { i } \right)$ is invariant, and we may form the invariant distribution $\nu _ { i } = c _ { i } / \textstyle \sum _ { j } c _ { j }$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 11.22: If no invariant distribution exists, then (21) holds by Lemma 11.25. Now let ν be an invariant distribution, and note that $\nu _ { i } > 0$ for all i by Proposition 11.20. By Lemma 11.23 the coupled chain in Lemma 11.24 is irreducible and recurrent, and so (22) holds for any initial distribution $\mu ,$ , and (20) follows since $P _ { \nu } \circ \theta _ { n } ^ { - 1 } = P _ { \nu }$ by Lemma 11.11. If even $\nu ^ { \prime }$ is invariant, then (20) yields $P _ { \nu ^ { \prime } } = P _ { \nu }$ , and so $\nu ^ { \prime } = \nu$ ✷ 

The limits in Theorem 11.22 may be expressed as follows in terms of the mean recurrence times $E _ { j } \tau _ { j }$ 

Theorem 11.26 (mean recurrence times, Kolmogorov) For a Markov chain in $S$ and states $i , j \in S$ with $j$ aperiodic, we have as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
p _ {i j} ^ {n} \rightarrow \frac {P _ {i} \{\tau_ {j} <   \infty \}}{E _ {j} \tau_ {j}}.\tag{24}
$$

Proof: First let $i = j , \ \mathrm { I f } \ j$ is transient, then $p _ { j j } ^ { n }  0$ and $E _ { j } \tau _ { j } = \infty$ , and so (24) is trivially true. If instead $j$ is recurrent, then the restriction of X to the set $S _ { j } = \{ i ; r _ { j i } > 0 \}$ is irreducible and recurrent by Lemma 11.21, and aperiodic by Proposition 11.20. Hence, $p _ { j j } ^ { n }$ converges by Theorem 11.22. 

To identify the limit, define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} L _ {n} = \sup \left\{k \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+};   \tau_ {j} ^ {k} \leq n \right\} \\ = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} 1 \{X _ {k} = j \}, \quad n \in \mathsf {N}. \end{array}
$$

The $\tau _ { j } ^ { n }$ form a random walk under $P _ { j }$ , and so the law of large numbers yields 

$$
\frac {L (\tau_ {j} ^ {n})}{\tau_ {j} ^ {n}} = \frac {n}{\tau_ {j} ^ {n}} \rightarrow \frac {1}{E _ {j} \tau_ {j}} \mathrm{a.s.} P _ {j}.
$$

By the monotonicity of $L _ { k }$ and $\tau _ { j } ^ { n }$ , we obtain $L _ { n } / n \to ( E _ { j } \tau _ { j } ) ^ { - 1 }$ a.s. $P _ { j }$ . Since $L _ { n } \leq n$ , we get by dominated convergence 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} p _ {j j} ^ {k} = \frac {E _ {j} L _ {n}}{n} \rightarrow \frac {1}{E _ {j} \tau_ {j}},
$$

and (24) follows. 

Now let $i \neq j$ . Using the strong Markov property, the disintegration theorem, and dominated convergence, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} p _ {i j} ^ {n} = P _ {i} \{X _ {n} = j \} \\ = P _ {i} \Big \{\tau_ {j} \leq n, (\theta_ {\tau_ {j}} X) _ {n - \tau_ {j}} = j \Big \} \\ = E _ {i} \big (p _ {j j} ^ {n - \tau_ {j}}; \tau_ {j} \leq n \big) \\ \to \frac {P _ {i} \{\tau_ {j} <   \infty \}}{E _ {j} \tau_ {j}}. \end{array}
$$

# Random Walks and Renewal Processes

Recurrence dichotomy and criteria, transience for $d \geq 3$ , Wald equations, first maximum and last return, duality, ladder times and heights, fluctuations, Wiener–Hopf factorization, ladder distributions, boundedness and divergence, stationary renewal process, occupation measure, two-sided renewal theorem, asymptotic delay, renewal equation 

Before turning to the continuous-time Markov chains, we consider the special case of space- and time-homogeneous processes in discrete time, where the increments are independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.), and thus determined by the single one-step distribution $\mu .$ Such processes are known as random walks. The corresponding continuous-time processes are the L´evy processes, to be discussed in Chapter 16. For simplicity, we consider only random walks in Euclidean spaces, though the definition makes sense in an arbitrary measurable group. 

Thus, a random walk in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is defined as a discrete-time random process $X = \left( X _ { n } \right)$ evolving by i.i.d. steps $\xi _ { n } = \Delta X _ { n } = X _ { n } - X _ { n - 1 }$ . For most purposes we may take $X _ { 0 } = 0$ , so that $X _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \ldots + \xi _ { n }$ for all $n .$ . Though random walks may be regarded as the simplest of all Markov chains, they exhibit many basic features of the more general discrete-time processes, and hence may serve as a good introduction to the general subject. We shall further see how random walks enter naturally into the description and analysis of certain continuoustime phenomena. 

Some basic facts about random walks have already been noted in previous chapters. Thus, we proved some simple 0 1 laws in Chapter 4, and in Chapters 5–6 we established the ultimate versions of the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem, both of which deal with the asymptotic behavior of $n ^ { - c } X _ { n }$ for suitable constants $c > 0$ . More sophisticated limit theorems of this kind will be derived in Chapters 22–23 and 30, often through approximation by a Brownian motion or a more general L´evy process. 

Random walks in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ are either recurrent or transient, and our first aim is to derive recurrence criteria in terms of the transition distribution $\mu .$ . We proceed with some striking connections between maxima and return times, anticipating the arcsine laws in Chapters 14 and 22. This is followed by a detailed study of ladder times and heights for one-dimensional random walks, culminating with the Wiener–Hopf factorization and Baxter’s formula. Finally, we prove a two-sided version of the renewal theorem, describing the asymptotic behavior of the occupation measure and its intensity for a transient random walk. 

In addition to the mentioned connections, we note the relevance of renewal theory for the study of continuous-time Markov chains, as considered in Chapter 13. Renewal processes are simple instances of regenerative sets, to be studied in full generality in Chapter 29, in connection with local time and excursion theory. 

To begin our systematic discussion of random walks, assume as before that $X _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ for all $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ , where the $\xi _ { n }$ are i.i.d. random vectors in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . The distribution of $X$ is then determined by the common distribution $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { n } )$ of the increments. By the efective dimension of X we mean the dimension of the linear subspace spanned by the support of $\mu .$ . For most purposes, we may assume that the efective dimension agrees with the dimension of the underlying space, since we may otherwise restrict our attention to the generated subspace. 

A random walk X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is said to be recurrent if lim in $\mathrm { f } _ { n  \infty } \vert X _ { n } \vert = 0$ a.s. and transient if $| X _ { n } | \to \infty { \mathrm { a . s } }$ . In terms of the occupation measure $\begin{array} { r } { \xi = \sum _ { n } \delta _ { X _ { n } } , } \end{array}$ transience means that $\xi$ is a.s. locally finite, and recurrence that $\xi B _ { 0 } ^ { \varepsilon } = \infty \mathrm { a . s }$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , where $B _ { x } ^ { r } = \{ y ; | x - y | < r \}$ . We define the recurrence set $A$ of X as the set of points $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\xi B _ { x } ^ { \varepsilon } = \infty$ a.s. for every $\varepsilon > 0$ 

We now state the basic dichotomy for random walks in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Here the intensity (measure) $E \xi$ of $\xi$ is defined by $( E \xi ) f = E ( \xi f )$ 

Theorem 12.1 (recurrence dichotomy) Let X be a random walk in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with occupation measure $\xi$ and recurrence set A. Then exactly one of these cases occurs: 

(i) X is recurrent with $A = \operatorname { s u p p } E \xi$ , which is then a closed subgroup of $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

(ii) X is transient and $E \xi$ is locally finite. 

Proof: The event $\left| X _ { n } \right| \to \infty$ has probability 0 or 1 by Kolmogorov’s 0 1 law. When $| X _ { n } |  \infty { \mathrm { a . s . } }$ , the Markov property at time m yields for any $m , n \in \mathbb { N }$ and $r > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{| X _ {m} | <   r, \inf _ {k \geq n} | X _ {m + k} | \geq r \Big \} \\ \quad \geq P \Big \{| X _ {m} | <   r, \inf _ {k \geq n} | X _ {m + k} - X _ {m} | \geq 2 r \Big \} \\ \quad = P \{| X _ {m} | <   r \}   P \Big \{\inf _ {k \geq n} | X _ {k} | \geq 2 r \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Noting that the event on the left can occur for at most n diferent values of $m$ , we get 

$$
P \Big \{\inf _ {k \geq n} | X _ {k} | \geq 2 r \Big \} \sum_ {m \geq 1} P \{| X _ {m} | <   r \} <   \infty , \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Since $\left| X _ { k } \right| \to \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ ., the probability on the left is positive for large enough $n ,$ and so for $r > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \xi B _ {0} ^ {r} = E \sum_ {m \geq 1} 1 \{| X _ {m} | <   r \} \\ = \sum_ {m \geq 1} P \{| X _ {m} | <   r \} <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

which shows that $E \xi$ is locally finite. 

Next let $| X _ { n } | \nrightarrow \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , so that $P \{ | X _ { n } | < r \ \mathrm { i . o . } \} \ > \ 0$ for some $r > 0$ Covering $B _ { 0 } ^ { r }$ by finitely many balls $G _ { 1 } , \ldots , G _ { n }$ of radius $\varepsilon / 2 .$ , we conclude that $P \{ X _ { n } \in G _ { k } { \mathrm { ~ i . o . } } \} > 0$ for at least one $k .$ . By the Hewitt–Savage $0 { - } 1$ law, the latter probability is in fact 1. Thus, the optional time $\tau = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n ; X _ { n } \in G _ { k } \}$ is a.s. finite, and so the strong Markov property yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & 1 = P \Bigl \{X _ {n} \in G _ {k} \text {i.o.} \Bigr \} \\ & \quad \leq P \Bigl \{| X _ {\tau + n} - X _ {\tau} | <   \varepsilon \text {i.o.} \Bigr \} \\ & \quad = P \Bigl \{| X _ {n} | <   \varepsilon \text {i.o.} \Bigr \} \\ & \quad = P \{\xi B _ {0} ^ {\varepsilon} = \infty \}, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $0 \in A$ , and X is recurrent. 

The set $S =$ supp $E \xi$ clearly contains A. To prove the converse, fix any $x \in S$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ . By the strong Markov property at $\sigma = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n \geq 0 ; | X _ { n } - x | <$ $\varepsilon / 2 \}$ and the recurrence of $X$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} P \{\xi B _ {x} ^ {\varepsilon} = \infty \} & = P \Big \{| X _ {n} - x | <   \varepsilon \text {i.o.} \Big \} \\ & \geq P \Big \{\sigma <   \infty , | X _ {\sigma + n} - X _ {\sigma} | <   \varepsilon / 2 \text {i.o.} \Big \} \\ & = P \{\sigma <   \infty \} P \Big \{| X _ {n} | <   \varepsilon / 2 \text {i.o.} \Big \} > 0. \end{array}
$$

By the Hewitt–Savage 0 1 law, the probability on the left then equals 1, which means that $x \in A$ . Thus, $S \subset A \subset S$ , and so in this case $A = S$ 

The set $S$ is clearly a closed additive semi-group in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . To see that in this case it is even a group, it remains to show that $x \in S$ implies $- x \in S$ . Defining σ as before and using the strong Markov property, along with the fact that $x \in S \subset A$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \{\xi B _ {- x} ^ {\varepsilon} = \infty \} = P \Big \{| X _ {n} + x | <   \varepsilon \text {i.o.} \Big \} \\ & \qquad = P \Big \{| X _ {\sigma + n} - X _ {\sigma} + x | <   \varepsilon \text {i.o.} \Big \} \\ & \qquad \geq P \Big \{| X _ {\sigma} - x | <   \varepsilon , | X _ {n} | <   \varepsilon / 2 \text {i.o.} \Big \} = 1, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $- x \in A = S$ 

We give some simple suficient conditions for recurrence. 

Theorem 12.2 (recurrence for $d \leq 2 )$ A random walk X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is recurrent under each of these conditions: 

for d = 1: n−<sup>1</sup>X<sub>n</sub> <sup>P</sup> 0, 

$$
\bullet \text {   for   } d = 2: E \xi_ {1} = 0 \text {   and   } E | \xi_ {1} | ^ {2} <   \infty .
$$

For $d = 1$ we recognize the weak law of large numbers, which was char acterized in Theorem 6.17. In particular, the condition holds when $E \xi _ { 1 } = 0$ 

By contrast, $E \xi _ { 1 } \in ( 0 , \infty ]$ implies $X _ { n }  \infty \mathrm { a . s }$ . by the strong law of large numbers, so in that case X is transient. 

Our proof of Theorem 12.2 is based on the following scaling relation<sup>1</sup>. 

Lemma 12.3 (scaling) For a random walk X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ ， 

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 0} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq r \varepsilon \} \leq r ^ {d} \sum_ {n \geq 0} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq \varepsilon \}, \quad r \geq 1, \varepsilon > 0.
$$

Proof: The ball $B _ { 0 } ^ { r \varepsilon }$ may be covered by balls $G _ { 1 } , \ldots , G _ { m }$ of radius $\varepsilon / 2$ , where $m \lesssim r ^ { d }$ . Introducing the optional times $\tau _ { k } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n ; X _ { n } \in G _ { k } \} , k = 1 , \ldots , m$ we see from the strong Markov property that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq r \varepsilon \} & \leq & \sum_ {k, n} P \{X _ {n} \in G _ {k} \} \\ & \leq & \sum_ {k, n} P \bigl \{| X _ {\tau_ {k} + n} - X _ {\tau_ {k}} | \leq \varepsilon ; \tau_ {k} <   \infty \bigr \} \\ & = & \sum_ {k} P \{\tau_ {k} <   \infty \} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq \varepsilon \} \\ & \lesssim & r ^ {d} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq \varepsilon \}. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 12.2 (Chung & Ornstein): $( d = 1 )$ Fix any $\varepsilon > 0$ and $r \geq 1$ , and conclude from Lemma 12.3 that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq \varepsilon \} & \geq & r ^ {- 1} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq r \varepsilon \} \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \bigl \{| X _ {[ r t ]} | \leq r \varepsilon \bigr \} d t. \end{array}
$$

Since the integrand on the right tends to 1 as $r  \infty$ , the integral tends to by Fatou’s lemma, and the recurrence of X follows by Theorem 12.1. 

(d = 2) We may take X to have efective dimension 2, since the 1-dimensional case is already covered by (i). Then the central limit theorem yields $n ^ { - 1 / 2 } X _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \zeta$ for a non-degenerate normal random vector $\zeta .$ . In particular, $P \{ | \zeta | \leq c \} \geq c ^ { 2 }$ for bounded $c > 0$ . Fixing any $\varepsilon > 0$ and $r \geq 1$ , we conclude from Lemma 12.3 that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq \varepsilon \} & \geq & r ^ {- 2} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq r \varepsilon \} \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \bigl \{| X _ {[ r ^ {2} t ]} | \leq r \varepsilon \bigr \} d t. \end{array}
$$

As $r  \infty$ , we get by Fatou’s lemma 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | \leq \varepsilon \} & \gtrsim & \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Bigl \{| \zeta | \leq \varepsilon t ^ {- 1 / 2} \Bigr \} d t \\ & \gtrsim & \varepsilon^ {2} \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} t ^ {- 1} d t = \infty , \end{array}
$$

and the recurrence follows again by Theorem 12.1. 

An exact recurrence criterion can be given in terms of the characteristic function $\hat { \mu }$ of $\mu .$ Here we write $B _ { \varepsilon } = B _ { 0 } ^ { \varepsilon }$ for an open ε-ball around the origin. 

Theorem 12.4 (recurrence criterion, Chung & Fuchs) Let X be a random walk in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ based on a distribution $\mu ,$ and fix an $\varepsilon > 0$ . Then X is recurrent $i f f$ 

$$
\sup _ {0 <   r <   1} \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \Re \frac {1}{1 - r \hat {\mu} _ {t}} d t = \infty .\tag{1}
$$

The proof is based on a classical identity. 

Lemma 12.5 (Parseval) Let μ, ν be probability measures on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with characteristic functions $\hat { \mu } , \hat { \nu }$ . Then 

$$
\int \hat {\mu} d \nu = \int \hat {\nu} d \mu .
$$

Proof: Use Fubini’s theorem. 

ProofofTheorem 12.4: The function $f ( s ) = ( 1 - | s | ) _ { + }$ has Fourier transform $\hat { f } ( t ) = { 2 t ^ { - 2 } } ( 1 - \cos t )$ , and so the tensor product $\begin{array} { r } { f ^ { \otimes d } ( s ) = \prod _ { k \leq d } f ( s _ { k } ) } \end{array}$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ has Fourier transform $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { f } ^ { \otimes d } ( t ) = \prod _ { k \le d } \hat { f } ( t _ { k } ) } \end{array}$ . Writing $\mu ^ { * n } = \mathcal { L } ( X _ { n } )$ , we get by Lemma 12.5 for any $a > 0$ and $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ 

$$
\int \hat {f} ^ {\otimes d} (x / a) \mu^ {* n} (d x) = a ^ {d} \int f ^ {\otimes d} (a t) \hat {\mu} _ {t} ^ {n} d t.
$$

By Fubini’s theorem, it follows that for any $r \in ( 0 , 1 )$ 

$$
\int \hat {f} ^ {\otimes d} (x / a) \sum_ {n \geq 0} r ^ {n} \mu^ {* n} (d x) = a ^ {d} \int \frac {f ^ {\otimes d} (a t)}{1 - r \hat {\mu} _ {t}} d t.\tag{2}
$$

Now assume that (1) fails. Putting $\delta = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } d ^ { 1 / 2 }$ , we get by (2) 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {n} P \{| X _ {n} | <   \delta \} & = & \sum_ {n} \mu^ {* n} (B _ {\delta}) \\ & \leq & \int \hat {f} ^ {\otimes d} (x / \delta) \sum_ {n} \mu^ {* n} (d x) \\ & = & \delta^ {d} \sup _ {r <   1} \int \frac {f ^ {\otimes d} (\delta t)}{1 - r \hat {\mu} _ {t}}   d t \\ & \leq & \varepsilon^ {- d} \sup _ {r <   1} \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {d t}{1 - r \hat {\mu} _ {t}} <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

and so X is transient by Theorem 12.1. 

To prove the converse, we note that $\hat { f } ^ { \otimes d }$ has Fourier transform $( 2 \pi ) ^ { d } f ^ { \otimes d } .$ Hence, (2) remains true with f and $\hat { f }$ interchanged, apart from a factor $( 2 \pi ) ^ { d }$ on the left. If X is transient, then for any $\varepsilon > 0$ with $\delta = \varepsilon ^ { - 1 } d ^ { 1 / 2 }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \sup _ {r <   1} \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {d t}{1 - r \hat {\mu} _ {t}} & \lesssim \sup _ {r <   1} \int \frac {\hat {f} ^ {\otimes d} (t / \varepsilon)}{1 - r \hat {\mu} _ {t}} d t \\ & \lesssim \varepsilon^ {d} \int f ^ {\otimes d} (\varepsilon x) \sum_ {n} \mu^ {* n} (d x) \\ & \leq \varepsilon^ {d} \sum_ {n} \mu^ {* n} (B _ {\delta}) <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

When $\mu$ is symmetric in the sense that $\xi _ { 1 } \overset { d } { = } - \xi _ { 1 }$ , then $\hat { \mu }$ is real valued, and the last criterion becomes 1 

$$
\int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {d t}{1 - \hat {\mu} _ {t}} = \infty .
$$

By a symmetrization of $X$ we mean a random walk $\tilde { X } = X - X ^ { \prime }$ , where $X ^ { \prime }$ is an independent copy of X. We may relate the recurrence behavior of $X$ to that of $\tilde { X }$ : 

Corollary 12.6 (symmetrization) Let X be a random walk in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with symmetrization $\tilde { X }$ . Then 

$$
X \text {is recurrent} \Rightarrow \tilde {X} \text {is recurrent.}
$$

Proof: Since clearly $( \Re z ) ( \Re z ^ { - 1 } ) \leq 1$ for any $z \neq 0$ in ${ \mathsf { C } } .$ we get 

$$
\Re \frac {1}{1 - r \hat {\mu} ^ {2}} \leq \frac {1}{1 - r \Re \hat {\mu} ^ {2}} \leq \frac {1}{1 - r | \hat {\mu} | ^ {2}}.
$$

Thus, if $\tilde { X }$ is transient, then so is the random walk $\left( X _ { 2 n } \right)$ by Theorem 12.4. But then $| X _ { 2 n } |  \infty$ a.s. by Theorem 12.1, and so $| X _ { 2 n + 1 } | \to \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . By combination, $\left| X _ { n } \right| \to \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , which means that X is transient. ✷ 

The following suficient conditions for recurrence or transience are often useful for applications: 

Corollary 12.7 (suficient conditions) Let X be a random walk in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and fix any $\varepsilon > 0$ . Then 

$$
\int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \Re \frac {1}{1 - \hat {\mu} _ {t}} d t = \infty \Rightarrow X i s r e c u r r e n t,
$$

$$
\mathrm{(ii)} \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {d t}{1 - \Re \hat {\mu} _ {t}} <   \infty \Rightarrow X i s t r a n s i e n t.
$$

Proof: (i) Under the stated condition, Fatou’s lemma yields for any $r _ { n } \uparrow 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \liminf _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \Re \frac {1}{1 - r _ {n} \hat {\mu}} \geq \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \lim _ {n \to \infty} \Re \frac {1}{1 - r _ {n} \hat {\mu}} \\ = \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \Re \frac {1}{1 - \hat {\mu}} = \infty . \end{array}
$$

Thus, (1) holds and X is recurrent. 

(ii) Let $\mu$ be such as stated. Decreasing $\varepsilon$ if necessary, we may assume that R $\hat { \mu } \geq 0$ on $B _ { \varepsilon }$ . Then as before, 

$$
\int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \Re \frac {1}{1 - r \hat {\mu}} \leq \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {1}{1 - r \Re \hat {\mu}} \leq \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {1}{1 - \Re \hat {\mu}} <   \infty ,
$$

and so (1) fails. Thus, X is transient. 

We may now supplement Theorem 12.2 with some conclusive information for $d \geq 3$ 

Theorem 12.8 (transience for $d \geq 3 )$ Let X be a random walk of efective dimension d. Then 

$$
d \geq 3 \Rightarrow X i s t r a n s i e n t.
$$

Proof: We may take the symmetrized distribution to be d -dimensional, since $\mu$ is otherwise supported by a hyper-plane outside the origin, and the transience follows by the strong law of large numbers. By Corollary 12.6 it is enough to prove that the symmetrized random walk $\tilde { X }$ is transient, and so we may assume that $\mu$ is symmetric. Considering the conditional distributions on $B _ { r }$ and $B _ { r } ^ { c }$ for large enough $r > 0$ , we may write $\mu$ as a convex combination $c \mu _ { 1 } + ( 1 - c ) \mu _ { 2 }$ , where $\mu _ { 1 }$ is symmetric and d -dimensional with bounded support. Writing $( r _ { i j } )$ for the covariance matrix of $\mu _ { 1 }$ , we get as in Lemma 6.9 

$$
\hat {\mu} _ {1} (t) = 1 - \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i, j} r _ {i j} t _ {i} t _ {j} + o (| t | ^ {2}), \quad t \to 0.
$$

Since the matrix $( r _ { i j } )$ is positive definite, it follows that $1 - \hat { \mu } _ { 1 } ( t ) \geq | t | ^ { 2 }$ for small enough t , say for $t \in B _ { \varepsilon }$ . A similar relation then holds for $\hat { \mu } ,$ , and so 

$$
\int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {d t}{1 - \hat {\mu} _ {t}} \leq \int_ {B _ {\varepsilon}} \frac {d t}{| t | ^ {2}} \leq \int_ {0} ^ {\varepsilon} r ^ {d - 3} d r <   \infty .
$$

Thus, X is transient by Theorem 12.4. 

For optional times $\tau _ { : }$ , some moments of $X _ { \tau }$ are the same as $\operatorname { i f } ^ { 2 } X \bot \lfloor \tau$ . Given a discrete filtration ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { : }$ , we say that X is an -random walk, if it is adapted to $\mathcal { F }$ and such that $\mathcal { F } _ { k } \bot \bot \xi _ { k + 1 }$ for all $k$ . 

Theorem 12.9 (Wald equations) Let $X _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ be an -random walk with $E \xi _ { 1 } = \mu$ and $\mathrm { V a r } ( \xi _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 }$ , and let $\tau$ be an -optional time. Then

$$
\begin{array}{l} E X _ {\tau} = E \sum_ {k} \xi_ {k} 1 \{\tau \geq k \} \\ \quad = \sum_ {k} E (\xi_ {k}; \tau \geq k) \\ \quad = \sum_ {k} E \xi_ {k} P \{\tau \geq k \} \\ \quad = \mu \sum_ {k} P \{\tau \geq k \} = \mu E \tau . \end{array}
$$

The general result follows by subtraction of the formulas for random walks with terms $\xi _ { k } ^ { \pm } = ( \pm \xi _ { k } ) \vee 0$ 

(ii) First let $\tau$ be bounded, so that all sums below are finite. Since $\mu = 0$ and $\xi _ { j } 1 \{ \tau \geq k \} \bot \bot \xi _ { k }$ when $j < k$ , we get by Lemma 4.4 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E X _ {\tau} ^ {2} = E \Big (\sum_ {k} \xi_ {k} 1 \{\tau \geq k \} \Big) ^ {2} \\ \quad = E \sum_ {k} \xi_ {k} ^ {2} 1 \{\tau \geq k \} + 2 E \sum_ {j <   k} \xi_ {j} \xi_ {k} 1 \{\tau \geq k \} \\ \quad = \sum_ {k} E \big (\xi_ {k} ^ {2};   \tau \geq k \big) + 2 \sum_ {j <   k} E \big (\xi_ {j}   \xi_ {k};   \tau \geq k \big) \\ \quad = \sum_ {k} E \xi_ {k} ^ {2} P \{\tau \geq k \} + 2 \sum_ {j <   k} E \big (\xi_ {j};   \tau \geq k \big) E \xi_ {k} \\ \quad = \sigma^ {2} \sum_ {k} P \{\tau \geq k \} = \sigma^ {2} E \tau . \end{array}

Similarly, we get for $m \leq n$

(iii) Using Lemma 8.2 (i), and noting that $\mathcal { L } ( \zeta , \tau | \tau ) = \mathcal { L } ( \zeta , t ) _ { t = \tau }$ when $\zeta \perp \perp \tau$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{Var} (X _ {\tau}) = E \operatorname{Var} (X _ {\tau} | \tau) + \operatorname{Var} \bigl \{E (X _ {\tau} | \tau) \bigr \} \\ = E \tau \operatorname{Var} (\xi_ {1}) + \operatorname{Var} (\tau E \xi_ {1}) \\ = \sigma^ {2} E \tau + \mu^ {2} \operatorname{Var} (\tau). \end{array}

We proceed with a detailed study of one-dimensional random walks $X _ { n } =$ $\xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n } , n \in Z _ { + }$ . Say that X is simple if $| \xi _ { 1 } | = 1 \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . For a simple, symmetric random walk X we note that 

$$
u _ {n} \equiv P \{X _ {2 n} = 0 \} = 2 ^ {- 2 n} \binom {2 n} {n}, \quad n \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+}.\tag{3}
$$

First we give a surprising connection between the $u _ { n }$ and the times of last return to the origin. 

Theorem 12.10 (last return, $F e l l e r )$ Let X be a simple, symmetric random walk in $Z ,$ put $\sigma _ { n } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ k \leq n ; X _ { 2 k } = 0 \}$ , and define $u _ { n } \ b y \ ( 3 )$ . Then 

$$
P \{\sigma_ {n} = k \} = u _ {k} u _ {n - k}, \quad 0 \leq k \leq n.

The proof is based on a classical symmetry property, which will also appear in a continuous-time version as Lemma 14.14. 

Lemma 12.11 (reflection principle, Andr´e) For any symmetric random walk X and optional time τ, we have ${ \tilde { X } } { \stackrel { d } { = } } X$ , where 

$$
\tilde {X} _ {n} = X _ {n \wedge \tau} - (X _ {n} - X _ {n \wedge \tau}), \quad n \geq 0.
$$

Proof: We may clearly assume that $\tau < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . Writing $X _ { n } ^ { \prime } = X _ { \tau + n } - X _ { \tau } ,$ $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ , we get by the strong Markov property $X \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ X ^ { \prime } { \bot } \bot ( X ^ { \tau } , \tau )$ , and by symmetry $- X \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ X$ . Hence, by combination $\left( - X ^ { \prime } , X ^ { \tau } , \tau \right) \stackrel { d } { = } \left( X ^ { \prime } , X ^ { \tau } , \tau \right)$ , and the assertion follows by suitable assembly. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 12.10: The Markov property at time 2k yields 

$$
P \{\sigma_ {n} = k \} = P \{X _ {2 k} = 0 \}   P \{\sigma_ {n - k} = 0 \}, \quad 0 \leq k \leq n,
$$

which reduces the proof to the case of $k = 0$ . Thus, it remains to show that 

$$
P \left\{X _ {2} \neq 0, \dots , X _ {2 n} \neq 0 \right\} = P \left\{X _ {2 n} = 0 \right\}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

By the Markov property at time 1, the left-hand side equals 

$$
\frac {1}{2} P \Bigl \{\min _ {k <   2 n} X _ {k} = 0 \Bigr \} + \frac {1}{2} P \Bigl \{\max _ {k <   2 n} X _ {k} = 0 \Bigr \} = P \{M _ {2 n - 1} = 0 \},
$$

where $M _ { n } = \operatorname* { m a x } _ { k \leq n } X _ { k }$ . Using Lemma 12.11 with $\tau = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ k ; X _ { k } = 1 \}$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 1 - P \bigl \{M _ {2 n - 1} = 0 \bigr \} \\ \quad = P \bigl \{M _ {2 n - 1} \geq 1 \bigr \} \\ \quad = P \Bigl \{M _ {2 n - 1} \geq 1,   X _ {2 n - 1} \geq 1 \Bigr \} + P \Bigl \{M _ {2 n - 1} \geq 1,   X _ {2 n - 1} \leq 0 \Bigr \} \\ \quad = P \bigl \{X _ {2 n - 1} \geq 1 \bigr \} + P \bigl \{X _ {2 n - 1} \geq 2 \bigr \} \\ \quad = 1 - P \bigl \{X _ {2 n - 1} = 1 \bigr \} \\ \quad = 1 - P \bigl \{X _ {2 n} = 0 \bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

We continue with a striking connection between the maximum of a symmetric random walk and the last return probabilities in Theorem 12.10. Related results for Brownian motion and more general random walks will appear in Theorems 14.16 and 22.11. 

Theorem 12.12 (first maximum, Sparre-Andersen) Let X be a random walk based on a symmetric, difuse distribution, and put 

$$
M _ {n} = \max _ {k \leq n} X _ {k}, \quad \tau_ {n} = \min \left\{k \geq 0; X _ {k} = M _ {n} \right\}.
$$

Define $\sigma _ { n }$ as in Proposition 12.10, in terms of a simple, symmetric random walk. Then $\tau _ { n } \stackrel { d } { = } \sigma _ { n }$ for every $n \geq 0$ 

Here and below, we will use the relation 

$$
\left(X _ {1}, \dots , X _ {n}\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left(X _ {n} - X _ {n - 1}, \dots , X _ {n} - X _ {0}\right), \quad n \in \mathbb {N},\tag{4}
$$

valid for any random walk X. The formula is obvious from the fact that $( \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } ) \overset { d } { = } \left( \xi _ { n } , \ldots , \xi _ { 1 } \right)$ 

Proof of Theorem 12.12: By the symmetry of X together with (4), we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & v _ {k} \equiv P \{\tau_ {k} = 0 \} \\ & \qquad = P \{\tau_ {k} = k \}, \quad k \geq 0. \end{array}\tag{5}
$$

Hence, the Markov property at time k yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \{\tau_ {n} = k \} = P \{\tau_ {k} = k \}   P \{\tau_ {n - k} = 0 \} \\ = v _ {k}   v _ {n - k}, \qquad \qquad 0 \leq k \leq n. \end{array}\tag{6}
$$

Clearly $\sigma _ { 0 } = \tau _ { 0 } = 0$ . Proceeding by induction, let $\sigma _ { k } \overset { d } { = } \tau _ { k }$ and hence $u _ { k } = v _ { k }$ for all $k < n$ . Comparing (6) with Theorem 12.10 gives 

$$
P \{\sigma_ {n} = k \} = P \{\tau_ {n} = k \}, \quad 0 <   k <   n,
$$

which extends to $0 \leq k \leq n$ by (5). Thus, $\sigma _ { n } \overset { d } { = } \tau _ { n }$ 

For a one-dimensional random walk X, the ascending ladder times $\tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } , . . . .$ are given recursively by 

$$
\tau_ {n} = \inf \Bigl \{k > \tau_ {n - 1}; X _ {k} > X _ {\tau_ {n - 1}} \Bigr \}, n \in \mathsf {N},\tag{7}
$$

starting with $\tau _ { 0 } = 0$ . The associated ascending ladder heights are defined as the random variables $X _ { \tau _ { n } } , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , where $X _ { \infty }$ may be interpreted as $\infty$ . In a similar way, we define the descending ladder times $\tau _ { n } ^ { - }$ and heights $X _ { \tau _ { n } ^ { - } } , n \in \mathsf { N }$ The times $\tau _ { n }$ and $\tau _ { n } ^ { - }$ are clearly optional. By the strong Markov property, the pairs $( \tau _ { n } , X _ { \tau _ { n } } )$ and $( \tau _ { n } ^ { - } , X _ { \tau _ { n } ^ { - } } )$ form possibly terminating random walks in $\bar { \mathsf { R } } ^ { 2 }$ 

Replacing the relation $X _ { k } > X _ { \tau _ { n - 1 } }$ in (7) by $X _ { k } \ge X _ { \tau _ { n - 1 } }$ , we obtain the weak ascending ladder times $\sigma _ { n }$ and heights $X _ { \sigma _ { n } }$ . Similarly, we may introduce the weak descending ladder times $\sigma _ { n } ^ { - }$ and heights $X _ { \sigma _ { n } ^ { - } }$ . The mentioned sequences are connected by a pair of simple but powerful duality<sup>3</sup> relations. 

Lemma 12.13 (duality) Let $\eta , \eta ^ { \prime } , \zeta , \zeta ^ { \prime }$ be the occupation measures of the sequences $( X _ { \tau _ { n } } ) , ( X _ { \sigma _ { n } } ) , \{ X _ { n } ; n < \tau _ { 1 } ^ { - } \}$ , and $\{ X _ { n } ; n < \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { - } \}$ , respectively. Then 

$$
E \eta = E \zeta^ {\prime}, \qquad E \eta^ {\prime} = E \zeta .
$$

Proof: By (4) we have for any $B \in B _ { ( 0 , \infty ) }$ and $n \in \mathsf N$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{X _ {1} \wedge \dots \wedge X _ {n - 1} > 0,   X _ {n} \in B \Big \} \\ \qquad = P \Big \{X _ {1} \vee \dots \vee X _ {n - 1} <   X _ {n} \in B \Big \} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {k} P \Big \{\tau_ {k} = n,   X _ {\tau_ {k}} \in B \Big \}. \end{array}\tag{8}
$$

Summing over $n \geq 1$ gives $E \zeta ^ { \prime } B = E \eta B$ , and the first assertion follows. The proof of the second assertion is similar. ✷ 

The last result yields some remarkable information. Thus, for a simple, symmetric random walk, the expected number of visits to an arbitrary state $k \neq 0$ , before the first return to 0, is constant and equal to 1. In particular, the mean recurrence time is infinite, and so X is a null-recurrent Markov chain. 

The asymptotic behavior of a random walk is related to the expected values of the ladder times: 

Proposition 12.14 (fluctuations and mean ladder times) For a non-degenerate random walk X in R, exactly one of these cases occurs:

In case (iii), all variables $\tau _ { n }$ and $\tau _ { n } ^ { - }$ are finite, and Lemma 12.13 yields $E \sigma _ { 1 } = E \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { - } = \infty$ . ✷ 

Next we explore the relationship between the asymptotic behavior of a random walk and the expected values of $X _ { 1 }$ and $X _ { \tau _ { 1 } }$ . Define $E \gamma = E \gamma ^ { + } - E \gamma ^ { - }$ whenever $E \gamma ^ { + } \wedge E \gamma ^ { - } < \infty$ 

Proposition 12.15 (fluctuations and mean ladder heights) Let X be a nondegenerate random walk in R. Then

Proof: (i) By symmetry, we may assume that lim su $\operatorname { p } _ { n } X _ { n } = \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . If $E \tau _ { 1 } < \infty$ , we may apply the law of large numbers to each of the three ratios in the equation

We proceed with a celebrated factorization, providing some more detailed information about the distributions of ladder times and heights. Here we write $\chi ^ { \pm }$ for the possibly defective distributions of the pairs $( \tau _ { 1 } , X _ { \tau _ { 1 } } )$ and $( \tau _ { 1 } ^ { - } , X _ { \tau _ { 1 } ^ { - } } )$ , respectively, and let $\psi ^ { \pm }$ denote the corresponding distributions of $( \sigma _ { 1 } , X _ { \sigma _ { 1 } } )$ and $( \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { - } , X _ { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { - } } )$ . Put $\chi _ { n } ^ { \pm } = \chi ^ { \pm } ( \{ n \} \times \cdot )$ and $\psi _ { n } ^ { \pm } = \psi ^ { \pm } ( \{ n \} \times \cdot )$ , and define a measure $\chi ^ { 0 }$ on N by

where the second equality holds by (4). 

Theorem 12.16 (Wiener–Hopf factorization) For a random walk in R based on a distribution $\mu$ , we have 

(i)

Proof: (i) Define the measures $\rho _ { 1 } , \rho _ { 2 } , . . . \mathrm { o n } \ ( 0 , \infty )$ by
