$$

Eliminating $\rho$ between the two equations yields the first relation in (i), and the second relation follows by symmetry. 

(ii) Since the restriction of $\psi ^ { + }$ to $( 0 , \infty )$ equals $\psi _ { n } ^ { + } - \chi _ { n } ^ { 0 }$ , we get for any $B \in B _ { ( 0 , \infty ) }$ 

$$
\left(\chi_ {n} ^ {+} - \psi_ {n} ^ {+} + \chi_ {n} ^ {0}\right) B = P \Bigl \{\max _ {k <   n} X _ {k} = 0, X _ {n} \in B \Bigr \}.
$$

Decomposing the event on the right according to the time of first return to $0 ,$ we get C n 1 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \chi_ {n} ^ {+} - \psi_ {n} ^ {+} + \chi_ {n} ^ {0} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n - 1} \chi_ {k} ^ {0} \chi_ {n - k} ^ {+} \\ = (\chi^ {0} * \chi^ {+}) _ {n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}, \end{array}
$$

and so $\chi ^ { + } - \psi ^ { + } + \chi ^ { 0 } = \chi ^ { 0 } * \chi ^ { + }$ , which is equivalent to the ‘plus’ version of (ii). The ‘minus’ version follows by symmetry. ✷ 

The preceding factorization yields an explicit formula for the joint distri bution of first ladder time and height. 

Theorem 12.17 (ladder distributions, Sparre-Andersen, Baxter) Let X be a random walk in R. Then for $| s | < 1$ and $u \geq 0$ , we have 

$$
E s ^ {\tau_ {1}} \exp (- u X _ {\tau_ {1}}) = 1 - \exp \left\{- \sum_ {n \geq 1} \frac {s ^ {n}}{n} E \left(e ^ {- u X _ {n}}; X _ {n} > 0\right) \right\}.\tag{12}
$$

A similar relation holds for $( \sigma _ { 1 } , X _ { \sigma _ { 1 } } )$ , with $X _ { n } > 0$ replaced by $X _ { n } \geq 0$ 

Proof: Consider the mixed generating and characteristic functions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {\chi} _ {s, t} ^ {+} = E s ^ {\tau_ {1}} \mathrm{exp} \Big (i t X _ {\tau_ {1}} \Big), \\ \hat {\psi} _ {s, t} ^ {-} = E s ^ {\sigma_ {1} ^ {-}} \mathrm{exp} \Big (i t X _ {\sigma_ {1} ^ {-}} \Big), \end{array}
$$

and note that the first relation in Theorem 12.16 (i) is equivalent to 

$$
1 - s \hat {\mu} _ {t} = (1 - \hat {\chi} _ {s, t} ^ {+}) (1 - \hat {\psi} _ {s, t} ^ {-}), \quad | s | <   1, t \in \mathsf {R}.
$$

Taking logarithms and expanding in Taylor series, we obtain 

$$
\sum_ {n} n ^ {- 1} (s \hat {\mu} _ {t}) ^ {n} = \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 1} (\hat {\chi} _ {s, t} ^ {+}) ^ {n} + \sum_ {n} n ^ {- 1} (\hat {\psi} _ {s, t} ^ {-}) ^ {n}.
$$

For fixed $s \in ( - 1 , 1 )$ , this equation is of the form $\hat { \nu } = \hat { \nu } ^ { + } + \hat { \nu } ^ { - }$ , where ν and $\nu ^ { \pm }$ are bounded signed measures on $\mathsf { R } , \mathsf { \Omega } ( 0 , \infty )$ , and $( - \infty , 0 ]$ , respectively. By the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions, we get $\nu = \nu ^ { + } + \nu ^ { - }$ . In particular, $\nu ^ { + }$ equals the restriction of ν to $( 0 , \infty )$ . Thus, the corresponding Laplace transforms agree, and (12) follows by summation of a Taylor series for the logarithm. A similar argument yields the formula for $( \sigma _ { 1 } , X _ { \sigma _ { 1 } } )$ ✷ 

The last result yields expressions for the probability that a random walk stays negative or non-positive, as well as criteria for its divergence to $- \infty$ 

Corollary 12.18 (boundedness and divergence) For a random walk $X$ in $\mathsf { R } ,$ 

(i) 

$$
P \{\tau_ {1} = \infty \} = \frac {1}{E \sigma_ {1} ^ {-}} = \exp \left\{- \sum_ {n \geq 1} n ^ {- 1} P \{X _ {n} > 0 \} \right\},\tag{ii}
$$

$$
P \{\sigma_ {1} = \infty \} = \frac {1}{E \tau_ {1} ^ {-}} = \exp \Bigl \{- \sum_ {n \geq 1} n ^ {- 1} P \{X _ {n} \geq 0 \} \Bigr \},
$$

and the a.s. divergence $X _ { n } \to - \infty$ is equivalent to each of the conditions: 

$$
\sum_ {n \geq 1} n ^ {- 1} P \{X _ {n} > 0 \} <   \infty , \quad \sum_ {n \geq 1} n ^ {- 1} P \{X _ {n} \geq 0 \} <   \infty .
$$

Proof: The last expression for $P \{ \tau _ { 1 } = \infty \}$ follows from (12) with $u = 0$ as we let $s \to 1$ . Similarly, the formula for $P \{ \sigma _ { 1 } = \infty \}$ is obtained from the version of (12) for the pair $( \sigma _ { 1 } , X _ { \sigma _ { 1 } } )$ . In particular, $P \{ \tau _ { 1 } = \infty \} > 0$ if the series in (i) converges, and similarly for the condition $P \{ \sigma _ { 1 } = \infty \} > 0$ in terms of the series in (ii). Since both conditions are equivalent to $X _ { n }  - \infty { \mathrm { a . s . } }$ ., the last assertion follows. Finally, the first equalities in (i) and (ii) are obtained most easily from Lemma 12.13, if we note that the number of strict or weak ladder times $\tau _ { n } < \infty \ \mathrm { o r } \ \sigma _ { n } < \infty$ is geometrically distributed. ✷ 

We turn to a detailed study of the occupation measure $\begin{array} { r } { \xi = \sum _ { n > 0 } \delta _ { X _ { n } } } \end{array}$ of a transient random walk in $\mathsf { R } ,$ based on the transition and initial distributions $\mu$ and $\nu .$ Recall from Theorem 12.1 that the associated intensity measure $\begin{array} { r } { E \xi = \nu * \sum _ { n } \mu ^ { * n } } \end{array}$ is locally finite. By the strong Markov property, the sequence $( X _ { \tau + n } - X _ { \tau } )$ has the same distribution for every finite optional time $\tau .$ . Thus, a similar invariance holds for the occupation measure, and the associated intensities agree. A renewal is then said to occur at time $\tau _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ and the whole subject is known as renewal theory. When $\mu$ and $\nu$ are supported by $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , we refer to $\xi$ as a renewal process based on $\mu$ and $\nu ,$ and to $E \xi$ as the associated renewal measure. The standard choice is to take $\nu = \delta _ { 0 }$ , though in general we may also allow a non-degenerate delay distribution $\nu .$ 

The occupation measure $\xi$ is clearly a random measure on $\mathsf { R } ,$ defined as a kernel from Ω to R. By Lemma 15.1 below, the distribution of a random measure on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ is determined by the distributions of the integrals $\textstyle \xi f = \int f d \xi$ , for all $f$ belonging to the space $\hat { C } _ { + } ( \mathsf { R } _ { + } )$ of continuous functions $f \colon { \mathsf { R } } _ { + } \to { \mathsf { R } } _ { + }$ with bounded support. For any measure $\mu$ on R and constant $t \in { \mathsf { R } }$ we define $\theta _ { t } \mu = \mu \circ \theta _ { t } ^ { - 1 }$ with $\theta _ { t } x = x + t$ , so that $( \theta _ { t } \mu ) B = \mu ( B - t )$ and $( \theta _ { t } \mu ) f = \mu ( f \circ \theta _ { t } )$ for any measurable set $B \subset { \mathsf { R } }$ and function $f \geq 0$ . A random measure $\xi$ is said to be stationary if $\theta _ { t } \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

When $\xi$ is a renewal process based on a transition distribution $\mu ,$ , the delayed process $\eta = \delta _ { \alpha } \ast \xi$ is called a stationary version of $\xi$ , if it is stationary on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with the same spacing distribution $\mu .$ . We show that such a version exists whenever $\mu$ has finite mean, in which case ν is uniquely determined by $\mu .$ . Recall that λ denotes Lebesgue measure on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

Theorem 12.19 (stationary renewal process) Let $\xi$ be a renewal process based on a distribution $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with mean $m > 0$ . Then 

(i) $\xi$ has a stationary version η on $\textsf { R + } i f f$ m $< \infty$ , 

(ii) the distribution of η is unique with $E \eta = m ^ { - 1 } \lambda$ and delay distribution 

$$
\nu [ 0, t ] = m ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \mu (s, \infty) d s, \quad t \geq 0,
$$

(iii) $\nu = \mu \textit { i f f } \xi$ is a stationary Poisson process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

Proof, (i) (ii): For a delayed renewal process $\xi$ based on $\mu$ and $\nu ,$ Fubini’s theorem yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \xi = E \sum_ {n \geq 0} \delta_ {X _ {n}} = \sum_ {n \geq 0} \mathcal {L} (X _ {n}) \\ \quad = \sum_ {n \geq 0} \nu * \mu^ {* n} \\ \quad = \nu + \mu * \sum_ {n \geq 0} \nu * \mu^ {* n} \\ \quad = \nu + \mu * E \xi , \end{array}
$$

and so $\nu = ( \delta _ { 0 } - \mu ) * E \xi$ . If $\xi$ is stationary, then $E \xi$ is shift invariant, and Theorem 2.6 yields $E \xi = c \lambda$ for some constant $c > 0$ . Thus, $\nu = c \left( \delta _ { 0 } - \mu \right) \ast \lambda$ 2 and the asserted formula follows with $m ^ { - 1 }$ replaced by $c .$ $\mathrm { A s } \ t  \infty$ , we get $1 = c m$ by Lemma 4.4, which implies $m < \infty$ and $c = m ^ { - 1 }$ 

Conversely, let $m < \infty$ , and choose ν as stated. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \xi = \nu * \sum_ {n \geq 0} \mu^ {* n} \\ \quad = m ^ {- 1} (\delta_ {0} - \mu) * \lambda * \sum_ {n \geq 0} \mu^ {* n} \\ \quad = m ^ {- 1} \lambda * \Big (\sum_ {n \geq 0} \mu^ {* n} - \sum_ {n \geq 1} \mu^ {* n} \Big) = m ^ {- 1} \lambda , \end{array}
$$

which shows that $E \xi$ is invariant. By the strong Markov property, the shifted random measure ${ { \theta } _ { t } } { { \xi } }$ is again a renewal process based on $\mu ,$ , say with delay distribution $\nu _ { t }$ . Since E $\theta _ { t } \xi = \theta _ { t } E \xi$ , we get as before 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \nu_ {t} = (\delta_ {0} - \mu) * (\theta_ {t} E \xi) \\ = (\delta_ {0} - \mu) * E \xi = \nu , \end{array}
$$

which implies $\theta _ { t } \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ , showing that $\xi$ is stationary. 

(iii) By Theorem 13.6 below, $\xi$ is a stationary Poisson process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with rate $c > 0$ , if it is a delayed renewal process based on the exponential distribu tion with mean $c ^ { - 1 }$ , in which case $\mu = \nu$ . Conversely, let $\xi$ be a stationary renewal process based on a common distribution $\mu = \nu$ with mean $m < \infty$ . Then the tail probability $f ( t ) = \mu ( t , \infty )$ satisfies the diferential equation $m f ^ { \prime } { + } f = 0$ with initial condition $f ( 0 ) = 1$ , and so $f ( t ) = e ^ { - t / m }$ , which shows that $\mu = \nu$ is exponential with mean m. As before, $\xi$ is then a stationary Poisson process with rate $m ^ { - 1 }$ ✷ 

The last result yields a similar statement for the occupation measure of a general random walk. 

Corollary 12.20 (stationary occupation measure) Let $\xi$ be the occupation measure of a random walk X in R based on distributions $\mu , \nu ,$ , where $\mu$ has mean $m \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , and $\nu$ is defined as in Theorem 12.19 in terms of the ladder height distribution $\tilde { \mu }$ and its mean $\tilde { m }$ . Then $\xi$ is stationary on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with intensity $m ^ { - 1 }$ 

Proof: Since $X _ { n }  \infty \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., Propositions 12.14 and 12.15 show that the ladder times $\tau _ { n }$ and heights $H _ { n } = X _ { \tau _ { n } }$ have finite mean, and by Proposition 12.19 the renewal process $\zeta = \sum _ { n } \delta _ { H _ { n } }$ is stationary for the prescribed choice of $\nu .$ Fixing $t \geq 0$ and putting $\sigma _ { t } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ n \in Z _ { + } ; X _ { n } \geq t \}$ , we note in particular that $X _ { \sigma _ { t } } \mathrm { ~ - ~ } t$ has distribution $\nu .$ By the strong Markov property at $\sigma _ { t } .$ , the sequence $X _ { \sigma _ { t } + n } - t , n \in Z _ { + }$ , has then the same distribution as $X$ . Since $X _ { k } < t$ for $k < \sigma _ { t }$ , we get $\theta _ { t } \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , which proves the asserted stationarity. 

To identify the intensity, let $\xi _ { n }$ be the occupation measure of the sequence $X _ { k } - H _ { n } , \tau _ { n } \leq k < \tau _ { n + 1 }$ , and note that $H _ { n } \bot \bot \xi _ { n } \overset { d } { = } \xi _ { 0 }$ for each n by the strong Markov property. Hence, Fubini’s theorem yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \xi = E \sum_ {n \geq 0} \xi_ {n} * \delta_ {H _ {n}} \\ \quad = \sum_ {n \geq 0} E (\delta_ {H _ {n}} * E \xi_ {n}) \\ \quad = E \xi_ {0} * E \sum_ {n \geq 0} \delta_ {H _ {n}} \\ \quad = E \xi_ {0} * E \zeta . \end{array}
$$

Noting that $E \zeta = \tilde { m } ^ { - 1 } \lambda$ by Proposition 12.19, that $E \xi _ { 0 } ( 0 , \infty ) = 0$ , and that $\tilde { m } = m E \tau _ { 1 }$ by Proposition 12.15, we get on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

$$
E \xi = \frac {E \xi_ {0} \mathsf {R} _ {-}}{\tilde {m}} \lambda = \frac {E \tau_ {1}}{\tilde {m}} \lambda = m ^ {- 1} \lambda .
$$

We proceed to study the asymptotic behavior of the occupation measure $\xi$ and its intensity $E \xi$ . Under weak restrictions on $\mu _ { ; }$ , we show that ${ \theta } _ { t } \xi$ approaches the stationary version $\tilde { \xi } .$ , whereas $\theta _ { t } E \xi$ is asymptotically proportional to Lebesgue measure. For simplicity, we assume that the mean of $\mu$ exists in $\bar { \mathsf { R } } = [ - \infty , \infty ]$ 

We will use the standard notation for convergence on measure spaces.<sup>4</sup> Thus, for locally finite measures $\nu , \nu _ { 1 } , \nu _ { 2 } , . . . \ \mathrm { o n } \ \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , the vague convergence $\nu _ { n } \ \xrightarrow { v } \ \nu$ means that $\nu _ { n } f \to \nu f$ for all $f \in \hat { C } _ { + } ( \mathsf { R } _ { + } )$ . Similarly, for random measures $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , the distributional convergence $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ is defined by the condition $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \xi f$ for every $f \in \hat { C } _ { + } ( \mathsf { R } _ { + } )$ . A measure $\mu$ on R is said to be non-arithmetic, if the additive subgroup generated by supp $\mu$ is dense in R. 

Theorem 12.21 (two-sided renewal theorem, Blackwell, Feller & Orey) Let $\xi$ be the occupation measure of a random walk X in R based on distributions $\mu$ and $\nu _ { ; }$ , where $\mu$ is non-arithmetic with mean $m \in \bar { \mathsf { R } } \setminus \{ 0 \}$ . (i) $\theta _ { t } \xi \xrightarrow { v d } \tilde { \xi } ,$ 

(ii) $\theta _ { t } E \xi \stackrel { v } {  } E \tilde { \xi } = ( m ^ { - 1 } \vee 0 ) \lambda .$

Lemma 12.22 (asymptotic delay) For X as in Theorem 12.21 with $m \in$ $( 0 , \infty )$ , let $\nu _ { t }$ be the distribution of the first ladder heigh $\ell \geq 0$ of the sequence $X - t$ . Then $\nu _ { t } \stackrel { w } { \to } \tilde { \nu }$ as $t \to \infty$

The preceding theory may be used to study the renewal equation $F =$ $f + F * \mu$ , which often arises in applications. Here the convolution $F * \mu$ is defined by t

$$

where $h > 0$ and $a _ { 1 } , a _ { 2 } , \dotsc \in { \textsf { R } }$ . A measurable function f on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ is said to be directly Riemann integrable, if $\lambda | f | < \infty$ , and there exist some regular step functions $f _ { n } ^ { \pm }$ with $f _ { n } ^ { - } \leq f \leq f _ { n } ^ { + }$ and $\lambda ( f _ { n } ^ { + } - f _ { n } ^ { - } ) \to 0$ 

Theorem 12.24 (renewal equation) Consider a distribution $\mu \ne \delta _ { 0 }$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with associated renewal measure $\bar { \mu }$ and a locally bounded, measurable function $f$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ . Then 

(i) equation $F = f + F * \mu$ has the unique, locally bounded solution $F = f * \bar { \mu }$ , 

(ii) when f is directly Riemann integrable and $\mu$ is non-arithmetic with mean m, we have 

$$
F _ {t} \rightarrow m ^ {- 1} \lambda f, t \rightarrow \infty .
$$

Proof: (i) Iterating the renewal equation gives 

$$
F = \sum_ {k <   n} f * \mu^ {* k} + F * \mu^ {* n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{14}
$$

Since $\mu ^ { * n } [ 0 , t ] \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ for fixed $t \geq 0$ by the weak law of large numbers, we have $F * \mu ^ { * n } \to 0$ for any locally bounded F. If even $f$ is locally bounded, then by (14) and Fubini’s theorem, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} F = \sum_ {k \geq 0} f * \mu^ {* k} \\ = f * \sum_ {k \geq 0} \mu^ {* k} = f * \bar {\mu}. \end{array}
$$

Conversely, $f + f * \bar { \mu } * \mu = f * \bar { \mu }$ , which shows that $F = f * { \bar { \mu } }$ solves the given equation. 

(ii) Let $\mu$ be non-arithmetic. If f is a regular step function as in (13), then by Theorem 12.21 and dominated convergence, we get as $t \to \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} F _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} f (t - s)   \bar {\mu} (d s) \\ = \sum_ {j \geq 1} a _ {j}   \bar {\mu} \Big \{(0, h ] + t - j h \Big \} \\ \to m ^ {- 1} h \sum_ {j \geq 1} a _ {j} = m ^ {- 1} \lambda f. \end{array}
$$

In general, we may introduce some regular step functions $f _ { n } ^ { \pm }$ with $f _ { n } ^ { - } \leq f \leq f _ { n } ^ { + }$ and $\lambda ( f _ { n } ^ { + } - f _ { n } ^ { - } ) \to 0$ , and note that 

$$
(f _ {n} ^ {-} * \bar {\mu}) _ {t} \leq F _ {t} \leq (f _ {n} ^ {+} * \bar {\mu}) _ {t}, \quad t \geq 0, n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Letting $t \to \infty$ and then $n \to \infty$ , we obtain $F _ { t }  m ^ { - 1 } \lambda f$

# Jump-Type Chains and Branching Processes

Strong Markov property, renewals in Poisson process, rate kernel, embedded Markov chain, existence and explosion, compound and pseudo-Poisson processes, backward equation, invariant distribution, convergence dichotomy, mean recurrence times, Bienaym´e process, extinction and asymptotics, binary splitting, Brownian branching tree, genealogy and Yule tree, survival rate and distribution, difusion approximation 

After our detailed study of discrete-time Markov chains in Chapter 11, we turn our attention to the corresponding processes in continuous time, where the paths are taken to be piecewise constant apart from isolated jumps. The evolution of the process is then governed by a rate kernel α, determining both the rate at which transitions occur and the associated transition probabilities. For bounded α we get a pseudo-Poisson process, which may be described as a discrete-time Markov chain with transition times given by an independent, homogeneous Poisson process. 

Of special interest is the space-homogeneous case of compound Poisson processes, where the underlying Markov chain is a random walk. In Chapter 17 we show how every Feller process can be approximated in a natural way by a sequence of pseudo-Poisson processes, characterized by the boundedness of their generators. A similar compound Poisson approximation of general L´evy processes plays a basic role in Chapter 16. 

The chapter ends with a brief introduction to branching processes in discrete and continuous time. In particular, we study the extinction probability and asymptotic population size, and identify the ancestral structure of a critical Brownian branching tree in terms of a suitable Yule process. For a critical Bienaym´e process, we further derive the asymptotic survival rate and distribution, and indicate how a suitably scaled version can be approximated by a Feller difusion. The study of spatial branching processes will be resumed in Chapter 30. 

A process X in a measurable space (S, ) is said to be of pure jump-type, if its paths are a.s. right-continuous and constant apart from isolated jumps. We may then denote the jump times of X by $\tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } , . . . ,$ , with the understanding that $\tau _ { n } = \infty$ if there are fewer than n jumps. By a simple approximation based on Lemma 9.3, the times $\tau _ { n }$ are optional with respect to the right-continuous filtration $\mathcal { F } = \left( \mathcal { F } _ { t } \right)$ induced by X. For convenience we may choose X to be the identity map on the canonical path space Ω. When X is Markov, we write $P _ { x }$ for the distribution with initial state $x ,$ and note that the mapping $x \mapsto P _ { x }$ is a kernel from (S, ) to $\left( \Omega , \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } \right)$ 

We begin our study of pure jump-type Markov processes by proving an extension of the elementary strong Markov property in Proposition 11.9. A further extension appears as Theorem 17.17. 

Theorem 13.1 (strong Markov property, Doob) A pure jump-type Markov process satisfies the strong Markov property at every optional time. 

Proof: For any optional time $\tau ,$ , we may choose some optional times $\sigma _ { n } \geq$ $\tau + 2 ^ { - n }$ taking countably many values, such that $\sigma _ { n }  \mathrm { ~ } \tau \mathrm { ~ a . s ~ }$ . When $A \in$ $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau } \cap \{ \tau < \infty \}$ and $B \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty }$ , we get by Proposition 11.9 

$$
P \Bigl \{\theta_ {\sigma_ {n}} X \in B; A \Bigr \} = E \Bigl (P _ {X _ {\sigma_ {n}}} B; A \Bigr).\tag{1}
$$

The right-continuity of X yields $P \{ X _ { \sigma _ { n } } \neq X _ { \tau } \}  0$ . If B depends on finitely many coordinates, it is also clear that 

$$
P \Big (\{\theta_ {\sigma_ {n}} X \in B \} \triangle \{\theta_ {\tau} X \in B \} \Big) \to 0, \quad n \to \infty .
$$

Hence, (1) remains true for such sets B with $\sigma _ { n }$ replaced by $\tau .$ , and the relation extends to the general case by a monotone-class argument. ✷ 

We now examine the structure of a general pure jump-type Markov process. Here the crucial step is to determine the distributions associated with the first jump, occurring at time $\tau _ { 1 }$ . A random variable $\gamma \geq 0$ is said to be exponentially distributed if $P \{ \gamma > t \} = e ^ { c t } , t \ge 0$ , for a constant $c > 0$ , in which case $\begin{array} { r } { E \gamma = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } e ^ { - c t } d t \stackrel { \cdot } { = } c ^ { - 1 } } \end{array}$ . Say that a state $x \in S$ is absorbing if 

$$
P _ {x} \{X \equiv x \} = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {1} = \infty \} = 1.
$$

Lemma 13.2 (first jump) Let X be a pure jump-type Markov process, and fix a non-absorbing state x. Then under $P _ { x }$ 

(i) $\tau _ { 1 }$ is exponentially distributed, 

(ii) $\theta _ { \tau _ { 1 } } X \bot \bot \tau _ { 1 }$ 

Proof: (i) Put $\tau _ { 1 } = \tau$ . By the Markov property at fixed times, we get for any $s , t \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r} P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau > s + t \bigr \} = P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau > s, \tau \circ \theta_ {s} > t \bigr \} \\ = P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau > s \bigr \} P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau > t \bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

This is a Cauchy equation in s and t, whose only non-increasing solutions are of the form $P _ { x } \{ \tau > t \} = e ^ { - c t }$ with $c \in [ 0 , \infty ]$ . Since x is non-absorbing and $\tau > 0$ a.s., we have $c \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , and so τ is exponentially distributed with parameter c. 

(ii) 

(ii) By the Markov property at fixed times, we get for any $B \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty }$ Q 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P _ {x} \Bigl \{\tau > t,   \theta_ {\tau} X \in B \Bigr \} = P _ {x} \Bigl \{\tau > t,   (\theta_ {\tau} X) \circ \theta_ {t} \in B \Bigr \} \\ = P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau > t \bigr \}   P _ {x} \Bigl \{\theta_ {\tau} X \in B \Bigr \}, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\tau \bot \bot \theta _ { \tau } X$ 

Writing $X _ { \infty } = x$ when X eventually gets absorbed at $x ,$ we define the rate function c and jump transition kernel $\mu$ by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} c (x) = (E _ {x} \tau_ {1}) ^ {- 1}, \\ \mu (x, B) = P _ {x} \{X _ {\tau_ {1}} \in B \}, \qquad x \in S, B \in \mathcal {S}, \end{array}
$$

combined into a rate kernel $\alpha = c \mu _ { ; }$ , or 

$$
\alpha (x, B) = c (x) \mu (x, B), \quad x \in S, B \in \mathcal {S}.
$$

The required measurability follows from that for the kernel $( P _ { x } )$ . Assuming in addition that $\mu ( x , \cdot ) = \delta _ { x }$ when $\alpha ( x , \cdot ) = 0$ , we may reconstruct $\mu$ from $\alpha _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , so that $\mu$ becomes a measurable function of $\alpha$ . 

We proceed to show how $X$ can be represented in terms of a discrete-time Markov chain and an independent sequence of exponential random variables. In particular, we will see how the distributions $P _ { x }$ are uniquely determined by the rate kernel $\alpha .$ . In the sequel, we always assume the existence of the required randomization variables. 

Theorem 13.3 (embedded Markov chain) For a pure jump-type Markov process X with rate kernel $\alpha = c \mu$ , there exist a Markov chain Y on $Z _ { + }$ with transition kernel $\mu$ and some i.i.d., exponential random variables $\gamma _ { 1 } , \gamma _ { 2 } , \ldots \ldots Y$ with mean 1, such that a.s. for all $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ , 

(i) $X _ { t } = Y _ { n } , \ : \ : \ : t \in [ \tau _ { n } , \tau _ { n + 1 } ) ,$ 

$$
\tau_ {n} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\gamma_ {k}}{c (Y _ {k - 1})}.
$$

Proof: Let $\tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } , . . . .$ . be the jump times of $X ,$ , and put $\tau _ { 0 } = 0$ , so that (i) holds with $Y _ { n } ~ = ~ X _ { \tau _ { n } }$ for $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ . Introduce some i.i.d., exponentially distributed random variables $\gamma _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , \gamma _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } , \ldots . \perp$ X with mean 1, and define for $n \in { \mathbb N }$ 

$$
\gamma_ {n} = \left(\tau_ {n} - \tau_ {n - 1}\right) c (Y _ {n})   1 \{\tau_ {n - 1} <   \infty \} + \gamma_ {n} ^ {\prime}   1 \Bigl \{c (Y _ {n}) = 0 \Bigr \}.
$$

By Lemma 13.2, we get for any $t \geq 0 , \ B \in { \mathcal { S } }$ , and $x \in S$ with $c ( x ) > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P _ {x} \Bigl \{\gamma_ {1} > t, Y _ {1} \in B \Bigr \} = P _ {x} \Bigl \{\tau_ {1} c (x) > t, Y _ {1} \in B \Bigr \} \\ = e ^ {- t} \mu (x, B), \end{array}
$$

which clearly remains true when $c ( x ) = 0$ . By the strong Markov property, we obtain for any n, a.s. on $\{ \tau _ { n } < \infty \}$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P _ {x} \Big \{\gamma_ {n + 1} > t, Y _ {n + 1} \in B   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau_ {n}} \Big \} = P _ {Y _ {n}} \Big \{\gamma_ {1} > t, Y _ {1} \in B \Big \} \\ = e ^ {- t} \mu (Y _ {n}, B). \end{array}\tag{2}
$$

The strong Markov property also gives $\tau _ { n + 1 } < \infty$ a.s. on the set $\{ \tau _ { n } < \infty ,$ $c ( Y _ { n } ) > 0 \}$ . Arguing recursively, we get $\{ c ( Y _ { n } ) = 0 \} = \{ \tau _ { n + 1 } = \infty \}$ a.s., and (ii) follows. The same relation shows that (2) remains a.s. true on $\{ \tau _ { n } = \infty \}$ , and in both cases we may replace $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau _ { n } }$ by $\mathcal { G } _ { n } = \mathcal { F } _ { \tau _ { n } } \vee \sigma \{ \gamma _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } , . ~ . ~ . ~ , \gamma _ { n } ^ { \prime } \}$ . Thus, the pairs $( \gamma _ { n } , Y _ { n } )$ form a discrete-time Markov chain with the desired transition kernel. By Proposition 11.2, the latter property along with the initial distribution determine uniquely the joint distribution of $Y$ and $( \gamma _ { n } )$ ✷ 

In applications we are often faced with the converse problem of constructing a Markov process X with a given rate kernel $\alpha .$ . Then write $\alpha ( x , B ) =$ $c ( \boldsymbol { x } ) \mu ( \boldsymbol { x } , B )$ for some rate function $c \colon S \to { \mathsf { R } } _ { + }$ and transition kernel $\mu$ on $S _ { i }$ such that $\mu ( x , \cdot ) = \delta _ { x }$ when $c ( x ) = 0$ and otherwise $\mu ( x , \{ x \} ) = 0$ . If X does exist, it may clearly be constructed as in Theorem 13.3. The construction fails when $\zeta \equiv \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } \tau _ { n } < \infty$ , in which case an explosion is said to occur at time $\zeta .$ 

Theorem 13.4 (synthesis) For a finite kernel $\alpha = c \mu$ on $S$ with $\alpha ( \boldsymbol { x } , \{ \boldsymbol { x } \} )$ $\equiv 0$ , let Y be a Markov chain in S with transition kernel $\mu _ { ; }$ , and let $\gamma _ { 1 } , \gamma _ { 2 } , \ldots$ $\perp Y$ be i.i.d., exponential random variables with mean 1. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { n } \gamma _ { n } / c ( Y _ { n - 1 } ) = \infty \ a . s } \end{array}$ . under every initial distribution for Y, 

(ii) there exists a pure jump-type Markov process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with rate kernel α. 

Proof: Assuming (i), let $P _ { x }$ be the joint distribution of the sequences $Y =$ $( Y _ { n } )$ and $\Gamma = ( \gamma _ { n } )$ when $Y _ { 0 } = x$ . Regarding $( Y , \Gamma )$ as the identity map on the canonical space $\Omega = ( S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + } ) ^ { \infty }$ , we may construct X from $( Y , \Gamma )$ as in Theorem 13.3, where $X _ { t } = x _ { 0 }$ is arbitrary for $t \geq \operatorname { s u p } _ { n } \tau _ { n } .$ , and introduce the filtrations ${ \mathcal G } = ( { \mathcal G } _ { n } )$ induced by $( Y , \gamma )$ and $\mathcal { F } = \left( \mathcal { F } _ { t } \right)$ induced by X. We need to verify the Markov property $\mathcal { L } _ { x } ( \theta _ { t } X \vert \mathcal { F } _ { t } ) = \mathcal { L } _ { X _ { t } } ( X )$ for the distributions under $P _ { x }$ and $P _ { X _ { t } }$ , since the rate kernel can then be identified via Theorem 13.3. 

For any $t \geq 0$ and $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ , put 

$$
\kappa = \sup \{k; \tau_ {k} \leq t \}, \quad \beta = (t - \tau_ {n}) c (Y _ {n}),
$$

and define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} T ^ {m} (Y, \Gamma) = \bigl \{(Y _ {k}, \gamma_ {k + 1}); k \geq m \bigr \}, \\ (Y ^ {\prime}, \Gamma^ {\prime}) = T ^ {n + 1} (Y, \Gamma), \qquad \gamma^ {\prime} = \gamma_ {n + 1}. \end{array}
$$

Since clearly 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {t} = \mathcal {G} _ {n} \vee \sigma \{\gamma^ {\prime} > \beta \} \mathrm{on} \{\kappa = n \},
$$

it sufices by Lemma 8.3 to prove that 

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {x} \left\{\left(Y ^ {\prime}, \Gamma^ {\prime}\right); \gamma^ {\prime} - \beta > r \mid \mathcal {G} _ {n}, \gamma^ {\prime} > \beta \right\} = \mathcal {L} _ {Y _ {n}} \left\{T (Y, \Gamma); \gamma_ {1} > r \right\}.
$$

Noting that $( Y ^ { \prime } , \Gamma ^ { \prime } ) \bot \bot \mathcal { G } _ { n } ( \gamma ^ { \prime } , \beta )$ since $\gamma ^ { \prime } \bot \bot ( { \mathcal { G } } _ { n } , Y ^ { \prime } , \Gamma ^ { \prime } )$ , we see that the left-hand side equals 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathcal {L} _ {x} \big \{(Y ^ {\prime} , \Gamma^ {\prime}) ;   \gamma^ {\prime} - \beta > r   \big |   \mathcal {G} _ {n} \big \}}{P _ {x} \{\gamma^ {\prime} > \beta   |   \mathcal {G} _ {n} \}} = \mathcal {L} _ {x} \left\{(Y ^ {\prime}, \Gamma^ {\prime})   \big |   \mathcal {G} _ {n} \right\} \frac {P _ {x} \{\gamma^ {\prime} - \beta > r   |   \mathcal {G} _ {n} \}}{P _ {x} \{\gamma^ {\prime} > \beta   |   \mathcal {G} _ {n} \}} \\ = (P _ {Y _ {n}} \circ T ^ {- 1})   e ^ {- r}, \end{array}
$$

as required. 

To complete the picture, we need a convenient criterion for non-explosion. 

Proposition 13.5 (explosion) For any rate kernel α and initial state $x ,$ , let $( Y _ { n } )$ and $\left( \tau _ { n } \right)$ be such as in Theorem 13.3. Then a.s. 

$$
\tau_ {n} \rightarrow \infty \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \sum_ {n} \frac {1}{c (Y _ {n})} = \infty .\tag{3}
$$

In particular, $\tau _ { n }  \infty \ a . s$ . when x is recurrent for $( Y _ { n } )$ 

Proof: Write $\beta _ { n } = \{ c ( Y _ { n - 1 } ) \} ^ { - 1 }$ . Noting that $E e ^ { - u \gamma _ { n } } = ( 1 + u ) ^ { - 1 }$ for all $u \geq 0$ , we get by Theorem 13.3 (ii) and Fubini’s theorem 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E (e ^ {- u \zeta} | Y) = \prod_ {n} (1 + u \beta_ {n}) ^ {- 1} \\ \qquad = \exp \Bigl \{- \sum_ {n} \log (1 + u \beta_ {n}) \Bigr \} \text {a.s.} \end{array}\tag{4}
$$

Since $\frac { 1 } { 2 } ( r \wedge 1 ) \leq \log ( 1 + r ) \leq r$ for all $r > 0$ , the series on the right converges for every $u > 0$ if $\textstyle \sum _ { n } { \beta _ { n } } < \infty$ . Letting $u \to 0$ in (4), we get by dominated convergence 

$$
P (\zeta <   \infty | Y) = 1 \left\{\sum_ {n} \beta_ {n} <   \infty \right\} \text {a.s.},
$$

which implies (3). If x is visited infinitely often, the series $\textstyle \sum _ { n } \beta _ { n }$ has infinitely many terms $c _ { x } ^ { - 1 } > 0$ , and the last assertion follows. ✷ 

The simplest and most basic pure jump-type Markov processes are the homogeneous Poisson processes, which are space and time homogeneous processes of this kind starting at 0 and proceeding by unit jumps. Here we define a stationary Poisson process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with rate $c > 0$ as a simple point process $\xi$ with stationary, independent increments, such that $\xi [ 0 , t )$ is Poisson distributed with mean c t. To prove the existence, we may use generating functions to see that the Poisson distributions $\mu _ { t }$ with mean t satisfy the semi-group property $\mu _ { s } * \mu _ { t } = \mu _ { s + t }$ . The desired existence now follows by Theorem 8.23. 

Theorem 13.6 (stationary Poisson process, Bateman) Let ξ be a simple point process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with points $\tau _ { 1 } < \tau _ { 2 } < \cdots$ , and put $\tau _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi$ is a stationary Poisson process, 

(ii) $\xi$ has stationary, independent increments,

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ : Under (ii), Theorem 11.5 shows that $X _ { t } = \xi [ 0 , t ] , t \geq 0$ , is a space- and time-homogeneous Markov process of pure jump type, and so by Lemma 13.2, $\tau _ { 1 }$ is exponential and independent of $\theta _ { \tau _ { 1 } } \xi .$ . $$

$$

By a pseudo-Poisson process in a measurable space $S$ we mean a process of the form $X = Y \circ N$ a.s., where $Y$ is a discrete-time Markov process in $S$ and N Y is an homogeneous Poisson process. Letting $\mu$ be the transition kernel of Y and writing c for the constant rate of $N$ , we may construct a kernel 

$$
\alpha (x, B) = c \mu \bigl (x, B \setminus \{x \} \bigr), \quad x \in S, B \in \mathcal {S},\tag{5}
$$

which is measurable since $\mu ( x , \{ x \} )$ is a measurable function of x. We may characterize pseudo-Poisson processes in terms of the rate kernel: 

Proposition 13.7 (pseudo-Poisson process, Feller) For a process X in a Borel space S, these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $X = Y \circ N$ a.s. for a discrete-time Markov chain Y in S with transition 

kernel $\mu$ and a Poisson process N Y with constant rate $c > 0$ , 

(ii) X is a pure jump-type Markov process with bounded rate kernel α. 

In that case, we may choose α and $( \mu , c )$ to be related by (5). 

Proof, ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ : Assuming (i), write $\tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } , . . . .$ for the jump times of N, and let $\mathcal { F }$ be the filtration induced by the pair $( X , N )$ . As in Theorem 13.4, we see that X is -Markov. To identify the rate kernel $\alpha _ { \mathrm { { : } } }$ , fix any initial state $x ,$ and note that the first jump of X occurs at the time $\tau _ { n }$ when $Y _ { n }$ first leaves x. For each transition of $Y$ , this happens with probability $p _ { x } = \mu ( x , \{ x \} ^ { c } )$ . By Proposition 15.3, the time until first jump is then exponentially distributed with parameter $c p _ { x }$ . If $p _ { x } \ > \ 0$ , the position of X after the first jump has distribution $p _ { x } ^ { - 1 } \mu ( x , \cdot \setminus \{ x \} )$ . Thus, α is given by (5). 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Assuming (ii), put $r _ { x } = \alpha ( x , S )$ and $c = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { x } r _ { x }$ , and note that the kernel 

$$
\mu (x, \cdot) = c ^ {- 1} \Bigl \{\alpha (x, \cdot) + (c - r _ {x})   \delta_ {x} \Bigr \}, \quad x \in S,
$$

satisfies (5). Thus, if $X ^ { \prime } = Y ^ { \prime } \circ N ^ { \prime }$ is a pseudo-Poisson process based on $\mu$ and $c ,$ then $X ^ { \prime }$ is again Markov with rate kernel $\alpha ,$ and so $X \ { \stackrel { d } { = } } \ X ^ { \prime }$ . Hence, Corollary 8.18 yields $X = Y \circ N$ a.s. for a pair $( Y , N ) \overset { d } { = } ( Y ^ { \prime } , N ^ { \prime } )$ ✷ 

If the underlying Markov chain Y is a random walk in a measurable Abelian group $S _ { ; }$ , then $X = Y \circ N$ is called a compound Poisson process. Thus, the distribution of $X - X _ { 0 }$ is determined by the characteristic measure<sup>1</sup> $\nu = c \mu$ , where c is the rate of the jump-time process and $\mu$ is the common jump distribution. 

Compound Poisson processes may be characterized analytically in terms of the rate kernel, and probabilistically in terms of the increments of the process. A kernel α on $S$ is said to be invariant if $\alpha _ { x } = \alpha _ { 0 } \circ \theta _ { x } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { o r } \alpha ( x , B ) = \alpha ( 0 , B - x )$ for all x and B. We also say that a process X in S has independent increments if $X _ { t } - X _ { s } \bot \bot \{ X _ { r } ; r \leq s \}$ for all $s < t$ 

Corollary 13.8 (compound Poisson process) For a pure jump-type process X in a measurable Abelian group, these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) X is Markov with invariant rate kernel,

We now derive a combined diferential and integral equation for the transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ . An abstract version of this result appears in Theorem 17.6. For any measurable and suitably integrable function $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ , we define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} T _ {t} f (x) = \int f (y)   \mu_ {t} (x, d y) \\ \qquad = E _ {x} f (X _ {t}), \quad x \in S, t \geq 0. \end{array}
$$

Theorem 13.9 (backward equation, Kolmogorov) Let α be the rate kernel of a pure jump-type Markov process in S, and fix a bounded, measurable function $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ . Then $T _ { t } f ( x )$ is continuously diferentiable in t for fixed x, and 

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial t} T _ {t} f (x) = \int \alpha (x, d y) \left\{T _ {t} f (y) - T _ {t} f (x) \right\}, \quad t \geq 0, x \in S.
$$

(6) 

Proof: Put $\tau = \tau _ { 1 }$ , and let $x \in S$ and $t \geq 0$ . By the strong Markov property at $\sigma = \tau \wedge t$ and Theorem 8.5, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & T _ {t} f (x) = E _ {x} f (X _ {t}) = E _ {x} f \bigl \{(\theta_ {\sigma} X) _ {t - \sigma} \bigr \} \\ & \qquad = E _ {x} T _ {t - \sigma} f (X _ {\sigma}) \\ & \qquad = f (x) P _ {x} \{\tau > t \} + E _ {x} \bigl \{T _ {t - \tau} f (X _ {\tau}); \tau \leq t \bigr \} \\ & \qquad = f (x) e ^ {- t c _ {x}} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- s c _ {x}} d s \int \alpha (x, d y) T _ {t - s} f (y), \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
e ^ {t c _ {x}} T _ {t} f (x) = f (x) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {s c _ {x}} d s \int \alpha (x, d y) T _ {s} f (y).\tag{7}
$$

Here the use of the disintegration theorem is justified by the fact that $X ( \omega , t )$ is product measurable on $\Omega \times \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , by the right continuity of the paths. 

From (7) we see that $T _ { t } f ( x )$ is continuous in t for each $x ,$ and so by dominated convergence the inner integral on the right is continuous in s. Hence, $T _ { t } f ( x )$ is continuously diferentiable in t, and (6) follows by an easy computation. ✷ 

Next we show how the invariant distributions of a pure jump-type Markov process are related to those of the embedded Markov chain. 

Proposition 13.10 (invariant measures) Let the processes X, Y be related as in Theorem 13.3, and fix a probability measure ν on $S$ with $\textstyle { \int c d \nu < \infty }$ Then 

ν is invariant for $X \quad \iff \quad c \cdot \nu$ is invariant for Y. 

Proof: By Theorem 13.9 and Fubini’s theorem, we have for any bounded measurable function $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ 

$$
E _ {\nu} f (X _ {t}) = \int f (x) \nu (d x) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} d s \int \nu (d x) \int \alpha (x, d y) \left\{T _ {s} f (y) - T _ {s} f (x) \right\}.
$$

Thus, ν is invariant for X if the second term on the right is identically zero. Now (6) shows that $T _ { t } f ( x )$ is continuous in t, and by dominated convergence this remains true for the integral 

$$
I _ {t} = \int \nu (d x) \int \alpha (x, d y) \left\{T _ {t} f (y) - T _ {t} f (x) \right\}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Thus, the condition becomes $I _ { t } \equiv 0$ . Since f is arbitrary, it is enough to take $t = 0$ . Our condition then reduces to $( \nu \alpha ) f \equiv \nu ( c f ) \mathrm { o r } ( c \cdot \nu ) \mu = c \cdot \nu ,$ , which means that $c \cdot \nu$ is invariant for Y. ✷ 

We turn to a study of pure jump-type Markov processes in a countable state space S, also called continuous-time Markov chains. Here the kernels $\mu _ { t }$ are determined by the transition functions $p _ { i j } ^ { t } = \mu _ { t } ( i , \{ j \} )$ ). The connectivity properties are simpler than in the discrete case, and the notion of periodicity has no continuous-time counterpart. 

Lemma 13.11 (positivity) Consider a continuous-time Markov chain in $S$ with transition functions $p _ { i j } ^ { t }$ . Then for fixed $i , j \in S$ , exactly one of these cases occurs: 

(i) $p _ { i j } ^ { t } > 0 , \ t > 0 ,$ 

(ii) $p _ { i j } ^ { t } = 0 , \ t \ge 0 .$ 

In particular, $p _ { i i } ^ { t } > 0$ for all t and $i .$ . 

Proof: Let $q \ = \ ( q _ { i j } )$ be the transition matrix of the embedded Markov chain $Y$ in Theorem 13.3. If $q _ { i j } ^ { n } = P _ { i } \{ Y _ { n } = j \} = 0$ for all $n \geq 0$ , then clearly $1 \{ X _ { t } \neq j \} \equiv 1 { \mathrm { ~ a . s . ~ } } P _ { i }$ , and so $\overset { \smile } { p _ { i j } ^ { t } } = 0$ for all $t \geq 0$ . If instead $q _ { i j } ^ { n } > 0$ for some $n \geq 0$ , there exist some states $i = i _ { 0 }$ and $i _ { 1 } , \ldots , i _ { n } = j$ with $q _ { i _ { k - 1 } , i _ { k } } > 0$ for $k = 1 , \dots , n$ . Since the distribution of $\left( \gamma _ { 1 } , \dots , \gamma _ { n + 1 } \right)$ has the positive density $\prod _ { k \leq n + 1 } e ^ { - x _ { k } } > 0$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { n + 1 }$ , we obtain for any $t > 0$ 

$$
p _ {i j} ^ {t} \geq P \left\{\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\gamma_ {k}}{c _ {i _ {k - 1}}} \leq t <   \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n + 1} \frac {\gamma_ {k}}{c _ {i _ {k - 1}}} \right\} \prod_ {k = 1} ^ {n} q _ {i _ {k - 1}, i _ {k}} > 0.
$$

Noting that $p _ { i i } ^ { 0 } = q _ { i i } ^ { 0 } = 1$ , we get in particular $p _ { i i } ^ { t } > 0$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

A continuous-time Markov chain is said to be irreducible if $p _ { i j } ^ { t } > 0$ for all $i , j \in S$ and $t > 0$ . This clearly holds if the underlying discrete-time process $Y$ in Theorem 13.3 is irreducible, in which case 

$$
\sup \left\{t > 0; X _ {t} = j \right\} <   \infty \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \sup \left\{n > 0; Y _ {n} = j \right\} <   \infty .
$$

Thus, when $Y$ is recurrent, the sets $\{ t ; X _ { t } = j \}$ are a.s. unbounded under $P _ { i }$ for all $i \in S ;$ otherwise they are a.s. bounded. The two possibilities are again referred to as recurrence and transience, respectively. 

The basic ergodic Theorem 11.22 for discrete-time Markov chains has the following continuous-time counterpart. Further extensions are considered in Chapter $1 7$ and 26. Recall that $\overset { u } { \to }$ means convergence in total variation, and let $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ be the class of probability measures on $S .$ 

Theorem 13.12 (convergence dichotomy, Kolmogorov) For an irreducible, continuous-time Markov chain in $S _ { i }$ , exactly one of these cases occurs: 

(i) there exists a unique invariant distribution $\nu ,$ , the latter satisfies $\nu _ { i } > 0$ for all $i \in S$ , and as $t \to \infty$ we have 

$$
P _ {\mu} \circ \theta_ {t} ^ {- 1} \stackrel {u} {\to} P _ {\nu}, \quad \mu \in \hat {\mathcal {M}} _ {S},
$$

(ii) no invariant distribution exists, and as $t \to \infty$ , 

$$
p _ {i j} ^ {t} \to 0, i, j \in S.
$$

Proof: By Lemma 13.11, the discrete-time chain $X _ { n h } , n \in Z _ { + }$ , is irreducible and aperiodic. Suppose that $\left( X _ { n h } \right)$ is positive recurrent for some $h > 0$ , say with invariant distribution $\nu .$ Then the chain $\left( X _ { n h ^ { \prime } } \right)$ is positive recurrent for every $h ^ { \prime }$ of the form $2 ^ { - m } h$ , and by the uniqueness in Theorem 11.22 it has the same invariant distribution. Since the paths are right-continuous, a simple approximation shows that $\nu$ is invariant even for the original process X. 

For any distribution $\mu$ on S, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \left\| P _ {\mu} \circ \theta_ {t} ^ {- 1} - P _ {\nu} \right\| & = \left\| \sum_ {i} \mu_ {i} \sum_ {j} (p _ {i j} ^ {t} - \nu_ {j}) P _ {j} \right\| \\ & \leq \sum_ {i} \mu_ {i} \sum_ {j} \bigl | p _ {i j} ^ {t} - \nu_ {j} \bigr |. \end{array}
$$

Thus, (i) will follow by dominated convergence, if we can show that the inner sum on the right tends to zero. This is clear if we put $n = [ t / h ]$ and $r = t - n h$ , and note that by Theorem 11.22, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {k} \Big | p _ {i k} ^ {t} - \nu_ {k} \Big | \leq \sum_ {j, k} \Big | p _ {i j} ^ {n h} - \nu_ {j} \Big | p _ {j k} ^ {r} \\ = \sum_ {j} \Big | p _ {i j} ^ {n h} - \nu_ {j} \Big | \to 0. \end{array}
$$

It remains to consider the case where $\left( X _ { n h } \right)$ is null-recurrent or transient for every $h > 0$ . Fixing any $i , k \in S$ and writing $n = [ t / h ]$ and $r = t - n h$ as before, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} p _ {i k} ^ {t} = \sum_ {j} p _ {i j} ^ {r} p _ {j k} ^ {n h} \\ \leq p _ {i k} ^ {n h} + \sum_ {j \neq i} p _ {i j} ^ {r} \\ = p _ {i k} ^ {n h} + (1 - p _ {i i} ^ {r}), \end{array}
$$

which tends to zero as $t  \infty$ and then $h  0$ , by Theorem 11.22 and the continuity of $p _ { i i } ^ { t }$ ✷ 

As in discrete time, condition (ii) of the last theorem holds for any transient Markov chain, whereas a recurrent chain may satisfy either condition. Recurrent chains satisfying (i) and (ii) are again referred to as positive-recurrent and null-recurrent, respectively. Note that X may be positive recurrent even if the embedded, discrete-time chain Y is null-recurrent, and vice versa. On the other hand, X clearly has the same asymptotic properties as the discrete-time processes $( X _ { n h } ) , h > 0$ 

For any $j \in S$ , we now introduce the first exit and recurrence times 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {j} = \inf \{t > 0; X _ {t} \neq j \}, \\ \tau_ {j} = \inf \{t > \gamma_ {j}; X _ {t} = j \}. \end{array}
$$

As for Theorem 11.26 in the discrete-time case, we may express the asymptotic transition probabilities in terms of the mean recurrence times $E _ { j } \tau _ { j }$ . To avoid trite exceptions, we consider only non-absorbing states. 

Theorem 13.13 (mean recurrence times, Kolmogorov) For a continuoustime Markov chain in $S$ and states $i , j \in S$ with j non-absorbing, we have as $t \to \infty$ DO 

$$
p _ {i j} ^ {t} \rightarrow \frac {P _ {i} \{\tau_ {j} <   \infty \}}{c _ {j} E _ {j} \tau_ {j}}.\tag{8}
$$

Proof: We may take $i = j$ , since the general statement will then follow as in the proof of Theorem 11.26. If $j$ is transient, then $1 \{ X _ { t } = j \}  0 \ \mathrm { a . s . } \ P _ { j } .$ and so by dominated convergence $p _ { j j } ^ { t } = P _ { j } \{ X _ { t } = j \}  0$ . This agrees with (8), since in this case $P _ { j } \{ \tau _ { j } = \infty \} > 0$ . Turning to the recurrent case, let $S _ { j }$ be the class of states i accessible from $j$ . Then $S _ { j }$ is clearly irreducible, and so $p _ { j j } ^ { t }$ converges by Theorem 13.12. 

To identify the limit, define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} L _ {t} ^ {j} = \lambda \Big \{s \leq t; X _ {s} = j \Big \} \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 \big \{X _ {s} = j \big \} d s, \quad t \geq 0, \end{array}
$$

and let $\tau _ { j } ^ { n }$ be the time of n -th return to $j .$ . Letting $m , n  \infty$ with $| m - n | \leq 1$ and using the strong Markov property and the law of large numbers, we get a.s. $P _ { j }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c}\frac {L ^ {j} (\tau_ {j} ^ {m})}{\tau_ {j} ^ {n}} = \frac {L ^ {j} (\tau_ {j} ^ {m})}{m} \cdot \frac {n}{\tau_ {j} ^ {n}} \cdot \frac {m}{n}\\\rightarrow \frac {E _ {j} \gamma_ {j}}{E _ {j} \tau_ {j}} = \frac {1}{c _ {j} E _ {j} \tau_ {j}}.\end{array}
$$

By the monotonicity of $L ^ { j }$ it follows that $t ^ { - 1 } L _ { t } ^ { j } \to ( c _ { j } E _ { j } \tau _ { j } ) ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { ~ a . s }$ . Hence, by Fubini’s theorem and dominated convergence,

We conclude with some applications to branching processes and their difusion approximations. By a Bienaym´e $p r o c e s s ^ { 2 }$ we mean a discrete-time branching process $X \ = \ ( X _ { n } )$ , where $X _ { n }$ represents the total number of individuals in generation n. Given that $X _ { n } ~ = ~ m$ , the individuals in the $n { \mathrm { - t h } }$ generation give rise to independent families of progeny $Y _ { 1 } , \dots , Y _ { m }$ starting at time $n ,$ each distributed like the original process X with $X _ { 0 } = 1$ . We say that X is critical when $E _ { 1 } X _ { 1 } = 1$ , and super- or sub-critical when $E _ { 1 } X _ { 1 } > 1 \mathrm { o r } < 1$ , respectively.<sup>3</sup> To avoid some trite exceptions, we assume that both possibilities $X _ { 1 } ~ = ~ 0$ and $X _ { 1 } > 1$ have positive probabilities. 

Theorem 13.14 (Bienaym´e process) Let X be a Bienaym´e process with $E _ { 1 } X _ { 1 }$ $= \mu$ and $\operatorname { V a r } _ { 1 } ( X _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 }$ , and put $f ( s ) = E _ { 1 } s ^ { X _ { 1 } }$ . Then

\{\gamma = 0 \} = \{X _ {n} \rightarrow 0 \} a. s. P _ {1}.

Lemma 13.15 (recursion and moments) Let X be a Bienaym´e process with $E _ { 1 } X _ { 1 } = \mu$ and $\operatorname { V a r } _ { 1 } ( X _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 }$ . Then 

(i) the functions $f ^ { ( n ) } ( s ) = E _ { 1 } s ^ { X _ { n } }$ on [0, 1] satisfy 

$$
f ^ {(m + n)} (s) = f ^ {(m)} \circ f ^ {(n)} (s), \quad m, n \in \mathbb {N},

(ii) $E _ { 1 } X _ { n } = \mu ^ { n }$ , and when $\sigma ^ { 2 } < \infty$ we have 

$$
\operatorname{Var} _ {1} (X _ {n}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} n   \sigma^ {2}, & \mu = 1, \\ \sigma^ {2} \mu^ {n - 1}   \frac {\mu^ {n} - 1}{\mu - 1}, & \mu \neq 1. \end{array} \right.

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & f ^ {(m + n)} (s) = E _ {1} s ^ {X _ {m + n}} = E _ {1} E _ {X _ {m}} s ^ {X _ {n}} \\ & \qquad = E _ {1} (E _ {1} s ^ {X _ {n}}) ^ {X _ {m}} \\ & \qquad = f ^ {(m)} (E _ {1} s ^ {X _ {n}}) \\ & \qquad = f ^ {(m)} \circ f ^ {(n)} (s). \end{array}

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mu_ {m + n} = E _ {1} X _ {m + n} = E _ {1} E _ {X _ {m}} X _ {n}} \\ & {\qquad = E _ {1} (X _ {m} E _ {1} X _ {n})} \\ & {\qquad = (E _ {1} X _ {m}) (E _ {1} X _ {n})} \\ & {\qquad = \mu_ {m} \mu_ {n},} \end{array}

\sigma_ {m + n} ^ {2} = \sigma_ {m} ^ {2} \mu_ {n} + \mu_ {m} ^ {2} \sigma_ {n} ^ {2}.

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\sigma_ {n + 1} ^ {2} = \sigma_ {n} ^ {2} + \sigma^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = n \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = (n + 1) \sigma^ {2}.} \end{array}
$$

The simplest case is when X proceeds by binary splitting, so that the of spring distribution is confined to the values 0 and 2. To obtain a continuoustime Markov chain, we may choose the life lengths until splitting or death to be independent and exponentially distributed with constant mean. Theorem 13.16 (binary splitting) Let X be a critical, unit rate binary-splitting process, and define $p _ { t } = ( 1 + t ) ^ { - 1 }$ . Then 

(i) $P _ { 1 } \{ X _ { t } > 0 \} = p _ { t } , \quad t > 0 ,$ 

$$

$$

Proof, (i) The generating functions 

$$
F (s, t) = E _ {1} s ^ {X _ {t}}, \quad s \in [ 0, 1 ], t > 0,

$$

where $q _ { t } = 1 - p _ { t }$ . In particular, $P _ { 1 } \{ X _ { t } = 0 \} = F ( 0 , t ) = q _ { t }$

$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \{Z _ {s} ^ {t} = 1 \} = E P \Big \{Z _ {s} ^ {t} = 1   \Big |   X _ {s} \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \Big (X _ {s}   p _ {t - s}   q _ {t - s} ^ {X _ {s} - 1} \Big) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {n \geq 1} n   p _ {s} ^ {2}   q _ {s} ^ {n - 1} p _ {t - s}   q _ {t - s} ^ {n - 1} \\ \qquad = p _ {s} ^ {2}   p _ {t - s} \sum_ {n \geq 1} n (q _ {s}   q _ {t - s}) ^ {n - 1} \\ \qquad = \frac {p _ {s} ^ {2}   p _ {t - s}}{(1 - q _ {s}   q _ {t - s}) ^ {2}} = \frac {1 + t - s}{(1 + t) ^ {2}}. \end{array}
$$

Writing $\tau _ { 1 } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ s \le t ; Z _ { s } ^ { t } > 1 \}$ , we conclude that

which shows that $\tau _ { 1 }$ has the defective probability density $( 1 + t ) ^ { - 1 }$ on $[ 0 , t ]$ By Proposition 10.23, the associated compensator has density $( 1 + t - s ) ^ { - 1 }$ The Markov and branching properties carry over to the process $Z _ { s } ^ { t }$ by Theorem 8.12. Using those properties and proceeding recursively, we see that $Z _ { s } ^ { t }$ is a Yule process in $s \in [ 0 , t ]$ with rate function $( 1 + t - s ) ^ { - 1 }$ ✷
