(iii) We may take $\| \mu \| < \infty$ , since the case of $\| \mu \| = \infty$ will then follow by a martingale or monotone-class argument. Then consider any mixed binomial process $\begin{array} { r } { \xi = \sum _ { k < \kappa } \delta _ { \sigma _ { k } } } \end{array}$ , where the $\sigma _ { k }$ are i.i.d. $\mu$ and independent of $\kappa .$ For any $B \in S$ , we note that $1 _ { B } \xi$ and $1 _ { B ^ { c } } \xi$ are conditionally independent binomial processes based on $1 _ { B } \mu$ and $1 _ { B ^ { c } } \mu$ , respectively, given the variables $\kappa$ and $\vartheta _ { k } = 1 \{ k \leq \kappa , \sigma _ { k } \in B \}$ , $k \in \mathsf { N }$ . Thus, $1 _ { B } \xi$ is conditionally a binomial process based on $\mu _ { B }$ and $\xi B$ , given $1 _ { B ^ { c } } \xi , \xi B$ , and $\vartheta _ { 1 } , \vartheta _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . Since the conditional distribution depends only on $\xi B$ , we obtain $1 _ { B } \xi \perp \perp _ { \xi B } \left( 1 _ { B ^ { c } } \xi , \vartheta _ { 1 } , \vartheta _ { 2 } , . . . \right)$ , and the assertion follows. ✷ 

Using the easy necessity part of Theorem 15.4, we may prove the existence of Cox processes and transforms. The result also covers the cases of binomial processes and randomizations. 

Theorem 15.5 (Cox and transform existence) 

(i) For any random measure η on $S _ { i }$ , there exists a Cox process $\xi$ directed by $\eta .$ . 

(ii) For any point process $\xi$ on $S$ and probability kernel $\nu : S  T$ , there exists a ν-transform $\zeta ~ o f ~ \xi$ 

Proof: (i) First let $\eta = \mu$ be non-random with $\mu S \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . By Corollary 8.25 we may choose a Poisson distributed random variable $\kappa$ with mean $\mu S$ and some independent i.i.d. random elements $\sigma _ { 1 } , \sigma _ { 2 } , . . . .$ . in $S$ with distribution $\mu / \mu S$ . By Theorem 15.4, the random measure $\begin{array} { r } { \xi = \sum _ { j \leq \kappa } \delta _ { \sigma _ { j } } } \end{array}$ is then Poisson with intensity $\mu .$ 

For general $\mu \in { \mathcal { M } } _ { \mu }$ , we may choose a partition of $S$ into disjoint subsets $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } , \ldots \in \hat { S }$ , such that $\mu B _ { k } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ for all k. As before, there exists for every k a Poisson process $\xi _ { k }$ on $S$ with intensity $\mu _ { k } = 1 _ { B _ { k } } \mu _ { ; }$ , and by Corollary 8.25 we may choose the $\xi _ { k }$ to be independent. Writing $\xi = \textstyle \sum _ { k } \xi _ { k }$ and using Lemma 15.2 (i), we get for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $S$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E e ^ {- \xi f} & = \prod_ {k} E e ^ {- \xi_ {k} f} \\ & = \prod_ {k} \exp \left\{- \mu_ {k} (1 - e ^ {- f}) \right\} \\ & = \exp \left\{- \sum_ {k} \mu_ {k} (1 - e ^ {- f}) \right\} \\ & = \exp \left\{- \mu (1 - e ^ {- f}) \right\}. \end{array}
$$

Using Lemmas 15.1 (ii) and 15.2 (i), we conclude that $\xi$ is a Poisson process with intensity $\mu .$ 

Now let $\xi _ { \mu }$ be a Poisson process with intensity $\mu$ . Then for any $m _ { 1 } , \ldots , m _ { n } \in$ $Z _ { + }$ and disjoint $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } \in \hat { S }$ 

$$
P \bigcap_ {k \leq n} \left\{\xi_ {\mu} B _ {k} = m _ {k} \right\} = \prod_ {k \leq n} e ^ {- \mu B _ {k}} (\mu B _ {k}) ^ {m _ {k}} / m _ {k}!,
$$

which is a measurable function of $\mu .$ . The measurability extends to arbitrary sets $B _ { k } \in \hat { S }$ , since the general probability on the left is a finite sum of such products. Now the sets on the left form a π-system generating the σ-field in $\mathcal { N } _ { S }$ , and so Theorem 1.1 shows that $P _ { \mu } = \mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { \mu } )$ is a probability kernel from $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ to $\mathcal { N } _ { S }$ . Then Lemma 8.16 ensures the existence, for any random measure η on S, of a Cox process $\xi$ directed by η. 

(ii) First let $\begin{array} { r } { \mu = \sum _ { k } \delta _ { s _ { k } } } \end{array}$ be non-random in $\mathcal { N } _ { S }$ . Then Corollary 8.25 yields some independent random elements $\tau _ { k }$ in $T$ with distributions $\nu _ { s _ { k } }$ , making $\begin{array} { r } { \zeta _ { \mu } = \sum _ { k } \delta _ { \tau _ { k } } } \end{array}$ a ν-transform of $\mu$ . Letting $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } \in \mathcal { T }$ and $s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , we get by Lemma 15.2 (iii) 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E \prod_ {k} s _ {k} ^ {\zeta_ {\mu} B _ {k}} & = E \exp \zeta_ {\mu} \sum_ {k} 1 _ {B _ {k}} \log s _ {k} \\ & = \exp \mu \log \nu \exp \sum_ {k} 1 _ {B _ {k}} \log s _ {k} \\ & = \exp \mu \log \nu \prod_ {k} (s _ {k}) ^ {1 _ {B _ {k}}}. \end{array}
$$

Using Lemma 3.2 (i) twice, we see that $\nu \prod _ { k } ( s _ { k } ) ^ { 1 _ { B _ { k } } }$ is a measurable function on $S$ for fixed $s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } .$ <sub>, and so the right-hand side is a measurable func-</sub> tion of $\mu .$ Diferentiating $m _ { k }$ times with respect to $s _ { k }$ for each k and setting $s _ { 1 } = \cdots = s _ { n } = 1$ , we conclude that the probability $P \cap _ { k } \{ \zeta _ { \mu } B _ { k } = m _ { k } \}$ is a measurable function of $\mu$ for any $m _ { 1 } , \ldots , m _ { n } \in { \sf Z } _ { + }$ <sub>. As before,</sub> $P _ { \mu } = { \mathcal { L } } ( \zeta _ { \mu } )$ is then a probability kernel from $\mathcal { N } _ { S }$ to $\mathcal { N } _ { T }$ , and the general result follows by Lemma 8.16. ✷ 

We proceed with some basic properties of Poisson and Cox processes. 

Lemma 15.6 (Cox simplicity and integrability) Let $\xi$ be a Cox process $d i -$ rected by a random measure η on $S$ . Then 

(i) $\xi$ is a.s. simple $\Leftrightarrow \quad \eta$ is a.s. difuse, 

(ii) $\left\{ \xi f < \infty \right\} = \left\{ \eta ( f \wedge 1 ) < \infty \right\} a . s . \ f o r \ a l l \ f \in S _ { + } .$ 

Proof: (i) First reduce by conditioning to the case where $\xi$ is Poisson with intensity $\mu .$ Since both properties are local, we may also assume that $\| \mu \| \in$ $( 0 , \infty )$ . By a further conditioning based on Theorem 15.4, we may then take $\xi$ to be a binomial process based on $\mu ,$ , say $\begin{array} { r } { \xi = \sum _ { k \le n } \delta _ { \sigma _ { k } } } \end{array}$ , where the $\sigma _ { k }$ are i.i.d. $\mu .$ . Then Fubini’s theorem yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \{\sigma_ {i} = \sigma_ {j} \} = \int \mu \{s \}   \mu (d s) \\ = \sum_ {s} (\mu \{s \}) ^ {2}, i \neq j, \end{array}
$$

which shows that the $\sigma _ { k }$ are a.s. distinct if $\mu$ is difuse. 

(ii) Conditioning on η and using Theorem 8.5, we may again reduce to the case where $\xi$ is Poisson with intensity $\mu .$ . For any $f \in S _ { + }$ , we get as $0 < r  0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \exp \Bigl \{- \mu (1 - e ^ {- r f}) \Bigr \} = E e ^ {- r \xi f} \\ \to P \{\xi f <   \infty \}. \end{array}
$$

Since $1 - e ^ { - f } \asymp f \wedge 1$ , we have $\mu ( 1 - e ^ { - r f } ) \equiv \infty$ when $\mu ( f \wedge 1 ) = \infty$ , whereas $\mu ( 1 - e ^ { - r f } ) \to 0$ by dominated convergence when $\mu ( f \wedge 1 ) < \infty$ ✷ 

The following uniqueness property will play an important role below. 

Lemma 15.7 (Cox and thinning uniqueness, Krickeberg) Let $\xi , \tilde { \xi }$ be Cox processes on S directed by some random measures $\eta , \tilde { \eta }$ , or p -thinnings of some point processes η, $\tilde { \eta } _ { ; }$ , for a fixed $p \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ . Then 

$$
\xi \stackrel {d} {=} \tilde {\xi} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \eta \stackrel {d} {=} \tilde {\eta}.
$$

Proof: The implications to the left are obvious. To prove the implication to the right for the Cox transform, we may invert Lemma 15.2 (ii) to get for $f \in \hat { S } _ { + }$ 

$$
E e ^ {- \eta f} = E \exp \Bigl \{\xi \log (1 - f) \Bigr \}, \quad f <   1.
$$

In case of $p$ -thinnings, we may use Lemma 15.2 (iv) instead to get 

$$
E e ^ {- \eta f} = E \exp \Bigl \{\xi \log \bigl (1 - p ^ {- 1} (1 - e ^ {- f}) \bigr) \Bigr \}, \quad f <   - \log (1 - p).
$$

In both cases, the assertion follows by Lemma 15.1 (ii). 

Using Cox and thinning transforms, we may partially strengthen the general uniqueness criteria of Theorem 15.1. Related convergence criteria are given in Chapter 23 and 30. 

Theorem 15.8 (one-dimensional uniqueness criteria, M¨onch, Grandell, OK) Let S be a Borel space with a dissecting ring $\mathcal { U } \subset \hat { \mathcal { S } }$ . Then 

(i) for any point processes $\xi , \eta$ on $S _ { i }$ , we have $\xi ^ { * } \overset { d } { = } \eta ^ { * }$ if 

$$
P \{\xi U = 0 \} = P \{\eta U = 0 \}, \quad U \in \mathcal {U},
$$

(ii) for any simple point processes or difuse random measures $\xi , \eta$ on $S$ , we have $\xi \overset { d } { = } \eta$ if for a fixed $c > 0$ , 

$$
E e ^ {- c \xi U} = E e ^ {- c \eta U}, \quad U \in \mathcal {U},
$$

(iii) for a simple point process or difuse random measure $\xi$ and an arbitrary random measure η on $S _ { i }$ , we have $\xi \stackrel { d } { = } \eta \ i f f$ 

$$
\xi U \stackrel {d} {=} \eta U, \quad U \in \mathcal {U}.
$$

Proof: (i) Let be the class of sets $\{ \mu ; \mu U = 0 \}$ in $\mathcal { N } _ { S }$ with $U \in \mathcal { U } .$ , and note that is a π-system, since for any B, $C \in { \mathcal { U } }$ 

$$
\left\{\mu B = 0 \right\} \cap \left\{\mu C = 0 \right\} = \left\{\mu (B \cup C) = 0 \right\} \in \mathcal {C},
$$

by the ring property of . Furthermore, the sets $M \ \in \ B _ { \mathcal { N } _ { S } }$ with $P \{ \xi \in$ $M \} = P \{ \eta \in M \}$ form a λ -system , which contains by hypothesis. Hence, Theorem 1.1 (i) yields ${ \mathcal { D } } \supset \sigma ( { \mathcal { C } } )$ , which means that $\xi \overset { d } { = } \eta$ on $\sigma ( \mathcal { C } )$ 

Since the ring is dissecting, it contains a dissecting system $( I _ { n j } )$ , and for any $\mu \in \mathcal { N } _ { S }$ we have 

$$
\sum_ {j} \left\{\mu (U \cap I _ {n j}) \wedge 1 \right\}\rightarrow \mu^ {*} U, \quad U \in \mathcal {U},
$$

since the atoms of $\mu$ are ultimately separated by the sets $I _ { n j }$ . Since the sum on the left is $\sigma ( \mathcal { C } )$ -measurable, so is the limit $\mu ^ { * } U$ for every $U \in \mathcal { U }$ . By the proof of Lemma 15.1, the measurability extends to the map $\mu \mapsto \mu ^ { * }$ , and we conclude that $\xi ^ { * } \overset { d } { = } \eta ^ { * }$ 

(ii) First let $\xi , \eta$ be difuse. Letting $\tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta }$ be Cox processes directed by $c \xi , c \eta$ , respectively, we get by conditioning and hypothesis 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \{\tilde {\xi} U = 0 \} = E e ^ {- c \xi U} = E e ^ {- c \eta U} \\ & \qquad = P \{\tilde {\eta} U = 0 \}, \quad U \in \mathcal {U}. \end{array}
$$

Since $\tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta }$ are a.s. simple by Lemma 15.6 (i), part (i) yields $\tilde { \xi } \ \triangleq \tilde { \eta }$ , and so $\xi \overset { d } { = } \eta$ by Lemma 15.7 (i). 

Next let $\xi , \eta$ be simple point processes. For $p = 1 - e ^ { - c }$ , let $\tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta }$ be $p \mathrm { - }$ thinnings of $\xi , \eta _ { ; }$ , respectively. Since Lemma 15.2 (iv) remains true when $0 \leq$ $f \leq \infty$ , we may take $f = \infty \cdot 1 _ { U }$ for any $U \in \mathcal { U }$ to get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \{\tilde {\xi} U = 0 \} = E \exp \Bigl \{\xi \log (1 - p 1 _ {U}) \Bigr \} \\ & \qquad = E \exp \Bigl \{\xi U \log (1 - p) \Bigr \} = E e ^ {- c \xi}, \end{array}
$$

and similarly for $\tilde { \eta }$ in terms of $\eta$ . Hence, the simple point processes $\tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta }$ satisfy the condition in (i), and so $\tilde { \xi } \ \triangleq \tilde { \eta }$ , which implies $\xi \overset { d } { = } \eta$ 

(iii) First let $\xi$ be a simple point process. The stated condition yields $\eta U \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ a.s. for every $U \in { \mathcal { U } } .$ , and so $\eta$ is a point process by Lemma 2.18. By (i) we get $\xi \overset { d } { = } \eta ^ { * }$ , and in particular $\eta U \overset { d } { = } \xi U \overset { d } { = } \eta ^ { * } U$ for all $U \in \mathcal { U }$ , which implies $\eta = \eta ^ { * }$ since the ring is covering. 

Next let $\eta$ be a.s. difuse. Letting $\tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta }$ be Cox processes directed by $\xi , \eta$ respectively, we get $\tilde { \xi } U \ \stackrel { d } { = } \ \tilde { \eta } U$ for any $U \in \mathcal { U }$ by Lemma 15.2 (ii). Since $\tilde { \xi }$ is simple by Lemma 15.6 (i), we conclude as before that $\tilde { \xi } \ \triangleq \tilde { \eta }$ , and so $\xi \overset { d } { = } \eta$ by Lemma 15.7 (i). ✷ 

The last result yields a nice characterization of Poisson processes: 

Corollary 15.9 (Poisson criterion, R´enyi) Let $\xi$ be a random measure on $S$ with $E \xi \{ s \} \equiv 0 \ a . s .$ , and fix a dissecting ring $u \subset { \hat { S } }$ .Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi$ is a Poisson process, 

(ii) $\xi U$ is Poisson distributed for every $U \in \mathcal { U }$ 

Proof: Assume (ii). Since $\lambda = E \xi \in \mathcal { M } _ { S }$ , Theorem 15.5 yields a Poisson process η on S with $E \eta = \lambda$ . Here $\xi U \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ \eta U$ for all $U \in \mathcal { U }$ , and since $\eta$ is simple by Corollary 15.6 (i), we get $\xi \overset { d } { = } \eta$ by Theorem 15.8 (iii), proving (i). ✷ 

Much of the previous theory extends to processes with marks. Given some Borel spaces $S$ and $T ,$ , we define a T-marked point process on $S$ as a point process $\xi$ on $S \times T$ with $\xi ( \{ s \} \times T ) \le 1$ for all $s \in \ S$ . Say that $\xi$ has independent increments, if the point processes $\xi ( B _ { 1 } \times \cdot ) , \ldots , \xi ( B _ { n } \times \cdot )$ on $T$ are independent for any disjoint sets $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } \in { \hat { S } }$ . We also say that $\xi$ is a Poisson process, if $\xi$ is Poisson in the usual sense on the product space $S { \times } T$ . We may now characterize Poisson processes in terms of the independence property, extending Theorem 13.6. The result plays a crucial role in Chapters 16 and 29. A related characterization in terms of compensators is given in Corollary 15.17. 

For future purposes, we consider a slightly more general case. For any $S _ { - }$ marked point process $\xi$ on $T ,$ , we introduce the discontinuity set $D = \{ t \in T$ ; 

$E \xi ( \{ t \} \times S ) > 0 \}$ , and say that $\xi$ is an extended Poisson process, if it is an ordinary Poisson process on $D ^ { c }$ , and the contributions $\xi _ { t }$ to the points $t \in D$ are independent point measures on $S$ with mass $\leq 1$ . Note that $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ is then uniquely determined by $E \xi$ 

Theorem 15.10 (independent-increment point processes, Bateman, Copeland & Regan, Itˆo, Kingman) For an S-marked point process $\xi$ on $T$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi$ has independent T-increments, 

(ii) $\xi$ is an extended Poisson process on $T \times S$ 

Proof (OK): Subtracting the fixed discontinuities, we may reduce to the case where $E \xi ( \{ t \} \times S ) \equiv 0$ . Here we first consider a simple point process $\xi$ on $T = [ 0 , 1 ]$ with $E \xi \{ t \} \equiv 0$ . Define a set function 

$$
\rho B = - \log E e ^ {- \xi B}, \quad B \in \hat {\mathcal {T}},
$$

and note that $\rho B \geq 0$ for all B since $\xi B \ge 0 \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . If $\xi$ has independent increments, then for disjoint $B , C \in { \hat { \cal T } }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \rho (B \cup C) & = - \log E e ^ {- \xi B - \xi C} \\ & = - \log \Bigl (E e ^ {- \xi B} E e ^ {- \xi C} \Bigr) \\ & = \rho B + \rho C, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\rho$ is finitely additive. It is even countably additive, since $B _ { n } \uparrow B$ in $\hat { \tau }$ implies $\rho B _ { n } \uparrow \rho B$ by monotone and dominated convergence. It is further difuse, since $\rho \{ t \} = -$ log $E e ^ { - \xi \{ t \} } = 0$ for all $t \in T$ 

Now Theorem 15.5 yields a Poisson process $\eta$ on $T _ { \ast }$ , such that $E \eta = c ^ { - 1 } \rho$ with $c = 1 - e ^ { - 1 }$ . For any $B \in \hat { S }$ , we get by Lemma 15.2 (ii) 

$$
\begin{array}{r} E e ^ {- \eta B} = \exp \Bigl \{- c ^ {- 1} \rho (1 - e ^ {- 1 _ {B}}) \Bigr \} \\ = e ^ {- \rho B} = E e ^ {- \xi B}. \end{array}
$$

Since $\xi , \eta$ are simple by hypothesis and Lemma 15.6 (i), we get $\xi \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ \eta$ by Theorem 15.8 (ii). 

In the marked case, fix any $B \in B _ { T \times S }$ , and define a simple point process on $T$ by $\eta = 1 _ { B } \xi ( \cdot \times S )$ . Then the previous case shows that $\xi B = \| \eta \|$ is Poisson distributed, and so $\xi$ is Poisson by Corollary 15.9. ✷ 

The last result extends to a representation of random measures with independent increments<sup>4</sup>. A extension to general processes on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ will be given in Theorem 16.3. 

Corollary 15.11 (independent-increment random measures, Kingman) A random measure $\xi$ on $S$ has independent increments if a.s. 

$$
\xi B = \alpha B + \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} x   \eta (B \times d x), \quad B \in \mathcal {S},\tag{2}
$$

for $a$ fixed measure $\alpha \in \mathcal { M } _ { S }$ and an extended Poisson process η on $S \times ( 0 , \infty )$ with f∞ 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} (x \wedge 1)   E   \eta (B \times d x) <   \infty , \quad B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}}.\tag{3}
$$

Proof (OK): On $S \times ( 0 , \infty )$ we define a point process $\begin{array} { r } { \eta = \sum _ { s } \delta _ { s , \xi \{ s \} } } \end{array}$ , where the required measurability follows by a simple approximation. Since $\eta$ has independent S-increments and 

$$
\eta \Big (\{s \} \times (0, \infty) \Big) = 1 \Big \{\xi \{s \} > 0 \Big \} \leq 1, \quad s \in S,
$$

Theorem 15.10 shows that $\eta$ is a Poisson process. Subtracting the atomic part from $\xi ,$ , we obtain a difuse random measure α satisfying (2), which has again independent increments and hence is a.s. non-random by Theorem 6.12. Next, Lemma 15.2 (i) yields for any $B \in S$ and $r > 0$ 

$$
- \log E \exp \left\{- r \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} x \eta (B \times d x) \right\} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} (1 - e ^ {- r x}) E \eta (B \times d x).
$$

As $r  0$ , we see by dominated convergence that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } x \eta ( B \times d x ) < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s } } \end{array}$ . if (3) holds. ✷ 

We summarize the various Poisson criteria, to highlight some remarkable equivalences. The last condition anticipates Corollary 15.17 below. 

Corollary 15.12 (Poisson criteria) Let $\xi$ be a simple point process on $S$ with $E \xi \{ s \} = 0$ for all $s \in S$ . Then these conditions are equivalent <sup>5</sup>: 

(i) $\xi$ is a Poisson process, 

(ii) $\xi$ has independent increments, 

(iii) $\xi B$ is Poisson distributed for every $B \in \hat { S }$ 

When $\xi$ is stationary on $S = \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , it is further equivalent that 

(iv) $\xi$ is a renewal process with exponential holding times, 

(v) $\xi$ has induced compensator cλ for a constant $c \geq 0$ 

Proof: Here $( \mathrm { i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ by Theorem 15.10 and $( \mathrm { i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ by Corollary 15.9. For stationary $\xi ,$ , the equivalence of (i)–(ii), (iv) was proved in Theorem 13.6. ✷ 

In the multi-variate case, we have a further striking equivalence: 

Corollary 15.13 (multi-variate Poisson criteria) Let $\xi$ be a point process on $S \times T$ with a simple, locally finite S-projection $\bar { \xi } = \xi ( \cdot \times T )$ , such that $E \bar { \xi } \{ s \} = 0$ for all $s \in S$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) ξ is a Poisson process on $S \times T$ , 

(ii) $\xi$ has independent S-increments, 

(iii) $\xi$ is a ν-randomization of a Poisson process $\bar { \xi }$ on $S$ , for a probability kernel $\nu \colon S \to T$ 

Proof: Since $( \mathrm { i i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ is obvious and $\mathrm { ( i i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i ) }$ by Theorem 15.10, it remains to prove that ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i i i ) } }$ . Then let $\xi$ be Poisson with intensity $\lambda = E \xi ,$ and note that $\bar { \xi }$ is again Poisson with intensity $\bar { \lambda } = \lambda ( \cdot \times T )$ . By Theorem 3.4 there exists a probability kernel $\nu \colon S \to T$ such that $\lambda = { \bar { \lambda } } \otimes \nu .$ . Letting $\eta$ be a ν -randomization of $\bar { \xi } ,$ we see from Theorem 15.3 (i) that η is again Poisson with intensity λ. Hence, $( \xi , \bar { \xi } ) \overset { d } { = } ( \eta , \bar { \xi } )$ , and so $\mathcal { L } ( \xi | \bar { \xi } ) = \mathcal { L } ( \eta | \bar { \xi } )$ , which shows that even $\xi$ is a ν -randomization of $\bar { \xi } .$ ✷ 

We may next characterize the mixed Poisson and binomial processes by a basic symmetry property. Related results for more general processes appear in Theorems 27.9 and 27.10. Given a random measure $\xi$ and a difuse measure λ on $S _ { ; }$ , we say that $\xi$ is λ -symmetric if $\xi \circ f ^ { - 1 } \overset { d } { = } \xi$ for every λ -preserving map $f$ on $S$ 

Theorem 15.14 (symmetry, Davidson, Matthes et al., OK) Let $S$ be a Borel space with a difuse measure $\lambda \in \mathcal { M } _ { S }$ . Then 

(i) a simple point process $\xi$ on $S$ is λ-symmetric if it is a mixed Poisson or binomial process based on λ, 

(ii) a difuse random measure $\xi$ on S is λ-symmetric if $\xi = \alpha \lambda$ a.s. for a random variable $\alpha \geq 0$ 

In both cases, this holds<sup>6</sup> if $\mathcal { L } ( \xi B )$ depends only on $\lambda B$ 

Proof: (i) If $S = [ 0 , 1 ]$ , then ξ is invariant under λ -preserving transformations, and so $\xi$ remains conditionally λ -symmetric, given $\| \xi \|$ . We may then reduce by conditioning to the case of a constant $\| \xi \| = n$ , so that $\begin{array} { r } { \xi = \sum _ { k < n } \delta _ { \sigma _ { k } } } \end{array}$ for some random variables $\sigma _ { 1 } < \cdots < \sigma _ { n }$ in [0, 1]. Now consider any subintervals $I _ { 1 } < \cdots < I _ { n }$ of $[ 0 , 1 ]$ , where $I < J$ means that $s < t$ for all $s \in I$ and $t \in J$ . By contractability, the probability 

$$
P \bigcap_ {k} \left\{\sigma_ {k} \in I _ {k} \right\} = P \bigcap_ {k} \left\{\xi I _ {k} > 0 \right\}
$$

is invariant under individual shifts of $I _ { 1 } , \ldots , I _ { n }$ , subject to the mentioned order restriction. Thus, $\mathcal { L } ( \sigma _ { 1 } , \ldots , \sigma _ { n } )$ is shift invariant on the set $\Delta _ { n } = \{ s _ { 1 } < \cdots <$ $s _ { n } \} \subset [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { n }$ , and hence equals n! $\lambda ^ { n }$ on $\Delta _ { n }$ , which means that $\xi$ is a binomial process on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ based on $\lambda$ and $n .$ If instead $S = \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , the restrictions $1 _ { [ 0 , t ] } \xi$ are mixed binomial processes based on $1 _ { [ 0 , t ] } \lambda$ , and so $\xi$ is mixed Poisson on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ by Theorem 15.4. 

(ii) We may take $S = [ 0 , 1 ]$ . As in (i), we may further reduce by conditioning to the case where $\| \xi \| = 1 ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . Then $E \xi = \lambda$ by contractability, and for any intervals $I _ { 1 } < I _ { 2 }$ in $I .$ , the moment $E \xi ^ { 2 } ( I _ { 1 } \times I _ { 2 } )$ is invariant under individual shifts of $I _ { 1 }$ and $I _ { 2 }$ , so that $E \xi ^ { 2 }$ is proportional to $\lambda ^ { 2 }$ on $\Delta _ { 2 }$ . Since $\xi$ is difuse, we have $E \xi ^ { 2 } = 0$ on the diagonal $\{ s _ { 1 } = s _ { 2 } \}$ in $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ . Hence, by symmetry and normalization, $E \xi ^ { 2 } = \lambda ^ { 2 }$ on $[ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 }$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{Var} (\xi B) = E (\xi B) ^ {2} - (E \xi B) ^ {2} \\ = \lambda^ {2} B ^ {2} - (\lambda B) ^ {2} = 0, \quad B \in \mathcal {B} _ {[ 0, 1 ]}. \end{array}
$$

Then $\xi B = \lambda B$ a.s. for all $B _ { : }$ and $\operatorname { s o } \xi = \lambda \operatorname { a . s }$ . by a monotone-class argument. 

Now suppose that $\mathcal { L } ( \xi B )$ depends only on $\lambda B$ , and define

and so $\xi ( f ^ { - 1 } B ) \ \stackrel { d } { = } \ \xi B$ by Theorem 6.3. Then Theorem 15.8 (iii) yields $\xi \circ f ^ { - 1 } \overset { d } { = } \xi$ , which shows that $\xi$ is λ -symmetric. ✷ 

A Poisson process $\xi$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ is said to be stationary with rate $c \geq 0$ if $E \xi = c \lambda$ . We show how a point process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , subject to a suitable regularity condition, can be transformed to Poisson by a predictable map. This leads to various time-change formulas for point processes, similar to those for continuous local martingales in Chapter 19. 

When $\xi$ is an S-marked point process on $( 0 , \infty )$ , it is automatically locally integrable, which ensures the existence of the associated compensator $\hat { \xi } .$ . Recall that $\xi$ is said to be $q l -$ continuous if $\xi ( [ \tau ] \times S ) = 0$ a.s. for every predictable time $\tau _ { : }$ , so that the process $\hat { \xi } _ { t } B$ is a.s. continuous for every $B \in \hat { S }$ 

Theorem 15.15 (predictable mapping to Poisson) For any Borel spaces $S , T$ and measure $\mu \in \mathcal { M } _ { T }$ , let $\xi$ be a ql-continuous, S-marked point process on $( 0 , \infty )$ with compensator $\hat { \xi } ,$ , and consider a predictable map $Y$ : $\Omega \times \mathsf { R } _ { + } \times S  T$ Then 

$$
\hat {\xi} \circ Y ^ {- 1} = \mu a. s. \Rightarrow \eta = \xi \circ Y ^ {- 1} i s P o i s s o n (\mu).
$$

In particular, any simple, ql-continuous point process $\xi$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ is unit rate Poisson, on the time scale given by the compensator $\hat { \xi } .$ . Note the analogy with the time-change reduction of continuous local martingales to Brownian motion in Theorem 19.4. 

Proof: For disjoint sets $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n } \in B _ { T }$ with finite μ-measure, we need to show that $\eta B _ { 1 } , \ldots , \eta B _ { n }$ are independent Poisson variables with means $\mu B _ { 1 } , \ldots ,$ $\mu B _ { n }$ . Then define for each $k \leq n$ the processes 

$$
\begin{array}{l} J _ {t} ^ {k} = \int_ {S} \int_ {0} ^ {t +} 1 _ {B _ {k}} (Y _ {s, x}) \xi (d s d x), \\ \hat {J} _ {t} ^ {k} = \int_ {S} \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 _ {B _ {k}} (Y _ {s, x}) \hat {\xi} (d s d x). \end{array}
$$

Here $\hat { J } _ { \infty } ^ { k } = \mu B _ { k } < \infty$ a.s. by hypothesis, and so the $J ^ { k }$ are simple, integrable point processes on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with compensators ${ \hat { J } } ^ { k }$ . For fixed $u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { n } \geq 0$ , we put 

$$
X _ {t} = \sum_ {k <   n} \left\{u _ {k} J _ {t} ^ {k} - (1 - e ^ {- u _ {k}}) \hat {J} _ {t} ^ {k} \right\}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

The process $M _ { t } = e ^ { - X _ { t } }$ has bounded variation and finitely many jumps, and so by an elementary change of variables, 

$$
\begin{array}{r} M _ {t} - 1 = \sum_ {s \leq t} \Delta e ^ {- X _ {s}} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- X _ {s}} d X _ {s} ^ {c} \\ = \sum_ {k \leq n} \int_ {0} ^ {t +} e ^ {- X _ {s -}} (1 - e ^ {- u _ {k}}) d \Big (\hat {J} _ {s} ^ {k} - J _ {s} ^ {k} \Big). \end{array}
$$

Since the integrands on the right are bounded and predictable, M is a uniformly integrable martingale, and so $E M _ { \infty } = 1$ . Thus, 

$$
E \exp \left(- \sum_ {k} u _ {k} \eta B _ {k}\right) = \exp \left\{- \sum_ {k} \left(1 - e ^ {- u _ {k}}\right) \mu B _ {k} \right\},
$$

and the assertion follows by Theorem 6.3. 

We also have a multi-variate time-change result, similar to Proposition 19.8 for continuous local martingales. Say that the simple point processes $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n }$ are orthogonal if $\textstyle \sum _ { k } \xi _ { k } \{ s \} \leq 1$ for all s. 

Corollary 15.16 (time-change reduction to Poisson, Papangelou, Meyer) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n }$ be orthogonal, ql-continuous point processes on $( 0 , \infty )$ with a.s. unbounded compensators $\hat { \xi } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \hat { \xi } _ { n } .$ , and define 

$$
Y _ {k} (t) = \inf \left\{s > 0; \hat {\xi} _ {k} [ 0, s ] > t \right\}, \quad t \geq 0, k \leq n.
$$

Then the processes $\eta _ { k } = \xi _ { k } \circ Y _ { k } ^ { - 1 }$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ are independent, unit-rate Poisson. 

Proof: The processes $\eta _ { k }$ are Poisson by Theorem 15.15, since each $Y _ { k }$ is predictable and 

$$
\hat {\xi} _ {k} [ 0, Y _ {k} (t) ] = \hat {\xi} _ {k} \left\{s \geq 0; \hat {\xi} _ {k} [ 0, s ] \leq t \right\} = t \text { a   .   s   . }, \quad t \geq 0,
$$

by the continuity of $\hat { \xi } _ { k }$ . The multi-variate statement follows from the same theorem, if we apply the predictable map $Y = ( Y _ { 1 } , \ldots , Y _ { n } ) $ to the marked point process ${ \boldsymbol \xi } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \dots , \xi _ { n } )$ on $( 0 , \infty ) \times \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ with compensator $\hat { \xi } =$ $( \hat { \xi } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \hat { \xi } _ { n } )$ ✷ 

From Theorem 15.15 we see that a ql-continuous, marked point process $\xi$ is Poisson if its compensator is a.s. non-random, similarly to the characterization of Brownian motion in Theorem 19.3. The following more general statement may be regarded as an extension of Theorem 15.10.

Poisson integrals of various kind occur frequently in applications. Here we give criteria for the existence of the integrals $\xi f , ( \xi - \xi ^ { \prime } ) f$ , and $( \xi - \mu ) f ,$ , where $\xi$ and $\xi ^ { \prime }$ are independent Poisson processes with a common intensity $\mu .$ . # Independent-Increment and L´evy Processes

Infinitely divisible distributions, independent-increment processes, L´evy processes and subordinators, orthogonality and independence, stable L´evy processes, first-passage times, coupling of L´evy processes, approximation of random walks, arcsine laws, time change of stable integrals, tangential existence and comparison 

Just as random walks are the most basic Markov processes in discrete time, so also the L´evy processes constitute the most fundamental among continuoustime Markov processes, as they are precisely the processes of this kind that are both space- and time-homogeneous. They may also be characterized as processes with stationary, independent increments, which suggests that they be thought of simply as random walks in continuous time. Basic special cases are given by Brownian motion and homogeneous Poisson processes. 

Dropping the stationarity assumption leads to the broader class of processes with independent increments, and since many of the basic properties are the same, it is natural to extend our study to this larger class. Under weak regular ity conditions, their paths are right-continuous with left-hand limits (rcll), and the one-dimensional distributions agree with the infinitely divisible laws studied in Chapter 7. As the latter are formed by a combination of Gaussian and compound Poisson distributions, the general independent-increment processes are composed of Gaussian processes and suitable Poisson integrals. 

The classical limit theorems of Chapters 6–7 suggest similar approximations of random walks by L´evy processes, which may serve as an introduction to the general weak convergence theory in Chapters 22–23. In this context, we will see how results for random walks or Brownian motion may be extended to a more general continuous-time context. In particular, two of the arcsine laws derived for Brownian motion in Chapter 14 remain valid for general symmetric L´evy processes. 

Independent-increment processes may also be regarded as the simplest special cases of semi-martingales, to be studied in full generality in Chapter 20. We conclude the chapter with a discussion of tangential processes, where the idea is to approximate a general semi-martingale X by a process X<sup>˜</sup> with conditionally independent increments, such that X and X<sup>˜</sup> have similar asymptotic properties. This is useful, since the asymptotic behavior of the latter processes can often be determined by elementary methods. 

To resume our discussion of general processes with independent increments, we say that an $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ -valued process X is continuous in $p r o b a b i l i t y ^ { 1 }$ if $X _ { s } \ { \overset { P } { \to } } \ X _ { t }$ whenever $s \to t$ . This clearly prevents the existence of fixed discontinuities. To examine the structure of processes with independent increments, we may first choose regular versions of the paths. Recall that X is said to be $r c l l ^ { 2 }$ , if it has finite limits $X _ { t \pm }$ from the right and left at every point $t \geq 0$ , and the former equals $X _ { t }$ . Then the only possible discontinuities are jumps, and we say that X has a fixed jump at a time $t > 0$ if $P \{ X _ { t } \neq X _ { t - } \} > 0$ 

Lemma 16.1 (infinitely divisible distributions, de Finetti) For a random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi$ is infinitely divisible, 

(ii) $\xi \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ X _ { 1 }$ for a process X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with stationary, independent increments and $X _ { 0 } = 0$ 

We may then choose X to be continuous in probability, in which case 

(iii) ${ \mathcal { L } } ( X )$ is uniquely determined by $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ 

(iv) $\xi \in \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } \ { a . s . } \ \Leftrightarrow \ X _ { t } \in \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d } \ { a . s . } , t \geq 0 .$

We first describe the processes with stationary, independent increments:

A process X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with stationary, independent increments is called a L´evy processes, and when X is $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ -valued it is also called a subordinator<sup>3</sup>. Furthermore, the measure ν is called the L´evy measure of X. The result follows easily from the theory of infinitely divisible distributions: 

Proof: Given Theorem 7.5, it is enough to show that X has an rcll version. The last result can also be proved by probabilistic methods. where the summations extend over all times $t > 0$ with $\Delta X _ { t } = X _ { t } - X _ { t - } \neq 0$

As for the fixed discontinuities, let $D \subset ( 0 , \infty )$ be the countable supporting set and write $\begin{array} { r } { \eta = \sum _ { t \in D } \delta _ { t , \xi _ { t } } } \end{array}$ , where the $\xi _ { t }$ are independent random vectors in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and we interpret $\delta _ { t , 0 }$ as 0. Proposition 16.6 (regularization) For a process X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with independent increments, these conditions are equivalent:

To separate the jump component from the remainder of $X$ , we need the following independence criterion: 

Lemma 16.8 (orthogonality and independence) Let $( X , Y )$ be an rcll processes in $( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } ) ^ { 2 }$ with independent increments and $X _ { 0 } = Y _ { 0 } = 0$ , where $Y$ is an elementary step process. Then

This shows that $E M _ { t } ^ { u } N _ { t } ^ { v } = 1$ , and so

E e ^ {i u X _ {t} + i v Y _ {t}} = E e ^ {i u X _ {t}} E e ^ {i v Y _ {t}}, \quad t <   t _ {u, v}, u, v \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.

Proposition 16.9 (Gaussian processes with independent increments) Let X be an rcll process in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with independent increments and $X _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then these conditions are equivalent:

By Proposition 11.5, a L´evy process X is Markov for the induced filtration $\mathcal { G } = \left( \mathcal { G } _ { t } \right)$ , with the translation-invariant transition kernels 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu_ {t} (x, B) = \mu_ {t} (0, B - x) \\ = P \{X _ {t} \in B - x \}, t \geq 0. \end{array}
$$

More generally, given any filtration ${ \mathcal { F } } ,$ we say that a process X is L´evy with respect to $\mathcal { F }$ or simply $\mathcal { F } _ { - } L e v y .$ if it is adapted to $\mathcal { F }$ and such that $( X _ { t } - X _ { s } )$ $\mathcal { F } _ { s }$ for all $s < t$ . $$

which is right-continuous by Corollary 9.26. Just as for Brownian motion in Theorem 14.11, we see that when X is -L´evy for a right-continuous, complete filtration ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { : }$ , it is a strong Markov process, in the sense that the process $X ^ { \prime } =$ $\theta _ { \tau } X - X ,$ satisfies $X \overset { d } { = } X ^ { \prime } \overset { \ldots } { \bot } \mathcal { F } _ { \tau }$ for every optional time $\tau < \infty$ 

Turning to some symmetry conditions, we say that a process X on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ is self-similar, if for every $r > 0$ the scaled process $X _ { r t } , ~ t \ge ~ 0 ,$ , has the same distribution as $s X$ for a constant $s = h ( r ) > 0$ . Excluding the trivial case of $E | X _ { t } | \equiv 0$ , we see that $h$ satisfies the Cauchy equation $h ( r s ) = h ( r ) h ( s )$ . If 

X is right-continuous, then h is continuous, and all solutions are of the form $h ( r ) = r ^ { \alpha }$ for some $\alpha \in \mathsf { R }$ 

A L´evy process X in R is said to be strictly stable if it is self-similar, and weakly stable if it is self-similar apart from a centering, so that for every $r > 0$ the process $X _ { r t }$ has the same distribution as $s X _ { t } + b t$ for some s and b. In either case, the symmetrized version $X - X ^ { \prime }$ is strictly stable with the same parameter $\alpha ,$ and so s is again of the form $r ^ { \alpha }$ . Since clearly $\alpha > 0$ , we may introduce the stability index $p = \alpha ^ { - 1 }$ , and say that X is strictly or weakly $p - s t a b l e$ . The terminology carries over to random variables or vectors with distribution $\mathcal { L } ( X _ { 1 } )$ 

Corollary 16.11 (stable L´evy processes) Let X be a non-degenerate L´evy process in R with characteristics $( a , b , \nu )$ Then X is weakly p-stable for a $p > 0 \ i f f$ one of these conditions holds:

For subordinators, it is further equivalent that 

(iii) $p \in ( 0 , 1 )$ and $\nu ( d x ) = c x ^ { - p - 1 }$ dx on (0, ) for a c > 0.

If X is weakly p -stable with $p \neq 1$ , it becomes strictly p -stable through a suitable centering. In particular, a weakly $p { \mathrm { - s t a b l e } }$ subordinator is strictly stable if its drift component vanishes, in which case X is simply said to be stable. We show how stable subordinators may arise naturally even in the context of continuous processes. Given a Brownian motion B in $\mathsf { R } ,$ , we introduce the maximum process $M _ { t } = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { s \leq t } B _ { s }$ with right-continuous inverse 

$$

Theorem 16.12 (first-passage times, L´evy) For a Brownian motion $B _ { i }$ , the process $T$ is a 1 -stable subordinator with L´evy measure

If we add a negative drift to a Brownian motion, the associated maximum process M becomes bounded, so that $T \ = \ M ^ { - 1 }$ terminates by a jump to infinity. Here it becomes useful to allow subordinators with infinite jumps. By an extended subordinator we mean a process of the form $X _ { t } \equiv Y _ { t } + \infty$ $1 \{ t \geq \zeta \}$ a.s., where $Y$ is an ordinary subordinator and $\zeta$ is an independent, exponentially distributed random variable, so that X is obtained from Y by exponential killing. The representation in Theorem 16.3 remains valid in the extended case, except for a positive mass of $\nu$ at $\infty$ 

The following characterization is needed in Chapter 29. 

Lemma 16.13 (extended subordinators) Let X be a non-decreasing, rightcontinuous process in $[ 0 , \infty ]$ with $X _ { 0 } = 0$ and induced filtration $\mathcal { F }$ . Then X is an extended subordinator $i f f$ 

$$
\mathcal {L} \left(X _ {s + t} - X _ {s} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {s}\right) = \mathcal {L} (X _ {t}) a. s. o n \{X _ {s} <   \infty \}, \quad s, t > 0.\tag{5}
$$

Proof: Writing $\zeta = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t ; X _ { t } = \infty \}$ , we get from (5) the Cauchy equation 

$$

Anticipating our more detailed treatment in Chapter 20, we define a semimartingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ as an adapted process X with rcll paths, admitting a centering into a local martingale. Thus, subtracting all suitably centered jumps yields a continuous semi-martingale, in the sense of Chapter 18. Here the centering of small jumps amounts to a subtraction of the compensator $\hat { \eta }$ rather than the intensity $E \eta$ of the jump point process $\eta ,$ to ensure that the resulting process will be a local martingale. The set of local characteristics of X is given by the triple $( \hat { \eta } , [ M ] , A )$ , where $M$ is a continuous local martingale and A is a continuous, predictable process of locally finite variation, such that X is the sum of the centered jumps and the continuous semi-martingale $M + A$ . Tangential processes have similar asymptotic properties at $\infty .$ . Here we state only the most basic result of this type. Say that the function $\varphi \colon \mathsf { R } _ { + } \to \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ has moderate growth, if it is non-decreasing and continuous with $\varphi ( 0 ) = 0$ , and there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that $\varphi ( 2 x ) \leq c \varphi ( x )$ for all $x > 0$ . In that case, there exists a function $h > 0$ on $( 0 , \infty )$ , such that $\varphi ( c x ) \leq h ( c ) \varphi ( x )$ for all $c , x > 0$ . Basic examples include the power functions $\varphi ( x ) = | x | ^ { p }$ with $p > 0$ , and the functions $\varphi ( x ) = x \wedge 1$ and $\varphi ( x ) = 1 - e ^ { - x }$ 

Theorem 16.22 (tangential comparison, Zinn, Hitchenko, OK) Let the processes X, Y be tangential and either increasing or locally symmetric. Then for any function $\varphi \colon \mathsf { R } _ { + } \to \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ of moderate growth, we have<sup>7</sup> 

$$
E \varphi (X ^ {*}) \asymp E \varphi (Y ^ {*}).
$$

Lemma 16.23 (tail comparison) Let the processes $X , Y$ be tangential and either increasing or locally symmetric. Then for any $c , x > 0$ ,

Proof: (i) Let $\xi , \eta$ be the jump point processes of $X , Y$ . Fix any $x > 0$ , and introduce the optional time 

$$
\tau = \inf \left\{t > 0; | \Delta Y _ {t} | > x \right\}.
$$

Since the set $( 0 , \tau ]$ is predictable by Lemma 10.2, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{(\Delta X) ^ {*} > x \Big \} \leq P \{\tau <   \infty \} + E   \xi \Big \{(0, \tau ] \times [ - x, x ] ^ {c} \Big \} \\ \qquad = P \{\tau <   \infty \} + E   \eta \Big \{(0, \tau ] \times [ - x, x ] ^ {c} \Big \} \\ \qquad = 2   P \{\tau <   \infty \} \\ \qquad = 2   P \Big \{(\Delta Y) ^ {*} > x \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

(ii) Fix any $c , x > 0$ . For increasing X, Y, form $\hat { X } , \hat { Y }$ by omitting all jumps greater than cx, which clearly preserves the tangential relation. If $X , Y$ are instead locally symmetric, we form $\hat { X } , \hat { Y }$ by omitting all jumps of modulus $> 2 c x$ By Lemma 20.5 below and its proof, $\hat { X } , \hat { Y }$ are then local L<sup>2</sup>-martingales with jumps a.s. bounded by 4cx. They also remain tangential, and the tangential relation carries over to the quadratic variation processes $[ { \hat { X } } ] , [ { \hat { Y } } ]$ 

Now introduce the optional time 

$$
\tau = \inf \left\{t > 0; | \hat {Y} _ {t} | > c x \right\}.
$$

For increasing $X , Y$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} x P \{\hat {X} _ {\tau} > x \} & \leq E \hat {X} _ {\tau} = E \hat {Y} _ {\tau} \\ & = E \hat {Y} _ {\tau -} + E \Delta \hat {Y} _ {\tau} \\ & \leq 3 c x. \end{array}
$$

f $X , Y$ are instead locally symmetric, then using the Jensen and Bernstein– L´evy inequalities in 4.5 and 9.16, the integration by parts formula in Theorem 20.6 below, and the tangential properties and bounds, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(x   P \{\hat {X} _ {\tau} ^ {*} > x \}\right) ^ {2} \leq (E | \hat {X} _ {\tau} |) ^ {2} \\ \quad \leq E \hat {X} _ {\tau} ^ {2} = E [ \hat {X} ] _ {\tau} \\ \quad = E [ \hat {Y} ] _ {\tau} = E \hat {Y} _ {\tau} ^ {2} \\ \quad \leq \left(| \hat {Y} _ {\tau -} | + | \Delta \hat {Y} _ {\tau} |\right) ^ {2} \\ \quad \leq (4 c x) ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

Thus, in both cases $P \{ \hat { X } _ { \tau } ^ { * } > x \} \leq 4 c .$ 

Since $Y ^ { * } \ge { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ( \Delta Y ) ^ { * }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left\{(\Delta X) ^ {*} \leq 2 c x \right\} \subset \{X = \hat {X} \}, \\ \{\tau <   \infty \} \subset \{\hat {Y} ^ {*} > c x \} \subset \{Y ^ {*} > c x \}. \end{array}
$$

Combining with the previous tail estimate and (i), we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \{X ^ {*} > x \} \leq P \bigl \{(\Delta X) ^ {*} > 2 c x \bigr \} + P \{X ^ {*} > x \} \\ & \quad \leq 2   P \bigl \{(\Delta Y) ^ {*} > 2 c x \bigr \} + P \{\tau <   \infty \} + P \{\hat {X} _ {\tau} ^ {*} > x \} \\ & \quad \leq 3   P \{Y ^ {*} > c x \} + 4 c. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 16.22: For any $c , x > 0$ , consider the optional times 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tau = \inf \Bigl \{t > 0; | X _ {t} | > x \Bigr \}, \\ \sigma = \inf \Bigl \{t > 0; P \bigl \{(\theta_ {t} Y) ^ {*} > c x | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \bigr \} > c \Bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

Since $\theta _ { \tau } X , \theta _ { \tau } Y$ remain conditionally tangential given $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau }$ , Lemma 16.23 (ii) yields a.s. on $\{ \tau < \sigma \}$

$$

and since $\{ \tau < \sigma \} \in \mathcal { F } _ { \tau }$ by Lemma 9.1, we get

\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{X ^ {*} > 3   x, (\Delta X) ^ {*} \leq x, \sigma = \infty \Big \} \\ \quad \leq P \Big \{(\theta_ {\tau} X) ^ {*} > x, \tau <   \sigma \Big \} \\ \quad = E \Big \{P \big \{(\theta_ {\tau} X) ^ {*} > x   |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \};   \tau <   \sigma \Big \} \\ \quad \leq 7 c   P \{\tau <   \infty \} \\ \quad = 7 c   P \{X ^ {*} > x \}. \end{array}

Furthermore, Lemma 16.23 (i) yields

\begin{array}{c} P \Bigl \{(\Delta X) ^ {*} > x \Bigr \} \leq 2   P \Bigl \{(\Delta Y) ^ {*} > x \Bigr \} \\ \leq 2   P \Bigl \{Y ^ {*} > \frac {1}{2}   x \Bigr \}, \end{array}

and Theorem 9.16 gives

\begin{array}{l} P \{\sigma <   \infty \} = P \Big \{\sup _ {t} P \Big \{(  \theta_ {t} Y) ^ {*} > c   x   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {t} \Big \} > c \Big \} \\ \qquad \leq P \Big \{\sup _ {t} P \Big (  Y ^ {*} > \frac {1}{2}   c   x   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {t} \Big) > c \Big \} \\ \qquad \leq c ^ {- 1} P \Big \{Y ^ {*} > \frac {1}{2}   c   x \Big \}. \end{array}

Combining the last three estimates, we obtain

$$

Since $\varphi$ is non-decreasing of moderate growth, so that $\varphi ( r x ) \leq h ( r ) \varphi ( x )$ for some function $h > 0$ , we obtain

\begin{array}{l} (h _ {3} ^ {- 1} - 7 c) E   \varphi (X ^ {*}) \leq E   \varphi (X ^ {*} / 3) - 7 c   E   \varphi (X ^ {*}) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}

Now choose $c < ( 7 h _ { 3 } ) ^ { - 1 }$ to get $E \varphi ( X ^ { * } ) \lesssim E \varphi ( Y ^ { * } )$ 

Combining the last two theorems, we may simplify the tangential comparison. Say that X, Y are weakly tangential if their local characteristics have the same distribution. Here there is no mention of associated filtrations, and the two processes may even be defined on diferent probability spaces. 

Corollary 16.24 (extended comparison) Theorem 16.22 remains true when X and $Y$ are weakly tangential. 

Proof: Let $X , Y$ be semi-martingales on some probability spaces $\Omega , \Omega ^ { \prime }$ with filtrations ${ \mathcal { F } } , { \mathcal { G } }$ , and write A, B for the associated local characteristics. By Theorem 16.20 we may choose some processes $\tilde { X } , \tilde { Y }$ with conditionally independent increments, on suitable extensions of $\Omega , \Omega ^ { \prime }$ , such that $X , { \tilde { X } }$ are <sup>˜</sup>-tangential while $Y , { \tilde { Y } }$ are <sup>˜</sup> -tangential, for some standard extensions $\tilde { \mathcal { F } }$ of $\mathcal { F }$ and $\tilde { \mathcal { G } }$ of $\mathcal { G }$ . Now suppose that $A \stackrel { d } { = } B$ , and conclude that also ${ \tilde { X } } { \stackrel { d } { = } } { \tilde { Y } }$ since $\tilde { X } , \tilde { Y }$ have conditionally independent increments. Assuming $X , Y$ to be either increasing or locally symmetric and letting $\varphi$ have moderate growth, we get by Theorem 16.22

$$

Chapter 17 

# Feller Processes and Semi-groups

Transition semi-groups, pseudo-Poisson processes, Feller properties, resolvents and generator, forward and backward equations, Yosida approximation, closure and cores, L´evy processes, Hille–Yosida theorem, positive-maximum principle, compactification, existence and regularization, strong Markov property, discontinuity sets, Dynkin’s formula, characteristic operator, difusions and elliptic operators, convergence ofFeller processes, approximation of Markov chains, quasi-left continuity 

As stressed before, Markov processes are among the most basic processes of modern probability. After studying several special cases in previous chapters, we now turn to a detailed study of the broad class of Feller processes. Those are Markov processes general enough to cover most applications of interest, yet restricted by some regularity conditions that allow for a reasonable flexibility, leading to a rich arsenal of basic tools and powerful properties. 

The crucial new idea is to regard the transition kernels as operators $T _ { t }$ on an appropriate function space. The Chapman–Kolmogorov relation then turns into the semi-group property $T _ { s } T _ { t } = T _ { s + t }$ , which suggests a formal representation $T _ { t } = e ^ { t A }$ in terms of a generator A. Under suitable regularity conditions— the so-called Feller properties—it is indeed possible to define a generator A describing the infinitesimal evolution of the underlying process X. Under further conditions, X will be shown to have continuous paths if A extends an elliptic diferential operator. In general, the powerful Hille–Yosida theorem provides precise conditions for the existence of a Feller process corresponding to a given operator A. 

Using the basic regularity theorem for sub-martingales from Chapter 9, we show that every Feller process has a right-continuous version with left-hand limits. Given this fundamental result, it is straightforward to extend the strong Markov property to arbitrary Feller processes. We also explore some profound connections with martingale theory. Finally, we establish a general continuity theorem for Feller processes, and deduce a corresponding approximation of discrete-time Markov chains by difusions and other continuous-time Markov processes, anticipating some weak convergence results from Chapter 23. 

To clarify the connection between transition kernels and operators, let $\mu$ be an arbitrary probability kernel on a measurable space (S, ). The associated transition operator T is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} T f (x) = (T f) (x) \\ \qquad = \int \mu (x, d y)   f (y), \quad x \in S, \end{array}\tag{1}
$$

where $f : S  \mathsf { R }$ is assumed to be measurable and either bounded or nonnegative. Approximating f by simple functions and using monotone convergence, we see that $T f$ is again a measurable function on S. We also note that $T$ is a positive contraction operator, in the sense that $0 \leq f \leq 1$ implies $0 \leq T f \leq 1 .$ . A special role is played by the identity operator I, corresponding to the kernel $\mu ( x , \cdot ) \equiv \delta _ { x }$ . The importance of transition operators for the study of Markov processes is due to the following simple fact. 

Lemma 17.1 (semi-group property) For each $t \geq 0$ , let $\mu _ { t }$ be a probability kernel on S with associated transition operator $T _ { t }$ . Then for any $s , t \geq 0$ , 

$$
\mu_ {s + t} = \mu_ {s} \mu_ {t} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad T _ {s + t} = T _ {s} T _ {t}.
$$

Proof: For any $B \in S$ , we have $T _ { s + t } 1 _ { B } ( x ) = \mu _ { s + t } ( x , B )$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} (T _ {s} T _ {t}) 1 _ {B} (x) & = T _ {s} (T _ {t} 1 _ {B}) (x) \\ & = \int \mu_ {s} (x, d y) (T _ {t} 1 _ {B}) (y) \\ & = \int \mu_ {s} (x, d y) \mu_ {t} (y, B) \\ & = (\mu_ {s} \mu_ {t}) (x, B). \end{array}
$$

Thus, the Chapman–Kolmogorov relation on the left is equivalent to $T _ { s + t } 1 _ { B } =$ $( T _ { s } T _ { t } ) \boldsymbol { 1 } _ { B }$ for any $B \in S$ , which extends to the semi-group property $T _ { s + t } = T _ { s } T _ { t }$ , by linearity and monotone convergence. ✷ 

By analogy with the situation for the Cauchy equation, we might hope to represent the semi-group in the form $T _ { t } = e ^ { t A } , t \geq 0$ , for a suitable generator A. For this formula to make sense, the operator A must be suitably bounded, so that the exponential function can be defined through a Taylor expansion. We consider a simple case where such a representation exists. 

Proposition 17.2 (pseudo-Poisson processes) Let $( T _ { t } )$ be the transition semigroup of a pure jump-type Markov process in S with bounded rate kernel α. Then $T _ { t } = e ^ { t A } , t \geq 0$ , where for bounded measurable functions $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ , 

$$
A f (x) = \int \left\{f (y) - f (x) \right\} \alpha (x, d y), \quad x \in S.
$$

Proof: Since $\alpha$ is bounded, we may write $\alpha ( x , B ) \equiv c \mu ( x , B \setminus \{ x \} )$ for a probability kernel $\mu$ and a constant $c \geq 0$ . By Proposition 13.7, X is then a pseudo-Poisson process of the form $X ~ = ~ Y ~ \circ ~ N$ , where $Y$ is a discretetime Markov chain with transition kernel $\mu _ { ; }$ , and $N$ is an independent Poisson process with fixed rate $c .$ . Letting $T$ be the transition operator associated with $\mu ,$ , we get for any $t \geq 0$ and $f$ as stated 

$$
\begin{array}{l} T _ {t} f (x) = E _ {x} f (X _ {t}) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {n \geq 0} E _ {x} \Big \{f (Y _ {n}); N _ {t} = n \Big \} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {n \geq 0} P \{N _ {t} = n \} E _ {x} f (Y _ {n}) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {n \geq 0} e ^ {- c t} \frac {(c t) ^ {n}}{n !} T ^ {n} f (x) \\ \qquad = e ^ {c t (T - I)} f (x). \end{array}
$$

Hence, $T _ { t } = e ^ { t A }$ for all $t \geq 0$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A f (x) = c \left(T - I\right) f (x) \\ \qquad = c \int \Big \{f (y) - f (x) \Big \} \mu (x, d y) \\ \qquad = \int \Big \{f (y) - f (x) \Big \} \alpha (x, d y). \end{array}
$$

For the further analysis, we take $S$ to be a locally compact, separable metric space, and write $C _ { 0 } = C _ { 0 } ( S )$ for the class of continuous functions $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ with $f ( x )  0$ as $x \to \infty$ . We can make $C _ { 0 }$ into a Banach space by introducing the norm $\| f \| = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { x } \left| f ( x ) \right|$ . A semi-group of positive contraction operators $T _ { t }$ on $C _ { 0 }$ is called a Feller semi-group, if it has the additional regularity properties 

$$
\left(\mathrm{F} _ {1}\right) T _ {t} C _ {0} \subset C _ {0}, t \geq 0,
$$

$$
\left(\mathrm{F} _ {2}\right) T _ {t} f (x) \rightarrow f (x) \text {   as   } t \rightarrow 0, \quad f \in C _ {0}, x \in S.
$$

In Theorem 17.6 we show that $\left( \mathrm { F _ { 1 } } \right) - \left( \mathrm { F _ { 2 } } \right)$ , together with the semi-group property, imply the strong continuity 

$$
\left(\mathrm{F} _ {3}\right) T _ {t} f \rightarrow f \text {as} t \rightarrow 0, f \in C _ {0}.
$$

To clarify the probabilistic significance of those conditions, we assume for simplicity that $S$ is compact, and also that $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ is conservative, in the sense that $T _ { t } 1 = 1$ for all t. For every initial state x, we may introduce an associated Markov process $X _ { t } ^ { x } , t \geq 0$ , with transition operators $T _ { t }$ 

Lemma 17.3 (Feller properties) Let $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ be a conservative transition semigroup on a compact metric space $( S , \rho )$ . Then the Feller properties $\left( \mathrm { F _ { 1 } } \right) \mathrm { - ( F _ { 3 } ) }$ are equivalent to, respectively, 

(i) $X _ { t } ^ { x } \overset { d } { \to } X _ { t } ^ { y }$ as $x  y , \quad t \geq 0 .$ 

(ii) $X _ { t } ^ { x } \overset { P } { \to } x$ as $t \to 0 , \quad x \in S .$ 

$$
\text {(iii)} \sup _ {x} E _ {x} \left\{\rho (X _ {s}, X _ {t}) \wedge 1 \right\}\rightarrow 0 a s | s - t | \rightarrow 0.
$$

Proof: The first two equivalences are obvious, so we prove only the third one. Then let the sequence $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be dense in $C = C _ { S }$ . By the compactness of S, we note that $x _ { n } \to x$ in S if $f _ { k } ( x _ { n } ) \to f _ { k } ( x )$ for each $k .$ . Thus, $\rho$ is topologically equivalent to the metric 

$$
\rho^ {\prime} (x, y) = \sum_ {k \geq 1} 2 ^ {- k} \left\{\left| f _ {k} (x) - f _ {k} (y) \right| \wedge 1 \right\}, \quad x, y \in S.
$$

Since $S$ is compact, the identity mapping on $S$ is uniformly continuous with respect to $\rho$ and $\rho ^ { \prime } .$ , and so we may assume that $\rho = \rho ^ { \prime }$ 

Next we note that, for any $f \in C , \ x \in S$ , and $t , h \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {x} \Big \{f (X _ {t}) - f (X _ {t + h}) \Big \} ^ {2} = E _ {x} \Big (f ^ {2} - 2 f   T _ {h} f - T _ {h} f ^ {2} \Big) (X _ {t}) \\ \qquad \leq \left\| f ^ {2} - 2 f   T _ {h} f + T _ {h} f ^ {2} \right\| \\ \qquad \leq 2 \| f \| \left\| f - T _ {h} f \right\| + \left\| f ^ {2} - T _ {h} f ^ {2} \right\|. \end{array}
$$

Assuming $\left( \mathrm { F _ { 3 } } \right)$ , we get $\mathrm { s u p } _ { x } E _ { x } | f _ { k } ( X _ { s } ) - f _ { k } ( X _ { t } ) | \to 0$ as $s - t \to 0$ for fixed $k ,$ and so by dominated convergence ${ \mathrm { s u p } } _ { x } E _ { x } \rho ( X _ { s } , X _ { t } ) \to 0$ . Conversely, the latter condition yields $T _ { h } f _ { k } \to f _ { k }$ for each k, which implies $\left( \mathrm { F _ { 3 } } \right)$ ✷ 

Our first aim is to construct the generator of a Feller semi-group $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ on $C _ { 0 }$ . Since in general there is no bounded linear operator A satisfying $T _ { t } = e ^ { t A }$ , we need to look for a suitable substitute. For motivation, note that if $p$ is a real-valued function on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with representation $p _ { t } = e ^ { a t }$ , we can recover a from $p$ by either a diferentiation or an integration: 

$$
t ^ {- 1} (p _ {t} - 1) \rightarrow a \mathrm{as} t \rightarrow 0,
$$

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \lambda t} p _ {t} d t = (\lambda - a) ^ {- 1}, \quad \lambda > 0.
$$

The latter formula suggests that we introduce, for every $\lambda > 0$ , the resolvent or potential $R _ { \lambda }$ , defined as the Laplace transform 

$$
R _ {\lambda} f = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \lambda t} (T _ {t} f) d t, \quad f \in C _ {0}.
$$

Note that the integral exists, since $T _ { t } f ( x )$ is bounded and right-continuous in $t \geq 0$ for fixed $x \in S$ 

Theorem 17.4 (resolvents and generator) Let $( T _ { t } )$ be a Feller semi-group on $C _ { 0 }$ with resolvents $R _ { \lambda } , \lambda > 0$ . Then 

(i) the $\lambda R _ { \lambda }$ are injective contraction operators on $C _ { 0 }$ , and $\lambda R _ { \lambda } \to I$ holds strongly as $\lambda \to \infty$ , 

(ii) the range $\mathcal { D } = R _ { \lambda } C _ { 0 }$ is independent of λ and dense in $C _ { 0 }$ 

(iii) there exists an operator A on $C _ { 0 }$ with domain ${ \mathcal { D } } ,$ such that $R _ { \lambda } ^ { - 1 } = \lambda - A$ on for every $\lambda > 0$ , 

(iv) A and $T _ { t }$ commute on for every $t \geq 0$ 

Proof, $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ : If $f \in C _ { 0 }$ , then $\left( \operatorname { F } _ { 1 } \right)$ yields $T _ { t } f \in C _ { 0 }$ for every t, and so by dominated convergence we have even $R _ { \lambda } f \in C _ { 0 }$ . To prove the stated contraction property, we may write for any $f \in C _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left\| \lambda R _ {\lambda} f \right\| \leq \lambda \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \lambda t} \| T _ {t} f \| d t} \\ & {\quad \leq \lambda \| f \| \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- \lambda t} d t = \| f \|.} \end{array}
$$

A simple computation yields the resolvent equation 

$$
R _ {\lambda} - R _ {\mu} = (\mu - \lambda) R _ {\lambda} R _ {\mu}, \quad \lambda , \mu > 0,\tag{2}
$$

which shows that the operators $R _ { \lambda }$ commute and have a common range . If $f = R _ { 1 } g$ for some $g \in C _ { 0 }$ , we get by (2) as $\lambda \to \infty$ 

$$

The convergence extends by a simple approximation to the closure of $\mathcal { D } .$ 

Now introduce the one-point compactification ${ \hat { S } } = S \cup \{ \Delta \}$ of S, and extend any $f \in C _ { 0 }$ to $\hat { C } = C ( \hat { S } )$ by putting $f ( \Delta ) = 0$ . The operator A in Theorem 17.4 is called the generator of the semi-group $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ . To emphasize the role of the domain , we often say that (T ) has generator $( A , D )$ . The term is justified by the following lemma. 

Lemma 17.5 (uniqueness) A Feller semi-group is uniquely determined by its generator. 

Proof: The operator A determines $R _ { \lambda } = ( \lambda - A ) ^ { - 1 }$ for all $\lambda > 0$ . We now show that any Feller semi-group is strongly continuous, and derive general versions of Kolmogorov’s forward and backward equations. 

Theorem 17.6 (strong continuity, forward and backward equations) Let $( T _ { t } )$ be a Feller semi-group with generator $( A , D )$ . Then

To identify $\tilde { T } _ { t }$ , we may use the resolvent equation (2) to obtain, for any $f \in C _ { 0 }$ and $\lambda , \mu > 0$ ,

Proof of Theorem 17.6: The semi-group $( T _ { t } ^ { \lambda } )$ is clearly norm continuous in t for each $\lambda > 0$ , and the strong continuity of $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ follows by Lemma 17.7 as $\lambda  \infty$ . For a given generator A, it is often hard to identify the domain , or the latter may simply be too large for convenient calculations. It is then useful to restrict A to a suitable sub-domain. An operator A with domain on a Banach space B is said to be closed, if its graph $G = \{ ( f , A f ) ; f \in { \mathcal { D } } \}$ is a closed subset of $B ^ { 2 }$ . In general, we say that A is closable, if the closure $\bar { G }$ is the graph of a single-valued operator ${ \bar { A } } ,$ , called the closure of A. Note that A is closable if the conditions $\mathcal { D } \ni f _ { n } \to 0$ and $A f _ { n } \to g$ imply $g = 0$ 

When A is closed, a core for A is defined as a linear sub-space $D \subset { \mathcal { D } } ,$ such that the restriction $A | _ { D }$ has closure A. Note that A is then uniquely determined by $A | _ { D }$ . We give conditions ensuring $D \subset \mathcal { D }$ to be a core, when A is the generator of a Feller semi-group (T ) on $C _ { 0 }$

A sub-space $D \subset C _ { 0 }$ is said to be invariant under $( T _ { t } )$ if $T _ { t } D \subset D$ for all $t \geq 0$ . Note that for any subset $B \subset C _ { 0 }$ , the linear span of $\cup _ { t } { T _ { t } } B$ is an invariant sub-space of $C _ { 0 }$

To deduce the semi-group property, fix any $f \in C _ { 0 }$ and $s , t \geq 0$ , and note that as $\lambda \to \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \big (T _ {s + t} - T _ {s} T _ {t} \big) f = \big (T _ {s + t} - T _ {s + t} ^ {\lambda} \big) f + T _ {s} ^ {\lambda} \big (T _ {t} ^ {\lambda} - T _ {t} \big) f \\ + \big (T _ {s} ^ {\lambda} - T _ {s} \big) T _ {t} f \to 0. \end{array}
$$

The positivity of the operators $T _ { t }$ will follow immediately, if we can show that $R _ { \lambda }$ is positive for each $\lambda > 0$ . Then fix any function $g \geq 0$ in $C _ { 0 }$ , and put $\begin{array} { r } { f \ = \ R _ { \lambda } g } \end{array}$ , so that $g = ( \lambda - { \bar { A } } ) f$ . By the definition of A<sup>¯</sup>, there exist some $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \dots \in \mathcal { D }$ with $f _ { n }  f$ and $A f _ { n }  \bar { A } f$ . If $\operatorname* { i n f } _ { x } f ( x ) < 0$ , we have in $⨏ _ { x } f _ { n } ( x ) < 0$ for all suficiently large $n _ { : }$ , and we may choose some $x _ { n } \in S$ with $f _ { n } ( x _ { n } ) \leq f _ { n } \land 0$ . By (iii) we have $A f _ { n } ( x _ { n } ) \geq 0$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\inf _ {x} (\lambda - A) f _ {n} (x) \leq (\lambda - A) f _ {n} (x _ {n})} \\ & {\qquad \leq \lambda f _ {n} (x _ {n})} \\ & {\qquad = \lambda \inf _ {x} f _ {n} (x).} \end{array}
$$

As $n \to \infty$ , we get the contradiction 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq \inf _ {x} g (x) \\ = \inf _ {x} (\lambda - \bar {A}) f (x) \\ \leq \lambda \inf _ {x} f (x) <   0. \end{array}
$$

To see that $\bar { A }$ is the generator of the semi-group $( T _ { t } )$ , we note that the operators $\lambda - { \bar { A } }$ are inverses of the resolvent operators $R _ { \lambda }$ ✷ 

The previous proof shows that, if an operator $A$ on $C _ { 0 }$ satisfies the positive maximum principle in (iii), then it is dissipative, in the sense that $\| ( \lambda - A ) f \| \geq$ $\lambda \| f \|$ for all $f \in \operatorname { d o m } ( A )$ and $\lambda > 0$ . This yields the following simple observation, needed later. 

Lemma 17.12 (maximality) Let $( A , D )$ be the generator of a Feller semigroup on $C _ { 0 }$ , and consider an extension of A to a linear operator $( A ^ { \prime } , D ^ { \prime } )$ satisfying the positive-maximum principle. Then $( A , { \mathcal { D } } ) = ( A ^ { \prime } , { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } )$ 

Proof: Fix any $f \in \mathcal { D } ^ { \prime }$ , and put $g = ( I - A ^ { \prime } ) f$ . Since $A ^ { \prime }$ is dissipative and $( I - A ) R _ { 1 } = I$ on $C _ { 0 }$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left\| f - R _ {1} g \right\| \leq \left\| (I - A ^ {\prime}) (f - R _ {1} g) \right\| \\ = \left\| g - (I - A) R _ {1} g \right\| = 0, \end{array}
$$

and so $f = R _ { 1 } g \in \mathcal { D }$ 

We proceed to show how a nice Markov process can be associated with every Feller semi-group $( T _ { t } )$ . For the corresponding transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ to have total mass 1, we need the operators $T _ { t }$ to be conservative, in the sense that $\mathrm { s u p } _ { f \le 1 } T _ { t } f ( x ) = 1$ for all $x \in S$ . This can be achieved by a suitable extension. 

Then introduce an auxiliary stat $\mathrm { e } ^ { 2 } \Delta \notin S$ , and form the compactified space ${ \hat { S } } = S \cup \{ \Delta \}$ , where $\Delta$ is chosen as the point at infinity when $S$ is non-compact, and otherwise is taken to be isolated from $S .$ Note that any function $f \in C _ { 0 }$ has $\mathrm { a }$ continuous extension to $\hat { S } _ { : }$ , achieved by putting $f ( \Delta ) = 0$ . The original semi-group on $C _ { 0 }$ extends as follows to a conservative semi-group on $\hat { C } = C _ { \hat { S } }$ 

Lemma 17.13 (compactification) Every Feller semi-group $( T _ { t } )$ on $C _ { 0 }$ extends to a conservative Feller semi-group $( \hat { T } _ { t } )$ on $\hat { C }$ , given by 

$$
\hat {T} _ {t} f = f (\Delta) + T _ {t} \bigl \{f - f (\Delta) \bigr \}, \quad t \geq 0, f \in \hat {C}.
$$

Proof: It is straightforward to verify that $( \hat { T } _ { t } )$ is a strongly continuous semigroup on ${ \hat { C } } .$ To show that the operators $\hat { T } _ { t }$ are positive, fix any $f \in { \hat { C } }$ with $f \geq 0$ , and note that $g \equiv f ( \Delta ) - f \in C _ { 0 }$ with $g \le f ( \Delta )$ . Hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} T _ {t} g \leq T _ {t} g ^ {+} \leq \| T _ {t} g ^ {+} \| \\ \leq \| g ^ {+} \| \leq f (\Delta), \end{array}
$$

and so $\hat { T } _ { t } f = f ( \Delta ) - T _ { t } g \ge 0$ . The contraction and conservation properties now follow from the fact that $\hat { T } _ { t } 1 = 1$ ✷ 

Next we construct an associated semi-group of Markov transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ on ${ \hat { S } } _ { : }$ satisfying 

$$
T _ {t} f (x) = \int f (y) \mu_ {t} (x, d y), \quad f \in C _ {0}.\tag{10}
$$

Say that a state $x \in { \hat { S } }$ is absorbing for $\left( \mu _ { t } \right)$ , if $\mu _ { t } ( x , \{ x \} ) = 1$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

Proposition 17.14 (existence) For any Feller semi-group $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ on $C _ { 0 }$ , there exists a unique semi-group of Markov transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ on $\hat { S }$ , satisfying (10) and such that $\Delta$ is absorbing for $\left( \mu _ { t } \right)$ 

Proof: For fixed $x \in S$ and $t \geq 0$ , the mapping $f \mapsto { \hat { T } } _ { t } f ( x )$ is a positive linear functional on $\hat { C }$ with norm 1. Hence, Riesz’ representation Theorem 2.25 yields some probability measures $\mu _ { t } ( x , \cdot )$ on $\hat { S }$ satisfying 

$$
\hat {T} _ {t} f (x) = \int f (y) \mu_ {t} (x, d y), \quad f \in \hat {C}, x \in \hat {S}, t \geq 0.\tag{11}
$$

The measurability on the right is clear by continuity. By a standard approximation followed by a monotone-class argument, we obtain the desired measurabil ity of $\mu _ { t } ( x , B )$ , for any $t \geq 0$ and Borel set $B \subset { \hat { S } }$ . The Chapman–Kolmogorov relation holds on $\hat { S }$ by Lemma 17.1. Formula (10) is a special case of (11), which also yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \int f (y)   \mu_ {t} (\Delta , d y) & = \hat {T} _ {t} f (\Delta) \\ & = f (\Delta) = 0, \quad f \in C _ {0}, \end{array}
$$

showing that $\Delta$ is absorbing. The uniqueness of $\left( \mu _ { t } \right)$ is clear from the last two properties. ✷ 

For any probability measure ν on ${ \hat { S } } _ { : }$ , Theorem 11.4 yields a Markov process $X ^ { \nu }$ in $\hat { S }$ with initial distribution $\nu$ and transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ . Let $P _ { \nu }$ be the distribution of $X ^ { \nu }$ with associated integration operator $E _ { \nu }$ . When $\nu = \delta _ { x }$ , we may write $P _ { x }$ and $E _ { x }$ instead, for simplicity. We now extend Theorem 16.3 to a basic regularization theorem for Feller processes. For an rcll process $X$ , we say that $\Delta$ is absorbing for $X ^ { \pm }$ if $X _ { t } = \Delta \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } X _ { t - } = \Delta$ implies $X _ { u } = \Delta$ for all $u \geq t$ 

Theorem 17.15 (regularization, Kinney) Let X be a Feller process in $\hat { S }$ with initial distribution ν. Then 

(i) X has an rcll version $\tilde { X }$ in ${ \hat { S } } ,$ such that $\Delta$ is absorbing for $\tilde { X } ^ { \pm }$ 

(ii) $\textit { i f } \left( T _ { t } \right)$ is conservative and ν is restricted to $S _ { i }$ , we can choose $\tilde { X }$ to be rcll even in S. 

For the proof, we introduce an associated class of super-martingales, to which we may apply the regularity theorems in Chapter 9. Let $C _ { 0 } ^ { + }$ be the class of non-negative functions in $C _ { 0 }$ 

Lemma 17.16 (resolvents and super-martingales) For any $f \in C _ { 0 } ^ { + }$ , the process

For any $f \in C _ { 0 }$ with $f > 0$ on $S _ { ; }$ the strong continuity of $( T _ { t } )$ yields even $R _ { 1 } f > 0$ on $S$ . Applying Lemma 9.32 to the super-martingale $Y _ { t } ~ =$ $e ^ { - t } R _ { 1 } f ( \tilde { X } _ { t } )$ we conclude that $X ~ \equiv ~ \Delta ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . on the interval $\lbrack \zeta , \infty )$ , where $\zeta = \operatorname* { i n f } \big \{ t \geq 0 ; \Delta \in \{ \tilde { X } _ { t } , \tilde { X } _ { t - } \} \big \}$ Discarding the exceptional null set, we can make this hold identically. Thus, $\zeta > t { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . for all t, and hence $\zeta = \infty \mathrm { a . s . }$ which may again be taken to hold identically. Then $\tilde { X } _ { t }$ and $\tilde { X } _ { t } .$ take values in $S _ { ; }$ and the stated regularity properties remain valid in $S$ ✷ 

By the last theorem, we may choose $\Omega$ as the space of rcll functions in $\hat { S }$ such that $\Delta$ is absorbing, and let X be the canonical process on $\Omega$ . Processes with diferent initial distributions ν are then distinguished by their distributions $P _ { \nu }$ on Ω. The process X is clearly Markov under each $P _ { \nu }$ , with initial distribution $\nu$ and transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ , and it has the regularity properties of Theorem 17.15. Let $( \mathcal { F } _ { t } )$ be the right-continuous filtration generated by $X$ , and put $\mathcal { A } = \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } =$ $\vee _ { t } \mathcal { F } _ { t }$ . As before, the shift operators $\theta _ { t }$ on Ω are given by

We now state a general version of the strong Markov property. The result extends the special versions obtained in Proposition 11.9 and Theorems 13.1 and 14.11. A further instant of this property is given in Theorem 32.11. 

Theorem 17.17 (strong Markov property, Dynkin & Yushkevich, Blumenthal) For any canonical Feller process $X$ , initial distribution ν, optional time $\tau _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , and random variable $\xi \ge 0$ , we have 

$$
E _ {\nu} \left(\xi \circ \theta_ {\tau} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\tau}\right) = E _ {X _ {\tau}} \xi a. s. P _ {\nu} o n \{\tau <   \infty \}.

Then the times $\tau _ { n } = 2 ^ { - n } [ 2 ^ { n } \tau + 1 ]$ are -optional by Lemma 9.4, and Lemma 9.3 gives $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau } \subset \mathcal { G } _ { \tau _ { n } }$ for all n. Thus, Proposition 11.9 yields 

$$
E _ {\nu} \left(\xi \circ \theta_ {\tau_ {n}}; A\right) = E _ {\nu} \left(E _ {X _ {\tau_ {n}}} \xi ; A\right), \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {\tau}, n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{12}

To extend this to $\tau .$ , we first take $\begin{array} { r } { \xi = \prod _ { k \le m } f _ { k } ( X _ { t _ { k } } ) } \end{array}$ for some $f _ { 1 } , \dots , f _ { m } \in C _ { 0 }$ and $t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { m }$ . Then $\xi \circ \theta _ { \tau _ { n } }  \xi \circ \theta _ { \tau }$ , by the right-continuity of X and continuity of $f _ { 1 } , \ldots , f _ { m }$ . Writing $h _ { k } = t _ { k } - t _ { k - 1 }$ with $t _ { 0 } = 0$ , and using Feller property $\left( \operatorname { F } _ { 1 } \right)$ and the right-continuity of $X$ , we obtain

Thus, (12) extends to $\tau$ by dominated convergence on both sides. Using standard approximation and monotone-class arguments, we may finally extend the result to arbitrary $\xi .$ ✷

The strong Markov property is often used in the following extended form. 

Corollary 17.19 (optional projection) For any canonical Feller process $X _ { \cdot }$ non-decreasing, adapted process Y, and random variable $\xi \ge 0$ , we have

Next we show that any martingale on the canonical space of a Feller process X is a.s. continuous outside the discontinuity set of X. For Brownian motion, this also follows from the integral representation in Theorem 19.11. 

Theorem 17.20 (discontinuity sets) Let X be a canonical Feller process with initial distribution $\nu ,$ and let M be a local P -martingale. Then

By a simple approximation, then contains all indicator functions of sets $\bigcap _ { k \leq n } \{ X _ { t _ { k } } \in G _ { k } \}$ with $G _ { 1 } , \ldots , G _ { n }$ <sub>open. A basic role in the theory is played by the processes 

$$
M _ {t} ^ {f} = f (X _ {t}) - f (X _ {0}) - \int_ {0} ^ {t} A f (X _ {s}) d s, \quad t \geq 0, f \in \mathcal {D}.

Lemma 17.21 (Dynkin’s formula) For a Feller process $X _ { i }$ 

(i) the processes $M ^ { f }$ are martingales under any initial distributions ν for $X$

$$

To prepare for the next major result, we introduce the optional times 

$$
\tau_ {h} = \inf \left\{t \geq 0; \rho (X _ {t}, X _ {0}) > h \right\}, \quad h > 0,

Lemma 17.22 (escape times) When $x \in S$ is non-absorbing, we have $E _ { x } \tau _ { h } <$ for $h > 0$ small enough. 

Proof: If x is not absorbing, then $\mu _ { t } ( x , B _ { x } ^ { \varepsilon } ) < p < 1$ for some $t , \varepsilon > 0$ where $B _ { x } ^ { \varepsilon } = \{ y ; \rho ( x , y ) \leq \varepsilon \}$ . By Lemma 17.3 and Theorem 5.25, we may choose $h \in ( 0 , \varepsilon ]$ so small that
