We turn to a probabilistic description of the generator and its domain. Say that A is maximal within a class of linear operators, if it extends every member of the class. 

Theorem 17.23 (characteristic operator, Dynkin) Let $( A , D )$ be the generator of a Feller process. Then 

(i) for $f \in \mathcal { D }$ we have $A f ( x ) = 0$ when x is absorbing, and otherwise 

$$
A f (x) = \lim _ {h \to 0} \frac {E _ {x} f (X _ {\tau_ {h}}) - f (x)}{E _ {x} \tau_ {h}},\tag{15}
$$

(ii) A is the maximal operator on $C _ { 0 }$ with those properties. 

Proof: (i) Fix any $f \in { \mathcal { D } }$ . If x is absorbing, then $T _ { t } f ( x ) = f ( x )$ for all $t \geq 0$ , and so $A f ( x ) = 0$ . For non-absorbing x, Lemma 17.21 yields instead 

$$
E _ {x} f (X _ {\tau_ {h} \wedge t}) - f (x) = E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {h} \wedge t} A f (X _ {s}) d s, \quad t, h > 0.\tag{16}
$$

By Lemma 17.22, we have $E \tau _ { h } < \infty$ for suficiently small $h > 0$ , and so (16) extends to $t = \infty$ by dominated convergence. Relation (15) now follows from the continuity of $A f$ , along with the fact that $\rho ( X _ { s } , x ) \le h$ for all $s < \tau _ { h }$ 

(ii) Since the positive-maximum principle holds for any extension of A with the stated properties, the assertion follows by Lemma 17.12. ✷ 

In the special case of $S = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , let $\hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ be the class of infinitely diferentiable functions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with bounded support. An operator $( A , D )$ with $\mathcal { D } \supset \hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ is said to be local on $\hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ , if $A f ( x ) = 0$ when f vanishes in a neighborhood of $x .$ For a local generator A on $\hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ , the positive-maximum principle yields a local positive-maximum principle, asserting that if $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ has a local maximum $\geq 0$ at a point x, then $A f ( x ) \leq 0$ 

We give a basic relationship between difusion processes and elliptic diferential operators. This connection is further explored in Chapters 21, 32, and 34–35. 

Theorem 17.24 (Feller difusions and elliptic operators, Dynkin) Let $( A , D )$ be the generator of a Feller process $X$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\hat { C } ^ { \infty } \subset \mathcal { D }$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) X is continuous on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ , a.s. $P _ { \nu }$ for every $\nu ,$ 

(ii) A is local on $\hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ 

In this case, there exist some functions $a ^ { i j } , b ^ { i } , c \in C _ { \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ with $c \geq 0$ and $( a ^ { i j } )$ symmetric, non-negative definite, such that for any $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ and $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , 

$$
A f (x) = \frac {1}{2} a ^ {i j} (x) \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f (x) + b ^ {i} (x) \partial_ {i} f (x) - c (x) f (x).\tag{17}
$$

Here the matrix $( a _ { i j } )$ gives the difusion rates of X, the vector (b<sup>i</sup>) represents the drift rate of X, and c is the rate of $k i l l i n g ^ { 3 }$ . For semi-groups of this type, we may choose Ω as the set of paths that are continuous on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ . The Markov process X is then referred to as a canonical Feller difusion. 

Proof: ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ : Use Theorem 17.23. 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Assume (ii). Fix any $x \in { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d }$ and $0 < h < m$ , and choose an $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ with $f \geq 0$ and support y; $h \leq | y - x | \leq m \}$ . Then $A f ( y ) = 0$ for all $y \in B _ { x } ^ { h }$ , and so Lemma 17.21 shows that $f ( X _ { t \wedge \tau _ { h } } )$ is a martingale under $P _ { x }$ By dominated convergence, we have $E _ { x } f ( X _ { \tau _ { h } } ) = 0$ , and since m was arbitrary, 

$$
P _ {x} \left\{\left| X _ {\tau_ {h}} - x \right| \leq h \text {or} X _ {\tau_ {h}} = \Delta \right\} = 1, \quad x \in \mathbb {R} ^ {d}, h > 0.
$$

By the Markov property at fixed times, we get for any initial distribution ν 

$$
P _ {\nu} \bigcap_ {t \in \mathbb {Q} _ {+}} \theta_ {t} ^ {- 1} \Bigl \{| X _ {\tau_ {h}} - X _ {0} | \leq h \text {or} X _ {\tau_ {h}} = \Delta \Bigr \} = 1, \quad h > 0,
$$

which implies 

$$
P _ {\nu} \Bigl \{\sup _ {t <   \zeta} | \Delta X _ {t} | \leq h \Bigr \} = 1, \quad h > 0,
$$

proving (i). 

Now fix any $x \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and choose $f _ { 0 } ^ { x } , f _ { i } ^ { x } , f _ { i j } ^ { x } \in \hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ , such that for any y in a neighborhood of $x ,$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f _ {0} ^ {x} (y) = 1, \quad f _ {i} ^ {x} (y) = y _ {i} - x _ {i}, \\ f _ {i j} ^ {x} (y) = (y _ {i} - x _ {i}) (y _ {j} - x _ {j}). \end{array}
$$

Putting 

$$
c (x) = - A f _ {0} ^ {x} (x), \qquad b _ {i} (x) = A f _ {i} ^ {x} (x), \qquad a _ {i j} (x) = A f _ {i j} ^ {x} (x),
$$

we see that (17) holds locally when $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ agrees near x with a second-degree polynomial. In particular, choosing $f _ { 0 } ( y ) = 1 , f _ { i } ( y ) = y _ { i }$ , and $f _ { i j } ( y ) = y _ { i } y _ { j }$ for y near x, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & A f _ {0} (x) = - c (x), \\ & A f _ {i} (x) = b _ {i} (x) - x _ {i} c (x), \\ & A f _ {i j} (x) = a _ {i j} (x) + x _ {i} b _ {j} (x) + x _ {j} b _ {i} (x) - x _ {i} x _ {j} c (x). \end{array}
$$

This shows that $c , b _ { i } .$ , and $a _ { i j } = a _ { j i }$ are continuous. 

Applying the local positive-maximum principle to $f _ { 0 } ^ { x }$ , we get $c ( x ) \geq 0$ . By the same principle applied to the function 

$$
f = - \left(u ^ {i} f _ {i} ^ {x}\right) ^ {2} = - u ^ {i} u ^ {j} f _ {i j} ^ {x},
$$

we obtain $u ^ { i } u ^ { j } a _ { i j } ( x ) \geq 0$ , which shows that $( a _ { i j } )$ is non-negative definite. Finally, let $f \in \hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ be arbitrary with a second-order Taylor expansion $\tilde { f }$ around x. Then each of the functions 

$$
g _ {\pm} ^ {\varepsilon} (y) = \pm \left\{f (y) - \tilde {f} (y) \right\} - \varepsilon | x - y | ^ {2}, \quad \varepsilon > 0,
$$

has a local maximum 0 at $x ,$ and so 

$$
A g _ {\pm} ^ {\varepsilon} (x) = \pm \left\{A f (x) - A \tilde {f} (x) \right\} - \varepsilon \sum_ {i} a _ {i i} (x) \leq 0, \quad \varepsilon > 0.
$$

As $\varepsilon \to 0$ we get $A f ( x ) = A { \tilde { f } } ( x )$ , showing that (17) is generally true. 

We turn to a basic limit theorem for Feller processes, extending some results for L´evy processes in Theorems 7.7 and 16.14. 

Theorem 17.25 (convergence, Trotter, Sova, Kurtz, Mackeviˇcius) Let $X , X ^ { 1 }$ $X ^ { 2 } , \dots$ . be Feller processes in S with semi-groups $( T _ { t } ) , \left( T _ { n , t } \right)$ and generators $( A , { \mathcal { D } } ) , ( A _ { n } , { \mathcal { D } } _ { n } )$ , respectively, and fix a core D for A. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) for any $f \in D$ , there exist some $f _ { n } \in { \mathcal { D } } _ { n }$ with $f _ { n }  f$ and $A _ { n } f _ { n } \to A f$ , 

(ii) $T _ { n , t } \to T _ { t }$ strongly for each $t > 0$ 

(iii) $T _ { n , t } f \to T _ { t } f$ for every $f \in C _ { 0 }$ , uniformly for bounded $t > 0$ 

(iv) $X _ { 0 } ^ { n } \overset { d } { \to } X _ { 0 }$ in $S \Rightarrow X ^ { n } \xrightarrow { s d }$ X in $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \hat { S } }$ 

Our proof is based on two lemmas, the former extending Lemma 17.7. 

Lemma 17.26 (norm inequality) Let $( T _ { t } ) , \ ( T _ { t } ^ { \prime } )$ be Feller semi-groups with generators $( A , { \mathcal { D } } ) , ( A ^ { \prime } , { \mathcal { D } } ^ { \prime } )$ , respectively, where $A ^ { \prime }$ is bounded. Then 

$$
\left\| T _ {t} f - T _ {t} ^ {\prime} f \right\| \leq \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left\| (A - A ^ {\prime}) T _ {s} f \right\| d s, \quad f \in \mathcal {D}, t \geq 0.\tag{18}
$$

Proof: Fix any $f \in \mathcal { D }$ and $t > 0$ . Since $( T _ { s } ^ { \prime } )$ is norm continuous, Theorem 17.6 yields 

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial s} (T _ {t - s} ^ {\prime} T _ {s} f) = T _ {t - s} ^ {\prime} (A - A ^ {\prime}) T _ {s} f, \quad 0 \leq s \leq t.
$$

Here the right-hand side is continuous in s, by the strong continuity of $\left( T _ { s } \right)$ , the boundedness of $A ^ { \prime }$ , the commutativity of A and $T _ { s }$ , and the norm continuity of $( T _ { s } ^ { \prime } )$ . Hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{r} T _ {t} f - T _ {t} ^ {\prime} f = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\partial}{\partial s} (T _ {t - s} ^ {\prime} T _ {s} f) d s \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} T _ {t - s} ^ {\prime} (A - A ^ {\prime}) T _ {s} f d s, \end{array}
$$

and (18) follows by the contractivity of $T _ { t - s } ^ { \prime }$ 

We may next establish a continuity property for the Yosida approximations $A ^ { \lambda } , A _ { n } ^ { \lambda }$ of the generators $A , A _ { n }$ , respectively. 

Lemma 17.27 (continuity of Yosida approximation) Let $( A , D ) , ( A _ { n } , D _ { n } )$ be generators of some Feller semi-groups, satisfying (i) of Theorem 17.25. Then $A _ { n } ^ { \lambda } \to A ^ { \lambda }$ strongly for every $\lambda > 0$ 

Proof: By Lemma 17.8, it is enough to show that $A _ { n } ^ { \lambda } f  A ^ { \lambda } f$ for every $f \in ( \lambda - A ) D$ . Then define $g \equiv R ^ { \lambda } f \in D$ . By (i) we may choose some $g _ { n } \in \mathcal { D } _ { n }$ with $g _ { n }  g$ and $A _ { n } g _ { n }  A g$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&f _ {n} \equiv (\lambda - A _ {n}) g _ {n}\\&\qquad \rightarrow (\lambda - A) g = f,\end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\| A _ {n} ^ {\lambda} f - A ^ {\lambda} f \right\| = \lambda^ {2} \left\| R _ {n} ^ {\lambda} f - R ^ {\lambda} f \right\| \\ \qquad \leq \lambda^ {2} \left\| R _ {n} ^ {\lambda} (f - f _ {n}) \right\| + \lambda^ {2} \left\| R _ {n} ^ {\lambda} f _ {n} - R ^ {\lambda} f \right\| \\ \qquad \leq \lambda \| f - f _ {n} \| + \lambda^ {2} \| g _ {n} - g \| \to 0. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 17.25, ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i i i ) } }$ : Assume (i). Since D is dense in $C _ { 0 } .$ , we may take $f \in D$ . Then choose some functions $f _ { n }$ as in (i), and conclude from Lemmas 17.7 and 17.26 that, for any $n \in \mathsf N$ and $t , \lambda > 0$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left\| T _ {n, t} f - T _ {t} f \right\| \leq \left\| T _ {n, t} (f - f _ {n}) \right\| + \left\| (T _ {n, t} - T _ {n, t} ^ {\lambda}) f _ {n} \right\| + \left\| T _ {n, t} ^ {\lambda} (f _ {n} - f) \right\| \\ \qquad + \left\| (T _ {n, t} ^ {\lambda} - T _ {t} ^ {\lambda}) f \right\| + \left\| (T _ {t} ^ {\lambda} - T _ {t}) f \right\| \\ \qquad \leq 2 \left\| f _ {n} - f \right\| + t \left\| (A ^ {\lambda} - A) f \right\| + t \left\| (A _ {n} - A _ {n} ^ {\lambda}) f _ {n} \right\| \\ \qquad + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left\| (A _ {n} ^ {\lambda} - A ^ {\lambda}) T _ {s} ^ {\lambda} f \right\| d s. \end{array}\tag{19}
$$

By Lemma 17.27 and dominated convergence, the last term tends to zero as $n \to \infty$ . For the third term on the right, we get 

$$

which tends to $\| ( A - A ^ { \lambda } ) f \|$ by the same lemma. Hence, by (19), 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \sup _ {t \leq u} \left\| T _ {n, t} f - T _ {t} f \right\| \leq 2 u \left\| (A ^ {\lambda} - A) f \right\|, \quad u, \lambda > 0,

and the desired convergence follows by Lemma 17.7, as we let $\lambda \to \infty$ 

$( \mathrm { i i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ : Obvious. 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Assume (ii), fix any $f \in D$ and $\lambda > 0$ , and define $g = ( \lambda - A ) f$ and $f _ { n } = R _ { n } ^ { \lambda } g$ . ${ \mathrm { ( i v ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ : Assume (iv). We may take S to be compact and the semi-groups $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ and $\left( T _ { n , t } \right)$ to be conservative. Then let $X _ { 0 } = x$ and $X _ { 0 } ^ { n } = x _ { n }$ . By Lemma 17.3, the process X is a.s. continuous at t. Thus, (iv) yields $X _ { t } ^ { n } \overset { d } { \to } X _ { t }$ , and the desired convergence follows. 

(i) – $( \mathrm { i i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i v } )$ : Assume (i) – (iii), and let $X _ { 0 } ^ { n } \overset { d } { \to } X _ { 0 }$ . To obtain $X ^ { n } { \xrightarrow { f d } } X$ it is enough to show that as $n  \infty$ , for any $f _ { 0 } , \dots , f _ { m } \in C$ and $0 = t _ { 0 } <$ $t _ { 1 } \cdots t _ { m }$

To strengthen the convergence to $X ^ { n } { \overset { d } { \to } } X$ , it sufices by Theorems 23.9 and 23.11 to show that $\rho ( X _ { \tau _ { n } } ^ { n } , X _ { \tau _ { n } + h _ { n } } ^ { n } ) \ \stackrel { P } {  }$ 0 for any finite optional times $\tau _ { n }$ and positive constants $h _ { n } \  \ 0 .$ . From the last theorem and its proof, we may derive a similar approximation of discrete-time Markov chains. This extends the approximations of random walks in Corollary 16.17 and Theorem 23.14. 

Theorem 17.28 (approximation of Markov chains) Let $\varGamma ^ { 1 } , Y ^ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be discrete-time Markov chains in $S$ with transition operators $U _ { 1 } , U _ { 2 } , \dots ,$ , and let X be a Feller process in S with semi-group $( T _ { t } )$ and generator A. $$
A _ {n} = h _ {n} ^ {- 1} (U _ {n} - I), \qquad T _ {n, t} = U _ {n} ^ {[ t / h _ {n} ]}, \qquad X _ {t} ^ {n} = Y _ {[ t / h _ {n} ]} ^ {n}.

We finally show that canonical Feller processes and their induced filtrations are quasi-left continuous. 

Proposition 17.29 (ql-continuity of Feller processes, Blumenthal, Meyer) Let X be a canonical Feller process with arbitrary initial distribution, and fix an optional time $\tau$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\tau$ is predictable, 

(ii) $\tau$ is accessible, 

(iii) $X _ { \tau - } = X _ { \tau } \ a . s . \ o n \ \{ \tau < \infty \}$ 

In particular we see that, when X is a.s. continuous, every optional time is predictable. 

Proof, $( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ : By Proposition 10.4, we may take $\tau$ to be finite and predictable. Now fix an announcing sequence $\left( \tau _ { n } \right)$ and a function $f \in C _ { 0 }$ . By the strong Markov property, we get for any $h > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \Big \{f (X _ {\tau_ {n}}) - f (X _ {\tau_ {n} + h}) \Big \} ^ {2} = E \Big (f ^ {2} - 2 f T _ {h} f + T _ {h} f ^ {2} \Big) (X _ {\tau_ {n}}) \\ & \qquad \leq \big \| f ^ {2} - 2 f T _ {h} f + T _ {h} f ^ {2} \big \| \\ & \qquad \leq 2 \| f \| \big \| f - T _ {h} f \big \| + \big \| f ^ {2} - T _ {h} f ^ {2} \big \|. \end{array}
$$

Letting $n \to \infty$ and then $h \downarrow 0$ , and using dominated convergence on the left and strong continuity on the right, we see that $E \{ f ( X _ { \tau - } ) - f ( X _ { \tau } ) \} ^ { 2 } = 0$ which implies $f ( X _ { \tau - } ) = f ( X _ { \tau } )$ a.s. Applying this to a separating sequence of functions $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots \in C _ { 0 }$ , we obtain $X _ { \tau - } = X _ { \tau }$ a.s. 

(iii) (i): By (iii) and Theorem 17.20, we have $\Delta M _ { \tau } = 0$ a.s. on $\{ \tau < \infty \}$ for every martingale M, and so $\tau$ is predictable by Theorem 10.14.

# Exercises

1. Show how the proofs of Theorems 17.4 and 17.6 can be simplified, if we assume $\left( \mathrm { F _ { 3 } } \right)$ instead of the weaker condition $\left( \mathrm { F _ { 2 } } \right)$ 

2. Consider a pseudo-Poisson process X on S with rate kernel α. Give conditions ensuring X to be Feller. 

3. Verify the resolvent equation (2), and conclude that the range of $R _ { \lambda }$ is inde pendent of λ. 

4. Show that a Feller semi-group $\left( T _ { t } \right)$ is uniquely determined by the resolvent operator $R _ { \lambda }$ for a fixed $\lambda > 0$ . Interpret the result probabilistically in terms of an independent, exponentially distributed random variable with mean $\lambda ^ { - 1 }$ . (Hint: Use Theorem 17.4 and Lemma 17.5.) 

5. Consider a discrete-time Markov process in S with transition operator T, and let τ be an independent random variable with a fixed geometric distribution. Show that T is uniquely determined by $E _ { x } f ( X _ { \tau } )$ for arbitrary $x \in S$ and $f \geq 0$ . (Hint: Apply the preceding result to the associated pseudo-Poisson process.) 

6. Give a probabilistic description of the Yosida approximation $T _ { t } ^ { \lambda }$ in terms the original process X and two independent Poisson processes with rate λ. 

7. Given a Feller difusion semi-group, write the diferential equation in Theorem 17.6 (ii), for suitable f, as a PDE for the function $T _ { t } f ( x )$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } \times \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Also show that the backward equation of Theorem 13.9 is a special case of the same equation. 

8. Consider a Feller process X and an independent subordinator T. Show that $Y = X \circ T$ is again Markov, and that Y is L´evy whenever this is true for X. If both T and X are stable, then so is Y. Find the relationship between the transition semi-groups, respectively between the indices of stability.

## VI. Stochastic Calculus and Applications

Stochastic calculus is rightfully recognized as one of the central areas of modern probability. In Chapter 18 we develop the classical theory of Itˆo integration with respect to continuous semi-martingales, based on a detailed study of the quadratic variation process. Chapter 19 deals with some basic applications to Brownian motion and related processes, including various martingale characterizations and transformations of martingales based on a random time change or a change of probability measure. In Chapter 20, the integration theory is extended to the more subtle case of semi-martingales with jump discontinuities, and in the final Chapter 21 we develop some basic aspects of the Malliavin calculus for functionals on Wiener space. The material of the first two chapters is absolutely fundamental, whereas the remaining chapters are more advanced and could be deferred to a later stage of studies. 

18. Itˆo integration and quadratic variation. After a detailed study of the quadratic variation and covariation processes for continuous local martingales, we introduce the stochastic integral via an ingenious martingale characterization. This leads easily to some basic continuity and iteration properties, and to the fundamental Itˆo formula, showing how continuous semi-martingales are transformed by smooth mappings. 

19. Continuous martingales and Brownian motion. Using stochastic calculus, we derive some basic properties of Brownian motion and continuous local martingales. Thus, we show how the latter can be reduced to Brownian motions by a random time change, and how the drift of a continuous semimartingale can be removed by a suitable change of measure. We further derive some integral representations of Brownian functionals and continuous martingales. 

20. Semi-martingales and stochastic integration. Here we extend the stochastic calculus for continuous integrators to the context of semi-martingales with jump discontinuities. Important applications include some general decompositions of semi-martingales, the Burkholder-type inequalities, the Bichteler– Dellacherie characterization of stochastic integrators, and a representation of the Dol´eans exponential. 

21. Malliavin calculus. Here we study the Malliavin derivative D and its dual $D ^ { * }$ , along with the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator $L .$ . Those three operators are closely related and admit simple representations in terms of multiple Wiener–Itˆo integrals. We further explain in what sense $D ^ { * }$ extends the Itˆo integral, derive a diferentiation property for the latter, and establish the Clark–Ocone representation of Brownian functionals. We also indicate how the theory can be used to prove the existence and smoothness of densities. 

Chapter 18 

# Itˆo Integration and Quadratic Variation

Local and finite-variation martingales, completeness, covariation, continuity, norm comparison, uniform integrability, Cauchy-type inequalities, martingale integral, semi-martingales, continuity, dominated convergence, chain rule, optional stopping, integration by parts, approximation of covariation, Itˆo’s formula, local integral, conformal mapping, Fisk–Stratonovich integral, continuity and approximation, random time change, dependence on parameter, functional representation 

Here we initiate the study of stochastic calculus, arguably the most powerful tool of modern probability, with applications to a broad variety of subjects throughout the subject. For the moment, we may only mention the timechange reduction and integral representation of continuous local martingales in Chapter 19, the Girsanov theory for removal of drift in the same chapter, the predictable transformations in Chapter 27, the construction of local time in Chapter 29, and the stochastic diferential equations in Chapters 32–33. 

In this chapter we consider only stochastic integration with respect to continuous semi-martingales, whereas the more subtle case of integrators with possible jump discontinuities is postponed until Chapter 20, and an extension to non-anticipating integrators appears in Chapter 21. The theory of stochastic integration is inextricably linked to the notions of quadratic variation and covariation, already encountered in Chapter 14 in the special case of Brownian motion, and together the two notions are developed into a theory of amazing power and beauty. 

We begin with a construction of the covariation process [M, N] of a pair of continuous local martingales M and N, which requires an elementary approximation and completeness argument. The processes M∗ and $[ M ] = [ M , M ]$ will be related by some useful continuity and norm relations, including the powerful BDG inequalities. 

Given the quadratic variation [M], we may next construct the stochastic integral VdM for suitable progressive processes V, using a simple Hilbert -<sub>space</sub> <sub>argument.</sub> <sub>Combining</sub> <sub>with</sub> <sub>the</sub> <sub>ordinary</sub> <sub>Stieltjes</sub> <sub>integral</sub>  <sub>V</sub> <sub>dA</sub> <sub>for</sub> -<sub>processes A of locally finite variation, we may finally extend the integral to</sub> arbitrary continuous semi-martingales $X = M + A$ . The continuity properties of quadratic variation carry over to the stochastic integral, and in conjunction with the obvious linearity they characterize the integration. 

A key result for applications is $I t { \hat { o } } ^ { \prime } s$ formula, which shows how semi-martingales are transformed under smooth mappings. Though the present substitution rule difers from the elementary result for Stieltjes integrals, the two formulas can be brought into agreement by a simple modification of the integral. We conclude the chapter with some special topics of importance for applications, such as the transformation of stochastic integrals under a random time-change, and the integration of processes depending on a parameter. 

The present material may be thought of as a continuation of the martingale theory of Chapters 9–10. Though no results for Brownian motion are used explicitly in this chapter, the existence of the Brownian quadratic variation in Chapter 14 may serve as a motivation. We also need the representation and measurability of limits obtained in Chapter 5. 

Throughout the chapter we take $\mathcal { F } = \left( \mathcal { F } _ { t } \right)$ to be a right-continuous and complete filtration on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathrm { ~ A ~ }$ process M is said to be a local martingale, if it is adapted to $\mathcal { F }$ and such that the stopped and centered processes $M ^ { \tau _ { n } } - M _ { 0 }$ are true martingales for some optional times $\tau _ { n } \uparrow \infty$ . By a similar localization we may define local $L ^ { 2 } .$ -martingales, locally bounded martingales, locally integrable processes, etc. The required optional times $\tau _ { n }$ are said to form a localizing sequence. 

Any continuous local martingale may clearly be reduced by localization to a sequence of bounded, continuous martingales. Conversely, we see by dominated convergence that every bounded local martingale is a true martingale. The following useful result may be less obvious.

Thus, $M ^ { \tau }$ is again a local martingale with localizing sequence $\left( \sigma _ { n } \right)$ 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Suppose that each process $M ^ { \tau _ { n } }$ is a local martingale with localizing sequence $\left( \sigma _ { k } ^ { n } \right)$ . Since $\sigma _ { k } ^ { n } $ a.s. for each $n$ , we may choose some indices $k _ { n }$ with

P \left\{\sigma_ {k _ {n}} ^ {n} <   \tau_ {n} \wedge n \right\} \leq 2 ^ {- n}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.

It remains to note that the processes $M ^ { \tau _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime } } = ( M ^ { \tau _ { n } ^ { \prime } } ) ^ { \overline { { \tau _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime } } } }$ are true martingales. ✷ 

Next we show that every continuous martingale of finite variation is a.s. constant. An extension appears as Lemma 10.11. 

Proposition 18.2 (finite-variation martingales) Let M be a continuous local martingale. Then

$$

In fact, let $V _ { t }$ denote the total variation of M on the interval $[ 0 , t ]$ , and note that V is continuous and adapted. For each $n \in \mathsf N$ 2 we may then introduce the optional time $\tau _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; V _ { t } = n \}$ , and note that $M ^ { \tau _ { n } } - M _ { 0 }$ is a continuous martingale with total variation bounded by $n .$ We further note that $\tau _ { n }  \infty$ , and that if $M ^ { \tau _ { n } } = M _ { 0 }$ a.s. for each $n ,$ , then even $M = M _ { 0 }$ a.s. In the reduced case, fix any $t > 0$ , write $t _ { n , k } = k t / n$ , and conclude from the continuity of M that a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \zeta_ {n} \equiv \sum_ {k \leq n} \left(M _ {t _ {n, k}} - M _ {t _ {n, k - 1}}\right) ^ {2} \\ \quad \leq V _ {t} \max _ {k \leq n} \left| M _ {t _ {n, k}} - M _ {t _ {n, k - 1}} \right| \to 0. \end{array}

Our construction of stochastic integrals depends on the quadratic variation and covariation processes, which therefore need to be constructed first. Here we use a direct approach, which has the further advantage of giving some insight into the nature of the basic integration-by-parts formula in Proposition 18.16. An alternative but less elementary approach would be to use the Doob–Meyer decomposition in Chapter 10. 

The construction utilizes predictable step processes of the form 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V _ {t} = \sum_ {k} \xi_ {k} 1 \{t > \tau_ {k} \} \\ = \sum_ {k} \eta_ {k} 1 _ {(\tau_ {k}, \tau_ {k + 1} ]} (t), \quad t \geq 0, \end{array}\tag{1}

where the $\tau _ { n }$ are optional times with $\tau _ { n } \uparrow \infty \mathrm { a . s . }$ , and the $\xi _ { k }$ and $\eta _ { k }$ are $\mathcal { F } _ { { \tau _ { k } } ^ { - } }$ measurable random variables for all $k \in { \mathsf N }$ . For any process X we consider the elementary integral process $V \cdot X$ , given as in Chapter 9 by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (V \cdot X) _ {t} \equiv \int_ {0} ^ {t} V d X = \sum_ {k} \xi_ {k} \Bigl (X _ {t} - X _ {t} ^ {\tau_ {k}} \Bigr) \\ = \sum_ {k} \eta_ {k} \Bigl (X _ {\tau_ {k + 1}} ^ {t} - X _ {\tau_ {k}} ^ {t} \Bigr), \end{array}\tag{2}
$$

where the series converge since they have only finitely many non-zero terms. Note that $( V \cdot X ) _ { 0 } = 0$ , and that $V \cdot X$ inherits the possible continuity properties of X. It is further useful to note that $V \cdot X = V \cdot ( X - X _ { 0 } )$ . The following simple estimate will be needed later. 

Lemma 18.3 (martingale preservation and $L ^ { 2 } \mathbf { - } b o u n d )$ For any continuous $L ^ { 2 } - m a r t i n g a l e$ M with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ and predictable step process V with $| V | \leq 1$ , the process $V \cdot M$ is again an $L ^ { 2 }$ -martingale satisfying

$$

Proof: First suppose that the sum in (1) has only finitely many non-zero terms. Then $V \cdot M$ is a martingale by Corollary 9.15, and the $L ^ { 2 } .$ -bound follows by the computation 

$$

Now consider the space $\mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ of all $L ^ { 2 } \mathrm { - b o u n d e d }$ , continuous martingales M with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ , equipped with the norm $\| M \| = \| M _ { \infty } \| _ { 2 }$ . Recall that $\| M ^ { * } \| _ { 2 } \leq$ $2 \| M \|$ by Proposition 9.17. 

Lemma 18.4 (completeness) Let $\mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ be the space of $L ^ { 2 }$ -bounded, continuous martingales with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ and norm $\| M \| = \| M _ { \infty } \| _ { 2 }$ . Then $\mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ is complete and hence a Hilbert space. 

Proof: For any Cauchy sequence $M ^ { 1 } , M ^ { 2 } , \ldots$ in $\mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ , the sequence $( M _ { \infty } ^ { n } )$ is Cauchy in $L ^ { 2 }$ and thus converges toward some $\xi \in L ^ { 2 }$ . and so $\lVert M ^ { n } - M \rVert \to 0$ . Moreover, $( M ^ { n } - M ) ^ { * } \to 0$ a.s. along a sub-sequence, which implies that M is a.s. continuous with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ ✷

Corollary 18.8 (uniform integrability) Let M be a continuous local martingale. Then M is a uniformly integrable martingale, whenever

Let $\mathcal { E }$ be the class of bounded, predictable step processes with jumps at finitely many fixed times. To motivate the construction of general stochastic integrals, and for subsequent needs, we derive a basic identity for elementary integrals. 

Lemma 18.10 (covariation identity) For any continuous local martingales M, N and processes U, $V \in \mathcal { E }$ , the integrals U M and $V \cdot N$ are again continuous local martingales, and we have 

$$

To prove (5), let $\begin{array} { r } { U _ { t } = \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } 1 _ { ( t _ { k } , t _ { k + 1 } ] } ( t ) } \end{array}$ , where $\xi _ { k }$ is bounded and $\mathcal { F } _ { t _ { k } }$ -measurable for each k. $$

Replacing M, N by $M ^ { \tau } , N ^ { \tau }$ for an arbitrary optional time $\tau ,$ we get

\begin{array}{c} E \left(U \cdot M\right) _ {\tau} N _ {\tau} = E \big (U \cdot M ^ {\tau} \big) _ {\infty} N _ {\infty} ^ {\tau} \\ = E \Big (U \cdot [ M ^ {\tau}, N ^ {\tau} ] \Big) _ {\infty} \\ = E \Big (U \cdot [ M, N ] \Big) _ {\tau}. \end{array}
$$

By Lemma $9 . 1 4$ , the process $( U \cdot M ) N - U \cdot [ M , N ]$ is then a martingale, and so $[ U \cdot M , N ] = U \cdot [ M , N ] \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . The general formula follows by iteration. ✷ 

To extend the stochastic integral $V \cdot M$ to more general processes $V .$ , we take (5) to be the characteristic property. For any continuous local martingale $M .$ let $L ( M )$ be the class of all progressive processes $V _ { \mathrm { : } }$ such that $( V ^ { 2 } \cdot [ M ] ) _ { t } < \infty$ a.s. for every $t > 0$

Taking $N = M ^ { \prime } - M ^ { \prime \prime }$ gives $[ M ^ { \prime } - M ^ { \prime \prime } ] = 0 \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., and so $M ^ { \prime } = M ^ { \prime \prime } \mathrm { a . s }$ . by Proposition 18.6.

Replacing $N$ by $N ^ { \tau }$ for an arbitrary optional time $\tau$ and using Theorem 18.5 and optional sampling, we get

Before continuing our study of basic properties, we extend the stochastic integral to a larger class of integrators. By a continuous semi-martingale we mean a process $X = M + A$ , where M is a continuous local martingale and $A$ is a continuous, adapted process with locally finite variation and $A _ { 0 } = 0$ The decomposition $X = M + A$ is then a.s. unique by Proposition 18.2, and it is often referred to as the canonical decomposition of X. A continuous semimartingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is defined as a process $X = ( X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { d } )$ , where $X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { d }$ are continuous semi-martingales in R. 

Let $L ( A )$ be the class of progressive processes V, such that the processes $( V \cdot A ) _ { t } = \textstyle { \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } V d A }$ exist as elementary Stieltjes integrals. For any continuous semi-martingale $X = M + A$ , we write $L ( X ) = L ( M ) \cap L ( A )$ , and define the X-integral of a process $V \in L ( X )$ as the sum $V { \cdot } X = V { \cdot } M + V { \cdot } A$ , which makes $V \cdot X$ a continuous semi-martingale with canonical decomposition $V \cdot M + V \cdot A$ For progressive processes V, it is further clear that 

$$
V \in L (X) \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad V ^ {2} \in L ([ M ]), V \in L (A).
$$

Lemma 18.12 yields the following stochastic version of the dominated convergence theorem. 

Corollary 18.13 (dominated convergence) For any continuous semi-martingale X and processes U, $V , V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \ldots \in L ( X )$ , we have 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{l} V _ {n} \to V \\ | V _ {n} | \leq U \end{array} \right\} \Rightarrow \big (V _ {n} \cdot X - V \cdot X \big) _ {t} ^ {*} \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} 0, t \geq 0.
$$

$$
\left\{\left(V _ {n} - V\right) ^ {2} \cdot [ M ] \right\} _ {t} + \left(V _ {n} \cdot A - V \cdot A\right) _ {t} ^ {*} \rightarrow 0.
$$

Here the former convergence implies $( V _ { n } \cdot M - V \cdot M ) _ { t } ^ { * } \stackrel { P } {  } 0$ by Lemma 18.12, and the assertion follows. ✷

Lemma 18.14 (chain rule) For any continuous semi-martingale X and progressive processes U, V with $V \in L ( X )$ , we have

(ii) $U \cdot ( V \cdot X ) = ( U V ) \cdot X \ a . s .$

$$

Since $\left[ V \cdot M \right] = V ^ { 2 } \cdot \left[ M \right]$ , the two pairs of conditions are equivalent. 

(ii) The relation $U \cdot ( V \cdot A ) = ( U V ) \cdot A$ is elementary. To see that even $U \cdot ( V \cdot M ) = ( U V ) \cdot M$ a.s., consider any continuous local martingale $N .$ , and note that

Lemma 18.15 (optional stopping) For any continuous semi-martingale X, process $V \in L ( X )$ , and optional time $\tau ,$ we have a.s.

Write $C ^ { k } = C ^ { k } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ for the class of k times continuously diferentiable functions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . When $f \in C ^ { 2 }$ , we write $\partial _ { i } f$ and $\partial _ { i j } ^ { 2 } f$ for the first and second order partial derivatives of f. Here and below, summation over repeated indices is understood. 

Theorem 18.18 (substitution rule, Itˆo) For any continuous semi-martingale X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and function $f \in C ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ , we have a.s.

$$

It is suggestive to write $d [ X ^ { i } , X ^ { j } ] = d X ^ { i } d X ^ { j }$ , and think of (10) as a second order Taylor expansion. 

If X has canonical decomposition $M + A$ , we get the corresponding de composition of $f ( X )$ by substituting $M ^ { i } + A ^ { i }$ for $X ^ { i }$ on the right side of (9). When $M = 0$ , the last term vanishes, and (9) reduces to the familiar substitu tion rule for ordinary Stieltjes integrals. In general, the appearance of this Itˆo correction term shows that the rules of ordinary calculus fail for the Itˆo integral.

Then suppose that (11) holds for both $f$ and $^ { g , }$ so that $F = f ( X )$ and $G = g ( X )$ are continuous semi-martingales. Using the definition of the integral, along with Proposition 18.14 and Theorem 18.16, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (f g) (X) - (f g) (X _ {0}) \\ \quad = F G - F _ {0} G _ {0} \\ \quad = F \cdot G + G \cdot F + [ F, G ] \\ \quad = F \cdot \left\{g ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot X + \frac {1}{2} g ^ {\prime \prime} (X) \cdot [ X ] \right\} \\ \quad \quad + G \cdot \left\{f ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot X + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} (X) \cdot [ X ] \right\} + \left[ f ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot X, g ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot X \right] \\ \quad = \left(f g ^ {\prime} + f ^ {\prime} g\right) (X) \cdot X + \frac {1}{2} \big (f g ^ {\prime \prime} + 2 f ^ {\prime} g ^ {\prime} + f ^ {\prime \prime} g \big) (X) \cdot [ X ] \\ \quad = (f g) ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot X + \frac {1}{2} (f g) ^ {\prime \prime} (X) \cdot [ X ]. \end{array}
$$

Now let $f \in C ^ { 2 }$ be arbitrary. By Weierstrass’ approximation theorem<sup>5</sup>, we may choose some polynomials $p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ , such that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { u p } _ { | x | \leq c } | p _ { n } ( x ) - f ^ { \prime \prime } ( x ) | \to 0 } \end{array}$ for every $c > 0$ . Integrating the $p _ { n }$ twice yields some polynomials $f _ { n }$ satisfying 

$$
\sup _ {| x | \leq c} \left\{\left| f _ {n} (x) - f (x) \right| \vee \left| f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (x) - f ^ {\prime} (x) \right| \vee \left| f _ {n} ^ {\prime \prime} (x) - f ^ {\prime \prime} (x) \right|\right\}\rightarrow 0, \quad c > 0.
$$

In particular, $f _ { n } ( X _ { t } ) \to f ( X _ { t } )$ for each $t ~ > ~ 0$ . Letting X have canonical decomposition $M + A$ and using dominated convergence for ordinary Stieltjes integrals, we get for any $t \geq 0$ 

$$
\left\{f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot A + \frac {1}{2} f _ {n} ^ {\prime \prime} (X) \cdot [ X ] \right\} _ {t} \rightarrow \left\{f ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot A + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} (X) \cdot [ X ] \right\} _ {t}.
$$

Similarly, $\{ f _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( X ) - f ^ { \prime } ( X ) \} ^ { 2 } \cdot [ M ] ) _ { t } \to 0$ for all $t ,$ and so by Lemma 18.12 

$$
\left\{f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot M \right\} _ {t} \xrightarrow {P} \left\{f ^ {\prime} (X) \cdot M \right\} _ {t}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Thus, formula (11) for the polynomials $f _ { n }$ extends in the limit to the same relation for $f .$ ✷ 

We also need a local version of the last theorem, involving stochastic integrals up to the first time $\zeta _ { D }$ when X exits a given domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . For continuous and adapted $X$ , the time $\zeta _ { D }$ is clearly predictable, in the sense of being announced by some optional times $\tau _ { n } \uparrow \zeta _ { D }$ with $\tau _ { n } < \zeta _ { D }$ a.s. on $\left\{ \zeta _ { D } > 0 \right\}$ for all $n .$ . Indeed, writing $\rho$ for the Euclidean metric in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ , we may choose 

$$
\tau_ {n} = \inf \left\{t \in [ 0, n ]; \rho (X _ {t}, D ^ {c}) \leq n ^ {- 1} \right\}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{12}
$$

We say that $X$ is a semi-martingale on $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ , if the stopped process $X ^ { \tau _ { n } }$ is a semi-martingale in the usual sense for every $n \in \mathsf N$ . To define the co variation processes $[ X ^ { i } , X ^ { j } ]$ on the interval $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ , we require $[ X ^ { i } , X ^ { j } ] ^ { \tau _ { n } } =$ $[ ( X ^ { i } ) ^ { \tau _ { n } } , ( X ^ { j } ) ^ { \tau _ { n } } ]$ a.s. for every n. Stochastic integrals with respect to $X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { d }$ are defined on $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ in a similar way. 

Corollary 18.19 (local Itˆo formula) For any domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , let X be a continuous semi-martingale on $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ . Then (9) holds a.s. on $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ for every $f \in C ^ { 2 } ( D )$ 

Proof: Choose some $f _ { n } \in C ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ with $f _ { n } ( x ) = f ( x )$ when $\rho ( x , D ^ { c } ) \geq n ^ { - 1 }$ Applying Theorem 18.18 to $f _ { n } ( X ^ { \tau _ { n } } )$ with $\tau _ { n }$ as in (12), we get (9) on $[ 0 , \tau _ { n } ]$ Since n was arbitrary, the result extends to $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ ✷ 

By a complex, continuous semi-martingale we mean a process of the form $Z = X + i Y$ , where $X , Y$ are real, continuous semi-martingales. The bilinearity of the covariation process suggests that we define the quadratic variation of $Z$ as 

$$
\begin{array}{c} [ Z ] = [ Z, Z ] = \left[ X + i Y, X + i Y \right] \\ = [ X ] + 2 i   [ X, Y ] - [ Y ]. \end{array}
$$

Let $L ( Z )$ be the class of processes $W = U + i V$ with U, $V \in L ( X ) \cap L ( Y )$ . For such a process $W$ , we define the integral by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} W \cdot Z = (U + i V) \cdot (X + i Y) \\ \qquad = U \cdot X - V \cdot Y + i \Big (U \cdot Y + V \cdot X \Big). \end{array}
$$

Corollary 18.20 (conformal mapping) Let f be an analytic function on a domain $D \subset \mathsf C$ . Then (9) holds for every continuous semi-martingale Z in D. 

Proof: Writing $f ( x + i y ) = g ( x , y ) + i h ( x , y )$ for any $x + i y \in D$ , we get 

$$
g _ {1} ^ {\prime} + i h _ {1} ^ {\prime} = f ^ {\prime}, \qquad g _ {2} ^ {\prime} + i h _ {2} ^ {\prime} = i f ^ {\prime},
$$

and so by iteration 

$$
g _ {1 1} ^ {\prime \prime} + i h _ {1 1} ^ {\prime \prime} = f ^ {\prime \prime}, \qquad g _ {1 2} ^ {\prime \prime} + i h _ {1 2} ^ {\prime \prime} = i f ^ {\prime \prime}, \qquad g _ {2 2} ^ {\prime \prime} + i h _ {2 2} ^ {\prime \prime} = - f ^ {\prime \prime}.
$$

Now (9) follows for $Z = X + i Y$ , as we apply Corollary 18.19 to the semi-martingale $( X , Y )$ and the functions $g , h$ ✷ 

Under suitable regularity conditions, we may modify the Itˆo integral so that it will obey the rules of ordinary calculus. Then for any continuous semimartingales $X , Y ,$ , we define the Fisk–Stratonovich integral by 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {t} X \circ d Y = (X \cdot Y) _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} [ X, Y ] _ {t}, \quad t \geq 0,\tag{13}
$$

or, in diferential form $X \circ d Y = X d Y + { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } d [ X , Y ]$ , where the first term on the right is an ordinary Itˆo integral. The point of this modification is that the substitution rule simplifies to $d f ( X ) = \partial _ { i } f ( X ) \circ d X ^ { i }$ , conforming with the chain rule of ordinary calculus. We may also prove a version for FS -integrals of the chain rule in Proposition 18.14. 

Theorem 18.21 (modified Itˆo integral, Fisk, Stratonovich) The integral in (13) satisfies the computational rules of elementary calculus. Thus, a.s., 

(i) for any continuous semi-martingale X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and function $f \in C ^ { 3 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ , 

$$
f (X _ {t}) = f (X _ {0}) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \partial_ {i} f (X) \circ d X ^ {i}, t \geq 0,
$$

(ii) for any real, continuous semi-martingales X, Y, Z, 

$$
X \circ (Y \circ Z) = (X Y) \circ Z.
$$

Proof: (i) By Itˆo’s formula, 

$$
\partial_ {i} f (X) = \partial_ {i} f (X _ {0}) + \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f (X) \cdot X ^ {j} + \frac {1}{2} \partial_ {i j k} ^ {3} f (X) \cdot [ X ^ {j}, X ^ {k} ].
$$

Using Itˆo’s formula again together with (5) and (13), we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \int_ {0} \partial_ {i} f (X) \circ d X ^ {i} & = \partial_ {i} f (X) \cdot X ^ {i} + \frac {1}{2} [ \partial_ {i} f (X), X ^ {i} ] \\ & = \partial_ {i} f (X) \cdot X ^ {i} + \frac {1}{2} \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f (X) \cdot [ X ^ {j}, X ^ {i} ] \\ & = f (X) - f (X _ {0}). \end{array}
$$

(ii) By Lemma 18.14 and integration by parts, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} X \circ (Y \circ Z) & = X \cdot (Y \circ Z) + \frac {1}{2} [ X, Y \circ Z ] \\ & = X \cdot (Y \cdot Z) + \frac {1}{2} X \cdot [ Y, Z ] + \frac {1}{2} [ X, Y \cdot Z ] + \frac {1}{4} [ X, [ Y, Z ] ] \\ & = X Y \cdot Z + \frac {1}{2} [ X Y, Z ] \\ & = X Y \circ Z. \end{array}
$$

The more convenient substitution rule of Corollary 18.21 comes at a high price: The FS -integral does not preserve the martingale property, and it requires even the integrand to be a continuous semi-martingale, which forces us to impose the stronger regularity constraint on the function $f$ in the substitution rule. 

Our next task is to establish a basic uniqueness property, justifying our reference to the process $V \cdot M$ in Theorem 18.11 as an integral. 

Theorem 18.22 (continuity) The integral $V \cdot M$ in Theorem 18.11 is the a.s. unique linear extension of the elementary stochastic integral, such that for any $t > 0 _ { i }$ V<sup>2</sup> [M] <sup>P</sup> 0 (V M)∗ <sup>P</sup> 0. 

This follows immediately from Lemmas 18.10 and 18.12, together with the following approximation of progressive processes by predictable step processes. 

Lemma 18.23 (approximation) For any continuous semi-martingale $X =$ $M + A$ and process $V \in L ( X )$ , there exist some processes $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots \in \mathcal { E }$ , such that $a . s .$ , simultaneously for all $t > 0$ 

$$
\left\{\left(V _ {n} - V\right) ^ {2} \cdot [ M ] \right\} _ {t} + \left\{\left(V _ {n} - V\right) \cdot A \right\} _ {t} ^ {*} \rightarrow 0.\tag{14}
$$

Proof: We may take $t = 1$ , since we can then combine the processes $V _ { n }$ for disjoint, finite intervals to construct an approximating sequence on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ . It is further enough to consider approximations in the sense of convergence in probability, since the a.s. versions will then follow for a suitable sub-sequence. This allows us to perform the construction in steps, first approximating $V$ by bounded and progressive processes $V ^ { \prime }$ , next approximating each $V ^ { \prime }$ by continuous and adapted processes $V ^ { \prime \prime }$ , and finally approximating each $V ^ { \prime \prime }$ by predictable step processes $V ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$ 

The first and last steps being elementary, we may focus on the second step. Then let V be bounded. We need to construct some continuous, adapted processes $V _ { n } .$ , such that (14) holds a.s. for $t = 1$ . Since the $V _ { n }$ can be chosen to be uniformly bounded, we may replace the first term by $( | V _ { n } - V | \cdot [ M ] ) _ { 1 }$ Thus, it is enough to establish the approximation $( | V _ { n } - V | \cdot A ) _ { 1 } \to 0$ when the process A is non-decreasing, continuous, and adapted with $A _ { 0 } = 0$ . Replacing $A _ { t }$ by $A _ { t } + t$ if necessary, we may even take A to be strictly increasing. 

To form the required approximations, we may introduce the inverse process $T _ { s } = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ t \geq 0 ; A _ { t } \leq s \}$ , and define for all $t , h > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} V _ {t} ^ {h} = h ^ {- 1} \int_ {T (A _ {t} - h)} ^ {t} V   d A \\ = h ^ {- 1} \int_ {(A _ {t} - h) _ {+}} ^ {A _ {t}} V (T _ {s})   d s. \end{array}
$$

Then Theorem 2.15 yields $V ^ { h } \circ T  V \circ T$ as $h  0$ , a.e. on $[ 0 , A _ { 1 } ]$ , and so by dominated convergence, 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} \left| V ^ {h} - V \right| d A = \int_ {0} ^ {A _ {1}} \left| V ^ {h} (T _ {s}) - V (T _ {s}) \right| d s \to 0.
$$

The processes $V ^ { h }$ are clearly continuous. To prove their adaptedness, we note that the process $T ( A _ { t } - h )$ is adapted for every $h > 0$ , by the definition of $T$ . Since $V$ is progressive, we further note that $V \cdot A$ is adapted and hence progressive. The adaptedness of $( V \cdot A ) _ { T ( A _ { t } - h ) }$ now follows by composition. ✷ 

Though the class $L ( X )$ of stochastic integrands is suficient for most purposes, it is sometimes useful to allow integration of slightly more general processes. Given any continuous semi-martingale $X = M + A$ , let ${ \hat { L } } ( X )$ denote the class of product-measurable processes $V .$ , such that $( V - \tilde { V } ) \cdot [ M ] = 0$ and $( V - \tilde { V } ) \cdot A = 0 \mathrm { a . s }$ . for some process $\tilde { V } \in L ( X )$ . For $V \in \hat { L } ( X )$ we define $\dot { V } \cdot X = \tilde { V } \cdot X \mathrm { a . s }$ . The extension clearly enjoys all the previously established properties of stochastic integration. 

We often need to see how semi-martingales, covariation processes, and stochastic integrals are transformed by a random time change. Then consider a non-decreasing, right-continuous family of finite optional times $\tau _ { s } , s \geq 0$ , here referred to as a finite random time change $\tau .$ . If even $\mathcal { F }$ is right-continuous, so is the induced filtration $\mathcal { G } _ { s } = \mathcal { F } _ { \tau { s } } , s \ge 0$ , by Lemma 9.3. A process $X$ is said to be τ-continuous, if it is a.s. continuous on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ and constant on every interval $[ \tau _ { s - } , \tau _ { s } ] , s \geq 0$ , where $\tau _ { 0 - } = X _ { 0 - } = 0$ by convention. 

Theorem 18.24 (random time change, Kazamaki) Let $\tau$ be a finite random time change with induced filtration $\mathcal { G }$ , and let $X = M + A$ be a τ-continuous ${ \mathcal { F } } .$ -semi-martingale. Then 

(i) X τ is a continuous -semi-martingale with canonical decomposition M $\circ \tau + A \circ \tau$ , such that $[ X \circ \tau ] = [ X ] \circ \tau \ a . s .$ , 

(ii) $V \in L ( X )$ implies $V \circ \tau \in \hat { L } ( X \circ \tau )$ and 

$$
(V \circ \tau) \cdot (X \circ \tau) = (V \cdot X) \circ \tau a. s.\tag{15}
$$

Proof: (i) It is easy to check that the time change $X \mapsto X \circ \tau$ preserves continuity, adaptedness, monotonicity, and the local martingale property. In particular, $X \circ \tau$ is then a continuous -semi-martingale with canonical decomposition M $\circ \tau + A \circ \tau$ . Since $M ^ { 2 } - \left\lceil M \right\rceil$ is a continuous local martingale, so is the time-changed process $M ^ { 2 } \circ \tau - [ M ] \circ \tau$ , and we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} {[ X \circ \tau ] = [ M \circ \tau ]} & \\ {= [ M ] \circ \tau} & \\ {= [ X ] \circ \tau} & {\mathrm{a.s.}} \end{array}
$$

If $V \in L ( X )$ , we also note that $V \circ \tau$ is product-measurable, since this is true for both V and $\tau$ . 

(ii) Fixing any $t \geq 0$ and using the τ-continuity of $X$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & (1 _ {[ 0, t ]} \circ \tau) \cdot (X \circ \tau) = 1 _ {[ 0, \tau_ {t} ^ {- 1} ]} \cdot (X \circ \tau) \\ & \qquad = (X \circ \tau) ^ {\tau_ {t} ^ {- 1}} \\ & \qquad = (1 _ {[ 0, t ]} \cdot X) \circ \tau , \end{array}
$$

which proves (15) when $V = 1 _ { [ 0 , t ] }$ . If X has locally finite variation, the result extends by a monotone-class argument and monotone convergence to arbitrary $V \in L ( X )$ . In general, Lemma 18.23 yields some continuous, adapted processes $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots ,$ such that a.s. 

$$
\int (V _ {n} - V) ^ {2} d [ M ] + \int \left| (V _ {n} - V) d A \right|\rightarrow 0.
$$

 <sub>By (15) the corresponding properties hold for the time-changed processes, and</sub> since the processes $V _ { n } \circ \tau$ are right-continuous and adapted, hence progressive, we obtain $V \circ \tau \in \hat { L } ( X \circ \tau )$ 

Now assume instead that the approximating processes $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots$ . are predictable step processes. Then (15) holds as before for each $V _ { n }$ , and the relation extends to V by Lemma 18.12. ✷ 

Next we consider stochastic integrals of processes depending on a parameter. Given a measurable space $( S , S )$ , we say that a process $V$ on $S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ is progressive<sup>6</sup>, if its restriction to $S \times [ 0 , t ]$ is $S \otimes B _ { t } \otimes \mathcal { F } _ { t }$ -measurable for every $t \geq 0 .$ , where $\boldsymbol { B } _ { t } = \boldsymbol { B } _ { [ 0 , t ] }$ . A simple version of the following result will be useful in Chapter 19. 

Theorem 18.25 (dependence on parameter, Dol´eans, Stricker $\mathcal { E A } \ Y o r )$ For measurable S, consider a continuous semi-martingale X and a progressive process $V _ { s } ( t )$ on $S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ such that $V _ { s } \in L ( X )$ for all $s \in S$ . Then the process $Y _ { s } ( t ) = ( V _ { s } \cdot X ) _ { t }$ has a version that is progressive and a.s. continuous at each $s \in S$ 

Proof: Let X have canonical decomposition of $M + A$ , and let the processes $V _ { s } ^ { n }$ on $S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ be progressive and such that for any $t \geq 0$ and $s \in S$ , 

$$
\left\{\left(V _ {s} ^ {n} - V _ {s}\right) ^ {2} \cdot [ M ] \right\} _ {t} + \left\{\left(V _ {s} ^ {n} - V _ {s}\right) \cdot A \right\} _ {t} ^ {*} \xrightarrow {P} 0.
$$

Then Lemma 18.12 yields $( V _ { s } ^ { n } \cdot X - V _ { s } \cdot X ) _ { t } ^ { * } \stackrel { P } {  } 0$ for every s and t. Proceeding as in the proof of Proposition 5.32, we may choose a sub-sequence $\{ n _ { k } ( s ) \} \subset \mathbb { N }$ depending measurably on $s ,$ such that the same convergence holds $\mathrm { a . s }$ . along $\{ n _ { k } ( s ) \}$ for any s and t. Define $Y _ { s , t } = \operatorname* { l i m } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { k } ( V _ { s } ^ { n _ { k } } \cdot X ) _ { t }$ whenever this is finite, and put $Y _ { s , t } = 0$ otherwise. If the processes $( V _ { s } ^ { n } \cdot X ) _ { t }$ have progressive versions on $S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ that are a.s. continuous for each $s ,$ then $Y _ { s , t }$ is clearly a version of the process $( V _ { s } \cdot X ) _ { t }$ with the same properties. We apply this argument in three steps. 

First we reduce to the case of bounded, progressive integrands by taking $V ^ { n } = V { 1 \{ | V | \leq n \} }$ . Next, we apply the transformation in the proof of Lemma 18.23, to reduce to the case of continuous and progressive integrands. Finally, we approximate any continuous, progressive process V by the predictable step processes $V _ { s } ^ { n } ( t ) = V _ { s } ( 2 ^ { - n } [ 2 ^ { n } t ] )$ . The integrals $V _ { s } ^ { n } \cdot X$ are then elementary, and the desired continuity and measurability are obvious by inspection. ✷ 

We turn to the related topic of functional representations. For motivation, we note that the construction of a stochastic integral $V \cdot X$ depends in a subtle way on the underlying probability measure $P$ and filtration $\mathcal { F }$ . Thus, we cannot expect a general representation $F ( V , X )$ of the integral process $V \cdot X$ . In view of Proposition 5.32, we might still hope for a modified representation of the form $F ( \mu , V , X )$ , where $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( V , X )$ . Even this may be too optimistic, since the canonical decomposition of X also depends on $\mathcal { F }$ 

Here we consider only a special case, suficient for our needs in Chapter 32. Fixing any progressive functions $\sigma _ { j } ^ { i }$ and $b ^ { i }$ of suitable dimension, defined on the path space $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ , we consider an adapted process X satisfying the stochastic diferential equation 

$$
d X _ {t} ^ {i} = \sigma_ {j} ^ {i} (t, X) d B _ {t} ^ {j} + b ^ {i} (t, X) d t,\tag{16}
$$

where $B$ is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { r }$ . A detailed discussion of such equations appears in Chapter 32. Here we need only the simple fact from Lemma 32.1 that the coeficients $\sigma _ { j } ^ { i } ( t , X )$ and $b ^ { i } ( t , X )$ are again progressive. Write $a ^ { i j } =$ $\sigma _ { k } ^ { i } \sigma _ { k } ^ { j }$ 

Proposition 18.26 (functional representation) For any progressive functions $\sigma , b , f$ of suitable dimension, there exists a measurable mapping 

$$
F \colon \hat {\mathcal {M}} \left(C _ {R _ {+}, R ^ {d}}\right) \times C _ {R _ {+}, R ^ {d}} \rightarrow C _ {R _ {+}, R},\tag{17}
$$

such that whenever X solves (16) with ${ \mathcal { L } } ( X ) = \mu$ and $f ^ { i } ( X ) \in L ( X ^ { i } )$ for all i, we have 

$$
f ^ {i} (X) \cdot X ^ {i} = F (\mu , X) a. s.
$$

Proof: From (16) we note that X is a semi-martingale with covariation processes $[ X ^ { i } , X ^ { j } ] = a ^ { i j } ( X ) \cdot \lambda$ and drift components $b ^ { i } ( X ) \cdot \lambda$ . Hence, $f ^ { i } ( X ) \in$ $L ( X ^ { i } )$ for all i if the processes $( f ^ { i } ) ^ { 2 } a ^ { i i } ( X )$ and $f ^ { i } b ^ { i } ( X )$ are a.s. Lebesgue integrable, which holds in particular when f is bounded. Letting $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be progressive with 

$$
\left(f _ {n} ^ {i} - f ^ {i}\right) ^ {2} a ^ {i i} (X) \cdot \lambda + \left|\left(f _ {n} ^ {i} - f ^ {i}\right) b ^ {i} (X) \right| \cdot \lambda \rightarrow 0,\tag{18}
$$

we get by Lemma 18.12 

$$
\left\{f _ {n} ^ {i} (X) \cdot X ^ {i} - f ^ {i} (X) \cdot X ^ {i} \right\} _ {t} ^ {*} \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} 0, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Thus, if $f _ { n } ^ { i } ( X ) \cdot X ^ { i } = F _ { n } ( \mu , X )$ a.s. for some measurable mappings $F _ { n }$ as in (17), Proposition 5.32 yields a similar representation for the limit $f ^ { i } ( X ) \cdot X ^ { i }$ 

As in the previous proof, we may apply this argument in steps, reducing first to the case where f is bounded, next to the case of continuous $f ,$ , and finally to the case where f is a predictable step function. Here the first and last steps are again elementary. For the second step, we may now use the simpler approximation 

$$
f _ {n} (t, x) = n \int_ {(t - n ^ {- 1}) _ {+}} ^ {t} f (s, x) d s, \qquad t \geq 0, n \in \mathbb {N}, x \in C _ {\mathbb {R} _ {+}, \mathbb {R} ^ {d}}.
$$

By Theorem 2.15 we have $f _ { n } ( t , x ) \to f ( t , x )$ a.e. in t for each $x \in C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ , and (18) follows by dominated convergence. ✷ 

## Exercises

1. Show that if M is a local martingale and $\xi$ is an $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ -measurable random variable, then the process $N _ { t } = \xi M _ { t }$ is again a local martingale. 

2. Show that every local martingale $M \geq 0$ with $E M _ { 0 } < \infty$ is a super-martingale. Also show by an example that M may fail to be a martingale. (Hint: Use Fatou’s lemma. Then take $M _ { t } = X _ { t / ( 1 - t ) + }$ , where X is a Brownian motion starting at 1, stopped when it reaches 0.) 

3. For a continuous local martingale M, show that M and [M] have a.s. the same intervals of constancy. (Hint: For any $r \in \mathsf { Q } _ { + }$ , put $\tau = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t > r ; [ M ] _ { t } > [ M ] _ { r } \}$ Then $M ^ { \tau }$ is a continuous local martingale on $\lbrack r , \infty )$ with quadratic variation 0, and so $M ^ { \tau }$ is a.s. constant on [s, τ]. Use a similar argument in the other direction.) 

4. For any continuous local martingales $M _ { n }$ starting at 0 and associated optional times $\tau _ { n }$ , show that $( M _ { n } ) _ { \tau _ { n } } ^ { \ast } \stackrel { P } {  }$ 0 if $[ M _ { n } ] _ { \tau _ { n } } \stackrel { P } {  } 0$ . Chapter 19 

# Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion

Real and complex exponential martingales, characterization of Brownian motion, time-change reduction, harmonic and analytic maps, point polarity and transience, skew-product representation, orthogonality and independence, Brownian invariance, Brownian functionals and martingales, Gauss and Poisson reduction, iterated and multiple integrals, chaos and integral representation, change of measure, transformation of drift, preservation properties, Cameron–Martin theorem, uniform integrability, Wald’s identity, removal of drift 

Here we deal with a wide range of applications of stochastic calculus, the principal tools of which were introduced in the previous chapter. A recurrent theme is the notion of exponential martingales, which appear in both a real and a complex variety. Exploring the latter yields an easy access to L´evy’s celebrated martingale characterization of Brownian motion, and to the basic time-change reduction of isotropic continuous local martingales to a Brownian motion. Applying the latter result to suitable compositions of a Brownian motion with harmonic or analytic maps, we obtain important information about Brownian motion in R<sup>d</sup>. Similar methods can be used to analyze a variety of other transformations leading to Gaussian processes. 

As a further application of the exponential martingales, we derive stochastic integral representations of Brownian functionals and martingales, and examine their relationship to the chaos expansions obtained by diferent methods in Chapter 14. In this context, we also note how the previously introduced multiple Wiener–Itˆo integrals can be expressed as iterated single Itˆo integrals. A related problem, of crucial importance for Chapter 32, is to represent a continuous local martingale with absolutely continuous covariation process in terms of stochastic integrals with respect to a suitable Brownian motion. 

As a final major topic, we examine the transformations induced by absolutely continuous changes of the probability measure. Here the density process turns out to be a real exponential martingale, and any continuous local martingale remains a martingale under the new measure, apart from an additional drift term. This observation is useful for applications, where it is often employed to remove the drift of a given semi-martingale. The appropriate change of measure then depends on the given process, and it becomes important to find efective criteria for a proposed exponential process to be a true martingale. 

The present exposition may be regarded as a continuation of our discussion of martingales and Brownian motion in Chapters 9 and 14, respectively. Changes of time and measure are both important for the theory of stochastic diferential equations, developed in Chapters 32–33. The time-change reductions of continuous martingales have counterparts for the point processes explored in Chapter 15, where the present Gaussian processes are replaced by suitable Poisson processes. The results about changes of measure are extended in Chapter 20 to the context of possibly discontinuous semi-martingales. 

To begin our technical discussion of the mentioned ideas, we consider first the complex exponential martingales, which are closely related to the real versions appearing in Lemma 19.22. 

Lemma 19.1 (complex exponential martingales) Let M be a real, continuous local martingale with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then 

$$
Z _ {t} = \exp \left(i M _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} [ M ] _ {t}\right), \quad t \geq 0,
$$

is a complex local martingale, satisfying 

$$
Z _ {t} = 1 + i (Z \cdot M) _ {t} a. s., \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Proof: Applying Corollary 18.20 to the complex-valued semi-martingale $\begin{array} { r } { X _ { t } = i M _ { t } + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left[ M \right] _ { t } } \end{array}$ and the entire function $f ( z ) = e ^ { z }$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d Z _ {t} = Z _ {t} \Big (d X _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} d [ X ] _ {t} \Big)} \\ & {\qquad = Z _ {t} \Big (i d M _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} d [ M ] _ {t} - \frac {1}{2} d [ M ] _ {t} \Big)} \\ & {\qquad = i Z _ {t} d M _ {t}.} \end{array}
$$

Then there exists an isonormal Gaussian process $\zeta \perp \perp F _ { 0 }$ on H, such that

$$

Then (1) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} [ N ] _ {\infty} = \sum_ {j, k} u _ {j} u _ {k} \left[ M ^ {h _ {j}}, M ^ {h _ {k}} \right] _ {\infty} \\ = \sum_ {j, k} u _ {j} u _ {k} \left\langle h _ {j}, h _ {k} \right\rangle = \| h \| ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

\begin{array}{l} P A = E (Z _ {\infty}; A) \\ \qquad = E \Big \{\exp \Big (i N _ {\infty} + \frac {1}{2}   [ N ] _ {\infty} \Big); A \Big \} \\ \qquad = E (e ^ {i \xi}; A)   \exp \Big (\frac {1}{2}   \| h \| ^ {2} \Big). \end{array}
$$

Since $u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { n }$ were arbitrary, we conclude from Theorem 6.3 that the random vector $( M _ { \infty } ^ { h _ { 1 } } , \ldots , M _ { \infty } ^ { h _ { n } } )$ is independent of $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ and centered Gaussian with covariances $\langle h _ { j } , h _ { k } \rangle$ 

For any element $\begin{array} { r } { h = \sum _ { i } a _ { i } h _ { i } } \end{array}$ , define $\begin{array} { r } { \zeta h = \sum _ { i } a _ { i } M _ { \infty } ^ { h _ { i } } } \end{array}$ . To see that $\zeta h$ is a.s. independent of the representation of h, suppose that also $h = \textstyle \sum _ { i } b _ { i } h _ { i }$ . Writing $c _ { i } = a _ { i } - b _ { i }$ , we get

For a first application, we may establish a celebrated martingale characterization of Brownian motion. 

Theorem 19.3 (Brownian criterion, $L e v y )$ For a continuous process $B =$ $( B ^ { 1 } , \ldots , B ^ { d } )$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $B _ { 0 } = 0$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) B is an -Brownian motion, 

(ii) B is a local -martingale with $[ B ^ { i } , B ^ { j } ] _ { t } \equiv \delta _ { i j } t ~ a . s .$ 

Proof $( O K )$ : Assuming (ii), we introduce for fixed $s < t$ the continuous local martingales 

$$
M _ {r} ^ {i} = B _ {r \wedge t} ^ {i} - B _ {r \wedge s} ^ {i}, r \geq s, i \leq d,
$$

and conclude from Lemma 19.2 that the diferences $B _ { t } ^ { i } - B _ { s } ^ { i }$ are i.i.d. $N ( 0 , t - s )$ and independent of $\mathcal { F } _ { s }$ , which proves (i). ✷ 

The last result suggests that we might transform a general continuous local martingale M into a Brownian motion through a suitable random time change. In higher dimensions, this requires M to be isotropic, in the sense that a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{c} [ M ^ {i} ] = [ M ^ {j} ], \\ [ M ^ {i}, M ^ {j} ] = 0, \qquad i \neq j, \end{array}
$$

which holds in particular when M is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . For continuous local martingales M in C, the condition is a.s. equivalent to $[ M ] = 0$ , or 

$$
\begin{array}{c} [ \Re M ] = [ \Im M ], \\ [ \Re M, \Im M ] = 0. \end{array}
$$

In the isotropic case, we refer to $[ M ^ { 1 } ] = \cdot \cdot \cdot = [ M ^ { d } ] \ \mathrm { o r } \ [ \Re M ] = [ \Im M ]$ as the rate process of $M .$ 

Though the proof is straightforward when $[ M ] _ { \infty } = \infty \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ , the general case requires a rather subtle extension of the filtered probability space. For two filtrations ${ \mathcal { F } } , { \mathcal { G } }$ on Ω, we say that $\mathcal { G }$ is a standard extension of $\mathcal { F }$ if 

$$
\mathcal {F} _ {t} \subset \mathcal {G} _ {t} \underset {\mathcal {F} _ {t}} {\perp} \mathcal {F}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

This is precisely the condition needed to ensure that all adaptedness and conditioning properties will be preserved. 

Theorem 19.4 (time-change reduction, Doeblin, Dambis, Dubins & Schwarz) Let M be an isotropic, continuous local -martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ , and define infSt > 0: [M1], > s} C T 0 

$$
\tau_ {s} = \inf \left\{t \geq 0; [ M ^ {1} ] _ {t} > s \right\}, \quad \mathcal {G} _ {s} = \mathcal {F} _ {\tau_ {s}}, \quad s \geq 0.
$$

Then there exists a Brownian motion $B$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ w.r.t. a standard extension $\hat { \mathcal G }$ of ${ \mathcal { G } } ,$ , such that a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{r} B = M \circ \tau o n [ 0, [ M ^ {1} ] _ {\infty}), \\ M = B \circ [ M ^ {1} ]. \end{array}
$$

Proof $( O K )$ : We may take $d = 1$ , the proof for $d > 1$ being similar. Introduce a Brownian motion X $\mathcal { F }$ with induced filtration $\mathcal { X } ,$ , and put $\hat { \mathcal G } _ { t } = \mathcal G _ { t } \vee \mathcal X _ { t }$ Since $\mathcal { G } \bot \bot \mathcal { X }$ , it is clear that $\hat { \mathcal G }$ is a standard extension of both $\mathcal { G }$ and . In particular, X remains a Brownian motion under $\hat { \mathcal G }$ . Now define 

$$
B _ {s} = M _ {\tau_ {s}} + \int_ {0} ^ {s} 1 \{\tau_ {r} = \infty \} d X _ {r}, \quad s \geq 0.\tag{2}
$$

Since M is τ-continuous by Proposition 18.6, Theorem 18.24 shows that the first term $M \circ \tau$ is a continuous -martingale, hence also a $\hat { \mathcal G }$ -martingale, with quadratic variation

Thus, $[ B ] _ { s } = s \mathrm { a . s . }$ , and so Theorem 19.3 shows that B is a <sup>ˆ</sup> -Brownian motion. Finally, $B _ { s } = M _ { \tau _ { s } }$ for $s < [ M ] _ { \infty }$ , which implies $M = B \circ [ M ]$ a.s. by the τ-continuity of M. ✷ 

In two dimensions, isotropic martingales arise naturally by composition of a complex Brownian motion $B$ with a possibly multi-valued analytic function $f .$ For any continuous process $X$ , we may clearly choose a continuous evolution of $f ( X )$ , as long as $X$ avoids all singularities of $f .$ Similar results hold for harmonic functions, which is especially useful in dimensions $d \geq 3$ , where no analytic functions exist. 

Theorem 19.5 (harmonic and analytic maps, $L e v y )$ 

(i) For an harmonic function f on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , consider an isotropic, continuous local martingale M in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ that a.s. avoids all singularities of $f .$ . Then $f ( M )$ is a local martingale satisfying 

$$
[ f (M) ] = | \nabla f (M) | ^ {2} \cdot [ M ^ {1} ] a. s.
$$

(ii) For an analytic function $f ,$ , consider a complex, isotropic, continuous local martingale M that a.s. avoids all singularities of f. Then $f ( M )$ is again a complex, isotropic local martingale satisfying 

$$
[ \Re f (M) ] = | f ^ {\prime} (M) | ^ {2} \cdot [ \Re M ] a. s.
$$

If B is a Brownian motion and $f ^ { \prime } \not \equiv 0$ , then $\left[ \Re f ( B ) \right]$ is a.s. unbounded and strictly increasing. 

Proof: (i) Since M is isotropic, we get by Corollary 18.19 

$$
f (M) = f (M _ {0}) + f _ {i} ^ {\prime} \cdot M ^ {i} + \frac {1}{2} \Delta f (M) \cdot [ M ^ {1} ].
$$

Here the last term vanishes since $f$ is harmonic, and so $f ( M )$ is a local martingale. The isotropy of M also yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} {[ f (M) ] = \sum_ {i} \Big [ f _ {i} ^ {\prime} (M) \cdot M ^ {i} \Big ]} \\ & {= \sum_ {i} \Big \{f _ {i} ^ {\prime} (M) \Big \} ^ {2} \cdot [ M ^ {1} ]} \\ & {= \big | \nabla f (M) \big | ^ {2} \cdot [ M ^ {1} ].} \end{array}
$$

(ii) Since f is analytic, Corollary 18.20 yields 

$$
f (M) = f \left(M _ {0}\right) + f ^ {\prime} (M) \cdot M + \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} (M) \cdot [ M ].
$$

Since M is isotropic, the last term vanishes, and we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} [ f (M) ] = \left[ f ^ {\prime} (M) \cdot M \right] \\ = \left\{f ^ {\prime} (M) \right\} ^ {2} \cdot [ M ] = 0, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $f ( M )$ is again isotropic. Writing $M = X + i Y$ and $f ^ { \prime } ( M ) =$ $U + i V$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \left[ \Re f (M) \right] & = \left[ U \cdot X - V \cdot Y \right] \\ & = \left(U ^ {2} + V ^ {2}\right) \cdot \left[ X \right] \\ & = | f ^ {\prime} (M) | ^ {2} \cdot \left[ \Re M \right]. \end{array}
$$

Noting that $f ^ { \prime }$ has at most countably many zeros, unless it vanishes identically, we obtain by Fubini’s theorem 

$$
E \lambda \Bigl \{t \geq 0; f ^ {\prime} (B _ {t}) = 0 \Bigr \} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Bigl \{f ^ {\prime} (B _ {t}) = 0 \Bigr \} d t = 0,
$$

and so $[ \Re f ( B ) ] = | f ^ { \prime } ( B ) | ^ { 2 } \cdot \lambda$ is a.s. strictly increasing. To see that it is also a.s. unbounded, we note that $f ( B )$ converges a.s. on the set $\{ [ \Re f ( B ) ] < \infty \}$ However, $f ( B )$ diverges a.s., since f is non-constant and the random walk $B _ { 0 } , B _ { 1 } , \ldots$ . is recurrent by Theorem 12.2. ✷

Combining (i) above with Theorem 17.11, we see that a complex, isotropic, continuous local martingale M with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ avoids every fixed point $a \neq 0$ Thus, Theorem 19.5 (ii) applies to any analytic function f with only isolated singularities. Since f is allowed to be multi-valued, the result applies even to functions with essential singularities, such as to $f ( z ) = \log ( 1 + z )$ . For a simple application, we consider the windings of planar Brownian motion about a fixed point. 

Corollary 19.7 (skew-product representation, Galmarino) Let B be a complex Brownian motion with $B _ { 0 } = 1$ , and choose a continuous version of $V =$ arg B with $V _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then there exists a real Brownian motion $Y \bot \bot | B |$ , such that a.s. (P|−2 1) 

$$
V _ {t} \equiv Y \circ \left(| B | ^ {- 2} \cdot \lambda\right) _ {t}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Hence, Theorem 19.4 yields a complex Brownian motion $Z = X + i Y$ with $M = Z \circ [ \Re M ]$ a.s., and the assertion follows. ✷ 

For a non-isotropic, continuous local martingale M in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , there is no single random time change that reduces the process to a Brownian motion. However, we may transform the components $M ^ { i }$ individually as in Theorem 19.4, to obtain a set of one-dimensional Brownian motions $B ^ { 1 } , \ldots , B ^ { d }$ . If the latter processes are independent, they may be combined into a d -dimensional Brownian motion $B = ( B ^ { 1 } , \ldots , B ^ { d } )$ . We show that the required independence arises automatically, whenever the original components $M ^ { i }$ are strongly orthogonal, in the sense that $[ M ^ { i } , M ^ { j } ] = 0 ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . for all $i \neq j$ 

Proposition 19.8 (multi-variate time change, Knight) Let $M ^ { 1 } , M ^ { 2 } , . . .$ . be strongly orthogonal, continuous local martingales starting at 0. Then there exist some independent Brownian motions $B ^ { 1 } , B ^ { 2 } , \ldots$ . with 

$$
M ^ {k} = B ^ {k} \circ [ M ^ {k} ] a. s., \quad k \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Proof: When $[ M ^ { k } ] _ { \infty } ~ = ~ \infty ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . for all $k ,$ , the result is an easy consequence of Lemma 19.2. In general, choose some independent Brownian motions $X ^ { 1 } , X ^ { 2 } , \ldots \bot \bot \mathcal { F }$ with induced filtration $\mathcal { X }$ , and define 

$$
B _ {s} ^ {k} = M ^ {k} \left(\tau_ {s} ^ {k}\right) + X ^ {k} \left\{\left(s - \left[ M ^ {k} \right] _ {\infty}\right) _ {+} \right\}, \quad s \geq 0, k \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Write $\psi _ { t } = - \log ( 1 - t ) _ { + }$ , and put $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \mathcal { F } _ { \psi _ { t } } + \mathcal { X } _ { ( t - 1 ) _ { + } } , t \geq 0$ . To check that $B ^ { 1 } , B ^ { 2 } , \ldots$ . have the desired joint distribution, we may take the $[ M ^ { k } ]$ to be bounded. Then the processes 

$$
N _ {t} ^ {k} = M _ {\psi_ {t}} ^ {k} + X _ {(t - 1) _ {+}} ^ {k}, \quad t \geq 0,
$$

are strongly orthogonal, continuous $\mathcal { G }$ -martingales with quadratic variations 

$$
[ N ^ {k} ] _ {t} = [ M ^ {k} ] _ {\psi_ {t}} + (t - 1) _ {+}, \quad t \geq 0,
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} B _ {s} ^ {k} = N _ {\sigma_ {s} ^ {k}} ^ {k}, \\ \sigma_ {s} ^ {k} = \inf \Bigl \{t \geq 0; [ N ^ {k} ] _ {t} > s \Bigr \}. \end{array}

The assertion now follows from the result for $[ M ^ { k } ] _ { \infty } = \infty \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ 

We turn to some general invariance properties of a Brownian motion or bridge. Then for any processes U, V on $I = { \mathsf { R } } _ { + }$ or [0, 1], we define<sup>1</sup> 

$$
\lambda V = \int_ {I} V _ {t} d t, \qquad \langle U, V \rangle = \int_ {I} U _ {t} V _ {t} d t, \qquad \| V \| _ {2} = \langle V, V \rangle^ {1 / 2}.
$$

A process B on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ is said to be a Brownian bridge w.r.t. a filtration ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { : }$ 7 if it is -adapted and such that, conditionally on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for every $t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , it is a Brownian bridge from $( t , B _ { t } )$ to (1, 0). We anticipate the fact that an $\mathcal { F } _ { - }$ Brownian bridge in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is a continuous semi-martingale on [0, 1]. The associated martingale component is clearly a standard Brownian motion 

## Theorem 19.9 (Brownian invariance)

(i) Consider an -Brownian motion X and some -predictable processes $V ^ { t }$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } , t \geq 0$ , such that 

$$
\langle V ^ {s}, V ^ {t} \rangle = s \wedge t a. s., \quad s, t \geq 0.
$$

Then $Y _ { t } = ( V ^ { t } \cdot X ) _ { \infty } , t \geq 0 ,$ , is a version of a Brownian motion. 

(ii) Consider an -Brownian bridge X and some -predictable processes $V ^ { t }$ on $[ 0 , 1 ] , t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , such that 

$$
\lambda V ^ {t} = t, \quad \langle V ^ {s}, V ^ {t} \rangle = s \wedge t a. s., \qquad s, t \in [ 0, 1 ].
$$

Then $Y _ { t } = ( V ^ { t } \cdot X ) _ { 1 } , t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , is a version of a Brownian bridge. 

The existence of the integrals $V ^ { t } \cdot X$ should be regarded as part of the assertions. In case of (ii) we need to convert the relevant Brownian-bridge integrals into continuous martingales. Then for any Lebesgue integrable process $V$ on [0, 1], we define 

$$
\bar {V} _ {t} = (1 - t) ^ {- 1} \int_ {t} ^ {1} V _ {s} d s, \quad t \in [ 0, 1 ].
$$

## Lemma 19.10 (Brownian bridge integral)

(i) Let X be an -Brownian bridge with martingale component B, and consider an -predictable process V on [0, 1], such that $\begin{array} { r } { E ^ { \mathcal { F } _ { 0 } } \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } V ^ { 2 } < \infty ~ a . s . } \end{array}$ and λV is -measurable. Then 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} V _ {t} d X _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {1} (V _ {t} - \bar {V} _ {t}) d B _ {t} a. s.
$$

(ii) For any processes $U , V \in L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 1 ]$ , we have $\bar { U } , \bar { V } \in L ^ { 2 } [ 0 , 1 ]$ and 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} (U _ {t} - \bar {U} _ {t}) (V _ {t} - \bar {V} _ {t}) d t = \int_ {0} ^ {1} U _ {t} V _ {t} d t - \lambda U \cdot \lambda V.
$$

Proof: (ii) We may take $U = V ,$ , since the general case will then follow by polarization. Writing $\begin{array} { r } { R _ { t } = \int _ { t } ^ { 1 } V _ { s } d s = ( 1 - t ) \bar { V } _ { t } } \end{array}$ and integrating by parts, we get on [0, 1) 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int \bar {V} _ {t} ^ {2} d t = \int (1 - t) ^ {- 2} R _ {t} ^ {2} d t} \\ & {\qquad = (1 - t) ^ {- 1} R _ {t} ^ {2} + 2 \int (1 - t) ^ {- 1} R _ {t} V _ {t} d t} \\ & {\qquad = (1 - t) \bar {V} _ {t} ^ {2} + 2 \int \bar {V} _ {t} V _ {t} d t.} \end{array}
$$

For bounded V, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {1} (V _ {t} - \bar {V} _ {t}) ^ {2} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {1} V _ {t} ^ {2} d t - (\lambda V) ^ {2} \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {1} (V _ {t} - \lambda V) ^ {2} d t, \end{array}\tag{3}
$$

and so by Minkowski’s inequality 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| \bar {V} \| _ {2} \leq \| V \| _ {2} + \| V - \bar {V} \| _ {2} \\ = \| V \| _ {2} + \| V - \lambda V \| _ {2} \\ \leq 2 \| V \| _ {2}, \end{array}
$$

which extends to the general case by monotone convergence. This gives $\bar { V } \in L ^ { 2 }$ , and the asserted relation follows from (3) by dominated convergence. 

(i) The process $M _ { t } = X _ { t } / ( 1 - t )$ is clearly a continuous martingale on [0, 1), and so $X _ { t } = ( 1 - t ) M _ { t }$ is a continuous semi-martingale on the same interval. Integrating by parts, we get for any $t \in [ 0 , 1 )$

Hence by combination,

\int_ {0} ^ {t} V _ {s} d X _ {s} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} (V _ {s} - \bar {V} _ {s}) d B _ {s} + X _ {t} \bar {V} _ {t}, t \in [ 0, 1).\tag{4}

By Cauchy’s inequality and dominated convergence, we get as $t  1$

\begin{array}{r l} & {\left(E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} | X _ {t} \bar {V} _ {t} |\right) ^ {2} \leq E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} (M _ {t} ^ {2}) E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} \Big (\int_ {t} ^ {1} | V _ {s} | d s \Big) ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad \leq (1 - t) E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} (M _ {t} ^ {2}) E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} \int_ {t} ^ {1} V _ {s} ^ {2} d s} \\ & {\qquad = t E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} \int_ {t} ^ {1} V _ {s} ^ {2} d s \to 0,} \end{array}

and so by dominated convergence $X _ { t } \bar { V } _ { t } \overset { P } {  } 0$ . By (4) and Corollary 18.13, it remains to note that V<sup>¯</sup> is B-integrable, which holds since $\bar { V } \in L ^ { 2 }$ by (ii). ✷

Theorem 19.11 (Brownian martingales) Let $B = ( B ^ { 1 } , \ldots , B ^ { d } )$ be a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with complete, induced filtration $\mathcal { F }$ . Then every local $\mathcal { F } _ { - }$ martingale M is a.s. continuous, and there exist some $( P \times \lambda ) – a . e$ . unique processes $V ^ { 1 } , \dots , V ^ { d } \in L ( B ^ { 1 } )$ , such that
