Lemma 19.12 (Brownian functionals, Itˆo) Let $B = ( B ^ { 1 } , \ldots , B ^ { d } )$ be a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and let ξ be a B-measurable random variable with $E \xi = 0$ and $E \xi ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . By the obvious completeness of $L ( B ^ { 1 } )$ , the same formula shows that K is closed. To obtain $K = H$ , we need to show that any $\xi \in H \ominus K$ vanishes a.s. 

Then fix any non-random functions $u ^ { 1 } , \ldots , u ^ { d } \in L ^ { 2 } ( { \mathsf { R } } )$ . Put $\begin{array} { r } { M = \sum _ { k } u ^ { k } { \cdot } B ^ { k } } \end{array}$ , and define the process $Z$ as in Lemma 19.1. Then Proposition 18.14 yields

and so $\xi \perp ( Z _ { \infty } - 1 )$ , or

Specializing to step functions $u ^ { k }$ and using Theorem 6.3, we get

E \left\{\xi ; \left(B _ {t _ {1}}, \dots , B _ {t _ {n}}\right) \in C \right\} = 0, \quad t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n} \in \mathsf {R} _ {+}, C \in \mathcal {B} ^ {n}, n \in \mathsf {N},

which extends by a monotone-class argument to $E ( \xi ; A ) = 0$ for any $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty }$ Thus, $\xi = E ( \xi | \mathcal { F } _ { \infty } ) = 0$ a.s. ✷

By Theorem 6.3, the variables $X _ { t _ { 1 } } , \ldots , X _ { t _ { m } }$ and $\eta B _ { 1 } , \ldots , \eta B _ { n }$ have then the required joint conditional distribution, and the assertion follows by a monotoneclass argument. ✷

Proposition 19.15 (discounted reduction maps) For $j \in \mathsf N$ , let $( \tau _ { j } , \chi _ { j } )$ be orthogonal, adapted pairs as in Theorem 10.27 with discounted compensators $\zeta _ { j } ,$ and let $Y _ { j } \colon { \mathsf { R } } _ { + } \times K _ { j } \to S _ { j }$ be predictable with $\zeta _ { j } \circ Y _ { j } ^ { - 1 } \leq \mu _ { j }$ a.s. for some $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ -measurable random distributions $\mu _ { j }$ on $S _ { j }$ . Put $\gamma _ { j } = Y _ { j } ( \tau _ { j } , \chi _ { j } )$ , and define $X$ as in Lemma 19.14 for a continuous local martingale M in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and some predictable processes $U _ { t } , t \in S$ , such that the process $\rho$ on $S ^ { 2 }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }  – m e a s u r a b l e$ Then conditionally on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ , we have 

(i) $X , \gamma _ { 1 } , \gamma _ { 2 } , . . .$ . are independent, 

(ii) $\mathcal { L } ( \gamma _ { j } ) = \mu _ { j }$ for all $j$ , 

(iii) X is centered Gaussian with covariance function $\rho .$ 

Proof: For $V _ { 1 } , \ldots , V _ { m }$ as before, we define the associated martingales $M _ { 1 }$ ， $\ldots , M _ { m }$ as in Lemma 10.25. Further introduce the exponential local martingale $\begin{array} { r } { Z = \exp ( i N + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \left[ N \right] ) } \end{array}$ , where N is such as in the proof of Lemma 19.14. Then $( Z - 1 ) \prod _ { j } M _ { j }$ is conditionally a uniformly integrable martingale, and we get as in Theorem 10.27 

$$
E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} (Z _ {\infty} - 1) \prod_ {j} \left\{1 _ {B _ {j}} (\gamma_ {j}) - \mu_ {j} B _ {j} \right\} = 0.
$$

Combining with the same relation without the factor $Z _ { \infty } - 1$ and proceeding recursively, we get as before 

$$
E ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} \exp (i N _ {\infty}) \prod_ {j} 1 _ {B _ {j}} (\gamma_ {j}) = \exp \left(- \frac {1}{2} [ N ] _ {\infty}\right) \prod_ {j} \mu_ {j} B _ {j}.
$$

Applying Theorem 6.3 to the bounded measure $\begin{array} { r } { \tilde { P } = \prod _ { j } 1 _ { B _ { j } } ( \gamma _ { j } ) \cdot P ^ { \mathcal { F } _ { 0 } } } \end{array}$ , we conclude that 

$$
P ^ {\mathcal {F} _ {0}} \Bigl \{X \in A; \gamma_ {j} \in B _ {j}, j \leq m \Bigr \} = \nu_ {\rho} (A) \prod_ {j} \mu_ {j} B _ {j},
$$

where $\nu _ { \rho }$ denotes the centered Gaussian distribution on $\mathsf { R } ^ { T }$ with covariance function $\rho .$ ✷ 

Next we show how the multiple Wiener–Itˆo integrals of Chapter 14 can be expressed as iterated single Itˆo integrals. Then introduce the tetrahedral sets 

$$
\Delta_ {n} = \left\{\left(t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}\right) \in \mathsf {R} _ {+} ^ {n}; t _ {1} <   \dots <   t _ {n} \right\}, \quad n \in \mathsf {N}.
$$

Given a function $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { n } , \lambda ^ { n } )$ , we write $\hat { f } = n ! \tilde { f } 1 _ { \Delta _ { n } }$ , where $\tilde { f }$ is the symmetrization of $f$ defined in Chapter 14. For any isonormal Gaussian process $\zeta$ on $L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda )$ , we may introduce an associated Brownian motion B on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ satisfying $B _ { t } = \zeta 1 _ { [ 0 , t ] }$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

Theorem 19.16 (multiple and iterated integrals) Let B be a Brownian motion on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ generated by an isonormal Gaussian process $\zeta$ on $L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda )$ . Then for any $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda ^ { n } )$ , we have 

$$
\zeta^ {n} f = \int d B _ {t _ {n}} \int d B _ {t _ {n - 1}} \dots \int \hat {f} (t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n}) d B _ {t _ {1}} a. s.\tag{6}
$$

Though a formal verification is easy, the existence of the integrals on the right depends in a subtle way on the choice of suitable versions in each step. The existence of such versions is regarded as part of the assertion. 

Proof: We prove by induction that the iterated integral 

$$
V _ {t _ {k + 1}, \dots , t _ {n}} ^ {k} = \int d B _ {t _ {k}} \int d B _ {t _ {k - 1}} \dots \int \hat {f} (t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}) d B _ {t _ {1}}
$$

exists for almost all $t _ { k + 1 } , \ldots , t _ { n } ,$ , and that $V ^ { k }$ has a version supported by $\Delta _ { n - k }$ which is progressive in the variable $t _ { k + 1 }$ for fixed $t _ { k + 2 } , \ldots , t _ { n }$ . We further need to establish the isometry 

$$
E \Big (V _ {t _ {k + 1}, \dots , t _ {n}} ^ {k} \Big) ^ {2} = \int \dots \int \Big \{\hat {f} (t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}) \Big \} ^ {2} d t _ {1} \dots d t _ {k},\tag{7}
$$

which allows us in the next step to define $V _ { t _ { k + 2 } , \dots , t _ { n } } ^ { k + 1 }$ for almost all $t _ { k + 2 } , \ldots , t _ { n }$ 

The integral $V ^ { 0 } = { \hat { f } }$ has clearly the stated properties. Now suppose that a version of the integral $V _ { t _ { k } , \dots , t _ { n } } ^ { k - 1 }$ has been constructed with the desired properties. For any $t _ { k + 1 } , \ldots , t _ { n }$ such that (7) is finite, Theorem 18.25 shows that the process 

$$
X _ {t, t _ {k + 1}, \dots , t _ {n}} ^ {k} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} V _ {t _ {k}, \dots , t _ {n}} ^ {k - 1} d B _ {t _ {k}}, \quad t \geq 0,
$$

has a progressive version that is a.s. continuous in t for fixed $t _ { k + 1 } , \ldots , t _ { n }$ . By Proposition 18.15 we obtain 

$$
V _ {t _ {k + 1}, \dots , t _ {n}} ^ {k} = X _ {t _ {k + 1}, t _ {k + 1}, \dots , t _ {n}} ^ {k} \mathrm{a.s.,} t _ {k + 1}, \dots , t _ {n} \geq 0,
$$

and the progressivity carries over to $V ^ { k }$ , regarded as a process in $t _ { k + 1 }$ for fixed $t _ { k + 2 } , \ldots , t _ { n }$ . Since $\dot { V } ^ { k - 1 }$ is supported by $\Delta _ { n - k + 1 }$ , we may choose $X ^ { k }$ to be supported by $\mathsf { R } _ { + } \times \Delta _ { n - k }$ , which ensures that $V ^ { k }$ will be supported by $\Delta _ { n - k }$ Finally, formula (7) for $V ^ { k - 1 }$ yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \Big (V _ {t _ {k + 1}, \ldots , t _ {n}} ^ {k} \Big) ^ {2} = E \int \Big (V _ {t _ {k}, \ldots , t _ {n}} ^ {k - 1} \Big) ^ {2} d t _ {k} \\ & \qquad = \int \dots \int \Big \{\hat {f} (t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n}) \Big \} ^ {2} d t _ {1} \dots d t _ {k}. \end{array}
$$

To prove $( 6 )$ , we note that the right-hand side is linear and $L ^ { 2 } .$ -continuous in $f$ . Furthermore, the two sides agree for indicator functions of rectangles in $\Delta _ { n }$ . The equality extends by a monotone-class argument to arbitrary indicator functions in $\Delta _ { n } .$ , and the further extension to $L ^ { 2 } ( \Delta _ { n } )$ is immediate. It remains to note that $\zeta ^ { n } f = \zeta ^ { n } \tilde { f } = \zeta ^ { n } \hat { f }$ for any $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda ^ { n } )$ ✷ 

For a Brownian functional with mean 0 and finite variance, we have established both a chaos expansion in Theorem 14.26 and a stochastic integral representation in Lemma 19.12. We proceed to examine how the two formulas are related. For any $f \in L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda ^ { n } )$ , we define $f _ { t } ( t _ { 1 } , \dots , t _ { n - 1 } ) = f ( t _ { 1 } , \dots , t _ { n - 1 } , t )$ , and write $\zeta ^ { n - 1 } f ( t ) = \zeta ^ { n - 1 } f _ { t }$ when $\| f _ { t } \| < \infty$ 

Proposition 19.17 (chaos and integral representations) Let $\zeta$ be an isonormal Gaussian process on $L ^ { 2 } ( \lambda )$ , generating a Brownian motion $B$ , and let $\xi \in L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ with chaos expansion $\textstyle \sum _ { n > 0 } \zeta ^ { n } f _ { n }$ . Then a.s. 

$$
\xi = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} V _ {t} d B _ {t}, \qquad V _ {t} = \sum_ {n > 0} \zeta^ {n - 1} \hat {f} _ {n} (t), \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Proof: Proceeding as in the previous proof, we get for any $m \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int \sum_ {n \geq m} E \Bigl \{\zeta^ {n - 1} \hat {f} _ {n} (t) \Bigr \} ^ {2} d t = \sum_ {n \geq m} \| \hat {f} _ {n} \| ^ {2} \\ = \sum_ {n \geq m} E (\zeta^ {n} f _ {n}) ^ {2} <   \infty . \end{array}\tag{8}
$$

Since the integrals $\zeta ^ { n } f$ are orthogonal for diferent $n _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , the series for $V _ { t }$ converges in $L ^ { 2 }$ for almost every $t \geq 0$ . On the exceptional null set, we may redefine $V _ { t } = 0$ . Choosing progressive versions of the integrals $\zeta ^ { n - 1 } \hat { f } _ { n } ( t )$ , as before, we see from the proof of Corollary 5.33 that even the sum $V$ can be chosen to be progressive. Applying (8) with $m = 1$ gives $V \in L ( B )$ 

Using Theorem 19.16, we get by a formal calculation 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \xi = \sum_ {n \geq 1} \zeta^ {n} f _ {n} \\ = \sum_ {n \geq 1} \int \zeta^ {n - 1} \hat {f} _ {n} (t)   d B _ {t} \\ = \int d B _ {t} \sum_ {n \geq 1} \zeta^ {n - 1} \hat {f} _ {n} (t) \\ = \int V _ {t}   d B _ {t}. \end{array}
$$

To justify the interchange of integration and summation, we may use (8) and let $m \to \infty$ to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \Big \{\int d B _ {t} \sum_ {n \geq m} \zeta^ {n - 1} \hat {f} _ {n} (t) \Big \} ^ {2} = \int \sum_ {n \geq m} E \Big \{\zeta^ {n - 1} \hat {f} _ {n} (t) \Big \} ^ {2} d t \\ = \sum_ {n \geq m} E (\zeta^ {n} f _ {n}) ^ {2} \to 0. \end{array}
$$

Now let $P , Q$ be probability measures on a common measurable space $( \Omega , A )$ , endowed with a right-continuous and P-complete filtration $( \mathcal { F } _ { t } )$ . When $Q \ll P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t } .$ , we write $Z _ { t }$ for the corresponding density, so that $Q = Z _ { t } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ . Since the martingale property depends on the choice of probability measure, we need to distinguish between P-martingales and Q -martingales. Let $E _ { P }$ denote integration with respect to $P ,$ and write $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty } ~ = ~ \forall _ { t } \mathcal { F } _ { t }$ We <sub>summarize the basic properties of such measure transformations. Recall from</sub> Theorem 9.28 that any ${ \mathcal { F } } .$ -martingale has an rcll version. 

Lemma 19.18 (change of measure) Let P, Q be probability measures on a measurable space Ω with a right-continuous, P-complete filtration $\mathcal { F } _ { : }$ , such that 

$$
Q = Z _ {t} \cdot P o n \mathcal {F} _ {t}, t \geq 0,
$$

for an adapted process $Z$ . Then for any adapted process $X _ { \cdot }$ 

(i) $Z$ is a P-martingale, 

(ii) $Z$ is uniformly integrable $\Leftrightarrow \ Q \ll P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty ; }$ 

(iii) X is a Q-martingale $\Leftrightarrow \ X Z$ is a P-martingale. 

When Z is right-continuous and X is rcll, we have also 

(iv) $Q = Z _ { \tau } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau } \cap \{ \tau < \infty \}$ for any optional time $\tau _ { \mathrm { : } }$ 

(v) X is a local Q-martingale $\Leftrightarrow \ X Z$ is a local P-martingale, 

(vi) $\operatorname* { i n f } _ { s \leq t } Z _ { s } > 0 a . s . \ Q , \quad t > 0 $ 

Proof: (iii) For any adapted process $X$ , we note that $X _ { t }$ is $Q$ -integrable if $X _ { t } Z _ { t }$ is P -integrable. When this holds for all $t ,$ the Q -martingale property of 

X becomes 

$$
\int_ {A} X _ {s} d Q = \int_ {A} X _ {t} d Q, \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {s}, s <   t.
$$

By the definition of $Z ,$ , this is equivalent to 

$$
E _ {P} \big (X _ {s} Z _ {s}; A \big) = E _ {P} \big (X _ {t} Z _ {t}; A \big), \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {s}, s <   t,
$$

which means that $X Z$ is a P -martingale. 

(i) (ii): Choosing $X _ { t } \equiv 1$ in (iii), we see that $Z$ is a P -martingale. Now let $Z$ be uniformly P -integrable, say with L<sup>1</sup>-limit $Z _ { \infty }$ . For any $t < u$ and $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { t }$ , we have $Q A = E _ { P } ( Z _ { u } ; A )$ . As $u \to \infty$ we get $Q A = E _ { P } ( Z _ { \infty } ; A )$ , which extends to arbitrary $A \in { \mathcal { F } } _ { \infty }$ by a monotone-class argument. Thus, $Q = Z _ { \infty } { \cdot } P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ . Conversely, if $Q = \xi \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { \infty }$ , then $E _ { P } \xi = 1$ , and the P -martingale $M _ { t } = E _ { P } ( \xi | \mathcal { F } _ { t } )$ satisfies $Q = M _ { t } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for every t. But then $Z _ { t } = M _ { t }$ a.s. for all t, and Z is uniformly P -integrable with limit $\xi .$ 

(iv) By optional sampling, 

$$
Q A = E _ {P} \left(Z _ {\tau \wedge t}; A\right), \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {\tau \wedge t}, t \geq 0,
$$

and so 

$$
Q \big (A; \tau \leq t \big) = E _ {P} \big (Z _ {\tau}; A \cap \{\tau \leq t \} \big), \quad A \in \mathcal {F} _ {\tau}, t \geq 0.
$$

The assertion now follows by monotone convergence as $t \to \infty$ 

(v) For any optional time $\tau _ { : }$ we need to show that $X ^ { \tau }$ is a Q -martingale if $( X Z ) ^ { \tau }$ is a P -martingale. This may be seen as in $( \mathrm { i v } )$ , once we note that $Q = Z _ { t } ^ { \tau } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau \wedge t }$ for all t. 

(vi) By Lemma 9.32 it is enough to show that $Z _ { t } > 0$ a.s. Q for every $t > 0$ This is clear from the fact that $Q \{ Z _ { t } = 0 \} = E _ { P } ( Z _ { t } ; Z _ { t } = 0 ) = 0$ ✷ 

The measure $Q$ is usually not given at the outset, but needs to be constructed from the martingale $Z .$ . This requires some regularity conditions on the underlying probability space. 

Lemma 19.19 (existence) Let $Z \ge 0$ be a martingale with $Z _ { 0 } = 1$ , on the canonical probability space $( \Omega , P )$ with induced filtration ${ \mathcal F } ,$ , where $\Omega = D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , S }$ for a Polish space $S _ { ☉ }$ . Then there exists a probability measure $Q$ on Ω with 

$$
Q = Z _ {t} \cdot P o n \mathcal {F} _ {t}, t \geq 0.
$$

Proof: For every $t \geq 0$ we may introduce the probability measure $Q _ { t } = Z _ { t } { \cdot } P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t } .$ , which may be regarded as defined on $D _ { [ 0 , t ] , S }$ . Since the latter spaces are again Polish for the Skorohod topology, Corollary 8.22 yields a probability measure $Q$ on $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , S }$ with projections $Q _ { t }$ . The measure $Q$ has clearly the required properties. ✷ 

We show how the drift of a continuous semi-martingale is transformed under a change of measure with a continuous density Z. An extension appears in Theorem 20.9. 

Theorem 19.20 (transformation of drift, Girsanov, van Schuppen & Wong) Consider some probability measures $P , \ Q$ and a continuous process $Z$ , such that Q = Z+ : P on Ft. t > 0 

$$
Q = Z _ {t} \cdot P o n \mathcal {F} _ {t}, t \geq 0.
$$

Then for any continuous local P-martingale M, we have the local Q-martingale 

$$
\tilde {M} = M - Z ^ {- 1} \cdot [ M, Z ].
$$

Proof: First let $Z ^ { - 1 }$ be bounded on the support of $[ M ]$ . Then $\tilde { M }$ is a continuous P -semi-martingale, and so by Proposition 18.14 and an integration by parts, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \tilde {M} Z - (\tilde {M} Z) _ {0} & = \tilde {M} \cdot Z + Z \cdot \tilde {M} + [ \tilde {M}, Z ] \\ & = \tilde {M} \cdot Z + Z \cdot M - [ M, Z ] + [ \tilde {M}, Z ] \\ & = \tilde {M} \cdot Z + Z \cdot M, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\tilde { M } Z$ is a local P-martingale. Hence, by Lemma 19.18, $\tilde { M }$ is a local Q -martingale. 

For general $M ,$ , define $\tau _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; Z _ { t } < 1 / n \}$ , and note as before that $\tilde { M } ^ { \tau _ { n } }$ is a local Q -martingale for every $n \in { \mathbb N }$ . Since $\tau _ { n }  \infty \mathrm { a . s . } Q$ by Lemma 19.18, $\tilde { M }$ is a local Q -martingale by Lemma 18.1. ✷ 

Next we show how the basic notions of stochastic calculus are preserved by a change of measure. Then let $[ X ] _ { P }$ be the quadratic variation of X under the probability measure $P ,$ write $L _ { P } ( X )$ for the class of processes V that are X-integrable under $P ,$ , and let $( V \cdot X ) _ { P }$ be the corresponding stochastic integral. 

Proposition 19.21 (preservation properties) Let $Q = Z _ { t } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ , where $Z$ is continuous. Then 

(i) a continuous P-semi-martingale X is also a Q -semi-martingale, and 

$$
[ X ] _ {P} = [ X ] _ {Q} a. s. Q,
$$

(ii) $L _ { P } ( X ) \subset L _ { Q } ( X )$ , and for any $V \in L _ { P } ( X )$ 

$$
(V \cdot X) _ {P} = (V \cdot X) _ {Q} a. s. Q,
$$

(iii) for any continuous local P-martingale M and process $V \in L _ { P } ( M )$ ， 

$$
(V \cdot M) ^ {\sim} = V \cdot \tilde {M} a. s. Q,
$$

whenever either side exists. 

Proof: (i) Consider a continuous P -semi-martingale $X = M + A$ , where M is a continuous local P -martingale and A is a process of locally finite variation. Under $Q$ we may write 

$$
X = \tilde {M} + Z ^ {- 1} \cdot [ M, Z ] + A,
$$

where $\tilde { M }$ is the continuous local Q -martingale of Theorem 19.20, and we note that $Z ^ { - 1 } \cdot \left[ M , Z \right]$ has locally finite variation, since $Z > 0$ a.s. Q by Lemma 19.18. Thus, X is also a semi-martingale under $Q .$ . The statement for $[ X ]$ is now clear from Proposition 18.17. 

(ii) If $V \in L _ { P } ( X )$ , then $V ^ { 2 } \in L _ { P } ( [ X ] )$ and $V \in L _ { P } ( A )$ , and so the same relations hold under $Q _ { i }$ , and we get $V \in L _ { Q } ( \tilde { M } + A )$ To get $V \in L _ { Q } ( X )$ it remains to show that $V \in L _ { Q } ( Z ^ { - 1 } \cdot [ M , \dot { Z } ] )$ ). Since $Z > 0$ under $Q .$ , it is equivalent to show that $V \in L _ { Q } ( [ M , Z ] )$ , which is clear by Proposition 18.9, since $[ M , Z ] _ { \cal Q } = [ \tilde { M } , Z ] _ { \cal Q }$ and $V \in L _ { Q } ( \tilde { M } )$ 

(iii) Note that ${ \cal L _ { Q } } ( M ) = { \cal L _ { Q } } ( { \tilde { M } } )$ as before. If V belongs to either class, then under $Q { \mathrm { : } }$ Proposition 18.14 yields the a.s. relations 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} (V \cdot M) ^ {\sim} & = V \cdot M - Z ^ {- 1} \cdot [ V \cdot M, Z ] \\ & = V \cdot M - V Z ^ {- 1} \cdot [ M, Z ] \\ & = V \cdot \tilde {M}. \end{array}
$$

In particular, Theorem 19.3 shows that if B is a P -Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , then $\tilde { B }$ is a Brownian motion under $Q _ { i }$ , since both processes are continuous martingales with the same covariation process. 

The preceding theory simplifies when $P$ and $Q$ are equivalent on each $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ since in that case $Z > 0 { \mathrm { ~ a . s . ~ } } P$ by Lemma 19.18. If $Z$ is also continuous, it can be expressed as an exponential martingale. More general processes of this kind are considered in Theorem 20.8. 

Lemma 19.22 (real exponential martingales) A continuous process $Z > 0$ is a local martingale if a.s. 

$$
Z _ {t} = \mathcal {E} (M) _ {t} \equiv \exp \left(M _ {t} - \frac {1}{2} [ M ] _ {t}\right), \quad t \geq 0,\tag{9}
$$

for a continuous local martingale M. Here M is a.s. unique, and for any continuous local martingale N, 

$$
[ M, N ] = Z ^ {- 1} \cdot [ Z, N ] a. s.
$$

Proof: If M is a continuous local martingale, so is $\mathcal { E } ( M )$ by $\mathrm { I t o } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s }$ formula. Conversely, let $Z > 0$ be a continuous local martingale. Then Corollary 18.19 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \log Z - \log Z _ {0} = Z ^ {- 1} \cdot Z - \frac {1}{2} Z ^ {- 2} \cdot [ Z ] \\ = Z ^ {- 1} \cdot Z - \frac {1}{2} [ Z ^ {- 1} \cdot Z ], \end{array}
$$

and (9) follows with $M = \log Z _ { 0 } + Z ^ { - 1 } \cdot Z$ . The last assertion is clear from this expression, and the uniqueness of M follows from Proposition 18.2. ✷ 

The drift of a continuous semi-martingale can sometimes be eliminated by a suitable change of measure. Beginning with the case of a Brownian motion $B$ with deterministic drift, we need to show that $\mathcal { E } ( B )$ is a true martingale, which follows easily by a direct computation. By $P \sim Q$ we mean that $P \ll Q$ and $Q \ll P .$ . Let $L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ be the class of measurable functions $f : { \mathsf { R } } _ { + } \to { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d } ,$ such that $| f | ^ { 2 }$ is locally Lebesgue integrable. For any $f \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ we define $f \cdot \lambda = ( f ^ { 1 } \cdot \lambda , \dots , f ^ { d } \cdot \lambda )$ , where the components on the right are ordinary Lebesgue integrals. 

Theorem 19.23 (shifted Brownian motion, Cameron & Martin) Let B be a canonical Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with induced, complete filtration $\mathcal { F }$ , fix a continuous function h : $\mathsf R _ { + } \to \mathsf R ^ { d }$ with $h _ { 0 } = 0$ , and put $P _ { h } = \mathcal { L } ( B + h )$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $P _ { h } \sim P _ { 0 }$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

(ii) $h = f \cdot \lambda$ for an $f \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ 

Under those conditions, 

(iii) $P _ { h } = \mathcal { E } ( f \cdot B ) _ { t } \cdot P _ { 0 }$ 

Proof, $( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i i ) - ( \mathrm { i i i } ) }$ : Assuming (i), Lemma 19.18 yields a $P _ { 0 }$ -martingale $Z > 0$ , such that $P _ { h } = Z _ { t } \cdot P _ { 0 }$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ . Here $Z$ is a.s. continuous by Theorem 19.11, and by Lemma 19.22 it equals $\mathcal { E } ( M )$ for a continuous local $P _ { 0 } -$ martingale M. Using Theorem 19.11 again, we note that $\begin{array} { r } { M = V \cdot B = \sum _ { i } V ^ { i } \cdot B ^ { i } } \end{array}$ a.s. for some processes $V ^ { i } \in L ( B ^ { 1 } )$ , and in particular $V \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { a . s . }$ 

By Theorem 19.20, the process 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \tilde {B} = B - [ B, M ] \\ = B - V \cdot \lambda \end{array}
$$

is a $P _ { h }$ -Brownian motion, and so under $P _ { h }$ the canonical process $B$ has the semi-martingale decompositions 

$$
\begin{array}{c} B = \tilde {B} + V \cdot \lambda \\ = (B - h) + h. \end{array}
$$

Since the decomposition is a.s. unique by Proposition 18.2, we get $V \cdot \lambda = h$ a.s. Then also $h = f \cdot \lambda$ for some measurable function $f$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ,$ , and since clearly $\lambda \{ t \geq 0 ; V _ { t } \neq f _ { t } \} = 0$ a.s., we have even $f \in L _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 } ,$ , proving (ii). Furthermore, $M = V \cdot B = f \cdot B \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ , and (iii) follows. 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Assume (ii). Since $M = f \cdot B$ is a time-changed Brownian motion under $P _ { 0 }$ , the process $Z = { \mathcal { E } } ( M )$ is a $P _ { \mathrm { 0 } } \mathrm { - m a r t i n g a l e } .$ , and Lemma 19.19 yields a probability measure $Q$ on $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ , such that $Q = Z _ { t } \cdot P _ { 0 }$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ Moreover, Theorem 19.20 shows that the process 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \tilde {B} = B - [ B, M ] \\ = B - h \end{array}
$$

is a Q -Brownian motion, and so $Q = P _ { h }$ . In particular, this proves (i). ✷ 

For more general semi-martingales, Theorem 19.20 and Lemma 19.22 suggest that we might remove the drift by a change of measure of the form $Q = { \mathcal { E } } ( M ) _ { t } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ , where M is a continuous local martingale with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then by Lemma 19.18 we need $Z = { \mathcal { E } } ( M )$ to be a true martingale, which can often be verified through the following criterion. 

Theorem 19.24 (uniform integrability, Novikov) Let M be a real, continuous local martingale with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then $\mathcal { E } ( M )$ is a uniformly integrable martingale, whenever 

$$
E \exp \left(\frac {1}{2} [ M ] _ {\infty}\right) <   \infty .
$$

This will first be proved in a special case. 

Lemma 19.25 (Wald’s identity) For any real Brownian motion B and optional time $\tau _ { \cdot }$ , we have 

$$
E e ^ {\tau / 2} <   \infty \quad \Rightarrow \quad E \exp \left(B _ {\tau} - \frac {1}{2} \tau\right) = 1.
$$

Proof: First consider the hitting times 

$$
\tau_ {b} = \inf \left\{t \geq 0; B _ {t} = t - b \right\}, \quad b > 0.
$$

Since the $\tau _ { b }$ remain optional with respect to the right-continuous, induced filtration, we may take B to be a canonical Brownian motion with associated distribution $P = P _ { 0 }$ . Defining $h _ { t } \equiv t$ and $Z = { \mathcal { E } } ( B )$ , we see from Theorem 19.23 that $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { h } = Z _ { t } \cdot P } \end{array}$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ . Since $\tau _ { b } < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . under both $P$ and $P _ { h }$ , Lemma 19.18 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \exp \Big (B _ {\tau_ {b}} - \frac {1}{2} \tau_ {b} \Big) = E Z _ {\tau_ {b}} \\ & \qquad = E \Big (Z _ {\tau_ {b}}; \tau_ {b} <   \infty \Big) \\ & \qquad = P _ {h} \{\tau_ {b} <   \infty \} = 1. \end{array}
$$

The stopped process $M _ { t } \equiv Z _ { t \wedge \tau _ { b } }$ is a positive local martingale, and by Fatou’s lemma it is also a super-martingale on $[ 0 , \infty ]$ . Since clearly $E M _ { \infty } =$ $E Z _ { \tau _ { b } } = 1 = E M _ { 0 }$ , we see from the Doob decomposition that $M$ is a true martingale on $[ 0 , \infty ]$ . For $\tau$ as stated, we get by optional sampling 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 1 = E M _ {\tau} = E Z _ {\tau \wedge \tau_ {b}} \\ \qquad = E \big (Z _ {\tau};   \tau \leq \tau_ {b} \big) + E \big (Z _ {\tau_ {b}};   \tau > \tau_ {b} \big). \end{array}\tag{10}
$$

Using the definition of $\tau _ { b }$ and the condition on $\tau .$ , we get as $b \to \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \Big (Z _ {\tau_ {b}}; \tau > \tau_ {b} \Big) = e ^ {- b} E \Big (e ^ {\tau_ {b} / 2}; \tau > \tau_ {b} \Big) \\ \leq e ^ {- b} E e ^ {\tau / 2} \to 0, \end{array}
$$

and so the last term in (10) tends to zero. Since also $\tau _ { b }  \infty$ , the first term on the right tends to $E Z _ { \tau }$ by monotone convergence, and we get $E Z _ { \tau } = 1$ . ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 19.24: Since $\mathcal { E } ( M )$ is a super-martingale on $[ 0 , \infty ]$ , it sufices to show that, under the stated condition, $E \mathcal { E } ( M ) _ { \infty } = 1$ . Using Theorem 19.4 and Proposition 9.9, we may then reduce to the statement of Lemma 19.25. ✷ 

This yields in particular a classical result for Brownian motion: 

Corollary 19.26 (drift removal, Girsanov) Consider a Brownian motion B and a progressive process V in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , such that 

$$
E \exp \Bigl \{\frac {1}{2} \left(| V | ^ {2} \cdot \lambda\right) _ {\infty} \Bigr \} <   \infty .
$$

Then 

(i) $Q = \mathcal { E } ( V \cdot B ) _ { \infty } \cdot P$ is a probability measure, 

(ii) $\tilde { B } = B - V \cdot \lambda$ is a Q-Brownian motion. 

Proof: Combine Theorems 19.20 and 19.24.

# Semi-Martingales and Stochastic Integration

Predictable covariation, L<sup>2</sup>-martingale and semi-martingale integrals, quadratic variation and covariation, substitution rule, Dol´eans exponential, change of measure, BDG inequalities, martingale integral, purely discontinuous semi-martingales, semi-martingale and martingale decompositions, exponential super-martingales and inequalities, quasi-martingales, stochastic integrators 

In the last two chapters, we have seen how the Itˆo integral with associated transformation rules leads to a powerful stochastic calculus for continuous semimartingales, defined as sums of continuous local martingales and continuous processes of locally finite variation. This entire theory will now be extended to semi-martingales with possible jump discontinuities. In particular, the semimartingales turn out to be precisely the processes that can serve as stochastic integrators with reasonable adaptedness and continuity properties. 

The present theory is equally important but much more subtle, as it depends crucially on the Doob–Meyer decomposition from Chapter 10 and the powerful BDG inequalities for general local martingales. Our construction of the general stochastic integral proceeds in three steps. First we imitate the definition of the L<sup>2</sup>-integral V M from Chapter 18, using a predictable version M, N of the covariation process. A suitable truncation then allows us to extend the integral to arbitrary semi-martingales X and bounded, predictable processes V. The ordinary covariation [X, Y] can now be defined by the integration-by-parts formula, and we may use the general BDG inequalities to extend the martingale integral V M to more general integrands V. 

Once the stochastic integral is defined, we may develop a stochastic calculus for general semi-martingales. In particular, we prove an extension of Itˆo’s formula, solve a basic stochastic diferential equation, and establish a general Girsanov-type theorem for absolutely continuous changes of the probability measure. The latter material extends the relevant parts of Chapters 18–19. 

The stochastic integral and covariation process, along with the Doob–Meyer decomposition from Chapter 10, provide the basic tools for a more detailed study of general semi-martingales. In particular, we may now establish two general decompositions, similar to the decompositions of optional times and increasing processes in Chapter 10. We further derive some exponential inequalities for martingales with bounded jumps, characterize local quasi-martingales as special semi-martingales, and show that no continuous extension of the predictable integral exists beyond the context of semi-martingales. 

Throughout this chapter, let $\mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ be the class of uniformly square-integrable martingales, and note as in Lemma 18.4 that $\mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ is a Hilbert space for the norm $\| { \bf \bar { M } } \| = ( E M _ { \infty } ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ . Let $\mathcal { M } _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ be the closed linear subspace of martingales $M \in \mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ . The corresponding classes $\mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ and $\mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { 0 , l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ are defined as the sets of processes M, such that the stopped versions $M ^ { \tau _ { n } }$ belong to $\mathcal { M } ^ { 2 }$ or $\mathcal { M } _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ , respectively, for suitable optional times $\tau _ { n } \to \infty$ 

For every $M \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 } ,$ we note that $M ^ { 2 }$ is a local sub-martingale. The corresponding compensator $\langle M \rangle$ is called the predictable quadratic variation of M. More generally, we define<sup>1</sup> the predictable covariation $\langle M , N \rangle$ of two processes M, $N \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ as the compensator of $M N$ , also obtainable through the polarization formula 

$$
4 \langle M, N \rangle = \langle M + N \rangle - \langle M - N \rangle .
$$

Note that $\langle M , M \rangle = \langle M \rangle$ . If M and N are continuous, then clearly $\langle M , N \rangle =$ $[ M , N ]$ a.s. Here we list some further useful properties. 

Proposition 20.1 (predictable covariation) For any M, $N , M ^ { n } \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 } ,$ , we have a.s. 

(i) $\langle M , N \rangle$ is symmetric, bilinear with $\langle M , N \rangle = \langle M - M _ { 0 } , N \rangle$ ， 

(ii) $\langle M \rangle = \langle M , M \rangle$ is non-decreasing, 

(iii) $\begin{array} { r } { | \langle M , N \rangle | \leq \int | d \langle M , N \rangle | \leq \langle M \rangle ^ { 1 / 2 } \langle N \rangle ^ { 1 / 2 } , } \end{array}$ 

(iv) $\langle M , N \rangle ^ { \tau } = \langle M ^ { \tau } , N \rangle = \langle M ^ { \tau } , N ^ { \tau } \rangle$ for any optional time $\tau ,$ 

(v) $\langle M ^ { n } \rangle _ { \infty } \stackrel { P } { \to } 0 \Rightarrow ( M ^ { n } - M _ { 0 } ^ { n } ) ^ { * } \stackrel { P } { \to } 0 .$ 

Proof, (i) (iv): Lemma 10.11 shows that $\langle M , N \rangle$ is the a.s. unique predictable process of locally integrable variation starting at 0, such that $M N -$ $\langle M , N \rangle$ is a local martingale. The symmetry and bilinearity follow immediately, as does last property in (i), since $M N _ { 0 } , M _ { 0 } N$ , and $M _ { 0 } N _ { 0 }$ are all local martingales. Moreover, we get (iii) as in Proposition 18.9, and (iv) as in Theorem 18.5. 

(v) Here we may take $M _ { 0 } ^ { n } = 0$ for all n. Let $\langle M ^ { n } \rangle _ { \infty } \overset { P } { \to } 0$ , fix any $\varepsilon > 0$ , and define $\tau _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t ; \langle M ^ { n } \rangle _ { t } \geq \varepsilon \}$ . Since $\langle M ^ { n } \rangle$ is predictable, even $\tau _ { n }$ is predictable by Theorem 10.14, say with announcing sequence $\tau _ { n k } \uparrow \tau _ { n }$ . The latter may be chosen such that $M ^ { n }$ becomes an L<sup>2</sup>-martingale and $( M ^ { n } ) ^ { 2 } - \langle M ^ { n } \rangle$ a uniformly integrable martingale on every interval $[ 0 , \tau _ { n k } ]$ . Then Proposition 9.17 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (M ^ {n}) _ {\tau_ {n k}} ^ {* 2} & \lesssim & E (M ^ {n}) _ {\tau_ {n k}} ^ {2} \\ & = & E \langle M ^ {n} \rangle_ {\tau_ {n k}} \leq \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

and as $k  \infty$ we get $E ( M ^ { n } ) _ { \tau _ { n } - } ^ { * 2 } \lesssim \varepsilon$ . Now fix any $\delta > 0$ , and write 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} P \Big \{(M ^ {n}) ^ {* 2} > \delta \Big \} & \leq & P \{\tau_ {n} <   \infty \} + \delta^ {- 1} E (M ^ {n}) _ {\tau_ {n} -} ^ {* 2} \\ & \lesssim & P \Big \{\langle M ^ {n} \rangle_ {\infty} \geq \varepsilon \Big \} + \delta^ {- 1} \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Here the right-hand side tends to zero as $n \to \infty$ and then $\varepsilon \to 0$ 

The predictable quadratic variation can be used to extend the Itˆo integral from Chapter 18. Then let be the class of bounded, predictable step processes V with jumps at finitely many fixed times. The corresponding integral $V \cdot X$ is referred to as an elementary predictable integral. 

Given any $M \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ , let $L ^ { 2 } ( M )$ be the class of predictable processes V, such that $( V ^ { 2 } \cdot \langle M \rangle ) _ { t } \tilde { \mathbf { \Gamma } } < \infty$ a.s. for all $t > 0$ . Assuming $M \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ and $V \in L ^ { 2 } ( M )$ , we may form an integral process V M belonging to $\mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { 0 , l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ . In the following statement, we assume that M, N, $M _ { n } \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ , and let $U , V , V _ { n }$ be predictable processes such that the appropriate integrals exist. 

Theorem 20.2 (L<sup>2</sup>-martingale integral, Courr`ege, Kunita & Watanabe) The elementary predictable integral extends a.s. uniquely to a bilinear map of any $M \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ and $V \in L ^ { 2 } ( M )$ into a process V $M \in \mathcal { M } _ { 0 , \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 } ,$ such that a.s. 

(i) $( V _ { n } ^ { 2 } \cdot \langle M _ { n } \rangle ) _ { t } \stackrel { P } {  } 0 \Rightarrow ( V _ { n } \cdot M _ { n } ) _ { t } ^ { \ast } \stackrel { P } {  } 0 , t > 0 ,$ 

(ii) $\langle V \cdot M , N \rangle = V \cdot \langle M , N \rangle , \ N \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 } ,$ 

(iii) $U \cdot ( V \cdot M ) = ( U V ) \cdot M ,$ 

(iv) $\Delta ( V \cdot M ) = V ( \Delta M )$ 

(v) $( V \cdot M ) ^ { \tau } = V \cdot M ^ { \tau } = ( V 1 _ { [ 0 , \tau ] } ) \cdot M$ for any optional time $\tau$ 

The integral V M is a.s. uniquely determined by (ii). 

The proof depends on an elementary approximation of predictable processes, similar to Lemma 18.23 in the continuous case. 

Lemma 20.3 (approximation) Let V be a predictable process with $| V | ^ { p } \in$ $L ( A )$ , where A is increasing and $p \geq 1$ . Then there exist some $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots \in \mathcal { E }$ with 

$$
\left(| V _ {n} - V | ^ {p} \cdot A\right) _ {t} \rightarrow 0 a. s., t > 0.
$$

Proof: It is enough to establish the approximation $( | V _ { n } - V | ^ { p } \cdot A ) _ { t } \stackrel { P } { \to } 0 .$ By Minkowski’s inequality we may then approximate in steps, and by dominated convergence we may first take V to be simple. Then each term can be approximated separately, and so we may next choose $V = 1 _ { B }$ for a predictable set B. Approximating separately on disjoint intervals, we may finally assume that $B \subset \Omega \times [ 0 , t ]$ for some $t > 0$ . The desired approximation then follows from Lemma 10.2 by a monotone-class argument. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 20.2: As in Theorem 18.11, we may construct the integral V M as the a.s. unique process in $\mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { 0 , l o c } } ^ { 2 }$ satisfying (ii). The mapping $( V , M ) \mapsto$ V M is clearly bilinear and extends the elementary predictable integral, just as in Lemma 18.10. Properties (iii) and (v) may be proved as in Propositions 18.14 and 18.15. The stated continuity follows immediately from (ii) and Proposition 20.1 (v). To prove the asserted uniqueness, it is then enough to apply Lemma 20.3 with $A = \langle M \rangle$ and $p = 2$ 

To prove (iv), we may apply Lemma 20.3 with 

$$
A _ {t} = \langle M \rangle_ {t} + \sum_ {s \leq t} (\Delta M _ {s}) ^ {2}, \quad t \geq 0,
$$

to ensure the existence of some processes $V _ { n } \in \mathcal { E }$ , such that a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{c} V _ {n} (\Delta M) \to V (\Delta M), \\ \left(V _ {n} \cdot M - V \cdot M\right) ^ {*} \to 0. \end{array}
$$

In particular, $\Delta ( V _ { n } \cdot M )  \Delta ( V \cdot M ) \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ , and (iv) follows from the corresponding relation for the elementary integrals $V _ { n } \cdot M$ , once we have shown that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { s < t } ( \Delta M _ { s } ) ^ { 2 } < \infty } \end{array}$ a.s. For the latter condition, we may take $M \in \mathcal { M } _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ and ≤<sub>define</sub> $t _ { n , k } = k t 2 ^ { - n }$ for $k \leq 2 ^ { n }$ . Then Fatou’s lemma yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \sum_ {s \leq t} (\Delta M _ {s}) ^ {2} \leq E \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \sum_ {k} \Big (M _ {t _ {n, k}} - M _ {t _ {n, k - 1}} \Big) ^ {2} \\ & \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E \sum_ {k} \Big (M _ {t _ {n, k}} - M _ {t _ {n, k - 1}} \Big) ^ {2} \\ & \quad = E M _ {t} ^ {2} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

A semi-martingale is defined as a right-continuous, adapted process $X ,$ admitting a decomposition $M + A$ into a local martingale M and a process A of locally finite variation starting at 0. If the variation of A is even locally integrable, we can write $X = ( M { + } \bar { A } { - } \hat { A } ) { + } \hat { A }$ , where $\hat { A }$ denotes the compensator of A. We may then choose A to be predictable, in which case the decomposition is a.s. unique by Propositions 18.2 and 10.16, and X is called a special semimartingale with canonical decomposition $M + A$ 

The L´evy processes constitute basic examples of semi-martingales, and we note that a L´evy process is a special semi-martingale if its L´evy measure ν satisfies $\textstyle \int ( x ^ { 2 } \wedge | x | ) \nu ( d x ) < \infty$ . From Theorem 10.5 we further see that any -<sub>local sub-martingale is a special semi-martingale.</sub> 

We may extend the stochastic integration to general semi-martingales. For the moment we consider only locally bounded integrands, which covers most applications of interest. 

Theorem 20.4 (semi-martingale integral, Dol´eans-Dade & Meyer) The $L ^ { 2 } .$ integral of Theorem 20.2 and the ordinary Lebesgue–Stieltjes integral extend a.s. uniquely to a bilinear map of any semi-martingale X and locally bounded, predictable process V into a semi-martingale V X. The integration map also satisfies 

(i) properties $( \mathrm { i i i } ) - ( \mathrm { v } )$ of Theorem 20.2, 

(ii) $V \geq | V _ { n } | \to 0 \Rightarrow ( V _ { n } \cdot X ) _ { t } ^ { * } \stackrel { P } { \to } 0 , t > 0 ,$ 

(iii) when X is a local martingale, so is $V \cdot X$ 

Our proof relies on a basic truncation: 

Lemma 20.5 (truncation, Dol´eans-Dade, Jacod & M´emin, Yan) Any local martingale M has a decomposition $M ^ { \prime } + M ^ { \prime \prime }$ into local martingales, such that 

(i) M has locally integrable variation, 

(ii) $\vert \Delta M ^ { \prime \prime } \vert \leq 1 \ a . s .$ 

Proof: Define 

$$
A _ {t} = \sum_ {s \leq t} (\Delta M _ {s}) 1 \left\{\left| \Delta M _ {s} \right| > \frac {1}{2} \right\}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

By optional sampling, A has locally integrable variation. Let $\hat { A }$ be the compensator of $A _ { i }$ , and put $M ^ { \prime } = A - \hat { A }$ and $M ^ { \prime \prime } = M - M ^ { \prime }$ . Then $M ^ { \prime }$ and $M ^ { \prime \prime }$ are again local martingales, and $M ^ { \prime }$ has locally integrable variation. Since also 

$$
\begin{array}{c} | \Delta M ^ {\prime \prime} | \leq \left| \Delta M - \Delta A \right| + | \Delta \hat {A} | \\ \leq \frac {1}{2} + | \Delta \hat {A} |, \end{array}
$$

it remains to show that $\begin{array} { r } { | \Delta \hat { \cal A } | \le { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \end{array}$ . Since the constructions of A and $\hat { A }$ commute with optional stopping, we may take M and $M ^ { \prime }$ to be uniformly integrable. Since $\hat { \boldsymbol A }$ is predictable, the times $\tau = n \wedge$ inf $\{ t ; | \Delta \hat { A } | > \frac { 1 } { 2 } \}$ are predictable by Theorem 10.14, and it sufices to show that $| \Delta \hat { A } _ { \tau } | \leq { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . Since clearly $E ( \Delta M _ { \tau } | \mathcal { F } _ { \tau - } ) = E ( \Delta M _ { \tau } ^ { \prime } | \mathcal { F } _ { \tau - } ) = 0$ a.s., Lemma 10.3 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \Delta \hat {A} _ {\tau} | = \left| E \Big (\Delta A _ {\tau} \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau -} \Big) \right| \\ \quad = \left| E \Big (\Delta M _ {\tau}; | \Delta M _ {\tau} | > \frac {1}{2} \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau -} \Big) \right| \\ \quad = \left| E \Big (\Delta M _ {\tau}; | \Delta M _ {\tau} | \leq \frac {1}{2} \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau -} \Big) \right| \leq \frac {1}{2}. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 20.4: By Lemma 20.5 we may write $X = M + A$ , where M is a local martingale with bounded jumps, hence a local $L ^ { 2 } .$ -martingale, and A has locally finite variation. For any locally bounded, predictable process $V ,$ we may then define $V \cdot X = V \cdot M + V \cdot A$ , where the first term is the integral in Theorem 20.2 and the second term is an ordinary Lebesgue–Stieltjes integral. \left(V _ {n} ^ {2} \cdot \langle M \rangle\right) _ {t} + \left(V _ {n} \cdot A\right) _ {t} ^ {*} \rightarrow 0,
$$

and so by Theorem 20.2 we have $( V _ { n } \cdot X ) _ { t } ^ { * } \stackrel { P } { \to } 0$ for all $t > 0$ 

For the uniqueness it sufices to prove that, if $M \ = \ A$ is a local $L ^ { 2 } \mathrm { _ - }$ martingale of locally finite variation, then $V \cdot M = V \cdot A$ a.s. for every locally bounded, predictable process $V ,$ where $V \cdot M$ is the integral in Theorem 20.2 and $V \cdot A$ is an ordinary Stieltjes integral. $$
\left\{\left(V _ {n} - V\right) ^ {2} \cdot \langle M \rangle \right\} ^ {*} + \left(\left| V _ {n} - V \right| \cdot A\right) ^ {*} \rightarrow 0.

Then for any $t > 0$ *

and the desired equality follows. 

(iii) By Lemma 20.5 and a suitable localization, we may assume that $V$ is bounded and X has integrable variation A. By Lemma 20.3 we may next choose some uniformly bounded processes $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots \in \mathcal { E }$ , such that $( | V _ { n } - V | \cdot A ) _ { t } \to 0$ a.s. for every $t \geq 0$ . For any semi-martingales $X , Y ,$ the left-continuous versions $( X _ { - } ) _ { t } = X _ { t - }$ and $( Y _ { - } ) _ { t } = Y _ { t - }$ are locally bounded and predictable, and hence may serve as integrands in general stochastic integrals. We may then $\mathrm { d e f i n e ^ { 2 } }$ the quadratic variation [X] and covariation $[ X , Y ]$ by the integration-by-parts formulas 

$$

$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} [ X, Y ] = X Y - X _ {0} Y _ {0} - X _ {-} \cdot Y - Y _ {-} \cdot X \\ = \frac {1}{4} \Big ([ X + Y ] - [ X - Y ] \Big), \end{array}\tag{1}

Theorem 20.6 (covariation) For any semi-martingales $X , Y$ , we have a.s. 

(i) $[ X , Y ]$ is symmetric, bilinear with $[ X , Y ] = [ X - X _ { 0 } , Y ]$ ,

(iii) $| \left[ X , Y \right] | \leq \int | d \left[ X , Y \right] | \leq [ X ] ^ { 1 / 2 } [ Y ] ^ { 1 / 2 } ,$

(v) $[ V \cdot X , Y ] = V \cdot [ X , Y ]$ for locally bounded, predictable $V ,$ 

(vi) $[ X ^ { \tau } , Y ] = [ X ^ { \tau } , Y ^ { \tau } ] = [ X , Y ] ^ { \tau }$ for any optional time $\tau ,$ 

(vii) $M , N \in \mathcal { M } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 2 } \Rightarrow [ M , N ]$ has compensator $\langle M , N \rangle$

Proof: (i) The symmetry and bilinearity of $[ X , Y ]$ are obvious from (1), and the last relation holds since $[ X , Y _ { 0 } ] = 0$ 

(ii) Proposition 18.17 extends with the same proof to general semi-martingales. In particular, $[ X ] _ { s } \leq [ X ] _ { t }$ a.s. for all $s \leq t .$ . By right-continuity, we can choose the exceptional null set to be independent of s and t, which means that [X] is a.s. non-decreasing.

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\Delta [ X, Y ] _ {t} = \Delta (X Y) _ {t} - \Delta (X _ {-} \cdot Y) _ {t} - \Delta (Y _ {-} \cdot X) _ {t}} \\ & {\qquad = X _ {t} Y _ {t} - X _ {t -} Y _ {t -} - X _ {t -} (\Delta Y _ {t}) - Y _ {t -} (\Delta X _ {t})} \\ & {\qquad = (\Delta X _ {t}) (\Delta Y _ {t}).} \end{array}
$$

Now let $V , V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots .$ be locally bounded and predictable with $V \geq | V _ { n } |  0$ . $$

A monotone-class argument yields an extension to arbitrary V. 

(vi) Use (v) with $V = 1 _ { [ 0 , \tau ] }$

We may now extend Itˆo’s formula in Theorem 18.18 to a substitution rule for general semi-martingales. By a semi-martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ we mean a process $X = ( X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { d } )$ composed by one-dimensional semi-martingales $X ^ { i }$ . Let $[ X ^ { i } , X ^ { j } ] ^ { c }$ denote the continuous components of the finite-variation processes $[ X ^ { i } , X ^ { j } ]$ , and write $\partial _ { i } f$ and $\partial _ { i j } ^ { 2 } f$ for the first and second order partial derivatives of $f _ { i }$ , respectively. 

Theorem 20.7 (substitution rule, Kunita & Watanabe) For any semi-martingale $X = ( X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { d } )$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and function $f \in C ^ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ , we have<sup>3</sup> 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (X _ {t}) = f (X _ {0}) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \partial_ {i} f (X _ {s -})   d X _ {s} ^ {i} + \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f (X _ {s -})   d [ X ^ {i}, X ^ {j} ] _ {s} ^ {c} \\ + \sum_ {s \leq t} \bigl \{\Delta f (X _ {s}) - \partial_ {i} f (X _ {s -}) (\Delta X _ {s} ^ {i}) \bigr \}. \end{array}\tag{2}
$$

Proof: Let $f \in C ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ satisfy (2), where the last term has locally finite variation. We show that (2) remains true for the functions $g _ { k } ( x ) = x _ { k } f ( x )$ ， $k = 1 , \dots , n$ . Then note that by (1), 

$$
g _ {k} (X) = g _ {k} \left(X _ {0}\right) + X _ {-} ^ {k} \cdot f (X) + f \left(X _ {-}\right) \cdot X ^ {k} + \left[ X ^ {k}, f (X) \right].\tag{3}
$$

Writing ${ \hat { f } } ( x , y ) = f ( x ) - f ( y ) - \partial _ { i } f ( y ) ( x _ { i } - y _ { i } )$ , we get by (2) and Theorem 20.2 (iii) 

$$
\begin{array}{c} X _ {-} ^ {k} \cdot f (X) = X _ {-} ^ {k}   \partial_ {i} f (X _ {-}) \cdot X ^ {i} + \frac {1}{2} X _ {-} ^ {k}   \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f (X _ {-}) \cdot [ X ^ {i}, X ^ {j} ] ^ {c} \\ + \sum_ {s} X _ {s -} ^ {k}   \hat {f} (X _ {s}, X _ {s -}). \end{array}\tag{4}
$$

Next we see from (ii), (iv), (v), and (viii) of Theorem 20.6 that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \left[ X ^ {k}, f (X) \right] & = \partial_ {i} f (X _ {-}) \cdot [ X ^ {k}, X ^ {i} ] + \sum_ {s} (\Delta X _ {s} ^ {k})   \hat {f} (X _ {s}, X _ {s -}) \\ & = \partial_ {i} f (X _ {-}) \cdot [ X ^ {k}, X ^ {i} ] ^ {c} + \sum_ {s} (\Delta X _ {s} ^ {k}) \{\Delta f (X _ {s}) \}. \end{array}\tag{5}
$$

Inserting (4) (5) into (3) and using the elementary formulas 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \partial_ {i} g _ {k} (x) = \delta_ {i k} f (x) + x _ {k} \partial_ {i} f (x), \\ \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} g _ {k} (x) = \delta_ {i k} \partial_ {j} f (x) + \delta_ {j k} \partial_ {i} f (x) + x _ {k} \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f (x), \\ \hat {g} _ {k} (x, y) = (x _ {k} - y _ {k}) \left\{f (x) - f (y) \right\} + y _ {k} \hat {f} (x, y), \end{array}
$$

followed by some simplification, we obtain the desired expression for $g _ { k } ( X )$ 

Formula (2) is trivially true for constant functions, and it extends by induction and linearity to arbitrary polynomials. By Weierstrass’ theorem, a general function $f \in C ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ can be approximated by polynomials, such that all derivatives up to second order tend to those of $f ,$ uniformly on every compact set. To prove (2) for $f ,$ , it is then enough to show that the right-hand side tends to zero in probability, as $f$ and its first and second order derivatives tend to zero, uniformly on compact sets. 

For the integrals in (2), this holds by the dominated convergence property in Theorem 20.4, and it remains to consider the last term. Writing $B _ { t } = \{ x \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } ;$ $| x | \leq X _ { t } ^ { * } \}$ and $\| g \| _ { B } = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { B } \left| g \right|$ , we get by Taylor’s formula in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \sum_ {s \leq t} \left| \hat {f} (X _ {s}, X _ {s -}) \right| & \lesssim & \sum_ {i, j} \left\| \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f \right\| _ {B _ {t}} \sum_ {s \leq t} | \Delta X _ {s} | ^ {2} \\ & \leq & \sum_ {i, j} \left\| \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f \right\| _ {B _ {t}} \sum_ {i} [ X ^ {i} ] _ {t} \to 0. \end{array}
$$

The same estimate shows that the last term has locally finite variation. □ 

To illustrate the use of the general substitution rule, we consider a partial extension of Lemma 19.22 and Proposition 32.2 to general semi-martingales. 

Theorem 20.8 (Dol´eans exponential) For a semi-martingale X with $X _ { 0 } = 0$ 2 the equation $Z = 1 + Z _ { - } \cdot X$ has the a.s. unique solution 

$$
Z _ {t} = \mathcal {E} (X) \equiv \exp \left(X _ {t} - \frac {1}{2} [ X ] _ {t} ^ {c}\right) \prod_ {s \leq t} \left(1 + \Delta X _ {s}\right) e ^ {- \Delta X _ {s}}, \quad t \geq 0.\tag{6}
$$

The infinite product in (6) is a.s. absolutely convergent, since $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { s < t } ( \Delta X _ { s } ) ^ { 2 } \le } \end{array}$ $[ X ] _ { t } < \infty$ . However, we may have $\Delta X _ { s } = - 1$ for some $s > 0$ , in which case $Z = 0$ for $t \geq s$ . The process $\mathcal { E } ( X )$ in (6) is called the Dol´eans exponential of X. For continuous X we get $\begin{array} { r } { \dot { \mathcal { E } } ( X ) = \exp ( X - \frac { 1 } { 2 } [ X ] ) } \end{array}$ , conforming with the notation of Lemma 19.22. For processes A of locally finite variation, formula (6) simplifies to 

$$
\mathcal {E} (A) = \exp (A _ {t} ^ {c}) \prod_ {s \leq t} (1 + \Delta A _ {s}), \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Proof of Theorem 20.8: To check that (6) is a solution, we may write $Z = e ^ { Y } V$ , where 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y _ {t} = X _ {t} - \frac {1}{2} \left[ X \right] _ {t} ^ {c}, \\ V _ {t} = \prod_ {s \leq t} \left(1 + \Delta X _ {s}\right) e ^ {- \Delta X _ {s}}. \end{array}
$$

Then Theorem 20.7 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} Z _ {t} - 1 = (Z _ {-} \cdot Y) _ {t} + (e ^ {Y _ {-}} \cdot V) _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} (Z _ {-} \cdot [ X ] ^ {c}) _ {t} \\ + \sum_ {s <   t} \Bigl (\Delta Z _ {s} - Z _ {s -} \Delta X _ {s} - e ^ {Y _ {s -}} \Delta V _ {s} \Bigr). \end{array}\tag{7}
$$

Now $\begin{array} { r } { e ^ { Y _ { - } } \cdot V = \sum e ^ { Y _ { - } } \Delta V } \end{array}$ since V is of pure jump type, and furthermore $\Delta Z =$ $Z _ { - } \Delta X$ . Hence, the right-hand side of (7) simplifies to $Z _ { - } \cdot X$ , as desired. 

To prove the uniqueness, let Z be an arbitrary solution, and put $V = Z e ^ { - Y }$ where $\begin{array} { r } { Y = X - \frac { 1 } { 2 } [ X ] ^ { c } } \end{array}$ as before. Then Theorem 20.7 gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V _ {t} - 1 = (e ^ {- Y _ {-}} \cdot Z) _ {t} - (V _ {-} \cdot Y) _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} (V _ {-} \cdot [ X ] ^ {c}) _ {t} - (e ^ {- Y _ {-}} \cdot [ X, Z ] ^ {c}) _ {t} \\ \qquad + \sum_ {s \leq t} \left(\Delta V _ {s} + V _ {s -} \Delta Y _ {s} - e ^ {- Y _ {s -}} \Delta Z _ {s}\right) \\ \qquad = (V _ {-} \cdot X) _ {t} - (V _ {-} \cdot X) _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} (V _ {-} \cdot [ X ] ^ {c}) _ {t} + \frac {1}{2} (V _ {-} \cdot [ X ] ^ {c}) _ {t} - (V _ {-} \cdot [ X ] ^ {c}) _ {t} \\ \qquad + \sum_ {s \leq t} \left(\Delta V _ {s} + V _ {s -} \Delta X _ {s} - V _ {s -} \Delta X _ {s}\right) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {s \leq t} \Delta V _ {s}. \end{array}
$$

Thus, V is purely discontinuous of locally finite variation. We may further compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Delta V _ {t} = Z _ {t}   e ^ {- Y _ {t}} - Z _ {t -}   e ^ {- Y _ {t -}} \\ \qquad = (Z _ {t -} + \Delta Z _ {t})   e ^ {- Y _ {t -} - \Delta Y _ {t}} - Z _ {t -}   e ^ {- Y _ {t -}} \\ \qquad = V _ {t -} \left\{(1 + \Delta X _ {t})   e ^ {- \Delta X _ {t}} - 1 \right\}, \end{array}
$$

which shows that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V _ {t} = 1 + (V _ {-} \cdot A) _ {t}, \\ A _ {t} = \sum_ {s \leq t} \Big \{(1 + \Delta X _ {t})   e ^ {- \Delta X _ {t}} - 1 \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

It remains to show that the homogeneous equation $V = V _ { - } \cdot A$ has the unique solution $V = 0$ . Then define $\begin{array} { r } { R _ { t } = \int _ { ( 0 , t ] } | d A | } \end{array}$ , and conclude from Theorem 20.7 and the convexity of the function $x \mapsto x ^ { n }$ that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} R _ {t} ^ {n} = n \left(R _ {-} ^ {n - 1} \cdot R\right) _ {t} + \sum_ {s \leq t} \Big (\Delta R _ {s} ^ {n} - n   R _ {s -} ^ {n - 1} \Delta R _ {s} \Big) \\ \geq n \left(R _ {-} ^ {n - 1} \cdot R\right) _ {t}. \end{array}\tag{8}
$$

We prove by induction that 

$$
V _ {t} ^ {*} \leq \frac {V _ {t} ^ {*} R _ {t} ^ {n}}{n !}, \quad t \geq 0, n \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+}.\tag{9}
$$

This is obvious for $n = 0$ , and if it holds for $n - 1$ , then by (8) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} V _ {t} ^ {*} = (V _ {-} \cdot A) _ {t} ^ {*} \\ \leq \frac {V _ {t} ^ {*} (R _ {-} ^ {n - 1} \cdot R) _ {t}}{(n - 1) !} \leq \frac {V _ {t} ^ {*} R _ {t} ^ {n}}{n !}, \end{array}
$$

as required. Since $R _ { t } ^ { n } / n ! \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } n \to \infty$ , relation (9) yields $V _ { t } ^ { * } = 0$ for all $t > 0$ ✷ 

The equation $Z = 1 + Z _ { - } \cdot X$ arises naturally in connection with changes of probability measure. Here we extend Theorem 19.20 to general local martingales. 

Theorem 20.9 (change of measure, van Schuppen & Wong) Consider some probability measures P, Q and a local martingale $Z \geq 0$ , such that $Q = Z _ { t } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ , and let M be a local P-martingale such that [M, Z] has locally integrable variation and P-compensator $\langle M , Z \rangle$ . Then we have the local Q-martingale 

$$
\tilde {M} = M - Z _ {-} ^ {- 1} \cdot \langle M, Z \rangle .
$$

A lemma is needed for the proof. 

Lemma 20.10 (integration by parts) For any semi-martingale X with $X _ { 0 } = 0$ and predictable process A of locally finite variation, we have 

$$
A X = A \cdot X + X _ {-} \cdot A a. s.
$$

Proof: We need to show that $\Delta A \cdot X = [ A , X ]$ a.s., which is equivalent to 

$$
\int_ {(0, t ]} (\Delta A _ {s}) d X _ {s} = \sum_ {s \leq t} (\Delta A _ {s}) (\Delta X _ {s}), \quad t \geq 0,
$$

by Theorem 20.6 (viii). Since the series on the right is absolutely convergent by Cauchy’s inequality, we may reduce, by dominated convergence on each side, to the case where A is constant apart from finitely many jumps. By Lemma 10.3 and Theorem 10.14, we may proceed to the case where A has at most one jump occurring at a predictable time $\tau .$ . Introducing an announcing sequence $\left( \tau _ { n } \right)$ and writing $Y = \Delta A \cdot X$ , we get by Theorem 20.2 (v) 

$$
Y _ {\tau_ {n} \wedge t} = 0 = Y _ {t} - Y _ {t \wedge \tau} \text {a.s.,} t \geq 0, n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Thus, even $Y$ is constant, apart from a possible jump at $\tau$ . Finally, Theorem 20.2 (iv) yields $\Delta Y _ { \tau } = ( \Delta A _ { \tau } ) ( \Delta X _ { \tau } )$ a.s. on $\{ \tau < \infty \}$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 20.9: Let $\tau _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t ; Z _ { t } < 1 / n \}$ for $n \in \mathsf N$ , and note that $\tau _ { n } \to \infty \mathrm { a . s . } Q$ by Lemma 19.18. Hence, $\tilde { M }$ is well defined under $Q ,$ , and it sufices as in Lemma 19.18 to show that $( \tilde { M } Z ) ^ { \tau _ { n } }$ is a local P -martingale for every $n .$ . Writing $\underline { m }$ for equality up to a local P -martingale, we see from Lemma 20.10 with $X = Z$ and $A = Z _ { - } ^ { - 1 } \cdot \langle M , Z \rangle$ that, on every interval $[ 0 , \tau _ { n } ]$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} M Z & \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} [ M, Z ] \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} \langle M, Z \rangle \\ & = Z _ {-} \cdot A \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} A Z. \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\tilde { M } Z = \left( M - A \right) Z \ \stackrel { m } { = } \ 0$ , as required. 

Using the last theorem, we may show that the class of semi-martingales is closed under absolutely continuous changes of probability measure. A special case of this result was previously obtained as part of Proposition 19.21. 

Corollary 20.11 (preservation law, Jacod) If $Q \ll P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t > 0$ then every P-semi-martingale is also a Q-semi-martingale. 

Proof: Let $Q = Z _ { t } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for all $t \geq 0$ . We need to show that every local P -martingale M is a semi-martingale under $Q .$ . By Lemma 20.5, we may then take $\Delta M$ to be bounded, so that $[ M ]$ is locally bounded. By Theorem 20.9 it sufices to show that $[ M , Z ]$ has locally integrable variation, and by Theorem 20.6 (iii) it is then enough to prove that $[ Z ] ^ { 1 / 2 }$ is locally integrable. By Theorem 20.6 (iv), 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} {[ Z ] _ {t} ^ {1 / 2} \leq [ Z ] _ {t -} ^ {1 / 2} + | \Delta Z _ {t} |} \\ & {\leq [ Z ] _ {t -} ^ {1 / 2} + Z _ {t -} ^ {*} + | Z _ {t} |, t \geq 0,} \end{array}
$$

and so the desired integrability follows by optional sampling. 

Next we extend the BDG inequalities of Theorem 18.7 to general local martingales. Such extensions are possible only for exponents $p \geq 1$ 

Theorem 20.12 (norm comparison, Burkholder, Davis, Gundy) For any local martingale M with $M _ { 0 } = 0$ , we have<sup>4</sup> 

$$
E M ^ {* p} \asymp E [ M ] _ {\infty} ^ {p / 2}, \quad p \geq 1.\tag{10}
$$

In particular, we conclude as in Corollary 18.8 that M is a uniformly integrable martingale whenever $E [ M ] _ { \infty } ^ { 1 / 2 } < \infty$ 

Proof for $p = 1 \ ( D a v i s )$ : Exploiting the symmetry of the argument, we write $M ^ { \flat }$ and $M ^ { \sharp }$ for the processes $M ^ { * }$ and $[ M ] ^ { 1 / 2 }$ , taken in either order. Putting $J = \Delta M$ , we define 

$$
A _ {t} = \sum_ {s \leq t} J _ {s} 1 \Bigl \{| J _ {s} | > 2 J _ {s -} ^ {*} \Bigr \}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Since $| \Delta A | \le 2 \Delta J ^ { * }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} | d A _ {s} | = \sum_ {s} | \Delta A _ {s} | \\ \leq 2 J ^ {*} \leq 4 M _ {\infty} ^ {\sharp}. \end{array}
$$

Writing $\hat { A }$ for the compensator of A and putting $D = A - { \hat { A } }$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E D _ {\infty} ^ {\flat} \vee E D _ {\infty} ^ {\sharp} & \leq & E \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} | d D _ {s} | \\ & \lesssim & E \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} | d A _ {s} | \lesssim E M _ {\infty} ^ {\sharp}. \end{array}\tag{11}
$$

To get a similar estimate for $N = M - D$ , we introduce the optional times

A semi-martingale $X = M + A$ is said to be purely discontinuous, if there exist some local martingales $M ^ { 1 } , M ^ { 2 } , . . .$ . of locally finite variation, such that $E ( M - M ^ { n } ) _ { t } ^ { * 2 } \to 0$ for every $t > 0$ . # Chapter 21

# Malliavin Calculus

Malliavin derivative, integration by parts, closure, chain rule, divergence operator, chaos representations, norms and domains, conditioning and adaptation, factorization, commutation, covariance, local properties, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semi-group and generator, elliptic operators, second order chain rule, extension and diferentiation of Itˆo integrals, Brownian functionals, existence of smooth density, absolute continuity 

The stochastic calculus of variations, known as Malliavin calculus, is an infinitedimensional calculus on Wiener space of amazing power and beauty. Here we develop only some basic results for the diferentiation and related operators, along with their representations and existence criteria in terms of multiple Wiener-Itˆo integrals. Already when developed that far, the theory is powerful enough to yield important new insights into various topics treated in earlier chapters. Unfortunately, we had to omit the more advanced aspects of the theory, including some fundamental Sobolev-type inequalities, with applications to solutions of SDEs, due to our obvious space limitations. 

In this chapter we give a fairly complete treatment of the three basic operators of the theory—the Malliavin derivative D, the adjoint divergence operator D∗, even known as the Skorohod integral, and the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator L. Highlights of the theory include the explicit representations of those operators and their domains in terms of multiple Wiener–Itˆo integrals, the remarkable identity $L = - D ^ { * } D$ , an expression of L as a second order diferential operator, and some surprising connections to ordinary Itˆo integrals. 

Most of the basic theory covered here relies on some standard functional analysis, combined with the theory of Wiener chaos expansions from Chapter 14. To ease the access for probabilists, I have replaced the sometimes peculiar traditional notation<sup>1</sup> by a more standard usage in probability theory, writing $\xi , \eta , \ldots$ . for random variables and X, Y, . . . for random processes, and similarly for some basic notions of functional analysis. I have also tried to clarify the customary confusion<sup>2</sup> between the OU-semi-group and generator in the sense of Feller processes, and the corresponding notions of Malliavin calculus. 

To begin our technical exposition of the theory, let ζ be an isonormal Gaussian process on a separable Hilbert space H, as defined in Chapter 14. Our first aim is to define a linear diferentiation operator D on a suitable class of ζ-measurable random variables. Our basic requirements are the relations $D ( \zeta h ) = h$ for all $h \in H$ , along with a suitable chain rule for diferentiation. 

For motivation, we consider first the class $s$ of smooth random variables of the form 

$$
\xi = f (\zeta \bar {h}) = f (\zeta h _ {1}, \dots , \zeta h _ {n}), \quad h _ {1}, \dots , h _ {n} \in H, n \in \mathsf {N},\tag{1}
$$

for functions $f \in C ^ { 1 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { n } )$ with bounded, first order partial derivatives $\partial _ { i } f$ where we write $\bar { h } \ : = \ : ( h _ { 1 } , \ldots , h _ { n } )$ . -<sub>To state the basic existence theorem, recall that a linear operator A between</sub> two Banach spaces S, T is said to be closed, if its graph is closed in $S \times T$ so that $x _ { n } \ \to \ x$ in S and $A x _ { n }  y$ in $T$ imply $x \in$ dom $A$ and $y = A x$ An operator $A : S  T$ is closable and hence admits a closed extension, if $x _ { n } \to 0$ in $S$ and $A x _ { n }  y$ in $T$ imply $y = 0$ . Let $L ^ { p } ( \zeta , H )$ be the space of ζ -measurable random elements $\eta$ in H with norm $E ( \| \eta \| ^ { p } ) ^ { 1 / p } < \infty$ , and write $\hat { C } ^ { 1 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { n } )$ for the class of diferentiable functions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ with bounded first derivatives. For convenience, we write ${ \boldsymbol { \xi } } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \dots , \xi _ { n } )$ 

Theorem 21.1 (Malliavin derivative) Let $\zeta$ be an isonormal Gaussian process on a separable Hilbert space H. Then for any $p \geq 1$ there exists a unique closed, linear operator $D _ { p } \colon L ^ { p } ( \zeta ) \to L ^ { p } ( \zeta , H )$ with domain $\mathcal { D } _ { p }$ containing $\zeta h$ for all $h \in H$ , such that for any $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } \in \mathcal { D } _ { p }$ 

(i) $D _ { p } ( \zeta h ) = h , h \in H ,$ 

$$
D _ {p} (f \circ \xi) = \sum_ {i \leq n} \partial_ {i} f (\xi) D _ {p} \xi_ {i}, \quad f \in \hat {C} ^ {1} (\mathsf {R} ^ {n}).
$$

Note that for $\xi \in S$ , the chain rule in (ii) reduces to $( 2 )$ . In general it is understood that $f ( \xi ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { p }$ . For the proof, we define $D$ on by means of (2). The resulting operator from $L ^ { p } ( \zeta )$ to $L ^ { p } ( \zeta , H )$ turns out to be closable, and we may define $D _ { p }$ as the associated closure. We need to show that $D$ is well-defined by (2) on the space $\boldsymbol { s }$ 

Lemma 21.2 (consistency) For any $\xi \in { \mathcal { S } }$ , the variable $D \xi$ in (2) is a.s. independent of the representation of ξ in (1). 

Proof: We need to show that, if also $\xi = g ( \zeta \bar { k } ) = g ( \zeta k _ { 1 } , \dots , \zeta k _ { m } )$ , then 

$$
\sum_ {i \leq n} \partial_ {i} f (\zeta \bar {h}) h _ {i} = \sum_ {j \leq m} \partial_ {i} g (\zeta \bar {k}) k _ {j}.
$$

Here we may choose the $k _ { j }$ to be ortho-normal with a linear span containing all $h _ { i }$ . Assuming $\begin{array} { r } { h _ { i } = \sum _ { j } T _ { i j } k _ { j } } \end{array}$ for a matrix $T .$ , we obtain 

$$
f \circ T (\zeta \bar {k}) = g (\zeta \bar {k}) \mathrm{a.s.}
$$

Since the variables $\zeta k _ { i }$ are i.i.d. $N ( 0 , 1 )$ and the functions $f \circ T$ and $g$ are contin uous, it follows that $f \circ T = g$ . By the elementary chain rule for diferentiation, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \sum_ {j} \partial_ {j} g (\zeta \bar {k}) k _ {j} & = \sum_ {j} \partial_ {j} (f \circ T) (\zeta \bar {k}) k _ {j} \\ & = \sum_ {i, j} \partial_ {i} (f \circ T) (\zeta \bar {k}) T _ {i j} k _ {j} \\ & = \sum_ {i} \partial_ {i} f (\zeta \bar {h}) h _ {i}. \end{array}
$$

We further need some elementary identities for the operator D on ${ \mathcal { S } } .$ 

Lemma 21.3 (integration by parts) Let $\xi , \eta$ be smooth functionals of $\zeta ,$ , and let $h \in H$ . Then 

(i) $E \langle D \xi , h \rangle = E \xi ( \zeta h ) .$ 

(ii) $E \xi \eta ( \zeta h ) = E \xi \langle D \eta , h \rangle + E \eta \langle D \xi , h \rangle .$ 

Proof: (i) We may choose $\xi$ as in (1) with ortho-normal $h _ { 1 } , \ldots , h _ { n } \in H$ and take $h = h _ { 1 }$ . Writing $\varphi$ for the standard normal density on $\mathsf { R } ,$ , and noting that $\varphi ^ { \prime } ( x ) = - x \varphi ( x )$ , we get by (2) and an elementary integration by parts 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \langle D \xi , h \rangle = \int \partial_ {1} f (x)   \varphi^ {\otimes n} (x)   d x \\ = \int f (x)   \varphi^ {\otimes n} (x)   x _ {1}   d x \\ = E   \xi (\zeta h). \end{array}
$$

(ii) Here we may represent $\xi , \eta$ as in (1) in terms of a common set of elements $h _ { 1 } , \ldots , h _ { n } \in H$ . Using (2) and the elementary product rule for diferentiation, we obtain $D ( \xi \eta ) = \xi D \eta + \eta D \xi$ a.s., and so by (i) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E   \xi \eta (\zeta h) = E \Big \langle D (\xi \eta), h \Big \rangle \\ \qquad = E \Big \langle \xi D \eta + \eta D \xi , h \Big \rangle \\ \qquad = E   \xi \langle D \eta , h \rangle + E   \eta \langle D \xi , h \rangle . \end{array}
$$

Next, we show that the operator D in (2) is closable. 

Lemma 21.4 (closure) For any $p \geq 1$ , the operator D on $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ is closable from $L ^ { p } ( \zeta )$ to $L ^ { p } ( \zeta , H )$ , and hence extends to a closed operator $( D _ { p } , D _ { p } )$ between those spaces. 

Proof: Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots \in S$ with $\xi _ { n } \to 0$ in $L ^ { p } ,$ , and such that $D \xi _ { n } \to \eta$ in $L ^ { p } ( \zeta , H )$ . To show that $\eta = 0$ a.s., fix any $h \in H$ , and let $\beta \in S$ be such that $\beta ( \zeta h )$ is bounded. Using Lemma 21.3 (ii), we get by dominated convergence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E   \beta \langle \eta , h \rangle \leftarrow E   \beta \langle D   \xi_ {n}, h \rangle \\ \qquad =   E \Big \{\beta   \xi_ {n} (\zeta h) - \xi_ {n} \langle D \beta , h \rangle \Big \} \to 0, \end{array}
$$

since $\beta ( \zeta h )$ and $\langle D \beta , h \rangle$ are bounded. Hence, $E \beta \langle \eta , h \rangle = 0$ , and so by approximation $\langle \eta , h \rangle = 0 ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . Since h was arbitrary, we obtain $\eta = 0 ~ \mathrm { a . s . }$ ✷ 

This extends D to a closed operator $D _ { p } \colon L ^ { p } ( \zeta ) \to L ^ { p } ( \zeta , H )$ , and we denote the associated domain by $\mathcal { D } _ { 1 , p }$ or simply $\mathcal { D } _ { p }$ . Since clearly $D _ { p } = D _ { q }$ on $\mathcal { D } _ { p } \cap \mathcal { D } _ { q }$ for any $p , q \geq 1$ , we may henceforth write simply $D _ { p } = D$ . It remains to show that the extended version of D satisfies the required chain rule. 

Lemma 21.5 (chain rule) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } \in { \mathcal { D } } _ { p }$ with $p \geq 1$ , and let $f \in C ^ { 1 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { n } )$ with bounded first derivatives. Then even $f ( \xi ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { p }$ , and

Lemma 21.14 (existence of $D ^ { * } )$ For an isonormal Gaussian process $\zeta$ on H and element $Y \in L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta , H )$ , these conditions are equivalent:

Now let $X \in { \mathcal { D } } ^ { * }$ . Comparing the above computation with Theorem 21.14 

(i), we get 

and so

An operator $T$ on a space of random variables $\xi$ is said to be local if $\xi = 0$ $\mathrm { a . s . }$ . on a set $A \in { \mathcal { F } }$ implies $T \xi = 0 \ \mathrm { a . e } .$ . on $A .$ . We show that $D ^ { * }$ is local on $\hat { \mathcal { D } } _ { 1 , 2 }$ and $D$ is local on $\mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 1 }$ . To make this more precise, we note that for any statement on $\Omega \times T$ , the qualification ‘a.e.’ is understood to be with respect to $P \otimes \mu$ 

Theorem 21.22 (local properties) For any set $A \subset \Omega$ in ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { z }$ , we have 

(i) $X \in \hat { \mathcal { D } } _ { 1 , 2 } , \ 1 _ { A } X = 0 \ a . e . \ \Rightarrow \ 1 _ { A } ( D ^ { * } X ) = 0 \ a . s . ,$

$$

$$

$$

As $n \to \infty$ , we note that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \eta \left(D ^ {*} X\right) f _ {n} (\| X \| ^ {2}) \to \eta \left(D ^ {*} X\right) 1 \{X = 0 \}, \\ f _ {n} (\| X \| ^ {2}) \left\langle X, D   \eta \right\rangle \to 0, \\ \eta   f _ {n} ^ {\prime} (\| X \| ^ {2}) \left\langle D X \cdot X,   X \right\rangle \to 0, \end{array}
$$

Since $S _ { c }$ is dense in $L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ , this implies $D ^ { * } X = 0 { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . on $A \subset \{ X = 0 \}$ , as required. 

To justify (7), we note that

$$

$$

$$

where both bounds are integrable. Hence, (7) follows from (6) by dominated convergence. 

(ii) It is enough to prove the statement for bounded variables $\xi \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 1 }$ since it will then follow for general $\xi$ by the chain rule for D, applied to the variable arctan $\xi$ . For $f$ and $f _ { n }$ as in (i), define $\begin{array} { r } { g _ { n } ( t ) = \int _ { - \infty } ^ { t } f _ { n } ( r ) d r } \end{array}$ , and note that $\| g _ { n } \| _ { \infty } \leq n ^ { - 1 } \| f \| _ { 1 }$ , and also $D g _ { n } ( \xi ) = f _ { n } ( \xi ) D \xi$ -<sub>by the chain rule.</sub> 

Now let $Y \in S _ { b } ( H )$ be arbitrary, and note that the $D / D ^ { * }$ -duality remains valid in the form $E ( \eta D ^ { * } Y ) = E \langle D \eta , Y \rangle$ , for any bounded variables $\eta \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 1 }$ Using the chain rule for D, the extended $D / D ^ { * } { \mathrm { - d u a l i t y } } ,$ and some easy estimates, we obtain

Since the operators $D$ and $D ^ { * }$ are local, we may extend their domains as follows. Say that a random variable $\xi$ lies locally in $\mathcal { D } _ { 1 , p }$ and write $\xi \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 , p } ;$ , if there exist some measurable sets $A _ { n } \uparrow \Omega$ with associated random variables $\xi _ { n } \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , p } ;$ , such that $\xi = \xi _ { n }$ on $A _ { n }$ . The definitions of $\mathcal { D } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { m , p }$ and $\hat { \mathcal { D } } _ { \mathrm { l o c } } ^ { 1 , 2 }$ are similar. 

To motivate our introduction of the third basic operator of the subject, let X be a standard Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process on H, defined as a centered Gaussian process on $\mathsf { R } \times H$ with covariance function 

$$
E (X _ {s} h) (X _ {t} k) = e ^ {- | t - s |} \langle h, k \rangle , \quad h, k \in H, s, t \in \mathsf {R}.
$$

This makes X a stationary Markov process on H, such that $X _ { t }$ is isonormal Gaussian on H for every $t \in { \mathsf { R } }$ , whereas $X _ { t } h$ is a real OU-process in t for each $h \in H$ with $\| h \| = 1$ . For the construction of X, fix any ONB $h _ { 1 } , h _ { 2 } , \ldots \in H$ , let the $X _ { t } h _ { j }$ be independent OU-processes in R, and extend to H by linearity and continui $\mathrm { 5 y ^ { 6 } }$ . 

For the present purposes, we may put $X _ { 0 } = \zeta _ { }$ , and define the associated transition operators $T _ { t }$ directly on $L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ by 

$$
T _ {t} (f \circ \zeta) = E \Big (f \circ X _ {t}   \big |   \zeta \Big), \quad t \geq 0,
$$

for measurable functions $f$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { H }$ with $f ( \zeta ) \in L ^ { 2 }$ . In fact, any $\xi \in L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ has such a representation by Lemma 1.14 or Theorem 14.26, and since $X _ { t } \overset { d } { = } \zeta$ , the right-hand side is a.s. independent of the choice of $f .$ 

To identify the operators $T _ { t }$ , we note that the Hermite polynomials $p _ { n }$ , normalized as in Theorem 14.25, satisfy the identity 

$$
\exp \left(x t - \frac {1}{2} t ^ {2}\right) = \sum_ {n \geq 0} p _ {n} (x) \frac {t ^ {n}}{n !}, \quad x, t \in \mathsf {R}.\tag{8}
$$

From the moving average representation in Chapter 14, we further note that for any $t \geq 0$ , 

$$
X _ {t} = e ^ {- t} \zeta + \sqrt {1 - e ^ {- 2 t}} \zeta_ {t},\tag{9}
$$

where $\zeta \ { \overset { d } { = } } \zeta _ { t } \bot \downarrow \zeta$ 

Theorem 21.23 (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semi-group) For a standard $O U - p r o -$ cess X on H with $X _ { 0 } = \zeta$ , the transition operators $T _ { t }$ on $L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ are given by

Proof: By Proposition 4.2 and Corollary 6.5, it is enough to consider random variables of the form $\xi = f ( \zeta h )$ with $\| h \| = 1$ . By the uniqueness theorem for moment-generating functions, we may take $f ( x ) = \textstyle \exp ( r x - { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } r ^ { 2 } )$ for an arbitrary $r \in { \mathsf { R } }$ . Using the representation (9) with $a = e ^ { - t }$ and $b = { \sqrt { 1 - e ^ { - 2 t } } }$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (X _ {t}) = \exp \Big (r X _ {t} h - \frac {1}{2} r ^ {2} \Big) \\ \qquad = \exp \Big (r a \zeta h + r b \zeta_ {t} - \frac {1}{2} r ^ {2} \Big) \\ \qquad = \exp \Big (r a \zeta h - \frac {1}{2} r ^ {2} a ^ {2} \Big) \exp \Big (r b \zeta_ {t} h - \frac {1}{2} r ^ {2} b ^ {2} \Big). \end{array}
$$

In particular, we get for $t = 0$ by (8) and Theorem 14.25 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \xi = f (\zeta) = \exp \Big (r   \zeta h - \frac {1}{2}   r ^ {2} \Big) \\ = \sum_ {n \geq 0} p _ {n} (\zeta h)   \frac {r ^ {n}}{n !} \\ = \sum_ {n \geq 0} \zeta^ {n} h ^ {\otimes h}   \frac {r ^ {n}}{n !}, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $J _ { n } \xi = \zeta ^ { n } h ^ { \otimes n } r ^ { n } / n !$ . For general t, we note that $\zeta _ { t } h$ is $N ( 0 , 1 )$ with $\zeta _ { t } \perp \perp \zeta .$ and conclude by the same calculation that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \Big \{f (X _ {t})   \Big |   \zeta \Big \} = \exp \Big (r a   \zeta h - \frac {1}{2}   r ^ {2} a ^ {2} \Big) \\ & \qquad = \sum_ {n \geq 0} \zeta^ {n} h ^ {\otimes h}   \frac {(r a) ^ {n}}{n !} \\ & \qquad = \sum_ {n \geq 0} e ^ {- n t} J _ {n} \xi . \end{array}
$$

The $T _ { t }$ clearly form a contraction semi-group on $L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ , and we proceed to determine the associated generator, in the sense of convergence in $L ^ { 2 }$ 

Theorem 21.24 (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck generator) For a standard OU-process $X$ on H with $X _ { 0 } = \zeta$ , the generator $L$ and its domain ${ \mathcal { L } } \subset L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ are given by 

(i) $\begin{array} { r } { \xi \in \mathcal { L } \Leftrightarrow \sum n ^ { 2 } \| J _ { n } \xi \| ^ { 2 } < \infty . } \end{array}$ 

(ii) $L \xi = \sum _ { n > 0 } L ( J _ { n } \xi ) = - \sum _ { n > 0 } n J _ { n } \xi i n L ^ { 2 } ,$ 

(iii) $\| L \xi \| ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { n > 0 } \| L ( J _ { n } \xi ) \| ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { n > 0 } n ^ { 2 } \| J _ { n } \xi \| ^ { 2 } .$

First let $\xi \in { \mathcal { L } }$ . Since $J _ { n }$ and $T _ { t }$ commute on $L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ and $n \geq t ^ { - 1 } ( 1 - e ^ { - n t } ) \to n$ as $t  0$ for fixed n, we get by dominated convergence as $t  0$
