and so $\xi \in \mathcal G$ with $G \xi = L \xi$ <sub>, proving that</sub> $G = L$ on ${ \mathcal { L } } \subset { \mathcal { G } }$ 

To show that $\mathcal G \subset \mathcal L$ , let $\xi \in \mathcal G$ be arbitrary. Since the $J _ { n }$ act continuously on $L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ , we get as before 

$$
J _ {n} (G \xi) \leftarrow t ^ {- 1} \Bigl \{T _ {t} (J _ {n} \xi) - J _ {n} \xi \Bigr \} \rightarrow - n J _ {n} \xi ,

We may now establish a remarkable relationship between the three basic operators of Malliavin calculus: 

Theorem 21.25 (operator relation) The operators D, D∗, L are related by 

(i) $\xi \in \mathcal { L } \ \Leftrightarrow \ \xi \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 2 } , \ D \xi \in \mathcal { D } ^ { * }$

It remains to show that $\mathcal { L } \subset \mathop { \mathrm { d o m } } ( D ^ { * } D )$ , so let $\xi \in { \mathcal { L } }$ be arbitrary. Then Theorem 21.24 yields 

$$
\sum_ {n} n \left\| J _ {n} \xi \right\| ^ {2} \leq \sum_ {n} n ^ {2} \left\| J _ {n} \xi \right\| ^ {2} <   \infty ,

We proceed to show that L behaves like a second order diferential operator, when acting on smooth random variables. For comparison, recall from Chapter 32 that an OU-process in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ solves the SDE $d X _ { t } = { \sqrt { 2 } } d B _ { t } - X _ { t } d t$ , and hence that its generator A agrees formally with the expression for L below. See also Theorem 17.24 for an equivalent formula in the context of general Feller difusions. 

Theorem 21.26 (L as elliptic operator) For smooth random variables $\xi =$ $f ( \zeta { \bar { h } } )$ with $\bar { h } = ( h _ { 1 } , \ldots , h _ { n } ) \in H ^ { n }$ , we have

$$
D ^ {*} (D \xi) = \sum_ {i \leq n} \partial_ {i} f (\zeta \bar {h}) \zeta h _ {i} - \sum_ {i, j \leq n} \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f (\zeta \bar {h}) \langle h _ {i}, h _ {j} \rangle ,

We may extend the last result to a chain rule for the OU-operator $L ,$ which may be regarded as a second order counterpart of the first order chain rule (3) for D. 

Corollary 21.27 (second order chain rule) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } \in \mathcal { D } _ { 2 , 4 }$ , and let $f \in C ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { n } )$ with bounded first and second order partial derivatives. We now come to the remarkable fact that the divergence operator $D ^ { * }$ here introduced as the adjoint of the diferentiation operator $D ,$ is a nonanticipating extension of the Itˆo integral of stochastic calculus. This is why it is often regarded as an integral and may even be denoted by an integral sign. 

Here we take $\zeta$ to be an isonormal Gaussian process on $H = L ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \lambda )$ generating a Brownian motion B with $B _ { t } = \zeta [ 0 , t ]$ a.s. for all $t \geq 0$ . For such a process $X$ , we know from -<sub>Chapter 18 that the Itˆo integral</sub> $X _ { t } d B _ { t }$ exists. 

Theorem 21.28 $\ d ( D ^ { * }$ as extended Itˆo integral) Let $\zeta$ be an isonormal process on $L ^ { 2 } ( \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \lambda )$ , generating a Brownian motion B with induced filtration $\mathcal { F }$ . Then

We proceed with a striking diferentiation property of the Itˆo integral. 

Theorem 21.29 (derivative of Itˆo integral, Pardoux & Peng) Let $\zeta$ be an isonormal Gaussian process on $L ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , 1 ] , \lambda )$ generating a Brownian motion $B _ { . }$ and consider a B-adapted process $X \in L ^ { 2 } ( P \otimes \lambda )$ . Then

(ii) X B <sup>ˆ</sup><sub>1,2</sub>, and (X B)<sub>t 1,2</sub>, t [0, 1], 

(iii) $D _ { s } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } X _ { r } d B _ { r } = X _ { s } 1 _ { s \leq t } + \int _ { s } ^ { t } ( D _ { s } X _ { r } ) d B _ { r } a . e . , s , t \in [ 0 , 1 ] .$

Equation (iii) remains true for $s > t ,$ , since all three terms then vanish by Corollary 21.13 (i). 

It remains to prove the implication $\cdot \Leftarrow$ in (i), so assume that $( \boldsymbol { X } \cdot \boldsymbol { B } ) _ { 1 } \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 2 }$ Let $X _ { t } ^ { n }$ denote the projection of $X _ { t }$ onto $\mathcal { P } _ { n } = \mathcal { H } _ { 0 } \oplus \dots \oplus \mathcal { H } _ { n }$ . Then $( X ^ { n } \cdot B ) _ { t }$ is the projection of $( X \cdot ) _ { t }$ onto $\mathcal { P } _ { n + 1 }$ , and so $( X ^ { n } \cdot B ) _ { 1 } \to ( X \cdot B ) _ { 1 }$ in the topology of $\mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 2 }$ . Applying (iii) to each process $X ^ { n }$ and using the martingale property of the Itˆo integral, we obtain

\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {1} E \Big \{D _ {s} (X ^ {n} \cdot B) _ {1} \Big \} ^ {2} d s = \int_ {0} ^ {1} E | X _ {s} ^ {n} | ^ {2} d s + \int_ {0} ^ {1} d s \int_ {0} ^ {s} E (D _ {r} X _ {s} ^ {n}) ^ {2} d r \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \int_ {0} ^ {1} d s \int_ {0} ^ {s} E (D _ {r} X _ {s} ^ {n}) ^ {2} d r \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = E \big \| D X ^ {n} \big \| _ {\lambda^ {2}} ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

By a similar estimate for $D X ^ { m } - D X ^ { n }$ we conclude that $D X ^ { n }$ converges in $L ^ { \dot { 2 } } ( \lambda ^ { 2 } )$ , and so $X \in \hat { \mathcal { D } } _ { 1 , 2 }$ by the closure of $D .$ . (Alternatively, we may use a version of Lemma $2 1 . 6 . )$ □ 

Next recall from Lemma 19.12 that any B-measurable random variable $\xi \in L ^ { 2 }$ with $E \xi = 0$ can be written as an Itˆo integral $\textstyle { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } X _ { t } d B _ { t } }$ , for an a.e. unique process $X \in L _ { \mathcal { F } } ^ { 2 } ( P \otimes \lambda )$ -<sub>. We may now give an explicit formula for the</sub> integrand X. 

Theorem 21.30 (Brownian functionals, Clark, Ocone) Let B be a Brownian motion on [0, 1] with induced filtration $\mathcal { F }$ . Then for any $\xi \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 2 }$ 

$$
\xi = E \xi + \int_ {0} ^ {1} E \left(D _ {t} \xi \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right) d B _ {t},
$$

$$
\text {(ii)} \quad E | \xi | ^ {p} \lesssim | E \xi | ^ {p} + \int_ {0} ^ {1} E | D _ {t} \xi | ^ {p} d t, \quad p \geq 2.
$$

For the stated formula to make sense, we need to choose a progressively measurable version of the integrand. Such an optional projection of $D _ { t } \xi$ is easily constructed by a suitable approximation. 

Proof: (i) Assuming $\xi = \textstyle \sum _ { n } \zeta ^ { n } f _ { n }$ , we get by Theorem 21.7 and Corollary 14.28 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \Big (D _ {t} \xi   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {t} \Big) = \sum_ {n > 0} n   E \Big \{\zeta^ {n - 1} f _ {n} (\cdot , t)   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {t} \Big \} \\ = \sum_ {n > 0} n   \zeta^ {n - 1} \Big \{1 _ {[ 0, t ] ^ {n - 1}} f _ {n} (\cdot , t) \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

The left-hand side is further adapted and square integrable, hence belongs to $\mathcal { D } ^ { * }$ by Theorem 21.28 (i). Applying $D ^ { * }$ to the last sum and using Theorems 21.15 and 21.28 (ii), we conclude that 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} E \left(D _ {t} \xi \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right) d B _ {t} = \sum_ {n > 0} \zeta^ {n} f _ {n} = \xi - E \xi ,
$$

where the earlier factor n is canceled out by the symmetrization. 

(ii) Using Jensen’s inequality (three times), along with Fubini’s theorem and the Burkholder inequality in Theorem 18.7, we get from (i) 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E | \xi | ^ {p} - | E \xi | ^ {p} & \lesssim & E \Big | \int_ {0} ^ {1} E \big (D _ {t} \xi   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big)   d B _ {t} \Big | ^ {p} \\ & \lesssim & E \Big | \int_ {0} ^ {1} \big \{E \big (D _ {t} \xi   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big) \big \} ^ {2} d t \Big | ^ {p / 2} \\ & \leq & E \int_ {0} ^ {1} \big | E \big (D _ {t} \xi   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big) \big | ^ {p}   d t \\ & \leq & \int_ {0} ^ {1} E | D _ {t} \xi | ^ {p}   d t. \end{array}
$$

The Malliavin calculus can often be used to show the existence and possible regularity of a density. The following simple result illustrates the idea. 

Theorem 21.31 (functionals with smooth density) For an isonormal Gaussian process $\zeta$ on H, let $\xi \in L ^ { 2 } ( \zeta )$ with 

$$
\xi \in \mathcal {D} _ {1, 2}, \quad D \xi \in \mathcal {D} ^ {*}, \quad \| D \xi \| > 0.
$$

Then $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { L } ( \boldsymbol { \xi } ) \ll \lambda } \end{array}$ with the bounded, continuous density<sup>8</sup> 

$$
g (x) = E \left\{D ^ {*} \left(\| D \xi \| ^ {- 2} D \xi\right); \xi > x \right\}, \quad x \in \mathsf {R}.
$$

Proof: Let $f \in { \hat { C } } ( \mathsf { R } )$ be arbitrary, and put $\textstyle F ( x ) = \int _ { - \infty } ^ { x } f ( y ) d y$ . Then the chain rule in Theorem 21.1 yields $F ( \xi ) \in { \mathcal { D } } _ { 1 , 2 }$ and 

$$
\left\langle D (F \circ \xi), D \xi \right\rangle = f (\xi) \| D \xi \| ^ {2}.
$$

Using the $D / D ^ { * }$ -duality and Fubini’s theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E f (\xi) = E \left\langle D (F \circ \xi), \| D \xi \| ^ {- 2} D \xi \right\rangle \\ \quad = E   D ^ {*} \Big (\| D \xi \| ^ {- 2} D \xi \Big) F (\xi) \\ \quad = E   D ^ {*} \Big (\| D \xi \| ^ {- 2} D \xi \Big) \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\xi} f (x)   d x \\ \quad = \int E \Big \{D ^ {*} \Big (\| D \xi \| ^ {- 2} D \xi \Big);   \xi > x \Big \} f (x)   d x. \end{array}
$$

Since $f$ was arbitrary, this gives the asserted density. 

Weaker conditions will often ensure the mere absolute continuity, though we may then be unable to give an explicit formula for the density. 

Theorem 21.32 (absolute continuity) For an isonormal Gaussian process $\zeta$ on H, let $\xi$ be a ζ-measurable random variable. Then 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{c} \xi \in \mathcal {D} _ {\text {loc}} ^ {1, 1} \\ D   \xi \neq 0 a. s. \end{array} \right\} \Rightarrow \mathcal {L} (\xi) \ll \lambda .
$$

Proof: By localization, we may let $\xi \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 1 }$ , and we may further assume that $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( \boldsymbol { \xi } )$ is supported by $[ - 1 , 1 ]$ . We need to show that if $A \in \mathcal { B } _ { [ - 1 , 1 ] }$ with $\lambda A = 0$ , then $\mu A = 0$ . As in Lemma 1.37, we may then choose some smooth functions $f _ { n } \colon [ - 1 , 1 ] \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ with bounded derivatives, such that $f _ { n }  1 _ { A }$ a.e. $\lambda + \mu .$ . Writing $\textstyle F _ { n } ( x ) = \int _ { - 1 } ^ { x } f _ { n } ( y ) d y$ , we see by dominated convergence that $F _ { n } ( x ) \to 0$ for all $x .$ -<sub>. Since the</sub> $F _ { n }$ are again smooth with bounded derivatives, the chain rule in Theorem 21.1 yields $F _ { n } ( \xi ) \in \mathcal { D } _ { 1 , 1 }$ with 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} D (F _ {n} \circ \xi) & = f _ {n} (\xi)   D \xi \\ & \to 1 \{\xi \in A \}   D   \xi \text { a.s. } \end{array}
$$

Since also $F _ { n } ( \xi ) \to 0$ , the closure property of $D$ gives $1 \{ \xi \in A \} D \xi = 0 \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ and since $D \xi \neq 0$ a.s. by hypothesis, we obtain $\mu A = P \{ \xi \in A \} = 0$ ✷

## VII. Convergence and Approximation

Here our primary objective is to derive functional versions of the major limit theorems of probability theory, through the development of general embedding and compactness arguments. The intuitive Skorohod embedding in Chapter 22 leads easily to functional versions of the central limit theorem and the law of the iterated logarithm, and allows extensions to renewal and empirical processes, as well as to martingales with small jumps. Though the compactness approach in Chapter 23 is more subtle, as it depends on the development of compactness criteria in the underlying function or measure spaces, it has a much wider scope, as it applies even to processes with jumps and to random sets and measures. In Chapter 24, we develop some powerful large deviation principles, providing precise exponential bounds for tail probabilities in a great variety of contexts. The first two chapters contain essential core material, whereas the last chapter is more advanced and might be postponed. 

22. Skorohod embedding and functional convergence. Here the key step is to express a centered random variable as the value of a Brownian motion B at a suitably bounded optional time. Iterating the construction yields an embedding of an entire random walk X into B. By estimating the associated approximation error, we can derive a variety of weak or strong limit theorems for X from the corresponding results for B, leading in particular to functional versions of the central limit theorem and the law of the iterated logarithm, with extensions to renewal and empirical processes. A similar embedding applies to martingales with uniformly small jumps. 

23. Convergence in distribution. Here we develop the compactness approach to convergence in distribution in function and measure spaces. The key result is Prohorov’s theorem, which shows how the required relative compactness is equivalent to tightness, under suitable conditions on the underlying space. The usefulness of the theory relies on our ability to develop eficient tightness criteria. Here we consider in particular the spaces $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , S }$ of functions in S with only jump discontinuities, and the space $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ of locally finite measures on S, leading to a wealth of useful convergence criteria. 

24. Large deviations. The large deviation principles (LDPs) developed in this chapter can be regarded as refinements of the weak law of large numbers in a variety of contexts. The theory involves some general extension principles, leading to an extremely versatile and powerful body of methods and results, covering a wide range of applications. In particular, we include Schilder’s LDP for Brownian motion, Sanov’s LDP for empirical distributions, the Freidlin– Wentzel LDP for stochastic dynamical systems, and Strassen’s functional law of the iterated logarithm. 

Chapter 22 

# Skorohod Embedding and Functional Convergence

Embedding of random walk, Brownian martingales, moment identities and estimates, rate of continuity, approximations of random walk, functional central limit theorem, laws of the iterated logarithm, arcsine laws, approximation of renewal processes, empirical distribution functions, embedding and approximation of martingales, martingales with small jumps, time-scale comparison 

In Chapter 6 we used analytic methods to derive criteria for sums of independent random variables to be approximately Gaussian. Though this may remain the easiest approach to the classical limit theorems, such results are best understood when viewed in the context of some general approximation results for random processes. The aim of this chapter is to develop the purely probabilistic technique of Skorohod embedding to derive such functional limit theorems. 

The scope of applications of the present method extends far beyond the classical limit theorems. This is because some of the most important functionals of a random process, such as the supremum up to a fixed time or the time at which the maximum occurs, can not be expressed in terms of the values at finitely many times. The powerful new technique allows us to extend some basic result for Brownian motion from Chapter 14, including the acsine laws and the law of the iterated logarithm, to random walks and related sequences. Indeed, the technique of Skorohod embedding extends even to a wide class of martingales with small jumps. 

From the statements for random walks, similar results can be deduced for various related processes. In particular, we prove a functional central limit theorem and a law of the iterated logarithm for renewal processes, and show how suitably normalized versions of the empirical distribution functions, based on a sample of i.i.d. random variables, can be approximated by a Brownian bridge. 

In the simplest setting, we may consider a random walk $( X _ { n } )$ , based on some i.i.d. random variables $\xi _ { k }$ with mean 0 and variance 1. Here we can prove the existence of a Brownian motion B and some optional times $\tau _ { 1 } \leq \tau _ { 2 } \leq \cdots$ such that $X _ { n } = B _ { \tau _ { n } }$ a.s. for every n. For applications, it is essential to choose the $\tau _ { n }$ such that the diferences $\Delta \tau _ { n }$ become i.i.d. with finite mean. The path of the step process $X _ { [ t ] }$ will then be close to that of B, and many results for Brownian motion carry over, at least approximately, to the random walk. 

The present account depends in many ways on material from previous chapters. Thus, we rely on the basic theory of Brownian motion, as set forth in Chapter 14. We also make frequent use of ideas and results from Chapter 9 on martingales and optional times. Finally, occasional references are made to Chapter 5 for empirical distributions, to Chapter $8$ for the transfer theorem, to Chapter 12 for random walks and renewal processes, and to Chapter 15 for Poisson processes. 

More general approximations and functional limit theorems will be obtained by diferent methods in Chapters 23–24 and 30. The present approximations of martingales with small jumps are closely related to the time-change results for continuous local martingales in Chapter 19. 

To clarify the basic ideas, we begin with a detailed discussion of the classical Skorohod embedding of random walks. Say that a random variable $\xi$ or its distribution is centered if $E \xi = 0$ 

Theorem 22.1 (embedding of random walk, Skorohod) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be i.i.d., centered random variables, and put $X _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ . $$
(B _ {\tau_ {n}}) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (X _ {n}), \qquad E \Delta \tau_ {n} = E \xi_ {1} ^ {2}, \qquad E (\Delta \tau_ {n}) ^ {2} \leq 4 E \xi_ {1} ^ {4}.

Here the moment conditions are crucial, since without them the statement would be trivially true and totally useless. In fact, we could then take $B \bot \bot ( \xi _ { n } )$ and choose recursively $\tau _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } \Big \{ t \geq \tau _ { n - 1 } ; B _ { t } = X _ { n } \Big \}$

Then each $X _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ is a.s. bounded with finitely many upcrossings of any non-degenerate interval, and so the process $\tilde { X } _ { n } ( t ) \stackrel { \cdot } { = } X _ { n } ^ { \prime } ( t { + } )$ exists a.s. with paths in $D _ { [ 0 , 1 ] }$ . From the right continuity of paths, it is also clear that $( { \tilde { X } } _ { n } , Y ) \stackrel { d } { = } ( X _ { n } , Y _ { n } )$ on [0, 1] for every n. 

To obtain the desired convergence, we note that 

$$
\left\| \tilde {X} _ {n} - Y \right\| \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left\| X _ {n} - Y _ {n} \right\| \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} 0,
$$

and hence $\textstyle f ( X _ { n } ) \triangleq f ( { \tilde { X } } _ { n } ) \to f ( Y )$ , as in Lemma 5.3. 

In particular, we may recover the central limit theorem in Proposition 6.10 by taking $f ( x ) = x _ { 1 }$ in Theorem 22.9. We may also obtain results that go beyond the classical theory, such as by choosing $f ( x ) = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { t } \left| x _ { t } \right|$ . For a less ob vious application, we may extend the arcsine laws of Theorem 14.16 to suitable random walks. Recall that a random variable $\xi$ is said to be arcsine distributed if $\xi \stackrel { d } { = } \sin ^ { 2 } \alpha$ , where α is $U ( 0 , 2 \pi )$ 

Theorem 22.11 (arcsine laws, Erd¨os & Kac, Sparre-Andersen) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be i.i.d., non-degenerate random variables, and put $X _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ . Define for $n \in { \mathbb N }$ 

$$
\tau_ {n} ^ {1} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k <   n} 1 \{X _ {k} > 0 \},
$$

$$
\tau_ {n} ^ {2} = n ^ {- 1} \min \Bigl \{k \geq 0; X _ {k} = \max _ {i <   n} X _ {i} \Bigr \},
$$

$$
\tau_ {n} ^ {3} = n ^ {- 1} \max \Bigl \{k \leq n; X _ {k} X _ {n} \leq 0 \Bigr \},
$$

and let $\tau$ be arcsine distributed. Then 

(i) $\tau _ { n } ^ { k } \xrightarrow [ ] { d } \tau$ for k = 1, 2, 3 when $E \xi _ { i } = 0$ and $E \xi _ { i } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , 

(ii) $\tau _ { n } ^ { k } \xrightarrow [ ] { d } \tau$ for $k = 1$ , 2 when $\mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { i } )$ is symmetric. 

For the proof, we introduce on $D _ { [ 0 , 1 ] }$ the functionals 

$$
f _ {1} (x) = \lambda \left\{t \in [ 0, 1 ]; x _ {t} > 0 \right\},
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

The following result is elementary. 

Lemma 22.12 (continuity of functionals) The functionals $f _ { i }$ are measurable, and 

$f _ { 1 }$ is continuous at $x \Leftrightarrow \lambda \{ t ; x _ { t } = 0 \} = 0 \mathrm { { } }$ 

$f _ { 2 }$ is continuous at $x  x _ { t } \lor x _ { t - }$ has a unique maximum, 

$f _ { 3 }$ is continuous at x, if all local extremes of $x _ { t }$ or $x _ { t }$ on $( 0 , 1 ]$ are $\neq 0$ 

Proof of Theorem 22.11: Clearly, $\tau _ { n } ^ { i } = f _ { i } ( X ^ { n } )$ for $n \in \mathsf N$ and $i = { 1 , 2 , 3 } ,$ 7 where 

$$
X _ {t} ^ {n} = n ^ {- 1 / 2} X _ {[ n t ]}, \quad t \in [ 0, 1 ], n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

(i) By Theorems 14.16 and 22.9, it sufices to show that each $f _ { i }$ is a.s. continuous at B. Thus, we need to verify that B a.s. satisfies the conditions in Lemma 22.12. This is obvious for $f _ { 1 }$ , since Fubini’s theorem yields

$$

The conditions for $f _ { 2 }$ and $f _ { 3 }$ follow easily from Lemma 14.15. 

(ii) Since $\tau _ { n } ^ { 1 } \ \stackrel { d } { = } \ \tau _ { n } ^ { 2 }$ by Corollary 27.8, it is enough to consider $\boldsymbol { \tau } _ { n } ^ { 1 }$ . Then introduce an independent Brownian motion $B ,$ and define 

$$
\sigma_ {n} ^ {\varepsilon} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k \leq n} 1 \left\{\varepsilon B _ {k} + (1 - \varepsilon) X _ {k} > 0 \right\}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}, \varepsilon \in (0, 1 ].

By (i) together with Theorem 12.12 and Corollary 27.8, we have $\sigma _ { n } ^ { \varepsilon } \overset { d } { = } \sigma _ { n } ^ { 1 } \overset { d } { \to } \tau$ Since $P \{ X _ { n } = 0 \}  0$ , e.g. by Theorem 5.17, we also note that 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \left| \sigma_ {n} ^ {\varepsilon} - \tau_ {n} ^ {1} \right| \leq n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k \leq n} 1 \{X _ {k} = 0 \} \xrightarrow {P} 0.

Hence, we may choose some $\varepsilon _ { n } \to 0$ with $\sigma _ { n } ^ { \varepsilon _ { n } } - \tau _ { n } ^ { 1 } \overset { P } {  } 0$ , and Theorem 5.29 yields $\tau _ { n } ^ { 1 } \stackrel { d } { \to } \tau$ ✷ 

Results like Theorem 22.9 are called invariance principles, since the limiting distribution of $f ( X ^ { n } )$ is the same<sup>5</sup> for all i.i.d. sequences $\left( \xi _ { k } \right)$ with $E \xi _ { i } = 0$ and $E \xi _ { i } ^ { 2 } = 1$ . This is often useful for applications, since a direct computation may be possible for a special choice of distribution, such as for $\begin{array} { r } { P \{ \xi _ { k } = \pm 1 \} = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ 

The approximations in Theorem 22.6 yield similar results for renewal processes, here regarded as non-decreasing step processes. 

Theorem 22.13 (approximation of renewal process) Let N be a renewal process based on a distribution $\mu$ with mean 1 and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ . Then there exists a Brownian motion $B$ , such that 

$$
t ^ {- 1 / 2} \sup _ {s \leq t} \left| N _ {s} - s - \sigma B _ {s} \right| \xrightarrow {P} 0, \quad t \to \infty ,\tag{i}
$$

(ii) $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \infty } { \frac { N _ { t } - t - \sigma B _ { t } } { \sqrt { 2 t \log \log t } } } = 0 ~ a . s .$ 

Proof: (ii) Let $\tau _ { 0 } , \tau _ { 1 } , . . . .$ . be the renewal times of N, and introduce the random walk $X _ { n } = n - \tau _ { n } + \tau _ { 0 } , n \in Z _ { + }$ . Choosing a Brownian motion $B$ as in Theorem 22.6, we get as $n \to \infty$ 

$$
\frac {N _ {\tau_ {n}} - \tau_ {n} - \sigma B _ {n}}{\sqrt {2 n \log \log n}} = \frac {X _ {n} - \sigma B _ {n}}{\sqrt {2 n \log \log n}} \rightarrow 0 \mathrm{a.s.}
$$

Since $\tau _ { n } \sim n$ a.s. by the law of large numbers, we may replace n in the denominator by $\tau _ { n }$ , and by Lemma 22.7 we may further replace $B _ { n }$ by $B _ { \tau _ { n } }$ . Hence, 

$$
\frac {N _ {t} - t - \sigma B _ {t}}{\sqrt {2 t \log \log t}} \rightarrow 0 \text { a.s.   along } (\tau_ {n}).
$$

By Lemma 22.7 it is enough to show that 

$$
\frac {\tau_ {n + 1} - \tau_ {n}}{\sqrt {2 \tau_ {n} \log \log \tau_ {n}}} \rightarrow 0 \text {a.s.},
$$

which is easily seen from Theorem 22.6. 

(i) From Theorem 22.6, we further obtain 

$$
n ^ {- 1 / 2} \sup _ {k \leq n} \left| N _ {\tau_ {k}} - \tau_ {k} - \sigma B _ {k} \right| = n ^ {- 1 / 2} \sup _ {k \leq n} \left| X _ {k} - \tau_ {0} - \sigma B _ {k} \right| \xrightarrow {P} 0,
$$

and by Brownian scaling, 

$$
n ^ {- 1 / 2} w (B, n, 1) \stackrel {d} {=} w (B, 1, n ^ {- 1}) \to 0.
$$

It is then enough to show that 

$$
n ^ {- 1 / 2} \sup _ {k \leq n} \left| \tau_ {k} - \tau_ {k - 1} - 1 \right| = n ^ {- 1 / 2} \sup _ {k \leq n} \left| X _ {k} - X _ {k - 1} \right| \xrightarrow {P} 0,
$$

which is again clear from Theorem 22.6. 

Proceeding as in Corollary 22.8 and Theorem 22.9, we may deduce an associated law of the iterated logarithm and a weak convergence result. 

Corollary 22.14 (limits of renewal process) Let N be a renewal process based on a distribution $\mu$ with mean 1 and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , and let the functional $f : D _ { [ 0 , 1 ] } \to \mathsf { R }$ be measurable and a.s. continuous at a Brownian motion B. 

$$
\limsup _ {t \to \infty} \frac {\pm (N _ {t} - t)}{\sqrt {2 t \log \log t}} = \sigma a. s.,\tag{i}
$$

(ii) $f ( X ^ { r } ) \stackrel { d } { \to } f ( B )$ as $r  \infty$ , where 

$$
X _ {t} ^ {r} = \frac {N _ {r t} - r t}{\sigma \sqrt {r}}, \quad t \in [ 0, 1 ], r > 0.

Part (ii) above yields a similar result for empirical distribution functions, based on a sequence of i.i.d. random variables. The asymptotic behavior can then be expressed in terms of a Brownian bridge. 

Theorem 22.15 (approximation of empirical distributions) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be $i . i . d .$ random variables with ordinary and empirical distribution functions $F$ and $\hat { F } _ { 1 } , \hat { F } _ { 2 } , \dots .$ . Then there exist some Brownian bridges $B ^ { 1 } , B ^ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ such that 

$$
\sup _ {x} \Big | n ^ {1 / 2} \Big \{\hat {F} _ {n} (x) - F (x) \Big \} - B ^ {n} \circ F (x) \Big | \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} 0, \quad n \to \infty .\tag{5}

Proof: Arguing as in the proof of Proposition 5.24, we may reduce to the case where the $\xi _ { n }$ are $U ( 0 , 1 )$ , and $F ( t ) \equiv t \mathrm { { o n } } \left[ 0 , 1 \right]$ . Then clearly

For the associated Brownian bridges $B _ { t } ^ { n } = W _ { t } ^ { n } - t W _ { 1 } ^ { n }$ , we get

We turn to a martingale version of the Skorohod embedding in Theorem 22.1 with associated approximation in Theorem 22.6. 

Theorem 22.16 (embedding ofmartingale) For a martingale $\left( M _ { n } \right)$ with $M _ { 0 } =$ 0 and induced filtration $\left( { \mathcal { G } } _ { n } \right)$ , there exists a Brownian motion B with associated optional times $0 = \tau _ { 0 } \leq \tau _ { 1 } \leq \cdot \cdot \cdot$ , such that a.s. for all $n \in \mathsf N$ ,

(ii) $E \big ( \Delta \tau _ { n } \big | \mathcal F _ { n - 1 } \big ) = E \big \{ ( \Delta M _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } \big | \mathcal G _ { n - 1 } \big \} ,$ 

(iii) $\begin{array} { r }  { E \Big \{ ( \Delta \tau _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } \Big | \mathcal { F } _ { n - 1 } \Big \} \leq 4 { E \Big \{ ( \Delta M _ { n } ) ^ { 4 } \Big | \mathcal { G } _ { n - 1 } \Big \} } , } \end{array}$ 

where $( \mathcal F _ { n } )$  <sub>denotes the filtration induced by the pairs</sub> $( M _ { n } , \tau _ { n } )$ 

Proof: Let $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be probability kernels satisfying 

$$

Define the associated measures $\tilde { \mu } _ { n } ( x ; \cdot )$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { 2 }$ as in Lemma 22.4, and conclude from the measurability part of the lemma that ${ \tilde { \mu } } _ { n }$ is a probability kernel from $\mathsf { R } ^ { n - 1 }$ to $\mathsf { R } ^ { 2 }$ . Next choose some measurable functions $f _ { n } \colon { \mathsf { R } } ^ { n } \to { \mathsf { R } } ^ { 2 }$ as in Lemma 4.22, such that ${ \mathcal { L } } \{ f _ { n } ( x , \vartheta ) \} = { \tilde { \mu } } _ { n } ( x , \cdot )$ when ϑ is $U ( 0 , 1 )$ 

Now fix a Brownian motion $B ^ { \prime }$ and some independent i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random variables $\vartheta _ { 1 } , \vartheta _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ . Let $\tau _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } = 0$ , and define recursively some random variables $\alpha _ { n } , \beta _ { n } , \tau _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ for $n \in { \mathbb N }$ by 

$$
(\alpha_ {n}, \beta_ {n}) = f _ {n} \big (B _ {\tau_ {1} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime}, \ldots , B _ {\tau_ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime}, \vartheta_ {n} \big),\tag{8}
$$

$$
\tau_ {n} ^ {\prime} = \inf \Bigl \{t \geq \tau_ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}; B _ {t} ^ {\prime} - B _ {\tau_ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime} \in \{\alpha_ {n}, \beta_ {n} \} \Bigr \}.\tag{9}
$$

Since $B ^ { \prime }$ is a Brownian motion for the filtration $\mathcal { B } _ { t } = \sigma \{ ( B ^ { \prime } ) ^ { t } , ( \vartheta _ { n } ) \} , t \geq 0$ , and each $\tau _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ is -optional, the strong Markov property shows that $B _ { t } ^ { ( n ) } = B _ { \tau _ { n } ^ { \prime } + t } ^ { \prime } -$ $B _ { \tau _ { n } ^ { \prime } } ^ { \prime }$ is again a Brownian motion independent of $\mathcal { F } _ { n } ^ { \prime } = \sigma \{ \tau _ { k } ^ { \prime } , B _ { \tau _ { k } ^ { \prime } } ^ { \prime } ; k \le n \}$ . Since also $\vartheta _ { n + 1 } \bot \bot ( B ^ { ( n ) } , \mathcal { F } _ { n } ^ { \prime } )$ , we have $( B ^ { ( n ) } , \vartheta _ { n + 1 } )$ Ⅱ $\mathcal { F } _ { n } ^ { \prime }$ . Writing $\mathcal { G } _ { n } ^ { \prime } = \sigma \{ B _ { \tau _ { k } ^ { \prime } } ^ { \prime } ; k \le n \}$ k , we conclude that 

$$

$$

Using (8) and Theorem 8.5, we get

\mathcal {L} \big (\Delta B _ {\tau_ {n} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime} \big | \mathcal {G} _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime} \big) = \mu_ {n} \big (B _ {\tau_ {1} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime}, \ldots , B _ {\tau_ {n - 1} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime}; \cdot \big),\tag{12}

$$

$$

$$
= E \Bigl \{(\Delta B _ {\tau_ {n} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime}) ^ {2} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime} \Bigr \},\tag{13}
$$

$$
E \left\{\left(\Delta \tau_ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime} \right\} = E \left\{\left(\Delta \tau_ {n} ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime} \right\}

$$
\leq 4 E \left\{\left(\Delta B _ {\tau_ {n} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {4} \mid \mathcal {G} _ {n - 1} ^ {\prime} \right\}.\tag{14}
$$

Comparing $( 7 )$ and (12), we get $( B _ { \tau _ { n } ^ { \prime } } ^ { \prime } ) \stackrel { d } { = } ( M _ { n } )$ . By Theorem 8.17, we may then choose a Brownian motion B with associated optional times $\tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } , . . . ,$ such that 

$$
\left\{B, (M _ {n}), (\tau_ {n}) \right\} \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left\{B ^ {\prime}, (B _ {\tau_ {n} ^ {\prime}} ^ {\prime}), (\tau_ {n} ^ {\prime}) \right\}.

All a.s. relations between the objects on the right, including their conditional expectations with respect to appropriate induced σ-fields, remain valid for the objects on the left. In particular, (i) holds for all $n _ { \mathrm { : } }$ and (13) (14) imply the corresponding formulas (ii) (iii). ✷ 

The last theorem allows us to approximate a martingale with small jumps by a Brownian motion. For discrete-time martingales $M .$ , we define the quadratic variation [M] and predictable variation $\langle M \rangle$ by 

$$
[ M ] _ {n} = \sum_ {k <   n} (\Delta M _ {k}) ^ {2},
$$

$$
\langle M \rangle_ {n} = \sum_ {k \leq n} E \left\{\left(\Delta M _ {k}\right) ^ {2} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {k - 1} \right\},
$$

<sub>in analogy with the continuous-time versions in Chapters 18 and 20.</sub> 

Theorem 22.17 (approximation of martingales with small jumps) For $n \in$ N, let $M ^ { n }$ be an ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { n }$ -martingale $M ^ { n }$ on $Z _ { + }$ satisfying 

$$
M _ {0} ^ {n} = 0, \qquad | \Delta M _ {k} ^ {n} | \leq 1, \qquad \sup _ {k} | \Delta M _ {k} ^ {n} | \xrightarrow {P} 0,\tag{15}
$$

put $\zeta _ { n } = [ M ^ { n } ] _ { \infty }$ , and define 

$$
X _ {t} ^ {n} = \sum_ {k} \Delta M _ {k} ^ {n} 1 \left\{\left[ M ^ {n} \right] _ {k} \leq t \right\}, \quad t \in [ 0, 1 ], n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Then 

(i) $( X ^ { n } - B ^ { n } ) _ { \zeta _ { n } \wedge 1 } ^ { \ast } \stackrel { P } { \to } 0$ for some Brownian motions $B ^ { n }$ 

(ii) claim (i) remains true with $[ M ^ { n } ]$ replaced by $\langle M ^ { n } \rangle$ 

(iii) the third condition in (15) can be replaced by 

$$
\sum_ {k} P \left\{\left| \Delta M _ {k} ^ {n} \right| > \varepsilon \mid \mathcal {F} _ {k - 1} ^ {n} \right\} \xrightarrow {P} 0, \quad \varepsilon > 0.\tag{16}
$$

Lemma 22.18 (time-scale comparison) In Theorem 22.17, let $M _ { k } ^ { n } = B ^ { n } ( \tau _ { k } ^ { n } )$ a.s. for some Brownian motions $B ^ { n }$ with associated optional times $\tau _ { k } ^ { n }$ as in Theorem 22.16, and put 

$$
\kappa_ {t} ^ {n} = \inf \left\{k; [ M ^ {n} ] _ {k} > t \right\}, \quad t \geq 0, n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

Then as $n \to \infty$ for fixed $t > 0$ 

$$
\sup _ {k \leq \kappa_ {t} ^ {n}} \left\{\left| \tau_ {k} ^ {n} - [ M ^ {n} ] _ {k} \right| \vee \left| [ M ^ {n} ] _ {k} - \langle M ^ {n} \rangle_ {k} \right| \right\} \xrightarrow {P} 0.\tag{17}
$$

Proof: By optional stopping, we may assume $\left[ M ^ { n } \right]$ to be uniformly bounded, and take the supremum in (17) over all k. To handle the second diference in $( 1 7 )$ , we note that $D ^ { n } = [ M ^ { n } ] - \langle M ^ { n } \rangle$ is a martingale for each $n .$ . Using the martingale property, Proposition 9.17, and dominated convergence, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (D ^ {n}) ^ {* 2} & \preceq & \sup _ {k} E (D _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \\ & = & \sum_ {k} E (\Delta D _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \\ & = & \sum_ {k} E E \bigl \{(\Delta D _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {k - 1} ^ {n} \bigr \} \\ & \leq & \sum_ {k} E E \bigl \{\bigl (\Delta [ M ^ {n} ] _ {k} \bigr) ^ {2} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {k - 1} ^ {n} \bigr \} \\ & = & E \sum_ {k} (\Delta M _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {4} \\ & \preceq & E \sup _ {k} (\Delta M _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \to 0, \end{array}
$$

and so $( D ^ { n } ) ^ { * } \xrightarrow { P } 0$ . This clearly remains true if each sequence $\langle M ^ { n } \rangle$ is defined in terms of the filtration ${ \mathcal { G } } ^ { n }$ induced by $M ^ { n }$ 

To complete the proof of (17), it is enough to show, for the latter versions of $\langle M ^ { n } \rangle$ , that $( \tau ^ { n } - \langle M ^ { n } \rangle ) ^ { * } \stackrel { P } {  } 0$ . Then write ${ \mathcal { T } } ^ { n }$ for the filtration induced by the pairs $( M _ { k } ^ { n } , \tau _ { k } ^ { n } ) , k \in \mathsf { N }$ , and conclude from Theorem 22.16 (ii) that 

$$
\left\langle M ^ {n} \right\rangle_ {m} = \sum_ {k \leq m} E \left(\Delta \tau_ {k} ^ {n} \mid \mathcal {T} _ {k - 1} ^ {n}\right), \quad m, n \in \mathsf {N}.
$$

Hence, $\tilde { D } ^ { n } = \tau ^ { n } - \langle M ^ { n } \rangle$ is a ${ \mathcal { T } } ^ { n } .$ -martingale. Using Theorem 22.16 (ii) (iii), we get as before 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E (\tilde {D} ^ {n}) ^ {* 2} & \preceq & \sup _ {k} E (\tilde {D} _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \\ & = & \sum_ {k} E E \bigl \{(\Delta \tilde {D} _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \Big | \mathcal {T} _ {k - 1} ^ {n} \bigr \} \\ & \leq & \sum_ {k} E E \bigl \{(\Delta \tau_ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \Big | \mathcal {T} _ {k - 1} ^ {n} \bigr \} \\ & \preceq & \sum_ {k} E E \bigl \{(\Delta M _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {4} \Big | \mathcal {G} _ {k - 1} ^ {n} \bigr \} \\ & = & E \sum_ {k} (\Delta M _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {4} \\ & \preceq & E \sup _ {k} (\Delta M _ {k} ^ {n}) ^ {2} \to 0. \end{array}

The suficiency of (16) is a consequence of the following simple estimate.

Though the Skorohod embedding has no natural extension to higher dimensions, we can still derive some multi-variate approximations by applying the previous results separately in each component. To illustrate the method, we show how suitable random walks in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ can be approximated by continuous processes with stationary, independent increments. Extensions to more general limits are obtained by diferent methods in Corollary 16.17 and Theorem 23.14.

By Theorem 5.31, or even simpler by Corollary 8.19 and Theorem A5.4, there exist some rcll processes ${ \tilde { Y } } ^ { n } { \overset { d } { = } } Y ^ { n }$ with $\tilde { Y } _ { t } ^ { n }  \sigma B _ { t }$ a.s. for all $t \in \mathsf { Q } _ { + }$ . Chapter 23 

# Convergence in Distribution

Tightness and relative compactness, convergence and tightness in function spaces, convergence of continuous and rcll processes, functional central limit theorem, moments and tightness, optional equi-continuity and tightness, approximation of random walks, tightness and convergence of random measures, existence via tightness, vague and weak convergence, Cox and thinning continuity, strong Cox continuity, measure-valued processes, convergence of random sets and point processes 

Distributional convergence is another of those indispensable topics, constantly used throughout modern probability. The basic notions were introduced already in Chapter 5, and in Chapter 6 we proved some fundamental limit theorems for sums of independent random variables. In the previous chapter we introduced the powerful method of Skorohod embedding, which enabled us to establish some functional versions of those results, where the Gaussian limits are replaced by entire paths of Brownian motion and related processes. 

Despite the amazing power of the latter technique, its scope of applicability is inevitably restricted by the limited class of possible limit laws. Here we turn to a systematic study of general weak convergence theory, based on some fundamental principles of compactness in appropriate function and measure spaces. In particular, some functional limit theorems, derived in the last chapter by cumbersome embedding and approximation techniques, will now be accessible by straightforward compactness arguments. 

The key result is Prohorov’s theorem, which gives the basic connection between tightness and relative distributional compactness. This result enables us to convert some classical compactness criteria into similar probabilistic versions. In particular, the Arzel`a–Ascoli theorem yields a corresponding criterion for distributional compactness of continuous processes. Similarly, an optional equi-continuity condition guarantees the appropriate compactness, for rightcontinuous processes with left-hand limits<sup>1</sup>. We will also derive some general criteria for convergence in distribution of random measures and sets, with special emphasis on the point process case. 

The general criteria will be applied to some interesting concrete situations. In addition to some already familiar results from Chapters 22, we will derive convergence criteria for Cox processes and thinnings of point processes. Further applications appear in other chapters, such as a general approximation result for Markov chains in Chapter 17, various limit theorems for exchangeable processes and particle systems in Chapters $2 7$ and 30, and a way of constructing weak solutions to SDEs in Chapter 32. To avoid overloading this chapter with technical detail, we outline some of the underlying analysis in Appendices $5 \mathrm { - 6 }$ 

Beginning with continuous processes, we fix some separable and complete metric spaces $( T , d ) , ( S , \rho )$ , where $T$ is also locally compact, and consider the space $C _ { T , S }$ of continuous functions from $T$ to $S _ { ; }$ , endowed with the locally uniform topology. The associated notion of convergence, written as $x _ { n } \xrightarrow { u l } x$ , is given by 

$$
\sup _ {t \in K} \rho (x _ {n, t}, x _ {t}) \to 0, \quad K \in \mathcal {K} _ {T},\tag{1}
$$

where $\kappa _ { T }$ denotes the class of compact sets $K \subset T$ . Since $T$ is locally compact, we may choose $K _ { 1 } , K _ { 2 } , \ldots \in \mathcal { K } _ { T }$ with $K _ { n } ^ { o } \uparrow T$ , and it is enough to verify (1) for all $K _ { n }$ . Using such a sequence, we may easily construct a separable and complete metrization of the topology. In Lemma A5.1 we show that the Borel σ-field in $C _ { T , S }$ is generated by the evaluation maps $\pi _ { t } \colon x \mapsto x _ { t } , t \in T$ . This is significant for our purposes, since the random elements in $C _ { T , S }$ are then precisely the continuous processes on $T$ taking values in $S .$ 

Given any such processes X and $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots$ , we need to find tractable conditions for the associated convergence in distribution, written as $X _ { n } \xrightarrow { u l d } X$ This mode of convergence is clearly strictly stronger than the finite-dimensional convergence $X _ { n } \xrightarrow { f d } X$ , defined $\mathrm { b y ^ { 2 } }$ 

$$
(X _ {t _ {1}} ^ {n}, \ldots , X _ {t _ {m}} ^ {n}) \xrightarrow {d} (X _ {t _ {1}}, \ldots , X _ {t _ {m}}), \quad t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {m} \in T, m \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{2}
$$

This is clear already in the non-random case, since the point-wise convergence $x _ { t } ^ { n } \to x _ { t }$ in $C _ { T , S }$ may not be locally uniform. 

The classical way around this dificulty is to require the functions $x _ { n }$ to be locally equi-continuous. Formally, we may impose suitable conditions on the associated local moduli of continuity 

$$
w _ {K} (x, h) = \sup \left\{\rho \left(x _ {s}, x _ {t}\right); s, t \in K, d (s, t) \leq h \right\}, \quad h > 0, K \in \mathcal {K} _ {T}.\tag{3}
$$

Using the Arzel`a–Ascoli compactness criterion, in the version of Theorem A5.2, we may easily characterize convergence in $C _ { T , S }$ . Though this case is quite elementary, it is discussed in detail below, since it sets the pattern for the more advanced criteria for distributional convergence, considered throughout the remainder of the chapter. 

Lemma 23.1 (convergence in $\left( { { C _ { T , S } } } \right)$ Let $x , x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be continuous, S-valued functions on $T$ , where S, T are separable, complete metric spaces and $T$ is locally compact with a dense subset $T ^ { \prime }$ . Then $x _ { n } \xrightarrow { u l }$ x in $C _ { T , S } \ i f f$ 

(i) $x _ { t } ^ { n } \to x _ { t }$ for all $t \in T ^ { \prime }$ 

$$
\text {(ii)} \lim _ {h \to 0} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} w _ {K} (x _ {n}, h) = 0, \quad K \in \mathcal {K} _ {T}.
$$

Proof: $\operatorname { I f } x _ { n } \xrightarrow { u l } x .$ , then (i) holds by continuity and (ii) holds by Theorem A5.2. Conversely, assume $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i } )$ . Then $( x _ { n } )$ is relatively compact by Theorem A5.2, and so for any sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ we have convergence $x _ { n } \xrightarrow { u l } y$ along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ . Then by continuity, $x _ { n } ( t )  y ( t )$ along $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ for all $t \in T$ , and so (i) yields $x ( t ) = y ( t )$ for all $t ^ { \prime } \in T ^ { \prime }$ . Since x and y are continuous and $T ^ { \prime }$ is dense in $T ,$ we get $x = y$ . The approach for random processes is similar, except that here we need to replace the compactness criterion in Theorem A5.2 by a criterion for compactness in distribution. The key result is Prohorov’s Theorem 23.2 below, which relates compactness in a given metric space $S$ to weak compactness<sup>3</sup> in the associated space $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ of probability measures on $S _ { ☉ }$ . For most applications of interest, we may choose $S$ to be a suitable function or measure space. 

To make this precise, let $\Xi$ be a family of random elements in a metric space S. Generalizing a notion from Chapter $5$ , we say that $\Xi$ is tight if 

$$
\inf _ {K \in \mathcal {K} _ {S}} \sup _ {\xi \in \Xi} P \{\xi \notin K \} = 0.\tag{4}
$$

We also say that $\Xi$ is relatively compact in distribution, if every sequence of random elements $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots \in \Xi$ has a sub-sequence converging in distribution toward a random element $\xi$ in S. 

We may now state the fundamental equivalence between tightness and relative compactness, for random elements in suficiently regular metric spaces. This extends the version for Euclidean spaces in Proposition 6.22. 

Theorem 23.2 (tightness and relative compactness, Prohorov) For a set $\Xi$ of random elements in a metric space $S$ , we have ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ with 

(i) Ξ is tight, 

(ii) $\Xi$ is relatively compact in distribution, 

and equivalence holds when S is separable and complete. 

In particular, we see that when S is separable and complete, a single random element $\xi$ in S is tight, in the sense that inf $ _ { \cal K } P \{ \xi \notin { \cal K } \} = 0$ . For sequences we may then replace the ‘sup’ in (4) by ‘lim sup’. 

For the proof of Theorem 23.2, we need a simple lemma. Recall from Lemma 1.6 that a random element in a sub-space of a metric space $S$ may also be regarded as a random element in S. 

Lemma 23.3 (tightness preservation) Tightness is preserved by continuous maps. Thus, if S is a metric space and $\Xi$ is a set of random elements in a subset $A \subset S$ , we have 

$$
\Xi \text {   is   tight   in   } A \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Xi \text {   is   tight   in   } S.
$$

Proof: Compactness is preserved by continuous maps. This applies in particular to the natural embedding $I \colon A \to S$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 23.2 (Varadarajan): For $S = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , the result was proved in Proposition 6.22. Turning to the case of $S = { \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ , consider a tight sequence of random elements ${ \xi } ^ { n } = ( { \xi } _ { 1 } ^ { n } , { \xi } _ { 2 } ^ { n } , \dots )$ in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ . Writing $\eta _ { k } ^ { n } = ( \xi _ { 1 } ^ { n } , \dots , \xi _ { k } ^ { n } )$ , we see from Lemma 23.3 that the sequence $( \eta _ { k } ^ { n } ; n \in \mathbb { N } )$ is tight in $\mathsf { R } ^ { k }$ for each $k \in { \mathsf N }$ For any sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , a diagonal argument yields $\eta _ { k } ^ { n } \stackrel { d } {  }$ some $\eta _ { k }$ for all $k \in \mathsf { N }$ , as $n \to \infty$ along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ . Hence, for any sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , we have $\xi _ { n } \ \overset { d } { \to }$ some $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { \infty }$ along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ . $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } , . . .$ . of radius r. Writing $G _ { k } = B _ { 1 } \cup \dots \cup B _ { k }$ , we claim that

For processes with possible jump discontinuities, the theory is similar but more complicated. Here we consider the space $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , S }$ of $\mathrm { r c l l ^ { 4 } }$ functions on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ taking values in a separable, complete metric space $( S , \rho )$ . For any $\varepsilon , t > 0 .$ 7 such a function x has clearly at most finitely many jumps of size $\rho ( x _ { t } , x _ { t - } ) > \varepsilon$ up to time t. 

Though it still makes sense to consider the locally uniform topology with associated mode of convergence $x _ { n } \xrightarrow { u l } x$ , it is technically convenient and more useful for applications to allow appropriate time changes, given by increasing bijections on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ . Note that such functions $\lambda$ are continuous and strictly increasing with $\lambda _ { 0 } ~ = ~ 0$ and $\lambda _ { \infty } = \infty$ . where the suprema extend over all optional times $\tau \leq t$ and $\sigma \in [ \tau - \delta , \tau ]$ . ✷ 

We also need the following elementary estimate. 

Lemma 23.13 (exponential bound) For any random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n } \geq 0$ with sum $X _ { n }$ , we have 

$$
E e ^ {- X _ {n}} \leq e ^ {- n c} + \max _ {k \leq n} P \{\xi_ {k} <   c \}, \quad c > 0.
$$

Proof: Let $p$ be the maximum on the right. By the H¨older and Chebyshev inequalities, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E e ^ {- X _ {n}} = E \prod_ {k} e ^ {- \xi_ {k}} \\ \leq \prod_ {k} (E e ^ {- n \xi_ {k}}) ^ {1 / n} \\ \leq \left\{(e ^ {- n c} + p) ^ {1 / n} \right\} ^ {n} \\ = e ^ {- n c} + p. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 23.11: Again we may assume that $\rho \leq 1$ , and by suitable approximation we may extend condition (14) to weakly optional times $\sigma$ and $\tau .$ . For all $n \in \mathsf N$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ , we define recursively the weakly $X ^ { n }$ -optional times 

$$
\sigma_ {k + 1} ^ {n} = \inf \Bigl \{s > \sigma_ {k} ^ {n}; \rho (X _ {\sigma_ {k} ^ {n}} ^ {n}, X _ {s} ^ {n}) > \varepsilon \Bigr \}, \quad k \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+},
$$

starting with $\sigma _ { 0 } ^ { n } = 0$ , and note that for $m \in \mathsf N$ and $t , h > 0$ , 

$$
\tilde {w} _ {t} (X ^ {n}, h) \leq 2 \varepsilon + \sum_ {k <   m} 1 \Bigl \{\sigma_ {k + 1} ^ {n} - \sigma_ {k} ^ {n} <   h, \sigma_ {k} ^ {n} <   t \Bigr \} + 1 \bigl \{\sigma_ {m} ^ {n} <   t \bigr \}.\tag{15}
$$

Writing $\nu _ { n } ( t , h )$ for the supremum in (14), we get by Chebyshev’s inequality and a simple truncation 

$$
P \Bigl \{\sigma_ {k + 1} ^ {n} - \sigma_ {k} ^ {n} <   h, \sigma_ {k} ^ {n} <   t \Bigr \} \leq \varepsilon^ {- 1} \nu_ {n} (t + h, h), k \in \mathbb {N}, t, h > 0,\tag{16}
$$

and so by (14) and (15), 

$$
\lim _ {h \to 0} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} E \tilde {w} _ {t} (X ^ {n}, h) \leq 2 \varepsilon + \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \{\sigma_ {m} ^ {n} <   t \}.\tag{17}
$$

Next we see from (16) and Lemma 23.13 that, for any $c > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \Bigl \{\sigma_ {m} ^ {n} <   t \Bigr \} \leq e ^ {t} E \Bigl (e ^ {- \sigma_ {m} ^ {n}}; \sigma_ {m} ^ {n} <   t \Bigr) \\ & \qquad \leq e ^ {t} \Bigl \{e ^ {- m c} + \varepsilon^ {- 1} \nu_ {n} (t + c, c) \Bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

By (14) the right-hand side tends to 0 as $m , n  \infty$ and then $c \to 0$ . Hence, the last term in (17) tends to 0 as $m  \infty$ , and (11) follows since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary. ✷ 

To illustrate the use of Theorem 23.11, we prove an extension of Theorem 23.6. A related result was obtained by diferent methods in Corollary 16.17. An extension to Markov chains appears in Theorem 17.28. 

Theorem 23.14 (approximation of random walks, Skorohod) Let $Y ^ { 1 } , Y ^ { 2 } , \ldots$ be random walks in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and form the rcll processes

When X is a.s. continuous, this holds if $X ^ { n } \xrightarrow { u l d } X$ 

Proof: By Corollary 7.9 we have $X ^ { n } \xrightarrow { f d } X$ , and so by Theorem 23.11 it is enough to show that $\vert X _ { \tau _ { n } + h _ { n } } ^ { n } - X _ { \tau _ { n } } ^ { n } \vert \ \overset { P } {  }$ 0 for any optional times $\tau _ { n } < \infty$ and constants $h _ { n } \to 0$ . Next we consider convergence in distribution of random measures on a separable, complete metric space $S _ { i }$ defined as locally finite kernels $\xi \colon \Omega  S$ Thus, $\xi ( \omega , B )$ is a measurable function of $\omega \in \Omega$ for fixed $B$ and a measure in $B \in S$ for fixed $\omega ,$ such that $\xi B < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . for all $B$ in the ring ${ \hat { S } } \subset S$ of bounded Borel sets. Equivalently, we may regard random measures as random elements in the space $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ of locally finite measures $\mu$ on $S _ { i }$ , endowed with the σ-field generated by all evaluation maps $\pi _ { B } \colon \mu \mapsto \mu B$ with $B \in S$ 

On $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ we introduce the vague topology, induced by the integration maps $\pi _ { f } : \mu \mapsto \mu f$ , for all $f$ in the space $\hat { C } _ { S }$ of bounded, continuous functions $f \geq 0$ with bounded support<sup>5</sup>. The corresponding notion of vague convergence $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { v } { \to } \mu$ is then given by $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ . For bounded measures $\mu$ on $S ,$ we also consider the weak topology with associated weak convergence $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } { \to } \mu .$ , given by $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ for all bounded, continuous functions $f \geq 0$ on $S .$ The basic properties of the vague and weak topologies are summarized in Lemma A5.5, and associated compactness criteria are given in Theorem A5.6. Using the latter, we may derive corresponding criteria for tightness of random measures: 

Theorem 23.15 (tightness of random measures, Matthes et al.) $L e t \equiv b e$ a set of random measures on a separable, complete metric space S. $T h e n \Xi$ is vaguely tight if 

(i) $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { r \to \infty } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { \xi \in \Xi } P \{ \xi B > r \} = 0 , B \in \hat { \mathcal { S } } ,$ 

(ii) $\operatorname* { i n f } _ { K \in { \mathcal K } } \operatorname* { s u p } _ { \xi \in \Xi } E \Big \{ \xi ( B \setminus K ) \wedge 1 \Big \} = 0 , { \mathcal B } \in \hat { \mathcal S } .$ 

When the $\xi \in \Xi \ a r e \ a . s .$ . bounded, the set Ξ is weakly tight $i f f \ ( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i } )$ hold with $B = S$ 

Proof: Let $\Xi$ be vaguely tight. Then for any $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a vaguely compact set $A \subset \mathcal { M } _ { S }$ , such that $P \{ \xi \notin A \} < \varepsilon$ for all $\xi \in \Xi$ . For fixed $\bar { B } \in \bar { \cal S }$ Theorem A5.6 yields $r = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { \mu \in A } \mu B < \infty$ , and so $\mathrm { s u p } _ { \xi \in \Xi } P \{ \xi B > r \} < \varepsilon$ The same lemma yields a $K \in \mathcal { K }$ with $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { \mu \in { \cal A } } \mu ( B \setminus K ) < \varepsilon .$ , which implies $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { \xi \in \Xi } E \{ \xi ( B \setminus K ) \wedge 1 \} \le 2 \varepsilon$ . Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, this proves the necessity of (i) and (ii). 

Now assume (i) (ii). Fix any $s _ { 0 } \in S$ , and put $B _ { n } = \{ s \in S ; \rho ( s , s _ { 0 } ) <$ $n \}$ . For any $\varepsilon > 0$ , we may choose some constants $r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , \dots > 0$ and sets $K _ { 1 } , K _ { 2 } , \ldots \in { \mathcal { K } }$ , such that for all $\xi \in \Xi$ and $n \in \mathsf N$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \{\xi B _ {n} > r _ {n} \} <   2 ^ {- n} \varepsilon , \\ E \Big \{\xi (B _ {n} \setminus K _ {n}) \wedge 1 \Big \} <   2 ^ {- 2 n} \varepsilon . \end{array}\tag{18}
$$

Writing A for the set of measures $\mu \in \mathcal { M } _ { S }$ with 

$$
\mu B _ {n} \leq r _ {n}, \quad \mu (B _ {n} \setminus K _ {n}) \leq 2 ^ {- n}, \qquad n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

we see from Theorem A5.6 that A is vaguely relatively compact. Noting that 

$$
P \left\{\xi (B _ {n} \setminus K _ {n}) > 2 ^ {- n} \right\} \leq 2 ^ {n} E \left\{\xi (B _ {n} \setminus K _ {n}) \wedge 1 \right\}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

we get from (18) for any $\xi \in \Xi$ 

$$
P \{\xi \notin A \} \leq \sum_ {n} P \{\xi B _ {n} > r _ {n} \} + \sum_ {n} 2 ^ {n} E \Bigl \{\xi (B _ {n} \setminus K _ {n}) \wedge 1 \Bigr \} <   2 \varepsilon ,
$$

We may now derive criteria for convergence in distribution with respect to the vague topology, written as $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ and defined<sup>6</sup> by $\mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { n } ) \xrightarrow { v w } \mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ , where $\xrightarrow { v w }$ denotes weak convergence on $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { \mathcal { M } _ { S } }$ with respect to the vague topology on $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ . Let $\hat { S } _ { \xi }$ be the class of sets $B \in \hat { S }$ with $\xi \partial B = 0 ~ \mathrm { a . s }$ . A non-empty class $\mathcal { T }$ of sets $I \subset S$ is called a semi-ring, if it is closed under finite intersections, and such that every proper diference in is a finite union of disjoint -sets; it is called a ring if it is also closed under finite unions. Typical semi-rings in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ are families of rectangular boxes $I _ { 1 } \times \cdots \times I _ { d }$ . By $\hat { \mathcal { Z } } _ { + }$ we denote the class of simple functions over $\mathcal { T }$ 

Theorem 23.16 (convergence of random measures, Harris, Matthes et $a l . )$ Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be random measures on a separable, complete metric space $S ,$ and fix a dissecting semi-ring $\mathcal { T } \subset \hat { \mathcal { S } } _ { \xi }$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi ,$ 

(ii) $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \xi f$ for all $f \in \hat { C } _ { S } o r \hat { \mathcal { T } } _ { + }$ 

(iii) $E e ^ { - \xi n f } \to E e ^ { - \xi f }$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ or $\hat { \mathcal { Z } } _ { + }$ with $f \leq 1$ 

Our proof relies on two simple lemmas. For any function $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ , let $D _ { f }$ be the set of discontinuity points of $f .$ 

Lemma 23.17 (limits of integrals) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be random measures on $S$ with $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ , and let $f \in \hat { S } _ { + }$ with $\xi D _ { f } = 0 \ a . s .$ . Then $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \xi f$ 

Proof: By Theorem 5.27 it is enough to prove that, if $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { v } { \to } \mu$ with $\mu D _ { f } = 0$ then $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ . By a suitable truncation and normalization, we may take all $\mu _ { n }$ and $\mu$ to be probability measures. Then the same theorem yields $\mu _ { n } \circ f ^ { - 1 } \stackrel { w } {  }$ $\mu \circ f ^ { - 1 }$ , which implies $\mu _ { n } f \to \mu f$ since $f$ is bounded. ✷ 

Lemma 23.18 (continuity sets) Let $\xi , \eta , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be random measures on $S$ with $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \eta$ , and fix a dissecting ring and a constant $r > 0$ . Then 

(i) $\hat { S } _ { \eta } \supset \hat { S } _ { \xi }$ whenever 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} E e ^ {- r \xi_ {n} U} \geq E e ^ {- r \xi U}, \quad U \in \mathcal {U},
$$

(ii) for point processes $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ , we may assume instead that 

lim inf $P \{ \xi _ { n } U = 0 \} \geq P \{ \xi U = 0 \} , \quad U \in \mathcal { U } .$ n→∞ 

Proof: Fix any $B \in \hat { S } _ { \xi }$ . Let $\partial B \subset F \subset U$ with $\boldsymbol { F } \in \hat { \boldsymbol { S } } _ { \eta }$ and $U \in \mathcal { U }$ , where $F$ is closed. By (i) and Lemma 23.17, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E e ^ {- r \eta \partial B} \geq E e ^ {- r \eta F} \\ = \lim _ {n \to \infty} E e ^ {- r \xi_ {n} F} \\ \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} E e ^ {- r \xi_ {n} U} \\ \geq E e ^ {- r \xi U}. \end{array}
$$

Letting $U \downarrow F$ and then $F \downarrow \partial B$ , we get $E e ^ { - r \eta \partial B } \geq E e ^ { - r \xi \partial B } = 1$ by dominated convergence. Hence, $\eta \partial B = 0 { \mathrm { a . s . } }$ , which means that $B \in \hat { S } _ { \eta }$ . The proof of (ii) is similar. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 23.16: Here $( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ holds by Lemma 23.17 and $( \mathrm { i i } ) \Leftrightarrow$ (iii) by Theorem 6.3. To prove $\mathrm { ( i i ) } \Rightarrow \mathrm { ( i ) }$ , assume that $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \xi f$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ or $\hat { \mathcal { Z } } _ { + }$ , respectively. For any $B \in \hat { S }$ we may choose an $f$ with $1 _ { B } \leq f ,$ , and so $\xi _ { n } B \leq \xi _ { n } f$ is tight by the convergence of $\xi _ { n } f$ . Thus, $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ satisfies (i) of Theorem 23.15. 

To prove (ii) of the same result, we may assume that $\xi \partial B = 0 \mathrm { a . s }$ . A simple approximation yields $( 1 _ { B } \xi _ { n } ) f \overset { d } { \to } ( 1 _ { B } \xi ) f$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ of $\hat { \mathcal { Z } } _ { + }$ , and so we may take $S = B$ , and let the measures $\xi _ { n }$ and $\xi$ be a.s. bounded with $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \xi f$ for all $f \in C _ { S }$ or $\mathcal { T } _ { + }$ . Here Corollary 6.5 yields $( \xi _ { n } f , \xi _ { n } S ) \overset { d } { \to } ( \xi f , \xi S )$ for all such $f ,$ and so $( \xi _ { n } S \vee 1 ) ^ { - 1 } \xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } ( \xi S \vee 1 ) ^ { - 1 } \xi f$ , which allows us to assume $\| \xi _ { n } \| \leq 1$ for all $n .$ . Then $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \xi f$ implies $E \xi _ { n } f \to E \xi f$ for all $f$ as above, and so $E \xi _ { n } \ { \overset { v } { \to } } \ E \xi$ by the definition of vague convergence. Here Lemma A5.6 yields in $\quad \ : \cdot \kappa \exp _ { n } E \xi _ { n } K ^ { c } = 0 \ :$ , which proves (ii) of Theorem 23.15 for the sequence $( \xi _ { n } )$ 

The latter theorem shows that $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is tight. If $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \eta$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ for a random measure $\eta$ on $S ,$ , then Lemma 23.17 yields $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \eta f$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ or $\mathcal { T } _ { + }$ . In the former case, $\eta f \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ \xi f$ for all $f \in C _ { S }$ , which implies $\eta \triangleq \xi .$ . In the latter case, Lemma 23.18 yields $\hat { S } _ { \eta } \supset \hat { S } _ { \xi } \supset \mathcal { I }$ , and so $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \eta f$ for all $f \in \hat { \mathcal { I } } _ { + }$ , which again implies $\eta \overset { d } { = } \xi$ . Since $N ^ { \prime }$ was arbitrary, we obtain $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ ✷ 

Corollary 23.19 (existence of limit) Let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be random measures on an lcscH space $S ,$ such that $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \alpha _ { f }$ for some random variables $\alpha _ { f } , f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ Then $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ for a random measure $\xi$ on $S$ satisfying 

$$
\xi f \stackrel {d} {=} \alpha_ {f}, \quad f \in \hat {C} _ {S}.
$$

Proof: Condition (ii) of Theorem 23.15 being void, the tightness of $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ follows already from the tightness of $( \xi _ { n } f )$ for all $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ . Hence, Theorem 23.2 yields $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , for a random measure $\xi$ on S, and so $\xi _ { n } f \overset { d } { \to } \xi f$ along $N ^ { \prime }$ for every $f \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ . The latter convergence extends to N by hypothesis, and so $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ by Theorem 23.16. ✷ 

Theorem 23.20 (weak and vague convergence) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be a.s. bounded random measures on $S$ with $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { w d } \xi ,$ 

(ii) $\xi _ { n } S \overset { d } { \to } \xi S$ 

(iii) inf lim sup $E \left( \xi _ { n } B ^ { c } \wedge 1 \right) = 0$ ˆ n 

Proof, ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ : Clear since $1 \in C _ { S }$ 

$( \mathrm { i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ : If (iii) fails, then a diagonal argument yields a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ with 

$$
\inf _ {B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}}} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \in N ^ {\prime}} E \Big (\xi_ {n} B ^ {c} \wedge 1 \Big) > 0.\tag{19}
$$

Since clearly $\tilde { \xi } \overset { d } { = } \xi$ , a transfer argument allows us to take $\tilde { \xi } = \xi$ . Then for any $B \in \hat { \cal S } _ { \xi }$ , we get along $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} 0 \leq \xi_ {n} B ^ {c} = \xi_ {n} S - \xi_ {n} B \\ \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} \alpha - \xi B, \end{array}
$$

and so $\xi B \le$ α a.s., which implies $\xi S \le \alpha \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . since $B$ was arbitrary. Since also $\alpha \stackrel { d } { = } \xi S$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r} E \Big | e ^ {- \xi S} - e ^ {- \alpha} \Big | = E e ^ {- \xi S} - E e ^ {- \alpha} \\ = E e ^ {- \xi S} - E e ^ {- \xi S} = 0, \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E \Big (\xi_ {n} B ^ {c} \wedge 1 \Big) & = E \Big \{(\xi_ {n} S - \xi_ {n} B) \wedge 1 \Big \} \\ & \to E \Big \{(\xi S - \xi B) \wedge 1 \Big \} \\ & = E \Big (\xi B ^ {c} \wedge 1 \Big), \end{array}
$$

which tends to 0 as $B \uparrow S$ by dominated convergence. This contradicts (19), and (iii) follows. 

$( \mathrm { i i i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i } )$ : Writing $K ^ { c } \subset B ^ { c } \cup ( B \setminus K )$ when $K \in \mathcal { K }$ and $B \in \hat { S }$ , and using the additivity of $P$ and $\xi _ { n }$ and the sub-additivity of $x \wedge 1$ for $x \geq 0$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} E \big (\xi_ {n} K ^ {c} \wedge 1 \big) \\ \quad \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} \big (E \big \{\xi_ {n} B ^ {c} \wedge 1 \big \} + E \big \{\xi_ {n} (B \setminus K) \wedge 1 \big \} \big) \\ \quad \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} E \big (\xi_ {n} B ^ {c} \wedge 1 \big) + \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} E \big \{\xi_ {n} (B \setminus K) \wedge 1 \big \}. \end{array}
$$

Taking the infimum over $K \in \mathcal { K }$ and then letting $B \uparrow S$ , we get by Theorem 23.15 and (iii) 

$$
\inf _ {K \in \mathcal {K}} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} E \big (\xi_ {n} K ^ {c} \wedge 1 \big) = 0.\tag{20}
$$
