$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} P \Big \{\xi_ {n} S > r \Big \} \\ \quad \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} \left(P \Big \{\xi_ {n} B > r - 1 \Big \} + P \Big \{\xi_ {n} B ^ {c} > 1 \Big \}\right) \\ \quad \leq \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} P \Big \{\xi_ {n} B > r - 1 \Big \} + \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} E \Big (\xi_ {n} B ^ {c} \wedge 1 \Big). \end{array}
$$

Letting $r  \infty$ and then $B \uparrow S$ , we get by Theorem 23.15 and (iii) 

$$
\lim _ {r \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} P \Bigl \{\xi_ {n} S > r \Bigr \} = 0.\tag{21}
$$

By Theorem 23.15, we see from (20) and (21) that $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is weakly tight. As suming $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { w d } \eta$ along a sub-sequence, we have also $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \eta$ , and so $\eta \stackrel { d } { = } \xi$ Since the sub-sequence was arbitrary, (i) follows by Theorem 23.2. ✷ 

For a first application, we prove some continuity properties of Cox processes and thinnings, extending the simple uniqueness properties in Lemma 15.7. Further limit theorems involving Cox processes and thinnings appear in Chapter 30. 

Theorem 23.21 (Cox and thinning continuity) For $n \in \mathsf N$ and a fixed $p \in$ (0, 1], let $\xi _ { n }$ be a Cox process on $S$ directed by a random measure $\eta _ { n }$ or a p -thinning of a point process $\eta _ { n }$ on S. Then 

$$
\xi_ {n} \stackrel {v d} {\longrightarrow} \xi \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \eta_ {n} \stackrel {v d} {\longrightarrow} \eta
$$

for some $\xi , \eta$ , where $\xi$ is a Cox process directed by η or a p -thinning of $\eta _ { i }$ respectively. In that case also 

$$
\left(\xi_ {n}, \eta_ {n}\right) \stackrel {v d} {\longrightarrow} (\xi , \eta) i n \mathcal {M} _ {S} ^ {2}.
$$

Proof: Let $\eta _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \eta$ for a random measure η on $S .$ . Then Lemma 15.2 yields for any $f , g \in { \hat { C } } _ { S }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E e ^ {- \xi_ {n} f - \eta_ {n} g} = & E \exp \Bigl \{- \eta_ {n} (1 - e ^ {- f} + g) \Bigr \} \\ & \to E \exp \Bigl \{- \eta (1 - e ^ {- f} + g) \Bigr \} \\ = & E e ^ {- \xi f - \eta g}, \end{array}
$$

where $\xi$ is a Cox process directed by η. Hence, Theorem 6.3 gives $\xi _ { n } f + \eta _ { n } g \overset { d } { \to }$ $\xi f + \eta g$ for all such $f$ and $g _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and so $\left( \xi _ { n } , \eta _ { n } \right) \xrightarrow { v d } \left( \xi , \eta \right)$ by Theorem 23.16. 

Conversely, let $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ for a point process $\xi$ on S. Then the sequence $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is vaguely tight, and so Theorem 23.15 yields for any $B \in \hat { S }$ and $u > 0$ 

$$
\lim _ {r \to 0} \inf _ {n \geq 1} E e ^ {- r \xi_ {n} B} = \sup _ {K \in \mathcal {K}} \inf _ {n \geq 1} E \exp \Bigl \{- u   \xi_ {n} (B \setminus K) \Bigr \} = 1.
$$

Similar relations hold for $( \eta _ { n } )$ by Lemma 15.2, with $r$ and $u$ replaced by $r ^ { \prime } = 1 - e ^ { - r }$ and $u ^ { \prime } = 1 - e ^ { - u }$ , and so even $( \eta _ { n } )$ is vaguely tight by Theorem 23.15, which implies that $( \eta _ { n } )$ is vaguely relatively compact. If $\eta _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \eta$ along a sub-sequence, then $\xi _ { n } \ \xrightarrow { v d } \ \xi ^ { \prime }$ as before, where $\xi ^ { \prime }$ is a Cox process directed by $\eta .$ Since $\xi ^ { \prime } \overset { d } { = } \xi ,$ , the distribution of $\eta$ is unique by Lemma 15.7, and so the convergence $\eta _ { n } \ \xrightarrow { v d } \ \eta$ extends to the entire sequence. The proof for $p$ -thinnings is similar. ✷ 

We also consider a stronger, non-topological version of distributional convergence for random measures, defined as follows. Beginning with non-random measures $\mu$ and $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , . . . \in \mathcal { M } _ { S }$ , we write $\mu _ { n } \ { \stackrel { u } { \to } } \ \mu$ for convergence in total variation and $\mu _ { n } \ \xrightarrow [ ] { u l } \ \mu$ for the corresponding local version, defined by $1 _ { B } \mu _ { n } \stackrel { u } { \to } 1 _ { B } \mu$ for all $B \in { \hat { S } }$ . For random measures ξ and $\xi _ { n }$ on S, we may now define the convergence $\xi _ { n } \ \xrightarrow { u d } \ \xi$ by ${ \mathcal { L } } ( \xi _ { n } ) ~ { \overset { u } { \to } } ~ { \mathcal { L } } ( \xi )$ , and let $\xi _ { n } \ \xrightarrow { u l d } \ \xi$ be the corresponding local version, given by $1 _ { B } \xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { u d } 1 _ { B } \xi$ for all $B \in \hat { S }$ . Finally, we define the convergence $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { u l P } \xi$ by $\| \xi _ { n } - \xi \| _ { B } \overset { P } { \to } 0$ for all $B \in \hat { S }$ , and similarly for the global version $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { u P } \xi$ 

The last result has the following partial analogue for strong convergence. 

Theorem 23.22 (strong Cox continuity) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be Cox processes directed by some random measures $\eta , \eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , . . . \ o n \ S$ . Then 

$$
\eta_ {n} \xrightarrow {u l P} \eta \quad \Rightarrow \quad \xi_ {n} \xrightarrow {u l d} \xi ,
$$

with equivalence when $\eta , \eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , . . .$ . are non-random. 

Proof: We may clearly take S to be bounded. First let $\eta = \lambda$ and all $\eta _ { n } = \lambda _ { n }$ be non-random. For any $n \in \mathsf N$ , put 

$$
\hat {\lambda} _ {n} = \lambda \wedge \lambda_ {n}, \qquad \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime} = \lambda - \hat {\lambda} _ {n}, \qquad \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime \prime} = \lambda_ {n} - \hat {\lambda} _ {n},
$$

so that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda = \hat {\lambda} _ {n} + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime}, \qquad \lambda_ {n} = \hat {\lambda} _ {n} + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime \prime}, \\ \| \lambda_ {n} - \lambda \| = \| \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime} \| + \| \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime \prime} \|. \end{array}
$$

Letting $\hat { \xi } _ { n } , \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime } , \xi _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime }$ be independent Poisson processes with intensities $\hat { \lambda } _ { n } , \lambda _ { n } ^ { \prime } , \lambda _ { n } ^ { \prime \prime }$ , respectively, we note that 

$$
\xi \stackrel {d} {=} \hat {\xi} _ {n} + \xi_ {n} ^ {\prime}, \qquad \xi_ {n} \stackrel {d} {=} \hat {\xi} _ {n} + \xi_ {n} ^ {\prime \prime}.
$$

Assuming $\lambda _ { n } \overset { u } { \to } \lambda$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \left\| \mathcal {L} (\xi) - \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {n}) \right\| & \leq \left\| \mathcal {L} (\xi) - \mathcal {L} (\hat {\xi} _ {n}) \right\| + \left\| \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {n}) - \mathcal {L} (\hat {\xi} _ {n}) \right\| \\ & \lesssim P \{\xi_ {n} ^ {\prime} \neq 0 \} + P \{\xi_ {n} ^ {\prime \prime} \neq 0 \} \\ & = \left(1 - e ^ {- \| \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime} \|}\right) + \left(1 - e ^ {- \| \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime \prime} \|}\right) \\ & \leq \| \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime} \| + \| \lambda_ {n} ^ {\prime \prime} \| \\ & = \| \lambda - \lambda_ {n} \| \to 0, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { u d } \xi$ 

Conversely, let $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { u d } \xi$ . Then for any $B \in S$ and $n \in \mathsf N$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l}P \{\xi_ {n} B = 0 \}&\geq P \{\xi_ {n} = 0 \}\\&\rightarrow P \{\xi = 0 \}\\&= e ^ {- \| \lambda \|} > 0.\end{array}
$$

Since $( \log x ) ^ { \prime } = x ^ { - 1 } \leq 1$ on every interval $[ \varepsilon , 1 ]$ with $\varepsilon > 0$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \| \lambda - \lambda_ {n} \| & \lesssim & \sup _ {B} | \lambda B - \lambda_ {n} B | \\ & = & \sup _ {B} \left| \log P \{\xi B = 0 \} - \log P \{\xi_ {n} B = 0 \} \right| \\ & \lesssim & \sup _ {B} \left| P \{\xi B = 0 \} - P \{\xi_ {n} B = 0 \} \right| \\ & \leq & \| \mathcal {L} (\xi) - \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {n}) \| \to 0, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\lambda _ { n } \overset { u } { \to } \lambda$ 

Now let $\eta$ and the $\eta _ { n }$ be random measures satisfying $\eta _ { n } \xrightarrow [ ] { u P } \eta$ . To obtain $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { u d } \xi$ , it is enough to show that, for any sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , the desired convergence holds along a further sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ . By Lemma 5.2 we may then assume that $\eta _ { n } \xrightarrow [ ] { u } \eta$ a.s. Letting the processes $\xi$ and $\xi _ { n }$ be conditionally independent and Poisson distributed with intensities $\eta$ and $\eta _ { n }$ , respectively, we conclude from the previous case that 

$$
\left\| \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {n} \mid \eta_ {n}) - \mathcal {L} (\xi \mid \eta) \right\|\rightarrow 0 \text { a.s. },
$$

and so by dominated convergence, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\| \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {n}) - \mathcal {L} (\xi) \right\| = \left\| E \Big \{\mathcal {L} (\xi_ {n} | \eta_ {n}) - \mathcal {L} (\xi | \eta) \Big \} \right\| \\ = \sup _ {| f | \leq 1} \left| E \Big (E \{f (\xi_ {n}) | \eta_ {n} \} - E \{f (\xi) | \eta \} \Big) \right| \\ \leq \sup _ {| f | \leq 1} E \Big | E \{f (\xi_ {n}) | \eta_ {n} \} - E \{f (\xi) | \eta \} \Big | \\ \leq E \Big \| \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {n} | \eta_ {n}) - \mathcal {L} (\xi | \eta) \Big \| \to 0, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { u d } \xi$ 

For measure-valued processes $X ^ { n }$ with rcll paths, we may characterize tightness in terms of the real-valued projections 

$$
X _ {t} ^ {n} f = \int f (s) X _ {t} ^ {n} (d s), \quad f \in \hat {C} ^ {+}.
$$

Theorem 23.23 (measure-valued processes) Let $X ^ { 1 } , X ^ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be vaguely rcll processes in $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ , where $S$ is lcscH. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $( X ^ { n } )$ is vaguely tight in $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathscr { M } _ { S } }$ , 

(ii) $( X ^ { n } f )$ is tight in $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } _ { + } }$ for every $f \in \hat { C } _ { S } ^ { + }$ 

Proof: Let $( X ^ { n } f )$ be tight for every $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { + }$ , and fix any $\varepsilon > 0$ . Let $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be such as in Theorem A5.7, and choose some compact sets $B _ { 1 } , B _ { 2 } , \ldots$ $\subset D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } _ { + } }$ with 

$$
P \left\{X ^ {n} f _ {k} \in B _ {k} \right\} \geq 1 - \varepsilon 2 ^ {- k}, \quad k, n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{22}
$$

Then $A = \cap _ { k } \{ \mu ; \mu f _ { k } \in B _ { k } \}$ is relatively compact in $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathscr { M } _ { S } }$ , and (22) yields $P \{ X ^ { n } \in A \} \geq 1 - \varepsilon$ ✷ 

Next we consider convergence of random sets. Given an lcscH space $S ,$ , let $\mathcal { F } , \mathcal { G }$ , be the classes of closed, open, and compact subsets of S. We endow $\mathcal { F }$ with the Fell topology, generated by the sets 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} \big \{F \in \mathcal {F};   F \cap G \neq \emptyset \big \}, & G \in \mathcal {G}, \\ \big \{F \in \mathcal {F};   F \cap K = \emptyset \big \}, & K \in \mathcal {K}. \end{array}
$$

Some basic properties of this topology are summarized in Theorem A6.1. In particular, $\mathcal { F }$ is compact and metrizable, and the set $\{ F ; F \cap B = \emptyset \}$ is universally measurable for every $B \in \hat { S }$ 

A random closed set in S is defined as a random element $\varphi$ in $\mathcal { F }$ . Write $\varphi \cap B = \varphi B$ for any $B \in \hat { S }$ , and note that the probabilities $P \{ \varphi B = \varnothing \}$ are well defined. For any random closed set $\varphi _ { : }$ , we introduce the class 

$$
\hat {\mathcal {S}} _ {\varphi} = \Big \{B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}}; P \{\varphi B ^ {o} = \emptyset \} = P \{\varphi \bar {B} = \emptyset \} \Big \},
$$

which is separating by Lemma A6.2. We may now state the basic convergence criterion for random sets. 

Theorem 23.24 (convergence of random sets, Norberg, OK) Let $\varphi , \varphi _ { 1 } , \varphi _ { 2 } ,$ . . . be random closed sets in an lcscH space $S _ { i }$ , and fix a separating class $\mathcal { U } \subset \hat { \mathcal { S } } _ { \varphi }$ Then $\varphi _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \varphi \ i f f$ 

$$
P \{\varphi_ {n} U = \emptyset \} \to P \{\varphi U = \emptyset \}, \quad U \in \mathcal {U}.\tag{23}
$$

In particular, we may take $\mathcal { U } = \hat { \mathcal { S } } _ { \varphi }$ 

Proof: Write 

$$
\begin{array}{c} h (B) = P \{\varphi B \neq \emptyset \}, \\ h _ {n} (B) = P \{\varphi_ {n} B \neq \emptyset \}. \end{array}
$$

If $\varphi _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \varphi$ , Theorem 5.25 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h (B ^ {o}) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} h _ {n} (B) \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} h _ {n} (B) \leq h (\bar {B}), \quad B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}}, \end{array}
$$

and so for any $\boldsymbol { B } \in \hat { \mathcal { S } } _ { \varphi }$ we have $h _ { n } ( B ) \to h ( B )$ 

Now consider a separating class satisfying (23). Fix any $B \in \hat { S } _ { \varphi }$ , and conclude from (23) that, for any $U , V \in { \mathcal { U } }$ with $U \subset B \subset V$ • 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h (U) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} h _ {n} (B) \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} h _ {n} (B) \leq h (V). \end{array}\tag{24}
$$

Since $\mathcal { U }$ is separating, we may choose some $U _ { k } , V _ { k } \in \mathcal { U }$ with $U _ { k } \ \uparrow \ B ^ { o }$ and $\bar { V } _ { k } \downarrow \bar { B }$ . Here clearly 

$$
\begin{array}{c} U _ {k} \uparrow B ^ {o} \Rightarrow \{\varphi U _ {k} \neq \emptyset \} \uparrow \{\varphi B ^ {o} \neq \emptyset \} \\ \Rightarrow h (U _ {k}) \uparrow h (B ^ {o}) = h (B), \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \bar {V} _ {k} \downarrow \bar {B} \Rightarrow \{\varphi \bar {V} _ {k} \neq \emptyset \} \downarrow \{\varphi \bar {B} \neq \emptyset \} \\ \Rightarrow h (\bar {V} _ {k}) \downarrow h (\bar {B}) = h (B), \end{array}
$$

where the finite-intersection property was used in the second line. In view of (24), we get $h _ { n } ( B ) \to h ( B )$ , and (23) follows with $\boldsymbol { \mathcal U } = \hat { \boldsymbol S } _ { \varphi }$ 

Since $\mathcal { F }$ is compact, the sequence $\left( \varphi _ { n } \right)$ is relatively compact by Theorem 23.2. For any sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , we obtain $\varphi _ { n } \ { \stackrel { d } { \to } } \ \psi$ along a further subsequence $N ^ { \prime \prime }$ , for a random closed set $\psi .$ . Combining the direct statement with (23), we get A 

$$
P \{\varphi B = \emptyset \} = P \{\psi B = \emptyset \}, \quad B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}} _ {\varphi} \cap \hat {\mathcal {S}} _ {\psi}.\tag{25}
$$

Since $\hat { S } _ { \varphi } \cap \hat { S } _ { \psi }$ is separating by Lemma A6.2, we may approximate as before to extend (25) to any compact set B. The class of sets $\{ F ; F \cap K = \emptyset \}$ with compact K is clearly a π-system, and so a monotone-class argument yields $\varphi \triangleq \psi$ . Since $N ^ { \prime }$ is arbitrary, we obtain $\varphi _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \varphi$ along N. ✷ 

Simple point processes allow the dual descriptions as integer-valued random measures or locally finite random sets. The corresponding notions of conver gence are diferent, and we proceed to clarify how they are related. Since the mapping $\mu \mapsto$ supp $\mu$ is continuous on $\mathcal { N } _ { S }$ , the convergence $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d }$ ξ implies supp $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to }$ supp ξ. Conversely, if $E \xi$ and $E \xi _ { n }$ are locally finite, then by Theorem 23.24 and Proposition 23.25, we have $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ whenever supp $\xi _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \operatorname { s u p p } \xi$ and $E \xi _ { n } \overset { v } { \to } E \xi$ . Here we give a precise criterion. 

Theorem 23.25 (convergence of point processes) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ . be point processes on S with ξ simple, and fix any dissecting ring $\mathcal { U } \subset \hat { S } _ { \xi }$ and semi-ring $\mathcal { T } \subset \mathcal { U }$ . Then $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi \mathrm { ~ } i f f$ 

$$
\text {(i)} \quad P \{\xi_ {n} U = 0 \} \rightarrow P \{\xi U = 0 \}, \qquad U \in \mathcal {U},
$$

(ii) lim sup P ξ<sub>n</sub>I > 1 P ξI > 1 , I . n→∞ 

Proof: The necessity holds by Lemma 23.17. Now assume $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i } )$ . We may choose and to be countable. Define $\eta ( U ) = \xi U \wedge 1$ and $\eta _ { n } ( U ) = \xi _ { n } U \wedge 1$ for $U \in \mathcal { U }$ . Taking repeated diferences in (i), we get $\eta _ { n } \overset { d } { \to } \eta$ for the product topology on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { u }$ . Hence, Theorem 5.31 yields some processes $\widetilde { \eta } \overset { d } { = } \eta$ and $\widetilde { \eta } _ { n } \overset { d } { = } \eta _ { n } ,$ such that a.s. $\tilde { \eta } _ { n } ( U ) \to \tilde { \eta } ( U )$ for all $U \in \mathcal { U }$ . By a transfer argument, we may choose $\tilde { \xi } _ { n } \overset { d } { = } \xi _ { n }$ and $\tilde { \xi } \overset { d } { = } \xi ,$ , such that a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \tilde {\eta} _ {n} (U) = \tilde {\xi} _ {n} U \wedge 1, \\ \tilde {\eta} (U) = \tilde {\xi} U \wedge 1, \quad U \in \mathcal {U}. \end{array}
$$

We may then assume that $\eta _ { n } ( U ) \to \eta ( U )$ for all $U \in \mathcal { U }$ a.s. 

Now fix an $\omega \in \Omega$ with $\eta _ { n } ( U ) \to \eta ( U )$ for all $U \in { \mathcal { U } } .$ , and let $U \in \mathcal { U }$ be arbitrary. Splitting U into disjoint sets $I _ { 1 } , \ldots , I _ { m } \in \mathcal { T }$ with $\xi I _ { k } \le 1$ for all $k \leq m$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \eta_ {n} (U) \to \eta (U) \leq \xi U \\ = \sum_ {j} \xi I _ {j} = \sum_ {j} \eta (I _ {j}) \\ \leftarrow \sum_ {j} \eta_ {n} (I _ {j}) \\ \leq \sum_ {j} \xi_ {n} I _ {j} = \xi_ {n} U, \end{array}
$$

and so as $n \to \infty$ , we have a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \left\{\xi_ {n} U \wedge 1 \right\} & \leq \xi U \\ & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \xi_ {n} U, \quad U \in \mathcal {U}. \end{array}\tag{26}
$$

Next we note that, for any $h , k \in Z _ { + }$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left\{k \leq h \leq 1 \right\} ^ {c} = \left\{h > 1 \right\} \cup \left\{h <   k \wedge 2 \right\} \\ = \left\{k > 1 \right\} \cup \left\{h = 0,   k = 1 \right\} \cup \left\{h > 1 \geq k \right\}, \end{array}
$$

where all unions are disjoint. Substituting $h = \xi I$ and $k = \xi _ { n } I$ , and using (ii) and (26), we get 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} P \Bigl \{\xi I <   \xi_ {n} I \wedge 2 \Bigr \} = 0, \quad I \in \mathcal {I}.\tag{27}
$$

Letting $U \in \mathcal { U }$ be a union of disjoint sets $I _ { 1 } , \ldots , I _ { m } \in \mathcal { T }$ , we get by (27) 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \bigl \{\xi_ {n} U > \xi U \bigr \} & \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} P \bigcup_ {j} \bigl \{\xi_ {n} I _ {j} > \xi I _ {j} \bigr \} \\ & \leq P \bigcup_ {j} \bigl \{\xi I _ {j} > 1 \bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

By dominated convergence, we can make the right-hand side arbitrarily small, and so $P \{ \xi _ { n } U > \xi U \}  0$ . Combining with (26) gives $P \{ \xi _ { n } U \neq \xi U \}  0$ 2 which means that $\xi _ { n } U \overset { P } {  } \xi U$ . Hence, $\xi _ { n } f \overset { P } { \to } \xi f$ for every $f \in \mathcal { U } _ { + }$ , and Theorem 23.16 (i) yields $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ ✷

Show that $\xi _ { n } \xrightarrow { v d } \xi$ implies $\varphi _ { n } \stackrel { d } { \to } \varphi$ . Further show by an example that the reverse implication may fail. 

17. For an lcscH space S, let $\mathcal { U } \subset \hat { \mathcal { S } }$ be separating. Show that if $K \subset G$ with K compact and $G$ open, there exists a $U \in \mathcal { U }$ with $K \subset U ^ { o } \subset \bar { U } \subset G$ . (Hint: First choose $B , C \in { \hat { S } }$ with $K \subset B ^ { o } \subset \bar { B } \subset C ^ { o } \subset \bar { C } \subset G . )$ 

Chapter 24 

# Large Deviations

Exponential rates, cumulant-generating function, Legendre–Fenchel transform, rate function, large deviations in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ , Schilder’s theorem, regularization and uniqueness, large deviation principle, goodness, exponential tightness, weak and functional LDPs, continuous mapping, random sequences, exponential equivalence, perturbed dynamical systems, empirical distributions, relative entropy, functional law of the iterated logarithm 

In many contexts throughout probability theory and its applications, we need to estimate the asymptotic rate of decline of various tail probabilities. Since such problems might be expected to lead to tedious technical calculations, we may be surprised and delighted to learn about the existence of a powerful general theory, providing such asymptotic rates with great accuracy. Indeed, in many cases of interest, the asymptotic rate turns out to be exponential, and the associated rate function can often be obtained explicitly from the underlying distributions. 

In its simplest setting, the theory of large deviation provides exponential rates of convergence in the weak law of large numbers. Here we consider some i.i.d. random variables $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . with mean m and cumulant-generating function $\Lambda ( u ) = \log E e ^ { u \xi _ { i } } < \infty$ , and write $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { \xi } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { k \le n } \xi _ { k } } \end{array}$ . For any $x > m$ we show that the tail probabilities $P \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } > x \}$ tend to 0 at an exponential rate $I ( x )$ , given by the Legendre–Fenchel transform $\Lambda ^ { * }$ of $\Lambda .$ . In higher dimensions, it is convenient to state the result in the more general form 

$$
- n ^ {- 1} \log P \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \} \rightarrow I (B) = \inf _ {x \in B} I (x),
$$

where B is restricted to a suitable class of continuity sets. In this standard form of a large-deviation principle with rate function $I ,$ the result extends to a wide range of contexts throughout probability theory. 

For a striking example of fundamental importance in statistical mechanics, we may mention Sanov’s theorem, which provides similar large deviation bounds for the empirical distributions of a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with a common distribution $\mu .$ . Here the rate function I, defined on the space of probability measures ν on $\mathsf { R } _ { : }$ , agrees with the relative entropy $H ( \nu | \mu )$ . Another important case is Schilder’s theorem for a family of rescaled Brownian motions in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , where the rate function becomes $I ( x ) = { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \| \dot { x } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ —the squared norm in the Cameron–Martin space first encountered in Chapter 19. The latter result can be used to derive the powerful Fredlin–Wentzell estimates for randomly perturbed dynamical systems. It also yields a short proof of Strassen’s law of the iterated logarithm, a stunning extension of the classical Khinchin law from Chapter 14. 

Modern proofs of those and other large deviation results rely on some general extension principles, which explains the wide applicability of the present ideas. In addition to some rather elementary and straightforward methods of continuity and approximation, we consider the more sophisticated and extremely powerful principles of inverse continuous mapping and projective limits, both of which play crucial roles in ensuing applications. We may also stress the significance of the notion of exponential tightness, and of the essential equivalence between the setwise and functional formulations of the large-deviation principle. 

Large deviation theory is arguably one of the most technical areas of modern probability. For a beginning student, it is then essential not to get distracted by topological subtleties or elaborate computations. Many results are therefore stated under simplifying assumptions. Likewise, we postpone our discussion of the general principles, until the reader has become well acquainted with some basic ideas in a simple and concrete setting. For those reasons, important applications appear both at the beginning and at the end of the chapter, separated by some more abstract discussions of general notions and principles. 

Returning to the elementary setting of i.i.d. random variables $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ we write $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } } \end{array}$ and $\bar { \xi } _ { n } = S _ { n } / n$ . If $m = E \xi$ exists and is finite, then $P \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } > x \}  0$ for all $x \ > \ m$ by the weak law of large numbers. Under stronger moment conditions, the rate of convergence turns out to be exponential and can be estimated with great accuracy. This elementary but quite technical observation, along with its multi-dimensional counterpart, lie at the core of large-deviation theory, and provide both a general pattern and a point of departure for the more advanced developments. For motivation, we begin with some simple observations. 

Lemma 24.1 (tail rate) For i.i.d. random variables $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots _ { n }$ 

(i) $n ^ { - 1 } \log P \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } \geq x \} \to \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } n ^ { - 1 } \log P \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } \geq x \} \equiv - h ( x ) , \ x \in { \mathsf { R } } ,$ 

(ii) h is [0, ]-valued, non-decreasing, and convex, 

(iii) $h ( x ) < \infty \Leftrightarrow P \{ \xi \geq x \} > 0 .$ 

Proof: (i) Writing $p _ { n } = P \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } \geq x \}$ , we get for any $m , n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & p _ {m + n} = P \bigl \{S _ {m + n} \geq (m + n) x \bigr \} \\ & \qquad \geq P \bigl \{S _ {m} \geq m x, S _ {m + n} - S _ {m} \geq n x \bigr \} = p _ {m} p _ {n}. \end{array}
$$

Taking logarithms, we conclude that the sequence $- \log p _ { n }$ is sub-additive, and the assertion follows by Lemma 25.19. 

(ii) The first two assertions are obvious. To prove the convexity, let x, $y \in \mathsf { R }$ be arbitrary, and proceed as before to get 

$$
P \left\{S _ {2 n} \geq n (x + y) \right\} \geq P \left\{S _ {n} \geq n x \right\} P \left\{S _ {n} \geq n y \right\}.
$$

Taking logarithms, dividing by $2 n$ , and letting $n \to \infty$ , we obtain 

$$
h \left\{\frac {1}{2} (x + y) \right\} \leq \frac {1}{2} \left\{h (x) + h (y) \right\}, \quad x, y > 0.
$$

(iii) If $P \{ \xi \ge x \} = 0$ , then $P \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } \ge x \} = 0$ for all $n _ { \colon }$ , and so $h ( x ) = \infty$ Conversely, (i) yields log $P \{ \xi \ \ge \ x \} \ \le \ - h ( x )$ , and so $h ( x ) \ = \ \infty$ implies $P \{ \xi \ge x \} = 0$ ✷ 

To identify the limit in Lemma 24.1, we need some further notation, here given for convenience directly in d dimensions. For any random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ we introduce the cumulant-generating function 

$$
\Lambda (u) = \Lambda_ {\xi} (u) = \log E e ^ {u \xi}, \quad u \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.\tag{1}
$$

Note that Λ is convex, since by H¨older’s inequality we have for any $u , v \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and $p , q > 0$ with $p + q = 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\Lambda (p u + q v) = \log E \exp \bigl \{(p u + q v) \xi \bigr \}} \\ & {\qquad \leq \log \bigl \{(E e ^ {u \xi}) ^ {p} (E e ^ {v \xi}) ^ {q} \bigr \}} \\ & {\qquad = p \Lambda (u) + q \Lambda (v).} \end{array}
$$

The surface $z = \Lambda ( u )$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d + 1 }$ is determined by the class of supporting hyper-planes<sup>1</sup> of diferent slopes, and we note that the plane with slope $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ (or normal vector $( 1 , - x ) )$ has equation 

$$
z + \Lambda^ {*} (x) = x u, \quad u \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d},
$$

where $\Lambda ^ { * }$ is the Legendre–Fenchel transform of $\Lambda ,$ , given by 

$$
\Lambda^ {*} (x) = \sup _ {u \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}} \Bigl \{u x - \Lambda (u) \Bigr \}, \quad x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.\tag{2}
$$

We can often compute $\Lambda ^ { * }$ explicitly. Here we consider two simple cases, both needed below. The results may be proved by elementary calculus. 

Lemma 24.2 (Gaussian and Bernoulli distributions) 

(i) When $\boldsymbol { \xi } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { d } )$ is standard Gaussian in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

$$
\Lambda_ {\xi} ^ {*} (x) \equiv \frac {1}{2} | x | ^ {2}, \quad x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d},
$$

(ii) when $\xi \in \{ 0 , 1 \}$ with $P \{ \xi = 1 \} = p \in ( 0 , 1 )$ 大

$$
\Lambda_ {\xi} ^ {*} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} x \log \frac {x}{p} + (1 - x) \log \frac {1 - x}{1 - p}, & x \in [ 0, 1 ], \\ \infty , & x \notin [ 0, 1 ]. \end{array} \right.
$$

The function $\Lambda ^ { * }$ is again convex, since for any $x , y \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and for $p , q$ as before, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Lambda^ {*} (p x + q y) = \sup _ {u} \Big (p \left\{u x - \Lambda (u) \right\} + q \left\{u y - \Lambda (u) \right\} \Big) \\ \qquad \leq p \sup _ {u} \Big \{u x - \Lambda (u) \Big \} + q \sup _ {u} \Big \{u y - \Lambda (u) \Big \} \\ \qquad = p \Lambda^ {*} (x) + q \Lambda^ {*} (y). \end{array}
$$

If $\Lambda < \infty$ near the origin, then $m = E \xi$ exists and agrees with the gradient $\nabla \Lambda ( 0 )$ . Thus, the surface $z = \Lambda ( u )$ has tangent hyper-plane $z =$ mu at 0, and we conclude that $\Lambda ^ { * } ( m ) = 0$ and $\Lambda ^ { * } ( x ) > 0$ for $x \neq m$ . If $\xi$ is truly d -dimensional, then Λ is strictly convex at 0, and $\Lambda ^ { * }$ is finite and continuous near m. For $d = 1$ , we sometimes need the corresponding one-sided statements, which are easily derived by dominated convergence. 

The following key result identifies the function h in Lemma 24.1. For simplicity, we assume that $m = E \xi$ exists in $[ - \infty , \infty )$ 

Theorem 24.3 (rate function, Cram´er, Chernof) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be i.i.d. random variables with $m = E \xi < \infty$ . Then 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \log P \left\{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq x \right\}\rightarrow - \Lambda^ {*} (x), \quad x \geq m.\tag{3}
$$

Proof: Using Chebyshev’s inequality and (1), we get for any $u > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \Big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq x \Big \} = P \Big \{e ^ {u S _ {n}} \geq e ^ {n u x} \Big \} \\ & \quad \leq e ^ {- n u x} E e ^ {u S _ {n}} \\ & \quad = \exp \Big \{n \Lambda (u) - n u x \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \log P \left\{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq x \right\} \leq \Lambda (u) - u x.
$$

This remains true for $u \leq 0$ , since in that case $\Lambda ( u ) - u x \geq 0$ for $x \ge m$ Hence, by (2), we have the upper bound 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \log P \left\{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq x \right\} \leq - \Lambda^ {*} (x), \quad x \geq m, n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{4}
$$

To derive a matching lower bound, we first assume that $\Lambda < \infty$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ Then Λ is smooth on $( 0 , \infty )$ with $\Lambda ^ { \prime } ( 0 + ) = m$ and $\Lambda ^ { \prime } ( \infty ) =$ ess sup $\xi \equiv b ,$ , and so for any $a \in ( m , b )$ we can choose a $u > 0$ with $\Lambda ^ { \prime } ( u ) = a$ . Let $\eta , \eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , . . .$ be i.i.d. with distribution 

$$
P \{\eta \in B \} = e ^ {- \Lambda (u)} E \left(e ^ {u \xi}; \xi \in B\right), \quad B \in \mathcal {B}.\tag{5}
$$

Then $\Lambda _ { \eta } ( r ) = \Lambda _ { \xi } ( r + u ) - \Lambda _ { \xi } ( u )$ , and so $E \eta = \Lambda _ { \eta } ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) = \Lambda _ { \xi } ^ { \prime } ( u ) = a$ . For any $\varepsilon > 0$ , we get by (5) 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Big \{\Big | \bar {\xi} _ {n} - a \Big | <   \varepsilon \Big \} = e ^ {n \Lambda (u)} E \Big \{\exp (- n u \bar {\eta} _ {n});   | \bar {\eta} _ {n} - a | <   \varepsilon \Big \} \\ \geq \exp \Big \{n \Lambda (u) - n u (a + \varepsilon) \Big \} P \Big \{| \bar {\eta} _ {n} - a | <   \varepsilon \Big \}. \end{array}\tag{6}
$$

Here the last probability tends to 1 by the law of large numbers, and so by (2) 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Big \{\Big | \bar {\xi} _ {n} - a \Big | <   \varepsilon \Big \} & \geq \Lambda (u) - u (a + \varepsilon) \\ & \geq - \Lambda^ {*} (a + \varepsilon). \end{array}
$$

Fixing any $x \in ( m , b )$ and putting $a = x + \varepsilon$ , we get for small enough $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
\liminf _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq x \Bigr \} \geq - \Lambda^ {*} (x + 2 \varepsilon).
$$

Since $\Lambda ^ { * }$ is continuous on $( m , b )$ by convexity, we may let $\varepsilon \to 0$ and combine with (4) to obtain (3). 

The result for $x > b$ is trivial, since in that case both sides of (3) equal $- \infty$ If instead $x = b < \infty$ , then both sides equal log $P \{ \xi = b \}$ , the left side by a simple computation and the right side by an elementary estimate. Finally, let $x = m > - \infty$ . Since the statement is trivial when $\xi = m { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , we may assume that $b > m$ . For any $y \in ( m , b )$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l}0 \geq n ^ {- 1} \log P \bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq m \bigr \}\\\geq n ^ {- 1} P \bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq y \bigr \}\\\rightarrow - \Lambda^ {*} (y) > - \infty .\end{array}
$$

Here $\Lambda ^ { * } ( y )  \Lambda ^ { * } ( m ) = 0$ by continuity, and (3) follows for $x \ = \ m$ . This completes the proof when $\Lambda < \infty$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

The case where $\Lambda ( u ) = \infty$ for some $u > 0$ may be handled by truncation. Thus, for any $r > m$ we consider the random variables $\xi _ { k } ^ { r } = \xi _ { k } \wedge r$ . Writing $\Lambda _ { r }$ and ${ \Lambda } _ { r } ^ { * }$ for the associated functions Λ and $\Lambda ^ { * }$ , we get for $x \ge m \ge E \xi ^ { r }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \geq x \Bigr \} \geq n ^ {- 1} \log P \Bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} ^ {r} \geq x \Bigr \} \\ \to - \Lambda_ {r} ^ {*} (x). \end{array}\tag{7}
$$

Now $\Lambda _ { r } ( u ) \uparrow \Lambda ( u )$ by monotone convergence as $r  \infty$ , and by Dini’s theorem<sup>2</sup> the convergence is uniform on every compact interval where $\Lambda < \infty$ . Since also $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ is unbounded on the set where $\Lambda < \infty$ , it follows easily that $\Lambda _ { r } ^ { * } ( x )  \Lambda ^ { * } ( x )$ for all $x \geq m$ . The required lower bound is now immediate from (7). ✷ 

We may supplement Lemma 24.1 with a criterion for exponential decline of the tail probabilities $P \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } \geq x \}$ 

Corollary 24.4 (exponential rate) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables with $m = E \xi < \infty$ and $b = \mathrm { e s s } \operatorname { s u p } \xi$ . Then 

(i) for any $x \in ( m , b )$ , the probabilities $P \big \{ \bar { \xi } _ { n } \ge x \big \}$ decrease exponentially if $\Lambda ( \varepsilon ) < \infty$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$ , 

(ii) the exponential decline extends to $x = b \ i f \ P \{ \xi = b \} \in ( 0 , 1 )$ 

Proof: If $\Lambda ( \varepsilon ) < \infty$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$ , then $\Lambda ^ { \prime } ( 0 + ) = m$ by dominated convergence, and so $\Lambda ^ { * } ( x ) > 0$ for all $x > m$ . If instead $\Lambda = \infty \ \mathrm { o n } \ ( 0 , \infty )$ , then $\Lambda ^ { * } ( x ) = 0$ for all $x \geq m$ . The statement for $x = b$ is trivial. ✷ 

The large deviation estimates in Theorem 24.3 are easily extended from intervals $[ x , \infty )$ to arbitrary open or closed sets, which leads to a large-deviation principle for i.i.d. sequences in R. To fulfill our needs in subsequent applications and extensions, we consider a version of the same result in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Motivated by the last result, and to avoid some technical complications, we assume that $\Lambda ( u ) < \infty$ for all $u .$ Write $B ^ { o }$ and $\bar { B } = B ^ { - }$ for the interior and closure of a set B. 

Theorem 24.5 (large deviations in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , Varadhan) Let $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be i.i.d. random vectors in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\Lambda = \Lambda _ { \xi } < \infty$ . Then for any $B \in B ^ { d }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} - \inf _ {x \in B ^ {o}} \Lambda^ {*} (x) & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Bigr \} \\ & \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Bigr \} \leq - \inf _ {x \in \bar {B}} \Lambda^ {*} (x). \end{array}
$$

Proof: To derive the upper bound, fix any $\varepsilon > 0$ . By (2) there exists for every $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ some $u _ { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , such that 

$$
u _ {x} x - \Lambda (u _ {x}) > \left\{\Lambda^ {*} (x) - \varepsilon \right\} \wedge \varepsilon^ {- 1},
$$

and by continuity we may choose an open ball $B _ { x }$ around $x ,$ such that 

$$
u _ {x} y > \Lambda (u _ {x}) + \left\{\Lambda^ {*} (x) - \varepsilon \right\} \wedge \varepsilon^ {- 1}, \quad y \in B _ {x}.
$$

By Chebyshev’s inequality and (1), we get for any $n \in \mathsf N$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B _ {x} \Bigr \} \leq E \exp \Bigl \{u _ {x} S _ {n} - n \inf \bigl (u _ {x} y; y \in B _ {x} \bigr) \Bigr \} \\ \leq \exp \Bigl \{- n \Bigl (\{\Lambda^ {*} (x) - \varepsilon \} \wedge \varepsilon^ {- 1} \Bigr) \Bigr \}. \end{array}\tag{8}
$$

Further note that $\Lambda < \infty$ implies $\Lambda ^ { * } ( x )  \infty$ as $| x | \to \infty$ , at least when $d = 1$ By Lemma 24.1 and Theorem 24.3, we may then choose $r > 0$ so large that 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \log P \left\{\left| \bar {\xi} _ {n} \right| > r \right\} \leq - 1 / \varepsilon , \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{9}
$$

Now let $B \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ be closed. Then the set $\{ x \in B ; | x | \leq r \}$ is compact and may be covered by finitely many balls $B _ { x _ { 1 } } , \ldots , B _ { x _ { m } }$ with centers $x _ { i } \in B$ . By (8) and (9), we get for any $n \in \mathsf N$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Big \} \leq \sum_ {i \leq m} P \Big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B _ {x _ {i}} \Big \} + P \Big \{| \bar {\xi} _ {n} | > r \Big \} \\ \quad \leq \sum_ {i \leq m} \exp \Big \{- n \Big (\{\Lambda^ {*} (x _ {i}) - \varepsilon \} \wedge \varepsilon^ {- 1} \Big) \Big \} + e ^ {- n / \varepsilon} \\ \quad \leq (m + 1) \exp \Big \{- n \Big (\{\Lambda^ {*} (B) - \varepsilon \} \wedge \varepsilon^ {- 1} \Big) \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

where $\Lambda ^ { * } ( B ) = \operatorname* { i n f } _ { x \in B } \Lambda ^ { * } ( x )$ . Hence, 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Bigl \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Bigr \} \leq - \left\{\Lambda^ {*} (B) - \varepsilon \right\} \wedge \varepsilon^ {- 1},
$$

and the upper bound follows since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary. 

Turning to the lower bound, we first assume that $\Lambda ( u ) / | u | \to \infty \mathrm { \ a s \ } | u | \to$ $\infty$ . Fix any open set $B \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and a point $x \in B$ . By compactness and the smoothness of Λ, there exists a $u \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\nabla \Lambda ( u ) = x .$ . Let $\eta , \eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be i.i.d. random vectors with distribution (5), and note as before that ${ E \eta = x }$ For $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough, we get as in (6) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Big \} \geq P \Big \{\Big | \bar {\xi} _ {n} - x \Big | <   \varepsilon \Big \} \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq \exp \Big \{n \Lambda (u) - n u x - n \varepsilon | u | \Big \}   P \Big \{| \bar {\eta} _ {n} - x | <   \varepsilon \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Hence, by the law of large numbers and (2), 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Big \} & \geq \Lambda (u) - u x - \varepsilon | u | \\ & \geq - \Lambda^ {*} (x) - \varepsilon | u |. \end{array}
$$

It remains to let $\varepsilon \to 0$ and take the supremum over $x \in B$ 

To eliminate the growth condition on Λ, let $\zeta , \zeta _ { 1 } , \zeta _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be i.i.d. standard Gaussian random vectors independent of $\xi$ and the $\xi _ { n }$ . Then for any $\sigma > 0$ and $u \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we have by Lemma 24.2 (i) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Lambda_ {\xi + \sigma \zeta} (u) = \Lambda_ {\xi} (u) + \Lambda_ {\zeta} (\sigma u) \\ \qquad = \Lambda_ {\xi} (u) + \frac {1}{2}   \sigma^ {2} | u | ^ {2} \\ \qquad \geq \Lambda_ {\xi} (u), \end{array}
$$

and in particular $\Lambda _ { \xi + \sigma \zeta } ^ { * } \ \leq \ \Lambda _ { \xi } ^ { * }$ . Since also $\Lambda _ { \xi + \sigma \zeta } ( u ) / | u | \geq \sigma ^ { 2 } | u | / 2 \to \infty$ , we note that the previous bound applies to $\xi _ { n } + \sigma \zeta _ { n }$ . Now fix any $x \in B$ as before, and choose $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough that B contains a 2ε-ball around x. Then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Big \{\big | \bar {\xi} _ {n} + \sigma \bar {\zeta} _ {n} - x \big | <   \varepsilon \Big \} \leq P \Big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Big \} + P \Big \{\sigma | \bar {\zeta} _ {n} | \geq \varepsilon \Big \} \\ \leq 2 \left(P \Big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \Big \} \vee P \Big \{\sigma | \bar {\zeta} _ {n} | \geq \varepsilon \Big \}\right). \end{array}
$$

Applying the lower bound to the variables $\bar { \xi } _ { n } + \sigma \bar { \zeta } _ { n }$ and the upper bound to $\bar { \zeta } _ { n } .$ , we get by Lemma 24.2 (i) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - \Lambda_ {\xi} ^ {*} (x) \leq - \Lambda_ {\xi + \sigma \zeta} ^ {*} (x) \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \Big \{\big | \bar {\xi} _ {n} + \sigma \bar {\zeta} _ {n} - x \big | <   \varepsilon \Big \} \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log \left(P \big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \big \} \vee P \big \{\sigma | \bar {\zeta} _ {n} | \geq \varepsilon \big \}\right) \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \log P \big \{\bar {\xi} _ {n} \in B \big \} \vee (- \varepsilon^ {2} / 2 \sigma^ {2}). \end{array}
$$

The desired lower bound now follows, as we let $\sigma \to 0$ and then take the supremum over all $x \in B$ ✷ 

We can also establish large-deviation results in function spaces. The following theorem is basic and sets the pattern for more complex results. For convenience, we may write $C = C _ { [ 0 , 1 ] , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ and $C _ { 0 } ^ { k } = \{ x \in \bar { C } ^ { k } ; x _ { 0 } = 0 \}$ . We also introduce the Cameron–Martin space $H _ { 1 }$ , consisting of all absolutely continuous functions $x \in C _ { 0 }$ with a Radon–Nikodym derivative ${ \dot { x } } \in L ^ { 2 }$ , so that $\begin{array} { r } { \| \dot { x } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } | \dot { x } _ { t } | ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ 

Theorem 24.6 (large deviations of Brownian motion, Schilder) Let X be a d-dimensional Brownian motion on [0, 1]. Then for any Borel set $B \subset C _ { [ 0 , 1 ] , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} - \inf _ {x \in B ^ {o}} I (x) & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^ {2} \log P \{\varepsilon X \in B \} \\ & \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^ {2} \log P \{\varepsilon X \in B \} \leq - \inf _ {x \in \bar {B}} I (x), \end{array}
$$

where 

$$
I (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {1}{2} \| \dot {x} \| _ {2} ^ {2}, & x \in H _ {1}, \\ \infty , & x \notin H _ {1}. \end{array} \right.
$$

The proof requires a simple topological fact. 

Lemma 24.7 (level sets) The level sets $L _ { r }$ below are compact in $C _ { [ 0 , 1 ] , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } \colon$ 

$$
L _ {r} = I ^ {- 1} [ 0, r ] = \left\{x \in H _ {1}; \| \dot {x} \| _ {2} ^ {2} \leq 2 r \right\}, \quad r > 0.
$$

Proof: Cauchy’s inequality gives 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} | x _ {t} - x _ {s} | \leq \int_ {s} ^ {t} | \dot {x} _ {u} |   d u \\ & \leq (t - s) ^ {1 / 2} \| \dot {x} \| _ {2}, \quad 0 \leq s <   t \leq 1, x \in H _ {1}. \end{array}
$$

By the Arzel`a–Ascoli Theorem A5.2, the set $L _ { r }$ is then relatively compact in C. It is also weakly compact in the Hilbert space $H _ { 1 }$ with norm $\lVert x \rVert = \lVert \dot { x } \rVert _ { 2 }$ Thus, every sequence $x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots \in L _ { r }$ has a sub-sequence that converges in both C and $H _ { 1 }$ , say with limits $x \in C$ and $y \in L _ { r }$ , respectively. For every $t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , the sequence $x _ { n } ( t )$ then converges in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ to both $x ( t )$ and $y ( t )$ , and we get $x = y \in L _ { r }$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 24.6: To establish the lower bound, fix any open set $B \subset C$ . Since $I = \infty$ outside $H _ { 1 }$ , it sufices to prove that 

$$
- I (x) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^ {2} \log P \{\varepsilon X \in B \}, \quad x \in B \cap H _ {1}.\tag{10}
$$

Then note as in Lemma 1.37 that $C _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ is dense in $H _ { 1 }$ , and also that $\| x \| _ { \infty } \leq$ $\| { \dot { x } } \| _ { 1 } \leq \| { \dot { x } } \| _ { 2 }$ for any $x \in H _ { 1 }$ . Hence, for every $x \in B \cap H _ { 1 }$ , there exist some functions $x _ { n } \in B \cap C _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ with $I ( x _ { n } ) \to I ( x )$ , and it sufices to prove (10) for $x \in B \cap C _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ 

For small enough $h > 0$ , Theorem 19.23 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \{\varepsilon X \in B \} \geq P \Big \{\| \varepsilon X - x \| _ {\infty} <   h \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \Big (\mathcal {E} \Big \{- (\dot {x} / \varepsilon) \cdot X \Big \} _ {1}; \| \varepsilon X \| _ {\infty} <   h \Big). \end{array}\tag{11}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \log \mathcal {E} \Bigl \{- (\dot {x} / \varepsilon) \cdot X \Bigr \} _ {1} = - \varepsilon^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {1} \dot {x} _ {t}   d X _ {t} - \varepsilon^ {- 2} I (x) \\ = - \varepsilon^ {- 1} \dot {x} _ {1} X _ {1} + \varepsilon^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {1} \ddot {x} _ {t}   X _ {t}   d t - \varepsilon^ {- 2} I (x), \end{array}
$$

and so by (11), 

$$
\varepsilon^ {2} \log P \{\varepsilon X \in B \} \geq - I (x) - h | \dot {x} _ {1} | - h \| \ddot {x} \| _ {1} + \varepsilon^ {2} \log P \Bigl \{\| \varepsilon X \| _ {\infty} <   h \Bigr \}.
$$

Now (10) follows as we let $\varepsilon \to 0$ and then $h  0$ 

Turning to the upper bound, fix any closed set $B \subset C$ , and let $B _ { h }$ be the closed h -neighborhood of B. Letting $X _ { n }$ be the n -segment, polygonal approximation of X with $X _ { n } ( k / n ) = X ( k / n )$ for $k \leq n$ , we note that

P \{\varepsilon X \in B \} \leq P \left\{\varepsilon X _ {n} \in B _ {h} \right\} + P \left\{\varepsilon \| X - X _ {n} \| > h \right\}.\tag{12}
$$

Writing $I ( B _ { h } ) = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ I ( x ) ; x \in B _ { h } \}$ , we obtain

P \Bigl \{\varepsilon X _ {n} \in B _ {h} \Bigr \} \leq P \Bigl \{I (\varepsilon X _ {n}) \geq I (B _ {h}) \Bigr \}.

Here $2 I ( X _ { n } )$ is a sum of nd variables $\xi _ { i k } ^ { 2 }$ , where the $\xi _ { i k }$ are i.i.d. $N ( 0 , 1 )$ , and so by Lemma 24.2 (i) and an interpolated version of Theorem 24.5,

$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \Big \{\varepsilon \| X - X _ {n} \| > h \Big \} \leq n   P \Big \{\varepsilon \| X \| > h \sqrt {n} / 2 \Big \} \\ & \qquad \leq 2   n d   P \Big \{\varepsilon^ {2} \xi^ {2} > h ^ {2} n / 4 d \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^ {2} \log P \Bigl \{\varepsilon \| X - X _ {n} \| > h \Bigr \} \leq - h ^ {2} n / 8 d.\tag{14}
$$

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon^ {2} \log P \{\varepsilon X \in B \} \leq - I (B _ {h}) \wedge (h ^ {2} n / 8 d),
$$

and as $n \to \infty$ we obtain the upper bound $- I ( B _ { h } )$ 

It remains to show that ${ \cal I } ( B _ { h } ) \ \uparrow \ { \cal I } ( B )$ as $h \  \ 0 .$ Then fix any $r \_ >$ $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { h } I ( B _ { h } )$ . For every $h > 0$ , we may choose an $x _ { h } \in B _ { h }$ with $I ( x _ { h } ) \leq r _ { : }$ and by Lemma 24.7 we may extract a convergent sequence $x _ { h _ { n } } \to x$ with $h _ { n }  0$ , such that even $I ( x ) \leq r$ . Since also $x \in \cap _ { h } B _ { h } \ = \ B$ , we obtain $I ( B ) \leq r$ , as required. ✷ 

The last two theorems suggest the following abstraction. Letting $\xi _ { \varepsilon } , \varepsilon > 0$ 2 be random elements in a metric space $S$ with Borel σ-field ${ \mathbf { } } S .$ , we say that the family $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ satisfies a large-deviation principle (LDP) with rate function $I \colon S  [ 0 , \infty ]$ , if for any $B \in S$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} - \inf _ {x \in B ^ {o}} I (x) & \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \} \\ & \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \} \leq - \inf _ {x \in \bar {B}} I (x). \end{array}\tag{15}
$$

For sequences $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots ,$ we require the same condition with the normalizing factor $\varepsilon$ replaced by $n ^ { - 1 }$ . It is often convenient to write $I ( B ) = \mathrm { i n f } _ { x \in B } I ( x )$ Writing $\boldsymbol { S _ { I } }$ for the class $\{ B \in { \mathcal { S } } ; I ( B ^ { o } ) = I ( { \bar { B } } ) \}$ of I-continuity sets, we note that (15) yields the convergence 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \} = - I (B), \quad B \in \mathcal {S} _ {I}.\tag{16}
$$

If $\xi , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . are i.i.d. random vectors in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\Lambda ( u ) = E e ^ { u \xi } < \infty$ for all $u ,$ then by Theorem 24.5 the averages $\bar { \xi } _ { n }$ satisfy the LDP in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with rate function $\Lambda ^ { * }$ . If instead X is a d -dimensional Brownian motion on [0, 1], then Theorem 24.6 shows that the processes $\varepsilon ^ { 1 / 2 } X$ satisfy the LDP in $C _ { [ 0 , 1 ] , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ , with rate function $\begin{array} { r } { I ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \| \dot { x } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ for $x \in H _ { 1 }$ and $I ( x ) = \infty$ otherwise. 

We show that the rate function I is essentially unique. 

Lemma 24.8 (regularization and uniqueness) Let $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ satisfy an LDP in a metric space S with rate function I. Then 

(i) I can be chosen to be lower semi-continuous, 

(ii) the choice of I in (i) is unique. 

Proof: (i) Assume (15) for some I. Then the function 

$$
J (x) = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {y \to x} I (y), \quad x \in S,
$$

is clearly lower semi-continuous with $J \ \leq \ I .$ . It is also easy to verify that $J ( G ) = I ( G )$ for all open sets $G \subset S$ . Thus, (15) remains true with I replaced by J. 

(ii) Suppose that (15) holds for each of the lower semi-continuous functions I and J, and let $I ( x ) < J ( x )$ for some $x \in S$ . By the semi-continuity of $J ,$ we may choose a neighborhood G of x with $J ( \bar { G } ) > I ( x )$ . Applying (15) to both I and J, we get the contradiction 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - I (x) \leq - I (G) \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in G \} \\ \quad \leq - J (\bar {G}) <   - I (x). \end{array}
$$

Justified by the last result, we may henceforth take the lower semi-continuity to be part of our definition of a rate function. (An arbitrary function I satisfying (15) will then be called a raw rate function.) No regularization is needed in Theorems 24.5 and 24.6, since the associated rate functions $\Lambda ^ { * }$ and I are already lower semi-continuous, the former as the supremum of a family of continuous functions, the latter by Lemma 24.7. 

It is sometimes useful to impose a slightly stronger regularity condition on the function I. Thus, we say that I is good, if the level sets $I ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ] = \{ x \in S \}$ $I ( x ) \ \leq \ r \}$ are compact (rather than just closed). Note that the infimum $I ( B ) = \mathrm { i n f } _ { x \in B } I ( x )$ is then attained for every closed set $B \neq \emptyset$ . The rate functions in Theorems 24.5 and 24.6 are clearly both good. 

A related condition on the family $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ is the exponential tightness 

$$
\inf _ {K} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K \Bigr \} = - \infty ,\tag{17}
$$

where the infimum extends over all compact sets $K \subset S$ . We actually need only the slightly weaker condition of sequential exponential tightness, where (17) is only required along sequences $\varepsilon _ { n } \to 0$ . To simplify our exposition, we often omit the sequential qualification from our statements, and carry out the proofs under the stronger non-sequential hypothesis. 

We finally say that (ξ ) satisfies the weak LDP with rate function I, if the lower bound in (15) holds as stated, while the upper bound is only required for compact sets B. We list some relations between the mentioned properties. 

Lemma 24.9 (goodness, exponential tightness, and weak LDP) Let $\xi _ { \varepsilon } , \varepsilon > 0$ , be random elements in a metric space S. Then 

(i) $i f \left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ satisfies an LDP with rate function I, then (16) holds, and the two conditions are equivalent when I is good,

Proof: (i) Let I be good and satisfy (16). Write $B ^ { h }$ for the closed $h -$ neighborhood of $B \in S$ . Since I is non-increasing on $s ,$ , we have $B ^ { h } \notin S _ { I }$ for at most countably many $h > 0$ . Hence, (16) yields for almost every $h > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \} & \leq \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B ^ {h} \Big \} \\ & = - I (B ^ {h}). \end{array}
$$

To see that $I ( B ^ { h } ) \ d t \ d t I ( \bar { B } )$ as $h  0$ , suppose that instead su $\ni _ { h } I ( B ^ { h } ) < I ( \bar { B } )$ Since I is good, we may choose for every $h > 0$ some $x _ { h } \in B ^ { h }$ with $I ( x _ { h } ) =$ $I ( B ^ { h } )$ , and then extract a convergent sequence $x _ { h _ { n } } \to x \in \hat { B }$ with $h _ { n } \to 0$ Then the lower semi-continuity of I yields the contradiction 

$$
\begin{array}{c} I (\bar {B}) \leq I (x) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} I (x _ {h _ {n}}) \\ \leq \sup _ {h > 0} I (B ^ {h}) <   I (\bar {B}), \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} - I (x) \leq - I (\{x \} ^ {h}) \\ = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in \{x \} ^ {h} \Big \} \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \big \}. \end{array}
$$

The lower bound now follows as we take the supremum over $x \in B ^ { o }$ 

(ii) By (17), we may choose some compact sets $K _ { r }$ satisfying 

$$
\limsup _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K _ {r} \} <   - r, \quad r > 0.\tag{18}
$$

For any closed set $B \subset S$ , we have 

$$
P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \} \leq 2 \left(P \left\{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \cap K _ {r} \right\} \vee P \left\{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K _ {r} \right\}\right), \quad r > 0,

and so, by the weak LDP and (18), 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B \} & \leq - I (B \cap K _ {r}) \wedge r \\ & \leq - I (B) \wedge r. \end{array}

The upper bound now follows as we let $r  \infty$ . Applying the lower bound and (18) to the sets $K _ { r } ^ { c }$ gives 

$$
- I (K _ {r} ^ {c}) \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K _ {r} \Bigr \} <   - r, \quad r > 0,
$$

and so $I ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ] \subset K _ { \iota }$ for all $r > 0$ , which shows that I is good. 

(iii) The suficiency follows from (ii), applied to an arbitrary sequence $\varepsilon _ { n } $ 0. Now let $S$ be separable and complete, and assume that the rate function I is good. For any $k \in \mathsf N$ , we may cover S by some open balls $B _ { k 1 } , B _ { k 2 } , \ldots$ of radius $1 / k$ . Putting $U _ { k m } = \cup _ { j \leq m } B _ { k j }$ , we have s $\begin{array} { r } { { \Psi _ { m } } I ( U _ { k m } ^ { c } ) = \infty } \end{array}$ , since any level set $I ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ <sub>is covered by finitely many sets</sub> $B _ { k j }$ . Now fix any sequence $\varepsilon _ { n } \to 0$ and constant $r > 0$ . By the LDP upper bound and the fact that $P \{ \xi _ { \varepsilon _ { n } } \in U _ { k m } ^ { c } \} \to 0$ as $m  \infty$ for fixed n and $k _ { ; }$ , we may choose $m _ { k } \in \mathbb { N }$ so large that

By analogy with weak convergence theory, we may look for a version of (16) for continuous functions. 

Theorem 24.10 (functional LDP, Varadhan, Bryc) Let $\xi _ { \varepsilon } , \varepsilon > 0$ , be random elements in a metric space S. 

(i) $I f \ ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } )$ satisfies an LDP with rate function I, and $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ is continuous and bounded above, then 

$$
\Lambda_ {f} \equiv \lim _ {\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \varepsilon \log E \exp \left\{f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) / \varepsilon \right\} = \sup _ {x \in S} \left\{f (x) - I (x) \right\}.
$$

$$
I (x) = \sup _ {f \in C _ {b}} \left\{f (x) - \Lambda_ {f} \right\}, \quad x \in S.
$$

Proof: (i) For every $n \in \mathsf N$ , we can choose finitely many closed sets $B _ { 1 } , \ldots ,$ $B _ { m } \subset S _ { \ l }$ , such that $f \leq - n$ on $\cap _ { j } B _ { j } ^ { c }$ , and the oscillation of f on each $B _ { j }$ is at most $n ^ { - 1 }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log E e ^ {f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) / \varepsilon} \leq \underset {j \leq m} {\max} \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log E \Big (e ^ {f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) / \varepsilon};   \xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B _ {j} \Big) \vee (- n) \\ \quad \leq \underset {j \leq m} {\max} \Big \{\underset {x \in B _ {j}} {\sup} f (x) - \inf _ {x \in B _ {j}} I (x) \Big \} \vee (- n) \\ \quad \leq \underset {j \leq m} {\max} \underset {x \in B _ {j}} {\sup} \Big \{f (x) - I (x) + n ^ {- 1} \Big \} \vee (- n) \\ = \underset {x \in S} {\sup} \Big \{f (x) - I (x) + n ^ {- 1} \Big \} \vee (- n). \end{array}
$$

The upper bound now follows as we let $n \to \infty$ . Next we fix any $x \in S$ with a neighborhood $G ,$ and write 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log E e ^ {f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) / \varepsilon} & \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log E \Big (e ^ {f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) / \varepsilon};   \xi_ {\varepsilon} \in G \Big) \\ & \geq \inf _ {y \in G} f (y) - \inf _ {y \in G} I (y) \\ & \geq \inf _ {y \in G} f (y) - I (x). \end{array}
$$

Here the lower bound follows as we let $G \downarrow \{ x \}$ , and then take the supremum over $x \in S$ 

(ii) Note that I is lower semi-continuous, as the supremum over a family of continuous functions. Since $\Lambda _ { f } = 0$ for $f = 0 ,$ , it is also clear that $I \geq 0$ . By Lemma 24.9 (ii), it remains to show that (ξ ) satisfies the weak LDP with rate function I. Then fix any $\delta > 0$ . For every $x \in S$ , we may choose a function $f _ { x } \in C _ { b }$ satisfying 

$$
f _ {x} (x) - \Lambda_ {f _ {x}} > \left\{I (x) - \delta \right\} \wedge \delta^ {- 1},

and by continuity there exists a neighborhood $B _ { x }$ of x such that 

$$
f _ {x} (y) > \Lambda_ {f _ {x}} + \left\{I (x) - \delta \right\} \wedge \delta^ {- 1}, \quad y \in B _ {x}.
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B _ {x} \} \leq E \exp \Big \{\varepsilon^ {- 1} \Big (f _ {x} (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) - \inf \big \{f _ {x} (y); y \in B _ {x} \big \} \Big) \Big \} \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}
$$

and so by the definition of $\Lambda _ { f _ { x } }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B _ {x} \Big \} \\ \quad \leq \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\lim} \varepsilon \log E \exp \left\{f _ {x} (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) / \varepsilon \right\} - \Lambda_ {f _ {x}} - \left\{I (x) - \delta \right\} \wedge \delta^ {- 1} \\ = - \left\{I (x) - \delta \right\} \wedge \delta^ {- 1}. \end{array}
$$

Now fix any compact set $K \subset S$ , and choose $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { m } \in K$ such that $K \subset$ $\cup _ { i } B _ { x _ { i } }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in K \bigr \} & \leq \underset {i \leq m} {\max} \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B _ {x _ {i}} \bigr \} \\ & \leq - \underset {i \leq m} {\min} \bigl \{I (x _ {i}) - \delta \bigr \} \wedge \delta^ {- 1} \\ & \leq - \bigl \{I (K) - \delta \bigr \} \wedge \delta^ {- 1}. \end{array}
$$

The upper bound now follows as we let $\delta  0$ 

Next consider any open set G and element $x \in G$ . For any $n \in { \mathbb N }$ , we may choose a continuous function $f _ { n } \colon S \to [ - n , 0 ]$ such that $f _ { n } ( x ) = 0$ and $f _ { n } = - n$ on $G ^ { c }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - I (x) = \inf _ {f \in C _ {b}} \left\{\Lambda_ {f} - f (x) \right\} \\ \leq \Lambda_ {f _ {n}} - f _ {n} (x) = \Lambda_ {f _ {n}} \\ = \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log E \exp \left\{f _ {n} (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) / \varepsilon \right\} \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \left\{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in G \right\} \vee (- n). \end{array}
$$

The lower bound now follows as we let $n \to \infty$ , and then take the supremum over all $x \in G$ ✷ 

We proceed to show how the $\mathrm { L D P }$ is preserved by continuous mappings. The following results are often referred to as direct and inverse contraction principles. Given a rate function I on $S$ and a map $f \colon S  T$ , we define the image $J = I \circ f ^ { - 1 }$ on $T$ as the function 

$$
\begin{array}{l} J (y) = I \Big (f ^ {- 1} \{y \} \Big) \\ \qquad = \inf \Big \{I (x); f (x) = y \Big \}, \quad y \in T. \end{array}\tag{19}
$$

Note that the corresponding set functions are related by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} J (B) \equiv \inf _ {y \in B} J (y) \\ \qquad = \inf \Bigl \{I (x); f (x) \in B \Bigr \} \\ \qquad = I (f ^ {- 1} B), \quad B \subset T. \end{array}
$$

Theorem 24.11 (continuous mapping) Let f be a continuous map between two metric spaces S, T, and let $\xi _ { \varepsilon }$ be random elements in S. 

(i) If (ξ ) satisfies an LDP in S with rate function I, then the images $f ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } )$ satisfy an LDP in T with the raw rate function $J = I \circ f ^ { - 1 }$ . Moreover, J is a good rate function on T, whenever the function I is good on $S$ 

(ii) $( I o f f e )$ Let $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ be exponentially tight in S, let f be injective, and let the images $f ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } )$ satisfy a weak LDP in T with rate function J. Then $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ satisfies an LDP in S with the good rate function $I = J \circ f$ 

Proof: (i) Since f is continuous, the set $f ^ { - 1 } B$ is open or closed whenever the corresponding property holds for B. Using the LDP for $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ , we get for any $B \subset T$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} - I (f ^ {- 1} B ^ {o}) & \leq \liminf _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in f ^ {- 1} B ^ {o} \bigr \} \\ & \leq \limsup _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in f ^ {- 1} \bar {B} \bigr \} \leq - I (f ^ {- 1} \bar {B}), \end{array}
$$

which proves the LDP for $\{ f ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } ) \}$ with the raw rate function $J = I \circ f ^ { - 1 }$ 

When I is good, we claim that 

$$
J ^ {- 1} [ 0, r ] = f \left(I ^ {- 1} [ 0, r ]\right), \quad r \geq 0.\tag{20}
$$

To see this, fix any $r \geq 0$ , and let $x \in I ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} J \circ f (x) = I \circ f ^ {- 1} \circ f (x) \\ \qquad = \inf \Bigl \{I (u);   f (u) = f (x) \Bigr \} \\ \qquad \leq I (x) \leq r, \end{array}
$$

which means that $f ( x ) \in J ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ . Conversely, let $y \in J ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ . Since I is good and f is continuous, the infimum in (19) is attained at some $x \in S .$ , and we get $y = f ( x )$ with $I ( x ) \leq r$ . Thus, $y \in f ( I ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ] )$ , which completes the proof of (20). Since continuous maps preserve compactness, (20) shows that the goodness of I carries over to J. 

(ii) Here I is again a rate function, since the lower semi-continuity of J is preserved by composition with the continuous map f. By Lemma 24.9 (ii), it is then enough to show that $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ satisfies a weak LDP in $S .$ To prove the upper bound, fix any compact set $K \subset S$ , and note that the image set $f ( K )$ is again compact, since f is continuous. Hence, the weak LDP for $\{ f ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } ) \}$ yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in K \Big \} = \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) \in f (K) \Big \} \\ \leq - J \big \{f (K) \big \} = - I (K). \end{array}
$$

Next we fix any open set $G \subset S$ , and let $x \in G$ be arbitrary with $I ( x ) = $ $r < \infty$ . Since $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ is exponentially tight, we may choose a compact set $K \subset S$ such that 

$$
\limsup _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K \Bigr \} <   - r.\tag{21}
$$

The continuous image $f ( K )$ is compact in $T ,$ , and so by (21) and the weak LDP for $\{ f ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } ) \}$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - I (K ^ {c}) = - J \Big \{f (K ^ {c}) \Big \} \\ \leq - J \Big (\{f (K) \} ^ {c} \Big) \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) \notin f (K) \Big \} \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K \Big \} <   - r. \end{array}
$$

Since $I ( x ) = r ,$ , we conclude that $x \in K$ 

As a continuous bijection from the compact set K onto $f ( K )$ , the function $f$ is a homeomorphism between the two sets with their subset topologies. Then Lemma 1.6 yields an open set $G ^ { \prime } \subset T$ , such that $f ( x ) \in f ( G \cap K ) = G ^ { \prime } \cap f ( K )$ Noting that 

$$
P \Big \{f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) \in G ^ {\prime} \Big \} \leq P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in G \Big \} + P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K \Big \},
$$

and using the weak LDP for $\{ f ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } ) \}$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - r = - I (x) = - J \{f (x) \} \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{f (\xi_ {\varepsilon}) \in G ^ {\prime} \bigr \} \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in G \bigr \} \vee \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \notin K \bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

Hence, by (21), 

$$
- I (x) \leq \liminf _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in G \Bigr \}, \quad x \in G,
$$

and the lower bound follows as we take the supremum over all $x \in G$ □ 

We turn to the powerful method of projective limits. The following sequential version is suficient for our needs, and will enable us to extend the LDP to a variety of infinite-dimensional contexts. Some general background on projective limits is provided by Appendix 6. 

Theorem 24.12 (random sequences, Dawson $\beta \ G a r t n e r )$ For any metric spaces $S _ { 1 } , S _ { 2 } , \ldots , l e t \xi _ { \varepsilon } = ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } ^ { n } )$ be random elements in $S ^ { \infty } = S _ { 1 } \times S _ { 2 } \times \cdots ,$ such that for each $n \in \mathsf N$ the vectors $\big ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } ^ { 1 } , \dots , \xi _ { \varepsilon } ^ { n } \big )$ satisfy an LDP in $S ^ { n } = S _ { 1 } \times \cdot \cdot \cdot \times S _ { n }$ with the good rate function $I _ { n }$ . Then $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ satisfies an LDP in $S ^ { \infty }$ with the good rate function 

$$
I (x) = \sup _ {n} I _ {n} (x _ {1}, \dots , x _ {n}), \quad x = (x _ {1}, x _ {2}, \dots) \in S ^ {\infty}.\tag{22}
$$

Proof: For any $m \leq n$ , we introduce the natural projections $\pi _ { n } \colon S ^ { \infty } \to S ^ { n }$ and $\pi _ { m n } : S ^ { n }  S ^ { m }$ Since the $\pi _ { m n }$ are continuous and the $I _ { n }$ are good, Theorem 24.11 yields ${ \cal I } _ { m } = { \cal I } _ { n } \circ \pi _ { m n } ^ { - 1 }$ for all $m \leq n ,$ , and so $\pi _ { m n } ( I _ { n } ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ] ) \subset$ $I _ { m } ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ for all $r \geq 0$ and $m \leq n$ . Hence, for each $r \geq 0$ the level sets $I _ { n } ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ form a projective sequence. Since they are also compact by hypothesis, and by (22), 

$$
I ^ {- 1} [ 0, r ] = \bigcap_ {n} \pi_ {n} ^ {- 1} I _ {n} ^ {- 1} [ 0, r ], \quad r \geq 0,\tag{23}
$$

the sets $I ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ are compact by Lemma A6.4. Thus, I is again a good rate function. 

Now fix any closed set $A \subset S$ , and put $A _ { n } = \pi _ { n } A .$ , so that $\pi _ { m n } A _ { n } = A _ { m }$ for all $m \leq n$ . Since the $\pi _ { m n }$ are continuous, we have also $\pi _ { m n } A _ { n } ^ { - } \subset A _ { m } ^ { - }$ for $m \leq n$ , which means that the sets $A _ { n } ^ { - }$ form a projective sequence. We claim that 

$$
A = \bigcap_ {n} \pi_ {n} ^ {- 1} A _ {n} ^ {-}.\tag{24}
$$

Here the relation $A \subset \pi _ { n } ^ { - 1 } A _ { n } ^ { - }$ is obvious. Now let x $\not \in A$ . By the definition of the product topology, we may choose a $k \in \mathsf { N }$ and an open set $U \subset S ^ { k }$ , such that $x \in \pi _ { k } ^ { - 1 } U \subset A ^ { c }$ . It follows easily that $\pi _ { k } x \in U \subset A _ { k } ^ { c }$ . Since U is open, we have even $\pi _ { k } x \in ( A _ { k } ^ { - } ) ^ { c }$ . Thus, $x \notin \cap _ { n } \pi _ { n } ^ { - 1 } A _ { n } ^ { - }$ , which completes the proof of <sub>(24). The projective property carries over to the intersections</sub> $A _ { n } ^ { - } \cap I _ { n } ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ]$ 2 and formulas (23) and (24) combine into the relation 

$$
A \cap I ^ {- 1} [ 0, r ] = \bigcap_ {n} \pi_ {n} ^ {- 1} \left\{A _ {n} ^ {-} \cap I _ {n} ^ {- 1} [ 0, r ] \right\}, \quad r \geq 0.\tag{25}
$$

Now let $I ( A ) > r \in { \mathsf { R } }$ . Then $A \cap I ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ] = \emptyset$ , and by (25) and Lemma A6.4 we get $A _ { n } ^ { - } \cap I _ { n } ^ { - 1 } [ 0 , r ] = \emptyset$ for some $n \in \mathsf { N } .$ , which implies $I _ { n } ( A _ { n } ^ { - } ) \geq r$ Noting that $A \subset \pi _ { n } ^ { - 1 } A _ { n }$ and using the LDP in $S ^ { n }$ , we conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in A \Big \} \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \Big \{\pi_ {n} \xi_ {\varepsilon} \in A _ {n} \Big \} \\ \leq - I _ {n} (A _ {n} ^ {-}) \leq - r, \end{array}

Finally, fix an open set $G \subset S ^ { \infty }$ , and let $x \in G$ be arbitrary. By the definition of the product topology, we may choose $n \in \mathsf { N }$ and an open set $U \subset S ^ { n }$ such that $x \in \pi _ { n } ^ { - 1 } U \subset G$ . The LDP in $S ^ { n }$ yields

\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in G \bigr \} & \geq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\pi_ {n} \xi_ {\varepsilon} \in U \bigr \} \\ & \geq - I _ {n} (U) \\ & \geq - I _ {n} \circ \pi_ {n} (x) \\ & \geq - I (x), \end{array}
