We consider yet another basic extension principle for the LDP, involving suitable approximations. The families of random elements $\xi _ { \varepsilon }$ and $\eta _ { \varepsilon }$ in a common separable metric space $( S , d )$ are said to be exponentially equivalent, if 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \varepsilon \log P \left\{d \left(\xi_ {\varepsilon}, \eta_ {\varepsilon}\right) > h \right\} = - \infty , \quad h > 0.\tag{26}
$$

The separability of $S$ is only needed to ensure measurability of the pairwise distances $d ( \xi _ { \varepsilon } , \eta _ { \varepsilon } )$ . In general, we may replace (26) by a similar condition involving the outer measure. 

Lemma 24.13 (approximation) Let $\xi _ { \varepsilon } , \eta _ { \varepsilon }$ be exponentially equivalent random elements in a separable metric space $S .$ . Then $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ satisfies an $L D P$ with the good rate function I, if the same LDP holds for $( \eta _ { \varepsilon } )$ 

Proof: Let the LDP hold for $\left( \xi _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ with rate function I. Fix any closed set $B \subset S$ , and write $B ^ { h }$ for the closed h -neighborhood of B. Then 

$$
P \left\{\eta_ {\varepsilon} \in B \right\} \leq P \left\{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B ^ {h} \right\} + P \left\{d \left(\xi_ {\varepsilon}, \eta_ {\varepsilon}\right) > h \right\},
$$

and so by (26) and the LDP for (ξ ), 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\eta_ {\varepsilon} \in B \bigr \} \\ \quad \leq \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in B ^ {h} \bigr \} \vee \underset {\varepsilon \to 0} {\limsup} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{d (\xi_ {\varepsilon}, \eta_ {\varepsilon}) > h \bigr \} \\ \quad \leq - I (B ^ {h}) \vee (- \infty) \\ = - I (B ^ {h}). \end{array}
$$

Since I is good, we have $I ( B ^ { h } ) \dag I ( B )$ as $h  0$ , and the required upper bound follows. 

Now fix any open set $G \subset S$ , and let $x \in G$ . If $d ( x , G ^ { c } ) > h > 0$ , we may choose a neighborhood U of x such that $U ^ { h } \subset G$ . Noting that 

$$
P \left\{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in U \right\} \leq P \left\{\eta_ {\varepsilon} \in G \right\} + P \left\{d \left(\xi_ {\varepsilon}, \eta_ {\varepsilon}\right) > h \right\},
$$

we get by (26) and the LDP for (ξ<sub>ε</sub>) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - I (x) \leq - I (U) \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\xi_ {\varepsilon} \in U \bigr \} \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\eta_ {\varepsilon} \in G \bigr \} \vee \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{d (\xi_ {\varepsilon}, \eta_ {\varepsilon}) > h \bigr \} \\ = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \varepsilon \log P \bigl \{\eta_ {\varepsilon} \in G \bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

The required lower bound now follows, as we take the supremum over all $x \in G$ ✷ 

We turn to some important applications, illustrating the power of the general theory. First we study the perturbations of an ordinary diferential equation ${ \dot { x } } = b ( x )$ by a small noise term. More precisely, we consider the unique solutions $X ^ { \varepsilon }$ with $X _ { 0 } ^ { \varepsilon } = 0$ of the d -dimensional SDEs<sup>3</sup> 

$$
d X _ {t} = \varepsilon^ {1 / 2} d B _ {t} + b (X _ {t}) d t, \quad t \geq 0, \varepsilon \geq 0,\tag{27}
$$

where $B$ is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and b is a bounded and uniformly Lipschitz continuous mapping on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ . Let $H _ { \infty }$ be the set of all absolutely continuous functions $x \colon { \mathsf { R } } _ { + } \to { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d }$ with $x _ { 0 } = 0$ , such that $\dot { x } \in L ^ { 2 }$ 

Theorem 24.14 (perturbed dynamical systems, Freidlin & Wentzell) For any bounded, uniformly Lipschitz continuous function $b \colon \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \to \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , the solutions $X ^ { \varepsilon }$ to (27) with $X _ { 0 } ^ { \varepsilon } = 0$ satisfy an $L D P$ in $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ with the good rate function 

$$
I (x) = \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \left| \dot {x} _ {t} - b (x _ {t}) \right| ^ {2} d t, x \in H _ {\infty}.\tag{28}
$$

Here it is understood that $I ( x ) = \infty$ when $x \notin H _ { \infty }$ . Note that the result for $b = 0$ extends Theorem 24.6 to processes on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

Proof: If $B ^ { 1 }$ is a Brownian motion on [0, 1], then for every $r > 0$ , the scaled process $B ^ { r } = \Phi ( B ^ { 1 } )$ given by $B _ { t } ^ { r } = \bar { r } ^ { 1 / 2 } \bar { B } _ { t / r } ^ { 1 }$ is a Brownian motion on $[ 0 , r ]$ . Since Φ is continuous from $C _ { [ 0 , 1 ] } \ \mathrm { t o } \ C _ { [ 0 , r ] } .$ , we see from Theorems 24.6 and 24.11 (i), combined with Lemma 24.7, that the processes $\varepsilon ^ { 1 / 2 } B ^ { r }$ satisfy an LDP in $C _ { [ 0 , r ] }$ with the good rate function $I _ { r } = I _ { 1 } \circ \Phi ^ { - 1 }$ , where $I _ { 1 } ( x ) = \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \| \dot { x } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ for $x \in H _ { 1 }$ and $I _ { 1 } ( x ) = \infty$ otherwise. Now Φ maps $H _ { 1 }$ onto $H _ { r }$ , and when $y = \Phi ( x )$ with $x \in H _ { 1 }$ , we have $\dot { x } _ { t } = r ^ { 1 / 2 } \dot { y } _ { r t }$ . Hence, a simple calculation yields $\begin{array} { r } { I _ { r } ( y ) = \frac 1 2 \int _ { 0 } ^ { r } | \dot { y } _ { s } | ^ { 2 } d s = \frac 1 2 \| \dot { y } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , which extends Theorem 24.6 to $[ 0 , r ]$ . For the -<sub>further extension to</sub> $\mathsf { R } _ { + } .$ , write $\pi _ { n } x$ for the restriction of a function $x \in C _ { \mathsf { R } }$ + to $[ 0 , n ]$ , and infer from Theorem 24.12 that the processes $\varepsilon ^ { 1 / 2 } B$ satisfy an LDP in $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { - } }$ with the good rate function $\begin{array} { r } { I _ { \infty } ( x ) = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } I _ { n } ( \pi _ { n } x ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \| \dot { x } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ 

By an elementary version of Theorem 32.3, the integral equation 

$$
x _ {t} = z _ {t} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} b (x _ {s}) d s, t \geq 0,\tag{29}
$$

has a unique solution $x = F ( z )$ in $C = C _ { \mathsf { R } }$ for every $z \in C$ . Letting $z ^ { 1 } , z ^ { 2 } \in C$ + be arbitrary, and writing a for the Lipschitz constant of $b ,$ we note that the corresponding solutions $x ^ { i } = F ( z ^ { i } )$ satisfy 

$$
\left| x _ {t} ^ {1} - x _ {t} ^ {2} \right| \leq \left\| z ^ {1} - z ^ {2} \right\| + a \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left| x _ {s} ^ {1} - x _ {s} ^ {2} \right| d s, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Hence, Gronwall’s Lemma 32.4 yields $\| x ^ { 1 } - x ^ { 2 } \| \leq \| z ^ { 1 } - z ^ { 2 } \| e ^ { a r }$ on the interval $[ 0 , r ]$ , which shows that $F$ is continuous. Using Schilder’s theorem on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , along with Theorem 24.11 (i), we conclude that the processes $X ^ { \varepsilon }$ satisfy an LDP in $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } }$ with the good rate function $I = I _ { \infty } \circ F ^ { - 1 }$ . Now $F$ is clearly bijective, and by (29) the functions $z$ and $x = F ( z )$ lie simultaneously in $H _ { \infty }$ , in which case $\dot { z } = \dot { x } - b ( x ) \ \mathrm { a . e }$ . Thus, I is indeed given by (28). ✷ 

Now consider a random element $\xi$ with distribution $\mu ,$ , in an arbitrary metric space S. Introduce the cumulant-generating functional 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \Lambda (f) & = \log E e ^ {f (\xi)} \\ & = \log \mu e ^ {f}, \quad f \in C _ {b} (S), \end{array}
$$

with associated Legendre–Fenchel transform 

$$
\Lambda^ {*} (\nu) = \sup _ {f \in C _ {b}} \Bigl \{\nu f - \Lambda (f) \Bigr \}, \quad \nu \in \hat {\mathcal {M}} _ {S},\tag{30}
$$

where $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ is the class of probability measures on $S _ { ; }$ , endowed with the topol ogy of weak convergence. Note that Λ and $\Lambda ^ { * }$ are both convex, by the same argument as for $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

For any measures $\mu , \nu \in \hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ , we define the relative entropy of $\nu$ with respect to $\mu$ by 

$$
H (\nu \mid \mu) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \nu \log p = \mu (p \log p), & \nu \ll \mu \text { with } \nu = p \cdot \mu , \\ \infty , & \nu \not \ll \mu . \end{array} \right.
$$

Since x log x is convex, the function $H ( \nu | \mu )$ is convex in $\nu$ for fixed $\mu ,$ , and Jensen’s inequality yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} H (\nu \mid \mu) \geq \mu p \log \mu p \\ = \nu S \log \nu S = 0, v \in \hat {\mathcal {M}} _ {S}, \end{array}
$$

with equality if $\nu = \mu$ 

Now let $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be i.i.d. random elements in $S .$ . The associated empirical distributions 

$$
\eta_ {n} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k \leq n} \delta_ {\xi_ {k}}, \quad n \in \mathsf {N},
$$

may be regarded as random elements in $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ , and we note that 

$$
\eta_ {n} f = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k \leq n} f (\xi_ {k}), \quad f \in C _ {b} (S), n \in \mathsf {N}.
$$

In particular, Theorem 24.5 applies to the random vectors $( \eta _ { n } f _ { 1 } , \dots , \eta _ { n } f _ { m } )$ , for fixed $f _ { 1 } , \dots , f _ { m } \in C _ { b } ( S )$ . The following result may be regarded as an infinitedimensional version of Theorem 24.5. It also provides an important connection to statistical mechanics, via the entropy function. 

Theorem 24.15 (large deviations of empirical distributions, Sanov) Let $\xi _ { 1 }$ $\xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . be i.i.d. random elements with distribution μ in a Polish space $S ,$ and put $\Lambda ( f ) = \log \mu e ^ { f }$ . Then the associated empirical distributions $\eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } , . . .$ satisfy an LDP in $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ with the good rate function 

$$
\Lambda^ {*} (\nu) = H (\nu \mid \mu), \quad \nu \in \hat {\mathcal {M}} _ {S}.\tag{31}
$$

A couple of lemmas will be needed for the proof. 

Lemma 24.16 (relative entropy, Donsker & Varadhan) For any μ, $\nu \in \hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ 

(i) the supremum in (30) may be taken over all bounded, measurable functions $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } } _ { : }$ 

(ii) then (31) extends to measures on any measurable space S. 

Proof: (i) Use Lemma 1.37 and dominated convergence. 

(ii) If $\nu \not \ll \mu .$ then $H ( \nu | \mu ) = \infty$ by definition. Choosing $B \in S$ with $\mu B =$ 0 and $\nu B > 0$ , and taking $f _ { n } = n 1 _ { B }$ , we obtain $\nu f _ { n } - \log \mu e ^ { f _ { n } } = n \nu B \to \infty$ Thus, even $\Lambda ^ { * } ( \nu ) = \infty$ in this case, and it remains to prove (31) when $\nu \ll \mu$ Assuming $\nu = p \cdot \mu$ and writing $f = \log p ,$ , we note that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \nu f - \log \mu e ^ {f} = \nu \log p - \log \mu p \\ = H (\nu | \mu). \end{array}
$$

If $f = \log p$ is unbounded, it may approximated by some bounded, measurable functions $f _ { n }$ satisfying $\mu e ^ { f _ { n } } \to 1$ and $\nu f _ { n } \to \nu f$ , and we get $\Lambda ^ { * } ( \nu ) \geq H ( \nu | \mu )$ 

To prove the reverse inequality, we first let $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ be finite and generated by a partition $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n }$ of $S .$ . Putting $\mu _ { k } = \mu B _ { k } , \nu _ { k } = \nu B _ { k }$ , and $p _ { k } = \nu _ { k } / \mu _ { k }$ , we may write our claim in the form 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & g (x) \equiv \sum_ {k} \nu_ {k} x _ {k} - \log \sum_ {k} \mu_ {k} e ^ {x _ {k}} \\ & \qquad \leq \sum_ {k} \nu_ {k} \log p _ {k}, \end{array}
$$

where $x = ( x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is arbitrary. Here the function $g$ is concave and satisfies $\nabla g ( x ) = 0$ for $x = ( \log p _ { 1 } , \ldots , \log p _ { n } )$ , asymptotically when $p _ { k } = 0$ for some k. Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sup _ {x} g (x) = g \Big (\log p _ {1}, \ldots , \log p _ {k} \Big) \\ = \sum_ {k} \nu_ {k} \log p _ {k}. \end{array}
$$

To prove the general inequality $\nu f - \log \mu e ^ { f } \leq \nu \log p ,$ we may choose $f$ to be simple. The generated σ-field $\mathcal { F } \subset \mathcal { S }$ is then finite, and we note that $\nu = \mu ( p | \mathcal { F } )$ μ on $\mathcal { F }$ . Using the result in the finite case, along with Jensen’s inequality for conditional expectations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \nu f - \log \mu e ^ {f} & \leq \mu \Bigl \{\mu (p | \mathcal {F}) \log \mu (p | \mathcal {F}) \Bigr \} \\ & \leq \mu   \mu \Bigl (p \log p   \big |   \mathcal {F} \Bigr) \\ & = \nu \log p. \end{array}
$$

Lemma 24.17 (exponential tightness) The empirical distributions $\eta _ { n }$ in Theorem 24.15 are exponentially tight in $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ 

Proof: If $B \in S$ with $P \{ \xi \in B \} = p \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , Theorem 24.3 and Lemmas 24.1 and 24.2 yield for any $x \in [ p , 1 ]$ 

$$
\sup _ {n} n ^ {- 1} \log P \left\{\eta_ {n} B > x \right\} \leq - x \log \frac {x}{p} - (1 - x) \log \frac {1 - x}{1 - p}.\tag{32}
$$

In particular, the right-hand side tends to $- \infty$ as $p  0$ for fixed $x \in ( 0 , 1 )$ Now fix any $r > 0$ . By (32) and Theorem 23.2, we may choose some compact sets $K _ { 1 } , K _ { 2 } , \ldots \subset S$ with

P \Bigl \{\eta_ {n} K _ {k} ^ {c} > 2 ^ {- k} \Bigr \} \leq e ^ {- k n r}, \quad k, n \in \mathbb {N}.

and it remains to note that the set

Proof of Theorem 24.15: By Theorem 1.8, we can embed $S$ as a Borel subset of a compact metric space K. The function space $C _ { b } ( K )$ is separable, and we can choose a dense sequence ${ f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , . . . \in C _ { b } ( K ) }$ . For any $m \in \mathsf N$ , the random vector $\{ f _ { 1 } ( \xi ) , \ldots , f _ { m } ( \xi ) \}$ has cumulant-generating function 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \Lambda_ {m} (u) = \log E \exp \sum_ {k \leq m} u _ {k} f _ {k} (\xi) \\ = \Lambda \circ \sum_ {k \leq m} u _ {k} f _ {k}, \quad u \in \mathsf {R} ^ {m}, \end{array}
$$

and so by Theorem 24.5 the random vectors $( \eta _ { n } f _ { 1 } , \dots , \eta _ { n } f _ { m } )$ satisfy an LDP in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { m }$ with the good rate function $\Lambda _ { m } ^ { * }$ . Then by Theorem 24.12, the infinite sequences $( \eta _ { n } f _ { 1 } , \eta _ { n } f _ { 2 } , . . . )$ satisfy an LDP in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ with the good rate function $J = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { m } ( \Lambda _ { m } ^ { * } \circ \pi _ { m } )$ , where $\pi _ { m }$ denotes the natural projection of ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ onto R<sup>m</sup>. Since $\dot { \mathcal { M } } _ { K }$ is compact by Theorem 23.2 and the mapping $\nu \mapsto ( \nu f _ { 1 } , \nu f _ { 2 } , . . . )$ is a continuous injection of $\hat { \mathscr { M } } _ { K }$ into ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ , Theorem 24.11 (ii) shows that the random measures $\eta _ { n }$ satisfy an LDP in $\dot { \mathcal { M } } _ { K }$ with the good rate function 

$$
\begin{array}{l} I _ {K} (\nu) = J \Big (\nu f _ {1}, \nu f _ {2}, \ldots \Big) \\ \qquad = \sup _ {m} \Lambda_ {m} ^ {*} \Big (\nu f _ {1}, \ldots , \nu f _ {m} \Big) \\ \qquad = \sup _ {m} \sup _ {u \in \mathbb {R} ^ {m}} \Big (\sum_ {k \leq m} u _ {k} \nu f _ {k} - \Lambda \circ \sum_ {k \leq m} u _ {k} f _ {k} \Big) \\ \qquad = \sup _ {f \in \mathcal {F}} \Big \{\nu f - \Lambda (f) \Big \} \\ \qquad = \sup _ {f \in C _ {b}} \Big \{\nu f - \Lambda (f) \Big \}, \end{array}\tag{33}
$$

where $\mathcal { F }$ is the set of all linear combinations of $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots$ 

Next, we note that the natural embedding $\hat { \mathscr { M } } _ { S }  \hat { \mathscr { M } } _ { K }$ is continuous, since for any $f \in C _ { b } ( K )$ the restriction of $f$ to S belongs to $C _ { b } ( S )$ . Since it is also trivially injective, we see from Theorem 24.11 (ii) and Lemma 24.17 that the $\eta _ { n }$ satisfy an LDP even in $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ , with a good rate function $I _ { S }$ equal to the restriction of $I _ { K }$ to $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ . It remains to note that $I _ { S } = \Lambda ^ { * }$ by (33) and Lemma 24.16. ✷ 

We conclude with a remarkable application of Schilder’s Theorem 24.6. Writing B for a standard Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we introduce for each $t > e$ the scaled process t B s > 0 (34)

Theorem 24.18 (functional law of the iterated logarithm, Strassen) For a Brownian motion B in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , define the processes $X ^ { t }$ by (34). Then these statements are equivalent and hold outside a fixed P-null set: 

(i) the set of paths $X ^ { t }$ with $t \geq 3$ is relatively compact in $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ , with set of limit points as $t $ ∞

In particular, we may recover the classical law of the iterated logarithm in Theorem 14.18 by choosing $F ( x ) = x _ { 1 }$ . Using Theorem 22.6, we can easily derive a correspondingly strengthened version for random walks. 

Proof: The equivalence $( \mathrm { i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ being elementary, it is enough to prove (i). Noting that $X ^ { t } \overset { d } { = } ( 2 \log \log t ) ^ { - 1 / 2 } B$ and using Theorem 24.6, we get for any measurable set $A \subset C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } }$ and constant $r > 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} \frac {\log P \left\{X ^ {r ^ {n}} \in A \right\}}{\log n} \leq \underset {t \to \infty} {\limsup} \frac {\log P \left\{X ^ {t} \in A \right\}}{\log \log t} \leq - 2   I (\bar {A}), \\ \underset {n \to \infty} {\liminf} \frac {\log P \left\{X ^ {r ^ {n}} \in A \right\}}{\log n} \geq \underset {t \to \infty} {\liminf} \frac {\log P \left\{X ^ {t} \in A \right\}}{\log \log t} \geq - 2   I (A ^ {o}), \end{array}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { I ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \| \dot { x } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ for $x \in H _ { \infty }$ and $I ( x ) = \infty$ otherwise. Hence, 

$$
\sum_ {n} P \Bigl \{X ^ {r ^ {n}} \in A \Bigr \} \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} <   \infty , & 2   I (\bar {A}) > 1, \\ = \infty , & 2   I (A ^ {o}) <   1. \end{array} \right.\tag{35}

Now fix any $r > 1$ , and let $G \supset K$ be open. Note that $2 I ( G ^ { c } ) > 1$ by Lemma 24.7. By the first part of (35) and the Borel–Cantelli lemma, we have $P \{ X ^ { r ^ { n } } \notin G { \mathrm { ~ i . o . } } \} = 0$ , or equivalently $1 _ { G } ( X ^ { r ^ { n } } ) \to 1$ a.s. Since $G$ was arbitrary, it follows that $\rho ( X ^ { r ^ { n } } , K ) \to 0$ a.s. for any metrization $\rho$ of $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ . $$

To extend the convergence to the entire family $\{ X ^ { t } \}$ , fix a path of $B$ with $\rho _ { 1 } ( X ^ { r ^ { n } } , K ) \to 0$ , and choose some functions $y ^ { r ^ { n } } \in K$ with $\rho _ { 1 } ( X ^ { r ^ { n } } , y ^ { r ^ { n } } ) \to 0$ For any $t \in [ r ^ { n } , r ^ { n + 1 } )$ , the paths $X ^ { r ^ { n } }$ and $X ^ { t }$ are related by

Defining $y ^ { t }$ in the same way in terms of $y ^ { r ^ { n } }$ , we note that also $y ^ { t } \in K$ , since $I ( y ^ { t } ) \leq I ( y ^ { r ^ { n } } )$ . Thus, $\rho _ { r } ( X ^ { t } , K ) \to 0$ . Since K is compact, we conclude that $\{ X ^ { t } \}$ is relatively compact, and that all its limit points as $t \to \infty$ belong to $K$ 

Now fix any $y \in K$ and $u \geq \varepsilon > 0$ . By the established part of the theorem and Cauchy’s inequality, we have a.s.

As $\varepsilon \to 0$ , we get lim inf $( X ^ { t } - y ) _ { u } ^ { * } = 0 \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., and so lim inf $\rho _ { 1 } ( X ^ { t } , y ) \le e ^ { - u }$ a.s. ## VIII. Stationarity, Symmetry and Invariance

Stationary and symmetric processes represent the third basic dependence structure of probability theory. In Theorem 25 we prove the pointwise and mean ergodic theorems in discrete and continuous time, along with various multi-variate and sub-additive extensions. Some main results admit extensions to transition semi-groups of Markov processes, which leads in Chapter 26 to some powerful limit theorems for the latter. Here we also study weak and strong ergodicity as well as Harris recurrence. In Chapter 27 we prove the basic representations and limit theorems for exchangeable processes, as well as the predictable sampling and mapping theorems. The final Chapter 28 provides representations of contractable, exchangeable, and rotatable arrays. For the novice we recommend especially Chapter 25 plus selected material from Chapters 26–27. Chapter 28 is more advanced and might be postponed. 

25. Stationary processes and ergodic theorems. After a general discussion of stationary and ergodic sequences and processes, we prove the basic discrete- and continuous-time ergodic theorems, along with various multivariate and sub-additive extensions. Next we consider the basic ergodic decomposition and prove some powerful coupling theorems. Among applications we note some limit theorems for entropy and information and for random matrices. We also include a very general version of the classical ballot theorem. 

26. Ergodic properties of Markov processes. Here we begin with the a.e. ergodic theorem for positive $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty }$ contractions on an abstract measure space, along with a related ratio ergodic theorem, leading to some powerful limit theorems for Markov processes. Next we characterize weak and strong ergodicity, and study the notion of Harris recurrence and the existence of invariant measures for regular Feller processes, using tools from potential theory. 

27. Symmetric distributions and predictable maps. Here the central result is the celebrated de Finetti-type representation of exchangeable and contractable sequences, along with various continuous-time extensions, allowing applications to sampling from a finite population. We further note the powerful predictable sampling and mapping theorems, where the original invariance property is extended to predictable times and mappings. 

28. Multi-variate arrays and symmetries. Here we establish the Aldous–Hoover-type coding representations of jointly exchangeable and contractable arrays of arbitrary dimension, and identify pairs of functions that can be used to represent the same array. After highlighting some special cases, we proceed to a representation of rotatable arrays in terms of Gaussian random variables, and conclude with an extension of Kingman’s paintbox representation for exchangeable and related partitions. 

# Stationary Processes and Ergodic Theory

Stationarity and invariance, two-sided extension, invariance and almost invariance, ergodicity, maximal ergodic lemma, discrete and continuoustime ergodic theorems, varying functions, moment and maximum inequalities, multi-variate ergodic theorem, commuting maps, convex averages, mean and sub-additive ergodic theorems, products of random matrices, ergodic decomposition, shift coupling and mixing criteria, group coupling, ballot theorems, entropy and information 

We now come to the subject of stationarity, the third basic dependence structure of modern probability, beside those of martingales and Markov processes<sup>1</sup>. Apart from their useful role in probabilistic modeling and in providing a natural setting for many general theorems, stationary processes often arise as limiting processes in a wide variety of contexts throughout probability. In particular, they appear as steady-state versions of various Markov and renewal-type processes. Their importance is further due to the existence of a range of fundamental limit theorems and maximum inequalities, belonging to the basic tool kit of every probabilist. 

A process is said to be stationary if its distribution is invariant<sup>2</sup> under shifts. A key result is Birkhof’s ergodic theorem, which may be regarded as a strong law of large numbers for stationary sequences and processes. After proving the classical ergodic theorems in discrete and continuous time, we turn to the multi-variate versions of Zygmund and Wiener, the former in a setting for non-commutative maps on rectangular regions, the latter in the commutative case and involving averages over increasing families of convex sets. We further consider a version of Kingman’s sub-additive ergodic theorem, and discuss a basic application to random matrices. 

In all the mentioned results, the limit is a random variable, measurable with respect to an appropriate invariant σ-field . Of special importance is the ergodic case, where is trivial and the limit reduces to a constant. For general stationary processes, we consider a decomposition of the distribution into ergodic components. We further consider some basic criteria for a suitable shift coupling of two processes, expressed in terms of the tail and invariant σ- fields  and $\mathcal { T } ,$ respectively. Those results will be helpful to prove some ergodic theorems in Chapters $2 7$ and 31. We conclude with some general versions of the classical ballot theorem, and prove the basic limit theorem for entropy and information. 

Our treatment of stationary sequences and processes is continued in Chapters 27 and 31 with some important applications and extensions of the present theory, including various ergodic theorems for Palm distributions. In Chapter 26, we show how the basic ergodic theorems allow extensions to suitable contraction operators, which leads to a profound unification of the present theory with the ergodic theory for Markov transition operators. In this context, we also prove some powerful ratio ergodic theorems. 

Returning to the basic notions of stationarity and invariance, we fix a general measurable space $( S , S )$ , often taken to be Borel. Given a measure $\mu$ and a measurable transformation $T$ on $S _ { ; }$ , we say that $T$ preserves $\mu$ or is μ -preserving if $\mu \circ T ^ { - 1 } = \mu$ . Thus, if $\xi$ is a random element in $S$ with distribution $\mu ,$ then $T$ is measure-preserving if $T \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ . In particular, we may consider a random sequence $\boldsymbol { \xi } = ( \xi _ { 0 } , \xi _ { 1 } , \dots )$ in a measurable space $( S ^ { \prime } , S ^ { \prime } )$ , and let $\theta$ denote the shift on $S = ( S ^ { \prime } ) ^ { \infty }$ , given by $\theta ( x _ { 0 } , x _ { 1 } , . . . ) = ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , . . . )$ . Then $\xi$ is said to be stationary<sup>3</sup> if $\theta \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ . We show that the general situation is equivalent to this special case. 

Lemma 25.1 (stationarity and invariance) For any random element $\xi$ in $S$ and measurable map $T$ on $S$ , we have 

(i) $T \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi \overset { . } { i } f f$ the sequence $( T ^ { n } \xi )$ is stationary, 

(ii) $f o r \ \xi \ a s$ in $( \mathrm { i } ) , ( f \circ T ^ { n } \xi )$ is stationary for every measurable function $f _ { i }$ , 

(iii) any stationary random sequence in $S$ can be represented as in (ii). 

Proof: Assuming $T \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \theta (f \circ T ^ {n} \xi) = (f \circ T ^ {n + 1} \xi) \\ = (f \circ T ^ {n} T \xi) \\ \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (f \circ T ^ {n} \xi), \end{array}
$$

and so $( f \circ T ^ { n } \xi )$ is stationary. Conversely, if $\eta = ( \eta _ { 0 } , \eta _ { 1 } , \dots )$ is stationary, we may write $\eta _ { n } = \pi _ { 0 } ( \theta ^ { n } \eta )$ with $\pi _ { 0 } ( x _ { 0 } , x _ { 1 } , . . . ) = x _ { 0 }$ , and note that $\theta \eta \overset { d } { = } \eta$ by the stationarity of $\eta$ . ✷ 

In particular, when $\xi _ { 0 } , \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots$ . is a stationary sequence of random elements in a measurable space $S$ , and $f$ is a measurable map of $S ^ { \infty }$ into a measurable space $S ^ { \prime }$ , we see that the random sequence 

$$
\eta_ {n} = f (\xi_ {n}, \xi_ {n + 1}, \dots), \quad n \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+},
$$

is again stationary. 

The definition of stationarity extends in an obvious way to random sequences indexed by $Z = \{ \dots , - 1 , 0 , 1 , \dots \}$ . A technical advantage of the twosided version is that the associated shift operators are invertible and form a group, rather than just a semi-group. We show that the two cases are essentially equivalent. Here we assume the existence of appropriate randomization variables, as explained in Chapter 8. 

Lemma 25.2 (two-sided extension) Every stationary random sequence $\xi _ { 0 } , \xi _ { 1 }$ 2 $\cdot \cdot \cdot$ in a Borel space can be extended to a two-sided stationary sequence 

$$
(\dots , \xi_ {- 1}, \xi_ {0}, \xi_ {1}, \xi_ {2}, \dots).
$$

Proof: Letting $\vartheta _ { 1 } , \vartheta _ { 2 } , . . .$ . be i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ and independent of $\xi = ( \xi _ { 0 } , \xi _ { 1 } , \ldots )$ we may construct the $\xi _ { - n }$ recursively as functions of ξ and $\vartheta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \vartheta _ { n }$ , such that $( \xi _ { - n } , \xi _ { - n + 1 } , \ldots ) \ \stackrel { d } { = } \ \xi$ for all $n .$ . In fact, once $\xi _ { - 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { - n }$ have been chosen, the existence of $\xi _ { - n - 1 }$ is clear from Theorem 8.17, if we note that $( \xi _ { - n } , \xi _ { - n + 1 } , . . . ) \overset { d } { = } \theta \xi$ . Finally, the extended sequence is stationary by Propo sition 4.2. ✷ 

Now fix a measurable transformation $T$ on a measure space $( S , S , \mu )$ , and let $S ^ { \mu }$ denote the μ -completion of $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ . We say that a set $I \subset S$ is invariant if $T ^ { - 1 } I = I$ and almost invariant if $T ^ { - 1 } I = I { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } \mu ,$ , in the sense that $\mu ( T ^ { - 1 } I \triangle I ) = 0$ . Since inverse maps preserve the basic set operations, the classes $\mathcal { T }$ and $\mathcal { T } ^ { \prime }$ of invariant sets in $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ and almost invariant sets in $S ^ { \mu }$ form σ-fields in $S$ , called the invariant and almost invariant $\sigma { - } f e l d s$ , respectively. 

A measurable function f on $S$ is said to be invariant if $f \circ T \equiv f$ , and almost invariant if $f \circ T = f \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } \mu$ . We show how invariant or almost invariant sets and functions are related. 

Lemma 25.3 (invariant sets and functions) Fix a measure $\mu$ and a measurable transformation $T$ on $S _ { i }$ , and let f be a measurable map of S into a Borel space U. Then 

(i) f is invariant if it is -measurable, 

(ii) f is almost invariant if it is $\mathcal { T } ^ { \prime }$ -measurable. 

Proof: Since $U$ is Borel, we may take $U = { \sf R }$ . If f is invariant or almost invariant, then so is the set $I _ { x } = f ^ { - 1 } ( - \infty , x )$ for any $x \in \mathsf { R }$ , and so $I _ { x } \in \mathcal { Z }$ or $\mathcal { T } ^ { \prime }$ respectively. Conversely, if f is measurable with respect to or $\mathcal { T } ^ { \prime } .$ , then $I _ { x } \in \mathcal { Z }$ or $\mathcal { T } ^ { \prime }$ , respectively, for every $x \in { \mathsf { R } }$ . Hence, the function $f _ { n } ( s ) = 2 ^ { - n } [ 2 ^ { n } f ( s ) ]$ , $s \in S$ , is invariant or almost invariant for every $n \in { \mathbb N }$ , and the invariance or almost invariance carries over to the limit $f .$ ✷ 

We proceed to clarify the relationship between the invariant and almost invariant σ-fields. Here ${ \mathcal { T } } ^ { \mu }$ denotes the μ -completion of $\mathcal { T }$ in $S ^ { \mu }$ , the σ-field generated by $\mathcal { T }$ and the μ -null sets in $S ^ { \mu }$ 

Lemma 25.4 (almost invariance) For any distribution $\mu$ and μ-preserving transformation $T$ on $S$ , the invariant and almost invariant σ-fields $\mathcal { T }$ and $\mathcal { T } ^ { \prime }$ are related by ${ \mathcal { T } } ^ { \prime } = { \mathcal { T } } ^ { \mu }$ 

Proof: If $J \in \mathcal { T } ^ { \mu }$ , there exists an $I \in \mathcal { Z }$ with $\mu ( I { \triangle } J ) = 0$ . Since $T$ is μ -preserving, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu \Big (T ^ {- 1} J \triangle J \Big) \leq \mu \Big (T ^ {- 1} J \triangle T ^ {- 1} I \Big) + \mu \Big (T ^ {- 1} I \triangle I \Big) + \mu (I \triangle J) \\ = \mu \circ T ^ {- 1} (J \triangle I) \\ = \mu (J \triangle I) = 0, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $J \in \mathcal { T } ^ { \prime }$ . Conversely, given any $J \in \mathcal { T } ^ { \prime }$ , we may choose a $J ^ { \prime } \in { \mathcal { S } }$ with $\mu ( J \triangle J ^ { \prime } ) = 0$ , and put $I = \cap _ { n } \cup _ { k \geq n } T ^ { - n } J ^ { \prime }$ . Then clearly $I \in \mathcal { Z }$ and $\mu ( I { \mit \triangle } J ) = 0$ , and so $J \in \mathcal { T } ^ { \mu }$ ✷ 

A measure-preserving map $T$ on a probability space $( S , S , \mu )$ is said to be ergodic for $\mu$ or simply $\mu - e r g o d i c .$ , if the invariant σ-field $\mathcal { T }$ is $\mu - t r i v i a l ,$ in the sense that $\mu I = 0$ or 1 for every $I \in \mathcal { Z }$ . Depending on viewpoint, we may prefer to say that $\mu$ is ergodic for $T _ { \ast }$ , or T-ergodic. The terminology carries over to any random element $\xi$ with distribution $\mu ,$ , which is said to be ergodic whenever this is true for $T$ or $\mu .$ . Thus, $\xi$ is ergodic if $P \{ \xi \in I \} = 0$ or 1 for any $I \in \mathcal { Z }$ , i.e., if the σ-field $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { I } _ { \xi } = \xi ^ { - 1 } \mathcal { I } } \end{array}$ in $\Omega$ is P-trivial. In particular, a stationary sequence $\xi = \left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is ergodic, if the shift-invariant $\sigma { - } \mathrm { f i e l d }$ is trivial for the distribution of $\xi$ . 

We show how the ergodicity of a random element $\xi$ is related to the ergodicity of the generated stationary sequence. 

Lemma 25.5 (ergodicity) Let $\xi$ be a random element in $S$ with distribution $\mu ,$ and let $T$ be a μ -preserving map on $S$ . Then 

$$
\xi \text {   is   } T \text {-ergodic } \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad (T ^ {n} \xi) \text {   is   } \theta \text {-ergodic},
$$

in which case $\eta = ( f \circ T ^ { n } \xi )$ is θ-ergodic for every measurable function f on $S$ 

Proof: Fix any measurable map $f \colon S  S ^ { \prime }$ , and define $F = \{ f \circ T ^ { n } ; n \geq 0 \}$ so that $F \circ T = \theta \circ F$ . If $I \subset ( S ^ { \prime } ) ^ { \infty }$ is θ -invariant, then $T ^ { - 1 } F ^ { - 1 } { \dot { I } } = F ^ { - 1 } \theta ^ { - 1 } { \dot { I } } =$ $F ^ { - 1 } I$ , and so $F ^ { - 1 } I$ is T-invariant in S. Assuming $\xi$ to be ergodic, we obtain $P \{ \eta \in I \} = P \{ \xi \in F ^ { - 1 } I \} = 0$ or 1, which shows that even η is ergodic. 

Conversely, let the sequence $( T ^ { n } \xi )$ be ergodic, and fix any T-invariant set I in S. Put $F = \{ T ^ { n } ; n \ge 0 \}$ , and define $A = \left\{ s \in S ^ { \infty } ; s _ { n } \in I \mathrm { { i . o . } } \right\}$ . Then $I = F ^ { - 1 } A$ and A is θ -invariant. Hence, $P \{ \xi \in I \} = P \{ ( T ^ { n } \xi ) \in A \} = 0$ or 1, which means that even $\xi$ is ergodic. ✷ 

We may now state the fundamental a.s. and mean ergodic theorem for stationary sequences of random variables. Recall that $( S , S )$ denotes an arbitrary measurable space, and write $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } = \xi ^ { - 1 } \mathcal { T } } \end{array}$ for convenience. 

Theorem 25.6 (ergodic theorem, Birkhof) Let $\xi$ be a random element in $S$ with distribution $\mu ,$ and let T be a μ-preserving map<sup>4</sup> on $S$ with invariant σ-field . Then for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on S, 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k <   n} f (T ^ {k} \xi) \rightarrow E \left\{f (\xi) \mid \mathcal {I} _ {\xi} \right\} a. s.\tag{1}
$$

When $f \in L ^ { p } ( \mu )$ for $a \ p \geq 1$ , the convergence extends to $L ^ { p }$ 

The proof is based on a simple but ingenious inequality. 

Lemma 25.7 (maximal ergodic lemma, Hopf) Let $\xi = \left( \xi _ { k } \right)$ be a stationary sequence of integrable random variables, and put $S _ { n } = \xi _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \xi _ { n }$ . Then 

$$
E \Big (\xi_ {1}; \sup _ {n \geq 1} S _ {n} > 0 \Big) \geq 0.
$$

Proof (Garsia): Put $M _ { n } = S _ { 1 } \lor \cdots \lor S _ { n }$ . Assuming $\xi$ to be defined on the canonical space ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {k} = \xi_ {1} + S _ {k - 1} \circ \theta \\ \leq \xi_ {1} + (M _ {n} \circ \theta) _ {+}, \quad k = 1, \ldots , n. \end{array}
$$

Taking maxima yields $M _ { n } \leq \xi _ { 1 } + ( M _ { n } \circ \theta ) _ { + }$ for all $n \in \mathsf N$ , and so by stationarity 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \Big (\xi_ {1}; M _ {n} > 0 \Big) \geq E \Big \{M _ {n} - (M _ {n} \circ \theta) _ {+}; M _ {n} > 0 \Big \} \\ \geq E \Big \{(M _ {n}) _ {+} - (M _ {n} \circ \theta) _ {+} \Big \} = 0. \end{array}
$$

Since $M _ { n } \uparrow \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } S _ { n }$ , the assertion follows by dominated convergence. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 25.6 (Yosida & Kakutani): First let $f \in L ^ { 1 }$ , and put $\eta _ { k } = f ( T ^ { k - 1 } \xi )$ for convenience. Since $E ( \eta _ { 1 } | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } )$ is an invariant function of $\xi$ by Lemmas 1.14 and 25.3, the sequence $\zeta _ { k } = \eta _ { k } - E ( \eta _ { 1 } | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } )$ is again stationary. Writing $S _ { n } = \zeta _ { 1 } + \cdots + \zeta _ { n }$ , we define for any $\varepsilon > 0$

and note that the sums $S _ { n } ^ { \varepsilon } = \zeta _ { 1 } ^ { \varepsilon } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \zeta _ { n } ^ { \varepsilon }$ satisfy

\begin{array}{c} \left\{\sup _ {n} S _ {n} ^ {\varepsilon} > 0 \right\} = \left\{\sup _ {n} (S _ {n} ^ {\varepsilon} / n) > 0 \right\} \\ = \left\{\sup _ {n} (S _ {n} / n) > \varepsilon \right\} \cap A _ {\varepsilon} = A _ {\varepsilon}. \end{array}

Since $A _ { \varepsilon } \in \mathcal { T } _ { \xi }$ , the sequence $\left( \zeta _ { n } ^ { \varepsilon } \right)$ is stationary, and Lemma 25.7 yields

Applying the same result to $- S _ { n }$ yields lim in $\operatorname { f } _ { n } ( S _ { n } / n ) \geq 0 { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , and so by combination $S _ { n } / n \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ 

Now let $f \in L ^ { p }$ for a $p \geq 1$ . Using Jensen’s inequality and the stationarity of $T ^ { k } \xi$ , we get for any $A \in { \mathcal { A } }$ and $r > 0$

which tends to 0 as $P A  0$ and then $r  \infty$ . Hence, by Lemma 5.10, the $p \mathrm { - t h }$ powers on the left are uniformly integrable, and the asserted $L ^ { p } .$ -convergence follows by Proposition 5.12. 

Finally, let $f \geq 0$ be arbitrary, and put $E \{ f ( \xi ) | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } \} = \bar { \eta }$ . Conditioning on the event $\{ \bar { \eta } \leq r \}$ for an arbitrary $r > 0$ , we see that (1) holds a.s. on $\{ \bar { \eta } < \infty \}$ Next, we have a.s. for any $r > 0$

Write and $\tau$ for the shift-invariant and tail $\sigma { \mathrm { - f i e l d s } }$ in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ , respectively, and note that $\mathcal { T } \subset \mathcal { T }$ . We may often allow the function $f = f _ { n , k }$ in Theorem 25.6 to depend on n or k. Here we consider a slightly more general situation. 

Corollary 25.8 (varying functions, Maker) Let $\xi$ be a random element in $S$ with distribution $\mu ,$ let T be a μ-preserving map on S with invariant σ-field , and let $f$ and $f _ { m , k }$ be measurable functions on S. Then 

(i) if $f _ { m , k } \to f \ a . s .$ . and $\mathrm { s u p } _ { m , k } \mathopen { } \mathclose \bgroup \left| f _ { m , k } \aftergroup \egroup \right| \in L ^ { 1 }$ , we have as $m , n  \infty$

n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k <   n} f _ {m, k} (T ^ {k} \xi) \rightarrow E \left\{f (\xi) \mid \mathcal {I} _ {\xi} \right\} a. s.,
$$

(ii) when $f _ { m , k } \to f$ in L<sup>p</sup> for a $p \geq 1$ <sub>, the convergence extends to</sub> $L ^ { p }$ 

Proof: (i) By Theorem 25.6 we may take $f = 0$ . Then put $g _ { r } = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { m , k > r } | f _ { m , k } |$ , and conclude from the same result that a.s.

Here $g _ { r } ( \xi ) \to 0 \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., and so by dominated convergence $E \{ g _ { r } ( \xi ) | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } \} \to 0 \mathrm { ~ a . s . }$

$$
\left\| n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k <   n} f _ {m, k} \circ T ^ {k} \right\| _ {p} \leq n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k <   n} \| f _ {m, k} \| _ {p} \to 0.
$$

To extend the ergodic theorem to continuous time, consider a family of transformations $T _ { t }$ on $S , t \geq 0$ , satisfying the semi-group property $T _ { s + t } = T _ { s } T _ { t }$ The latter is called a flow if it is also measura $. b l e ,$ , in the sense that the map $( x , t ) \mapsto T _ { t } x$ is product measurable from $S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ to $S .$ . The invariant $\sigma { - } f i e l d \mathcal { T }$ now consists of all sets $I \in S$ with $T _ { t } ^ { - 1 } I = I$ for all t. A random element $\xi$ in $S$ is said to be $( T _ { t } )$ -stationary if $T _ { t } \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ for all $t \geq 0$ 

Corollary 25.9 (continuous-time ergodic theorem) Let $\xi$ be a random element in $S$ with distribution $\mu _ { ; }$ , and let $\left( T _ { s } \right)$ be a μ-preserving $f l o w ^ { 5 }$ on $S$ with invariant $\sigma { - } f i e l d \mathcal { T }$ . Then for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $S _ { i }$ 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} t ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f (T _ {s} \xi) d s = E \Bigl \{f (\xi)   \big |   \mathcal {I} _ {\xi} \Bigr \} a. s.\tag{2}
$$

When $f \in L ^ { p } ( \mu )$ for a $p \geq 1$ , the convergence extends to $L ^ { p }$ 

Proof: In both cases we may assume that $f \geq 0$ . Writing $X _ { s } = f ( T _ { s } \xi )$ , we get by Jensen’s inequality and Fubini’s theorem 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \left| t ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {s}   d s \right| ^ {p} \leq E   t ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} X _ {s} ^ {p}   d s \\ = t ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} E X _ {s} ^ {p}   d s \\ = E X _ {0} ^ {p} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

The required convergence now follows, as we apply Theorem 25.6 to the function $\begin{array} { r } { g ( x ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } f ( T _ { s } x ) } \end{array}$ ds and the discrete shift $T = T _ { 1 }$ 

-<sub>To identify the limit, take</sub> $f \in L ^ { 1 }$ , and introduce the invariant version 

$$
\bar {f} (\xi) = \lim _ {r \to \infty} \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \int_ {r} ^ {r + n} f (T _ {s} \xi)   d s,
$$

which is also -measurable. The stationarity of $T _ { s } \xi$ yields $E ^ { Z _ { \xi } } f ( T _ { s } \xi ) ~ = ~$ $E ^ { Z _ { \xi } } f ( \xi )$ a.s. for all $s \geq 0$ . Using Fubini’s theorem, the $L ^ { 1 } .$ -convergence in (2), and the contraction property of conditional expectations, we get as $t \to \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E ^ {\mathcal {I} _ {\xi}} f (\xi) & = t ^ {- 1} E ^ {\mathcal {I} _ {\xi}} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f (T _ {s} \xi)   d s \\ & \stackrel {{P}} {{\to}} E ^ {\mathcal {I} _ {\xi}} \bar {f} (\xi) \\ & = \bar {f} (\xi), \end{array}
$$

as required. The result extends as before to arbitrary $f \geq 0$ 

We return to the case of a stationary sequence $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . of integrable random variables, and put $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } . } \end{array}$ . Since $S _ { n } / n$ converges a.s. by Theorem 25.6, the maximum $M = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } ( \bar { S _ { n } } / n )$ is a.s. finite. The following result, relating the moments of ξ and M, is known as the dominated ergodic theorem. Here we write log $\mathbf { \Phi } _ { + } { x } = \log ( x \vee 1 )$ , for convenience. 

Proposition 25.10 (maximum inequalities, Hardy & Littlewood, Wiener) Let $\xi = ( \xi _ { k } )$ be a stationary sequence of random variables, and put $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } } \end{array}$ and $M = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } ( S _ { n } / n )$ . Then 

(i) $E | M | ^ { p } \lesssim E | \xi _ { 1 } | ^ { p } , \ p > 1$ 

(ii) $\begin{array} { r } { E \Big ( | M | \log _ { + } ^ { m } | M | \Big ) \lesssim 1 + E \Big ( | \xi _ { 1 } | \log _ { + } ^ { m + 1 } | \xi _ { 1 } | \Big ) , ~ m \geq 0 . } \end{array}$ 

The proof requires a simple estimate related to Lemma 25.7. 

Lemma 25.11 (tail estimate) When $\xi = ( \xi _ { k } )$ is stationary in $L ^ { 1 }$ 

$$
r P \left\{\sup _ {n} \left(S _ {n} / n\right) > 2 r \right\} \leq E \left(\xi_ {1}; \xi_ {1} > r\right), \quad r > 0.
$$

Proof: For any $r > 0$ , put $\xi _ { k } ^ { r } = \xi _ { k } { 1 } \{ \xi _ { k } > r \}$ , and note that $\xi _ { k } \le \xi _ { k } ^ { r } + r$ Assuming $\xi$ to be defined on the canonical space $\mathsf { R } ^ { \infty }$ , and writing $A _ { n } = S _ { n } / n$ we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} A _ {n} - 2 r = A _ {n} \circ (\xi - 2 r) \\ \leq A _ {n} \circ (\xi^ {r} - r), \end{array}
$$

which implies $M - 2 r \leq M \circ ( \xi ^ { r } - r )$ . Applying Lemma 25.7 to the sequence $\xi ^ { r } - r$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r   P \{M > 2 r \} \leq r   P \Big \{M \circ (\xi^ {r} - r) > 0 \Big \} \\ \qquad \leq E \Big \{\xi_ {1} ^ {r}; M \circ (\xi^ {r} - r) > 0 \Big \} \\ \qquad \leq E \xi_ {1} ^ {r} = E \big (\xi_ {1}; \xi_ {1} > r \big). \end{array}
$$

Proof of Proposition 25.10: We may clearly assume that $\xi _ { 1 } \ge 0$ a.s. 

(i) By Lemma 25.11, Fubini’s theorem, and calculus, 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} E M ^ {p} = & p E \int_ {0} ^ {M} r ^ {p - 1} d r \\ = & p \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \{M > r \} r ^ {p - 1} d r \\ \leq & 2 p \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E \big (\xi_ {1};   2   \xi_ {1} > r \big) r ^ {p - 2} d r \\ = & 2 p E \xi_ {1} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \xi_ {1}} r ^ {p - 2} d r \\ = & 2 p (p - 1) ^ {- 1} E \big \{\xi_ {1} (2   \xi_ {1}) ^ {p - 1} \big \} \\ \lesssim & E \xi_ {1} ^ {p}. \end{array}
$$

(ii) For $m = 0 ,$ , we may write 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} E M - 1 & \leq E (M - 1) _ {+} \\ & = \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} P \{M > r \} d r \\ & \leq 2 \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} E \big (\xi_ {1};   2   \xi_ {1} > r \big)   r ^ {- 1} d r \\ & = 2   E   \xi_ {1} \int_ {1} ^ {2   \xi_ {1} \vee 1} r ^ {- 1} d r \\ & = 2   E \big (\xi_ {1} \log_ {+} 2 \xi_ {1} \big) \\ & \leq e + 2 E \big (\xi_ {1} \log 2   \xi_ {1};   2   \xi_ {1} > e \big) \\ & \lesssim 1 + E \big (\xi_ {1} \log_ {+} \xi_ {1} \big). \end{array}
$$

For $m > 0$ , we may write instead 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} E \Big (M \log_ {+} ^ {m} M \Big) & = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Big \{M \log_ {+} ^ {m} M > r \Big \} d r \\ & = \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} P \{M > t \} \left(m \log^ {m - 1} t + \log^ {m} t\right) d t \\ & \leq 2 \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} E \Big (\xi_ {1};   2   \xi_ {1} > t \Big) \Big (m \log^ {m - 1} t + \log^ {m} t \Big)   t ^ {- 1} d t \\ & = 2   E   \xi_ {1} \int_ {0} ^ {\log_ {+} 2 \xi_ {1}} \Big (m x ^ {m - 1} + x ^ {m} \Big)   d x \\ & = 2   E   \xi_ {1} \left(\log_ {+} ^ {m} 2   \xi_ {1} + \frac {\log_ {+} ^ {m + 1} 2   \xi_ {1}}{m + 1}\right) \\ & \leq 2 e + 4   E \Big (\xi_ {1} \log^ {m + 1} 2   \xi_ {1};   2   \xi_ {1} > e \Big) \\ & \lesssim 1 + E \Big (\xi_ {1} \log_ {+} ^ {m + 1}   \xi_ {1} \Big). \end{array}
$$

Given a measure space $( S , S , \mu )$ , we introduce for any $m \geq 0$ the class $L \log ^ { m } L ( \mu )$ of measurable functions $f$ on $S$ satisfying $\textstyle \int | f | \log _ { + } ^ { m } | f | d \mu < \infty$ Note in particular that $L \log ^ { 0 } L = \dot { L } ^ { 1 }$ -<sub>. Using the maximum inequalities of</sub> Proposition 25.10, we may prove the following multi-variate version of Theorem 25.6, for possibly non-commuting, measure-preserving transformations $T _ { 1 } , \dots , T _ { d }$ 

Theorem 25.12 (multi-variate ergodic theorem, Zygmund) Let $\xi$ be a random element in S with distribution $\mu _ { ; }$ , let $T _ { 1 } , \ldots , T _ { d }$ be μ-preserving maps on $S$ with invariant σ-fields $\mathcal { T } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \mathcal { T } _ { d }$ , and put $\mathcal { T } _ { k } = \xi ^ { - 1 } \mathcal { T } _ { k }$ . Then for any $f \in L \log ^ { d - 1 } L ( \mu )$ , we have as $n _ { 1 } , \ldots , n _ { d } $ ∞ 

$$
(n _ {1} \dots n _ {d}) ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k _ {1} <   n _ {1}} \dots \sum_ {k _ {d} <   n _ {d}} f \left(T _ {1} ^ {k _ {1}} \dots T _ {d} ^ {k _ {d}} \xi\right)\rightarrow E ^ {\mathcal {J} _ {d}} \dots E ^ {\mathcal {J} _ {1}} f (\xi) a. s.\tag{3}
$$

When $f \in L ^ { p } ( \mu )$ for a $p \geq 1$ , the convergence extends to $L ^ { p }$ 

Proof: Since $E \{ f ( \xi ) | \mathcal { T } _ { k } \} = \mu ( f | \mathcal { T } _ { k } ) \circ \xi \mathrm { ~ a . s . , ~ e . g . }$ . by Theorem 25.6, we may choose $\xi$ to be the identity map on S. For $d = 1$ , the result reduces to Theorem 25.6. Now assume the statement to be true up to dimension d. Proceeding by induction, consider any $\mu { \mathrm { - p r e s e r v i n g } }$ maps $T _ { 1 } , \ldots , T _ { d + 1 }$ on $S _ { ; }$ and let $f \in L \log ^ { d } L$ . By the induction hypothesis, the d -dimensional version of (3) holds as stated, and we may write the result in the form $f _ { m } \ \to \ \bar { f }$ a.s., where $m = ( n _ { 1 } , \ldots , n _ { d } ) $ . Iterating Proposition 25.10, we also note that $\mu \operatorname* { s u p } _ { m } | f _ { m } | < \infty$ . Hence, Corollary 25.8 (i) yields as m, $n \to \infty$ 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k <   n} f _ {m} \circ T _ {d + 1} ^ {k} \rightarrow \mu (\bar {f} | \mathcal {I} _ {d + 1}) \text {a.s.},
$$

as required. The proof of the L<sup>p</sup>-version is similar. 

In the commutative case, the last result yields an interesting relationship between the associated conditional expectations. Let $L ^ { 1 } ( \xi )$ denote the set of all integrable, ξ -measurable random variables. 

Corollary 25.13 (commuting maps and expectations) Let the maps $T _ { 1 } , \ldots , T _ { d }$ in Theorem 25.12 commute, and put $\mathcal { I } = \cap _ { k } \mathcal { I } _ { k }$ . Then 

$$
E ^ {\mathcal {J} _ {1}} \dots E ^ {\mathcal {J} _ {d}} = E ^ {\mathcal {J}} o n L ^ {1} (\xi).
$$

Proof: Since even $T _ { 1 } ^ { k _ { 1 } } , \ldots , T _ { d } ^ { k _ { d } }$ commute for arbitrary $k _ { 1 } , \dots , k _ { d } \in Z _ { + }$ , Theorem 25.12 yields 

$$
E ^ {\mathcal {I} _ {1}} \dots E ^ {\mathcal {I} _ {d}} f (\xi) = E ^ {\mathcal {I} _ {p _ {1}}} \dots E ^ {\mathcal {I} _ {p _ {d}}} f (\xi) \text {a.s.}\tag{4}
$$

for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $S$ and permutation $p _ { 1 } , \ldots , p _ { d }$ of $1 , \ldots , d .$ In particular, the expression in (4) is a.s. -measurable for every k, and therefore $\mathcal { I }$ -measurable. It remains to note that 

$$
E \left\{E ^ {\mathcal {J} _ {1}} \dots E ^ {\mathcal {J} _ {d}} f (\xi); A \right\} = E \left\{f (\xi); A \right\}, \quad A \in \mathcal {J}.
$$

For commuting maps $T _ { 1 } , \ldots , T _ { d }$ on $S _ { ; }$ , the compositions $T ^ { k } = T _ { 1 } ^ { k _ { 1 } } \cdot \cdot \cdot T _ { d } ^ { k _ { d } }$ form a d -dimensional semi-group indexed by $Z _ { + } ^ { d }$ . Similarly, when $( T _ { 1 } ^ { s } ) , \ldots , ( T _ { d } ^ { s } )$ are commuting flows on $S _ { i }$ , the compositions $T ^ { s } = T _ { 1 } ^ { s _ { 1 } } \cdot \cdot \cdot \ T _ { d } ^ { s _ { d } }$ form a $d -$ dimensional, measurable semi-group or flow indexed by $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ^ { d }$ . In the continuous parameter case, it may be more natural to consider flows indexed by $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ , corresponding to the case of stationary processes on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . In this context, one may also want to average over more general sets than rectangles. Here we consider a basic ergodic theorem for increasing sequences of convex sets. Given such a set $B$ , we define the inner radius $r ( B )$ as the radius of the largest open ball contained in B. 

Theorem 25.14 (convex averages, Wiener) Consider a random element $\xi$ in $S$ with distribution $\mu$ and a flow of μ-preserving maps $T _ { s }$ on $S , s \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , with invariant σ-field $\mathcal { T } ,$ and let $B _ { 1 } \subset B _ { 2 } \subset \cdots$ be bounded, convex sets in $B ^ { d }$ with $r ( B _ { n } ) \to \infty$ . Then for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $S$ , 

$$
\left(\lambda^ {d} B _ {n}\right) ^ {- 1} \int_ {B _ {n}} f (T _ {s} \xi) d s \rightarrow E \left\{f (\xi) \mid \mathcal {I} _ {\xi} \right\} a. s.
$$

When $f \in L ^ { p } ( \mu )$ for a $p \geq 1$ , the convergence extends to $L ^ { p }$ 

Several lemmas will be needed for the proof, beginning with a simple geometric estimate. 

Lemma 25.15 (space filling) For any bounded, convex sets $B _ { 1 } \subset \cdots \subset B _ { m }$ in $B ^ { d }$ with $\lambda ^ { d } B _ { 1 } > 0$ , a bounded set $K \in B ^ { d }$ , and a function h: $K  \{ 1 , \ldots , m \}$ , there exists a finite subset $M \subset K$ , such that the sets $B _ { h ( x ) } + x , x \in M$ , are disjoint and satisfy (2d) □ )d 

$$
\lambda^ {d} K \leq \binom {2 d} {d} \sum_ {x \in M} \lambda^ {d} B _ {h (x)}.
$$

Proof: Put $\begin{array} { r } { C _ { x } = B _ { h ( x ) } + x } \end{array}$ , and choose $x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \dotsc \in K$ recursively, as follows. Once $x _ { 1 } , \dotsc , x _ { j - 1 }$ have been selected, choose $x _ { j } \in K$ with the largest possible $h ( x )$ , such that $C _ { x _ { i } } \cap C _ { x _ { i } } = \emptyset$ for all $i < j$ . The construction terminates when no such $x _ { j }$ exists. Put $\Breve { M } = \{ x _ { i } \}$ , and note that the sets $C _ { x }$ with $x \in M$ are disjoint. Now fix any $y \in K$ . By the construction of $M .$ , we have $C _ { x } \cap C _ { y } \neq \emptyset$ for some $x \in M$ with $h ( x ) \geq h ( y )$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{c} y \in B _ {h (x)} - B _ {h (y)} + x \\ \subset B _ {h (x)} - B _ {h (x)} + x. \end{array}
$$

Hence, $K \subset \bigcup _ { x \in M } ( B _ { h ( x ) } - B _ { h ( x ) } + x )$ , and so by Lemma A6.5 (i), 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \lambda^ {d} K \leq \sum_ {x \in M} \lambda^ {d} \Big (B _ {h (x)} - B _ {h (x)} \Big) \\ \leq \binom {2 d} {d} \sum_ {x \in M} \lambda^ {d} B _ {h (x)}. \end{array}
$$

Next we prove a multi-variate version of Lemma 25.11, stated for convenience in terms of random measures. For motivation, we note that the set function $\begin{array} { r } { \eta B = \int _ { B } f ( T _ { s } \xi ) } \end{array}$ ds in Theorem 25.14 is a stationary random measure on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ -<sub>, and that the intensity m of</sub> $\eta ,$ defined by the relation $E \eta = m \lambda ^ { d }$ , is equal to $E f ( \xi )$ 

Lemma 25.16 (maximum inequality) Let ξ be a stationary random measure on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with intensity m, and let $B _ { 1 } \subset B _ { 2 } \subset \cdots$ be bounded, convex sets in $B ^ { d }$ with $\lambda ^ { d } B _ { 1 } > 0$ . Then 

$$
r   P \Bigl \{\sup _ {k} \frac {\xi B _ {k}}{\lambda^ {d} B _ {k}} > r \Bigr \} \leq m \binom {2 d} {d}, \quad r > 0.
$$

Proof: Fix any $r , a > 0$ and $n \in \mathsf N$ , and define a process ν on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and a random set K in $S _ { a } = \{ x \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } ; | x | \leq a \}$ by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \nu (x) = \inf \Bigl \{k \in \mathsf {N};   \xi (B _ {k} + x) > r   \lambda^ {d} B _ {k} \Bigr \}, \quad x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}, \\ K = \Bigl \{x \in S _ {a};   \nu (x) \leq n \Bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

By Lemma 25.15 we may choose a finite, random subset $M \subset K$ , such that the sets $B _ { \nu ( x ) } + x , \ x \in M$ , are disjoint and $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda ^ { d } K \le \binom { 2 d } { d } \sum _ { x \in M } \lambda ^ { d } B _ { \nu ( x ) } } \end{array}$ . Writing $b = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ | x | ; x \in B _ { n } \}$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \xi S _ {a + b} \geq \sum_ {x \in M} \xi \Big (B _ {\nu (x)} + x \Big) \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq r \sum_ {x \in M} \lambda^ {d} B _ {\nu (x)} \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \geq r \binom {2 d} {d} ^ {- 1} \lambda^ {d} K. \end{array}
$$

Taking expectations and using Fubini’s theorem and the stationarity and measurability of $\nu _ { \mathrm { { ; } } }$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} m \binom {2 d} {d} \lambda^ {d} S _ {a + b} & \geq r E \lambda^ {d} K \\ & = r \int_ {S _ {a}} P \Bigl \{\nu (x) \leq n \Bigr \} d x \\ & = r \lambda^ {d} S _ {a}   P \Bigl \{\max _ {k \leq n} \frac {\xi B _ {k}}{\lambda^ {d} B _ {k}} > r \Bigr \}. \end{array}
$$

Now divide by $\lambda ^ { d } S _ { a }$ , and then let $a  \infty$ and $n \to \infty$ in this order. 

We finally need an elementary Hilbert-space result. By a contraction on a Hilbert space H we mean a linear operator $T ,$ such that $\| T x \| \leq \| x \|$ for all $x \in H$ . For any linear subspace $M \subset H$ , write $M ^ { \perp }$ for the orthogonal complement and $\bar { M }$ for the closure of M. The adjoint $T ^ { * }$ of an operator $T$ is determined by the identity $\langle x , T y \rangle = \langle T ^ { * } x , y \rangle$ , where $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle$ denotes the inner product in H. 

Lemma 25.17 (invariant subspace) Let be a set of contraction operators on a Hilbert space H, and write N for the -invariant subspace of H. Then 

$$
N ^ {\perp} \subset \bar {R}, \qquad R = \operatorname{span} \left\{x - T x; x \in H, T \in \mathcal {T} \right\}.
$$

Proof: If $x \perp R ,$ 

$$
\langle x - T ^ {*} x, y \rangle = \langle x, y - T y \rangle = 0, \quad T \in \mathcal {T}, y \in H,
$$

which implies $T ^ { * } x = x$ for every $T \in \mathcal { T }$ . Hence, for any $T \in \mathcal { T }$ , we have $\langle T x , x \rangle = \langle x , T ^ { * } x \rangle = \| x \| ^ { 2 }$ , and so by contraction 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq \| T x - x \| ^ {2} \\ = \| T x \| ^ {2} + \| x \| ^ {2} - 2 \langle T x, x \rangle \\ \leq 2 \| x \| ^ {2} - 2 \| x \| ^ {2} = 0, \end{array}
$$

which implies $T x = x$ . This gives $R ^ { \perp } \subset N$ , and so $N ^ { \perp } \subset ( R ^ { \perp } ) ^ { \perp } = \bar { R } .$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 25.14: First let $f \in L ^ { 1 }$ , and define 

$$
\tilde {T} _ {s} f = f \circ T _ {s}, \qquad A _ {n} = (\lambda^ {d} B _ {n}) ^ {- 1} \int_ {B _ {n}} \tilde {T} _ {s} d s.
$$

For any $\varepsilon > 0$ , Lemma 25.17 yields a measurable decomposition 

$$
f = f ^ {\varepsilon} + \sum_ {k \leq m} \left(g _ {k} ^ {\varepsilon} - \tilde {T} _ {s _ {k}} g _ {k} ^ {\varepsilon}\right) + h ^ {\varepsilon},
$$

where $f ^ { \varepsilon } \in L ^ { 2 }$ is $\tilde { T } _ { s }$ -invariant for all $s \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ , the functions $g _ { 1 } ^ { \varepsilon } , \ldots , g _ { m } ^ { \varepsilon }$ are bounded, and $E | h ^ { \varepsilon } ( \xi ) | < \varepsilon$ . Here clearly $A _ { n } f ^ { \varepsilon } \equiv f ^ { \varepsilon }$ . Using Lemma A6.5 (ii), we get as $n \to \infty$ for fixed $k \leq m$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left\| A _ {n} \Big (g _ {k} ^ {\varepsilon} - \tilde {T} _ {s _ {k}} g _ {k} ^ {\varepsilon} \Big) \right\| \leq \frac {\lambda^ {d} \Big \{(B _ {n} + s _ {k}) \triangle B _ {n} \Big \}}{\lambda^ {d} B _ {n}} \| g _ {k} ^ {\varepsilon} \| \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad 2 \left\{\big (1 + | s _ {k} | / r (B _ {n}) \big) ^ {d} - 1 \right\} \| g _ {k} ^ {\varepsilon} \| \to 0. \end{array}
$$

Finally, Lemma 25.16 gives 

$$
r   P \Bigl \{\sup _ {n} A _ {n} | h ^ {\varepsilon} (\xi) | \geq r \Bigr \} \leq \binom {2 d} {d} E | h ^ {\varepsilon} (\xi) | \leq \binom {2 d} {d} \varepsilon , \quad r, \varepsilon > 0,
$$

and so $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } A _ { n } | h ^ { \varepsilon } ( \xi ) | \overset { P } { \to } 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$ . In particular, lim $\operatorname* { i n f } _ { n } A _ { n } f ( \xi ) < \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , which ensures that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \Big (\lim _ {n \to \infty} \sup - \lim _ {n \to \infty} \inf \Big) A _ {n} f (\xi) & = \Big (\lim _ {n \to \infty} \sup - \lim _ {n \to \infty} \inf \Big) A _ {n} h ^ {\varepsilon} (\xi) \\ & \leq 2 \sup _ {n} A _ {n} | h ^ {\varepsilon} (\xi) | \xrightarrow {P} 0. \end{array}
$$

Thus, the left-hand side vanishes $\mathrm { a . s . }$ , and the required a.s. convergence follows. 

When $f \in L ^ { p }$ for a $p \geq 1$ , the asserted L<sup>p</sup>-convergence follows as before, by the uniform integrability of the powers $| A _ { n } f ( \xi ) | ^ { p }$ . We may now identify the limit, as in the proof of Corollary 25.9, and the a.s. convergence extends to arbitrary $f \geq 0$ , as in case of Theorem 25.6. ✷ 

The L<sup>p</sup>-version of Theorem 25.14 remains valid under weaker conditions. For a simple extension, say that the distributions $\mu _ { n }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ are asymptotically invariant if $\| \mu _ { n } - \mu _ { n } * \delta _ { s } \| \to 0$ for every $s \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , where $\| \cdot \|$ denotes the total variation norm. Note that the conclusion of Theorem 25.14 can be written as $\mu _ { n } X \to \bar { X }$ a.s., where 

$$
\mu_ {n} = \frac {1 _ {B _ {n}} \lambda^ {d}}{\lambda^ {d} B _ {n}}, \qquad X _ {s} = f (T _ {s} \xi), \qquad \bar {X} = E \bigl \{f (\xi)   \big |   \mathcal {I} _ {\xi} \bigr \}.
$$

Corollary 25.18 (mean ergodic theorem) Let X be a stationary, measurable, and L<sup>p</sup>-valued process on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , where $p \geq 1$ . Then for any asymptotically invariant distributions $\mu _ { n }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , 

$$
\mu_ {n} X \to \bar {X} \equiv E \left(X _ {s} \mid \mathcal {I} _ {X}\right) i n L ^ {p}.
$$

Proof: By Theorem 25.14 we may choose some distributions $\nu _ { m }$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\nu _ { m } X  \bar { X }$ in $L ^ { p }$ . Using Minkowski’s inequality and its extension in Corollary 1.32, along with the stationarity of $X$ , the invariance of $\bar { X }$ , and dominated convergence, we get as $n $ and then $m \to \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left\| \mu_ {n} X - \bar {X} \right\| _ {p} \leq \left\| \mu_ {n} X - (\mu_ {n} * \nu_ {m}) X \right\| _ {p} + \left\| (\mu_ {n} * \nu_ {m}) X - \bar {X} \right\| _ {p}} \\ & {\qquad \leq \left\| \mu_ {n} - \mu_ {n} * \nu_ {m} \right\| \| X \| _ {p} + \int \left\| (\delta_ {s} * \nu_ {m}) X - \bar {X} \right\| _ {p} \mu_ {n} (d s)} \\ & {\qquad \leq \| X \| _ {p} \int \left\| \mu_ {n} - \mu_ {n} * \delta_ {t} \right\| \nu_ {m} (d t) + \left\| \nu_ {m} X - \bar {X} \right\| _ {p} \to 0.} \end{array}
$$

We turn to a sub-additive version of Theorem 25.6. For motivation and subsequent needs, we begin with a simple result for non-random sequences. A sequence $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } , \ldots \in { \textsf { R } }$ is said to be sub-additive, if $c _ { m + n } \leq c _ { m } + c _ { n }$ for all $m , n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

Lemma 25.19 (sub-additivity) For any sub-additive sequence $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } , \dotsc \in { \mathsf { R } }$ , 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \frac {c _ {n}}{n} = \inf _ {n} \frac {c _ {n}}{n} \in [ - \infty , \infty).
$$

Proof: Iterating the sub-additivity relation, we get for any $k , n \in \mathbb { N }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} c _ {n} \leq [ n / k ] c _ {k} + c _ {n - k [ n / k ]} \\ \leq [ n / k ] c _ {k} + c _ {0} \vee \dots \vee c _ {k - 1}, \end{array}
$$

where $c _ { 0 } = 0$ . Noting that $[ n / k ] \sim n / k$ as $n  \infty$ , we get lim $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } ( c _ { n } / n ) \leq$ $c _ { k } / k$ for all k, and so 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \inf _ {n} \frac {c _ {n}}{n} \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {c _ {n}}{n} \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {c _ {n}}{n} \leq \inf _ {n} \frac {c _ {n}}{n}. \end{array}
$$

For two-dimensional arrays $c _ { j k } , \ 0 \leq j < k .$ , sub-additivity is defined by $c _ { 0 , n } \leq c _ { 0 , m } + c _ { m , n }$ for all $m \ : < \ : n$ , which reduces to the one-dimensional notion when $c _ { j k } = c _ { k - j }$ for some sequence $c _ { k }$ . Note that sub-additivity holds automatically for arrays of the form $c _ { j k } = a _ { j + 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + a _ { k }$ 

We now extend the ergodic theorem to sub-additive arrays of random variables $\xi _ { j k } , \ 0 \ \le \ j \ < \ k$ . For motivation, recall from Theorem 25.6 that, if $\xi _ { j k } = \eta _ { j + 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \eta _ { k }$ for a stationary sequence of integrable random variables $\eta _ { k }$ , then $\xi _ { 0 , n } / n$ converges a.s. and in $L ^ { 1 }$ . A similar result holds for general subadditive arrays $( \xi _ { j k } )$ , stationary under simultaneous shifts in the two indices, so that $\left( \xi _ { j + 1 , k + 1 } \right) \overset { d } { = } \left( \xi _ { j , k } \right)$ . To allow a wider range of applications, we introduce the slightly weaker hypotheses 

$$
\left(\xi_ {k, 2 k}, \xi_ {2 k, 3 k}, \dots\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left(\xi_ {0, k}, \xi_ {k, 2 k}, \dots\right), \quad k \in \mathsf {N},\tag{5}
$$

$$
\left(\xi_ {k, k + 1}, \xi_ {k, k + 2}, \dots\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left(\xi_ {0, 1}, \xi_ {0, 2}, \dots\right), \quad k \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{6}
$$

For convenience, we also restate the sub-additivity condition 

$$
\xi_ {0, n} \leq \xi_ {0, m} + \xi_ {m, n}, \quad 0 <   m <   n.\tag{7}
$$

Theorem 25.20 (sub-additive ergodic theorem, Kingman, Liggett) Let $( \xi _ { j k } )$ be a sub-additive array of random variables with $E \xi _ { 0 , 1 } ^ { + } < \infty$ , satisfying $( 5 ) - ( 6 )$ Then 

(i) $n ^ { - 1 } \xi _ { 0 , n }  \bar { \xi }$ a.s. in $[ - \infty , \infty )$ , where $E \bar { \xi } = \operatorname* { i n f } _ { n } ( E \xi _ { 0 , n } / n ) \equiv c ;$ 

(ii) the convergence in (i) extends to $L ^ { 1 }$ when $c > - \infty$ 

(iii) $\bar { \xi }$ is a.s. constant when the sequences in (5) are ergodic. 

Proof: Put $\xi _ { 0 , n } ~ = ~ \xi _ { n }$ for convenience. By (6) and (7) we have $E \xi _ { n } ^ { + } \ \leq$ n $E \xi _ { 1 } ^ { + } < \infty$ . First let $c > - \infty$ , so that the variables $\xi _ { m , n }$ are integrable. Iterating (7) gives 

$$

We turn to the decomposition of an invariant distribution into ergodic components. For motivation, consider the setting of Theorem 25.6 or 25.14, and let $S$ be Borel, to ensure the existence of regular conditional distributions. Writing $\eta = \mathcal { L } ( \xi | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } )$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {L} (\xi) = E \mathcal {L} (\xi   |   \mathcal {I} _ {\xi}) = E \eta \\ = \int m   P \{\eta \in d m \}. \end{array}
$$

Furthermore, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\eta I = P \Big \{\xi \in I   \Big |   \mathcal {I} _ {\xi} \Big \}} \\ & {\qquad = 1 \big \{\xi \in I \big \} \mathrm{a.s.}, \quad I \in \mathcal {I},} \end{array}\tag{14}
$$

and so $\eta I = 0$ or 1 a.s. for any fixed $I \in \mathcal { T }$ . If we can choose the exceptional null set to be independent of $I ,$ then η is a.s. ergodic, and (14) gives the desired ergodic decomposition of $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( \boldsymbol { \xi } )$ . Though the suggested statement is indeed true, its proof requires a diferent approach. 

Proposition 25.22 (ergodicity by conditioning, Farrell, Varadarajan) Let ξ be a random element in a Borel space $S$ with distribution $\mu ,$ , and consider a measurable group G of μ-preserving maps $T _ { s }$ on $S , \ s \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , with invariant σ-field . $$

$$

By Theorem 25.14, we have $\eta _ { n } f \to \eta f { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . for every bounded, measurable function $f$ on $S ,$ , where $\eta =$ $\mathcal { L } ( \xi | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } )$ . Say that a class $\mathcal { C } \subset S$ is measure-determining, if every distribution on $S$ is uniquely determined by its values on $\mathcal { C }$ . 

Lemma 25.23 (degenerate limit) Let $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \ldots \in S$ be measure-determining with empirical distributions $\eta _ { n } = \mu _ { n } ( \xi , \cdot )$ , where the $\mu _ { n }$ are given by (15). Then $\xi$ is ergodic whenever

In (14) we saw that, for stationary $\xi ,$ the distribution $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( \boldsymbol { \xi } )$ is a mixture of invariant, ergodic probability measures. We show that this representation is unique<sup>6</sup> and characterizes the ergodic measures as extreme points in the convex set of invariant measures. 

To explain the terminology, we say that a subset M of a linear space is convex if $c m _ { 1 } + ( 1 - c ) m _ { 2 } \in M$ for all $m _ { 1 } , m _ { 2 } \in M$ and $c \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . In that case, an element $m \in M$ is extreme if for any $m _ { 1 } , m _ { 2 } , c$ as above, the relation $m = c m _ { 1 } + ( 1 - c )$ m implies $m _ { 1 } = m _ { 2 } = m$ . With any set of measures $\mu$ on a measurable space $( S , S )$ , we associate the σ-field generated by all evaluation maps $\pi _ { B } \colon \mu \mapsto \mu B , B \in \mathcal { S }$ 

Theorem 25.24 (ergodic decomposition, Krylov & Bogolioubov) Let ${ \cal G } =$ $\{ T _ { s } ; s \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \}$ be a measurable group of transformations on a Borel space S. Then 

(i) the G-invariant distributions on S form a convex set M, whose extreme points are precisely the ergodic measures in M,

Thus, for any $A _ { 1 } , A _ { 2 } , \ldots \in S$ , we have 

$$
m \bigcap_ {k} \left\{x \in S; \mu_ {n} (x, A _ {k}) \rightarrow \eta (x, A _ {k}) \right\} = 1 \text { a.e. } \nu .
$$

The same relation holds with $\eta ( x , A _ { k } )$ replaced by $m A _ { k }$ , since ν is restricted to the class of ergodic measures in M. Assuming the sets $A _ { k }$ to be measuredetermining, we conclude that $m \{ x ; \eta ( x , \cdot ) = m \} = 1$ a.e. ν. Hence, for any measurable set $A \subset M$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu \{\eta \in A \} = \int m \{\eta \in A \} \nu (d m) \\ = \int 1 _ {A} (m) \nu (d m) = \nu A, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $\nu = \mu \circ \eta ^ { - 1 }$ 

To prove the equivalence of ergodicity and extremality, fix any measure $\mu \in M$ with ergodic decomposition $\begin{array} { r } { \int m \nu ( d m ) } \end{array}$ . First let $\mu$ be extreme. If it is not ergodic, then ν is non-degenerate, and we have $\nu = c \nu _ { 1 } + \left( 1 - c \right) \nu _ { 2 }$ for some $\nu _ { 1 } \bot \nu _ { 2 }$ and $c \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . Since $\mu$ is extreme, we obtain m $\nu _ { 1 } ( d m ) = \textstyle { \int } m \nu _ { 2 } ( d m )$ , and so $\nu _ { 1 } ~ = ~ \nu _ { 2 }$ - -<sub>by the uniqueness of the decomposition. The contradiction</sub> shows that $\mu$ is ergodic. 

Next let $\mu$ be ergodic, so that $\nu ~ = ~ \delta _ { \mu }$ , and let $\mu \ : = \ : c \mu _ { 1 } + ( 1 - c ) \mu _ { 2 }$ with $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } \in M$ and $c \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . If $\begin{array} { r } { \mu _ { i } = \int { m \nu _ { i } ( d m ) } } \end{array}$ for $i = 1 , 2$ , then $\delta _ { \mu } =$ $c \nu _ { 1 } + ( 1 - c ) \nu _ { 2 }$ -<sub>by the uniqueness of the decomposition. Hence,</sub> $\nu _ { 1 } = \nu _ { 2 } = \delta _ { \mu } ,$ and so $\mu _ { 1 } = \mu _ { 2 }$ , which shows that $\mu$ is extreme. ✷ 

We turn to some powerful coupling results, needed for the ergodic theory of Markov processes in Chapter 26 and for our discussion of Palm distributions in Chapter 31. Theorem 25.25 (coupling on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , Goldstein, Berbee, Aldous $\mathcal { E A }$ Thorisson) Let X, Y be S-valued, product-measurable processes on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ . Then these conditions are equivalent:

We turn to a striking relationship between the sample intensity $\bar { \xi } \ =$ $E \big ( \xi [ 0 , 1 ] \big | \mathcal { Z } _ { \xi } \big )$ of a stationary, a.s. singular random measure $\xi$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ and the corresponding maximum over increasing intervals. Recall that $\xi$ is said to be singular if its absolutely continuous component vanishes, which holds in particular for purely atomic measures $\xi$ 

Theorem 25.27 (ballot theorem, Whitworth, Tak´acs, OK) Let $\xi$ be a stationary, a.s. singular random measure on ${ \sf R } _ { + } ~ o r ~ [ 0 , 1 )$ . Then there exists a $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random variable $\sigma \bot \bot \mathcal { T } _ { \xi }$ , such that

Now it is easy to check that the singularity of $F$ can be described by countably many conditions, each involving the increments of $F$ over finitely many intervals with rational endpoints.

Then put $X _ { t } = \xi ( 0 , t ]$ , and define 

$$

Noting that $A _ { t } \le t - X _ { t }$ and using the monotonicity of X, we get for any $s < t$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A _ {s} = \inf _ {r \in [ s, t)} (r - X _ {r}) \wedge A _ {t} \\ \qquad \geq (s - X _ {t}) \wedge A _ {t} \\ \qquad \geq (s - t + A _ {t}) \wedge A _ {t} \\ \qquad = s - t + A _ {t}. \end{array}

and by (22) it follows that $A _ { s } \ = \ A _ { t }$ for $| s - t | < \varepsilon$ . In particular, A has derivative $A _ { t } ^ { \prime } = 0 = \alpha _ { t }$ at t.

Corollary 25.28 (discrete-time ballot theorem) Let ${ \boldsymbol { \xi } } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \dots . )$ be a finite or infinite, stationary random sequence in $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , and put $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } = \sum _ { k < n } \xi _ { k } } \end{array}$ . Then

To state the next result, let $\xi$ be a random element in a countable space $S _ { ; }$ , and put $p _ { j } = P \{ \xi = j \}$ . For any σ-field $\mathcal { F }$ , we define the information $I ( j )$ and conditional information $I ( j \mid { \mathcal { F } } )$ by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} I (j) = - \log p _ {j}, \\ I (j   |   \mathcal {F}) = - \log P \Bigl \{\xi = j   \Big |   \mathcal {F} \Bigr \}, \qquad j \in S. \end{array}
$$

For motivation, we note the additivity 

$$
I \left(\xi_ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n}\right) = I (\xi_ {1}) + I \left(\xi_ {2} \mid \xi_ {1}\right) + \dots + I \left(\xi_ {n} \mid \xi_ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n - 1}\right),\tag{26}
$$

valid for any random elements $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n }$ in S. Next, we form the associated entropy $H ( \xi ) = E I ( \xi )$ and conditional entropy $H ( \xi | \mathcal { F } ) = E I ( \xi | \mathcal { F } )$ , and note that 

$$
H (\xi) = E I (\xi) = - \sum_ {j} p _ {j} \log p _ {j}.
$$

By (26), even H is additive, in the sense that 

$$
H \left(\xi_ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n}\right) = H \left(\xi_ {1}\right) + H \left(\xi_ {2} \mid \xi_ {1}\right) + \dots + H \left(\xi_ {n} \mid \xi_ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n - 1}\right).\tag{27}
$$

When the sequence $\left( \xi _ { n } \right)$ is stationary and ergodic with $H ( \xi _ { 0 } ) < \infty$ , we show that the averages in (26) and (27) converge toward a common limit. 

Theorem 25.29 (entropy and information, Shannon, McMillan, Breiman, Ionescu Tulcea) Let $\xi \mathrm { ~ = ~ } ( \xi _ { k } )$ be a stationary, ergodic sequence in a countable space $S _ { i }$ , such that $H ( \xi _ { 0 } ) < \infty$ . Then 

$$
n ^ {- 1} I \left(\xi_ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n}\right)\rightarrow H \left(\xi_ {0} \mid \xi_ {- 1}, \xi_ {- 2}, \dots\right) a. s. a n d i n L ^ {1}.
$$

Note that $H ( \xi _ { 0 } ) < \infty$ holds automatically when the state space is finite. Our proof will be based on a technical estimate. 

Lemma 25.30 (maximum inequality, Chung, Neveu) For any countably valued random variable $\xi$ and discrete filtration $( \mathcal F _ { n } )$ , we have 

$$
E \sup _ {n} I (\xi | \mathcal {F} _ {n}) \leq H (\xi) + 1.
$$

Proof: Write $p _ { j } = P \{ \xi = j \}$ and $\eta = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } I ( \xi | \mathcal { F } _ { n } )$ . For fixed $r > 0$ , we introduce the optional times 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tau_ {j} = \inf \Big \{n; I (j   |   \mathcal {F} _ {n}) > r \Big \} \\ \qquad = \inf \Big \{n; P \Big \{\xi = j   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {n} \Big \} <   e ^ {- r} \Big \}, \quad j \in S. \end{array}
$$

By Lemma 8.3, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{\eta > r, \xi = j \Big \} = P \Big \{\tau_ {j} <   \infty , \xi = j \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \Big (P \Big \{\xi = j   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau_ {j}} \Big \}; \tau_ {j} <   \infty \Big) \\ \qquad \leq e ^ {- r} P \{\tau_ {j} <   \infty \} \leq e ^ {- r}. \end{array}
$$

Since the left-hand side is also bounded by $p _ { j }$ , Lemma 4.4 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \eta = \sum_ {j} E \Big (\eta ; \xi = j \Big) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \Big \{\eta > r, \xi = j \Big \} d r \\ \qquad \leq \sum_ {j} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \left(e ^ {- r} \wedge p _ {j}\right) d r \\ \qquad = \sum_ {j} p _ {j} \left(1 - \log p _ {j}\right) \\ \qquad = H (\xi) + 1. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 25.29 (Breiman): We may choose $\xi$ to be defined on the canonical space $S ^ { \infty }$ . Then introduce the functions 

$$
\begin{array}{c} g _ {k} (\xi) = I \Bigl (\xi_ {0}   \big |   \xi_ {- 1}, \ldots , \xi_ {- k + 1} \Bigr), \\ g (\xi) = I \Bigl (\xi_ {0}   \big |   \xi_ {- 1}, \xi_ {- 2}, \ldots \Bigr). \end{array}

$$

Here $g _ { k } ( \xi ) \to g ( \xi )$ a.s. by martingale convergence, and $E \operatorname* { s u p } _ { k } g _ { k } ( \xi ) < \infty$ by Lemma 25.30. Hence, (28) follows by Corollary 25.8. ✷
