Chapter 26 

# Ergodic Properties of Markov Processes

Transition and contraction operators, operator ergodic theorem, maximum inequalities, ratio ergodic theorem, filling operators and functionals, ratio limit theorem, space-time invariance, strong and weak ergodicity and mixing, tail and invariant triviality, Harris recurrence and ergodicity, potential and resolvent operators, convergence dichotomy, recurrence dichotomy, invariant measures, distributional and pathwise limits 

The primary aim of this chapter is to study the asymptotic behavior of broad classes of Markov processes. First, we will see how the ergodic theorems of the previous chapter admit some powerful extensions to suitable contraction operators, leading to some pathwise and distributional ratio limit theorems for fairly general Markov processes. Next, we establish some basic criteria for strong or weak ergodicity of conservative Markov semi-groups, and show that Harris recurrent Feller processes are strongly ergodic. Finally, we show that any regular Feller process is either Harris recurrent or uniformly transient, examine the existence of invariant measures, and prove some associated distributional and pathwise limit theorems. The latter analysis relies crucially on some profound tools from potential theory. 

For a more detailed description, we first extend the basic ergodic theorem of Chapter 25 to suitable contraction operators on an arbitrary measure space, and establish a general operator version of the ratio ergodic theorem. The relevance of those results for the study of Markov processes is due to the fact that their transition operators are positive $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty }$ -contractions with respect to any invariant measure λ on the state space S. The mentioned results cover both the positive-recurrent case where $\lambda S < \infty$ , and the null-recurrent case where $\lambda S = \infty$ . Even more remarkably, the same ergodic theorems apply to both the transition probabilities and the sample paths, in both cases giving conclusive information about the asymptotic behavior. 

Next we prove, for an arbitrary Markov process, that a certain condition of strong ergodicity is equivalent to the triviality of the tail σ-field, the constancy of all bounded, space-time invariant functions, and a uniform mixing condition. We also consider a similar result where all four conditions are replaced by suitably averaged versions. For both sets of equivalences, one gets very simple and transparent proofs by applying the general coupling results of Chapter 25. 

In order to apply the mentioned theorems to specific Markov processes, we need to find regularity conditions ensuring the existence of an invariant measure or the triviality of the tail σ-field. Here we consider a general class of Feller processes satisfying either a strong recurrence or a uniform transience condition. In the former case, we prove the existence of an invariant measure, required for the application of the mentioned ergodic theorems, and show that the space-time invariant functions are constant, which implies the mentioned strong ergodicity. Our proofs of the latter results depend on some potential theoretic tools, related to those developed in Chapter 17. 

To set the stage for the technical developments, we consider a Markov transition operator $T$ on an arbitrary measurable space $( S , S )$ . Note that $T$ is positive, in the sense that $f \geq 0$ implies $T f \geq 0$ , and also that $T 1 = 1$ $\mathrm { A s }$ before, we write $P _ { x }$ for the distribution of a Markov process on $Z _ { + }$ with transition operator $T$ , starting at $x \in S$ . More generally, we define $P _ { \mu } =$ $\textstyle \int P _ { x } \mu ( d x )$ for any measure $\mu$ on $S$ . A measure $\lambda$ on $S$ is said to be invariant -<sub>if</sub> $\lambda T f = \lambda f$ for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ . Writing $\theta$ for the shift on the path space $S ^ { \infty }$ , we define the associated operator $\tilde { \theta }$ by $\tilde { \theta } f = f \circ \theta$ 

For any $p \geq 1$ , an operator $T$ on a measure space $( S , S , \mu )$ is called an $L ^ { p } .$ -contraction, if $\| T f \| _ { p } \leq \| f \| _ { p }$ for every $f \in L ^ { p }$ . We further say that $T$ is an $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty } .$ -contraction, if it is an L<sup>p</sup>-contraction for every $p \in [ 1 , \infty ]$ . The following result shows the relevance of the mentioned notions for the theory of Markov processes. 

Lemma 26.1 (transition and contraction operators) Let $T$ be a Markov transition operator on $( S , S )$ with invariant measure λ. Then 

(i) $T$ is a positive $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty }$ -contraction on $( S , \lambda )$ 

(ii) $\tilde { \theta }$ is a positive $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty }$ -contraction on $( S ^ { \infty } , P _ { \lambda } )$ 

Proof: (i) Applying Jensen’s inequality to the transition kernel $\mu ( x , B ) =$ $T 1 _ { B } ( x )$ and using the invariance of $\lambda _ { i }$ , we get for any $p \in [ 1 , \infty )$ and $f \in L ^ { p }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \| T f \| _ {p} ^ {p} = \lambda | \mu f | ^ {p} \\ \leq \lambda \mu | f | ^ {p} \\ = \lambda | f | ^ {p} = \| f \| _ {p} ^ {p}. \end{array}
$$

The result for $p = \infty$ is obvious. 

(ii) Proceeding as in Lemma 11.11, we see that $\theta$ is a measure-preserving transformation on $( S ^ { \infty } , P _ { \lambda } )$ . Hence, for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $S ^ { \infty }$ and constant $p \geq 1$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P _ {\lambda} \big | \tilde {\theta} f \big | ^ {p} = P _ {\lambda} \big | f \circ \theta \big | ^ {p} \\ & \qquad = \Big (P _ {\lambda} \circ \theta^ {- 1} \Big) | f | ^ {p} \\ & \qquad = P _ {\lambda} | f | ^ {p}. \end{array}
$$

The contraction property for $p = \infty$ is again obvious. 

Some crucial results from Chapter 25 carry over to the context of positive $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty }$ -contractions on an arbitrary measure space. First we consider an operator version of Birkhof’s ergodic theorem. To simplify the writing, we introduce the operators 

$$
S _ {n} = \sum_ {k <   n} T ^ {k}, \qquad A _ {n} = S _ {n} / n, \qquad M f = \sup _ {n} A _ {n} f.
$$

Say that f is T-invariant if $T f = f$ 

Theorem 26.2 (operator ergodic theorem, Hopf, Dunford & Schwartz) Let T be a positive $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty }$ -contraction on a measure space $( S , S , \mu )$ . Then for any $f \in L ^ { 1 }$ there exists a T-invariant function $A f \in L ^ { 1 }$ , such that 

$$
A _ {n} f \to A f a. e., \quad f \in L ^ {1}.
$$

For the proof, we need to extend the inequalities in Lemmas 25.7 and 25.11 and Proposition 25.10 (i) to an operator setting. 

Lemma 26.3 (maximum inequalities) For a positive L<sup>1</sup>-contraction T on a measure space $( S , S , \mu )$ , we have 

(i) $\mu \big ( f ; M f > 0 \big ) \geq 0 , \ f \in L ^ { 1 }$ 

If T is even an $L ^ { 1 } - L ^ { \infty }$ -contraction, then also 

(ii) $r \mu \{ M f > 2 r \} \leq \mu ( f ; f > r ) , f \in L ^ { 1 } , \ r > 0 ,$ 

(iii) $\| M f \| _ { p } \lesssim \| f \| _ { p } , \ f \in L ^ { p } , \ p > 1 .$ 

Proof: (i) For any $f \in L ^ { 1 }$ , write $M _ { n } f = S _ { 1 } f \lor \cdots \lor S _ { n } f$ , and conclude that by positivity 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & S _ {k} f = f + T S _ {k - 1} f \\ & \qquad \leq f + T (M _ {n} f) _ {+}, \quad k = 1, \ldots , n. \end{array}
$$

Hence, $M _ { n } f \leq f + T ( M _ { n } f ) .$ for all $n ,$ and so by positivity and contractivity, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu \Big (f; M _ {n} f > 0 \Big) \geq \mu \Big \{M _ {n} f - T (M _ {n} f) _ {+}; M _ {n} f > 0 \Big \} \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qend{array}
$$

As before, it remains to let $n \to \infty$ 

(ii) Put $f _ { r } = f { 1 \{ f > r \} }$ . By the $L ^ { \infty }$ -contractivity and positivity of $A _ { n }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} A _ {n} f - 2 r & \leq A _ {n} (f - 2 r) \\ & \leq A _ {n} (f _ {r} - r), \quad n \in \mathbb {N}, \end{array}
$$

which implies $M f - 2 r \leq M ( f _ { r } - r )$ . Hence, by part (i), 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} r   \mu \{M f > 2 r \} & \leq r   \mu \Bigl \{M (f _ {r} - r) > 0 \Bigr \} \\ & \leq \mu \Bigl \{f _ {r}; M (f _ {r} - r) > 0 \Bigr \} \\ & \leq \mu f _ {r} = \mu \bigl (f; f > r \bigr). \end{array}
$$

(iii) Here the earlier proof applies with only notational changes. 

Proof of Theorem 26.2: Fix any $f \in L ^ { 1 }$ . By dominated convergence, $f$ may be approximated in $L ^ { 1 }$ by functions $\tilde { f } \in L ^ { 1 } \cap L ^ { \infty } \subset L ^ { 2 }$ . By Lemma 25.17 we may next approximate $\tilde { f }$ in $L ^ { 2 }$ by functions of the form ${ \hat { f } } + ( g - T g )$ , where $\hat { f } , g \in L ^ { 2 }$ and $\dot { T } \hat { f } = \hat { f }$ . Finally, we may approximate $g$ in $L ^ { 2 }$ by functions $\tilde { g } \in L ^ { 1 } \cap L ^ { \infty }$ . Since $T$ contracts $L ^ { 2 }$ , the functions $\tilde { g } - T \tilde { g }$ will then approximate $g - T g$ in $L ^ { 2 }$ . Combining the three approximations, we have for any $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
f = f _ {\varepsilon} + \left(g _ {\varepsilon} - T g _ {\varepsilon}\right) + h _ {\varepsilon} + k _ {\varepsilon},\tag{1}
$$

where $f _ { \varepsilon } \in L ^ { 2 }$ with $T f _ { \varepsilon } = f _ { \varepsilon } , g _ { \varepsilon } \in L ^ { 1 } \cap L ^ { \infty }$ , and $\| h _ { \varepsilon } \| _ { 2 } \vee \| k _ { \varepsilon } \| _ { 1 } < \varepsilon$ 

Since $f _ { \varepsilon }$ is invariant, we have $A _ { n } f _ { \varepsilon } \equiv f _ { \varepsilon }$ . Next, we note that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\left\| A _ {n} (g _ {\varepsilon} - T g _ {\varepsilon}) \right\| _ {\infty} = n ^ {- 1} \left\| g _ {\varepsilon} - T ^ {n} g _ {\varepsilon} \right\| _ {\infty}} \\ & {\qquad \leq 2 n ^ {- 1} \| g _ {\varepsilon} \| _ {\infty} \to 0.} \end{array}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\limsup _ {n \to \infty} A _ {n} f \leq f _ {\varepsilon} + M h _ {\varepsilon} + M k _ {\varepsilon} <   \infty \text { a.e., }\tag{2}
$$

and similarly for lim $\operatorname { i n f } _ { n } A _ { n } f$ . Combining the two estimates gives 

$$
\Big (\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} - \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \Big) A _ {n} f \leq 2 M | h _ {\varepsilon} | + 2 M | k _ {\varepsilon} |.
$$

Now Lemma 26.3 yields for any $\varepsilon , r > 0$ 

$$
\left\| M | h _ {\varepsilon} | \right\| _ {2} \leq \| h _ {\varepsilon} \| _ {2} <   \varepsilon ,
$$

$$
\mu \Bigl \{M | k _ {\varepsilon} | > 2 r \Bigr \} \leq r ^ {- 1} \| k _ {\varepsilon} \| _ {1} <   \varepsilon / r,
$$

and so $M | h _ { \varepsilon } | + M | k _ { \varepsilon } | \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ a s ~ } } \varepsilon \to 0$ along a suitable sequence. Thus, $A _ { n } f$ converges a.e. toward a limit $A f$ 

To prove that $A f$ is T-invariant, we see from (1) and (2) that the a.e. limits $A h _ { \varepsilon }$ and $A k _ { \varepsilon }$ exist and satisfy $T A f - A f = ( T A - A ) ( h _ { \varepsilon } + k _ { \varepsilon } )$ . By the contraction property and Fatou’s lemma, the right-hand side tends a.e. to 0 as $\varepsilon \to 0$ along a sequence, and we get $T A f = A f$ a.e. ✷ 

The limit $A f$ in the last theorem may be 0, in which case the a.s. convergence $A _ { n } f  A f$ gives little information about the asymptotic behavior of $A _ { n } f$ . For example, this happens when $\mu S = \infty$ and $T$ is the operator induced by a μ -preserving and ergodic transformation $\theta$ on $S .$ . Then $A f$ is a constant, and the condition $A f \in L ^ { 1 }$ implies $A f = 0$ . To get around this dificulty, we may instead compare the asymptotic behavior of $S _ { n } f$ with that of $S _ { n } g$ for a suitable reference function $g \in L ^ { 1 }$ . This idea leads to a far-reaching and powerful extension of Birkhof’s theorem. 

Theorem 26.4 (ratio ergodic theorem, Chacon & Ornstein) Let T be a positive L<sup>1</sup>-contraction on a measure space $( S , S , \mu )$ , and let $f \in L ^ { 1 }$ and $g \in L _ { + } ^ { 1 }$ Then Sn f 

$$
\frac {S _ {n} f}{S _ {n} g} \text {   converges   a.e.   on   } \{S _ {\infty} g > 0 \}.
$$

Three lemmas are needed for the proof. 

Lemma 26.5 (individual terms) In the context of Theorem ${ 2 6 . 4 }$ 

$$
\frac {T ^ {n} f}{S _ {n + 1} g} \rightarrow 0 a. e. o n \{S _ {\infty} g > 0 \}.
$$

Proof: We may take $f \geq 0$ . Fix any $\varepsilon > 0$ , and define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h _ {n} = T ^ {n} f - \varepsilon S _ {n + 1} g, \\ A _ {n} = \{h _ {n} > 0 \}, \qquad n \geq 0. \end{array}
$$

By positivity, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h _ {n} = T h _ {n - 1} - \varepsilon g \\ \leq T h _ {n - 1} ^ {+} - \varepsilon g, \quad n \geq 1. \end{array}
$$

Examining separately the cases $A _ { n }$ and $A _ { n } ^ { c }$ , we conclude that 

$$
h _ {n} ^ {+} \leq T h _ {n - 1} ^ {+} - \varepsilon 1 _ {A _ {n}} g, n \geq 1,
$$

and so by contractivity, 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \varepsilon \mu (g; A _ {n}) \leq \mu (T h _ {n - 1} ^ {+}) - \mu h _ {n} ^ {+} \\ \leq \mu h _ {n - 1} ^ {+} - \mu h _ {n} ^ {+}. \end{array}
$$

Summing over n gives 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \varepsilon   \mu \sum_ {n \geq 1} 1 _ {A _ {n}} g \leq \mu h _ {0} ^ {+} = \mu (f - \varepsilon g) \\ \leq \mu f <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

which implies $\mu ( g ; A _ { n } \ \mathrm { i . o . } ) \ = \ 0$ and hence lim su $) _ { n } ( T ^ { n } f / S _ { n + 1 } g ) \leq \varepsilon { \mathrm { ~ a . e ~ } }$ . on $\{ g > 0 \}$ . Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, we obtain $T ^ { n } f / S _ { n + 1 } g \to 0$ a.e. on $\{ g > 0 \}$ Applying this result to the functions $T ^ { m } f$ and $T ^ { m } g$ gives the same convergence on $\{ S _ { m - 1 } g = 0 < S _ { m } g \}$ , for arbitrary $m > 1$ ✷ 

To state the next result, we introduce the non-linear filling operator $F$ on $L ^ { 1 }$ , given by $F h = T h _ { + } - h _ { - }$ . We may think of the sequence $F ^ { n } h$ as arising from successive attempts to fill a hole $h _ { - } .$ , where in each step we are only mapping matter that has not yet fallen into the hole. We also define $M _ { n } h = S _ { 1 } h \lor \cdots \lor S _ { n } h$ 

Lemma 26.6 (filling operator) For any $h \in L ^ { 1 }$ and $n \in \mathsf N$ 

$$
F ^ {n - 1} h \geq 0 o n \{M _ {n} h > 0 \}.
$$

Proof: Writing $h _ { k } = h _ { + } + ( F h ) _ { + } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + ( F ^ { k } h ) _ { + }$ , we claim that 

$$
h _ {k} \geq S _ {k + 1} h, \quad k \geq 0.\tag{3}
$$

This is clear for $k = 0$ since $h _ { + } = h + h _ { - } \geq h$ . Proceeding by induction, let (3) be true for $k = m \ge 0$ . Using the induction hypothesis and the definitions of $S _ { k } , h _ { k }$ , and $F _ { ; }$ , we get for $m + 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {m + 2} h = h + T S _ {m + 1} h \\ \leq h + T h _ {m} \\ = h + \sum_ {k \leq m} T (F ^ {k} h) _ {+} \\ = h + \sum_ {k \leq m} \left\{F ^ {k + 1} h + (F ^ {k} h) _ {-} \right\} \\ = h + \sum_ {k \leq m} \left\{(F ^ {k + 1} h) _ {+} - (F ^ {k + 1} h) _ {-} + (F ^ {k} h) _ {-} \right\} \\ = h + h _ {m + 1} - h _ {+} + h _ {-} - (F ^ {m + 1} h) _ {-} \leq h _ {m + 1}. \end{array}
$$

This completes the proof of (3). 

If $M _ { n } h > 0$ at some point in $S ,$ then $S _ { k } h > 0$ for some $k \leq n$ , and so by (3) we have $h _ { k } > 0$ for some $k < n$ . To state our third and crucial lemma, write $g \in { \mathcal { T } } _ { 1 } ( f )$ for a given $f \in L _ { + } ^ { 1 }$ , if there exists a decomposition $f = f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 }$ with $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } \in L _ { + } ^ { 1 }$ such that $g = T f _ { 1 } + f _ { 2 }$ Note in particular that $f , g \in L _ { + } ^ { 1 }$ implies $U ( f - g ) = f ^ { \prime } - g$ for some $f ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { T } _ { 1 } ( f )$ The classes $\mathcal { T } _ { n } ( f )$ are defined recursively by ${ \mathcal { T } } _ { n + 1 } ( f ) = { \mathcal { T } } _ { 1 } \{ { \mathcal { T } } _ { n } ( f ) \}$ , and we put ${ \mathcal { T } } ( f ) = \cup _ { n } { \mathcal { T } } _ { n } ( f )$ . Now introduce the functionals 

$$
\psi_ {B} f = \sup \left\{\mu (g; B); g \in \mathcal {T} (f) \right\}, \quad f \in L _ {+} ^ {1}, B \in \mathcal {S}.

Lemma 26.7 (filling functionals) For any $f , g \in L _ { + } ^ { 1 }$ and $B \in S$ 

$$
B \subset \left\{\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} S _ {n} (f - g) > 0 \right\} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \psi_ {B} f \geq \psi_ {B} g.
$$

$$
\left\{\limsup _ {n \to \infty} S _ {n} (f - g) > 0 \right\} \subset \left\{\limsup _ {n \to \infty} S _ {n} (c f - g ^ {\prime}) > 0 \right\} \text {   a.e.   }\tag{4}

$$
\begin{array}{c} S _ {n} (c f - g ^ {\prime}) = \sum_ {k <   n} T ^ {k} (c f - r - T s) \\ = S _ {n} (f - g) + (c - 1) S _ {n} f + s - T ^ {n} s. \end{array}
$$

Since 

$$
\frac {T ^ {n} s}{S _ {n} f} = \frac {T ^ {n - 1} T s}{S _ {n} f} \rightarrow 0 \text {a.e. on} \{S _ {\infty} f > 0 \}

by Lemma 26.5, we conclude that eventually $S _ { n } ( c f - g ^ { \prime } ) \geq S _ { n } ( f - g )$ a.e. on the same set, and (4) follows. 

Combining the given hypothesis with (4), we obtain the a.e. relation $B \subset$ $\{ M ( c f - g ^ { \prime } ) > 0 \}$ . Now Lemma 26.6 yields

F ^ {n - 1} (c f - g ^ {\prime}) \geq 0 \text { on } B _ {n} \equiv B \cap \left\{M _ {n} (c f - g ^ {\prime}) > 0 \right\}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}.

$$
\begin{array}{l} 0 \leq \mu \bigl \{F ^ {n - 1} (c f - g ^ {\prime}); B _ {n} \bigr \} \\ = \mu (f ^ {\prime}; B _ {n}) - \mu (g ^ {\prime}; B _ {n}) \\ \leq \psi_ {B} (c f) - \mu (g ^ {\prime}; B _ {n}) \\ \to c   \psi_ {B} f - \mu (g ^ {\prime}; B), \end{array}
$$

and so $c \psi _ { B } f \geq \mu ( g ^ { \prime } ; B )$ . It remains to let $c \to 1$ and take the supremum over $g ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { T } ( g )$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 26.4: We may take $f \geq 0$ . On $\{ S _ { \infty } g > 0 \}$ , put 

$$
\alpha = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {S _ {n} f}{S _ {n} g} \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \to \infty} \frac {S _ {n} f}{S _ {n} g} = \beta ,

and define $\alpha = \beta = 0$ otherwise. Since $S _ { n } g$ is non-decreasing, we have for any 

$$
c > 0
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \{\beta > c \} & \subset \Big \{\underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} \frac {S _ {n} (f - c g)}{S _ {n} g} > 0, S _ {\infty} g > 0 \Big \} \\ & \subset \Big \{\underset {n \to \infty} {\limsup} S _ {n} (f - c g) > 0 \Big \}. \end{array}

Writing $B = \{ \beta = \infty , S _ { \infty } g > 0 \}$ , we see from Lemma 26.7 that

\mu \{\alpha <   \beta \} \leq \sum_ {a <   b} \mu \Bigl \{\alpha <   a <   b <   \beta \Bigr \} = 0,

To illustrate the use of the last theorem, we consider a striking application to discrete-time Markov processes. For such a process $X$ on $S$ and a measurable function $f$ on $S ^ { \infty }$ , we define $\begin{array} { r } { S _ { n } f = \sum _ { k < n } f ( \theta _ { k } X ) } \end{array}$ 

Corollary 26.8 (ratio limit theorem) Let λ be an invariant measure of a discrete-time Markov process in $S$ , and let $f \in L ^ { 1 } ( P _ { \lambda } )$ and $g \in L _ { + } ^ { 1 } ( P _ { \lambda } )$ . Then

\begin{array}{r l} & {\lambda \tilde {f} = \int \tilde {f} (x) \lambda (d x)} \\ & {\quad = \int E _ {x} f (X) \lambda (d x)} \\ & {\quad = E _ {\lambda} f (X) = P _ {\lambda} f.} \end{array}

Now consider a conservative, continuous-time Markov process on an arbitrary state space $( S , S )$ with distributions $P _ { x }$ and associated expectation operators $E _ { x }$ . On the canonical path space $\Omega = S ^ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } }$ , we introduce the shift operators $\theta _ { t }$ and filtration $\mathcal { F } = \left( \mathcal { F } _ { t } \right)$ . A bounded function $f \colon S  { \mathsf { R } }$ is said to be invariant or harmonic, if it is measurable and such that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (x) = T _ {t} f (x) \\ \qquad = E _ {x} f (X _ {t}), \quad x \in S, t \geq 0. \end{array}
$$

More generally, we say that a bounded function $f \colon S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + } \to \mathsf { R }$ is space-time invariant or harmonic, if it is measurable and satisfies 

$$
f (x, s) = E _ {x} f (X _ {t}, s + t), \quad x \in S, s, t \geq 0.\tag{5}
$$

For motivation, we note that f is then invariant for the associated spacetime process $\tilde { X } _ { t } ~ = ~ ( X _ { t } , s + t )$ in $S \times { \sf R } _ { + }$ , where the second component is deterministic, apart from a possibly random initial value $s \geq 0$ . Note that $\tilde { X }$ is again a time-homogeneous Markov process with transition operators $\tilde { T } _ { t } f ( x , s ) = E _ { x } f ( X _ { t } , s + t )$ . We need the following useful martingale connection. 

Lemma 26.9 (space-time invariance) For any bounded, measurable function $f \colon S \times \mathsf { R } _ { + } \to \mathsf { R }$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $f$ is space-time invariant, 

(ii) $M _ { t } = f ( X _ { t } , s + t )$ is a $P _ { \mu }$ -martingale for every $\mu$ and $s \geq 0$ 

Proof, ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ : Assume (i), and let $s , t , h \geq 0$ . Using the Markov property of X, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E _ {\mu} \Big (M _ {t + h} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \Big) = E _ {\mu} \Big \{f \Big (X _ {t + h}, s + t + h \Big) \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \Big \} \\ & \qquad = E _ {X _ {t}} f \Big (X _ {h}, s + t + h \Big) \\ & \qquad = f (X _ {t}, s + t) = M _ {t}. \end{array}
$$

(ii) (i): By (ii) with $\mu = \delta _ { x }$ , we have for any $x \in S$ and $s , t \geq 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} E _ {x} f (X _ {t}, s + t) & = E _ {x} M _ {t} \\ & = E _ {x} M _ {0} \\ & = f (x, s). \end{array}
$$

The tail $\sigma { - } f i e l d$ on Ω is defined as $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { T } = \bigcap _ { t } \mathcal { T } _ { t } . } \end{array}$ , where $\mathcal { T } _ { t } = \sigma ( \theta _ { t } ) = \sigma \{ X _ { s } ; s \geq$ $t \}$ . A σ-field on Ω is said to be $P _ { \mu } { - } t r i v i a l ,$ if $P _ { \mu } A = 0$ or 1 for every $A \in { \mathcal { G } }$ Writing $P _ { \mu } ^ { B } = P _ { \mu } ( \cdot | B )$ , we say that $P _ { \mu }$ is mixing, if 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \left\| P _ {\mu} \circ \theta_ {t} ^ {- 1} - P _ {\mu} ^ {B} \circ \theta_ {t} ^ {- 1} \right\| = 0, \quad B \in \mathcal {F} _ {\infty} \text { with } P _ {\mu} B > 0.
$$

The following properties define the notion of strong ergodicity, as opposed to the weak ergodicity in Theorem 26.11. 

Theorem 26.10 (strong ergodicity and mixing, Orey) For a conservative Markov semi-group on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ~ o r ~ \mathsf { Z } _ { + }$ with distributions $P _ { \mu }$ , these conditions are equivalent:

$\mathrm { ( i ) } \Leftrightarrow \mathrm { ( i i ^ { \prime } ) }$ : If $P _ { \mu } A = 0$ or 1, then clearly also $P _ { \mu } ^ { B } A = 0$ or 1, which shows that $\mathrm { ( i ) \ \Rightarrow \ ( i i ^ { \prime } ) }$ . Theorem 26.11 (weak ergodicity and mixing) For a conservative Markov semi-group on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } ~ o r ~ \mathsf { Z } _ { + }$ with distributions $P _ { \mu } ,$ these conditions are equivalent:

${ \mathrm { ( i v ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i i ) } }$ : Let f be bounded and invariant. Then $f ( x ) = E _ { x } f ( X _ { t } ) =$ $T _ { t } f ( x )$ , and therefore $\begin{array} { r } { f ( x ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } T _ { s t } f ( x ) } \end{array}$ ds. Using (iv) gives

We now specialize to conservative Feller processes $X$ with distributions $P _ { x } .$ defined on an lcscH<sup>1</sup> space $S$ with Borel σ-field $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ . Say that the process is regular, if there exist a locally finite measure $\rho$ on $S$ and a continuous function $( x , y , t ) \mapsto p _ { t } ( x , y ) > 0$ on $S ^ { 2 } \times ( 0 , \infty )$ , such that 

$$
P _ {x} \{X _ {t} \in B \} = \int_ {B} p _ {t} (x, y) \rho (d y), x \in S, B \in \mathcal {S}, t > 0.
$$

The supporting measure $\rho$ is then unique up to an equivalence, and supp $\rho = S$ by the Feller property. A Feller process is said to be Harris recurrent, if it is regular with a supporting measure $\rho$ satisfying 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} 1 _ {B} (X _ {t}) d t = \infty \text { a.s. } P _ {x}, x \in S, B \in \mathcal {S} \text { with } \rho B > 0.\tag{6}
$$

Theorem 26.12 (Harris recurrence and ergodicity, Orey) For a Feller process $X$ , we have 

$$
X \text {   is   Harris   recurrent   } \Rightarrow X \text {   is   strongly   ergodic. }
$$

Theorem 26.18 (invariant measure, Harris, Watanabe) For a Harris recurrent Feller process on S with supporting measure $\rho ,$

Lemma 26.19 (invariance equivalence) Let $( T _ { t } )$ be a Feller semi-group on $S$ with resolvent $( U _ { a } )$ , and fix a locally finite measure λ on $S$ and a constant $c > 0$ . Then these conditions are equivalent:

Chapter 27 

# Symmetric Distributions and Predictable Maps

Asymptotically invariant sampling, exchangeable and contractable, mixed and conditionally i.i.d. sequences, coding representation and equivalence criteria, urn sequences and factorial measures, strong stationarity, prediction sequence, predictable sampling, optional skipping, sojourns and maxima, exchangeable and mixed L´evy processes, compensated jumps, sampling processes, hyper-contraction and tightness, rotatable sequences and processes, predictable mapping 

Classical results in probability typically require both an independence and an invariance condition<sup>1</sup>. It is then quite remarkable that, under special circumstances, the independence follows from the invariance assumption alone. We have already seen some notable instances of this phenomenon, such as in Theorems 11.5 and 11.14 for Markov processes and in Theorems 10.27 and 19.8 for martingales. Here and in the next chapter, we will study some broad classes of random phenomena, where a symmetry or invariance condition alone yields some very precise structural information, typically involving properties of independence. 

For a striking example, recall that an infinite sequence of random variables ${ \boldsymbol { \xi } } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \dots . )$ is said to be stationary if $\theta _ { n } \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi$ for every $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ , where $\theta _ { n }$ denotes the n -step shift operator on ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { \infty }$ . Replacing n by an arbitrary optional time $\tau$ in $Z _ { + }$ yields the notion of strong stationarity, where $\theta _ { \tau } \xi \ \overset { d } { = } \xi$ . We will show that $\xi$ is strongly stationary if it is conditionally i.i.d., given a suitable σ-field . This statement is essentially equivalent to de Finetti’s theorem—the fact that $\xi$ is exchangeable, defined as invariance in distribution under finite permutations, if it is mixed i.i.d. Thus, apart from a randomization, a simple symmetry condition leads us back to the elementary setting of i.i.d. sequences. 

This is by modern standards a quite elementary result that can be proved in just a few lines. The same argument yields the remarkable extension by Ryll-Nardzewski—the fact that the mere contractability<sup>2</sup>, where all sub-sequences are assumed to have the same distribution, sufices for $\xi$ to be mixed i.i.d. Further highlights of the theory include the predictable sampling theorem, extending of the exchangeablity property of a finite or infinite sequence to arbitrary predictable permutations. In Chapters 14, 16, and 22, we saw how the latter result yields short proofs of the classical arcsine laws. 

All the mentioned results have continuous-time counterparts. In particular, a process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with exchangeable or contractable increments is a mixture of L´evy processes. The more subtle representation of exchangeable processes on [0, 1] will be derived from some asymptotic properties for sequences obtained by sampling without replacement from a finite population. Similarly, the predictable sampling theorem turns into the quite subtle predictable mapping theorem—the invariance in distribution of an exchangeable process on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ or [0, 1] under predictable and pathwise measure-preserving transformations. Here some predictable mapping properties from Chapter 19, involving ordinary or discounted compensators, will be helpful for the proof. 

The material in this chapter is related in many ways to other parts of the book. In particular, we note some links to various applications and extensions in Chapters 14–16, for results involving exchangeable sequences or processes. The predictable sampling theorem is further related to results for random time change in Chapters 15–16 and 19. 

To motivate our first main topic, we consider a simple limit theorem for multi-variate sampling from a stationary process. Here we consider a measurable process $X$ on an index set $T ,$ , taking values in a space $S ,$ and let ${ \boldsymbol \tau } = ( \tau _ { 1 } , \tau _ { 2 } , \dots )$ be an independent sequence of random elements in $T$ with joint distribution $\mu .$ Define the associated sampling sequence $\xi = X \circ \tau$ in $S ^ { \infty }$ by C (5 (V V 

$$
\xi = (\xi_ {1}, \xi_ {2}, \ldots) = (X _ {\tau_ {1}}, X _ {\tau_ {2}}, \ldots)
$$

henceforth referred to as a $\mu - s a m p l e$ from X. The sampling distributions $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , . . .$ . on $T ^ { \infty }$ are said to be asymptotically invariant, if their projections onto $T ^ { k }$ are asymptotically invariant for every $k \in \mathsf { N }$ . Recall that $\mathcal { T } _ { X }$ denotes the invariant σ-field of $X$ , and note that the conditional distribution $\eta =$ $\mathcal { L } ( X _ { 0 } | \mathcal { T } _ { X } )$ exists by Theorem 8.5 when $S$ is Borel. 

Lemma 27.1 (asymptotically invariant sampling) Let X be a stationary, measurable process on $T = { \mathsf { R } }$ or Z with values in a Polish space S. For $n \in \mathsf N$ let $\xi _ { n }$ be a μ -sample from X, where $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . are asymptotically invariant distributions on $T ^ { \infty }$ . Then 

$$
\xi_ {n} \xrightarrow {d} \xi i n S ^ {\infty}, \quad \mathcal {L} (\xi) = E \eta^ {\infty} w i t h \eta = \mathcal {L} (X _ {0} | \mathcal {I} _ {X}).
$$

Proof: Write $\xi \ = \ ( \xi ^ { k } )$ and $\xi _ { n } = ( \xi _ { n } ^ { k } )$ . Fix any asymptotically invariant distributions $\nu _ { 1 } , \nu _ { 2 } , . . .$ . on $T ,$ , and let $f _ { 1 } , \ldots , f _ { m }$ be measurable functions on $S$ bounded by $\pm 1$ . Proceeding as in the proof of Corollary 25.18 (i), we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| E \prod_ {k} f _ {k} (\xi_ {n} ^ {k}) - E \prod_ {k} f _ {k} (\xi^ {k}) \right| \\ \leq E \left| \mu_ {n} \bigotimes_ {k} f _ {k} (X) - \prod_ {k} \eta f _ {k} \right| \\ \leq \left\| \mu_ {n} - \mu_ {n} * \nu_ {r} ^ {m} \right\| + \int E \left| (\nu_ {r} ^ {m} * \delta_ {t}) \bigotimes_ {k} f _ {k} (X) - \prod_ {k} \eta f _ {k} \right| \mu_ {n} (d t) \\ \leq \int \left\| \mu_ {n} - \mu_ {n} * \delta_ {t} \right\| \nu_ {r} ^ {m} (d t) + \sum_ {k} \sup _ {t} E \left| (\nu_ {r} * \delta_ {t}) f _ {k} (X) - \eta f _ {k} \right|. \end{array}
$$

Using the asymptotic invariance of $\mu _ { n }$ and $\nu _ { r }$ , together with Corollary 25.18 (i) and dominated convergence, we see that the right-hand side tends to 0 as $n \to \infty$ and then $r  \infty$ . The assertion now follows by Theorem 5.30. ✷ 

The last result leads immediately to a version of de Finetti’s theorem. For a precise statement, consider a finite or infinite random sequence $\boldsymbol { \xi } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \dots )$ with index set I, and say that $\xi$ is exchangeable if 

$$
\left(\xi_ {k _ {1}}, \xi_ {k _ {2}}, \dots\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left(\xi_ {1}, \xi_ {2}, \dots\right),\tag{1}
$$

for any $\mathrm { f i n i t e ^ { 3 } }$ permutation $( k _ { 1 } , k _ { 2 } , \ldots )$ of I. For infinite sequences $\xi ,$ we also consider the seemingly weaker property of contractability<sup>4</sup>, where $I = \mathsf { N }$ and (1) is only required for increasing sequences $k _ { 1 } < k _ { 2 } < \cdots ,$ . Then $\xi$ is stationary, and every sub-sequence has the same distribution as $\xi .$ . By Lemma 27.1 we obtain ${ \mathcal L } ( \xi ) ~ = ~ E \eta ^ { \infty }$ with $\eta ~ = ~ \mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { 1 } | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } )$ , here called the directing random measure of $\xi$ . We may also give a stronger conditional statement. Recall that, for any random measure η on a measurable space $( S , S )$ , the associated σ-field is generated by the random variables ηB for arbitrary $B \in S$ 

Theorem 27.2 (exchangeable sequences, de Finetti, Ryll-Nardzewski) For an infinite random sequence $\xi$ in a Borel space $S$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi$ is exchangeable, 

(ii) $\xi$ is contractable, 

(iii) $\xi$ is mixed i.i.d., 

(iv) $\mathcal { L } ( \xi | \eta ) = \eta ^ { \infty }$ a.s. for a random distribution η on $S$ 

Here η is a.s. unique and equal to $\mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { 1 } | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } )$ 

Since $\eta ^ { \infty }$ is a.s. the distribution of an i.i.d. sequence in $S$ based on the measure $\eta , \mathrm { ( i v ) }$ means that $\xi$ is conditionally i.i.d. $\eta .$ . Taking expectations of both sides in (iv), we obtain the seemingly weaker condition $\mathcal { L } ( \xi ) = E \eta ^ { \infty }$ , stating that $\xi$ is mixed i.i.d. The latter condition implies that $\xi$ is exchangeable, and so the two versions of (iii) are indeed equivalent. 

First proof of Theorem ${ \it 2 7 . 2 4 } \ : ( O K )$ : Since S is Borel, we may take $S =$ [0, 1]. Write $\mu _ { n }$ for the uniform distribution on the product set $\begin{array} { r l } {  { \prod _ { k } \{ ( k - 1 ) n + } } \quad  & { { } } \end{array}$ $1 , \ldots , k n \}$ . Assuming (ii), we see from Lemma 27.1 that $\mathcal { L } ( \xi ) = E \eta ^ { \infty }$ . More generally, we may extend (1) to 

$$
\left\{1 _ {A} (\xi), \xi_ {k _ {1}}, \xi_ {k _ {2}}, \dots \right\} \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left\{1 _ {A} (\xi), \xi_ {1}, \xi_ {2}, \dots \right\}, \quad k _ {1} <   k _ {2} <   \dots ,

Applying Lemma 27.1 to the sequence of pairs $\{ \xi _ { k } , 1 _ { A } ( \xi ) \}$ , we get as before ${ \mathcal { L } } ( \xi ; \xi \in A ) = E ( \eta ^ { \infty } ; \xi \in A )$ , and since $\eta$ is $\mathcal { T } _ { \xi } .$ -measurable, it follows that $\mathcal { L } ( \xi | \eta ) = \eta ^ { \infty }$ a.s. 

To see that $\eta$ is a.s. unique, we may use the law of large numbers and Theorem 8.5 to obtain 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {k \leq n} 1 _ {B} (\xi_ {k}) \to \eta B \text { a.s., } B \in \mathcal {S}.
$$

We can also prove de Finetti’s theorem by a simple martingale argument: 

Second proof of Theorem 27.2 (Aldous): If $\xi$ is contractable, then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} (\xi_ {m}, \theta_ {m} \xi) & \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (\xi_ {k}, \theta_ {m} \xi) \\ & \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (\xi_ {k}, \theta_ {n} \xi), k \leq m \leq n. \end{array}
$$

Now write $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } = \cap _ { n } \sigma ( \theta _ { n } \xi ) } \end{array}$ . Using Lemma 8.10 followed by Theorem 9.24 as $n \to \infty$ <sub>, we get a.s. for a fixed set</sub> $B \in S$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {m} | \theta_ {m} \xi) & = \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {k} | \theta_ {m} \xi) \\ & = \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {k} | \theta_ {n} \xi) \\ & \to \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {k} | \mathcal {T} _ {\xi}), \end{array}
$$

which shows that the extreme members agree a.s. In particular, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {m} \mid \theta_ {m} \xi) = \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {m} \mid \mathcal {T} _ {\xi}) \\ = \mathcal {L} (\xi_ {1} \mid \mathcal {T} _ {\xi}) \text {a.s.} \end{array}
$$

Here the first relation gives $\xi _ { m } \perp \perp \tau _ { \xi } \theta _ { m } \xi$ for all $m \in \mathsf { N }$ , and so by iteration $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . are conditionally independent given $\mathcal { T } _ { \xi }$ . The second relation shows that the conditional distributions agree a.s. This proves that ${ \mathcal { L } } ( \xi | { \mathcal { T } } _ { \xi } ) = \nu ^ { \infty }$ with $\nu = \mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { 1 } | \mathcal { T } _ { \xi } )$ ✷ 

The nature of de Finetti’s criterion is further clarified by the following functional representation, here included to prepare for the much more subtle higher-dimensional versions in Chapter 28. 

Corollary 27.3 (coding representation) Let $\xi = ( \xi _ { j } )$ be an infinite random sequence in a Borel space S. Then $\xi$ is exchangeable if

$$

The last expression shows that the $\tilde { \xi } _ { j }$ are conditionally independent given ${ \tilde { \nu } } _ { : }$ and by (2) their common conditional distribution equals $\tilde { \nu } .$ . Hence, the sequence $\tilde { \xi } = ( \tilde { \xi } _ { j } )$ satisfies $( \tilde { \nu } , \tilde { \xi } ) \overset { d } { = } ( \nu , \xi )$ , and Corollary 8.18 yields a.s. 

$$

for some i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ variables α and $\zeta _ { 1 } , \zeta _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ 

To identify $\nu ,$ let $B \in S$ be arbitrary, and use (3), Fubini’s theorem, and the definition of ν to get

$$

Theorem 27.2 fails for finite sequences. Here we need instead to replace the inherent i.i.d. sequences by suitable urn sequences, generated by successive drawing without replacement from a finite set. To make this precise, fix a measurable space $S _ { i }$ , and consider a measure of the form $\begin{array} { r } { \mu = \sum _ { k < n } \delta _ { s _ { k } } } \end{array}$ with $s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n } \in S$ . As in Lemma 2.20, we introduce on $S ^ { n }$ the associated factorial

where $\mathcal { P } _ { n }$ is the set of permutations $p = ( p _ { 1 } , \dotsc , p _ { n } )$ of $1 , \ldots , n$ , and $s \circ p =$ $( s _ { p _ { 1 } } , \ldots , s _ { p _ { n } } )$ . Note that $\mu ^ { ( n ) }$ is independent of the order of $s _ { 1 } , \ldots , s _ { n }$ and depends measurably on $\mu .$ 

Lemma 27.5 (finite exchangeable sequences) Let ${ \boldsymbol { \xi } } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \dots , \xi _ { n } )$ be a finite random sequence in $S _ { i }$ , and put $\begin{array} { r } { \eta = \sum _ { k } \delta _ { \xi _ { k } } } \end{array}$ . Then $\xi$ is exchangeable $i f f$ 

$$
\mathcal {L} (\xi \mid \eta) = \frac {\eta^ {(n)}}{n !} a. s.
$$

Proof: Since $\eta$ is invariant under permutations of $\xi _ { 1 } , \ldots , \xi _ { n }$ , we have $( \xi \circ$ $p , \eta ) \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ ( \xi , \eta )$ for any $p \in \mathcal { P } _ { n }$ . Now introduce an exchangeable permutation $\pi \bot \bot \xi$ of $1 , \ldots , n$ . Using Fubini’s theorem twice, we get for any measurable sets $A$ and $B$ in appropriate spaces 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{\xi \in B,   \eta \in A \Big \} = P \Big \{\xi \circ \pi \in B,   \eta \in A \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \Big \{P \Big (\xi \circ \pi \in B   \big |   \xi \Big);   \eta \in A \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \Big (\eta^ {(n)} B / n!  ;   \eta \in A \Big). \end{array}
$$

Just as for martingales and Markov processes, we may relate the defining properties to a filtration $\mathcal { F } ~ = ~ \left( \mathcal { F } _ { n } \right)$ Thus, a finite or infinite sequence of random elements ${ \boldsymbol { \xi } } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \dots . )$ is said to be ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { - }$ exchangeable, if it is -adapted and such that, for every $n \geq 0$ , the shifted sequence $\theta _ { n } \xi = ( \xi _ { n + 1 } , \xi _ { n + 2 } , . ~ . ~ . )$ is conditionally exchangeable given $\mathcal { F } _ { n }$ . For infinite sequences $\xi ,$ , the definition of ${ \mathcal { F } } .$ contractability is similar.<sup>6</sup> When $\mathcal { F }$ is the filtration induced by $\xi ,$ , the stated properties reduce to the unqualified versions considered earlier. 

An infinite, adapted sequence $\xi$ is said to be strongly stationary or $\mathcal { F } _ { - }$ stationary if $\begin{array} { r } { \theta _ { \tau } \xi \overset { d } { = } \xi } \end{array}$ for every optional time $\tau < \infty$ . By the prediction sequence of $\xi$ we mean the set of conditional distributions 

$$
\pi_ {n} = \mathcal {L} (\theta_ {n} \xi | \mathcal {F} _ {n}), \quad n \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+}.\tag{4}
$$

The random probability measures $\pi _ { 0 } , \pi _ { 1 } , . . . .$ . on $S$ are said to form a measurevalued martingale, if $( \pi _ { n } B )$ is a real-valued martingale for every measurable set $B \subset S$ . We show that strong stationarity is equivalent to exchangeability,<sup>7</sup> and exhibit an interesting martingale connection. 

Corollary 27.6 (strong stationarity) Let $\xi$ be an infinite, -adapted random sequence with prediction sequence $\pi _ { i }$ , taking values in a Borel space $S$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\xi$ is -exchangeable, 

(ii) $\xi$ is -contractable, 

(iii) $\xi$ <sup>is</sup> F<sup>-stationary,</sup> 

(iv) $\pi$ is a measure-valued -martingale. 

Proof: Conditions (i) and (ii) are equivalent by Theorem 27.2. Assuming (ii), we get a.s. for any $B \in S ^ { \infty }$ and $n \in { \cal Z } _ { + }$ + 

$$
\begin{array}{r} E \Big (\pi_ {n + 1} B \big | \mathcal {F} _ {n} \Big) = P \Big \{\theta_ {n + 1} \xi \in B \big | \mathcal {F} _ {n} \Big \} \\ = P \Big \{\theta_ {n} \xi \in B \big | \mathcal {F} _ {n} \Big \} = \pi_ {n} B, \end{array}\tag{5}
$$

which proves (iv). Conversely, (ii) follows by iteration from the second equality in (5), and so (ii) and (iv) are equivalent. 

Next we note that (4) extends by Lemma 8.3 to 

$$
\pi_ {\tau} B = P \Bigl \{\theta_ {\tau} \xi \in B   \big |   \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Bigr \} \text { a.s., } B \in \mathcal {S} ^ {\infty},
$$

for any finite optional time $\tau .$ . By Lemma 9.14, condition (iv) is then equivalent to 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Bigl \{\theta_ {\tau} \xi \in B \Bigr \} = E \pi_ {\tau} B = E \pi_ {0} B \\ = P \{\xi \in B \}, \qquad B \in \mathcal {S} ^ {\infty}, \end{array}
$$

which is in turn equivalent to (iii). 

The exchangeability property extends to a broad class of random permutations. Say that an integer-valued random variable $\tau$ is predictable with respect to a given filtration $\mathcal { F }$ , if the shifted time $( \tau - 1 ) _ { + }$ is -optional. 

Theorem 27.7 (predictable sampling) Let ${ \boldsymbol { \xi } } = ( \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \dots . )$ be a finite or infinite, ${ \mathcal { F } } .$ -exchangeable random sequence indexed by I. Then for any a.s. distinct, -predictable times $\tau _ { 1 } , \ldots , \tau _ { n }$ in I, we have 

$$
\left(\xi_ {\tau_ {1}}, \dots , \xi_ {\tau_ {n}}\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left(\xi_ {1}, \dots , \xi_ {n}\right).\tag{6}
$$

Note that we do not require $\xi$ to be infinite or the $\tau _ { k }$ to be increasing. A simple special case is that of optional skipping, where $I = \mathsf { N }$ and $\tau _ { 1 } < \tau _ { 2 } < \cdots$ If $\tau _ { k } \equiv \tau + k$ for some optional time $\tau < \infty$ , then (6) reduces to the strong stationarity in Proposition 27.6. For both applications and proof, it is useful to consider the inverse allocation sequence 

$$
\alpha_ {j} = \inf \left\{k; \tau_ {k} = j \right\}, \quad j \in I.
$$

When $\alpha _ { j }$ is finite, it gives the position of $j$ in the permuted sequence $\left( \tau _ { k } \right)$ . The times $\tau _ { k }$ are clearly predictable if the sequence $\left( \alpha _ { j } \right)$ is predictable in the sense of Chapters 9–10. 

Proof of Theorem 27.7: First let $\xi$ be indexed by $I _ { n } = \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , so that $\left( \tau _ { 1 } , \ldots , \tau _ { n } \right)$ and $\left( \alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } \right)$ are mutually inverse random permutations of $I _ { n }$ For each $m \in \{ 0 , \ldots , n \}$ , put $\alpha _ { j } ^ { m } = \alpha _ { j }$ for all $j \leq m$ , and define recursively 

$$
\alpha_ {j + 1} ^ {m} = \min \left(I _ {n} \backslash \{\alpha_ {1} ^ {m}, \dots , \alpha_ {j} ^ {m} \}\right), \quad m \leq j \leq n.
$$

Then $\left( \alpha _ { 1 } ^ { m } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } ^ { m } \right)$ is a predictable, $\mathcal { F } _ { m }$ -measurable permutation of $I _ { n }$ . $$
\begin{array}{l} E \prod_ {j} f _ {\alpha_ {j} ^ {m}} (\xi_ {j}) = E E \Big \{\prod_ {j} f _ {\alpha_ {j} ^ {m}} (\xi_ {j})   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {m - 1} \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \prod_ {j <   m} f _ {\alpha_ {j} ^ {m}} (\xi_ {j})   E \Big \{\prod_ {j \geq m} f _ {\alpha_ {j} ^ {m}} (\xi_ {j})   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {m - 1} \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \prod_ {j <   m} f _ {\alpha_ {j} ^ {m - 1}} (\xi_ {j})   E \Big \{\prod_ {j \geq m} f _ {\alpha_ {j} ^ {m - 1}} (\xi_ {j})   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {m - 1} \Big \} \\ \qquad = E \prod_ {j} f _ {\alpha_ {j} ^ {m - 1}} (\xi_ {j}). \end{array}

Summing over $m \in \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ and noting that $\alpha _ { j } ^ { n } = \alpha _ { j }$ and $\alpha _ { j } ^ { 0 } = j$ for all $j ,$ we get 

$$
E \prod_ {k \leq n} f _ {k} (\xi_ {\tau_ {k}}) = E \prod_ {j \leq n} f _ {\alpha_ {j}} (\xi_ {j}) = E \prod_ {k \leq n} f _ {k} (\xi_ {k}),

which extends to (6) by a monotone-class argument. 

Next let $I = I _ { m }$ with $m > n$ . The sequence $\left( \tau _ { k } \right)$ may then be extended recursively to $I _ { m }$ , through the formula

Finally, let $I = \mathsf { N }$ . For each $m \in \mathbb { N }$ , consider the predictable times

As $m  \infty$ we get $\tau _ { k } ^ { m } \to \tau _ { k }$ , and (6) follows from (8) by dominated convergence. ✷

Turning to the continuous-time case, we say that a process X in a topological space is continuous in probability<sup>8</sup> if $X _ { s } \ { \overset { P } { \to } } \ X _ { t }$ as $s  t$ . An R<sup>d</sup>-valued process X on [0, 1] or $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ is said to be exchangeable or contractable, if it is continuous in probability with $X _ { 0 } = 0$ , and such that the increments $X _ { t } - X _ { s }$ over disjoint intervals (s, t] of equal length form exchangeable or contractable sequences. Finally, we say that X has conditionally stationary, independent increments, given a σ-field , if the stated property holds conditionally for any finite collection of intervals.

Theorem 27.10 (exchangeable processes on $[ 0 , 1 ] )$ Let X be an $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ -valued process on [0, 1], continuous in probability with $X _ { 0 } = 0$ . Then X is exchangeable if it has a version 

$$

Using the martingale property of $( X _ { 1 } - X _ { t } ) / ( 1 - t )$ and the symmetry of X, we further see that 

$$
\begin{array}{l l} E \Big (\int_ {0} ^ {1} | d \hat {X _ {n}} |   \Big |   \mathcal {F} _ {0} \Big) & \preceq E (X _ {n} ^ {*} |   \mathcal {F} _ {0}) \\ & \preceq \big (\operatorname{tr} [ X _ {n} ] \big) _ {1} ^ {1 / 2} \\ & = \Big (\sum_ {j > n} | \beta_ {j} | ^ {2} \Big) ^ {1 / 2} \to 0. \end{array}
$$

Hence, $( X _ { n } \circ V ^ { - 1 } ) _ { t } \overset { P } { \to } 0$ for all $t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , which reduces the proof to the case of finitely many jumps. 

It is then enough to consider a jointly exchangeable pair, consisting of a marked point process $\xi$ on [0, 1] and a Brownian bridge $B$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . By a simple randomization, we may further reduce to the case where $\xi$ has a.s. distinct marks. It is then equivalent to consider finitely many optional times $\tau _ { 1 } , \ldots , \tau _ { m } ,$ such that B and the point processes $\xi _ { j } = \delta _ { \tau _ { j } }$ are jointly exchangeable. 

To apply Proposition 19.15, we may express the continuous martingale M as an integral with respect to the Brownian motion in Lemma 19.10, with the predictable process $V$ replaced by the associated indicator functions $U _ { r } ^ { t } =$ $1 \{ V _ { r } \leq t \} , r \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ ]. Then the covariations of the lemma become 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int_ {0} ^ {1} \Big (U _ {r} ^ {s} - \bar {U} _ {r} ^ {s} \Big) \Big (U _ {r} ^ {t} - \bar {U} _ {r} ^ {t} \Big) d r = \int_ {0} ^ {1} U _ {r} ^ {s} U _ {r} ^ {t} d r - \lambda U ^ {s} \cdot \lambda U ^ {t}} \\ & {\qquad = \lambda U ^ {s \wedge t} - \lambda U ^ {s} \cdot \lambda U ^ {t}} \\ & {\qquad = s \wedge t - s t} \\ & {\qquad = E (B _ {s} B _ {t}),} \end{array}
$$

as required. 

As for the random measures $\xi _ { j } = \delta _ { \tau _ { j } }$ , Proposition 10.23 yields the associated compensators at∆τ 1 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \eta_ {j} [ 0, t ] = \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \tau_ {j}} \frac {d s}{1 - s} \\ = - \log (1 - t \wedge \tau_ {j}), \quad t \in [ 0, 1 ]. \end{array}
$$

Since the $\eta _ { j }$ are difuse, we get by Theorem 10.24 (ii) the corresponding discounted compensators 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \zeta_ {j} [ 0, t ] = 1 - \exp \bigl (- \eta_ {j} [ 0, t ] \bigr) \\ = 1 - (1 - t \wedge \tau_ {j}) \\ = t \wedge \tau_ {j}, \quad t \in [ 0, 1 ]. \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\zeta _ { j } = \lambda ( [ 0 , \tau _ { j } ] \cap \cdot ) \leq \lambda$ a.s., and so $\zeta _ { j } \circ V ^ { - 1 } \leq \lambda \circ V ^ { - 1 } = \lambda$ a.s. Hence, Proposition 19.15 yields 

$$
\left(B \circ V ^ {- 1}, V _ {\tau_ {1}}, \dots , V _ {\tau_ {m}}\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (B, \tau_ {1}, \dots , \tau_ {m}),
$$

which implies $X \circ V ^ { - 1 } \overset { d } { = } X$

Chapter 28 

# Multi-variate Arrays and Symmetries

Separately or jointly exchangeable arrays, contraction and extension properties, coding representations, equivalent coding functions, coupling, conditional independence, shell σ-field, independent entries, invariant coding, symmetric functions, inversion, conditioning and independence, shell-measurable and dissociated arrays, separate or joint rotatability, totally rotatable arrays, symmetric partitions 

Our survey of modern probability would be incomplete without a discussion of higher-dimensional random arrays, which appear frequently in a wide range of applications. The most obvious use may be to describe the interactions between the nodes in a random graph or network, where $X _ { i j }$ represents the interaction between nodes i and j. Here even higher order interactions such as $X _ { i j k }$ are conceivable. The interactions may take values in an abstract space S, and we may allow the one-sided interactions $i \mapsto j$ and $j \mapsto i$ to be diferent, in general. The simplest example is the adjacency matrix between the nodes of a random graph. 

For a totally diferent application, consider a Hilbert-space valued random process $\xi _ { h } , h \in H$ , with associated inner products $\rho _ { h , k } = \langle \xi _ { h } , \xi _ { k } \rangle$ , for arbitrary $h , k \in H$ . Fixing an ortho-normal basis (ONB) $h _ { 1 } , h _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . in H, we obtain a discrete array $X _ { i j } = \rho _ { h _ { i } , h _ { j } }$ . We may also think of $X = ( X _ { i j } )$ as the coordinate representation of an operator on H, representing an observable quantity in quantum mechanics. More mundane examples of random arrays appear frequently in statistics, such as in the context of U-statistics. We may further mention the case of random partitions of a fixed, countable set. 

In all those applications, it is natural to impose suitable symmetry conditions. For the graph interactions, we may think of all nodes as equivalent, or we may enumerate them in random order, which leads to a condition of joint exchangeability of the interaction array X. If X instead codifies the interactions between two diferent kinds of nodes, those may be numbered separately, which suggests an assumption of separate exchangeability. For processes on a Hilbert space, we may think of all ortho-normal bases as equivalent, which leads to a condition of joint rotatability. Indeed, for operators in quantum mechanics there is no preferred ONB, simply because the individual coordinate representations are not observable. 

In this chapter, we derive representations of multi-variate random arrays with exchangeable, contractable, or rotatable symmetries. In the exchangeable case, there are no simple mixing representations in terms of i.i.d. arrays, and all higher-dimensional representations are instead extensions of the coding representation in Corollary 27.3. They yield in particular a remarkable extension property, generalizing the classical equivalence between exchangeable and contractable sequences. 

The higher-dimensional proofs are quite intricate, and involve a subtle use of notions and results for conditional independence from Chapter 8. The rotatable case is even harder, as it leads in general to representations in terms of multiple Wiener-Itˆo integrals such as in Chapter 14. Here we discuss only the relatively elementary representations in two dimensions, which can be stated in terms of i.i.d. Gaussian random variables. We finally include a version of Kingman’s paintbox representation for exchangeable and related partitions. 

To prepare for our more precise technical discussions, we say that a random array $X ~ = ~ \left( X _ { k } \right)$ , indexed by vectors $k = ( k _ { 1 } , \ldots , k _ { d } ) \in \mathsf { N } ^ { d }$ , is separately exchangeable, if its distribution is invariant under arbitrary permutations $p ^ { 1 } , \ldots , p ^ { d }$ in the d indices. We also consider the weaker property of joint exchangeability, where the same invariance is only required for a single permutation $p = ( p _ { 1 } , p _ { 2 } , . . . )$ of N, so that 

$$
X _ {k _ {1}, \dots , k _ {d}} \stackrel {d} {=} X _ {p (k _ {1}), \dots , p (k _ {d})}, \quad k \in \mathsf {N} ^ {d}.\tag{1}
$$

In the latter case, it is equivalent and more natural to consider arrays X indexed by the non-diagonal set ${ \mathsf { N } } ^ { ( d ) }$ , where all indices $k _ { 1 } , \ldots , k _ { d }$ are diferent. 

Replacing the permutations in (1) by sub-sequences $p _ { 1 } < p _ { 2 } < \cdots$ yields the even weaker notion of (joint) contractability<sup>1</sup>. Here it is equivalent and often preferable to consider arrays indexed by the tetrahedral set ${ \mathsf { N } } ^ { \uparrow d }$ of increasing sequences $k _ { 1 } < \ldots < k _ { d }$ , which may be identified with the corresponding sets of components $\tilde { k } = \{ k _ { 1 } , \ldots , k _ { d } \}$ . Define 

$$
\hat {\mathsf {N}} ^ {d} = \bigcup_ {k \leq d} \mathsf {N} ^ {k}, \quad \tilde {\mathsf {N}} ^ {d} = \bigcup_ {k \leq d} \mathsf {N} ^ {\uparrow k}, \quad \hat {\mathsf {N}} ^ {(d)} = \bigcup_ {k \leq d} \mathsf {N} ^ {(k)}.
$$

By a U-array we mean an indexed set of i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random variables<sup>2</sup>. For any U-array $\xi$ on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ and vector $k \in \mathbb { N } ^ { ( d ) }$ or set $J \in  { \mathbb { N } } ^ { \uparrow d }$ , we write 

$$
\hat {\xi} _ {k} = \{\xi_ {\tilde {h}}; h \subset k \}, \qquad \hat {\xi} _ {J} = \{\xi_ {I}; I \subset J \},
$$

where $h \subset k$ means that h is a sub-sequence of $k ,$ , and $\tilde { h }$ denotes the set of components of the vector h. Here the order of enumeration, important for subsequent representations, is determined by the order of the k-components. Thus, the index set for $d = 2$ consists of the sets $\emptyset , \{ k _ { 1 } \} , \{ k _ { 2 } \} , \{ k _ { 1 } , k _ { 2 } \}$ , whereas for $d = 3$ we have the index set 

$$
\emptyset , \{k _ {1} \}, \{k _ {2} \}, \{k _ {3} \}, \{k _ {1}, k _ {2} \}, \{k _ {1}, k _ {3} \}, \{k _ {2}, k _ {3} \}, \{k _ {1}, k _ {2}, k _ {3} \}.
$$

The jointly exchangeable and contractable arrays can be characterized by the following coding representations, extending the one-dimensional version in Corollary 27.3. Its proof will take up much of the present chapter. 

Theorem 28.1 (jointly exchangeable and contractable arrays, Aldous, Hoover, $O K )$ For a d-dimensional random array X in a Borel space $S _ { i }$ , we have 

(i) $X ~ = ~ ( X _ { k } )$ is jointly exchangeable on $\hat { \mathsf { N } } ^ { ( d ) }$ if there exist a measurable function $f \colon [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 ^ { d } } \to S$ and a U-array $\xi = ( \xi _ { J } )$ on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ , such that 

$$
X _ {k} = f (\hat {\xi} _ {k}) a. s., \quad k \in \hat {\mathsf {N}} ^ {(d)},
$$

(ii) $X \ = \ ( X _ { J } )$ is contractable on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d } \ i f f$ it can be extended to a jointly exchangeable array on $\hat { \mathsf { N } } ^ { ( d ) }$ , and hence can be represented as in (i), 

(iii) the array in (ii) is exchangeable on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ if we can choose the representing function f to be symmetric. 

When $d = 2$ , the representation in (i) becomes 

$$
X _ {i j} = f (\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}), \quad i \neq j \text {in} \mathsf {N},\tag{2}
$$

for a measurable function $f \colon [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 4 } \to S$ and some i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random variables $\alpha , \xi _ { i }$ , and $\zeta _ { i j } = \zeta _ { j i }$ . Part (i) yields a similar representation of separately exchangeable arrays, where the representing U-array is now indexed by $\hat { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d } .$ and $\hat { \xi } _ { k }$ is indexed by all sub-sequences $h \subset k$ . Thus, the index set for $d = 2$ has elements $\emptyset , k _ { 1 } , k _ { 2 } , ( k _ { 1 } , k _ { 2 } )$ , where denotes the empty sequence, whereas for $d = 3$ we have the index set 

$$
\emptyset , k _ {1}, k _ {2}, k _ {3}, (k _ {1}, k _ {2}), (k _ {1}, k _ {3}), (k _ {2}, k _ {3}), (k _ {1}, k _ {2}, k _ {3}).
$$

The representation in the separately exchangeable case is the same as before, apart from the dependencies between coding variables. 

Corollary 28.2 (separately exchangeable arrays) An S-valued array $\boldsymbol { X } \ =$ $( X _ { k } )$ on $\mathsf { N } ^ { d }$ is separately exchangeable if there exist a measurable function $f \colon [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 2 ^ { d } } \to S$ and a U-array $\xi = ( \xi _ { h } )$ on $\hat { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ , such that 

$$
X _ {k} = f (\hat {\xi} _ {k}) a. s., k \in \mathbb {N} ^ {d}.\tag{3}
$$

Thus, for $d = 2$ we get the representation 

$$
X _ {i j} = f (\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \eta_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}), \quad i, j \in \mathsf {N},\tag{4}
$$

for a measurable function $f \colon [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { 4 } \to S$ and some i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random vari ables $\alpha , \xi _ { i } , \eta _ { j } , \zeta _ { i j }$ 

Proof: If X is separately exchangeable, it is also jointly exchangeable and hence can be represented as in Theorem 28.1 (i), in terms of a U-array $\xi = ( \xi _ { J } )$ on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ . Now choose any disjoint, countable sets $N _ { 1 } , \ldots , N _ { d } \subset \mathsf { N }$ , and let Y be the restriction of $X$ to $N _ { 1 } \times \cdots \times N _ { d }$ . Then the representation of $Y$ reduces to the form (3), and since $X \stackrel { d } { = } Y$ apart from index sets, Theorem 8.17 yields the same representation for X. ✷ 

Before proceeding to the proof of Theorem 28.1, we note that the representing functions are far from unique. It then becomes important to determine when two functions $f$ and $g$ can be used to represent the same array. The answer difers in the three cases, and for convenience we consider only jointly exchangeable arrays of dimension $2 ,$ where the more explicit statements may clarify the basic ideas. See also the one-dimensional version in Lemma 27.4. Put $I = [ 0 , 1 ]$ for convenience. 

Theorem 28.3 (equivalent coding functions, Hoover, OK) For any measurable functions $f , g \colon I ^ { 4 }  S$ and i.i.d. $U ( 0 , 1 )$ random variables α, $\xi _ { i } , \zeta _ { i j } = \zeta _ { j i }$ and $\alpha ^ { \prime } , \xi _ { i } ^ { \prime } , \zeta _ { i j } ^ { \prime } = \zeta _ { j i } ^ { \prime }$ , these conditions are equivalent <sup>3</sup>: 

(i) there exist some variables $\{ \tilde { \alpha } , \tilde { \xi } _ { i } , \tilde { \zeta } _ { i j } ; i \neq j \} \stackrel { d } { = } \{ \alpha , \xi _ { i } , \zeta _ { i j } ; i \neq j \}$ , such that 

$$
f (\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}) = g (\tilde {\alpha}, \tilde {\xi} _ {i}, \tilde {\xi} _ {j}, \tilde {\zeta} _ {i j}) a. s., i \neq j,\tag{ii}
$$

$$
\left\{f \left(\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}\right); i \neq j \right\} \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left\{g \left(\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}\right); i \neq j \right\},
$$

(iii) there exist some measurable functions 

$$
T, T ^ {\prime} \colon I \to I, \qquad U, U ^ {\prime} \colon I ^ {2} \to I, \qquad V, V ^ {\prime} \colon I ^ {4} \to I,
$$

where $V , V ^ { \prime }$ are symmetric and all functions preserve λ in the highest order arguments, such that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & f \Big \{T (\alpha), U (\alpha , \xi_ {i}), U (\alpha , \xi_ {j}), V (\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}) \Big \} \\ & \qquad = g \Big \{T ^ {\prime} (\alpha), U ^ {\prime} (\alpha , \xi_ {i}), U ^ {\prime} (\alpha , \xi_ {j}), V ^ {\prime} (\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}) \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

(iv) there exist some measurable functions 

$$
T \colon I ^ {2} \to I, \qquad U \colon I ^ {4} \to I, \qquad V \colon I ^ {8} \to I,
$$

where V is symmetric and all functions map $\lambda ^ { 2 }$ into λ in the highest order arguments, such that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f (\alpha , \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {j}, \zeta_ {i j}) = g \Big \{T (\alpha , \alpha^ {\prime}), U (\alpha , \alpha^ {\prime}, \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {i} ^ {\prime}), U (\alpha , \alpha^ {\prime}, \xi_ {j}, \xi_ {j} ^ {\prime}), \\ V (\alpha , \alpha^ {\prime}, \xi_ {i}, \xi_ {i} ^ {\prime}, \xi_ {j}, \xi_ {j} ^ {\prime}, \zeta_ {i j}, \zeta_ {i j} ^ {\prime}) \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Note that (iii) is expressed in terms of six functions $T , T ^ { \prime } , U , U ^ { \prime } , V , V ^ { \prime } ,$ whereas (iv) requires only the three functions $T , U , V$ . On the other hand, we need<sup>4</sup> in (iv) (but not in (iii)) some external randomization variables $\alpha ^ { \prime } , \xi _ { i } ^ { \prime } ,$ $\zeta _ { i j } ^ { \prime } = \zeta _ { j i } ^ { \prime }$ 

To prepare for the proofs of Theorems 28.1 and 28.3, we begin with some general lemmas of independent interest. 

Lemma 28.4 (coupling) Let $X , Y , Z$ be S-valued arrays with $X \bot \bot _ { Y } Z$ . Then 

(i) $i f ~ ( X , Y ) , ( Y , Z )$ are exchangeable on $\hat { \mathsf { N } } ^ { ( d ) }$ , so is $( X , Y , Z )$ 

(ii) $i f ~ ( X , Y ) , ( Y , Z )$ are contractable on $\tilde { \mathsf { Q } } ^ { d }$ , so is $( X , Y , Z )$ 

Proof: (i) Writing $\mu ( Y , \cdot ) = \mathcal { L } ( X \mid Y )$ , we get for any measurable sets $A , B$ and permutation p on N 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \Big \{(X, Y, Z) \circ p \in A \times B \Big \} \\ \quad = E \Big (P \Big \{X \circ p \in A   \big |   (Y, Z) \circ p \Big \}; (Y, Z) \circ p \in B \Big) \\ \quad = E \Big (P \Big \{X \circ p \in A   \big |   Y \circ p \Big \}; (Y, Z) \circ p \in B \Big) \\ \quad = E \Big \{\mu (Y \circ p, A); (Y, Z) \circ p \in B \Big \} \\ \quad = E \Big \{\mu (Y, A); (Y, Z) \in B \Big \} \\ \quad = E \Big (P \{X \in A   |   Y, Z \}; (Y, Z) \in B \Big) \\ \quad = P \Big \{(X, Y, Z) \in A \times B \Big \}, \end{array}
$$

which extends immediately to $( X , Y , Z ) \circ p \overset { d } { = } ( X , Y , Z )$ 

(ii) For any $a < b$ in $\mathsf Q _ { + }$ and $t \in \mathsf { Q }$ , we define on Q the functions 

$$
\begin{array}{c} p _ {a, t} (x) = x + a   1 \{x > t \}, \qquad p _ {a} = p _ {a, 0}, \\ p _ {a} ^ {b} (x) = x + a   (1 - b ^ {- 1} x)   1 \{0 <   x <   b \}, \end{array}
$$

and note that $p _ { a } ^ { b } \circ p _ { b } = p _ { b }$ . The contractability of $( X , Y )$ yields $( X , Y ) \circ p _ { a } ^ { b } \overset { d } { = }$ $( X , Y )$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (X \circ p _ {b}, Y) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \Big (X \circ p _ {a} ^ {b} \circ p _ {b}, Y \circ p _ {a} ^ {b} \Big) \\ = \Big (X \circ p _ {b}, Y \circ p _ {a} ^ {b} \Big). \end{array}
$$

By Corollary 8.10, we get 

$$
\left(X \circ p _ {b}\right) \underset {Y \circ p _ {a} ^ {b}} {\coprod} Y,
$$

and since $\sigma ( Y \circ p _ { a } ^ { b } ) = \sigma ( Y \circ p _ { a } )$ and $\sigma ( Y \circ p _ { b } ; b > a ) = \sigma ( Y \circ p _ { a } )$ , a monotoneclass argument yields the extended relation 

$$
\left(X \circ p _ {a}\right) \underset {Y \circ p _ {a}} {\perp} Y.
$$

Since also $( X \circ p _ { a } ) \bot \bot _ { Y } ( Z \circ p _ { a } )$ by hypothesis, Theorem 8.12 gives 

$$
(X \circ p _ {a}) \underset {Y \circ p _ {a}} {\mathbb {I}} (Z \circ p _ {a}).
$$

Combining this with the hypothetical relations 

$$

we see as in case (i) that

Lemma 28.5 (conditional independence) Let $( X , \xi )$ be a contractable array on $\tilde { Z } ^ { d }$ with restriction $( Y , \eta )$ to $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d } { } _ { : }$ , where $\xi$ has independent entries. Then

Proposition 28.6 (shell σ-field, Aldous, Hoover) Let the array X on $Z _ { + } ^ { d }$ be separately exchangeable under permutations on N, and write $X ^ { + }$ for the restriction of X to $\mathsf { N } ^ { d }$ . Then 

$$
X ^ {+} \underset {\mathcal {S} (X ^ {+})} {\coprod} (X \setminus X ^ {+}).
$$

Proof: When $d = 1 , X$ is just a random sequence $( \eta , \xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . . ) = ( \eta , \xi )$ ， and $S ( X ^ { + } )$ reduces to the tail σ-field $\tau$ . Applying de Finetti’s theorem to both $\xi$ and $( \xi , \eta )$ gives 

$$
\mathcal {L} (\xi \mid \mu) = \mu^ {\infty}, \qquad \mathcal {L} (\xi \mid \nu , \eta) = \nu^ {\infty},
$$

for some random probability measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ on ${ \mathcal { S } } .$ . By the law of large numbers, $\mu$ and $\nu$ are -measurable with $\mu = \nu \mathrm { a . s . }$ , and so $\xi \bot \bot \tau \eta$ by Corollary 8.10. 

Assuming the truth in dimension $d - 1$ , we turn to the d -dimensional case. Define an $S ^ { \infty }$ -valued array $Y$ on $Z _ { + } ^ { d - 1 }$ by 

$$
Y _ {m} = \left(X _ {m, k}; k \geq 0\right), \quad m \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+} ^ {d - 1},
$$

and note that $Y$ is separately exchangeable under permutations on N. Writing $Y ^ { + }$ for the restriction of $Y$ to $\mathsf { N } ^ { d - 1 }$ and $X ^ { 0 }$ for the restriction of $X$ to $\mathsf { N } ^ { d - 1 } \times \{ \boldsymbol { 0 } \}$ , we get by the induction hypothesis 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (X ^ {+}, X ^ {0}) = Y ^ {+} \bigsqcup_ {\mathcal {S} (Y ^ {+})} (Y \setminus Y ^ {+}) \\ = X \setminus (X ^ {+}, X ^ {0}). \end{array}
$$

Since also 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {S} (Y ^ {+}) \subset \mathcal {S} (X ^ {+}) \vee \sigma (X ^ {0}) \\ \subset \sigma (Y ^ {+}), \end{array}
$$

we obtain 

$$
X ^ {+} \underset {\mathcal {S} (X ^ {+}), X ^ {0}} {\coprod} (X \setminus X ^ {+}).\tag{5}
$$

Next we apply the result for $d = 1$ to the $S ^ { \infty }$ -valued sequence 

$$
Z _ {k} = \left(X _ {m, k}; m \in \mathsf {N} ^ {d - 1}\right), \quad k \geq 0,
$$

to obtain 

$$
X ^ {+} = \left(Z \setminus Z _ {0}\right) \underset {\mathcal {S} (Z)} {\amalg} Z _ {0} = X ^ {0}.
$$

Since clearly 

$$
\mathcal {S} (Z) \subset \mathcal {S} (X ^ {+}) \subset \sigma (X ^ {+}),
$$

we conclude that 

$$
X ^ {+} \underset {\mathcal {S} (X ^ {+})} {\perp \mid \mid} X ^ {0}.
$$

Now combine with (5) and use Theorem 8.12 to get the desired relation. ✷ 

We need only the following corollary. Given an array $\xi$ on $Z _ { + } ^ { d }$ and a set $I \subset$ $\mathsf { N } _ { d } = \{ 1 , \dots , d \}$ , we write $\xi ^ { I }$ for the sub-array on the index set $\mathring { \mathsf { N } } ^ { I } \times \{ 0 \} ^ { I ^ { c } }$ , and put $\hat { \xi } ^ { J } = ( \xi ^ { I } ; \bar { I } \subset J )$ . Further define $\xi ^ { m } = ( \xi ^ { I } ; | I | = m )$ and $\hat { \xi } ^ { m } = \mathcal { \bar { ( } } \bar { \xi ^ { I } } ; | I | \leq$ m), and similarly for arrays on ${ \hat { \mathsf { N } } } ^ { \uparrow d }$ . Recall that $\mathsf { N } ^ { \uparrow d } = ( J \subset \mathsf { N } ; | J | = d )$ and $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d } = ( J \subset \mathsf { N } ; | J | \leq d )$ 

Corollary 28.7 (independent entries) 

(i) Let $\xi$ be a random array on $Z _ { + } ^ { d }$ with independent entries, separately exchangeable under permutations on N, and define 

$$
\eta_ {k} = f (\hat {\xi} _ {k}), \quad k \in \mathbb {Z} _ {+} ^ {d},
$$

for a measurable function f. Then even η has independent entries $i f$ 

$$
\eta_ {k} \perp \bot (\hat {\xi} _ {k} \setminus \xi_ {k}), \quad k \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+} ^ {d},\tag{6}
$$

in which case 

$$
\eta^ {I} \perp \bot (\xi \setminus \xi^ {I}), \quad I \subset \mathsf {N} _ {d}.\tag{7}
$$

(ii) Let $\xi$ be a contractable array on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ with independent entries, and define 

$$
\eta_ {J} = f (\hat {\xi} _ {J}), \quad J \in \tilde {\mathsf {N}} ^ {d},\tag{8}
$$

for a measurable function f. Then even η has independent entries $i f$ 

$$
\eta_ {J} \perp \bot (\hat {\xi} _ {J} \setminus \xi_ {J}), \quad J \in \tilde {\mathbb {N}} ^ {d},\tag{9}
$$

in which case 

$$
\eta^ {k} \perp (\xi \setminus \xi^ {k}), \quad k \leq d.\tag{10}
$$

Proof: (i) Assume (6). Since also $\hat { \xi } _ { k } \bot \bot ( \xi \setminus \hat { \xi } _ { k } )$ , we get $\eta _ { k } \bot \bot ( \xi \setminus \xi _ { k } )$ , and so 

$$
\eta_ {k} \perp \left(\xi \setminus \xi_ {k},   \hat {\eta} ^ {| k |} \setminus \eta_ {k}\right), \quad k \in \mathbb {Z} _ {+} ^ {d},
$$

where $| k |$ is the number of k -components in N. As in Lemma 4.8, this yields both (7) and the independence of the η -entries. 

Conversely, let $\eta$ have independent entries. Then $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } } ( \eta ^ { I } )$ is trivial for $\emptyset \neq$ $I \subset { \mathsf { N } } _ { d }$ by Kolmogorov’s $0 { - } 1$ law. Applying Lemma 28.6 to the $Z _ { + } ^ { I }$ -indexed array $( \eta ^ { I } , \hat { \xi } ^ { I } \setminus \xi ^ { I } )$ , which is clearly separately exchangeable on $\mathsf { N } ^ { I }$ , we obtain $\eta ^ { I } \bot \bot ( \hat { \xi } ^ { I } \setminus \xi ^ { I } )$ , and (6) follows. 

(ii) Assume (9). Since also $\hat { \xi } _ { J } \underline { { { \mathrm { 1 1 } } } } ( \xi \backslash \hat { \xi } _ { J } )$ , we obtain $\eta _ { J } \underline { { \perp | } } ( \xi \backslash \xi _ { J } )$ , and so 

$$
\eta_ {J} \perp \left(\xi \setminus \xi^ {d},   \hat {\eta} ^ {d} \setminus \eta^ {J}\right), \quad J \in \tilde {\mathsf {N}} ^ {d}.
$$

Thus, $\eta$ has independent entries and satisfies (10). 

Conversely, let $\eta$ have independent entries. Extend $\xi$ to a contractable array on $\mathsf Q ^ { \uparrow d }$ , and extend η accordingly to $\mathsf Q ^ { \uparrow d }$ by means of (8). Define 

$$
\left(\xi_ {k} ^ {\prime}, \eta_ {k} ^ {\prime}\right) = \left(\xi , \eta\right) _ {r (1, k _ {1}), \dots , r (d, k _ {d})}, \quad k \in \mathbb {Z} _ {+} ^ {d},
$$

where $r ( i , k ) = i + k ( k + 1 ) ^ { - 1 }$ . Then $\xi ^ { \prime }$ is separately exchangeable on $\mathsf { N } ^ { d }$ with independent entries, and (8) yields $\eta _ { k } ^ { \prime } = f ( \hat { \xi } _ { k } ^ { \prime } )$ for all $k \in Z _ { + } ^ { d }$ . Since $\eta ^ { \prime } \subset \eta$ has again independent entries, (i) yields $\eta _ { k } ^ { \prime } \bot \bot ( \hat { \xi } _ { k } ^ { \prime } \setminus \xi _ { k } ^ { \prime } )$ for all $k \in \mathsf { N } ^ { d }$ , or equivalently $\eta _ { J } \underline { { \bot \bot } } ( \hat { \xi } _ { J } \backslash \xi _ { J } )$ for suitable $J \in \mathsf { Q } ^ { \uparrow d }$ . The general relation (9) now follows by the contractability of $\xi .$ . ✷ 

Lemma 28.8 (coding) Let $\xi ~ = ~ ( \xi _ { j } )$ and $\eta ~ = ~ ( \eta _ { j } )$ be random arrays on a countable index set $I ,$ satisfying 

$$
(\xi_ {i}, \eta_ {i}) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (\xi_ {j}, \eta_ {j}), \quad i, j \in I,\tag{11}
$$

$$
\xi_ {j} \underset {\eta_ {j}} {\mathop {\coprod}} (\xi \setminus \xi_ {j}, \eta), \quad j \in I.\tag{12}
$$

Then there exist some measurable functions $f , g .$ , such that for any U-array $\vartheta \bot \bot ( \xi , \eta )$ on $I _ { i }$ , the random variables 

$$

$$

$$
\xi_ {j} = f (\eta_ {j}, \zeta_ {j}) a. s., \quad j \in I.\tag{14}
$$

Proof: For any $i \in I .$ , Theorem 8.17 yields a measurable function $f _ { : }$ , such that 

$$
\left(\xi_ {i}, \eta_ {i}\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} \left\{f \left(\eta_ {i}, \vartheta_ {i}\right), \eta_ {i} \right\}.
$$

The same theorem provides some measurable functions g and $h$ , such that the random elements 

satisfy 

$$
\zeta_ {i} = g (\xi_ {i}, \eta_ {i}, \vartheta_ {i}), \quad \tilde {\eta} _ {i} = h (\xi_ {i}, \eta_ {i}, \vartheta_ {i})
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\xi_ {i}, \eta_ {i}) = \left\{f (\tilde {\eta} _ {i}, \zeta_ {i}),   \tilde {\eta} _ {i} \right\} \text { a.s. }, \\ (\tilde {\eta} _ {i}, \zeta_ {i}) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (\eta_ {i}, \vartheta_ {i}). \end{array}
$$

In particular $\tilde { \eta } _ { i } ~ = ~ \eta _ { i }$ a.s., and so (14) holds for $j ~ = ~ i$ with $\zeta _ { i }$ as in (13). Furthermore, $\zeta _ { i }$ is $U ( 0 , 1 )$ and independent of $\eta _ { i }$ . The two statements extend by (11) to arbitrary $j \in I$ 

Combining (12) with the relations $\vartheta \bot \bot ( \xi , \eta )$ and $\vartheta _ { j } \bot \bot ( \vartheta \setminus \vartheta _ { j } )$ , we get 

$$
\left(\xi_ {j}, \eta_ {j}, \vartheta_ {j}\right) \underset {\eta_ {j}} {\mathop {\|}} \left(\xi \setminus \xi_ {j},   \eta ,   \vartheta \setminus \vartheta_ {j}\right), \quad j \in I,
$$

which implies 

$$

$$

Since also $\zeta _ { j } \bot \bot \eta _ { j }$ , Theorem 8.12 yields $\zeta _ { j } \bot \bot ( \zeta \setminus \zeta _ { j } , \eta )$ . Then Lemma 4.8 shows that the array η and the elements $\zeta _ { j } , j \in I$ , are all independent. Thus, $\zeta$ is indeed a U-array independent of $\eta .$ ✷

$$

$$

(ii) Defining $r t \ = \ t$ for $r \in G$ and $t \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ , we have by (i) and the independence $\zeta \perp \perp \eta$

Proof: (i) Write $\xi ^ { d } , \hat { \xi } ^ { d }$ for the restrictions of $\xi$ to ${ \mathsf { N } } ^ { \uparrow d }$ and ${ \tilde { \mathsf { N } } } ^ { d } .$ , respectively, and similarly for $\eta , \zeta , \vartheta$ . For $d = 0$ , Lemma 28.8 applied to the pair $( \xi _ { \varnothing } , \eta _ { \varnothing } )$ yields some functions $g , h$ , such that when $\vartheta _ { \varnothing \bot \bot } \xi$ is $U ( 0 , 1 )$ , the variable $\zeta _ { \varnothing } =$ $g ( \xi _ { \varnothing } , \vartheta _ { \varnothing } )$ becomes $U ( 0 , 1 )$ with $\zeta _ { \varnothing } \bot \bot \eta _ { \varnothing }$ and $\xi _ { \varnothing } = h ( \eta _ { \varnothing } , \zeta _ { \varnothing } )$ a.s. 

Proceeding by recursion on d, let $g , h$ be such that (16) defines a U-array $\hat { \zeta } ^ { d - 1 } \bot \bot \hat { \eta } ^ { d - 1 }$ on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d - 1 }$ satisfying (17) on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d - 1 }$ . $$
\xi_ {J} \underset {\hat {\xi} _ {J} ^ {\prime}} {\mathop {\coprod}} (\hat {\xi} ^ {d} \setminus \xi_ {J}), \quad J \in \mathsf {N} ^ {\uparrow d},

since $\xi$ has independent entries. Then (15) yields

\xi_ {J} \underset {\hat {\xi} _ {J} ^ {\prime}, \eta_ {J}} {\mathbb {I I}} \left(\hat {\xi} ^ {d} \setminus \xi_ {J},   \hat {\eta} ^ {d}\right), \quad J \in \mathsf {N} ^ {\uparrow d},

and by contractability we see that $( \hat { \xi } _ { J } , \eta _ { J } ) = ( \xi _ { J } , \hat { \xi } _ { J } ^ { \prime } , \eta _ { J } )$ has the same distribution for all $J \in \mathbb { N } ^ { \uparrow \bar { d } }$ . \begin{array}{r l} & {\zeta_ {J} = g _ {d} \Big \{\hat {\xi} _ {J}, f (\hat {\xi} _ {J}), \vartheta_ {J} \Big \},} \\ & {\xi_ {J} = h _ {d} \Big \{\hat {h} ^ {\prime} (\hat {\eta} _ {J} ^ {\prime}, \hat {\zeta} _ {J} ^ {\prime}), \eta_ {J}, \zeta_ {J} \Big \} \mathrm{a.s.}, J \in \mathsf {N} ^ {\uparrow d},} \end{array}

To complete the recursion, we need to show that $\hat { \zeta } ^ { d - 1 } , \zeta ^ { d } , \hat { \eta } ^ { d }$ are independent. Then note that $\hat { \vartheta } ^ { d - 1 } \underline { { \mathrm { \tiny ~ \cdot ~ } } } \underline { { \mathrm { \tiny ~ \cdot ~ } } } ( \hat { \xi } ^ { d } , \vartheta ^ { d } )$ , since $\vartheta$ is a U-array independent of $\xi .$ . Hence, (15) and (16) yield

Combining this with (19) gives

and so by (15) and (16) we have $\zeta ^ { d } \perp \perp ( \hat { \eta } ^ { d } , \hat { \zeta } ^ { d - 1 } )$ 

Now only $\hat { \eta } ^ { d } \bot \bot \hat { \zeta } ^ { d - 1 }$ remains to be proved. Since $\xi$ and $\eta$ are related by (15) and have independent entries, Lemma 28.7 (ii) yields $\eta ^ { d } \perp \perp \hat { \xi } ^ { d - 1 }$ , which extends to $\eta ^ { d } \bot \lfloor \hat { \xi } ^ { d - 1 } , \hat { \mathcal { V } } ^ { d - 1 } )$ since $\vartheta \bot \bot ( \xi , \eta )$ . Hence, $\eta ^ { \dot { d } } \dot { \perp } 1 ( \hat { \eta } ^ { d - 1 } , \hat { \zeta } ^ { d - 1 } )$ by (15) and (16). (ii) Here a similar recursive argument applies, except that now we need to invoke Lemmas 28.9 and 28.11 in each step, to ensure the desired symmetry of $g , h$ . We omit the details. ✷ 

For the next result, we say that an array is representable, if it can be represented as in Theorem 28.1. 

Lemma 28.13 (augmentation) Suppose that all contractable arrays on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ are representable, and let $( X , \xi )$ be a contractable array on $\tilde { \mathsf { N } } ^ { d }$ , where $\xi$ has independent entries. We are now ready to prove the main results, beginning with Theorem 28.1 (i). Here our proof is based on the following lemma.

Define ${ \tilde { T } } ^ { \prime } = { \tilde { T } } \setminus \{ \varnothing \}$ and $Z _ { - } = - Z _ { + } = Z \backslash \mathsf { N }$ 

Lemma 28.15 (key construction) Let X be a contractable array on $\tilde { Z } _ { \cdot }$ , and define for $J \in \tilde { \mathsf { N } }$ and $n \in \mathsf N$

Writing $Y = ( U \otimes V ) X$ for the mapping $X \mapsto Y$ , we say that X is separately rotatable if $( U \otimes V ) X \overset { d } { = } X$ for all $U , V$ , and jointly rotatable if the same condition holds with $U = V$
