Chapter 31 

# Palm and Gibbs Kernels, Local Approximation

Palm kernel, supporting measure, invariant Palm disintegration, uniqueness and inversion, time–cycle duality, local approximation, Palm averages, mixed Poisson and binomial processes, Poisson criterion, conditioning and iteration, Palm–density duality, reduced Palm measures, compound Cambell measure, Gibbs and Papangelou kernels, invariance and Cox property, Palm–Gibbs duality, inner and outer conditioning 

Palm measures may be regarded as extensions of regular conditional distributions, which explains their fundamental importance. Their study leads in particular to an amazingly rich theory of conditioning in point processes. We consider first the case of stationary random measures ξ, where there is only a single Palm measure, describing the local behavior of the entire process. Here a highlight of the theory is the fundamental theorem of Kaplan, giving a remarkable connection between stationary processes in discrete and continuous time. 

Dropping the condition of stationarity, we get a whole family of Palm measures, one for each point in the underlying space S, combining into a kernel on S formed by disintegration of the underlying Campbell measure<sup>1</sup>. Among the key results in the non-stationary case, we note the local approximations in Theorem 31.9, justifying the interpretation of the Palm distribution of a point process $\xi$ at a point $s \in S$ as the conditional distribution, given that ξ has a point at s. We further note the iteration approach in Theorem 31.12, where the Palm construction may be simplified through a preliminary conditioning, and the duality relation in Theorem 31.13, which enables us to derive smoothness properties of the Palm kernel from the possible smoothness of an associated conditional intensity. 

We also call attention to the higher order Palm measures of a point process, obtained by disintegration of a compound Campbell measure, and allowing an interpretation in terms of inner conditioning. This leads naturally to the dual notion of Gibbs kernel, describing the corresponding outer conditioning. We further derive some basic characterizations involving the Papangelou kernel, obtained by restricting the Gibbs kernel to individual point masses. 

Random measures have already appeared in various contexts in earlier chapters, including the more comprehensive treatments in Chapters 15 and 30. Here we just recall the definition of a random measure on $S$ as a locally finite kernel from the basic probability space $\Omega$ into S, and a point process as an integervalued random measure, supported by a locally finite random set. Given a random measure $\xi$ on $S$ and a random element $\eta$ in $T .$ , we define the associated Campbell measure $C _ { \xi , \eta }$ on $S \times T$ by 

$$
C _ {\xi , \eta} f = E \int \xi (d s) f (s, \eta), \quad f \geq 0.
$$

Theorem 31.1 (Palm disintegration) Consider a random measure $\xi$ on $S$ and a random element η in $T$ , such that $C _ { \xi , \eta }$ is σ-finite. Then 

(i) there exist a σ-finite measure $\nu \sim E \xi$ on $S$ and a kernel $\mathcal { L } ( \eta \| \xi ) \colon S \to T$ such that Q μ) 

$$
C _ {\xi , \eta} = \nu \otimes \mathcal {L} (\eta \| \xi),
$$

(ii) when $E \xi = \nu$ is σ-finite, we can choose $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi )$ to be a probability kernel. 

Proof: Use Theorem 3.4. 

The σ-finiteness of the Campbell measure is not a serious restriction, since we can always replace $\eta$ by the pair $( \xi , \eta )$ , for which it holds automatically. Putting $\mu = \mathcal { L } ( \eta \| \xi )$ , we can write the Palm disintegration as 

$$
E \int \xi (d s) f (s, \eta) = \int \nu (d s) \int \mu_ {s} (d t) f (s, t), \quad f \geq 0,
$$

just as for the conditional distributions in Theorem 8.5. Here $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi )$ is called the Palm kernel of $\eta$ with respect to $\xi ,$ and its values $\mathcal { L } ( \eta \parallel \xi ) _ { i }$ are known as Palm measures or, in case of (ii), as Palm distributions at the points s. Furthermore, $\nu$ is called a supporting measure of $\xi ,$ . When $\xi = \delta _ { \tau }$ for a random element $\tau$ in $S ,$ we may choose $\nu = E \xi = \mathcal { L } ( \tau )$ to obtain 

$$
\mathcal {L} (\eta \parallel \xi) _ {s} = \mathcal {L} (\eta \mid \tau) _ {s}, s \in S \mathrm{a.e.} \mathcal {L} (\tau),
$$

which justifies our notation and suggests that we think of the Palm measures as extensions of the regular conditional distributions from Chapter 8. Further justifications are provided by Theorems 31.5 and 31.9 below. 

Now let $G$ be a measurable group with Haar measure $\lambda ,$ acting measurably on the Borel spaces $S$ and $T$ . Given a random measure $\xi$ on $S$ and a random element $\eta$ in $T$ , we say that the pair $( \xi , \eta )$ is G -stationary if $\theta _ { r } ( \xi , \eta ) \overset { d } { = } ( \xi , \eta )$ for all $r \in G$ , where $\theta _ { r } \eta = r \eta$ and $\theta _ { r } \xi = \xi \circ \theta _ { r } ^ { - 1 }$ , so that 

$$
(\theta_ {r} \xi) B = \xi (\theta_ {r} ^ {- 1} B), \qquad (\theta_ {r} \xi) f = \xi (f \circ \theta_ {r}).
$$

If $S = G ,$ , we assume $\xi B < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . when $\lambda B < \infty$ , which makes λ an invariant supporting measure for $\xi$ . In particular we may choose $\eta = \xi$ , or replace $\eta$ by the pair (ξ, η). 

If the pair $( \xi , \eta )$ is jointly stationary with respect to a group $G ,$ we may choose the Palm disintegration to be G -invariant. When $S = G$ , the entire Palm kernel $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi )$ is determined by the single measure $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi ) _ { i }$ , then referred to as the Palm measure of $\eta$ with respect to $\xi$ 

Theorem 31.2 (invariant Palm disintegration) Let G be a measurable group with Haar measure $\lambda ,$ acting properly on $S$ and measurably on $T _ { \cdot }$ , where $S ,$ $T$ are Borel. Consider a random measure $\xi$ on S and a random element η in $T$ where $( \xi , \eta )$ is stationary and $C _ { \xi , \eta }$ is $\sigma { - } f i n i t e$ . Then 

(i) there exist a σ-finite, G-invariant measure $\nu \sim E \xi$ on $S$ and a G-invariant kernel $\mathcal { L } ( \eta \| \xi ) \colon S \to T$ , such that 

$$
C _ {\xi , \eta} = \nu \otimes \mathcal {L} (\eta \| \xi),
$$

(ii) when $S = G$ we may choose $\nu = \lambda$ , in which case $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi )$ is given, for any $B \in { \mathcal { G } }$ with $\lambda B = 1$ , by 

$$
E \left\{f (\eta) \| \xi \right\} _ {r} = E \int_ {B} f (r p ^ {- 1} \eta) \xi (d p), \quad r \in G, f \geq 0.\tag{1}
$$

Proof: Use Theorem 3.14. 

When $G = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with Lebesgue measure $\lambda ^ { d }$ , the Palm definition in Theorem 31.2 (ii) is essentially a 1 1 correspondence, and we proceed to derive some useful inversion formulas. If $\xi$ is a simple point process, then so is any ‘Palm version’ $\tilde { \xi }$ with distribution $\mathcal { L } ( \xi \| \xi ) _ { 0 }$ , and furthermore $\tilde { \xi } \{ 0 \} = 1$ . The inversion may then be stated in terms of the Voronoi cell around 0, given by 

$$
V _ {\mu} = \left\{x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d};   \mu B _ {x} ^ {| x |} = 0 \right\}, \quad \mu \in \mathcal {N} _ {\mathsf {R} ^ {d}},
$$

where $B _ { x } ^ { r }$ denotes the open ball around x of radius $r > 0$ . When $d = 1$ , the supporting points of $\mu$ may be enumerated in increasing order as $t _ { n } ( \mu )$ , subject to the convention $t _ { 0 } ( \mu ) \leq 0 < t _ { 1 } ( \mu )$ 

To avoid repetitions, we assume throughout that R or $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ acts measurably on the Borel space T. We further write $E ^ { \xi } = E ( \cdot \| \xi ) _ { 0 }$ , for convenience. 

Theorem 31.3 (uniqueness and inversion) For a stationary pair ofa random measure $\xi$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and a random element η in T, the measure $\mathcal { L } ( \xi , \eta ; \xi \neq 0 )$ is determined by $\mathcal { L } ( \xi , \eta \| \xi ) _ { 0 }$ , and for any measurable functions $f \geq 0$ on $T$ and $g > 0$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\xi g < \infty \ a . s .$ , we have 

$$
E \left\{f (\eta); \xi \neq 0 \right\} = E ^ {\xi} \int \frac {f \left(\theta_ {x} \eta\right)}{\xi \left(g \circ \theta_ {x}\right)} g (x) d x,\tag{i}
$$

(ii) when $\xi$ is a simple point process on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

$$
E \Bigl \{f (\eta); \xi \neq 0 \Bigr \} = E ^ {\xi} \int_ {V _ {0} (\xi)} f (\theta_ {- x} \eta) d x,
$$

(iii) when $\xi$ is a simple point process on $\mathsf { R } ,$ 

$$
E \left\{f (\eta); \xi \neq 0 \right\} = E ^ {\xi} \int_ {0} ^ {t _ {1} (\xi)} f \left(\theta_ {- r} \eta\right) d r.
$$

Replacing η by $( \xi , \eta )$ yields inversion formulas for the Palm measures $\mathcal { L } ( \xi , \eta \| \xi ) _ { 0 }$ . A similar remark applies to subsequent theorems. 

Proof: We may prove the stated formulas with η replaced by $\zeta = ( \xi , \eta )$ 

(i) Multiplying (1) by $\lambda ^ { d } B$ and extending by a monotone-class argument, we get for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ 

$$
E ^ {\xi} \int f (\zeta , x) d x = E \int f \left(\theta_ {- x} \zeta , x\right) \xi (d x),
$$

and so by substitution, 

$$
E ^ {\xi} \int f (\theta_ {x} \zeta , x) d x = E \int f (\zeta , x) \xi (d x).\tag{2}
$$

We turn to some general ergodic theorems for Palm distributions, showing how the mappings $\mathcal { L } ( \eta )  \mathcal { L } ( \tilde { \eta } )$ can be achieved by suitable averaging. Given a function $f \in \mathcal { T } _ { + }$ and a bounded measure $\nu \ne 0$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we introduce the average f

Say that the weight functions (probability densities) $g _ { 1 } , g _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . on R<sup>d</sup> are asymp- $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ totically invariant, if the corresponding property holds for the associated measures $g _ { n } \cdot \lambda ^ { d }$ . We often omit the dot in $f \cdot \mu$ 

Since such results apply to the proper Palm distributions, only when the sample intensity $\bar { \xi }$ is a.s. constant, we also need to introduce the modified Palm distributions $\bar { \mathcal { L } } ( \eta \| \xi ) _ { 0 }$ , defined for measurable functions $f \geq 0$ by 

$$

$$

whenever $0 < \bar { \xi } < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . For ergodic $\xi$ we have $\bar { \xi } = E \bar { \xi } \mathrm { a . s . }$ , and $\bar { \mathcal { L } } ( \eta \parallel \xi ) _ { 0 }$ agrees with $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi ) _ { 0 }$ . We may think of $\bar { \mathcal { L } } ( \eta \parallel \xi ) _ { 0 }$ as the distribution of $\eta$ when the pair $( \xi , \eta )$ is shifted to a ‘typical’ point of $\xi ,$ an interpretation that fails for $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi ) _ { 0 }$ in general. The pair $( \tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta } )$ is called a modified Palm version of $( \xi , \eta )$ if $\mathcal { L } ( \tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta } ) = \bar { \mathcal { L } } ( \xi , \eta \| \xi ) _ { 0 }$ 

Theorem 31.6 (Palm averaging) For a stationary pair of a random measure $\xi$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $\bar { \xi } \in ( 0 , \infty )$ a.s. and a random element η in $T$ , consider a modified Palm version $( \tilde { \xi } , \tilde { \eta } )$ . (i) $\bar { f } _ { \mu _ { n } } ( \tilde { \eta } ) \overset { P } {  } E f ( \eta )$

\begin{array}{r l} & {\xi_ {n} B = \int_ {B} 1 \Bigl \{\xi I _ {n} (s) = 1 \Bigr \} \xi (d s)} \\ & {\qquad = \sum_ {s \in B} \delta_ {s} 1 \Bigl \{\xi \{s \} = \xi I _ {n} (s) = 1 \Bigr \},} \end{array}

for any $B \in \hat { S }$ . Since $\xi$ is simple and $( I _ { n j } )$ is separating, we have $\xi _ { n } \uparrow \xi$ , and so by monotone convergence $E \eta \xi _ { n } \uparrow E \bar { \eta } \xi$ . \begin{array}{r} \int_ {B} f (s) E \xi (d s) = (f \cdot E \xi) B = E \eta \xi B \\ = \int_ {B} E \xi (d s) E (\eta \| \xi) _ {s}, \end{array}

which implies $f ( s ) = E ( \eta \| \xi ) _ { s }$ a.e. $E \xi$ 

For any $n \in { \mathbb N }$ and $s \in S { \mathrm { ~ a . e . ~ } } E \xi$ , we may choose $B = I _ { n } ( s )$ . Since $\xi _ { n } B \leq 1$ a.s., we get

\begin{array}{r l} E \eta \xi_ {n} B & = E \big (\eta ; \xi_ {n} B > 0 \big) \\ & \leq E (\eta ; \xi B > 0) \\ & \leq E \eta \xi B, \end{array}

\begin{array}{l} f _ {n} (s) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {B \downarrow \{s \}} \frac {E (\eta ;   \xi B > 0)}{E   \xi B} \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {B \downarrow \{s \}} \frac {E (\eta ;   \xi B > 0)}{E   \xi B} \leq f (s). \end{array}

which is equivalent to (iii). 

(ii) Using (i) along with some basic definitions and elementary estimates, we get

We consider a special case where the Palm measures can be computed explicitly. Note that if $\xi$ is a mixed Poisson process on $S$ directed by $\rho \lambda$ for a random variable $\rho \geq 0$ , then 

$$
P \{\xi B = 0 \} = \varphi (\lambda B), \quad B \in \mathcal {S},
$$

where $\varphi ( t ) = E e ^ { - t \rho }$ denotes the Laplace transform of $\rho .$ . When $0 < \lambda S < \infty$ , the same formula holds for a mixed binomial process $\xi$ based on the probability measure $\hat { \lambda } = \lambda / \lambda S$ and a $Z _ { + }$ -valued random variable $\kappa ,$ provided we choose 

$$
\varphi (t) = E (1 - t / \lambda S) ^ {\kappa}, \quad 0 \leq t \leq \lambda S.
$$

In either case, $\xi$ has Laplace functional 

$$
E e ^ {- \xi f} = \varphi \Bigl \{\lambda (1 - e ^ {- f}) \Bigr \}, \quad f \in \mathcal {S} _ {+},\tag{6}
$$

and so $\mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ is uniquely determined by the pair $( \lambda , \varphi )$ , which justifies that we write $M ( \lambda , \varphi )$ for the distribution of the point process $\xi$ in (6). For convenience, we allow the underlying probability measure $P$ to be σ-finite, so that $M ( \lambda , - \varphi ^ { \prime } )$ makes sense as the pseudo-distribution of a point process on $S .$ 

Theorem 31.10 (mixed Poisson and binomial processes) Let $\xi$ be a mixed Poisson or binomial process on $S$ with distribution $M ( \lambda , \varphi )$ , where $\lambda$ is $\sigma \mathrm { - }$ finite. Choosing $\lambda$ as supporting measure for $\xi _ { i }$ , we have 

$$
\text {(i)} \quad \mathcal {L} \left(\xi - \delta_ {s} \| \xi\right) _ {s} = M (\lambda , - \varphi^ {\prime}), s \in S a. e. \lambda ,
$$

(ii) $\mathcal { L } ( \xi ) \equiv \mathcal { L } \Big ( \xi - \delta _ { s } \Big \Vert \xi \Big ) _ { s } \ \Leftrightarrow \ \xi \ i s \ P o i s s o n \ ( \lambda )$ 

Proof: (i) First let $E \xi$ be σ-finite. For any $f \in S _ { + }$ and $B \in S$ with $\lambda f < \infty$ and $\lambda B < \infty$ , we have by (6) 

$$
E e ^ {- \xi f - t \xi B} = \varphi \Bigl \{\lambda \Bigl (1 - e ^ {- f - t 1 _ {B}} \Bigr) \Bigr \}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Taking right derivatives at $t = 0$ , we get by dominated convergence on each side

E \left(\xi B e ^ {- \xi f}\right) = - \varphi^ {\prime} \left\{\lambda \left(1 - e ^ {- f}\right) \right\} \lambda \left(1 _ {B} e ^ {- f}\right).
$$

Hence, by disintegration,

\int_ {B} \lambda (d s)   E \Big (e ^ {- \xi f} \left\| \xi\right) _ {s} = - \varphi^ {\prime} \Big \{\lambda (1 - e ^ {- f}) \Big \} \int_ {B} e ^ {- f (s)}   \lambda (d s).
$$

Since B was arbitrary, we obtain 

$$
E \Big (e ^ {- \xi f} \| \xi \Big) _ {s} = - \varphi^ {\prime} \Big \{\lambda (1 - e ^ {- f}) \Big \} e ^ {- f (s)}, \quad s \in S \text { a.e. } \lambda ,
$$

which implies 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \Big (e ^ {- (\xi - \delta_ {s}) f} \Big \| \xi \Big) _ {s} = E \Big (e ^ {- \xi f} \Big \| \xi \Big) _ {s} e ^ {f (s)} \\ = - \varphi^ {\prime} \Big \{\lambda (1 - e ^ {- f}) \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Equation (i) now follows by (6). For general $E \xi ,$ we may take $f \geq \varepsilon 1 _ { B }$ for fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ to justify the diferentiation. The resulting formulas extend by monotone convergence to arbitrary $f \geq 0$ 

(ii) The equation $\varphi = - \varphi ^ { \prime }$ with initial condition $\varphi ( 0 ) = 1$ has the unique solution $\varphi ( t ) = e ^ { - t }$ ✷

Noting that $\varphi ( 0 ) = 1$ and $\varphi ( 1 ) = E e ^ { - \xi f }$ , we obtain

It is often helpful to calculate the Palm distributions via a preliminary conditioning, similar to the approach in Theorem 8.15. Then consider a random measure $\xi$ on $S$ and some random elements $\eta$ in $T$ and $\zeta$ in $U _ { i }$ , where S, T, U are Borel and the Campbell measures $C _ { \xi , \eta }$ and $C _ { \xi , \zeta }$ are σ-finite. Regarding $\xi$ as a random element in the Borel space $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ and fixing a supporting measure $\rho$ of $\xi ,$ , we may introduce the Palm measures and conditional distributions 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {L} (\eta , \zeta \parallel \xi) _ {s} = \mu (s, \cdot), \\ \mathcal {L} (\xi , \zeta \mid \eta) _ {t} = \mu^ {\prime} (t, \cdot), \end{array}
$$

in terms of some kernels $\mu \colon S  T \times U$ and $\mu ^ { \prime } \colon T \to \mathcal { M } _ { S } \times U$ . For fixed s, t, we may next form the Palm and conditional measures 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu_ {s} \Big (\tilde {\zeta} \in \cdot \Big | \tilde {\eta} \Big) = \nu_ {s} (\tilde {\eta}, \cdot), \\ \mu_ {t} ^ {\prime} \Big (\tilde {\zeta} \in \cdot \Big \| \tilde {\xi} \Big) _ {s} = \nu_ {t} ^ {\prime} (s, \cdot), \end{array}
$$

where the former conditioning makes sense, since the measures $\mu _ { s }$ are a.e. $\sigma -$ finite. By Corollary 3.6, we can choose $\nu , \nu ^ { \prime }$ to be product-measurable, hence as kernels on $S \times T$ , in which case we may write suggestively 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P (\cdot | \eta \| \xi) _ {s, t} = \Big \{P (\cdot \| \xi) _ {s} \Big \} (\cdot | \eta) _ {t}, \\ P (\cdot \| \xi | \eta) _ {t, s} = \Big \{P (\cdot | \eta) _ {t} \Big \} (\cdot \| \xi) _ {s}. \end{array}
$$

Finally, we may take $t = \eta$ and put ${ \mathcal { F } } = \sigma ( \eta )$ and $\mathcal { H } = \sigma ( \zeta )$ , to form on $S$ the product-measurable, measure-valued processes 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P _ {\mathcal {F}} (\cdot \| \xi) _ {s} = P (\cdot \| \xi | \eta) _ {s, \eta}, \\ \Bigl \{P (\cdot \| \xi) _ {s} \Bigr \} _ {\mathcal {F}} = \bigl \{P (\cdot | \eta \| \xi) _ {\eta , s}. \end{array}
$$

Using this notation, we may state the iteration properties in the following suggestive form. In particular, part (iii) enables us to calculate the Palm kernel via a preliminary conditioning on $\eta ,$ which is especially useful in the contexts of randomizations and Cox processes. Say that a σ-field $\mathcal { F }$ on $\Omega$ is Borel generated, if ${ \mathcal { F } } = \sigma ( \beta )$ for some random element $\beta$ in a Borel space. 

Theorem 31.12 (iteration) Let $\xi$ be a random measure on a Borel space $S ,$ and let , be Borel-generated σ-fields in Ω, such that $C _ { \xi , \mathcal { F } }$ and $C _ { \xi , \mathcal { H } }$ are $\sigma { - } f i n i t e$ . Then for a fixed supporting measure $\nu \sim E \xi$ , we have on 

(i) $E _ { \mathcal { F } } \xi$ is a.s. σ-finite, 

(ii) $P _ { \mathcal { F } } ( \cdot \parallel \xi ) = \Big \{ P ( \cdot \parallel \xi ) \Big \} _ { \mathcal { F } } ~ a . e . ~ C _ { \xi , \mathcal { F } } ,$ 

(iii) $P ( \cdot \parallel \xi ) _ { s } = E \Big \{ P _ { \mathcal F } ( \cdot \parallel \xi ) _ { s } \Big \| \xi \Big \} _ { s } , s \in S \ a . e . \ E \xi .$ 

Proof: Let ${ \mathcal F } = \sigma ( \eta )$ and $\mathcal { H } = \sigma ( \zeta )$ for some random elements $\eta , \zeta$ in the Borel spaces T, U, and introduce the measures 

$$
\begin{array}{c c c} \mu_ {1} = \nu , & \mu_ {2} = \mathcal {L} (\eta), & \mu_ {3} = \mathcal {L} (\zeta), \\ \mu_ {1 2} = C _ {\xi , \eta}, & \mu_ {1 3} = C _ {\xi , \zeta}, & \mu_ {1 2 3} = C _ {\xi , \eta , \zeta}, \end{array}

which are all σ-finite. Since the support conditions of Theorem 3.7 are clearly fulfilled, the result yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \mu_ {3 | 2 | 1} \stackrel {{\simeq}} {{=}} \mu_ {3 | 1 | 2} \mathrm{a.e.} \mu_ {1 2}, \\ \mu_ {3 | 1} = \mu_ {2 | 1} \mu_ {3 | 1 | 2} \mathrm{a.e.} \mu_ {1}. \end{array}\tag{7}

Further note that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mu_ {1 2} = C _ {\xi , \eta} \\ \qquad \cong \mathcal {L} (\eta) \otimes E _ {\mathcal {F}} \xi \\ \qquad = \mu_ {2} \otimes E _ {\mathcal {F}} \xi , \end{array}

and so the uniqueness in Theorem 3.4 yields $\mu _ { 1 | 2 } = E _ { \mathcal { F } } \xi \mathrm { a . s }$ . In particular this implies (i), and the relations (7) are equivalent to (ii) and (iii). ✷ 

When looking for versions of the Palm measures with desired regularity properties, the following duality approach may be helpful. Then recall that, for any Borel spaces $S , T$ , a σ-finite measure $\rho$ on $S \times T$ admits the dual disintegrations 

$$
\rho = \nu \otimes \mu \stackrel {\sim} {=} \nu^ {\prime} \otimes \mu^ {\prime},
$$

for some σ-finite measures ν on $S$ and $\nu ^ { \prime }$ on $T ,$ , and some kernels $\mu \colon S  T$ and $\mu ^ { \prime } \colon T \to S$ . Here either disintegration may give useful information about the other one, as illustrated by the following simple case: 

Theorem 31.13 (Palm–density duality) Consider a random measure $\xi$ on $S$ and a random element η in $T _ { i }$ , where S, T are Borel, and fix a supporting measure ν of $\xi$ . Then 

(i) $E ( \xi | \eta )$ and $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi )$ exist simultaneously as σ-finite kernels between $S$ and $T _ { i }$ , 

(ii) for $E ( \xi | \eta )$ and $\mathcal { L } ( \eta | | \xi )$ as in (i), 

$$
E (\xi \mid \eta) \ll \nu a. s. \Leftrightarrow \mathcal {L} (\eta \| \xi) _ {s} \ll \mathcal {L} (\eta) a. e. \nu ,
$$

in which case both kernels have product-measurable a.e. densities, 

(iii) for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $S \times T$ , 

$$
E (\xi \mid \eta) = f (\cdot , \eta) \cdot \nu a. s. \Leftrightarrow \mathcal {L} (\eta \| \xi) _ {s} = f (s, \cdot) \cdot \mathcal {L} (\eta) a. e. \nu .
$$

Proof: (i) If $E \xi$ is σ-finite, then for any $B \in S$ and $C \in \mathcal { T }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \Big (\xi B; \eta \in C \Big) = E \Big \{E (\xi B | \eta); \eta \in C \Big \} \\ & \qquad = \int_ {C} P \{\eta \in d t \} E (\xi B | \eta) _ {t}, \end{array}
$$

which extends immediately to the dual disintegration 

$$
C _ {\xi , \eta} \cong \mathcal {L} (\eta) \otimes E (\xi | \eta).\tag{8}
$$

In general, $\xi$ is a countable sum of bounded random measures, and we may use Fubini’s theorem to extend (8) to the general case, for a suitable version of $E ( \xi | \eta )$ . In particular, the latter kernel has a σ-finite version if $C _ { \xi , \eta }$ is σ-finite. Since this condition is also equivalent to the existence of a σ-finite Palm kernel, the assertion follows. 

(iii) Assuming $E ( \xi | \eta ) = f ( \cdot , \eta ) \cdot \nu \mathrm { ~ a . s }$ ., we get for any $B \in S$ and $C \in \mathcal { T }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \Big (\xi B; \eta \in C \Big) = E \Big \{E (\xi B | \eta); \eta \in C \Big \} \\ & \qquad = E \int_ {B} f (s, \eta)   \nu (d s)   1 _ {C} (\eta) \\ & \qquad = \int_ {B} \nu (d s)   E \Big \{f (s, \eta); \eta \in C \Big \} \\ & \qquad = \int_ {B} \nu (d s) \int_ {C} P \{\eta \in d t \}   f (s, t), \end{array}
$$

which implies $\mathcal { L } ( \eta \| \xi ) _ { s } = f ( s , \cdot ) \cdot \mathcal { L } ( \eta ) \ \mathrm { a . e . } \ \nu$ . Conversely, the latter relation yields 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \Big (\xi B; \eta \in C \Big) = \int_ {B} \nu (d s) P \Big (\eta \in C \left\| \xi\right) _ {s} \\ & \qquad = \int_ {B} \nu (d s) \int_ {C} P \{\eta \in d t \} f (s, t) \\ & \qquad = \int_ {B} \nu (d s) E \Big \{f (s, \eta); \eta \in C \Big \} \\ & \qquad = E \int_ {B} f (s, \eta) \nu (d s) 1 _ {C} (\eta), \end{array}
$$

which shows that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E (\xi B \mid \eta) = \int_ {B} f (s, \eta)   \nu (d s) \\ = \Big \{f (\cdot , \eta) \cdot \nu \Big \} B \text {a.s.}, \end{array}
$$

and therefore $E ( \xi | \eta ) = f ( \cdot , \eta ) \cdot \nu \mathrm { ~ a . s }$ 

(ii) Since S, T are Borel, Theorem 9.27 yields a product-measurable density in each case. The assertion now follows from (iii). ✷ 

Higher order Palm measures are defined in the obvious way as univariate Palm measures with respect to the product random measures $\xi ^ { n } = \xi ^ { \otimes n }$ on $S ^ { n }$ We are especially interested in the Palm distributions of $\xi$ itself with respect to $\xi ^ { n }$ , here written as $\mathcal { L } ( \xi \parallel \xi ^ { n } )$ . When $\xi$ is a simple point process with σ-finite moment measures $E \xi ^ { n }$ , we note that 

$$
P \Big (\prod_ {i} \xi \{s _ {i} \} = 1 \left\| \xi^ {(n)}\right) _ {s} = 1, s \in S ^ {(n)} \text {a.e.} E \xi^ {n},
$$

where $S ^ { ( n ) }$ denotes the non-diagonal part of $S ^ { n }$ . This suggests that we consider instead the reduced Palm measures 

$$
\mathcal {L} \Big (\xi^ {\prime} \left\| \xi^ {(n)}\right) _ {s} \equiv \mathcal {L} \Big (\xi - \sum_ {i} \delta_ {s _ {i}} \Big \| \xi^ {(n)} \Big) _ {s}, \quad s \in S ^ {(n)},
$$

formed by disintegration of the n -th order reduced Campbell measures 

$$
C _ {\xi} ^ {(n)} f = E \int \xi^ {(n)} (d s)   f \Big (s;   \xi - \sum_ {i} \delta_ {s _ {i}} \Big), \quad f \geq 0 \text { on } S ^ {(n)} \times \mathcal {N} _ {S}.
$$

Since the latter are symmetric under permutation of coordinates in $S ^ { ( n ) }$ , we may regard the reduced Palm measures $P ( \xi ^ { \prime } \parallel \xi ^ { ( n ) } )$ as functions of the associated point measures $\textstyle \sum _ { i } \delta _ { s _ { i } }$ . By Lemma 2.20 they can then be obtained, simultaneously for all $n \in \mathsf { N }$ , by disintegration of the compound Campbell measure 

$$
\begin{array}{c} C _ {\xi} f = \sum_ {n \geq 0} C _ {\xi} ^ {(n)} f / n! \\ = E \sum_ {\mu \leq \xi} f (\mu , \xi - \mu), \end{array}
$$

where $C _ { \xi } ^ { ( 0 ) } = \mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ for consistency, and the last summation extends over all bounded point measures $\mu \le \xi$ . More precisely, assuming $\textstyle \xi = \sum _ { i \in J } \delta _ { \sigma _ { i } }$ for a countable index set $J ,$ , we $\mathrm { s u m ^ { 4 } }$ over all measures $\textstyle \mu = \sum _ { i \in I } \delta _ { \sigma _ { i } }$ with finite $I \subset J$ 

We now define the Gibbs kernel of $\xi$ as the maximal random measure $\Gamma =$ $G ( \xi )$ on $\hat { \mathcal { N } } _ { S }$ satisfying 

$$
E \int \Gamma (d \mu) f (\mu , \xi) \leq E \sum_ {\mu \leq \xi} f (\mu , \xi - \mu),\tag{9}
$$

for all measurable functions $f \geq 0$ on $\hat { \mathcal { N } } _ { S } \times \mathcal { N } _ { S }$ . Such a partial disintegration kernel exists uniquely by Corollary 3.5. 

Lemma 31.14 (boundedness and support) Let $\xi$ be a point process on $S$ with Gibbs kernel Γ. Then a.s. 

(i) $\Gamma \{ \mu S = \infty \} = 0 ,$ 

(ii) $\Gamma \big \{ \mu B = \mu S = n \big \} < \infty , \quad B \in \hat { S } , n \in \mathsf { Z } _ { + } ,$ 

(iii) $\int \mu ( \operatorname { s u p p } \xi ) \Gamma ( d \mu ) = 0$ when $\xi$ is simple. 

Proof, (i)–(ii): For any $B \in \hat { S }$ and m, $n \in { \mathsf { Z } } _ { + }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E \Big (\Gamma \Big \{\mu B = \mu S = n \Big \};   \xi B = m \Big) \\ \qquad \leq C \Big (\Big \{\nu B = m \Big \} \times \Big \{\mu B = \mu S = n \Big \} \Big) \\ \qquad = E   1 \Big \{\xi B = m + n \Big \} \sum_ {\mu \leq \xi} 1 \Big \{\mu B = \mu S = n \Big \} \\ \qquad = \binom {m + n} {n} P \Big \{\xi B = m + n \Big \} <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

and so $\Gamma \{ \nu B = \nu S = n \} < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ . on $\{ \xi B = m \}$ 

(iii) Approximating supp m by means of dissections of $S$ and using dominated convergence, we see that the function $f ( m , \mu ) = \mu ( \operatorname { s u p p } m )$ is productmeasurable on $\mathcal { N } _ { S } \times \hat { \mathcal { N } } _ { S }$ . Hence, (9) yields for simple $\xi$ 

$$
E \int \mu (\operatorname{supp} \xi) \Gamma (d \mu) \leq C f = E \sum_ {\mu \leq \xi} \mu \left\{\operatorname{supp} (\xi - \mu) \right\} = 0,
$$

and so the inner integral on the left vanishes a.s. 

The definition of Γ is justified by some remarkable properties: 

Theorem 31.15 (Gibbs kernel) Let $\Gamma = G ( \xi )$ be the Gibbs kernel of a point process $\xi$ on $S$ . Then for any $B \in \hat { S }$ and measurable $f \geq 0$ on $\hat { \mathcal { N } } _ { S }$ ,

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \int \Gamma (d \mu)   f (\xi + \mu)   1 \Bigl \{\xi B = \mu B ^ {c} = 0 \Bigr \} \\ = E \Bigl \{f (\xi);   P (\xi B = 0   |   1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi) > 0 \Bigr \}, \end{array}\tag{ii}
$$

$$
\Gamma (\cdot ; \mu B ^ {c} = 0) = \frac {\mathcal {L} \left(1 _ {B} \xi \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi\right)}{P \left(\xi B = 0 \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi\right)} a. s. o n \{\xi B = 0 \},\tag{iii}
$$

$$
\mathcal {L} \left(1 _ {B} \xi \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi\right) = \Gamma (\cdot | \mu B ^ {c} = 0) a. s. o n \{\xi B = 0 \}.
$$

and so $C ( \cdot \times \{ \mu B ^ { c } = 0 \} ) \ll \mathcal { L } ( \xi )$ on $M _ { 0 }$ . Of special importance is the restriction of the Gibbs kernel to the class of single point masses $\delta _ { s }$ . Identifying $\delta _ { s }$ with the point $s \in S$ yields a random measure $\eta = g ( \xi , \cdot )$ on S, known as the Papangelou kernel of $\xi ,$ , which can also be defined directly as the maximal kernel satisfying the partial disintegration

Corollary 31.16 (Papangelou kernel) The Papangelou kernel $\eta$ of a point process $\xi$ on $S$ is a.s. locally finite, and for simple $\xi$ we have $\eta ( \mathrm { s u p p } \xi ) = 0$ a.s. Furthermore, for any $B \in \hat { S }$ , 

$$
1 _ {B} \eta = \frac {E \left(1 _ {B} \xi ; \xi B = 1 \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi\right)}{P \left(\xi B = 0 \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi\right)} a. s. o n \{\xi B = 0 \},\tag{ii}
$$

$$
\mathcal {L} \left(\tau_ {B} \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi , \xi B = 1\right) = \frac {1 _ {B} \eta}{\eta B} a. s. o n \{\xi B = 0, \eta B > 0 \}.
$$

$$
\eta B = \Gamma \left\{\mu B = \mu S = 1 \right\} <   \infty \text { a.s., } \quad B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}}.
$$

When $\xi$ is simple, part (ii) of the same lemma yields a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \eta (\operatorname{supp} \xi) = \Gamma \Bigl \{\mu (\operatorname{supp} \xi) = \mu S = 1 \Bigr \} \\ = \int \Gamma (d \mu)   \mu (\operatorname{supp} \xi) = 0. \end{array}
$$

(i) By Theorem 31.15 (ii), we get for any $C \subset B$ in $\hat { S }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \eta C = \Gamma \Big \{\mu C = \mu S = 1 \Big \} \\ = \frac {P \Big (\xi C = \xi B = 1   \big |   1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi \Big)}{P \Big (\xi B = 0   \big |   1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi \Big)} \text { a.s. on } \{\xi B = 0 \}. \end{array}
$$

(ii) By (i), we have 

$$
\eta B = \frac {P (\xi B = 1 \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi)}{P (\xi B = 0 \mid 1 _ {B ^ {c}} \xi)} \text { a.s. on } \{\xi B = 0 \}.
$$

When this is positive, the assertion follows by division. 

The theory simplifies under the classical regularity condition

Lemma 31.17 (regularity) For a simple point process $\xi$ on $S$ satisfying (Σ), we have

and (Σ) yields $P A ^ { c } = 0$ 

To illustrate the usefulness of the Papangelou kernel $\eta ,$ we show how invariance of $\eta$ may imply that the underlying point process $\xi$ is Cox. 

Theorem 31.18 (invariance and Cox property, Papangelou) Let $\xi$ be a $T \cdot$ marked point process on R satisfying (Σ), let $\nu$ be a random measure on $T$ and define $\eta = \lambda \otimes \nu$ . Then these conditions are equivalent:

When $\xi$ is a.s. bounded, the compound Campbell measure becomes symmetric in its two components, and the Palm and Gibbs kernels agree. ## X. SDEs, Difusions, and Potential Theory

Stochastic diferential equations (SDEs) form a central topic of modern probability theory with a wealth of applications. In the autonomous case, the solutions provide probabilistic descriptions of continuous, strong Markov processes, known as difusions. In particular, we explore the relations between weak and strong solutions, and characterize the solutions in terms of a martingale problem. In the one-dimensional case, difusions may be described in terms of a scale function and a speed measure. Potential theoretic tools are used throughout Markov process theory, and some classical problems in the area have beautiful solutions in terms of Brownian motion. Our final chapter on stochastic diferential geometry deals primarily with martingales and semimartingales in a general diferentiable manifold. For beginners we recommend a careful study of Chapter 32 and selected parts of Chapter 33, whereas the remaining material is more advanced and might be postponed. 

32. Stochastic equations and martingale problems. Using a Picard iteration, we may construct pathwise solutions to suitable SDEs, combining into a stochastic flow on the underlying space. Next, we examine the relationship between weak solutions and the associated martingale problems, and explore the connections between weak and strong existence and uniqueness. 

33. One-dimensional SDEs and difusions. For a one-dimensional SDE without a drift term, we give precise conditions for existence and uniqueness. We proceed with a detailed study of one-dimensional difusions, leading to a complete description in terms of a scale function and a speed measure. We further examine the recurrence and ergodic properties of difusions on a natural scale, depending on the speed measure and nature of the endpoints. 

34. PDE connections and potential theory. Here we explore some connections between Brownian motion and classical potential theory, including solutions to the three classical problems of electrostatics. Next, we explore the relationship between alternating capacities and random closed sets, as well as between excessive functions and super-martingales, leading to a probabilistic version of the classical Riesz decomposition. 

35. Stochastic diferential geometry. Here we consider semi-martingales and their covariation processes in a general diferential manifold S, define martingales in terms of a connection, and explore criteria involving afine and convex functions. We further introduce the local characteristics of a semimartingale in S, and justify their definitions by some natural embedding and projection properties. Finally, we specialize to the difusion case, and characterize Brownian motion and related processes in a Riemannian manifold. 

Chapter 32 

# Stochastic Equations and Martingale Problems

Progressive functions, drift and difusion rates, Langevin equation, linear equations, weak, strong, and functional solutions, stochastic flows, Picard iteration, explosion, uniqueness, path-wise and in law, martingale problems, weak existence and continuity, measurability and mixtures, strong Markov and Feller properties, transformation of drift, scaling, transfer of solutions 

Just as ordinary diferential equations (ODEs) describe the evolution of suitably smooth dynamical systems, so the stochastic diferential equations (SDEs) model the evolution of the random counterparts, the difusion processes. The corresponding theories are in many ways analogous, except that the stochastic version involves an additional noise term, given by an Itˆo-type stochastic integral with respect to a Brownian motion. This leads to a close connection between the present SDE theory and the stochastic calculus developed in Chapters 18–19, which in turn depends in a crucial way on the martingale theory of Chapter 9. 

The study of SDEs and associated difusion processes leads far beyond the mentioned analogy with classical dynamical systems. In fact, the coeficients of such an equation determine a possibly time-dependent elliptic operator A, as in Theorem 17.24, which suggests the associated martingale problem of finding a process X, such that the processes $M ^ { f }$ in Lemma 17.21 become martingales. It turns out to be essentially equivalent for X to be a weak solution to the given SDE, as will be seen from the fundamental Theorem 32.7. 

The general theory of SDEs involves both weak and strong solutions. Here it is important to distinguish between the notions of strong and weak existence, and the associated notions of pathwise uniqueness and uniqueness in law. In this connection, we will establish the powerful result of Yamada and Watanabe, asserting that weak existence and pathwise uniqueness imply strong existence and uniqueness in law. Under the same conditions, we can in fact express the general solution in functional form as $X = F ( X _ { 0 } , B )$ a.s. 

The SDEs studied in this chapter are typically of the form 

$$
d X _ {t} ^ {i} = \sigma_ {j} ^ {i} (t, X) d B _ {t} ^ {j} + b ^ {i} (t, X) d t,\tag{1}
$$

which may also be written in integrated form as 

$$
X _ {t} ^ {i} = X _ {0} ^ {i} + \sum_ {j} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma_ {j} ^ {i} (s, X) d B _ {s} ^ {j} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} b ^ {i} (s, X) d s, \quad t \geq 0.\tag{2}
$$

Here $B = ( B ^ { 1 } , \ldots , B ^ { r } )$ is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { r }$ with respect to a filtration ${ \mathcal { F } } ,$ and the solution $X = ( X ^ { 1 } , \ldots , X ^ { d } )$ is a continuous -semi-martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Furthermore, the coeficients $\sigma$ and b are progressive<sup>1</sup> functions of suitable dimension, defined on the canonical path space $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ , equipped with the induced filtration $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \sigma \{ x _ { s } ; s \le t \} , t \ge 0$ . For convenience, we shall often refer to (1) as equation $( \sigma , b )$ 

For the integrals in (2) to exist, in the sense of Itˆo and Lebesgue integration, $X$ must fulfill the integrability conditions 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {t} \left\{\left| a ^ {i j} (s, X) \right| + \left| b ^ {i} (s, X) \right| \right\} d s <   \infty \mathrm{a.s.}, t \geq 0,\tag{3}
$$

where $a ^ { i j } = \sigma _ { k } ^ { i } \sigma _ { k } ^ { j }$ or $a = \sigma \sigma ^ { \prime }$ , and the bars denote any norms in the spaces of d d -matrices and d -vectors, respectively. For the existence and adaptedness of the right-hand side, we also need the integrands in (2) be progressive, which is ensured by the following result. 

Lemma 32.1 (progressive functions) Let f be a progressive function on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } \times$ $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } \ f o r$ the induced filtration , and let X be a continuous, -adapted process in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Then the process $Y _ { t } = f ( t , X )$ is -progressive. 

Proof: Fix any $t \geq 0$ . Since X is adapted, we note that $\pi _ { s } ( X ) = X _ { s }$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { t } -$ measurable for every $s \leq t$ , where $\pi _ { s } ( x ) = x _ { s }$ on $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ . Since $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \sigma \{ \pi _ { s } ; s \le$ $t \}$ , Lemma 1.4 shows that X is $\mathcal { F } _ { t } / \mathcal { G } _ { t }$ -measurable. Hence, by Lemma 1.9, the mapping $\varphi ( s , \omega ) = \{ s , X ( \omega ) \}$ is $( B _ { t } \otimes \mathcal { F } _ { t } ) / ( B _ { t } \otimes \mathcal { G } _ { t } )$ -measurable from $[ 0 , t ] \times \Omega$ to $[ 0 , t ] \times C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ , where $\boldsymbol { B } _ { t } = \boldsymbol { B } [ 0 , t ]$ . Also note that f is $( B _ { t } \otimes \mathcal { G } _ { t } )$ -measurable on $[ 0 , t ] \times C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } }$ since f is progressive. Then Lemma 1.7 shows that $Y = f \circ \varphi$ is $( B _ { t } \otimes \mathcal { F } _ { t } ) / \bar { B }$ -measurable on $[ 0 , t ] \times \Omega$ ✷ 

Equation (2) exhibits the solution process X as a semi-martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with drift components $b ^ { i } ( X ) \cdot \lambda$ and covariation processes $[ X ^ { i } , X ^ { j } ] = a ^ { i j } ( X ) \cdot \lambda .$ where $a ^ { i j } ( x ) = a ^ { i j } ( \cdot , x )$ and $b ^ { i } ( x ) = b ^ { i } ( \cdot , x )$ . The densities $a ( t , X )$ and $b ( t , X )$ may be regarded as local characteristics of X at time t. Of special interest is the difusion case, where σ and b have the form 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sigma (t, x) = \sigma (x _ {t}), \\ b (t, x) = b (x _ {t}), \qquad t \geq 0, x \in C _ {\mathsf {R} _ {+}, \mathsf {R} ^ {d}}, \end{array}
$$

for some measurable functions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Then the local characteristics at time t depend only on the current position $X _ { t }$ of the process, and the progressivity holds automatically. 

We will distinguish between strong and weak solutions to an SDE $( \sigma , b )$ For the former, we regard the filtered probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ as given, along with an ${ \mathcal { F } } .$ -Brownian motion B and an $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ -measurable random vector $\xi .$ A strong solution is then defined as an adapted process X with $X _ { 0 } = \xi$ a.s. 

satisfying (1). For a weak solution, only the initial distribution $\mu$ is given, and the solution consists of a triple $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ , along with an -Brownian motion B and an adapted process X with ${ \mathcal { L } } ( X _ { 0 } ) = \mu$ satisfying (1). 

This leads to diferent notions of existence and uniqueness, for a given equation $( \sigma , b )$ . We say that weak existence holds for the initial distribution $\mu _ { : }$ , if there exists a corresponding weak solution $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P , B , X )$ . By contrast, strong existence for the given $\mu$ means that, for any basic triple $( \mathcal { F } , B , \xi )$ with ${ \mathcal { L } } ( \xi ) = \mu$ , there exists a strong solution X with $X _ { 0 } = \xi$ a.s. Next, we say that uniqueness in law holds for the initial distribution $\mu ,$ if all weak solutions X with ${ \mathcal { L } } ( X _ { 0 } ) = \mu$ have the same distribution. Finally, pathwise uniqueness for a given distribution $\mu$ means that, whenever X and $Y$ are two solutions with $X _ { 0 } = Y _ { 0 } = \xi \mathrm { a . s }$ . and ${ \mathcal { L } } ( \xi ) = \mu ,$ , defined on a common filtered probability space with a given Brownian motion $B .$ , we have $X = Y$ a.s. 

One of the simplest SDEs is the Langevin equation 

$$
d X _ {t} = d B _ {t} - X _ {t} d t,\tag{4}
$$

of importance for both theory and applications. Integrating by parts gives 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & d \Big (e ^ {t} X _ {t} \Big) = e ^ {t} d X _ {t} + e ^ {t} X _ {t} d t \\ & \qquad = e ^ {t} d B _ {t}, \end{array}
$$

which yields the explicit solution 

$$
X _ {t} = e ^ {- t} X _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} e ^ {- (t - s)} d B _ {s}, \quad t \geq 0,\tag{5}
$$

recognized as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Conversely, the latter process is easily seen to satisfy (4). We further note that $\theta _ { t } X \stackrel { d } { \to } Y$ as $t \to \infty$ , where Y denotes the stationary version of the process, encountered in Chapters 14 and 21. We can also get a stationary version<sup>2</sup> directly from (5) by choosing $X _ { 0 }$ to be $N ( 0 , { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } )$ and independent of $B .$ 

We turn to a more general class of equations that can be solved explicitly. A further extension appears in Theorem 20.8. 

Proposition 32.2 (linear equations) Let U, V be continuous semi-martingales, and put $\begin{array} { r } { Z = \exp \bigl ( V - V _ { 0 } - \frac { 1 } { 2 } [ V ] \bigr ) } \end{array}$ . Then the equation $d X = d U + X d V$ has the unique solution 

$$
X = Z \left\{X _ {0} + Z ^ {- 1} \cdot (U - [ U, V ]) \right\}.\tag{6}
$$

Proof: Define $Y = X / Z$ . Integrating by parts and noting that $d Z = Z d V$ 2 we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} d U & = d X - X d V \\ & = Y d Z + Z d Y + d [ Y, Z ] - X d V \\ & = Z d Y + d [ Y, Z ]. \end{array}\tag{7}
$$

In particular, 

$$
[ U, V ] = Z \cdot [ Y, V ] = [ Y, Z ].
$$

Substituting this into (7) yields $Z d Y = d U - d \lbrack U , V \rbrack$ , which implies $d Y =$ $Z ^ { - 1 } d ( U - [ U , V ] )$ . Now (6) follows as we integrate from 0 to t and note that $Y _ { 0 } = X _ { 0 }$ . Since all steps are reversible, the same argument shows that (6) is indeed a solution. ✷ 

Though most SDEs can not be solved explicitly, we may still derive some general conditions for strong existence, pathwise uniqueness, and continuous dependence on initial conditions, using the classical method of Picard iteration, originally devised for ordinary diferential equations. 

Theorem 32.3 (strong solutions and stochastic flows, Itˆo) Let σ, b be bounded, progressive functions satisfying a Lipschitz condition<sup>3</sup> 

$$
\left\{\sigma (w) - \sigma (w ^ {\prime}) \right\} _ {t} ^ {*} + \left\{b (w) - b (w ^ {\prime}) \right\} _ {t} ^ {*} \leq (w - w ^ {\prime}) _ {t} ^ {*}, \quad t \geq 0,\tag{8}
$$

and consider a Brownian motion B in $\mathsf { R } ^ { r }$ w.r.t. a complete filtration $\mathcal { F }$ . Then there exists a jointly continuous process $X = \left( X _ { t } ^ { x } \right)$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } \times \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , such that for any -measurable random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , equation $( \sigma , b )$ has the a.s. unique solution $X ^ { \xi }$ starting at $\xi$ . 

For one-dimensional difusion equations, a stronger result is established in Theorem 33.3. The solution process $X \ = \ ( X _ { t } ^ { x } )$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } \times \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is called the stochastic flow generated by B. Our proof is based on two lemmas, beginning with an elementary classical estimate. 

Lemma 32.4 (Gronwall) Let f be a continuous function on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , such that 

$$
f (t) \leq a + b \int_ {0} ^ {t} f (s) d s, \quad t \geq 0,\tag{9}
$$

for some constants $a , b \geq 0$ . Then 

$$
f (t) \leq a e ^ {b t}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Proof: We may write (9) as 

$$
\frac {d}{d t} \Bigl \{e ^ {- b t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f (s) d s \Bigr \} \leq a e ^ {- b t}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Now integrate over $[ 0 , t ]$ and combine with (9). 

To state the next result, let $S _ { X }$ denote the process given by the right-hand side of (2). 

Lemma 32.5 (L<sup>p</sup>-contraction) Let $\sigma , b$ be bounded, progressive functions satisfying (8). Then for any $p \geq 2$ , there exists a non-decreasing function $c \geq 0$ on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ such that, for any continuous, adapted processes $X , Y$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

$$
E \left(S _ {X} - S _ {Y}\right) _ {t} ^ {* p} \leq 2 E \left| X _ {0} - Y _ {0} \right| ^ {p} + c _ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} E (X - Y) _ {s} ^ {* p} d s, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Proof: By Theorem 18.7, condition (8), and Jensen’s inequality, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \Big (S _ {X} - S _ {Y} \Big) _ {t} ^ {* p} - 2 E \Big | X _ {0} - Y _ {0} \Big | ^ {p} \\ & \lesssim E \Big \{\big (\sigma_ {X} - \sigma_ {Y} \big) \cdot B \Big \} _ {t} ^ {* p} + E \Big \{(b _ {X} - b _ {Y}) \cdot \lambda \Big \} _ {t} ^ {* p} \\ & \lesssim E \Big (\big | \sigma_ {X} - \sigma_ {Y} \big | ^ {2} \cdot \lambda \Big) _ {t} ^ {p / 2} + E \Big (\big | b _ {X} - b _ {Y} \big | \cdot \lambda \Big) _ {t} ^ {p} \\ & \lesssim E \left| \int_ {0} ^ {t} (X - Y) _ {s} ^ {* 2} d s \right| ^ {p / 2} + E \left| \int_ {0} ^ {t} (X - Y) _ {s} ^ {*} d s \right| ^ {p} \\ & \leq \left(t ^ {p / 2 - 1} + t ^ {p - 1}\right) \int_ {0} ^ {t} E (X - Y) _ {s} ^ {* p} d s. \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 32.3: To prove the existence, fix any $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ -measurable random vector $\xi$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , put $X _ { t } ^ { 0 } \equiv \xi$ , and define recursively $X ^ { n } = S _ { X ^ { n - 1 } }$ for $n \geq 1$ . Since $\sigma , b$ are bounded, we have $E ( X ^ { 1 } - X ^ { 0 } ) _ { t } ^ { * 2 } < \infty$ , and Lemma 32.5 yields 

$$
E \left(X ^ {n + 1} - X ^ {n}\right) _ {t} ^ {* 2} \leq c _ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} E \left(X ^ {n} - X ^ {n - 1}\right) _ {s} ^ {* 2} d s, \quad t \geq 0, n \geq 1.
$$

Hence, by induction, 

$$
E \left(X ^ {n + 1} - X ^ {n}\right) _ {t} ^ {* 2} \leq \frac {c _ {t} ^ {n} t ^ {n}}{n !} E \left(X ^ {1} - \xi\right) _ {t} ^ {* 2} <   \infty , \quad t, n \geq 0.
$$

For any $k \in \mathsf { N }$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Big \| \sup _ {n \geq k} \Big (X ^ {n} - X ^ {k} \Big) _ {t} ^ {*} \Big \| _ {2} \leq \sum_ {n \geq k} \Big \| \Big (X ^ {n + 1} - X ^ {n} \Big) _ {t} ^ {*} \Big \| _ {2} \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \Big \| \Big (X ^ {1} - \xi \Big) _ {t} ^ {*} \Big \| _ {2} \sum_ {n \geq k} \Big (c _ {t} ^ {n}   t ^ {n} / n! \Big) ^ {1 / 2} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

Thus, Lemma 5.6 yields a continuous, adapted process X with $X _ { 0 } = \xi$ , such that $( X ^ { n } - X ) _ { t } ^ { * } \to 0$ a.s. and in $L ^ { 2 }$ for each $t \geq 0$ . To see that X solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ , we conclude from Lemma 32.5 that 

$$
E \left(X ^ {n} - S _ {X}\right) _ {t} ^ {* 2} \leq c _ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} E \left(X ^ {n - 1} - X\right) _ {s} ^ {* 2} d s, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

As $n \to \infty$ , we get $E ( X - S _ { X } ) _ { t } ^ { * 2 } = 0$ for all t, which implies $X = S _ { X }$ a.s. 

Now consider two solutions $X , Y$ with $| X _ { 0 } - Y _ { 0 } | \leq \varepsilon \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . By Lemma 32.5, we get for any $p \geq 2$ 

$$
E (X - Y) _ {t} ^ {* p} \leq 2 \varepsilon^ {p} + c _ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} E (X - Y) _ {s} ^ {* p} d s, t \geq 0,
$$

and by Lemma 32.4 it follows that 

$$
E (X - Y) _ {t} ^ {* p} \leq 2 \varepsilon^ {p} e ^ {c _ {t} t}, \quad t \geq 0.\tag{10}
$$

If $X _ { 0 } = Y _ { 0 }$ a.s., we may take $\varepsilon = 0$ and conclude that $X = Y$ a.s., which proves the asserted uniqueness. Letting $X ^ { x }$ denote the solution X with $X _ { 0 } = x { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ ， we get by (10) 

$$
E \left| X ^ {x} - X ^ {y} \right| _ {t} ^ {* p} \leq 2 | x - y | ^ {p} e ^ {c _ {t} t}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Taking $p > d$  and applying Theorem 4.23 for each $T > 0$ with the metric $\rho _ { T } ( f , g ) = ( f - g ) _ { T } ^ { * }$ , we conclude that the process $( X _ { t } ^ { x } )$ has a jointly continuous version on $\mathsf { R } _ { + } \times \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

The construction shows that if $X , Y$ are solutions with $X _ { 0 } = \xi$ and $Y _ { 0 } = \eta$ a.s., then $X = Y$ a.s. on the set $\{ \xi = \eta \}$ . In particular, $X = X ^ { \xi }$ a.s. when $\xi$ takes only countably many values. In general, $\xi$ may be uniformly approximated by some random vectors $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , . . .$ . in $\mathsf { Q } ^ { d } .$ , and (10) yields $X _ { t } ^ { \xi _ { n } } \to X _ { t }$ in $L ^ { 2 }$ for all $t \geq 0$ . Since also $X _ { t } ^ { \xi _ { n } }  X _ { t } ^ { \xi }$ a.s. by the continuity of the flow, it follows that $X _ { t } = X _ { t } ^ { \xi } \ \mathrm { a . s }$ ✷ 

For many SDEs, the solutions may explode after a finite time. To deal with this possibility, we introduce as in Chapter 17 an extra absorbing sta $\mathrm { t e } ^ { 4 } \Delta$ at infinity, so that the path space becomes $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \overline { { \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } } }$ with $\overline { { \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } } = \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \cup \mathsf { \bar { \{ \Delta \} } }$ . Define $\zeta _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t ; | X _ { t } | \geq n \}$ for each $n ,$ put $\zeta = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } \zeta _ { n }$ , and let $X _ { t } = \Delta$ for $t \geq \zeta$ Given a Brownian motion B in $\mathsf { R } ^ { r }$ and an adapted process X in the extended path space, we say that $X$ or the pair $( X , B )$ solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ on the interval $[ 0 , \zeta )$ , if 

$$
X _ {t \wedge \zeta_ {n}} = X _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \zeta_ {n}} \sigma (s, X) d B _ {s} + \int_ {0} ^ {t \wedge \zeta_ {n}} b (s, X) d s, \quad t \geq 0, n \in \mathbb {N}.\tag{11}
$$

When $\zeta < \infty$ , we have $| X _ { \zeta _ { n } } | \to \infty$ , and X is said to explode at time $\zeta .$ 

Conditions for existence and uniqueness of possibly exploding solutions are obtainable from Theorem 32.3 by suitable localization. The following result can sometimes be used to exclude the possibility of explosion. 

Proposition 32.6 (explosion) For solutions to equation $( \sigma , b )$ , no explosion occurs a.s. when 2 (12) 

$$
\sigma (x) _ {t} ^ {*} + b (x) _ {t} ^ {*} \leq 1 + x _ {t} ^ {*}, \quad t \geq 0.\tag{12}
$$

Proof: By Proposition 18.15 we may assume that $X _ { 0 }$ is bounded. From (11) and (12), we get for suitable constants $c _ { t } < \infty$ 

$$
E X _ {t \wedge \zeta_ {n}} ^ {* 2} \leq 2 E | X _ {0} | ^ {2} + c _ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left(1 + E X _ {s \wedge \zeta_ {n}} ^ {* 2}\right) d s, \quad t \geq 0, n \in \mathbb {N},
$$

and so by Lemma 32.4 

$$
1 + E X _ {t \wedge \zeta_ {n}} ^ {* 2} \leq \left(1 + 2   E | X _ {0} | ^ {2}\right) \exp (c _ {t}   t) <   \infty , \quad t \geq 0, n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

As $n \to \infty$ we obtain $E X _ { t \wedge \zeta } ^ { * 2 } < \infty$ , which implies $\zeta > t { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ 

Our next aim is to characterize weak solutions to equation $( \sigma , b )$ by a martingale property, involving only the solution process X. Then define 

$$
M _ {t} ^ {f} = f (X _ {t}) - f (X _ {0}) - \int_ {0} ^ {t} A _ {s} f (X) d s, \quad t \geq 0, f \in \hat {C} ^ {\infty},\tag{13}
$$

where the operators $A _ { s }$ are given by 

$$
A _ {s} f (x) = \frac {1}{2} a ^ {i j} (s, x) f _ {i j} ^ {\prime \prime} (x _ {s}) + b ^ {i} (s, x) f _ {i} ^ {\prime} (x _ {s}), \quad s \geq 0, f \in \hat {C} ^ {\infty}.\tag{14}
$$

In the difusion case we may replace the integrand $A _ { s } f ( \boldsymbol { X } )$ in (13) by the expression $A f ( X _ { s } )$ , where A denotes the elliptic operator 

$$
A f (x) = \frac {1}{2} a ^ {i j} (x) f _ {i j} ^ {\prime \prime} (x) + b ^ {i} (x) f _ {i} ^ {\prime} (x), \quad f \in \hat {C} ^ {\infty}, x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.\tag{15}
$$

A continuous process X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , or its distribution $P ,$ is said to solve the local martingale problem for $( a , b )$ , if $M ^ { f }$ is a local martingale for every $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ For bounded $a ,$ b it is clearly equivalent that $M ^ { f }$ be a true martingale, and the original problem turns into a martingale problem. The (local) martingale problem for $( a , b )$ with initial distribution $\mu$ is said to be well posed if it has a unique solution $P _ { \mu }$ . For degenerate initial distributions $\delta _ { x }$ , we may write $P _ { x }$ instead of $P _ { \delta _ { x } }$ . We state the basic equivalence between weak solutions to an SDE and solutions to the associated local martingale problem. Here $\hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ denotes the class of probability measures on $S .$ 

Theorem 32.7 (weak solutions and martingale problems, Stroock & Varadhan) For progressive functions $\sigma ,$ b and distributions $P \in \hat { \mathcal { M } } ( C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } )$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) equation $( \sigma , b )$ has a weak solution with distribution $P _ { i }$ 

(ii) $P$ solves the local martingale problem for $( \sigma \sigma ^ { \prime } , b )$ 

Proof: Write $a = \sigma \sigma ^ { \prime } . \mathrm { ~ I f ~ } ( X , B )$ solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} [ X ^ {i}, X ^ {j} ] = \left[ \sigma_ {k} ^ {i} (X) \cdot B ^ {k},   \sigma_ {l} ^ {j} (X) \cdot B ^ {l} \right] \\ = \sigma_ {k} ^ {i} \sigma_ {l} ^ {j} (X) \cdot [ B ^ {k}, B ^ {l} ] \\ = a ^ {i j} (X) \cdot \lambda . \end{array}
$$

By Itˆo’s formula, we get for any $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d f (X _ {t}) = f _ {i} ^ {\prime} (X _ {t})   d X _ {t} ^ {i} + \frac {1}{2}   f _ {i j} ^ {\prime \prime} (X _ {t})   d [ X ^ {i}, X ^ {j} ] _ {t} \\ = f _ {i} ^ {\prime} (X _ {t})   \sigma_ {j} ^ {i} (t, X)   d B _ {t} ^ {j} + A _ {t} f (X)   d t. \end{array}
$$

Hence, $d M _ { t } ^ { f } = f _ { i } ^ { \prime } ( X _ { t } ) \sigma _ { i } ^ { i } ( t , X ) d B _ { t } ^ { j }$ , and so $M ^ { f }$ is a local martingale. 

Conversely, let X solve the local martingale problem for $( a , b )$ . When $f _ { n } ^ { i } \in$ $\hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ with $f _ { n } ^ { i } ( x ) ~ = ~ x ^ { i }$ for $| x | \le n$ , a localization argument shows that the processes 

$$
M _ {t} ^ {i} = X _ {t} ^ {i} - X _ {0} ^ {i} - \int_ {0} ^ {t} b ^ {i} (s, X) d s, \quad t \geq 0,\tag{16}
$$

are continuous local martingales. Similarly, choosing $f _ { n } ^ { i j } \in \hat { C } ^ { \infty }$ with $f _ { n } ^ { i j } ( x ) =$ $x ^ { i } x ^ { j }$ for $| x | \leq n$ , we may form the local martingales 

$$
M ^ {i j} = X ^ {i} X ^ {j} - X _ {0} ^ {i} X _ {0} ^ {j} - \left(X ^ {i} \beta^ {j} + X ^ {j} \beta^ {i} + \alpha^ {i j}\right) \cdot \lambda ,
$$

where $\alpha ^ { i j } = a ^ { i j } ( X )$ and $\beta ^ { i } = b ^ { i } ( X )$ . Integrating by parts and using (16), we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} M ^ {i j} = X ^ {i} \cdot X ^ {j} + X ^ {j} \cdot X ^ {i} + [ X ^ {i}, X ^ {j} ] - (X ^ {i} \beta^ {j} + X ^ {j} \beta^ {i} + \alpha^ {i j}) \cdot \lambda \\ = X ^ {i} \cdot M ^ {j} + X ^ {j} \cdot M ^ {i} + [ M ^ {i}, M ^ {j} ] - \alpha^ {i j} \cdot \lambda . \end{array}
$$

Here the last two terms on the right form a local martingale, and so by Proposition 18.2, t 

$$
[ M ^ {i}, M ^ {j} ] _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} a ^ {i j} (s, X) d s, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Hence, Theorem 19.13 yields a Brownian motion B with respect to a standard extension of the original filtration, such that 

$$
M _ {t} ^ {i} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma_ {k} ^ {i} (s, X) d B _ {s} ^ {k}, t \geq 0.
$$

Substituting this into (16) yields (2), which means that the pair $( X , B )$ solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ ✷ 

For subsequent needs, we note that the previous construction can be made measurable, in the following sense. 

Lemma 32.8 (functional representation) For any progressive functions σ, b, there exists a measurable map 

$$
F \colon \hat {\mathcal {M}} (C _ {\mathsf {R} _ {+}, \mathsf {R} ^ {d}}) \times C _ {\mathsf {R} _ {+}, \mathsf {R} ^ {d}} \times [ 0, 1 ] \to C _ {\mathsf {R} _ {+}, \mathsf {R} ^ {r}},
$$

such that when X solves the local martingale problem for $( \sigma \sigma ^ { \prime } , b )$ with distribution $P _ { i }$ , and ϑ X is $U ( 0 , 1 )$ , we have 

(i) $B = F ( P , X , \vartheta )$ is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { r }$

Proof: In the previous construction of $B ,$ , the only non-elementary step is the stochastic integration with respect to $( X , Y )$ in Theorem 19.13, where $Y$ is an independent Brownian motion and the integrand is a progressive function of $X$ , obtained by some elementary matrix algebra. Since the pair $( X , Y )$ is again a solution to a local martingale problem, Proposition 18.26 yields the desired functional representation. ✷ 

Combining the martingale formulation with a compactness argument, we may deduce some general existence and continuity properties. 

Theorem 32.9 (weak existence and continuity, Skorohod) Let σ, b be bounded, progressive functions, such that $\sigma ( t , \cdot )$ and $b ( t , \cdot )$ are continuous on $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ for every $t \geq 0$ . Then 

(i) the martingale problem for $( \sigma \sigma ^ { \prime } , b )$ has a solution $P _ { \mu }$ for every initial distribution $\mu _ { ; }$ 

(ii) when the $P _ { \mu }$ are unique, the mapping $\mu \mapsto P _ { \mu }$ is weakly continuous. 

Proof: (i) For any $\varepsilon > 0 , \ t \geq 0$ , and $x \in C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } }$ , define 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \sigma_ {\varepsilon} (t, x) = \sigma \{(t - \varepsilon) _ {+}, x \}, \\ b _ {\varepsilon} (t, x) = b \{(t - \varepsilon) _ {+}, x \}, \end{array}
$$

and let $a _ { \varepsilon } ~ = ~ \sigma _ { \varepsilon } \sigma _ { \varepsilon } ^ { \prime }$ . Since $\sigma , b$ are progressive, the processes $\sigma _ { \varepsilon } ( s , X )$ and $b _ { \varepsilon } ( s , X ) , \ s \ \leq \ t ,$ are measurable functions of $X$ on $[ 0 , ( t - \varepsilon ) _ { + } ]$ . Hence, a strong solution $X ^ { \varepsilon }$ to equation $\left( \sigma _ { \varepsilon } , b _ { \varepsilon } \right)$ may be constructed recursively on the intervals $[ ( n - 1 ) \varepsilon , n \varepsilon ] , n \in \mathsf { N }$ , starting from an arbitrary random vector $\xi \perp \perp B$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with distribution $\mu .$ . In particular, $X ^ { \varepsilon }$ solves the martingale problem for the pair $( a _ { \varepsilon } , b _ { \varepsilon } )$ 

Applying Theorem 18.7 to equation $( \sigma _ { \varepsilon } , b _ { \varepsilon } )$ and using the boundedness of $\sigma , b _ { \cdot }$ , we get for any $p > 0$ 

$$
E \sup _ {0 \leq r \leq h} \left| X _ {t + r} ^ {\varepsilon} - X _ {t} ^ {\varepsilon} \right| ^ {p} \leq h ^ {p / 2} + h ^ {p} \leq h ^ {p / 2}, \quad t, \varepsilon \geq 0, h \in [ 0, 1 ].
$$

Taking $p \ > \ 2 d ,$ , we see from Corollary 23.7 that the family $\{ X ^ { \varepsilon } \}$ is tight in $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ . By Theorem 23.2, we may then choose some $\varepsilon _ { n } \to 0$ , such that $X ^ { \varepsilon _ { n } } { \overset { d } { \to } } X$ for a suitable X. To see that X solves the martingale problem for $( a , b )$ , let $f \in { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ and $s < t$ be arbitrary, and consider any bounded, continuous function $g \colon C _ { [ 0 , s ] , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } \to \mathsf { R }$ . We need to show that 

$$
E \left\{f (X _ {t}) - f (X _ {s}) - \int_ {s} ^ {t} A _ {r} f (X) d r \right\} g (X) = 0.
$$

Then note that $X ^ { \varepsilon }$ satisfies the corresponding equation for the operators $A _ { r } ^ { \varepsilon } .$ constructed from the pair $( a _ { \varepsilon } , b _ { \varepsilon } )$ . Writing the two conditions as $E \varphi ( X ) = 0$ and $E \varphi _ { \varepsilon } ( X ^ { \varepsilon } ) ~ = ~ 0$ , respectively, it sufices by Theorem 5.27 to show that $\varphi _ { \varepsilon } ( x _ { \varepsilon } ) ~  ~ \varphi ( x )$ , whenever $x _ { \varepsilon } \to x$ in $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ . This follows easily from the continuity conditions imposed on $\sigma , b$ 

(ii) Assuming the solutions $P _ { \mu }$ to be unique, let $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } {  } \mu$ . Arguing as before, we see that $\left( P _ { \mu _ { n } } \right)$ is tight, and so by Theorem 23.2 it is also relatively compact. If $P _ { \mu _ { n } } \stackrel { w } {  } \dot { Q }$ along a sub-sequence, we see as before that Q solves the martingale problem for $( a , b )$ with initial distribution $\mu$ . Hence $Q = P _ { \mu } ,$ and the convergence extends to the original sequence. ✷ 

The well-posedness of the local martingale problem for $( a , b )$ may now be extended from degenerate to arbitrary initial distributions. This requires a basic measurability property, which will also be needed later. 

Theorem 32.10 (measurability and mixtures, Stroock $\mathcal { E A }$ Varadhan) Let a, b be progressive functions, such that for any $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ the local martingale problem $f o r \ ( a , b )$ with initial distribution $\delta _ { x }$ has a unique solution $P _ { x }$ . Then

Proof: By the proof of Theorem 32.7, it is enough to state the local martingale problem in terms of functions f belonging to some countable subclass ${ \mathcal { C } } \subset { \hat { C } } ^ { \infty }$ , consisting of suitably truncated versions of the coordinate functions $x ^ { i }$ and their products $x ^ { i } x ^ { j }$ . Now define $\mathcal { P } = \hat { \mathcal { M } } ( C _ { \mathsf { R } ^ { d } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } )$ and $\mathcal { P } _ { M } = \{ P _ { x } ; x \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \}$ , and write X for the canonical process in $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ .
