Then clearly $\mathcal { P } _ { M } = D \cap I \cap L$ 

(i) It sufices to show that $\mathcal { P } _ { M }$ is a measurable subset of $\mathcal { P }$ , since the desired measurability will then follow by Theorem A1.1 and Lemma 3.2. The measurability of $D$ is clear from Theorem 2.18. Even I is measurable, since the integrals on the left of (3) are measurable by Fubini’s theorem. Finally, $L \cap I$ is a measurable subset of $I ,$ since the defining condition is equivalent to countably many relations of the form $E \big ( M _ { t } ^ { f , n } - \tilde { M } _ { s } ^ { f , n } ; F \big ) = 0$ with $f \in { \mathcal { C } } ,$ $n \in \mathbb { N } , s < t$ in $\mathsf { Q } _ { + }$ , and $F \in \mathcal { F } _ { s }$ 

(ii) For any probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , the measure $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { \mu } = \int P _ { x } \mu ( d x ) } \end{array}$ has clearly initial distribution $\mu ,$ -<sub>and the previous argument shows that even</sub> $P _ { \mu }$ solves the local martingale problem for $( a , b )$ . To prove the uniqueness, let $P$ be any measure with the stated properties. Then $E \big ( M _ { t } ^ { f , n } - M _ { s } ^ { f , n } ; F \big | X _ { 0 } \big ) = 0$ a.s. for all $f , n , s < t$ , and $F$ as above, and so $\textstyle P ( \cdot | X _ { 0 } )$ a.s. solves the local martingale problem with initial distribution $\delta _ { X _ { 0 } }$ . Thus, $P ( \cdot | X _ { 0 } ) = P _ { X _ { 0 } } \ \mathrm { a . s . } ,$ and we get $\begin{array} { r } { P = E P _ { X _ { 0 } } = \int P _ { x } \mu ( d x ) = P _ { \mu } } \end{array}$ . This extends the well-posedness to -<sub>arbitrary initial distributions.</sub> ✷ 

We return to the problem of constructing a Feller difusion with generator A as in (15), solving a suitable SDE or the associated martingale problem. The following result may be regarded as a converse to Theorem 17.24. 

Theorem 32.11 (strong Markov and Feller properties, Stroock & Varadhan) Let a, b be measurable functions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , such that for any $x \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ the local martingale problem for $( a , b )$ with initial distribution $\delta _ { x }$ has a unique solution $P _ { x }$ . Then 

(i) the family $( P _ { x } )$ satisfies the strong Markov property, 

(ii) when a, b are bounded, continuous, $T _ { t } f ( x ) = E _ { x } f ( X _ { t } )$ defines a Feller semigroup on $C _ { 0 }$ , and the operator A in (15) extends uniquely to the associated generator. 

Proof: (i) By Theorem 32.10 it remains to prove that, for any state $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and bounded optional time $\tau$ 

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {x} \Big (X \circ \theta_ {\tau} \Big | \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \Big) = P _ {X _ {\tau}} \text { a.s. }
$$

As in the previous proof, this is equivalent to countably many relations of the form 

$$
E _ {x} \left\{1 _ {F} \left(M _ {t} ^ {f, n} - M _ {s} ^ {f, n}\right) \circ \theta_ {\tau} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \right\} = 0 \text { a.s. }\tag{17}
$$

with $s \_ t$ and $F ~ \in ~ \mathcal { F } _ { s }$ , where $M ^ { f , n }$ denotes the process $M ^ { f }$ stopped at $\tau _ { n } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t ; | M ^ { f } | \geq n \}$ . Now $\theta _ { \tau } ^ { - 1 } \mathcal { F } _ { s } \subset \mathcal { F } _ { \tau + s }$ by Lemma 9.5, and in the difusion case 

$$
\left(M _ {t} ^ {f, n} - M _ {s} ^ {f, n}\right) \circ \theta_ {\tau} = M _ {(\tau + t) \wedge \sigma_ {n}} ^ {f} - M _ {(\tau + s) \wedge \sigma_ {n}} ^ {f},
$$

where $\sigma _ { n } = \tau + \tau _ { n } \circ \theta _ { \tau }$ , which is again optional by Proposition 11.8. Thus, (17) follows by optional sampling from the local martingale property of $M ^ { f }$ under $P _ { x }$ 

(ii) Assume that $a , b$ are also bounded and continuous, and define $T _ { t } f ( x ) =$ $E _ { x } f ( X _ { t } )$ . By Theorem 32.9, the function $T _ { t } f$ is continuous for every $f \in C _ { 0 }$ and $t > 0$ , and the path continuity implies that $T _ { t } f ( x )$ is continuous in t for every x. To see that $T _ { t } f \in C _ { 0 }$ , it remains to show that $| X _ { t } ^ { x } | \overset { P } {  } \infty \mathrm { a s } | x |  \infty$ 2 where $X ^ { x }$ has distribution $P _ { x }$ . This follows from the SDE by the boundedness of $\sigma , b .$ , if for $0 < r < | x |$ we write 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \Big \{| X _ {t} ^ {x} | <   r \Big \} \leq P \Big \{\Big | X _ {t} ^ {x} - x \Big | > | x | - r \Big \} \\ \leq \frac {E \big | X _ {t} ^ {x} - x \big | ^ {2}}{(| x | - r) ^ {2}} \lesssim \frac {t + t ^ {2}}{(| x | - r) ^ {2}}, \end{array}
$$

and let $| x | \to \infty$ for fixed $r , t .$ . The last assertion is obvious from the uniqueness in law together with Theorem 17.23. ✷ 

Uniqueness in law is usually harder to prove than the weak existence. Some fairly general uniqueness criteria will be obtained in Theorems 33.1 and 34.2. For the moment, we will only exhibit some transformations that may simplify the problem. First we show how the drift may sometimes be eliminated by a change of probability measure. 

Proposition 32.12 (transformation of drift) Let $\sigma , b , c$ be progressive functions of suitable dimension, where c is bounded. Then 

(i) weak existence holds simultaneously for equations $( \sigma , b )$ and $( \sigma , b + \sigma c )$ ， 

(ii) when $c = \sigma ^ { \prime } h$ for a progressive function h, uniqueness in law holds simultaneously for the two equations. 

Proof: (i) Let X be a weak solution to equation $( \sigma , b )$ , defined on the canonical space for $( X , B )$ with induced filtration $\mathcal { F }$ and probability measure P. Put $V = c ( X )$ , and note that $( V ^ { 2 } \cdot \lambda ) _ { i }$ is bounded for each t. By Lemma 19.19 and Corollary 19.26, there exists a probability measure Q with $Q = \mathcal { E } ( V ^ { \prime } \cdot B ) _ { t } \cdot P$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { t }$ for each $t \geq 0$ , and we note that $\tilde { B } = \stackrel { \cdot } { B } - V \cdot \lambda$ is a Q -Brownian motion. Under $Q .$ , we further get by Proposition 19.21 

$$
\begin{array}{c} X - X _ {0} = \sigma (X) \cdot \Big (\tilde {B} + V \cdot \lambda \Big) + b (X) \cdot \lambda \\ = \sigma (X) \cdot \tilde {B} + (b + \sigma c) (X) \cdot \lambda , \end{array}
$$

which shows that X is a weak solution to the SDE $( \sigma , b + \sigma c )$ . Since the same argument applies to equation $( \sigma , b + \sigma c )$ with c replaced by $- c ,$ , we conclude that weak existence holds simultaneously for the two equations. 

(ii) Let $c = \sigma ^ { \prime } h$ , and suppose that uniqueness in law holds for equation $( \sigma , b + a h )$ . Further, let $( X , B )$ solve equation $( \sigma , b )$ under both P and $Q$ Choosing V and $\tilde { B }$ as before, it follows that $( X , { \tilde { B } } )$ solves equation $( \sigma , b + \sigma c )$ under the transformed distributions $\mathcal { E } ( V ^ { \prime } \cdot B ) _ { t } \cdot P$ and $\mathcal { E } ( V ^ { \prime } \cdot B ) _ { t } \cdot Q$ for $( X , B )$ By hypothesis, the latter measures have then the same X-marginal, and the stated condition shows that $\mathcal { E } ( V ^ { \prime } \cdot B )$ is X-measurable. Thus, the X-marginals agree even for $P , Q$ , which proves the uniqueness in law for equation $( \sigma , b )$ Reversing the argument yields an implication in the other direction. ✷ 

Next we show how an SDE of difusion type can be transformed by a random time change. The method will be used systematically in Chapter 33, to analyze the one-dimensional case. 

Proposition 32.13 (scaling) Let $\sigma , b , c$ be measurable functions on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , where the range of c has compact closure in $( 0 , \infty )$ . Then weak existence and uniqueness in law hold simultaneously for equations $( \sigma , b )$ and $( c \sigma , c ^ { 2 } b )$ 

Proof: Let X solve the local martingale problem for the pair $( a , b )$ , and introduce the process $V = c ^ { 2 } ( X ) \cdot \lambda$ with inverse $\left( \tau _ { s } \right)$ . By optional sampling, we note that $M _ { \tau _ { s } } ^ { f } , s \ge 0$ , is again a local martingale, and the process $Y _ { s } = X _ { \tau _ { s } }$ satisfies cs 

$$
M _ {\tau_ {s}} ^ {f} = f (Y _ {s}) - f (Y _ {0}) - \int_ {0} ^ {s} c ^ {2} A f (Y _ {r}) d r.
$$

Thus, $Y$ solves the local martingale problem for $( c ^ { 2 } a , c ^ { 2 } b )$ 

Now let T be the map on $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ transforming X into $Y ,$ and write $T ^ { \prime }$ for the corresponding map based on $c ^ { - 1 }$ , so that $T$ and $T ^ { \prime }$ are mutual inverses. Applying the previous argument to both maps, we conclude that a measure $P \in \hat { \mathcal { M } } ( C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } } )$ solves the local martingale problem for $( a , b )$ if $P \circ T ^ { - 1 }$ solves the corresponding problem for $( c ^ { 2 } a , c ^ { 2 } b )$ . Thus, both existence and uniqueness hold simultaneously for the two problems. By Theorem 32.7, the last statement translates immediately into a corresponding assertion for the SDEs. ✷ 

We finally explore the relationship between weak and strong solutions. Under suitable conditions, we further prove the existence of a universal functional solution. To explain the terminology, let be the filtration induced by the identity map $( \xi , B )$ on the canonical space $\Omega = \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \times C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { r } }$ , so that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } = \sigma \{ \xi , B ^ { t } )$ , $t \geq 0$ , where $B _ { s } ^ { t } = B _ { s \wedge t }$ . Writing $W ^ { r }$ for the r-dimensional Wiener measure, we introduce for every $\mu \in \hat { \mathcal { M } } _ { \sf R ^ { d } }$ the $( \mu \otimes W ^ { r } )$ -completion $\mathcal { G } _ { t } ^ { \mu }$ of $\mathcal { G } _ { t }$ . The universal completion $\bar { \mathcal { G } } _ { t }$ is defined as $\cap _ { \mu } \mathcal { G } _ { t } ^ { \mu }$ , and we say that a function 

$$
F \colon \mathsf {R} ^ {d} \times C _ {\mathsf {R} _ {+}, \mathsf {R} ^ {r}} \to C _ {\mathsf {R} _ {+}, \mathsf {R} ^ {d}}\tag{18}
$$

is universally adapted if it is adapted to the filtration $\bar { \mathcal { G } } = ( \bar { \mathcal { G } } _ { t } )$ 

Theorem 32.14 (existence, uniqueness, and functional solution, Yamada & Watanabe, OK) Let the functions σ, b be progressive and such that weak existence and pathwise uniqueness hold for solutions to equation $( \sigma , b )$ starting at fixed points. Then 

(i) strong existence and uniqueness in law hold for any initial distribution, 

(ii) there exists a measurable, universally adapted function $F$ as in (18), such that every solution $( X , B )$ to equation $( \sigma , b )$ satisfies $X = F ( X _ { 0 } , B )$ a.s. 

Note that the function $F$ in (ii) can be chosen to be independent of initial distribution $\mu .$ . A couple of lemmas are needed for the proof, beginning with a statement clarifying the relationship between adaptedness, strong existence, and functional solutions. 

Lemma 32.15 (transfer of strong solution) Let $( X , B )$ solve equation $( \sigma , b )$ , where X is adapted to the complete filtration induced by $X _ { 0 }$ and B. Then 

(i) $X = F ( X _ { 0 } , B )$ a.s. for a Borel measurable function F as in (18), 

(ii) for any basic triple $( \mathcal { F } , \tilde { B } , \xi )$ with $\xi \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ X _ { 0 }$ , the process $\tilde { X } = F ( \xi , \tilde { B } )$ is -adapted, and the pair $( { \tilde { X } } , { \tilde { B } } )$ solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ 

Proof: By Lemma 1.14, we have $X = F ( X _ { 0 } , B )$ a.s. for some Borel measurable function F as stated. The same result yields for every $t \geq 0$ a representation $X _ { t } = G _ { t } ( X _ { 0 } , B ^ { t } )$ a.s., and so $F ( X _ { 0 } , B ) _ { t } = G _ { t } ( X _ { 0 } , B ^ { t } )$ a.s. Hence, $\tilde { X } _ { t } ~ = ~ G _ { t } ( \xi , \tilde { B } ^ { t } )$ a.s., and so $\tilde { X }$ is -adapted. Since also $( \tilde { X } , \tilde { B } ) \ { \stackrel { d } { = } } \ ( X , B )$ , Proposition 18.26 shows that even the former pair solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ □ 

Even weak solutions can be transferred to any probability space with a specified Brownian motion: 

Lemma 32.16 (transfer of weak solution) Let $( X , B )$ solve equation $( \sigma , b )$ and let $( \mathcal { F } , \tilde { B } , \xi )$ be a basic triple with $\xi \overset { d } { = } X _ { 0 }$ . Then 

(i) there exists a process $\tilde { X }$ with 

$$
\tilde {X} \underset {\xi , \tilde {B}} {\perp \sqcup} \mathcal {F}, \qquad \tilde {X} _ {0} = \xi a. s., \qquad (\tilde {X}, \tilde {B}) \stackrel {{d}} {{=}} (X, B),
$$

(ii) the filtration induced by $( { \tilde { X } } , { \mathcal { F } } )$ is a standard extension of $\mathcal { F }$ , 

(iii) the pair $( \tilde { X } , \tilde { B } )$ with filtration solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ 

Proof: (i) By Theorem 8.17 and Proposition 8.20, there exists a process $\tilde { X } \perp \perp _ { \xi , \tilde { B } } \mathcal { F }$ with $( \tilde { X } , \xi , \tilde { B } ) \overset { d } { = } ( X , X _ { 0 } , B )$ , and in particular $\tilde { X } _ { 0 } = \xi \ \mathrm { a . s }$ 

(ii) Fix any $t \geq 0$ , and put $\tilde { B } ^ { \prime } = \tilde { B } - \tilde { B } ^ { t }$ . Then $( \tilde { X } ^ { t } , \tilde { B } ^ { t } )$ Ⅱ ${ \tilde { B } } ^ { \prime }$ , since the corresponding relation holds for $( X , B )$ , and so $\tilde { X } ^ { t } \dot { \perp } \perp _ { \xi , \tilde { B } ^ { t } } \tilde { B } ^ { \prime }$ . Since also $\tilde { X } ^ { t } \bot \bot _ { \xi , \tilde { B } } \mathcal { F }$ , Proposition 8.12 yields $\tilde { X } ^ { t } \bot \bot _ { \xi , \tilde { B } ^ { t } } ( \tilde { B } ^ { \prime } , \mathcal { F } )$ , and hence $\tilde { X } ^ { t } \bot \bot _ { \mathcal { F } _ { t } } \mathcal { F }$ . Then also $( \tilde { X } ^ { t } , \mathcal { F } _ { t } ) \bot \bot _ { \mathcal { F } _ { t } } \mathcal { F }$ by Corollary 8.11, which means that $\mathcal { G } _ { t } \bot \bot _ { \mathcal { F } _ { t } } \mathcal { F }$ 

(iii) Since standard extensions preserve martingales, Theorem 19.3 shows that $\tilde { B }$ remains a Brownian motion with respect to $\mathcal { G }$ . As in Proposition 18.26, we conclude that the pair $( { \tilde { X } } , { \tilde { B } } )$ solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 32.14: For clarity, we begin with a special case. 

1. Fixed initial distribution. Let $( X , B )$ solve equation $( \sigma , b )$ with initial distribution $\mu$ and filtration $\mathcal { F }$ . Then Lemma 32.16 yields a process Y ${ \cal X } _ { 0 } , { \cal B }  \mathcal { F }$ with $Y _ { 0 } = X _ { 0 } \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., such that $( Y , B )$ solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ for the filtration $\mathcal { G }$ induced by $( Y , { \mathcal { F } } )$ . Since $\mathcal { G }$ is a standard extension of ${ \mathcal { F } } ,$ , the pair $( X , B )$ remains a solution for ${ \mathcal { G } } _ { : }$ , and the pathwise uniqueness yields $X = Y$ a.s. 

For every $t \geq 0$ , we have $X ^ { t } \bot \bot _ { X _ { 0 } , B } X ^ { t }$ and $( X ^ { t } , B ^ { t } ) \bot \bot ( B - B ^ { t } )$ , and so $X ^ { t } \bot \bot _ { X _ { 0 } , B ^ { t } } X ^ { t } { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . by Proposition 8.12. Hence, Lemma 32.15 yields a measurable function $F _ { \mu }$ with $X = F _ { \mu } ( X _ { 0 } , B )$ a.s., such that for any basic triple $( \tilde { \mathcal { F } } , \tilde { B } , \xi )$ with $\xi \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ X _ { 0 }$ , the process $\tilde { X } = F _ { \mu } ( \xi , \tilde { B } ) \mathrm { ~ i s ~ } \tilde { \mathcal { F } } .$ adapted and solves equation $( \sigma , b )$ along with $\tilde { B }$ . In particular, ${ \tilde { X } } { \stackrel { d } { = } } X$ since $( \xi , { \tilde { B } } ) \overset { d } { = } ( X _ { 0 } , B )$ , and the pathwise uniqueness shows that $\tilde { X }$ is the a.s. unique solution for the given triple $( \tilde { \mathcal { F } } , \tilde { B } , \xi )$ . This proves the uniqueness in law. 

2. General case. The previous case yields uniqueness in law for solutions starting at fixed points, and Theorem 32.10 shows that the corresponding distributions $P _ { x }$ form a kernel from $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ to $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ . Writing $Q _ { x }$ for the distribution of $( X , B )$ , we see from Theorem 2.19 (v) and Lemma 3.2 (ii) that the mapping $x \mapsto Q _ { x }$ is a kernel from $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ to $C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d + r } }$

$$
Q _ {x} (X \in \cdot | B) = \delta_ {F _ {x} (B)} \text { a.s., } x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.\tag{19}
$$

By Proposition 9.27, we may choose versions $\nu _ { x , w } \ = \ Q _ { x } ( X \ \in \ \cdot \vert B \ \in \ d w )$ combining into a probability kernel $\nu : \mathbb { R } ^ { d } \times C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { r } } \to C _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ . Here (19) shows that $\nu _ { x , w }$ is a.s. degenerate for each $x ,$ and since the set D of degenerate measures is measurable by Lemma 2.18, we can modify ν to get $\nu _ { x , w } D \equiv 1$ Then Dd 

$$

Chapter 33 

# One-Dimensional SDEs and Difusions

Removal of drift, weak existence and uniqueness, path-wise uniqueness, weak and strict comparison, hitting times, scale function, speed measure, time-change reduction, Green function, accessible and reflecting boundaries, entrance and exit boundaries, entrance laws and Feller properties, ratio ergodic theorem, recurrence and ergodicity, strong ergodicity, positive recurrence and invariant distribution 

We have already recognized martingales and Markov processes as the most important dependence structures of modern probability. In both cases, Brownian motion is the prototype and most fundamental example. In fact, we proved in Theorem 19.4 that a real, continuous local martingale is nothing but a suitably time-changed Brownian motion. Similarly, we will show in Theorem 33.9 below that even a real and suficiently regular continuous Markov process is essentially a Brownian motion, up to a natural transformation in both space and time. 

Much more can be said in the one-dimensional case of continuous strong Markov processes—also known as difusion processes—which motivates that we spend a whole chapter to explore their basic properties. We begin with a study of the basic difusion equation 

$$
d X _ {t} = \sigma (X _ {t}) d B _ {t} + b (X _ {t}) d t,\tag{1}
$$

referred to below as equation $( \sigma , b )$ . Here we will see how the drift term can often be removed by a simple spatial transformation. This reduces (1) to the simple equation $d X _ { t } = \sigma ( X _ { t } ) d B _ { t }$ , where precise criteria can be given for weak existence and uniqueness in law, in terms of the function σ. For more general σ and b, we may give conditions for pathwise uniqueness and strict or weak comparison. From Theorem 32.11 we know that, if weak existence and uniqueness in law hold for (1), the solution process X is a continuous strong Markov process. It is clearly also a semi-martingale. 

We proceed with a study of general, one-dimensional difusion processes X. Our first aim is then to show how a spatial transformation, based on a suitable scale function, reduces X to a continuous local martingale, which is then said to be on a natural scale. In the latter case, we may next identify a suitable speed measure, determining the time-change reduction of X into a Brownian motion. The tools for this construction are purely probabilistic, as they are based on an analysis of the hitting times $\tau _ { a }$ and $\tau _ { a , b }$ of states a or interval endpoints $a < b$ . The ergodic behavior of X also depends in a crucial way on the properties at the boundary points, which may be absorbing or reflecting, as well as of entrance or exit type. 

Preparing for a more detailed discussion of equation $( \sigma , b )$ , we recall from Proposition 32.12 how the drift term can sometimes be eliminated through a change of the underlying probability measure. Under suitable regularity conditions on the coeficients, we may use the alternative approach of transforming the state space. Then assume that X solves (1), and put $Y _ { t } = p ( X _ { t } )$ for some function $p \in C ^ { 1 }$ , possessing an absolutely continuous derivative $p ^ { \prime }$ with density $p ^ { \prime \prime }$ . By the generalized Itˆo formula of Theorem 29.5, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d Y _ {t} = p ^ {\prime} (X _ {t})   d X _ {t} + \frac {1}{2}   p ^ {\prime \prime} (X _ {t})   d [ X ] _ {t} \\ \qquad = (\sigma p ^ {\prime}) (X _ {t})   d B _ {t} + \Big (\frac {1}{2}   \sigma^ {2} p ^ {\prime \prime} + b   p ^ {\prime} \Big) (X _ {t})   d t. \end{array}
$$

Here the drift term vanishes if $p$ solves the ordinary diferential equation 

$$
\frac {1}{2} \sigma^ {2} p ^ {\prime \prime} + b p ^ {\prime} = 0.\tag{2}
$$

When $b / \sigma ^ { 2 }$ is locally integrable, (2) has the explicit solutions 

$$
p ^ {\prime} (x) = c \exp \Bigl \{- 2 \int_ {0} ^ {x} (b / \sigma^ {2}) (u) d u \Bigr \}, \quad x \in \mathsf {R},
$$

for an arbitrary constant $c .$ . The desired scale function $p$ is then determined up to an afine transformation, and for $c > 0$ it is strictly increasing with a unique inverse $p ^ { - 1 }$ . A mapping by $p$ reduces (1) to the form $d Y _ { t } = \widetilde { \sigma } ( Y _ { t } ) d B _ { t }$ , where $\tilde { \sigma } = ( \sigma p ^ { \prime } ) \circ p ^ { - 1 }$ . Since the new equation is equivalent, it is clear that weak or strong existence or uniqueness hold simultaneously for the two equations. 

Once the drift is removed, we are left with an equation of the form 

$$
d X _ {t} = \sigma (X _ {t}) d B _ {t}.\tag{3}
$$

Here exact criteria for weak existence and uniqueness in law may be given in terms of the singularity sets 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {\sigma} = \Big \{x \in \mathsf {R}; \int_ {x -} ^ {x +} \sigma^ {- 2} (y)   d y = \infty \Big \}, \\ N _ {\sigma} = \Big \{x \in \mathsf {R};   \sigma (x) = 0 \Big \}. \end{array}
$$

Theorem 33.1 (existence and uniqueness, Engelbert & Schmidt) For equation (3) with initial distribution $\mu _ { ; }$ 

(i) weak existence holds for all $\mu \iff S _ { \sigma } \subset N _ { \sigma . }$ 

(ii) uniqueness in law then holds for all $\mu \Leftrightarrow S _ { \sigma } = N _ { \sigma }$ 

We begin with a lemma, which will also be useful later on. Given any measure ν on $\mathsf { R } ,$ we may introduce the associated singularity set 

$$
S _ {\nu} = \left\{x \in \mathsf {R};   \nu (x -, x +) = \infty \right\}.
$$

Letting B be a one-dimensional Brownian motion with associated local time $L _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , we may also introduce the additive functional 

$$
A _ {s} = \int L _ {s} ^ {x} \nu (d x), \quad s \geq 0.\tag{4}
$$

Lemma 33.2 (singularity set) Let B be a Brownian motion with local time $L$ and initial distribution $\mu _ { ; }$ and define A by (4) for a measure ν on $\mathsf { R }$ . Then a.s. $P _ { \mu }$ , infSβ > 0: 4 

$$
\inf \left\{s \geq 0; A _ {s} = \infty \right\} = \inf \left\{s \geq 0; B _ {s} \in S _ {\nu} \right\}.
$$

Proof: Fix any $t > 0$ , and let R be the event where $B _ { s } \notin S _ { \nu }$ on $[ 0 , t ]$ . Noting that $L _ { t } ^ { x } = 0$ a.s. for x outside the range $B [ 0 , t ]$ , we get a.s. on R 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A _ {t} = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} L _ {t} ^ {x}   \nu (d x) \\ \qquad \leq \nu \big (B [ 0, t ] \big) \sup _ {x} L _ {t} ^ {x} <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

since $B [ 0 , t ]$ is compact and $L _ { t } ^ { x }$ is a.s. continuous and hence bounded. 

Conversely, let $B _ { s } \in S _ { \nu }$ for some $s < t$ . To show that $A _ { t } = \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . on this event, we may use the strong Markov property to reduce to the case where $B _ { 0 } = a$ is non-random in $S _ { \nu }$ . But then $L _ { t } ^ { a } > 0$ a.s. by Tanaka’s formula, and so the continuity of L yields for small enough $\varepsilon > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} A _ {t} = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} L _ {t} ^ {x}   \nu (d x) \\ \qquad \geq \nu \Big (a - \varepsilon , a + \varepsilon \Big) \inf _ {| x - a | <   \varepsilon} L _ {t} ^ {x} = \infty . \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 33.1: (i) Let $S _ { \sigma } ~ \subset ~ N _ { \sigma }$ . To prove the asserted weak existence, let Y be a Brownian motion with arbitrary initial distribution $\mu _ { ; }$ and define $\zeta = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ s \geq 0 ; Y _ { s } \in S _ { \sigma } \}$ . By Lemma 33.2, the additive functional 

$$

$$

is continuous and strictly increasing on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ , and $A _ { t } = \infty$ for $t > \zeta$ . Further note that $A _ { \zeta } = \infty$ when $\zeta = \infty$ , whereas $A _ { \zeta }$ may be finite when $\zeta < \infty$ . In the latter case, A jumps from $A _ { \zeta }$ to at time $\zeta .$

$$

The process $\tau$ is clearly continuous and strictly increasing on $[ 0 , A _ { \zeta } ]$ , and for $t \geq A _ { \zeta }$ we have $\tau _ { t } = \zeta$ . Further note that $X _ { t } ~ = ~ Y _ { \tau _ { t } }$ is a continuous loca martingale, and τt 

$$
\begin{array}{r} t = A _ {\tau_ {t}} = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t}} \sigma^ {- 2} (Y _ {r}) d r \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma^ {- 2} (X _ {s}) d \tau_ {s}, t <   A _ {\zeta}. \end{array}
$$

Hence, for $t \leq A _ { \zeta } .$ 

$$
[ X ] _ {t} = \tau_ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma^ {2} (X _ {s}) d s.\tag{7}
$$

Here both sides remain constant after time $A _ { \zeta } ,$ , since $S _ { \sigma } ~ \subset ~ N _ { \sigma }$ , and so (7) remains true for all $t \geq 0$ . Hence, Theorem 19.13 yields a Brownian motion B satisfying (3), which means that X is a weak solution with initial distribution $\mu .$ 

Conversely, assume weak existence for any initial distribution. To show that $S _ { \sigma } \subset N _ { \sigma }$ , fix any $x \in S _ { \sigma }$ , and choose a solution X with $X _ { 0 } = x$ . Since X is a continuous local martingale, Theorem 19.4 yields $X _ { t } = Y _ { \tau _ { t } }$ for a Brownian motion $Y$ starting at x and a random time-change $\tau$ satisfying (7). For A as in (5) and $t \geq 0$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & A _ {\tau_ {t}} = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t}} \sigma^ {- 2} (Y _ {r}) d r \\ & \quad = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \sigma^ {- 2} (X _ {s}) d \tau_ {s} \\ & \quad = \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 \Bigl \{\sigma (X _ {s}) > 0 \Bigr \} d s \leq t. \end{array}\tag{8}
$$

Since $A _ { s } = \infty$ for $s > 0$ by Lemma 33.2, we get $\tau _ { t } = 0 \ \mathrm { a . s }$ ., and so $X _ { t } \equiv x { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ But then $x \in N _ { \sigma }$ by (7). 

(ii) Let $N _ { \sigma } \subset S _ { \sigma }$ , and consider a solution X with initial distribution $\mu .$ . As before, we may write $X _ { t } = Y _ { \tau _ { t } }$ a.s., where Y is a Brownian motion with initial distribution $\mu _ { ; }$ and $\tau$ is a random time-change satisfying (7). Define A as in (5), put $\chi = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } \in S _ { \sigma } \}$ , and note that $\tau _ { \chi } = \zeta \equiv \operatorname* { i n f } \{ s \geq 0 ; Y _ { s } \in S _ { \sigma } \}$ Since $N _ { \sigma } \subset S _ { \sigma }$ , we get as in (8)

A _ {\tau_ {t}} = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {t}} \sigma^ {- 2} (Y _ {s}) d s = t, \quad t \leq \chi .
$$

As before, we may form a solution $X _ { t } = Y _ { \tau _ { t } }$ starting at $x ,$ where Y is a Brownian motion starting at $x ,$ and $\tau$ is defined as in (6) from the process $A$ in (5). Since $x \in N _ { \sigma }$ , (3) has also the trivial solution $X _ { t } \equiv x$ . Thus, uniqueness in law fails for solutions starting at x. ✷ 

Proceeding with a study of pathwise uniqueness, we return to equation (1), writing $w ( \sigma , \cdot )$ for the modulus of continuity of $\sigma$ . 

Theorem 33.3 (pathwise uniqueness, Skorohod, Yamada & Watanabe) Let σ, b be bounded, measurable functions on R, such that 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\varepsilon} \left\{w (\sigma , h) \right\} ^ {- 2} d h = \infty , \quad \varepsilon > 0,\tag{9}
$$

and either b is Lipschitz continuous or $\sigma \neq 0$ . Then pathwise uniqueness holds for equation $( \sigma , b )$ 

The significance of (9) is clear from the following lemma, where for any semi-martingale Y we write $L _ { t } ^ { x } ( Y )$ for the associated local time. 

Lemma 33.4 (local time) Let $X ^ { i }$ solve equation $( \sigma , b _ { i } )$ for $i = 1 , 2$ , where $\sigma$ satisfies (9). Then 10(x1 y2) 

$$
L ^ {0} \left(X ^ {1} - X ^ {2}\right) = 0 a. s.
$$

Proof: Write $Y = X ^ { 1 } - X ^ { 2 } , L _ { t } ^ { x } = L _ { t } ^ { x } ( Y )$ , and $w ( x ) = w ( \sigma , \vert x \vert )$ . Using (1) and Theorem 29.5, we get for any $t > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} w _ {x} ^ {- 2} L _ {t} ^ {x}   d x = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Big |   w (Y _ {s}) \Big | ^ {- 2} d [ Y ] _ {s} \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Big |   \frac {\sigma (X _ {s} ^ {1}) - \sigma (X _ {s} ^ {2})}{w \big (X _ {s} ^ {1} - X _ {s} ^ {2} \big)} \Big | ^ {2} d s \leq t <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

By (1) and the right-continuity of L it follows that $L _ { t } ^ { 0 } = 0 { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ 

Proof of Theorem 33.3 for $\sigma \ne 0$ : By Propositions 32.12 and 32.13 along with a simple localization argument, uniqueness in law holds for equation $( \sigma , b )$ when $\sigma \neq 0$ . To prove the pathwise uniqueness, consider any two solutions X and Y with $X _ { 0 } = Y _ { 0 }$ a.s. Using Tanaka’s formula, Lemma 33.4, and equation $( \sigma , b )$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} d (X _ {t} \vee Y _ {t}) = d X _ {t} + d (Y _ {t} - X _ {t}) ^ {+} \\ \qquad = d X _ {t} + 1 \{Y _ {t} > X _ {t} \}   d (Y _ {t} - X _ {t}) \\ \qquad = 1 \{Y _ {t} \leq X _ {t} \}   d X _ {t} + 1 \{Y _ {t} > X _ {t} \}   d Y _ {t} \\ \qquad = \sigma (X _ {t} \vee Y _ {t})   d B _ {t} + b (X _ {t} \vee Y _ {t})   d t, \end{array}
$$

which shows that $X \vee Y$ is again a solution. The uniqueness in law gives $X \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ X \ \vee \ Y$ . Since $X \leq X \vee Y$ , it follows that $X = X \vee Y$ a.s., which implies $Y \le X { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . The symmetric argument yields $X \leq Y { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ ✷ 

The assertion for Lipschitz continuous b is a special case of the following comparison result. 

Theorem 33.5 (weak comparison, Skorohod, Yamada) For $i = 1 , 2$ , let $X ^ { i }$ solve equation $( \sigma , b _ { i } )$ , where σ satisfies (9) and $b _ { 1 }$ or $b _ { 2 }$ is Lipschitz continuous. Then b1 > b2 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{c} b _ {1} \geq b _ {2} \\ X _ {0} ^ {1} \geq X _ {0} ^ {2} a. s. \end{array} \right\} \Rightarrow X ^ {1} \geq X ^ {2} a. s. o n \mathsf {R} _ {+}.
$$

Proof: By symmetry we may take $b _ { 1 }$ to be Lipschitz continuous. Since $X _ { 0 } ^ { 2 } \le X _ { 0 } ^ { 1 }$ a.s., we get by Tanaka’s formula and Lemma 33.4 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \left(X _ {t} ^ {2} - X _ {t} ^ {1}\right) ^ {+} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 \Bigl \{X _ {s} ^ {2} > X _ {s} ^ {1} \Bigr \} \Bigl \{\sigma (X _ {t} ^ {2}) - \sigma (X _ {t} ^ {1}) \Bigr \} d B _ {t} \\ + \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 \Bigl \{X _ {s} ^ {2} > X _ {s} ^ {1} \Bigr \} \Bigl \{b _ {2} (X _ {s} ^ {2}) - b _ {1} (X _ {s} ^ {1}) \Bigr \} d s. \end{array}
$$

Using the martingale property of the first term, the Lipschitz continuity of $b _ { 1 }$ , and the condition $b _ { 2 } \leq b _ { 1 }$ , we conclude that 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} E \Big (X _ {t} ^ {2} - X _ {t} ^ {1} \Big) ^ {+} & \leq & E \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 \Big \{X _ {s} ^ {2} > X _ {s} ^ {1} \Big \} \Big \{b _ {1} (X _ {s} ^ {2}) - b _ {1} (X _ {s} ^ {1}) \Big \} d s \\ & \lesssim & E \int_ {0} ^ {t} 1 \Big \{X _ {s} ^ {2} > X _ {s} ^ {1} \Big \} \left| X _ {s} ^ {2} - X _ {s} ^ {1} \right| d s \\ & = & \int_ {0} ^ {t} E \Big (X _ {s} ^ {2} - X _ {s} ^ {1} \Big) ^ {+} d s. \end{array}
$$

Then $E ( X _ { t } ^ { 2 } - X _ { t } ^ { 1 } ) ^ { + } = 0$ by Gronwall’s lemma, and so $X _ { t } ^ { 2 } \le X _ { t } ^ { 1 }$ a.s. 

By imposing stronger restrictions on the coeficients, we may strengthen the last conclusion to a strict inequality. 

Theorem 33.6 (strict comparison) For $i = 1 , 2$ , let $X ^ { i }$ solve equation $( \sigma , b _ { i } )$ where $\sigma$ is Lipschitz continuous and $b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 }$ are continuous. Then 

$$
\left. \begin{array}{c} b _ {1} > b _ {2} \\ X _ {0} ^ {1} \geq X _ {0} ^ {2} a. s. \end{array} \right\} \Rightarrow X ^ {1} > X ^ {2} a. s. o n (0, \infty).
$$

Proof: Since the $b _ { i }$ are continuous with $b _ { 1 } ~ > ~ b _ { 2 }$ , there exists a locally Lipschitz continuous function b on R with $b _ { 1 } > b > b _ { 2 }$ . By Theorem 32.3, equation $( \sigma , b )$ has a solution X with $X _ { 0 } = X _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } \geq X _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ a.s., and it sufices to show that $X ^ { 1 } > X > X ^ { 2 }$ a.s. on $( 0 , \infty )$ . This yields a reduction to the case where one of the functions $b _ { i }$ is locally Lipschitz. By symmetry we may take that function to be $b _ { 1 }$ 

By the Lipschitz continuity of $\sigma$ and $b _ { 1 }$ , we may introduce the continuous semi-martingales 

$$
\begin{array}{l} {U _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \left\{b _ {1} (X _ {s} ^ {2}) - b _ {2} (X _ {s} ^ {2}) \right\} d s,} \\ {V _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {\sigma (X _ {s} ^ {1}) - \sigma (X _ {s} ^ {2})}{X _ {s} ^ {1} - X _ {s} ^ {2}} d B _ {s} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {b _ {1} (X _ {s} ^ {1}) - b _ {1} (X _ {s} ^ {2})}{X _ {s} ^ {1} - X _ {s} ^ {2}} d s,} \end{array}
$$

subject to the convention $0 / 0 = 0$ , and we note that 

$$
d \left(X _ {t} ^ {1} - X _ {t} ^ {2}\right) = d U _ {t} + \left(X _ {t} ^ {1} - X _ {t} ^ {2}\right) d V _ {t}.
$$

Letting $Z = \mathrm { e x p } { \big ( } V - { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } [ V ] { \big ) } > 0$ , we get by Proposition 32.2 

$$
X _ {t} ^ {1} - X _ {t} ^ {2} = Z _ {t} \left(X _ {0} ^ {1} - X _ {0} ^ {2}\right) + Z _ {t} \int_ {0} ^ {t} Z _ {s} ^ {- 1} \left\{b _ {1} \left(X _ {s} ^ {2}\right) - b _ {2} \left(X _ {s} ^ {2}\right) \right\} d s,
$$

and the assertion follows since $X _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } \geq X _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ a.s. and $b _ { 1 } > b _ { 2 }$ 

We turn to a systematic study of one-dimensional difusions. By a difusion in an interval $I \subset \mathsf { R }$ we mean a continuous strong Markov process taking values in I. Termination is only permitted at open end-points of I. Define $\tau _ { y } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } = y \}$ , and say that X is regular if $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { y } < \infty \} > 0$ for any $x \in I ^ { o }$ and $y \in I$ . Further write $\tau _ { a , b } = \tau _ { a } \wedge \tau _ { b }$ 

Our first step is to transform the general difusion process into a continuous local martingale, using a suitable change of scale. This corresponds to a removal of drift in the SDE (1). 

Theorem 33.7 (scale function, Feller, Dynkin) Let X be a regular difusion in an interval $I \subset \mathsf { R }$ . Then 

(i) there exists a continuous, strictly increasing function p on $I ,$ such that $p ( X ^ { \tau _ { a , b } } )$ is a P -martingale for every $x \in [ a , b ] \subset I$ 2 

(ii) an increasing function $p$ is such as in $( \mathrm { i } ) \ i f f$ 

$$
P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \} = \frac {p _ {x} - p _ {a}}{p _ {b} - p _ {a}}, \quad x \in [ a, b ].
$$

A function $p$ with the stated property is called a scale function for $X$ , and X is said to be defined on a natural scale if the scale function can be chosen to be linear. In general, the process $Y = p ( X )$ is a regular difusion on a natural scale. We begin with a study of the functions 

$$
\begin{array}{l} p _ {a, b} (x) = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \}, \\ h _ {a, b} (x) = E _ {x} \tau_ {a, b}, \qquad a \leq x \leq b, \end{array}
$$

which play a basic role in the sequel. 

Lemma 33.8 (hitting times) For any regular difusion and constants $a < b$ in I, we have 

(i) $p _ { a , b }$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $[ a , b ]$ 

(ii) $h _ { a , b }$ is bounded on $[ a , b ]$ 

In particular, (ii) yields $\tau _ { a , b } < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ . under $P _ { x }$ for any $a \leq x \leq b$ 

Proof: (i) First we show that $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { b } < \tau _ { a } \} > 0$ for any $a < x < b$ . Then introduce the optional time $\sigma _ { 1 } = \tau _ { a } + \tau _ { x } \circ \theta _ { \tau _ { a } }$ , and define recursively $\sigma _ { n + 1 } =$ $\sigma _ { n } + \sigma _ { 1 } \circ \theta _ { \sigma _ { n } }$ . By the strong Markov property, the $\sigma _ { n }$ form a random walk in $[ 0 , \infty ]$ under each $P _ { x }$ . If $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { b } < \tau _ { a } \} = 0$ , we get $\tau _ { b } \geq \sigma _ { n } $ a.s. $P _ { x }$ , and so $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { b } = \infty \} = 1$ , which contradicts the regularity of $X$ . 

Using the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { y }$ , we next obtain 

$$
P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \} = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {y} <   \tau_ {a} \}   P _ {y} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \}, \quad a <   x <   y <   b.\tag{10}
$$

Since $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { a } < \tau _ { y } \} > 0$ , we have $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { y } < \tau _ { a } \} < 1$ , which shows that $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { b } < \tau _ { a } \}$ is strictly increasing. 

By symmetry it remains to prove that $P _ { y } \{ \tau _ { b } < \tau _ { a } \}$ is left-continuous on $( a , b ]$ . By (10) it is equivalent to show that, for any $x \in ( a , b )$ , the mapping $y \mapsto P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { y } < \tau _ { a } \}$ is left-continuous on $( x , b ]$ . Then let $y _ { n } \uparrow y$ , and note that $\tau _ { y _ { n } }$ $\tau _ { y }$ a.s. $P _ { x }$ by the continuity of $X$ . Hence, $\left\{ \tau _ { y _ { n } } < \tau _ { a } \right\} \downarrow \left\{ \tau _ { y } < \tau _ { a } \right\}$ , which implies convergence of the corresponding probabilities. 

(ii) Fix any $c \in ( a , b )$ . By the regularity of X, we may choose $h > 0$ so large that 

$$
P _ {c} \{\tau_ {a} \leq h \} \wedge P _ {c} \{\tau_ {b} \leq h \} = \delta > 0.
$$

When $x \in ( a , c )$ , the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { x }$ yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \delta \leq P _ {c} \{\tau_ {a} \leq h \} \\ \quad \leq P _ {c} \{\tau_ {x} \leq h \}   P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} \leq h \} \\ \quad \leq P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} \leq h \} \\ \quad \leq P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau_ {a, b} \leq h \bigr \}, \end{array}
$$

and similarly for $x \in \left( c , b \right)$ . By the Markov property at h and induction on $n ,$ we obtain 

$$
P _ {x} \left\{\tau_ {a, b} > n h \right\} \leq (1 - \delta) ^ {n}, \quad x \in [ a, b ], \quad n \in \mathsf {Z} _ {+},
$$

and Lemma 4.4 yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {x} \tau_ {a, b} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau_ {a, b} > t \bigr \} d t \\ \leq h \sum_ {n \geq 0} (1 - \delta) ^ {n} <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 33.7: Let p be a locally bounded and measurable function on I, such that $M = p ( X ^ { \tau _ { a , b } } )$ is a martingale under $P _ { x }$ for any $a < x < b$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} p _ {x} = E _ {x} M _ {0} = E _ {x} M _ {\infty} \\ \qquad = E _ {x} p (X _ {\tau_ {a, b}}) \\ \qquad = p _ {a} P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} <   \tau_ {b} \} + p _ {b} P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \} \\ \qquad = p _ {a} + (p _ {b} - p _ {a}) P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \}, \end{array}
$$

and (ii) follows provided that $p _ { a } \neq p _ { b }$ 

To construct a function p with the stated properties, fix any points $u < v$ in I, and define for arbitrary $a \leq u$ and $b \geq v$ in I 

$$
p (x) = \frac {p _ {a , b} (x) - p _ {a , b} (u)}{p _ {a , b} (v) - p _ {a , b} (u)}, \quad x \in [ a, b ].\tag{11}
$$

To see that p is independent of a and $b ,$ consider a larger interval $[ a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } ] \subset I _ { \mathrm { \Omega } }$ and conclude from the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { a , b }$ that, for any $x \in [ a , b ]$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r} P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b ^ {\prime}} <   \tau_ {a ^ {\prime}} \} = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} <   \tau_ {b} \} P _ {a} \{\tau_ {b ^ {\prime}} <   \tau_ {a ^ {\prime}} \} \\ + P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \} P _ {b} \{\tau_ {b ^ {\prime}} <   \tau_ {a ^ {\prime}} \}, \end{array}
$$

or 

$$
p _ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} (x) = p _ {a, b} (x) \left\{p _ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} (b) - p _ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} (a) \right\} + p _ {a ^ {\prime} b ^ {\prime}} (a).
$$

Thus, $p _ { a , b }$ and $p _ { a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } }$ agree on $[ a , b ]$ up to an afine mapping, and so they yield the same value in (11). 

By Lemma 33.8, the constructed function is continuous and strictly increasing, and it remains to show that $p ( X ^ { \tau _ { a , b } } )$ is a martingale under $P _ { x }$ for any $a < b$ in I. Since the martingale property is preserved by afine transformations, it is equivalent to show that $p _ { a , b } ( X ^ { \tau _ { a , b } } )$ is a $P _ { x } { \mathrm { - m a r t i n g a l e } }$ . Then fix any optional time $\sigma ,$ and write $\tau = \sigma \land \tau _ { a , b }$ . By the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { : }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E _ {x} p _ {a, b} (X _ {\tau}) = E _ {x} P _ {X _ {\tau}} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \} \\ & \qquad = P _ {x} \theta_ {\tau} ^ {- 1} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \} \\ & \qquad = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \} \\ & \qquad = p _ {a, b} (x), \end{array}
$$

and the desired martingale property follows by Lemma 9.14. 

To prepare for the next result, consider a Brownian motion B in R with jointly continuous local time L. For any measure ν on $\mathsf { R } ,$ we introduce as in (4) the additive functional $\begin{array} { r } { A = \int L ^ { x } \nu ( d x ) } \end{array}$ with right-continuous inverse 

$$
\sigma_ {t} = \inf \left\{s > 0; A _ {s} > t \right\}, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

If $\nu \neq 0$ , the recurrence of B shows that A is a.s. unbounded. Hence, $\sigma _ { t } < \infty$ a.s. for all t, and we may define $X _ { t } ~ = ~ B _ { \sigma { t } } , ~ t ~ \ge ~ 0$ . We refer to $\sigma = \left( \sigma _ { t } \right)$ as the random time-change based on $\nu ,$ and to the process $X = B \circ \sigma$ as a correspondingly time-changed Brownian motion. 

Theorem 33.9 (speed measure and time change, Feller, Volkonsky, Itˆo & McKean) 

(i) For a regular difusion X on a natural scale in I, there exists a unique measure ν on I with $\nu [ a , b ] \in ( 0 , \infty )$ for all $a < b$ in $I ^ { o } .$ , such that X is a time-changed Brownian motion based on an extension of ν to <sup>¯</sup>I. 

(ii) Any time-changed Brownian motion as above is a regular difusion in I. 

The extended version of ν is called the speed measure of the difusion. Contrary to what the term suggests, the process moves slowly through regions where ν is large. For Brownian motion itself, the speed measure is clearly Lebesgue measure. More generally, the speed measure of a regular difusion solving equation (3) has density $\sigma ^ { - 2 }$ 

To prove the uniqueness of $\nu ,$ we need the following lemma, which is also useful for the subsequent classification of boundary behavior. Here we write $\sigma _ { a , b } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ s > 0 ; B _ { s } \notin ( a , b ) \}$ 

Lemma 33.10 (Green function) Let X be a time-changed Brownian motion based on ν. Then for any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on I and points $a < b$ in ${ \bar { I } } ,$ we have 

$$
E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {a, b}} f (X _ {t}) d t = \int_ {a} ^ {b} g _ {a, b} (x, y) f (y) \nu (d y), \quad x \in [ a, b ],\tag{12}
$$

where 

$$
g _ {a, b} (x, y) = E _ {x} L _ {\sigma_ {a, b}} ^ {y} = \frac {2 (x \wedge y - a) (b - x \vee y)}{b - a}, \quad x, y \in [ a, b ].\tag{13}
$$

When X is recurrent, this remains true for $a = - \infty \ o r \ b = \infty$ 

Taking $f \equiv 1$ in (12), we get in particular 

$$
h _ {a, b} (x) = E _ {x} \tau_ {a, b} = \int_ {a} ^ {b} g _ {a, b} (x, y) \nu (d y), \quad x \in [ a, b ],\tag{14}
$$

which will be useful later on. 

Proof: Clearly $\tau _ { a , b } = A ( \sigma _ { a , b } )$ for any $a , b \in { \bar { I } } .$ and also for $a = - \infty$ or $b = \infty$ when X is recurrent. Since $L ^ { y }$ is supported by $\{ y \}$ , we see from (4) 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {a, b}} f (X _ {t})   d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\sigma_ {a, b}} f (B _ {s})   d A _ {s} \\ = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (y)   L _ {\sigma_ {a, b}} ^ {y}   \nu (d y). \end{array}
$$

Taking expectations gives (12) with $g _ { a , b } ( x , y ) = E _ { x } L _ { \sigma _ { a , b } } ^ { y }$ . To prove (13), we get by Tanaka’s formula and optional sampling 

$$
E _ {x} L _ {\sigma_ {a, b} \wedge s} ^ {y} = E _ {x} \big | B _ {\sigma_ {a, b} \wedge s} - y \big | - | x - y |, \quad s \geq 0.
$$

If a, b are finite, we may let $s \to \infty$ and conclude by monotone and dominated convergence that 

$$
g _ {a, b} (x, y) = \frac {(y - a) (b - x)}{b - a} + \frac {(b - y) (x - a)}{b - a} - | x - y |,
$$

which simplifies to (13). The result for infinite a or b follows immediately by monotone convergence. ✷ 

The next lemma will enable us to construct the speed measure ν from the functions $h _ { a , b }$ in Lemma 33.8. 

Lemma 33.11 (consistence) For a regular difusion on a natural scale in I, there exists a strictly concave function h on $I ^ { o } ,$ such that for any $a < b$ in I, 

$$
h _ {a, b} (x) = h (x) - \frac {x - a}{b - a} h (b) - \frac {b - x}{b - a} h (a), \quad x \in [ a, b ].\tag{15}
$$

Proof: Fix any $u < v$ in I, and define for any $a \leq u$ and $b \geq v$ in I 

$$
h (x) = h _ {a, b} (x) - \frac {x - u}{v - u} h _ {a, b} (v) - \frac {v - x}{v - u} h _ {a, b} (u), \quad x \in [ a, b ].\tag{16}
$$

To see that h is independent of a and b, consider any larger interval $[ a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } ] \subset I$ and conclude from the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { a , b }$ that, for any $x \in [ a , b ]$ 

$$
E _ {x} \tau_ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} = E _ {x} \tau_ {a, b} + P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} <   \tau_ {b} \}   E _ {a} \tau_ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} + P _ {x} \{\tau_ {b} <   \tau_ {a} \}   E _ {b} \tau_ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}},
$$

or 

$$
h _ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} (x) = h _ {a, b} (x) + \frac {b - x}{b - a} h _ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} (a) + \frac {x - a}{b - a} h _ {a ^ {\prime}, b ^ {\prime}} (b).\tag{17}
$$

Thus, $h _ { a , b }$ and $h _ { a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } }$ agree on $[ a , b ]$ up to an afine function and therefore yield the same value in (16). 

If $a \leq u$ and $b \geq v .$ , then (16) shows that h and $h _ { a , b }$ agree on $[ a , b ]$ up to an afine function, and (15) follows since $h _ { a , b } ( a ) = h _ { a , b } ( b ) = 0$ . The formula extends by (17) to arbitrary $a < b$ in I. ✷ 

Since h is strictly concave, its left derivative $h _ { - } ^ { \prime }$ is strictly decreasing and left-continuous, and hence determines a measure ν on $I ^ { o }$ satisfying 

$$
2 \nu [ a, b) = h _ {-} ^ {\prime} (a) - h _ {-} ^ {\prime} (b), \quad a <   b \text { in } I ^ {o}.\tag{18}
$$

For motivation, we note that this expression is consistent with (14). 

To prove Theorem 33.9, we first need to clarify the behavior of X at the endpoints of I. If $b \neq I$ for an endpoint b, then by hypothesis the motion terminates when X reaches $b ,$ and we may attach b to I as an absorbing state. For convenience, we may then assume that I is a compact interval of the form $[ a , b ]$ , where either endpoint may be inaccessible, in the sense that a.s. it can not be reached in finite time from a point in $I ^ { o } ,$ 

For either endpoint b, the set $\Xi _ { b } = \{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } = b \}$ is regenerative under $P _ { b }$ in the sense of Chapter 29. In particular, Theorem 29.7 shows that b is either absorbing, in the sense that $\Xi _ { b } = \mathsf { R } _ { + } \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., or reflecting, in the sense that $\Xi _ { b } ^ { o } = \emptyset$ a.s. In the latter case, the reflection is said to be fast if $\lambda \Xi _ { b } = 0$ and slow if $\lambda \Xi _ { b } > 0$ . We give a more detailed discussion of the boundary behavior after the proof of the main theorem. 

First we establish Theorem 33.9 in a special case. The general result will then be deduced by a pathwise comparison. 

Proof of Theorem 33.9, absorbing endpoints (M´el´eard): Let X have distri bution $P _ { x } .$ where $x \in I ^ { o }$ , and put $\zeta = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t > 0 ; X _ { t } \neq I ^ { o } \}$ . For any $a < b$ in $I ^ { o }$ with $x \in [ a , b ]$ , the process $X ^ { \tau _ { a , b } }$ is a continuous martingale, and so by Theorem 29.5 

$$
h (X _ {t}) = h (x) + \int_ {0} ^ {t} h _ {-} ^ {\prime} (X) d X - \int_ {I} \tilde {L} _ {t} ^ {x} \nu (d x), \quad t \in [ 0, \zeta),\tag{19}

where $L$ is the local time of B. Hence, $\tilde { L } _ { t } ^ { x } = L _ { [ X ] _ { t } } ^ { x }$ a.s. for $t < \zeta$ , and so the last term in (19) equals $A _ { [ X ] _ { \ l } }$ a.s. 

For any optional time $\sigma ,$ put $\tau = \sigma \wedge \tau _ { a , b }$ , and conclude from the strong Markov property that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E _ {x} \Big \{\tau + h _ {a, b} (X _ {\tau}) \Big \} = E _ {x} \Big (\tau + E _ {X _ {\tau}} \tau_ {a, b} \Big) \\ & \qquad = E _ {x} \Big (\tau + \tau_ {a, b} \circ \theta_ {\tau} \Big) \\ & \qquad = E _ {x} \tau_ {a, b} = h _ {a, b} (x). \end{array}
$$

Writing $M _ { t } = h ( X _ { t } ) + t$ , it follows by Lemma 9.14 that ${ \cal M } ^ { \tau _ { a , b } }$ is a $P _ { x } { \mathrm { - m a r t i n g a l e } }$ e whenever $x \in [ a , b ] \subset I ^ { o }$ . Comparing with (19) and using Proposition 18.2, we obtain $A _ { [ X ] _ { t } } = t$ a.s. for all $t \in [ 0 , \zeta )$ . Since A is continuous and strictly increasing on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ with inverse $\sigma .$ , we get $[ X ] _ { t } = \sigma _ { t }$ a.s. for $t < \zeta$ . The last relation extends to $\lbrack \zeta , \infty )$ , provided we give infinite mass to $\nu$ at each endpoint. Then $X = B \circ \sigma { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . on $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ 

Conversely, we note that $B \circ \sigma$ is a regular difusion on $I .$ , whenever $\sigma$ is a random time-change based on a measure ν with the stated properties. To prove the uniqueness of $\nu ,$ , fix any $a < x < b$ in $I ^ { o }$ , and apply Lemma 33.10 with $f ( y ) = \{ g _ { a , b } ( x , y ) \} ^ { - 1 }$ to see that $\nu ( a , b )$ is determined by $P _ { x }$ ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 33.9, general case: Define $\nu$ on $I ^ { o }$ as in (18), and extend the definition to $\bar { I } .$ , by assigning infinite mass to any absorbing endpoint. To reflecting endpoints we attach finite mass, to be specified later. Given a Brownian motion $B .$ , we see as before that the correspondingly time-changed process $\tilde { X } = B \circ \sigma$ is a regular difusion in I. Letting $\zeta = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ t ; X _ { t } \in I ^ { o } \}$ and $\tilde { \zeta } = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ t ; \tilde { X } _ { t } \in I ^ { o } \}$ , we further see from the previous case that $X ^ { \zeta }$ and $\tilde { X } ^ { \tilde { \zeta } }$ have the same distribution for any starting position $x \in I ^ { o }$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \chi_ {1} = \zeta + \tau_ {a, b} \circ \theta_ {\zeta}, \\ \chi_ {n + 1} = \chi_ {n} + \chi_ {1} \circ \theta_ {\chi_ {n}}, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}. \end{array}
$$

Then the processes $Y _ { n } ^ { a , b } = X ^ { \zeta } \circ \theta _ { \chi _ { n } }$ form a Markov chain in the path space. A similar construction for $\tilde { X }$ yields some processes ${ \tilde { Y } } _ { n } ^ { a , b }$ , and we note that $( Y _ { n } ^ { a , b } ) \overset { d } { = } ( \tilde { Y } _ { n } ^ { a , b } )$ for fixed a and b. Since the process $Y _ { n } ^ { a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } }$ , obtained for a smaller interval $[ a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } ]$ , can be measurably recovered from that for $[ a , b ]$ , and similarly for $\tilde { Y } _ { n } ^ { a ^ { \prime } , b ^ { \prime } }$ , the entire collections $\left( Y _ { n } ^ { a , b } \right)$ and $( \tilde { Y } _ { n } ^ { a , b } )$ have the same distribution. By Theorem 8.17, we may then assume that the two families agree a.s. 

Now let $I = [ a , b ]$ , where a is reflecting. By the nature of Brownian motion, the level sets $\Xi _ { a }$ and $\tilde { \Xi } _ { a }$ for $X$ and $\tilde { X }$ are a.s. perfect, and so we may form the corresponding excursion point processes $\xi$ and $\tilde { \xi } ,$ local times $L$ and ${ \tilde { L } } .$ , and inverse local times $T$ and $\tilde { T }$ . Since excursions within $[ a , b )$ agree a.s. for X and $\tilde { X }$ , we can normalize the excursion laws of the two processes, using the law of large numbers, such that the corresponding parts of $\xi$ and $\dot { \xi }$ agree a.s. Then even $T$ and $\tilde { T }$ agree, possibly apart from the lengths of excursions reaching $b$ and the drift coeficient $c$ in Theorem 29.13. For $\tilde { X }$ the latter is proportional to the mass $\nu \{ a \}$ , which can now be chosen such that $c$ becomes the same as for X. This choice of $\nu \{ a \}$ is clearly independent of starting position x for X and $\tilde { X }$ . 

If the other endpoint b is absorbing, then clearly $X = \tilde { X } \mathrm { a . s . }$ , and the proof is complete. If b is instead reflecting, the excursions from b agree a.s. for X and $\tilde { X }$ . Repeating the argument with the roles of a and b interchanged, we get $X = \tilde { X } \mathrm { a . s . }$ , after a suitable adjustment of the mass $\nu \{ b \}$ ✷ 

We proceed to classify the boundary behavior of a regular difusion on a natural scale, in terms of the speed measure ν. A right endpoint b is called an entrance boundary for X if it is inaccessible, and yet 

$$
\lim _ {r \to \infty} \inf _ {y > x} P _ {y} \{\tau_ {x} \leq r \} > 0, \quad x \in I ^ {o}.\tag{20}
$$

By the Markov property at times nr, $n \in { \mathsf N }$ , the limit in (20) then equals 1, and in particular $P _ { y } \{ \tau _ { x } < \infty \} = 1$ for all $x < y$ in $I ^ { o }$ . In Theorem 33.13 below, we show that an entrance boundary is an endpoint where X may enter but not exit. 

The opposite behavior occurs at an exit boundary, defined as an endpoint b that is accessible and naturally absorbing, in the sense of remaining absorbing when the charge $\nu \{ b \}$ is reduced to zero. If b is accessible but not naturally absorbing, we have already seen how the boundary behavior of X depends on the value of $\nu \{ b \}$ . Thus, in this case, b is absorbing when $\nu \{ b \} = \infty$ , slowly reflecting when $\nu \{ b \} \in ( 0 , \infty )$ , and fast reflecting when $\nu \{ b \} = 0$ . For reflecting $b ,$ we further see from Theorem 33.9 that the set $\Xi _ { b } = \{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } = b \}$ is a.s. perfect. 

Theorem 33.12 (boundary behavior, Feller) Consider a regular difusion on a natural scale in $I = [ a , b ]$ with speed measure ν. Then for fixed $u \in I ^ { o }$ , we have 

(i) b is accessible if 

$$
b <   \infty , \quad \int_ {u} ^ {b} (b - x) \nu (d x) <   \infty ,
$$

(ii) b is accessible, reflecting if 

$$
b <   \infty , \quad \nu (u, b ] <   \infty ,
$$

(iii) b is an entrance boundary if 

$$
b = \infty , \quad \int_ {u} ^ {b} x   \nu (d x) <   \infty .
$$

The stated conditions can be translated into similar criteria for any regular difusion. In general, exit and other accessible boundaries may clearly be infinite, whereas entrance boundaries may be finite. Explosion is said to occur when X reaches an infinite boundary in finite time. A basic example of a regular difusion on $( 0 , \infty )$ with an entrance boundary at 0 is given by the Bessel process $X _ { t } = | B _ { t } |$ , where B is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $d \geq 2$ 

Proof of Theorem 33.12: (i) Since lim sup $_ s ( \pm B _ { s } ) = \infty \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., Theorem 33.9 shows that X cannot explode, so any accessible endpoint is finite. Now assume that $a < c < u < b < \infty$ . Then Lemma 33.8 shows that b is accessible if $h _ { c , b } ( u ) < \infty$ , which holds by (14) if $\textstyle \int _ { u } ^ { b } ( b - x ) \nu ( d x ) < \infty$ 

(ii) Here $b < \infty$ by (i), in which case Lemma 33.2 shows that b is absorbing if $\nu ( u , b ] = \infty$ 

(iii) An entrance boundary b is inaccessible by definition, and therefore $\tau _ { u } = \tau _ { u , b }$ a.s. when $a < u < b$ . Arguing as in the proof of Lemma 33.8, we also note that $E _ { y } \tau _ { u }$ is bounded for $y > u$ . If $b < \infty$ , we obtain the contradiction $E _ { y } \tau _ { u } = h _ { u , b } ( y ) = \infty$ , and so b must be infinite. From (14), we get by monotone convergence as $y  \infty$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&E _ {y} \tau_ {u} = h _ {u, \infty} (y) = 2 \int_ {u} ^ {\infty} (x \wedge y - u) \nu (d x)\\&\qquad \rightarrow 2 \int_ {u} ^ {\infty} (x - u) \nu (d x),\end{array}
$$

which is finite if $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { u } ^ { \infty } x \nu ( d x ) < \infty . } \end{array}$ 

We proceed to establish an important regularity property, which also clarifies the nature of entrance boundaries. 

Theorem 33.13 (entrance laws and Feller properties) For a regular difusion X on I, form $\bar { I } \supset I$ by attaching the entrance boundaries of X. Then X extends to a continuous Feller process on $\bar { I } .$ 

Proof: For any $f \in C _ { b } , \ a , x \in I$ , and $r , t \geq 0$ , the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { x } \wedge r$ yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {a} f (X _ {\tau_ {x} \wedge r + t}) = E _ {a} T _ {t} f \bigl (X _ {\tau_ {x} \wedge r} \bigr) \\ = T _ {t} f (x) P _ {a} \{\tau_ {x} \leq r \} + E _ {a} \bigl \{T _ {t} f (X _ {r});   \tau_ {x} > r \bigr \}. \end{array}\tag{21}
$$

To show that $T _ { t } f$ is left-continuous at any $y \in I$ , fix an $a ~ < ~ y$ in $I ^ { o } .$ , and choose $r > 0$ so large that $P _ { a } \{ \tau _ { y } \leq r \} > 0$ . As $x \uparrow y$ we have $\tau _ { x } \uparrow \tau _ { y }$ , and so $\left\{ \tau _ { x } \leq r \right\} \downarrow \left\{ \tau _ { y } \leq r \right\}$ . Thus, the probabilities and expectations in (21) converge to the corresponding expressions for $\tau _ { y }$ , and we get $T _ { t } f ( x )  T _ { t } f ( y )$ . The proof of the right-continuity is similar. 

If an endpoint b is inaccessible but not of entrance type, and if $f ( x )  0$ as $x  b$ , then clearly even $T _ { t } f ( x )  0$ at b for each $t > 0$ . Now let be an entrance boundary, and consider a function f with a finite limit at $\infty$ . We need to show that even $T _ { t } f ( x )$ converges, as $x \to \infty$ for fixed t. Then conclude from Lemma 33.10 that, as $a  \infty$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sup _ {x \geq a} E _ {x} \tau_ {a} = 2 \sup _ {x \geq a} \int_ {a} ^ {\infty} (x \wedge r - a) \nu (d r) \\ = 2 \int_ {a} ^ {\infty} (r - a) \nu (d r) \to 0. \end{array}\tag{22}
$$

Next we note that, for any $a < x < y$ and $r \geq 0$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P _ {y} \{\tau_ {a} \leq r \} \leq P _ {y} \bigl \{\tau_ {x} \leq r,   \tau_ {a} - \tau_ {x} \leq r \bigr \} \\ & \qquad = P _ {y} \{\tau_ {x} \leq r \} P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} \leq r \} \\ & \qquad \leq P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} \leq r \}. \end{array}
$$

Thus, $P _ { x } \circ \tau _ { a } ^ { - 1 }$ converges vaguely as $x \to \infty$ for fixed $a _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and (22) shows that the convergence holds even in the weak sense. 

Now fix any t and $f ,$ , and introduce for every a the continuous function $g _ { a } ( s ) = E _ { a } f \{ X _ { ( t - s ) _ { + } } \}$ . By the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { a } \wedge t$ and Theorem 8.5, we get for any $x , y \geq a$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \big | T _ {t} f (x) - T _ {t} f (y) \big | \leq \big | E _ {x}   g _ {a} (\tau_ {a}) - E _ {y}   g _ {a} (\tau_ {a}) \big | \\ + 2   \| f \| \big (P _ {x} + P _ {y} \big) \{\tau_ {a} > t \}. \end{array}
$$

Here the right-hand side tends to 0 as $x , y \to \infty$ and then $a  \infty .$ , by (22) and the weak convergence of $P _ { x } \circ \tau _ { a } ^ { - 1 }$ . Thus, $T _ { t } f ( x )$ is Cauchy convergent as $x \to \infty ,$ and we may denote the limit by $T _ { t } f ( \infty )$ 

It is now easy to check that the extended operators $T _ { t }$ form a Feller semi group on $C _ { 0 } ( \bar { I } )$ . Finally, Theorem 17.15 shows that the associated process, starting at a possible entrance boundary, has again a continuous version in the topology of <sup>¯</sup>I. ✷ 

We may next establish a ratio ergodic theorem, for elementary additive functionals of a recurrent difusion. It is instructive to compare with the general ratio limit theorems in Chapter 26. 

Theorem 33.14 (ratio ergodic theorem, Derman, Motoo $\mathcal { E A }$ Watanabe) Let $X$ be a regular, recurrent difusion on a natural scale in I with speed measure ν. Then for any measurable functions f, $g \geq 0$ on I with $\nu f < \infty$ and $\nu g > 0$ , we have as $t \to \infty$ 

$$
\frac {\int_ {0} ^ {t} f (X _ {s}) d s}{\int_ {0} ^ {t} g (X _ {s}) d s} \to \frac {\nu f}{\nu g} a. s. P _ {x}, x \in I.
$$

Proof: Fix any $a < b$ in I, put $\tau _ { a } ^ { b } = \tau _ { b } + \tau _ { a } \circ \theta _ { \tau _ { b } }$ , and define recursively some optional times $\sigma _ { 0 } , \sigma _ { 1 } , . . . .$ by 

$$
\sigma_ {n + 1} = \sigma_ {n} + \tau_ {a} ^ {b} \circ \theta_ {\sigma_ {n}}, n \geq 0,
$$

starting with $\sigma _ { 0 } = \tau _ { a }$ . Write 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\sigma_ {n}} f (X _ {s}) d s = \int_ {0} ^ {\sigma_ {0}} f (X _ {s}) d s + \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {\sigma_ {k - 1}} ^ {\sigma_ {k}} f (X _ {s}) d s,\tag{23}
$$

and note that the last sum has i.i.d. terms. By the strong Markov property and Lemma 33.10, we get for any $x \in I$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {x} \int_ {\sigma_ {k - 1}} ^ {\sigma_ {k}} f (X _ {s})   d s = E _ {a} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {b}} f (X _ {s})   d s + E _ {b} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau_ {a}} f (X _ {s})   d s \\ \qquad = \int f (y) \left\{g _ {- \infty , b} (y, a) + g _ {a, \infty} (y, b) \right\} \nu (d y) \\ \qquad = 2 \int f (y) \left\{\left(b - y \vee a\right) _ {+} + \left(y \wedge b - a\right) _ {+} \right\} \nu (d y) \\ \qquad = 2 \left(b - a\right) \nu f. \end{array}
$$

The same lemma shows that the first term in (23) is a.s. finite. Hence, the law of large numbers yields 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} n ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {\sigma_ {n}} f (X _ {s}) d s = 2 (b - a) \nu f \text { a   .   s   . } P _ {x}, \quad x \in I.
$$

Writing $\kappa _ { t } = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ n \geq 0 ; \sigma _ { n } \leq t \}$ , we get by monotone interpolation 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \kappa_ {t} ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f (X _ {s}) d s = 2 (b - a) \nu f \mathrm{a.s.} P _ {x}, x \in I.\tag{24}
$$

This remains true when $\nu f = \infty$ , since we can then apply (24) to some approximating functions $f _ { n } \uparrow f$ with $\nu f _ { n } < \infty$ , and let $n  \infty$ . The assertion now follows as we apply (24) to both f and $g$ . ✷ 

We may finally classify the asymptotic behavior of the process, depending on the boundedness of the speed measure ν and the nature of the endpoints. Applying a suitable afine mapping, we may transforms $I ^ { o }$ into one of the intervals $( 0 , 1 ) , ( 0 , \infty ) , \mathrm { o r } ( - \infty , \infty )$ . We need to distinguish between the three possibilities of boundary behavior at finite endpoints, codified as follows: 

( — inaccessible boundary, 

[ — absorbing boundary, 

[[ — reflecting boundary. 

Thus, we end up with totally ten diferent cases. 

A difusion is said to be ν -ergodic if it is recurrent and such that $\mathcal { L } _ { x } ( X _ { t } ) \stackrel { w } {  }$ $\nu / \nu I$ for all x. A recurrent difusion may be either null-recurrent or positive recurrent, depending on whether $| X _ { t } | \overset { P } { \to } \infty$ or not. We further say that absorption occurs at an endpoint b, when $X _ { t } = b$ for all suficiently large t, so that $1 \{ X _ { t } = b \}  1$ 

Theorem 33.15 (recurrence and ergodicity, Feller, Maruyama & Tanaka) Let X be a regular difusion on a natural scale with speed measure ν. Then the ergodic behavior of X depends as follows on the initial position x and the nature of the boundaries: 

$( - \infty , \infty )$ : X is ν-ergodic when ν is bounded, otherwise null-recurrent, 

$( 0 , \infty ) \colon X _ { t } \to 0 \ a . s .$ 

$[ 0 , \infty ) \colon 1 \{ X _ { t } = 0 \} \to 1 \ a . s . ,$ 

$[ [ 0 , \infty ) \colon X$ is ν-ergodic when ν is bounded, otherwise null-recurrent, 

$( 0 , 1 ) \colon X _ { t } \to 0 \ o r \ 1$ , with probabilities $1 - x$ and x, respectively, 

$[ 0 , 1 ) \colon 1 \{ X _ { t } = 0 \} \to 1 \ o r \ X _ { t } \to 1$ , with probabilities $1 - x$ and x, 

$[ 0 , 1 ] \colon 1 \{ X _ { t } = 0 \}  1 \ o r 1 \{ X _ { t } = 1 \}  1$ , with probabilities $1 - x$ and $x _ { i }$ , 

$[ [ 0 , 1 ) \colon X _ { t } \to 1 \ a . s .$ 

$[ [ 0 , 1 ] \colon 1 \{ X _ { t } = 1 \} \to 1 \ { a . s . } _ { ; }$ 

[[0, 1]]: X is ν-ergodic. 

First we prove the relatively elementary recurrence properties, distinguish ing between the cases of absorption, convergence, and recurrence. 

Proof of recurrence properties: 

[0, 1]: Theorem 33.7 (ii) yields $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { 0 } < \infty \} = 1 - x$ and $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { 1 } < \infty \} = x$ 

$[ 0 , \infty )$ : The same theorem yields for any $b > x$ 

$$
P _ {x} \{\tau_ {0} <   \infty \} \geq P _ {x} \{\tau_ {0} <   \tau_ {b} \} = \frac {b - x}{b},
$$

which tends to 1 as $b \to \infty$ 

$( - \infty , \infty )$ : The recurrence follows from the previous case. 

$[ [ 0 , \infty )$ : Since 0 is reflecting, $P _ { 0 } \{ \tau _ { y } < \infty \} > 0$ for some $y > 0$ , which extends to arbitrary y by the strong Markov property and the regularity of X. Arguing as in the proof of Lemma 33.8, we conclude that $P _ { 0 } \{ \tau _ { y } < \infty \} = 1$ for all $y > 0$ . The asserted recurrence now follows, as we combine with the statement for $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ 

(0, ): Here $X = B \circ [ X ]$ a.s. for a Brownian motion B. Since $X > 0$ , we have $[ X ] _ { \infty } < \infty { \mathrm { ~ a . s . } }$ , and so X converges a.s. Now $P _ { y } \{ \tau _ { a , b } < \infty \} = 1$ for any $0 < a \le y \le b$ . Applying the Markov property at an arbitrary time $t > 0$ , we conclude that a.s. either lim $\operatorname { i n f } _ { t } X _ { t } \leq a$ or lim $\operatorname { s u p } _ { t } X _ { t } \geq b$ Since a and b are arbitrary, $X _ { \infty }$ is then an endpoint of $( 0 , \infty )$ , and hence equals 0. 

(0, 1): As in the previous case, we have a.s. convergence to either 0 or 1. To find the corresponding probabilities, we see from Theorem 33.7 that 

$$
P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} <   \infty \} \geq P _ {x} \{\tau_ {a} <   \tau_ {b} \} = \frac {b - x}{b - a}, \quad 0 <   a <   x <   b <   1.
$$

Letting $b  1$ and then $a \to 0$ , we obtain $P _ { x } \{ X _ { \infty } = 0 \} \ge 1 - x$ . Similarly, $P _ { x } \{ X _ { \infty } = 1 \} \ge x$ , and so equality holds in both relations. 

[0, 1): Once again, $X  0$ or 1 with probabilities $1 - x$ and x, respectively. Further note that 

$$
P _ {x} \{\tau_ {0} <   \infty \} \geq P _ {x} \{\tau_ {0} <   \tau_ {b} \} = \frac {b - x}{b}, \quad 0 \leq x <   b <   1,
$$

which tends to $1 - x$ as $b \to 1$ . Thus, absorption occurs when $X  0$ [[0, 1]]: As in the previous case, we get $P _ { 0 } \{ \tau _ { 1 } < \infty \} = 1$ , and by symmetry also $P _ { 1 } \{ \tau _ { 0 } < \infty \} = 1$ 

[[0, 1]: As before $P _ { 0 } \{ \tau _ { 1 } < \infty \} = 1$ , and so the same relation holds for $P _ { x }$ 

[[0, 1): Again $P _ { 0 } \{ \tau _ { b } < \infty \} = 1$ for all $b \in \mathsf { \Gamma } ( 0 , 1 )$ . By the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { b }$ and the result for [0, 1), it follows that $P _ { 0 } \{ X _ { t } \to 1 \} \ge b .$ Letting $b  1$ gives $X _ { t } \to 1$ , a.s. under $P _ { 0 }$ . The result for $P _ { x }$ now follows by the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { x }$ , applied under $P _ { 0 }$ ✷ 

The ergodic properties will be proved along the lines of Theorem 11.22, which requires some additional lemmas. 

Lemma 33.16 (coupling) For any Feller processes $X \bot \bot Y$ , the pair $( X , Y )$ is again Feller. 

Proof: Use Theorem 5.30 and Lemma 17.3. 

We proceed with a continuous-time counterpart of Lemma 11.24. 

Lemma 33.17 (strong ergodicity) For a regular, recurrent difusion with initial distribution $\mu _ { 1 } ~ o r ~ \mu _ { 2 }$ , we have 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \left\| P _ {\mu_ {1}} \circ \theta_ {t} ^ {- 1} - P _ {\mu_ {2}} \circ \theta_ {t} ^ {- 1} \right\| = 0.
$$

Proof: Let X and Y be independent with distributions $P _ { \mu _ { 1 } }$ and $P _ { \mu _ { 2 } }$ , respectively. By Theorem 33.13 and Lemma 33.16, the pair $( X , Y )$ can be extended to a Feller difusion, and so by Theorem 17.17 it is again strong Markov with respect to the induced filtration $\mathcal { G }$ . Define $\tau = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } = Y _ { t } \}$ , and note that $\tau$ is $\mathcal { G } \mathrm { - o p t i o n a l }$ by Lemma 9.6. The assertion now follows as for Lemma 11.24, provided we can show that $\tau < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ 

Here we first assume that $I = { \sf R }$ . The processes X and $Y$ are then continuous local martingales. By independence they remain local martingales for the extended filtration $\mathcal { G }$ , and so even $X - Y$ is a local -martingale. Using the independence and recurrence of X and $Y$ , we get $[ X - Y ] _ { \infty } = [ X ] _ { \infty } + [ Y ] _ { \infty } = \infty$ a.s., which shows that even $X - Y$ is recurrent. In particular, $\tau < \infty \ \mathrm { a . s }$ 

Next let $I = [ [ 0 , \infty )$ or [[0, 1]], and define $\tau _ { 1 } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } = 0 \}$ and $\tau _ { 2 } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; Y _ { t } = 0 \}$ . By the continuity and recurrence of X and Y, we get $\tau \leq \tau _ { 1 } \vee \tau _ { 2 } <$ a.s. ✷ 

Our next result is similar to the discrete-time version in Lemma 11.25. 

Lemma 33.18 (existence) Every regular, positive-recurrent difusion has an invariant distribution. 

Proof: By Theorem 33.13 we may regard the transition kernels $\mu _ { t }$ with associated operators $T _ { t }$ as defined on <sup>¯</sup>I—the interval I with possible entrance boundaries attached. Since X is not null-recurrent, we may choose a bounded 

Borel set B and some $x _ { 0 } \in I$ and $t _ { n } \to \infty$ , such that in $\dot { \bar { \mathbf { \rho } } } _ { n } \mu _ { t _ { n } } ( x _ { 0 } , B ) > 0$ . Then Theorem 6.20 yields a measure μ on <sup>¯</sup>I with $\mu I > 0$ , such that $\mu _ { t _ { n } } ( x _ { 0 } , \cdot ) \stackrel { v } {  } \mu$ along a sub-sequence, in the topology of <sup>¯</sup>I. The convergence extends by Lemma 33.17 to arbitrary $x \in I$ , and so 

$$
T _ {t _ {n}} f (x) \to \mu f, \quad f \in C _ {0} (\bar {I}), x \in I.\tag{25}
$$

Now fix any $h \geq 0$ and $f \in C _ { 0 } ( \bar { I } )$ , and note that even $T _ { h } f \in C _ { 0 } ( \bar { I } )$ by Theorem 33.13. Using (25), the semi-group property, and dominated convergence, we get for any $x \in I$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mu (T _ {h} f) \leftarrow T _ {t _ {n}} \bigl (T _ {h} f \bigr) (x) \\ = T _ {h} \bigl (T _ {t _ {n}} f \bigr) (x) \to \mu f. \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\mu \mu _ { h } = \mu$ for all $h _ { ; }$ , which means that $\mu$ is invariant on ${ \bar { I } } .$ In particular, $\mu ( \bar { I } \setminus I ) = 0$ by the nature of entrance boundaries, and so $\mu / \mu I$ is an invariant distribution on I. ✷ 

Our final lemma provides the crucial connection between speed measure and invariant distributions. 

Lemma 33.19 (positive recurrence) For a regular, recurrent difusion X on a natural scale in I with speed measure ν, these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) $\nu I < \infty$ 

(ii) X is positive-recurrent, 

(iii) X has an invariant distribution. 

The invariant distribution is then unique and given by $\nu / \nu I$ 

Proof: If the process is null-recurrent, then clearly no invariant distribution exists. The converse is also true by Lemma 33.18, and so $( \mathrm { i i } ) \Leftrightarrow ( \mathrm { i i i } )$ . Now fix any bounded, measurable function $f : I \to \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ with bounded support. By Theorem 33.14, Fubini’s theorem, and dominated convergence, we have for any distribution $\mu$ on I 

$$
t ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} E _ {\mu} f (X _ {s}) d s = E _ {\mu} t ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {t} f (X _ {s}) d s \to \frac {\nu f}{\nu I}.
$$

If $\mu$ is invariant, then $\mu f = \nu f / \nu I$ , and so $\nu I < \infty$ . If instead X is null recurrent, then $E _ { \mu } f ( X _ { s } ) \to 0 { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } s \to \infty$ , and we get $\nu f / \nu I = 0$ , which implies $\nu I = \infty$ ✷ 

End of proof of Theorem 33.15: It remains to consider the cases where I equals $( \infty , \infty ) , [ [ 0 , \infty )$ , or [[0, 1]], since otherwise we have convergence or absorption at some endpoint. In case of [[0, 1]], Theorem 33.12 (ii) shows that $\nu$ is bounded. In the remaining cases, ν may be unbounded, so that X is null-recurrent by Lemma 33.19. If $\nu$ is bounded, then $\mu = \nu / \nu I$ is invariant by the same lemma, and the asserted ν -ergodicity follows from Lemma 33.17 with $\mu _ { 1 } = \mu$ ✷

For $N _ { \sigma } ^ { c }$ , choose X to be absorbed when it first reaches $N _ { \sigma \cdot } )$
