Chapter 34 

# PDE Connections and Potential Theory

Cauchy problem, Feynman–Kac formula, PDE existence and SDE uniqueness, harmonic functions, regularity, Dirichlet’s problem, transition and occupation densities, Greenian domain, Green function and potential, hitting and quitting kernels, sweeping measure and hitting, equilibrium measure and quitting, dependence on conductor and domain, time reversal, capacities and random sets, super-harmonic and excessive functions, additive functional as compensator, Riesz decomposition, measure-induced additive functional 

In Chapters 17 and 32 we saw how elliptic diferential operators arise naturally as the generators of nice difusion processes. This is the ultimate cause of some profound connections between probability theory and partial diferential equations (PDEs). In particular, a suitable extension of the operator $\scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \Delta$ appears as the generator of Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , which leads to a close relationship between classical potential theory and the theory of Brownian motion. More specifically, many basic problems in potential theory can be solved by probabilistic methods. Conversely, various hitting distributions for Brownian motion can be given a potential-theoretic interpretation. 

This chapter explores some of the mentioned connections. First we derive the celebrated Feynman–Kac formula, and show how the existence of solutions to a given Cauchy problem implies uniqueness of solutions to the associated SDE. We then proceed with a probabilistic construction of Green functions and potentials, and solve the Dirichlet, sweeping, and equilibrium problems of classical potential theory in terms of Brownian motion. We further show how Green capacities and alternating set functions can be represented in a natural way in terms of random sets. 

We conclude with a discussion of excessive and super-harmonic functions, along with their relations to modern martingale theory. To indicate the main ideas, let f be an excessive function of Brownian motion X on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . Then $f ( X )$ is a continuous super-martingale under $P _ { x }$ for every x, and so it has a Doob– Meyer decomposition M A. Here A can be chosen to be a continuous additive functional (CAF) of X, and we obtain an associated Riesz decomposition $f =$ $U _ { A } + h$ , where $U _ { A }$ is the potential of A and h is the greatest harmonic minorant of f. 

Some stochastic calculus from Chapters 18 and 32 is used at the beginning of the chapter, and we also rely on the theory of Feller processes from Chapter 

17. As for Brownian motion, the present discussion is essentially self-contained, apart from some elementary facts from Chapters 14 and 19. Occasionally, we refer to Chapters 5 and 23 for some basic weak convergence theory. Finally, the results at the end of the chapter require the existence of Poisson processes from Proposition 15.6, as well as some basic facts about the Fell topology listed in Theorem A6.1. Potential-theoretic ideas are used in several other chapters, and some additional, essentially unrelated results appear in especially Chapters 26 and 29. 

To begin with the general PDE connections, we consider an arbitrary Feller difusion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with associated semi-group operators $T _ { t }$ and generator $( A , D )$ Recall from Theorem 17.6 that, for any $f \in { \mathcal { D } } .$ , the function 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} u (t, x) & = T _ {t} f (x) \\ & = E _ {x} f (X _ {t}), \quad t \geq 0, x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}, \end{array}
$$

satisfies Kolmogorov’s backward equation ${ \dot { u } } = A u$ , where $\dot { u } = \partial u / \partial t$ . Thus, u provides a probabilistic solution to the Cauchy problem 

$$
\dot {u} = A u, \qquad u (0, x) = f (x).\tag{1}
$$

Adding a potential term vu to (1), where $v \colon \mathsf { R } ^ { d } \to \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , we obtain the more general problem 

$$
\dot {u} = A u - v u, \qquad u (0, x) = f (x).\tag{2}
$$

Here the solution may be expressed in terms of the elementary multiplicative functional $e ^ { - V }$ , where 

$$
V _ {t} = \int_ {0} ^ {t} v (X _ {s}) d s, \quad t \geq 0.
$$

Let $C ^ { 1 , 2 }$ be the class of functions $f \colon { \mathsf { R } } _ { + } \times { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d }$ of class $C ^ { 1 }$ in the time variable and class $C ^ { 2 }$ in the space variables. Write $C _ { b } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ and $C _ { b } ^ { + } ( { \mathsf { R } } ^ { d } )$ for the classes of bounded, continuous functions from $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ to R and $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , respectively. 

Theorem 34.1 (Cauchy problem, Feynman, Kac) Let (A, ) be the generator of a Feller difusion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } { } _ { : }$ , and fix any $f \in C _ { b } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ and $v \in C _ { b } ^ { + } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { d } )$ . Then 

(i) any bounded solution $u \in C ^ { 1 , 2 }$ to (2) is given by 

$$
u (t, x) = E _ {x} e ^ {- V _ {t}} f (X _ {t}), \quad t \geq 0, x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.
$$

(ii) the function in (i) solves (2) whenever $f \in \mathcal { D }$ 

Formula (i) can be interpreted in terms of killing. Then consider an exponential random variable $\gamma .$ X with mean 1, and define $\zeta = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t \geq 0 ; V _ { t } > \gamma \}$ Letting $\tilde { X }$ be the process X killed at time $\zeta ,$ we may express the right-hand side in (i) as $E _ { x } f ( { \tilde { X } } _ { t } )$ , with the understanding that $f ( \tilde { X } _ { t } ) = 0$ when $t \geq \zeta$ . Thus, $u ( t , x ) = \tilde { T } _ { t } f ( x )$ , where $\tilde { T } _ { t }$ is the transition operator of the killed process. It is easy to verify, directly from (i), that the family $( \tilde { T } _ { t } )$ is again a Feller semigroup.

$$
M _ {s} = e ^ {- V _ {s}} u (t - s, X _ {s}), \quad s \in [ 0, t ].
$$

Writing $\underline { { \underline { { m } } } }$ for equality apart from a continuous local martingale or its diferential, we see from Lemma 17.21, Itˆo’s formula, and (2) that, for any $s < t$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d M _ {s} = e ^ {- V _ {s}} \Big \{d u (t - s, X _ {s}) - u (t - s, X _ {s})   v (X _ {s})   d s \Big \}} \\ & {\quad \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} e ^ {- V _ {s}} \big \{A u (t - s, X _ {s}) - \dot {u} (t - s, X _ {s}) - u (t - s, X _ {s})   v (X _ {s}) \big \}   d s = 0.} \end{array}
$$

Thus, M is a continuous local martingale on $[ 0 , t )$ . Since M is bounded, the martingale property extends to t, and we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} u (t, x) & = E _ {x} M _ {0} = E _ {x} M _ {t} \\ & = E _ {x} u (0, X _ {t}) \\ & = E _ {x} e ^ {- V _ {t}} f (X _ {t}). \end{array}
$$

Next let u be given by (i) for some $f \in \mathcal { D }$ . Integrating by parts and using Lemma 17.21, we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{c} d \Big \{e ^ {- V _ {t}} f (X _ {t}) \Big \} = e ^ {- V _ {t}} \Big \{d f (X _ {t}) - (v f) (X _ {t})   d t \Big \} \\ \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} e ^ {- V _ {t}} \Big (A f - v f \Big) (X _ {t})   d t. \end{array}
$$

Taking expectations and diferentiating at $t = 0$ , we conclude that the semigroup $\tilde { T } _ { t } f ( x ) = E _ { x } f ( \tilde { X } _ { t } ) = u ( t , x )$ has generator $\tilde { A } = A - v$ on $\mathcal { D } _ { \ell }$ . Now (2) follows by the last assertion in Theorem 17.6. ✷ 

Part (ii) of Theorem 34.1 can often be improved in special cases. In particular, if $v = 0$ and $\begin{array} { r } { A = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \Delta = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \sum _ { i } \partial ^ { 2 } / \partial x _ { i } ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , so that X is a Brownian motion and (2) reduces to the standard heat equation, then $u ( t , x ) = E _ { x } f ( X _ { t } )$ solves (2) for any bounded, continuous function f on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . To see this, we note that $u \in C ^ { 1 , 2 }$ on $( 0 , \infty ) \times \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , by the smoothness of the Brownian transition density. Now consider the SDE in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$

with associated elliptic operator<sup>1</sup>

A v (x) = \frac {1}{2} a ^ {i j} (x) \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} v (x) + b ^ {i} (x) \partial_ {i} v (x), x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}, v \in C ^ {2},

where $a ^ { i j } = \sigma _ { k } ^ { i } \sigma _ { k } ^ { j }$ . We show how uniqueness in law for solutions to (3) may be inferred from the existence of solutions to the associated Cauchy problem (1). 

Theorem 34.2 (existence and uniqueness, Stroock $\mathcal { C }$ Varadhan) For any $f \in$ $C _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ we have $( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ , where 

(i) equation (1) has a bounded solution on a set $[ 0 , \varepsilon ] \times \mathsf { R } ^ { d } ;$ 

(ii) uniqueness in law holds for the SDE (3). 

Proof: Fix any $f \in C _ { 0 } ^ { \infty }$ and $t \in ( 0 , \varepsilon ]$ , and let u be a bounded solution to (1) on $[ 0 , t ] \times \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . If X solves (3), we see as before that $M _ { s } = u ( t - s , X _ { s } )$ is a martingale on $[ 0 , t ]$ , and so

\begin{array}{r l} & E f (X _ {t}) = E u (0, X _ {t}) \\ & \qquad = E M _ {t} = E M _ {0} \\ & \qquad = E u (t, X _ {0}). \end{array}

Now let X and $Y$ be solutions with the same initial distribution. To prove that $X \ { \stackrel { f d } { = } } \ Y .$ it is enough to consider times $0 = t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n }$ with $t _ { k } - t _ { k - 1 } \leq \varepsilon$ for all k. Assume that the distributions agree at $t _ { 0 } , \ldots , t _ { n - 1 } = t$ 2 and fix any set $C = \pi _ { t _ { 0 } , \dots , t _ { n - 1 } } ^ { - 1 } B$ with $B \in B ^ { n d }$ . If $P \{ X \ \in \ C \} \ =$ $P \{ Y \in C \} > 0$ , Theorem 32.11 yields the same property for the conditional measures $\mathcal { L } ( \theta _ { t } X \mid X \in C )$ and $\mathcal { L } ( \theta _ { t } Y | Y \in C )$ . Since the corresponding initial distributions agree by hypothesis, the 1-dimensional result yields the extension 

$$
\mathcal {L} \left(X _ {t + h}; X \in C\right) = \mathcal {L} \left(Y _ {t + h}; Y \in C\right), \quad h \in (0, \varepsilon ].

We now specialize to the case of a Brownian motion X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . For any closed set $B \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we introduce the hitting time $\tau _ { B } = \operatorname* { i n f } \{ t > 0 ; X _ { t } \in B \}$ and associated hitting kernel 

$$
H _ {B} (x, d y) = P _ {x} \left\{\tau_ {B} <   \infty , X _ {\tau_ {B}} \in d y \right\}, \quad x \in \mathsf {R} ^ {d}.
$$

For suitable functions $f ,$ we write $\begin{array} { r } { H _ { B } f ( x ) = \int f ( y ) H _ { B } ( x , d y ) } \end{array}$ 

By a domain in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ we mean an open, connected subset $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ . A function $u : D  { \mathsf { R } }$ is said to be harmonic, if it belongs to $C ^ { 2 } ( D )$ and satisfies the Laplace equation $\Delta u = 0$ . We also say that u has the mean-value property, if it is locally bounded and measurable, and such that for any ball $B \subset D$ with center $x ,$ the average of u over the boundary ∂B equals $u ( x )$ . The following analytic result is crucial for the probabilistic developments. 

Lemma 34.3 (harmonic function, Gauss, Koebe) For functions u on a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , these conditions are equivalent and imply $u \in C _ { D } ^ { \infty }$ 

(i) u is harmonic, 

(ii) u has the mean-value property. 

Proof: First let $u \in C ^ { 2 } ( D )$ , and fix a ball $B \subset D$ with center x. Writing $\tau = \tau _ { \partial B }$ and noting that $E _ { x } \tau < \infty$ , we get by Itˆo’s formula 

$$
E _ {x} u (X _ {\tau}) - u (x) = \frac {1}{2} E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \Delta u (X _ {s}) d s.
$$

Here the first term on the left equals the average of u over $\partial B$ , by the spherical symmetry of Brownian motion. If u is harmonic, then the right-hand side vanishes, and the mean-value property follows. If instead u is not harmonic, we may choose B such that $\Delta u \neq 0$ on B. Then the right-hand side is non-zero, and the mean-value property fails. 

It remains to show that every function u with the mean-value property is infinitely diferentiable. Then fix any infinitely diferentiable, spherically symmetric probability density $\varphi _ { : }$ supported by a ball of radius $\varepsilon > 0$ around the origin. Here the mean-value property yields $u = u * \varphi$ , on the set where the right-hand side is defined, and by dominated convergence the infinite diferentiability of $\varphi$ carries over to $u * \varphi = u$ ✷ 

Before proceeding to the potential-theoretic developments, we need to introduce a regularity condition on the domain D. Writing $\zeta = \zeta _ { D } = \tau _ { D ^ { c } }$ , we note that $P _ { x } \{ \zeta = 0 \} = 0$ or 1 for every $x \in \partial D$ by Corollary 17.18. When this probability is 1, we say that x is regular for $D ^ { c }$ or simply regular. If this holds for every $x \in \partial D$ , the boundary $\partial D$ is said to be regular, and we refer to D as a regular domain. 

Regularity is a fairly weak condition. In particular, any domain with a smooth boundary is regular, and we shall see that even various edges and corners are allowed, provided they are not too sharp and directed inward. By a spherical cone in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with vertex v and axis $a \neq 0$ we mean a set of the form $C = \left\{ x ; \langle x - v , a \rangle \geq c | x - v | \right\}$ , where $c \in ( 0 , | a | ]$ 

Lemma 34.4 (cone condition, Zaremba) For a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , let $x \in \partial D$ be such that $C \cap G \subset D ^ { c }$ for a spherical cone $C$ with vertex x and a neighborhood G of x. Then x is regular for $D ^ { c }$ 

Proof: By compactness of the unit sphere in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ , we may cover $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ by $C _ { 1 } =$ $C$ along with finitely many congruent cones $C _ { 2 } , \ldots , C _ { n }$ with vertex x. By rotational symmetry, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 1 = P _ {x} \Bigl \{\min _ {k \leq n} \tau_ {C _ {k}} = 0 \Bigr \} \\ \leq \sum_ {k \leq n} P _ {x} \Bigl \{\tau_ {C _ {k}} = 0 \Bigr \} \\ = n   P _ {x} \{\tau_ {C} = 0 \}, \end{array}
$$

and so $P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { C } = 0 \} > 0$ . Hence, Corollary 17.18 yields $P \{ \tau _ { C } = 0 \} = 1$ , and we get $\zeta _ { D } \leq \tau _ { C \cap G } = 0 \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ $P _ { x }$ ✷ 

Now fix a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and a continuous function $f : \partial D  { \sf R }$ . A function u on $\bar { D }$ is said to solve the Dirichlet problem $( D , f )$ , if u is harmonic on D and continuous on $\bar { D }$ with $u = f \mathrm { o n } \partial D$ . The solution may be interpreted as the electrostatic potential in D, when the potential on the boundary is given by $f .$ . 

Theorem 34.5 (Dirichlet problem, Kakutani, Doob) For any regular domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and function $f \in C _ { b } ( \partial D )$ , we have 

(i) the Dirichlet problem $( D , f )$ has a solution 

$$
u (x) = E _ {x} \left\{f \left(X _ {\zeta_ {D}}\right); \zeta_ {D} <   \infty \right\} = H _ {D ^ {c}} f (x), \quad x \in \bar {D},\tag{4}

(ii) when $\zeta _ { D } < \infty \ a . s .$ , this is the only bounded solution,

(i) a is regular for $D ^ { c }$

To prepare for the probabilistic construction of the Green function in an arbitrary domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we need to study the transition densities of a Brownian motion, killed upon hitting the boundary $\partial D$ . Recall that the unrestricted Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ has transition densities 

$$

By the strong Markov property and Theorem 8.5, we get for any $t > 0 , x \in D$ 2 and $B \subset B _ { D }$

Theorem 34.7 (transition density, Hunt) For any domain D in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and time $t > 0$ , we have

Proof: (i) From (6) we note that $p _ { t } ( x , y )$ is uniformly continuous in $( x , y )$ for fixed $t > 0$ , as well as in $( x , y , t )$ for $| x - y | > \varepsilon > 0$ and $t > 0$ . By (7) it follows that $p _ { t } ^ { D } ( x , y )$ is equi-continuous in $y \in D$ for fixed $t > 0$ . To prove the continuity in $x \in D$ for fixed $t > 0$ and $y \in D$ , it is then enough to show that $P _ { x } \{ X _ { t } \in B , t \le \zeta \}$ is continuous in x for fixed $t > 0$ and $B \in B _ { D }$ . For any $h \in ( 0 , t )$ , the Markov property gives 

$$
P _ {x} \left\{X _ {t} \in B, \zeta \geq t \right\} = E _ {x} \left(P _ {X _ {h}} \left\{X _ {t - h} \in B, \zeta \geq t - h \right\}; \zeta > h\right).
$$

Thus, for any $x , y \in D$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\Big | (P _ {x} - P _ {y}) \{X _ {t} \in B, t \leq \zeta \} \Big |} \\ & {\qquad \leq (P _ {x} + P _ {y}) \{\zeta \leq h \} + \big \| \mathcal {L} _ {x} (X _ {h}) - \mathcal {L} _ {y} (X _ {h}) \big \|,} \end{array}
$$

which tends to 0 as $y  x$ and then $h  0$ . Combining the continuity in x with the equi-continuity in $y _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , we conclude that $p _ { t } ^ { D } ( x , y )$ is continuous in $( x , y ) \in D ^ { 2 }$ for fixed $t > 0$ 

To prove the symmetry in x and y, it is now enough to establish the integrated version 

$$
\int_ {C} P _ {x} \{X _ {t} \in B, \zeta > t \} d x = \int_ {B} P _ {x} \{X _ {t} \in C, \zeta > t \} d x,\tag{8}
$$

for bounded $B , C \in B _ { D }$ . Then fix any compact set $F \subset D$ . Letting $n \in \mathsf N$ , and writing $h = 2 ^ { - n } t$ and $t _ { k } = k h$ , we get by Proposition 11.2 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {C} P _ {x} \bigl \{X _ {t _ {k}} \in F,   k \leq 2 ^ {n};   X _ {t} \in B \bigr \} d x \\ = \int_ {F} \dots \int_ {F} 1 _ {C} (x _ {0})   1 _ {B} (x _ {2 ^ {n}})   \prod_ {k \leq 2 ^ {n}} p _ {h} (x _ {k - 1}, x _ {k})   d x _ {0} \dots d x _ {2 ^ {n}}. \end{array}
$$

Here the right-hand side is symmetric in the pair $( B , C )$ , by the symmetry of $p _ { h } ( x , y )$ . By dominated convergence as $n \to \infty$ , we obtain (8) with $F$ in place of $D _ { \circ }$ , and the stated version follows by monotone convergence as $F \uparrow D$ 

(ii) From the proof of Lemma 34.6, recall that ${ \mathcal L } _ { x } ( \zeta , X ) \ \stackrel { w } { \to } \ { \mathcal L } _ { a } ( 0 , X )$ as $x \to a$ with a regular $a \in \partial D$ . In particular, $\mathcal { L } _ { x } ( \zeta , X _ { \zeta } ) \overset { w } { \to } \delta _ { 0 , a }$ . By the boundedness and continuity of $p _ { t } ( x , y )$ for $| x - y | > \varepsilon > 0$ , we see from (7) that $p _ { t } ^ { D } ( x , y )  0$ ✷ 

A domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ is said to be Greenian, if either d $\geq 3$ , or if $d \leq 2$ and $P _ { x } \{ \zeta _ { D } < \infty \} = 1$ for all $x \in D$ . Since the latter probability is harmonic in $x ,$ it sufices by Lemma 34.3 to verify the stated property for a single $x \in D$ Given a Greenian domain D, we introduce the Green function 

$$
g ^ {D} (x, y) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} p _ {t} ^ {D} (x, y) d t, \quad x, y \in D.
$$

For any measure $\mu$ on $D _ { : }$ , we further introduce the associated Green potential 

$$
G ^ {D} \mu (x) = \int g ^ {D} (x, y) \mu (d y), \quad x \in D.
$$

Writing $G ^ { D } \mu = G ^ { D } f$ when $\mu ( d y ) = f ( y ) d y$ , we get by Fubini’s theorem 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\zeta} f (X _ {t})   d t = \int g ^ {D} (x, y)   f (y)   d y \\ = G ^ {D} f (x), \quad x \in D, \end{array}
$$

which identifies $g ^ { D }$ as an occupation density of the killed process. 

The next result shows that $g ^ { D }$ and $G ^ { D }$ agree with the Green function and Green potential of classical potential theory. Thus, $G ^ { D } \mu ( x )$ may be interpreted as the electrostatic potential at $x ,$ arising from a charge distribution $\mu$ in $D _ { : }$ when the boundary ∂D is grounded. 

Theorem 34.8 (Green function) For a Greenian domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ 

(i) the function $g ^ { D }$ is symmetric on $D ^ { 2 }$ 

(ii) $g ^ { D } ( x , y )$ is harmonic in $x \in D \setminus \{ y \}$ for fixed $y \in D$ , 

(iii) for regular $b \in \partial D$ 

$$
\lim _ {x \to b} g ^ {D} (x, y) = 0, \quad y \in D.
$$

The proof is straightforward when $d \geq 3$ , but for $d \ \leq \ 2$ we need two technical lemmas. We begin with a uniform estimate for large t. 

Lemma 34.9 (uniform integrability) For a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , bounded when $d \leq 2$ , we have f∞ 

$$
\lim _ {t \to \infty} \sup _ {x, y \in D} \int_ {t} ^ {\infty} p _ {s} ^ {D} (x, y) d s = 0.
$$

Proof: For $d \geq 3$ we may take $D = \mathsf { R } ^ { d } .$ , in which case the result is obvious from (6). Now let $d = 2$ . By obvious domination and scaling arguments, we may then assume that $| x | \le 1 , y = 0 , D = \{ z ; | z | \le 2 \}$ , and $t > 1$ . Writing $p _ { t } ( x ) = p _ { t } ( x , 0 )$ , we get by (7) 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} p _ {t} ^ {D} (x, 0) & \leq & p _ {t} (x) - E _ {0} \bigl \{p _ {t - \zeta} (1);   \zeta \leq t / 2 \bigr \} \\ & \leq & p _ {t} (0) - p _ {t} (1)   P _ {0} \{\zeta \leq t / 2 \} \\ & \leq & p _ {t} (0)   P _ {0} \{\zeta > t / 2 \} + p _ {t} (0) - p _ {t} (1) \\ & \leq & t ^ {- 1} P _ {0} \{\zeta > t / 2 \} + t ^ {- 2}. \end{array}
$$

As in Lemma 33.8 (ii), we have $E _ { 0 } \zeta < \infty$ , and so by Lemma 4.4 the right-hand side is integrable in $t \in [ 1 , \infty )$ . The proof for $d = 1$ is similar. ✷ 

We also need to show that bounded sets have bounded Green potential. 

Lemma 34.10 (boundedness) For a Greenian domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and bounded set $B \in B _ { D }$ , the function $G ^ { D } 1 _ { B }$ is bounded. 

Proof: By domination and scaling, along with the strong Markov property, we may take $B = \{ x ; | x | \le 1 \}$ , and show that $G ^ { D } 1 _ { B } ( 0 ) < \infty$ . For $d \geq 3$ we may further choose $D = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , in which case the result follows by a simple computation. For $d = 2$ , we may assume that $D \supset C \equiv \{ x ; | x | < 2 \}$ . Write $\sigma = \zeta _ { C } + \tau _ { B } \circ \theta _ { \zeta _ { C } }$ and $\tau _ { 0 } = 0$ , and define recursively $\tau _ { k + 1 } = \tau _ { k } + \sigma \circ \theta _ { \tau _ { k } } , k \geq 0$ Putting $b = ( 1 , 0 )$ and using the strong Markov property at the times $\tau _ { k } .$ , we get 

$$
G ^ {D} 1 _ {B} (0) = G ^ {C} 1 _ {B} (0) + G ^ {C} 1 _ {B} (b) \sum_ {k \geq 1} P _ {0} \left\{\tau_ {k} <   \zeta \right\}.
$$

Here $G ^ { C } 1 _ { B } ( 0 ) \vee G ^ { C } 1 _ { B } ( b ) < \infty$ by Lemma 34.9. Furthermore, the strong Markov property yields $P _ { 0 } \{ \tau _ { k } < \zeta \} \le p ^ { k }$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { p = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { x \in B } P _ { x } \{ \sigma < \zeta \} } \end{array}$ . Finally, we note that $p < 1$ , since $P _ { x } \{ \sigma < \zeta \}$ is harmonic and hence continuous on $B$ . The proof for $d = 1$ is similar. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 34.8: (i) This is clear by Theorem 34.7. 

(ii) If $d \geq 3$ , or if $d = 2$ and D is bounded, we see from Theorem 34.7, Lemma 34.9, and dominated convergence that $g ^ { D } ( x , y )$ is continuous in $x \in$ $D \backslash \{ y \}$ for fixed $y \in D$ . Moreover, $G ^ { D } 1 _ { B }$ has the mean-value property in $D \backslash { \bar { B } }$ for bounded $\boldsymbol { B } \in \boldsymbol { B } _ { D }$ . The latter property extends by continuity to the density $g ^ { D } ( x , y )$ , which is then harmonic in $x \in D \setminus \{ y \}$ for fixed $y \in D$ , by Lemma 34.3. 

For $d = 2$ and unbounded $D _ { : }$ , define $D _ { n } = \{ x \in D ; | x | < n \}$ , and note as before that $g ^ { D _ { n } } ( x , y )$ has the mean-value property in $x \in D _ { n } \setminus \{ y \}$ for fixed $y \in D _ { n }$ . Since $p _ { t } ^ { D _ { n } } \uparrow p _ { t } ^ { D }$ by dominated convergence, we have $g ^ { D _ { n } } \uparrow g ^ { D }$ , and so the mean-value property extends to the limit. For any $x \neq y$ in $D _ { i }$ choose a circular disk B around y with radius $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough that x $\notin \hat { B } \subset D$ . Then $\pi \varepsilon ^ { 2 } g ^ { D } ( x , y ) = G ^ { D } 1 _ { B } ( x ) < \infty$ by Lemma 34.10. Thus, Lemma 34.3 shows that even $g ^ { D } ( x , y )$ is harmonic in $x \in D \setminus \{ y \}$ 

(iii) Fix any $y \in D ,$ , and assume that $x  b \in \partial D$ . Choose a Greenian domain $D ^ { \prime } \supset D$ with $b \in D ^ { \prime }$ . Since $p _ { t } ^ { D } \leq p _ { t } ^ { D ^ { \prime } }$ , and both $p _ { t } ^ { D ^ { \prime } } ( \cdot , y )$ and $g ^ { D ^ { \prime } } ( \cdot , y )$ are continuous at $b ,$ whereas $p _ { t } ^ { D } ( x , y )  0$ by Theorem 34.7, we get $g ^ { D } ( x , y )  0$ by Theorem 1.23. ✷ 

We proceed to show that a measure is determined by its Green potential, whenever the latter is finite. An extension appears as part of Theorem 34.12. For convenience, we write 

$$
P _ {t} ^ {D} \mu (x) = \int p _ {t} ^ {D} (x, y) \mu (d y), \quad x \in D, t > 0.
$$

Theorem 34.11 (uniqueness) For measures $\mu , \nu$ on a Greenian domain $D \subset$ $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we have D CD 

$$
G ^ {D} \mu = G ^ {D} \nu <   \infty \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mu = \nu .
$$

Proof: For any $t > 0$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\int_ {0} ^ {t} (P _ {s} ^ {D} \mu) d s = G ^ {D} \mu - P _ {t} ^ {D} G ^ {D} \mu} \\ & {\qquad = G ^ {D} \nu - P _ {t} ^ {D} G ^ {D} \nu} \\ & {\qquad = \int_ {0} ^ {t} (P _ {s} ^ {D} \nu) d s.} \end{array}\tag{9}
$$

By the symmetry of $p ^ { D }$ , we further get for any measurable function $f \colon D \to { \mathsf { R } } _ { + }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \int f (x) P _ {s} ^ {D} \mu (x) d x & = \int f (x) d x \int p _ {s} ^ {D} (x, y) \mu (d y) \\ & = \int \mu (d y) \int f (x) p _ {s} ^ {D} (x, y) d x \\ & = \int P _ {s} ^ {D} f (y) \mu (d y). \end{array}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int f (x) d x \int_ {0} ^ {t} P _ {s} ^ {D} \mu (x) d s = \int_ {0} ^ {t} d s \int P _ {s} ^ {D} f (y) \mu (d y) \\ = \int \mu (d y) \int_ {0} ^ {t} P _ {s} ^ {D} f (y) d s, \end{array}
$$

and similarly for $\nu .$ By (9), we obtain 

$$
\int \mu (d y) \int_ {0} ^ {t} P _ {s} ^ {D} f (y) d s = \int \nu (d y) \int_ {0} ^ {t} P _ {s} ^ {D} f (y) d s.\tag{10}
$$

Assuming $f \in C _ { K } ^ { + } ( D )$ , we get $P _ { s } ^ { D } f \to f$ as $s \to 0$ , and so $\begin{array} { r } { t ^ { - 1 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } P _ { s } ^ { D } f d s \to f } \end{array}$ . If -<sub>we can take limits in the outer integrations of (10), we obtain</sub> $\mu f = \nu f$ , which implies $\mu = \nu$ since $f$ is arbitrary. 

To justify the argument, it is enough to show that sup $P _ { s } ^ { D } f$ is $\mu -$ and $\nu -$ integrable. Then conclude from Theorem 34.7 that $f \lesssim p _ { s } ^ { D } ( \cdot , y )$ for fixed $s > 0$ and $y \in D$ , and from Theorem 34.8 that $f \lesssim G ^ { D } f$ . Here the latter property yields $P _ { s } ^ { D } f \leqslant P _ { s } ^ { D } G ^ { D } f \leqslant G ^ { D } f$ , whereas the former property yields for any $y \in D$ and $s > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mu (G ^ {D} f) & = & \int G ^ {D} \mu (x) f (x) d x \\ & \leq & P _ {s} ^ {D} G ^ {D} \mu (y) \\ & \leq & G ^ {D} \mu (y) <   \infty , \end{array}
$$

and similarly for $\nu .$ 

Now let $\mathcal { F } _ { D }$ and $\displaystyle { \kappa _ { D } }$ be the classes of closed and compact subsets of $D _ { i }$ , and write $\mathcal { F } _ { D } ^ { r }$ and ${ \boldsymbol { \kappa } } _ { D } ^ { r }$ for the subclasses of sets with regular boundary. For any $B \in \mathcal { F } _ { D }$ , we introduce the associated hitting kernel 

$$
H _ {B} ^ {D} (x, d y) = P _ {x} \left\{\tau_ {B} <   \zeta_ {D}, X _ {\tau_ {B}} \in d y \right\}, \quad x \in D.
$$

Note that when X has initial distribution $\mu _ { : }$ , the hitting distribution of $X ^ { \zeta }$ in $B$ equals $\begin{array} { r } { \mu H _ { B } ^ { D } = \int \mu ( d x ) H _ { B } ^ { D } ( x , \cdot ) } \end{array}$ 

The next result solves the sweeping problem of classical potential theory. To avoid some technical distractions, here and below, we consider only subsets with regular boundary. In general, the irregular part of the boundary can be shown to be polar, in the sense of being a.s. avoided by a Brownian motion. Given this result, one can easily remove all regularity restrictions. 

Theorem 34.12 (sweeping and hitting) For a Greenian domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with subset $\boldsymbol { B } \in \mathcal { F } _ { D } ^ { r }$ , let μ be a bounded measure on D with $G ^ { D } \mu < \infty$ on B. Then $\mu H _ { B } ^ { D }$ is the unique measure ν on B with 

$$
G ^ {D} \mu = G ^ {D} \nu o n B.
$$

For an electrostatic interpretation, suppose we insert a grounded conductor B into a domain D with grounded boundary and charge distribution $\mu .$ . Then a charge distribution $- \mu H _ { B } ^ { D }$ arises on B. 

A lemma is needed for the proof. Here we define $g ^ { D \setminus B } ( x , y ) = 0$ when either x or y lies in B. 

Lemma 34.13 (fundamental identity) For a Greenian domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with subset $\boldsymbol { B } \in \mathcal { F } _ { D } ^ { r }$ 

$$
g ^ {D} (x, y) = g ^ {D \setminus B} (x, y) + \int_ {B} H _ {B} ^ {D} (x, d z) g ^ {D} (z, y), \quad x, y \in D.
$$

Proof: Write $\zeta = \zeta _ { D }$ and $\tau = \tau _ { B }$ . Subtracting relations (7) for the domains $D$ and $D \backslash B$ , and using the strong Markov property at $\tau$ together with Theorem 8.5, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} p _ {t} ^ {D} (x, y) - p _ {t} ^ {D \setminus B} (x, y) \\ \quad = E _ {x} \big \{p _ {t - \tau} (X _ {\tau}, y);   \tau <   \zeta \wedge t \big \} - E _ {x} \big \{p _ {t - \zeta} (X _ {\zeta}, y);   \tau <   \zeta <   t \big \} \\ \quad = E _ {x} \big \{p _ {t - \tau} (X _ {\tau}, y);   \tau <   \zeta \wedge t \big \} \\ \qquad - E _ {x} \Big (E _ {X _ {\tau}} \big \{p _ {t - \tau - \zeta} (X _ {\zeta}, y);   \zeta <   t - \tau \big \};   \tau <   \zeta \wedge t \Big) \\ \quad = E _ {x} \big \{p _ {t - \tau} ^ {D} (X _ {\tau}, y);   \tau <   \zeta \wedge t \big \}. \end{array}
$$

Integrating with respect to t yields 

$$
\begin{array}{c} g ^ {D} (x, y) - g ^ {D \setminus B} (x, y) = E _ {x} \Big \{g ^ {D} (X _ {\tau}, y); \tau <   \zeta \Big \} \\ = \int H _ {B} ^ {D} (x, d z)   g ^ {D} (z, y). \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 34.12: Since $\partial B$ is regular, we have $H _ { B } ^ { D } ( x , \cdot ) = \delta _ { x }$ for all $x \in B$ , and so by Lemma 34.13 we get for all $x \in B$ and $z \in D$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int g ^ {D} (x, y) H _ {B} ^ {D} (z, d y) = \int g ^ {D} (z, y) H _ {B} ^ {D} (x, d y) \\ = g ^ {D} (z, x). \end{array}
$$

Integrating with respect to $\mu ( d z )$ gives $G ^ { D } ( \mu H _ { B } ^ { D } ) ( x ) = G ^ { D } \mu ( x )$ , which shows that $\nu = \mu H _ { B } ^ { D }$ has the stated property. 

Now consider any measure ν on B with $G ^ { D } \mu = G ^ { D } \nu$ on B. Noting that $g ^ { D \setminus B } ( x , \cdot ) = 0$ on $B$ , whereas $H _ { B } ^ { D } ( x , \cdot )$ is supported by B, we get by Lemma 34.13 for any $x \in D$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & G ^ {D} \nu (x) = \int \nu (d z) g ^ {D} (z, x) \\ & \quad = \int \nu (d z) \int g ^ {D} (z, y) H _ {B} ^ {D} (x, d y) \\ & \quad = \int H _ {B} ^ {D} (x, d y) G ^ {D} \nu (y) \\ & \quad = \int H _ {B} ^ {D} (x, d y) G ^ {D} \mu (y). \end{array}
$$

Thus, $\mu$ determines $G ^ { D } \nu$ on D, and so ν is unique by Theorem 34.11. ✷ 

Turning to the classical equilibrium problem, we introduce for any $K \in { \mathcal { K } } _ { D }$ the last exit or quitting time 

$$
\gamma_ {K} ^ {D} = \sup \Bigl \{t <   \zeta_ {D}; X _ {t} \in K \Bigr \},
$$

along with the associated quitting kernel 

$$
L _ {K} ^ {D} (x, d y) = P _ {x} \left\{\gamma_ {K} ^ {D} > 0; X (\gamma_ {K} ^ {D}) \in d y \right\}.
$$

Theorem 34.14 (equilibrium measure and quitting, Chung) For a Greenian domain $D \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with subset $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D }$ , 

(i) there exists a measure $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ on ∂K with 

$$
L _ {K} ^ {D} (x, d y) = g ^ {D} (x, y) \mu_ {K} ^ {D} (d y), \quad x \in D,
$$

(ii) $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ is difuse when $d \geq 2$ 

(iii) when $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r } , \mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ is the unique measure μ on K with $G ^ { D } \mu = 1$ on $K$ 

Here $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ is called the equilibrium measure of K relative to D, and its total mass $C _ { K } ^ { D }$ is called the capacity of K in D. For an electrostatic interpretation, suppose we insert a conductor K with potential 1 into a domain D with grounded boundary. Then a charge distribution $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ arises on the boundary of K. 

Proof: Write $\gamma = \gamma _ { K } ^ { D }$ , and define 

$$
l _ {\varepsilon} (x) = \varepsilon^ {- 1} P _ {x} \Bigl \{0 <   \gamma \leq \varepsilon \Bigr \}, \quad \varepsilon > 0.
$$

Using Fubini’s theorem, the simple Markov property, and dominated convergence $\mathrm { a s } \ \varepsilon \to 0$ , we get for any $f \in C _ { b } ( D )$ and $x \in D$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} G ^ {D} (f l _ {\varepsilon}) (x) = E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\zeta} f (X _ {t})   l _ {\varepsilon} (X _ {t})   d t \\ \qquad = \varepsilon^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E _ {x} \Big \{f (X _ {t})   P _ {X _ {t}} \{0 <   \gamma \leq \varepsilon \}; t <   \zeta \Big \}   d t \\ \qquad = \varepsilon^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} E _ {x} \Big \{f (X _ {t}); t <   \gamma \leq t + \varepsilon \Big \}   d t \\ \qquad = \varepsilon^ {- 1} E _ {x} \int_ {(\gamma - \varepsilon) _ {+}} ^ {\gamma} f (X _ {t})   d t \\ \qquad \to E _ {x} \Big \{f (X _ {\gamma}); \gamma > 0 \Big \} \\ \qquad = L _ {K} ^ {D} f (x). \end{array}
$$

If $f$ has compact support, then for every x we may replace $f$ by the bounded, continuous function $f / g ^ { D } ( x , \cdot )$ , to get as $\varepsilon \to 0$ 

$$
\int f (y) l _ {\varepsilon} (y) d y \rightarrow \int \frac {L _ {K} ^ {D} (x , d y) f (y)}{g ^ {D} (x , y)}.\tag{11}
$$

Since the left-hand side is independent of $x _ { i }$ , the same thing is true for the measure 

$$
\mu_ {K} ^ {D} (d y) = \frac {L _ {K} ^ {D} (x , d y)}{g ^ {D} (x , y)}.\tag{12}
$$

When $d = 1$ we have $g ^ { D } ( x , x ) < \infty ,$ , and (12) is trivially equivalent to (i). If instead $d \geq 2$ , then singletons are polar, and so the measure $L _ { K } ^ { D } ( x , \cdot )$ is difuse, which implies the same property for $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ . Thus, (12) is again equivalent to (i). Furthermore, the continuity of X implies that $L _ { K } ^ { D } ( x , \cdot )$ , and then also $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ is supported by $\partial K$ 

Integrating equation (i) over $D$ yields 

$$
P _ {x} \left\{\tau_ {K} <   \zeta_ {D} \right\} = G ^ {D} \mu_ {K} ^ {D} (x), \quad x \in D,
$$

and so for $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r }$ we get $G ^ { D } \mu _ { K } ^ { D } = 1$ on K. If ν is another measure on K with $G ^ { D } \nu = 1$ on K, then $\nu = \mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ by the uniqueness in Theorem 34.12. ✷ 

Now we will see how the equilibrium measures and capacities depend on the sets $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r }$ . 

Proposition 34.15 (consistency) For a Greenian domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with subsets $K \subset B$ in $\mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r }$ , 

(i) $\mu _ { K } ^ { D } = \mu _ { B } ^ { D } H _ { K } ^ { D } = \mu _ { B } ^ { D } L _ { K } ^ { D } ,$ 

$$
\mathrm{(ii)} C _ {K} ^ {D} = \int_ {B} P _ {x} \Bigl \{\tau_ {K} <   \zeta_ {D} \Bigr \} \mu_ {B} ^ {D} (d x).
$$

Proof: By Theorem 34.12 and the defining properties of $\mu _ { B } ^ { D }$ and $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ , we have on K 

$$
\begin{array}{r} G ^ {D} \Big (\mu_ {B} ^ {D} H _ {K} ^ {D} \Big) = G ^ {D} \mu_ {B} ^ {D} \\ = 1 = G ^ {D} \mu_ {K} ^ {D}, \end{array}
$$

and so $\mu _ { B } ^ { D } H _ { K } ^ { D } = \mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ by the same result. To prove the second equality in (i), we see from Theorem 34.14 that, for any $A \in B _ { K }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \mu_ {B} ^ {D} L _ {K} ^ {D} (A) = \int \mu_ {B} ^ {D} (d x) \int_ {A} g ^ {D} (x, y) \mu_ {K} ^ {D} (d y) \\ = \int_ {A} G ^ {D} \mu_ {B} ^ {D} (y) \mu_ {K} ^ {D} (d y) = \mu_ {K} ^ {D} (A), \end{array}
$$

since $G ^ { D } \mu _ { B } ^ { D } = 1$ on $A \subset B$ . Finally ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } \Rightarrow { \mathrm { ( i i ) } }$ , since $H _ { K } ^ { D } ( x , K ) = P _ { x } \{ \tau _ { K } <$ $\zeta _ { D } \}$ ✷ 

Some basic properties of capacities and equilibrium measures follow immediately from Proposition 34.15. To explain the terminology, fix a space $S$ along with a class $\mathcal { U }$ of subsets, closed under finite unions. For any function $h \colon \mathcal { U } \to \mathsf { R }$ and sets $U , U _ { 1 } , U _ { 2 } , \dots \in \mathcal { U }$ , we define recursively the diferences 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \Delta_ {U _ {1}} h (U) = h (U \cup U _ {1}) - h (U), \\ \Delta_ {U _ {1}, \ldots , U _ {n}} h (U) = \Delta_ {U _ {n}} \bigl \{\Delta_ {U _ {1}, \ldots , U _ {n - 1}} h (U) \bigr \}, \quad n > 1, \end{array}
$$

where the diference $\Delta _ { U _ { n } }$ in the last formula is taken with respect to U. Note that the higher-order diferences $\Delta _ { U _ { 1 } , \dots , U _ { n } }$ are invariant under permutations of $U _ { 1 } , \ldots , U _ { n }$ . Say that h is alternating or completely monotone if 

$$
(- 1) ^ {n + 1} \Delta_ {U _ {1}, \dots , U _ {n}} h (U) \geq 0, \quad n \in \mathbb {N}, U, U _ {1}, U _ {2}, \dots \in \mathcal {U}.
$$

Corollary 34.16 (dependence on conductor, Choquet) For a Greenian $d o -$ main $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , 

(i) the capacity $C _ { K } ^ { D }$ is an alternating function of $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r }$ 

(ii) $\mu _ { K _ { n } } ^ { D } \overset { w } { \to } \mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ as K<sub>n</sub> K or $K _ { n } \uparrow K$ in ${ \boldsymbol { \kappa } } _ { D } ^ { r }$ 

Proof: (i) Let ψ denote the path of $X ^ { \zeta }$ , regarded as a random closed set in D. Writing C 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h _ {x} (K) = P _ {x} \bigl \{\psi K \neq \emptyset \bigr \} \\ \qquad = P _ {x} \{\tau_ {K} <   \zeta \}, \quad x \in D \setminus K, \end{array}
$$

we get by induction 

$$
\begin{array}{l} (- 1) ^ {n + 1} \Delta_ {K _ {1}, \ldots , K _ {n}} h _ {x} (K) \\ \qquad = P _ {x} \Big \{\psi K = \emptyset ,   \psi K _ {1} \neq \emptyset ,   \ldots ,   \psi K _ {n} \neq \emptyset \Big \} \geq 0, \end{array}
$$

and the assertion follows by Proposition 34.15 with $K \subset B ^ { o }$ 

(ii) Trivially, $\tau _ { K _ { n } } \downarrow \tau _ { K }$ when $K _ { n } \uparrow K$ , and $\tau _ { K _ { n } } \uparrow \tau _ { K }$ when $K _ { n } \downarrow K$ since the $K _ { n }$ are closed. In the latter case, we have also $\bigcap _ { n } \left\{ \tau _ { K _ { n } } < \zeta \right\} = \left\{ \tau _ { K } < \zeta \right\}$ by compactness. Thus, in both cases $H _ { K _ { n } } ^ { D } ( x , \cdot ) \stackrel { w } {  } H _ { K } ^ { D } ( \stackrel { . } { x } , \cdot )$ for all $x \in D \setminus \bigcup _ { n } K _ { n }$ , and by dominated convergence in Proposition 34.15 with $B ^ { o } \supset \cup _ { n } K _ { n }$ <sub>, we get</sub> $\mu _ { K _ { n } } ^ { D } \overset { w } { \to } \mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ ✷ 

The next result solves the equilibrium problem for two conductors. 

Corollary 34.17 (condenser theorem) For any disjoint sets $B \in \mathcal { F } _ { D } ^ { r }$ and $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r }$ , there exists a unique signed measure ν on $B \cup K$ with $G ^ { D } \nu = 0$ on B and $G ^ { D } \nu = 1$ on $K$ , given by 

$$
\nu = \mu_ {K} ^ {D \backslash B} - \mu_ {K} ^ {D \backslash B} H _ {B} ^ {D}.
$$

Proof: Applying Theorem 34.14 to the domain $D \backslash B$ with subset $K$ , we get $\nu = \mu _ { K } ^ { D \setminus B }$ on $K$ , and then $\nu = - \mu _ { K } ^ { D \setminus B } H _ { B } ^ { D }$ on B by Theorem 34.12. ✷ 

The symmetry between hitting and quitting kernels in Proposition 34.15 can be extended to an invariance under time reversal of the whole process. More precisely, putting $\gamma = \gamma _ { K } ^ { D }$ , we may relate the stopped process $X _ { t } ^ { \zeta } = X _ { \gamma \wedge t }$ to its reversal $\tilde { X } _ { t } ^ { \gamma } = X _ { ( \gamma - t ) + }$ . For convenience, write $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { \mu } = \int P _ { x } \mu ( d x ) } \end{array}$ , and refer to the induced measures as distributions, even when $\mu$ -<sub>is not normalized.</sub> 

Theorem 34.18 (time reversal) For a Greenian domain $D \in \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with subset $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r }$ , put $\gamma = \gamma _ { K } ^ { D }$ and $\mu = \mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ . Then $X ^ { \gamma } \overset { d } { = } \tilde { X } ^ { \gamma }$ under $P _ { \mu }$ 

Proof: Let $P _ { x }$ and $E _ { x }$ refer to the process $X ^ { \zeta }$ . Fix any times $0 = t _ { 0 } <$ $t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n }$ , and write $s _ { k } = t _ { n } - t _ { k }$ and $h _ { k } = t _ { k } - t _ { k - 1 }$ . For any continuous functions $f _ { 0 } , \ldots , f _ { n }$ with compact supports in D, define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} f ^ {\varepsilon} (x) = E _ {x} \prod_ {k \geq 0} f _ {k} (X _ {s _ {k}})   l _ {\varepsilon} (X _ {t _ {n}}) \\ = E _ {x} \prod_ {k > 1} f _ {k} (X _ {s _ {k}})   E _ {X _ {s _ {1}}} (f _ {0}   l _ {\varepsilon}) (X _ {t _ {1}}), \end{array}
$$

where the last equality holds by the Markov property at $s _ { 1 }$ . Proceeding as in the proof of Theorem 34.14, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int \Big (f ^ {\varepsilon} G ^ {D} \mu \Big) (x)   d x = \int G ^ {D} f ^ {\varepsilon} (y)   \mu (d y) \\ \to E _ {\mu} \prod_ {k} f _ {k} (\tilde {X} _ {t _ {k}} ^ {\gamma})   1 \{\gamma > t _ {n} \}. \end{array}\tag{13}
$$

On the other hand, (11) shows that the measure $l _ { \varepsilon } ( x )$ dx tends vaguely to $\mu ,$ and so by Theorem 34.7 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {x} (f _ {0}   l _ {\varepsilon}) (X _ {t _ {1}}) = \int p _ {t _ {1}} ^ {D} (x, y)   (f _ {0}   l _ {\varepsilon}) (y)   d y \\ \to \int p _ {t _ {1}} ^ {D} (x, y)   f _ {0} (y)   \mu (d y). \end{array}
$$

Using dominated convergence, Fubini’s theorem, Proposition 11.2, Theorem 34.7, and the relation $G ^ { D } \mu ( x ) = P _ { x } \{ \gamma > 0 \}$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{\int \Big (f ^ {\varepsilon} G ^ {D} \mu \Big) (x) d x}\\&{\quad \rightarrow \int G ^ {D} \mu (x) d x \int f _ {0} (y) \mu (d y) E _ {x} \prod_ {k > 0} f _ {k} (X _ {s _ {k}}) p _ {t _ {1}} ^ {D} (X _ {s _ {1}}, y)}\\&{\quad = \int f _ {0} (x _ {0}) \mu (d x _ {0}) \int \dots \int G ^ {D} \mu (x _ {n}) \prod_ {k > 0} p _ {h _ {k}} ^ {D} (x _ {k - 1}, x _ {k}) f _ {k} (x _ {k}) d x _ {k}}\\&{\quad = E _ {\mu} \prod_ {k} f _ {k} (X _ {t _ {k}}) G ^ {D} \mu (X _ {t _ {n}})}\\&{\quad = E _ {\mu} \prod_ {k} f _ {k} (X _ {t _ {k}}) 1 \{\gamma > t _ {n} \}.}\end{array}
$$

Comparing with (13), we see that $X ^ { \gamma }$ and $\tilde { X } ^ { \gamma }$ have the same finite-dimensional distributions. ✷ 

We now extend Proposition 34.15 to exhibit the dependence on Greenian domains $D \subset D ^ { \prime }$ as well. Then for fixed $K \in { \mathcal { K } } _ { D }$ , we define recursively the optional times 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tau_ {j} = \gamma_ {j - 1} + \tau_ {K} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} \circ \theta_ {\gamma_ {j - 1}}, \\ \gamma_ {j} = \tau_ {j} + \gamma_ {K} ^ {D} \circ \theta_ {\tau_ {j}}, \qquad j \geq 1, \end{array}
$$

starting with $\gamma _ { 0 } = 0$ . Thus, $\tau _ { k }$ and $\gamma _ { k }$ are the hitting or quitting times of $K _ { i }$ during the k-th excursion in D reaching K, prior to the exit time $\zeta _ { D ^ { \prime } }$ . The extended hitting and quitting kernels are given by 

$$
\begin{array}{r} H _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}} (x, \cdot) = E _ {x} \sum_ {k} \delta_ {X (\tau_ {k})}, \\ L _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}} (x, \cdot) = E _ {x} \sum_ {k} \delta_ {X (\gamma_ {k})}, \end{array}
$$

where the summations extend over all $k \in { \mathsf N }$ with $\tau _ { k } < \infty$ 

Theorem 34.19 (dependence on conductor and domain) For a Greenian domains $D \subset D ^ { \prime }$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with regular, compact subsets $K \subset K ^ { \prime }$ , 

$$
\mu_ {K} ^ {D} = \mu_ {K ^ {\prime}} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} H _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}} = \mu_ {K ^ {\prime}} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} L _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}}.
$$

Proof: Define 

$$
l _ {\varepsilon} = \varepsilon^ {- 1} P _ {x} \{\gamma_ {K} ^ {D} \in (0, \varepsilon ] \}, \quad \varepsilon > 0.
$$

Proceeding as in the proof of Theorem 34.14, we get for any $x \in D ^ { \prime }$ and $f \in C _ { b } ( D ^ { \prime } )$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} G ^ {D ^ {\prime}} (f   l _ {\varepsilon}) (x) = \varepsilon^ {- 1} E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\zeta_ {D ^ {\prime}}} f (X _ {t})   1 \Big \{\gamma_ {K} ^ {D} \circ \theta_ {t} \in (0, \varepsilon ] \Big \}   d t \\ \to L _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}} f (x). \end{array}
$$

If f has compact support in $D _ { : }$ we may conclude as before that 

$$
\int f (y) \mu_ {K} ^ {D} (d y) \leftarrow \int (f l _ {\varepsilon}) (y) d y \rightarrow \int \frac {L _ {K} ^ {D , D ^ {\prime}} (x , d y) f (y)}{g ^ {D ^ {\prime}} (x , y)},
$$

and so 

$$
L _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}} (x, d y) = g ^ {D ^ {\prime}} (x, y) \mu_ {K} ^ {D} (d y).
$$

Integrating with respect to $\mu _ { K ^ { \prime } } ^ { D ^ { \prime } }$ and noting that $G ^ { D ^ { \prime } } \mu _ { K ^ { \prime } } ^ { D ^ { \prime } } = 1$ on $K ^ { \prime } \supset K$ , we obtain the second expression for $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ 

To deduce the first expression for $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ , note that $H _ { K } ^ { D ^ { \prime } } H _ { K } ^ { D , D ^ { \prime } } = H _ { K } ^ { D , D ^ { \prime } }$ , by the strong Markov property at $\tau _ { K }$ . Combining with the second expression for $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ and using Theorem 34.18 and Proposition 34.15, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mu_ {K} ^ {D} = \mu_ {K} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} L _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}} = \mu_ {K} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} H _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}}} \\ & {\qquad = \mu_ {K ^ {\prime}} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} H _ {K} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} H _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}}} \\ & {\qquad = \mu_ {K ^ {\prime}} ^ {D ^ {\prime}} H _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}}.} \end{array}
$$

The last result enables us to study the equilibrium measure $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ and capacity $C _ { K } ^ { D }$ as functions of both D and $K$ . In particular, we obtain the following continuity and monotonicity properties. 

Corollary 34.20 (dependence on domain) For a fixed regular, compact set $K \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , the equilibrium measure $\mu _ { K } ^ { D }$ is a decreasing, upper continuous function of the Greenian domain $D \supset K$ 

Proof: The monotonicity is clear from Theorem 34.19 with $K = K ^ { \prime }$ , since 

$$
H _ {K} ^ {D, D ^ {\prime}} (x, \cdot) \geq \delta_ {x}, \quad x \in K \subset D \subset D ^ {\prime}.
$$

It remains to prove that $C _ { K } ^ { D }$ is continuous from above and below in D for fixed $K$ . By dominated convergence, it is then enough to show that $\kappa _ { K } ^ { D _ { n } }  \kappa _ { K } ^ { D }$ where $\kappa _ { K } ^ { D } = \operatorname* { s u p } \{ j ; \tau _ { j } < \infty \}$ is the number of D -excursions hitting K. 

Assuming $D _ { n } \uparrow D$ , we need to show that if $X _ { s } , X _ { t } \in K$ and $X \in D$ on $[ s , t ]$ , then $X \in D _ { n }$ on $[ s , t ]$ for suficiently large n. But this is clear, since the path is compact on the interval $[ s , t ]$ . If instead $D _ { n } \downarrow D$ , we need to show that, for any $r < s < t$ with $X _ { r } , X _ { t } \in K$ and $X _ { s } \notin D$ , we have $X _ { s } \notin D _ { n }$ for suficiently large n. But this is obvious. ✷ 

Next we show how Green capacities can be expressed in terms of random sets. Let χ denote the identity mapping on $\mathcal { F } _ { D }$ . Given any measure ν on ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { D } \setminus \{ \emptyset \}$ with $\nu \{ \chi K \neq \emptyset \} < \infty$ for all $K \in { \mathcal { K } } _ { D }$ , we may introduce a Poisson process η on ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { D } \backslash \{ \emptyset \}$ with intensity measure $\nu ,$ and form the associated random closed set $\varphi = \cup \left\{ F ; \eta \{ F \} > 0 \right\}$ in $D$ . Letting $\pi _ { \nu }$ be the distribution of $\varphi _ { i }$ , we note that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \pi_ {\nu} \{\chi K = \emptyset \} = P \Big \{\eta \{\chi K \neq \emptyset \} = 0 \Big \} \\ \qquad = \exp \Big (- \nu \{\chi K \neq \emptyset \} \Big), \quad K \in \mathcal {K} _ {D}. \end{array}
$$

Theorem 34.21 (Green capacities and random sets, Choquet) For any Greenian domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , there exists a unique measure ν on ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { D } \setminus \{ \emptyset \}$ such that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & C _ {K} ^ {D} = \nu \{\chi K \neq \emptyset \} \\ & \quad = - \log \pi_ {\nu} \{\chi K = \emptyset \}, \quad K \subset \mathcal {K} _ {D} ^ {r}. \end{array}
$$

Proof: Let $\psi$ denote the path of $X ^ { \zeta }$ in $D$ . Choose sets $K _ { n } \uparrow D$ in ${ \boldsymbol { \mathcal { K } } } _ { D } ^ { r }$ with $K _ { n } \subset K _ { n + 1 } ^ { o }$ for all $n _ { : }$ , and put $\mu _ { n } = \mu _ { K _ { n } } ^ { D } , \ \psi _ { n } = \psi K _ { n } ,$ , and $\chi _ { n } = \chi K _ { n }$ . Define 

$$
\nu_ {n} ^ {p} = \int P _ {x} \bigl \{\psi_ {p} \in \cdot , \psi_ {n} \neq \emptyset \bigr \} \mu_ {p} (d x), \quad n \leq p,\tag{14}
$$

and conclude by the strong Markov property and Proposition 34.15 that 

$$
\nu_ {n} ^ {q} \left\{\chi_ {p} \in \cdot , \chi_ {m} \neq \emptyset \right\} = \nu_ {m} ^ {p}, \quad m \leq n \leq p \leq q.\tag{15}
$$

By Corollary 8.22, there exist some measures $\nu _ { n }$ on $\mathcal { F } _ { D } , \ n \in \mathbb { N }$ , with 

$$
\nu_ {n} \{\chi_ {p} \in \cdot \} = \nu_ {n} ^ {p}, n \leq p,\tag{16}
$$

and from (15) we note that 

$$
\nu_ {n} \Bigl \{\cdot , \chi_ {m} \neq \emptyset \Bigr \} = \nu_ {m}, \quad m \leq n.\tag{17}
$$

Hence, the measures $\nu _ { n }$ agree on $\{ \chi _ { m } \neq \emptyset \}$ for $n \geq m$ , and so we may define $\nu = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } \nu _ { n }$ . By (17) we have $\nu \{ \cdot , \chi _ { n } \neq \emptyset \} = \nu _ { n }$ for all n. Assuming $K \in \mathcal { K } _ { D } ^ { r }$ with $K \subset K _ { n } ^ { o } .$ , we conclude from (14), (16), and Proposition 34.15 that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\nu \{\chi K \neq \emptyset \} = \nu_ {n} \{\chi K \neq \emptyset \}} \\ & {\qquad = \nu_ {n} ^ {n} \{\chi K \neq \emptyset \}} \\ & {\qquad = \int P _ {x} \bigl \{\psi_ {n} K \neq \emptyset \bigr \} \mu_ {n} (d x)} \\ & {\qquad = \int P _ {x} \bigl \{\tau_ {K} <   \zeta \bigr \} \mu_ {n} (d x) = C _ {K} ^ {D}.} \end{array}
$$

The uniqueness of ν is clear by a monotone-class argument. 

We next explore the connection between alternating set functions and random closed sets. As in Chapter 23, we then fix an lcscH space S with Borel σ-field and classes ${ \mathcal { G } } , { \mathcal { F } } , { \mathcal { K } }$ of open, closed, and compact sets. Write $\hat { S } = \{ B \in { \mathcal S } ; \bar { B } \in { \mathcal K } \}$ , and say that a class $\mathcal { U } \subset \hat { \mathcal { S } }$ is separating, if for any $K \in \mathcal { K }$ and $G \in { \mathcal { G } }$ with $K \subset G$ , there exists a set $U \in \mathcal { U }$ with $K \subset U \subset G$ 

For any non-decreasing function $h$ on a separating class $u \subset { \hat { S } }$ , we define the associated inner and outer capacities $h ^ { o }$ and h<sup>¯</sup> by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h ^ {o} (G) = \sup \Bigl \{h (U); U \in \mathcal {U}, \bar {U} \subset G \Bigr \}, \quad G \in \mathcal {G}, \\ \bar {h} (K) = \inf \Bigl \{h (U); U \in \mathcal {U}, U ^ {o} \supset K \Bigr \}, \quad K \in \mathcal {K}. \end{array}
$$

Those formulas clearly remain valid with replaced by any separating subclass. For any random closed set $\varphi$ in $S _ { ☉ }$ , we introduce the associated hitting function 

$$
h (B) = P \{\varphi B \neq \emptyset \} \quad B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}}.
$$

Theorem 34.22 (alternating functions and random sets, Choquet) Let S be an lcscH space with classes ${ \mathcal { G } } , { \mathcal { F } } , { \mathcal { K } }$ of open, closed, and compact sets, and let $\mathcal { U } \subset \hat { \mathcal { S } }$ be separating and closed under finite unions. Then 

(i) the hitting function h of a random closed set in S is alternating with $h = \bar { h }$ on and $h = h ^ { o }$ on $\mathcal { G }$ 

(ii) for any alternating function $p : \mathcal { U } \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ with $p ( \emptyset ) = 0$ , there exists a random closed set with hitting function h, such that $h = \bar { p }$ on $\mathcal { \kappa }$ and $h = p ^ { o }$ on $\mathcal { G }$ . 

First we clarify the algebraic part of the construction: 

Lemma 34.23 (discrete case) Let the class $\mathcal { U } \subset \hat { \mathcal { S } }$ be finite and closed under unions, and consider an alternating function $h : \mathcal { U } \to [ 0 , 1 ]$ with $h ( \emptyset ) = 0$ Then there exists a point process $\xi$ on S with 

$$
P \{\xi U > 0 \} = h (U), \quad U \in \mathcal {U}.
$$

Proof: This is obvious when $\mathcal { U } = \{ \emptyset \}$ . Proceeding by induction, assume the statement to be true when $\mathcal { U }$ is generated by up to $n - 1$ sets, and consider a class generated by n non-empty sets $B _ { 1 } , \ldots , B _ { n }$ . By scaling we may assume that $h ( B _ { 1 } \cup \dots \cup B _ { n } ) = 1$ 

For any $j \in \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , let $\mathcal { U } _ { j }$ be the class of unions formed by the sets $B _ { i } \setminus B _ { j } , i \neq j$ , and define 

$$
\begin{array}{l} h _ {j} (U) = \Delta_ {U} h (B _ {j}) \\ \qquad = h (B _ {j} \cup U) - h (B _ {j}), \quad U \in \mathcal {U} _ {j}. \end{array}
$$

Then each $h _ { j }$ is again alternating with $h _ { j } ( \emptyset ) = 0$ , and so the induction hypothesis yields a point process $\xi _ { j }$ on $\textstyle \bigcup _ { i } B _ { i } \setminus B _ { j }$ with hitting function $h _ { j }$ . Note that $h _ { j }$ <sub>remains the hitting function of</sub> $\xi _ { j }$ on all of $\mathcal { U } .$ . We further introduce a point process $\xi _ { n + 1 }$ with 

$$
P \bigcap_ {i} \left\{\xi_ {n + 1} B _ {i} > 0 \right\} = (- 1) ^ {n + 1} \Delta_ {B _ {1}, \dots , B _ {n}} h (\emptyset).
$$

For $1 \leq j \leq n + 1$ , write $\nu _ { j }$ for the restriction of $\mathcal { L } ( \xi _ { j } )$ to the set $A _ { j } \ =$ $\cap _ { i < j } \{ \mu B _ { i } \ > \ 0 \}$ , and put $\begin{array} { r } { \nu = \sum _ { j } \nu _ { j } } \end{array}$ . Choose $\xi$ to be the canonical point <sub>process on S with distribution ν.</sub> 

To see that $\xi$ has hitting function h, we note that for any $U \in \mathcal { U }$ and $j \le n$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \nu_ {j} \{\mu U > 0 \} & = P \Big \{\xi_ {j} B _ {1} > 0, \ldots , \xi_ {j} B _ {j - 1} > 0, \xi_ {j} U > 0 \Big \} \\ & = (- 1) ^ {j + 1} \Delta_ {B _ {1}, \ldots , B _ {j - 1}, U} h _ {j} (\emptyset) \\ & = (- 1) ^ {j + 1} \Delta_ {B _ {1}, \ldots , B _ {j - 1}, U} h (B _ {j}). \end{array}
$$

It remains to show that, for any $U \in \mathcal { U } \setminus \{ \emptyset \}$ , 

$$
\sum_ {j \leq n} (- 1) ^ {j + 1} \Delta_ {B _ {1}, \dots , B _ {j - 1}, U} h (B _ {j}) + (- 1) ^ {n + 1} \Delta_ {B _ {1}, \dots , B _ {n}} h (\emptyset) = h (U),
$$

which is clear from the fact that 

$$
\Delta_ {B _ {1}, \dots , B _ {j - 1}, U} h (B _ {j}) = \Delta_ {B _ {1}, \dots , B _ {j}, U} h (\emptyset) + \Delta_ {B _ {1}, \dots , B _ {j - 1}, U} h (\emptyset).
$$

Proof of Theorem 34.22: The direct assertion can be proved in the same way as Corollary 34.16. Conversely, let and $p$ be such as stated. By Lemma A6.3 we may take $\mathcal { U }$ to be countable, say ${ \mathcal { U } } = \{ U _ { 1 } , U _ { 2 } , . . . \}$ . For every $n _ { \colon }$ , let $\mathcal { U } _ { n }$ be the class of unions of sets from $U _ { 1 } , \ldots , U _ { n }$ . By Lemma 34.23 there exist some point processes $\xi _ { 1 } , \xi _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ . on $S$ , such that 

$$
P \{\xi_ {n} U > 0 \} = p (U), \quad U \in \mathcal {U} _ {n}, n \in \mathbb {N}.
$$

The space $\mathcal { F }$ is compact by Theorem A6.1, and so Theorem 23.2 yields a random closed set $\varphi$ in $S$ with supp $\xi _ { n } \ \overset { d } { \to } \ \varphi$ along a sub-sequence $N ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { N }$ Writing $h _ { n }$ and $h$ for the associated hitting functions, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & h (B ^ {o}) \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \in N ^ {\prime}} h _ {n} (B) \\ & \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n \in N ^ {\prime}} h _ {n} (B) = h (\bar {B}), \quad B \in \hat {\mathcal {S}}, \end{array}
$$

and in particular, 

$$
h (U ^ {o}) \leq p (U) \leq h (\bar {U}), \quad U \in \mathcal {U}.
$$

Using the stronger separation property $K \subset U ^ { o } \subset \bar { U } \subset G$ , we may easily conclude that $h = p ^ { o }$ on $\mathcal { G }$ and $h = \bar { p }$ on $\kappa$ ✷ 

Turning to a discussion of super-harmonic and excessive functions, fix a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and let $T _ { t } = T _ { t } ^ { D }$ be the transition operators of a Brownian motion X in D, killed on the boundary ∂D. A function $f \geq 0$ on $D$ is said to be excessive, if $T _ { t } f \leq f$ for all $t > 0$ and $T _ { t } f  f$ as $t  0$ . Then clearly $T _ { t } f \uparrow f$ . Note that if f is excessive, then $f ( X )$ is a super-martingale under $P _ { x }$ for every $x \in D$ . The basic example of an excessive function is the Green potential $G ^ { D } \nu$ of a measure ν on a Greenian domain $D ,$ provided this potential is finite. 

Though excessivity is defined globally in terms of the operators $T _ { t } ^ { D }$ , it is in fact a local property. For a precise statement, say that a measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $D$ is super-harmonic, if for any ball B in D with center x, the average of $f$ over the sphere ∂B is bounded by $f ( x )$ . As we shall see, it is enough to consider balls in D of radius less than an arbitrary $\varepsilon > 0$ . Recall that $f$ is lower semi-continuous if $x _ { n } \to x$ implies lim in $\operatorname { f } _ { n } f ( x _ { n } ) \geq f ( x )$ 

Theorem 34.24 (super-harmonic and excessive functions, Doob) For any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) f is excessive, 

(ii) f is super-harmonic and lower semi-continuous. 

Our proof is based on two lemmas, beginning with a relationship between the two continuity properties. 

Lemma 34.25 (semi-continuity) Let $f \geq 0$ be a measurable function on a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , such that $T _ { t } f \leq f$ for all $t > 0$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) f is excessive, 

(ii) f is lower semi-continuous. 

Proof: Assume (i), and let $x _ { n } \to x$ in D. By Theorem 34.7 and Fatou’s lemma, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} T _ {t} f (x) = \int p _ {t} ^ {D} (x, y)   f (y)   d y \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} \int p _ {t} ^ {D} (x _ {n}, y)   f (y)   d y \\ \quad = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} T _ {t} f (x _ {n}) \\ \quad \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {n \to \infty} f (x _ {n}), \end{array}
$$

and as $t  0$ we get $f ( x ) \leq \operatorname* { l i m } \operatorname* { i n f } _ { n } f ( x _ { n } )$ , which implies (ii). 

Next assume (ii). Using the continuity of X and Fatou’s lemma, we get as $t  0$ along an arbitrary sequence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (x) = E _ {x} f (X _ {0}) \\ \leq E _ {x} \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {t \to 0} f (X _ {t}) \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {t \to 0} E _ {x} f (X _ {t}) \\ = \operatorname * {l i m i n f} _ {t \to 0} T _ {t} f (x) \\ \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {t \to 0} T _ {t} f (x) \leq f (x). \end{array}
$$

Thus, $T _ { t } f \to f ,$ , proving (i). 

For smooth functions, the super-harmonic property is easily described. 

Lemma 34.26 (smooth functions) For any function $f \geq 0$ in ${ C } _ { D } ^ { 2 }$ , 

f is super-harmonic Δf 0 f is excessive. 

Proof: By Itˆo’s formula, the process 

$$
M _ {t} = f (X _ {t}) - \frac {1}{2} \int_ {0} ^ {t} \Delta f (X _ {s}) d s, \quad t \in [ 0, \zeta),\tag{18}
$$

is a continuous local martingale. Now fix any closed ball $B \subset D$ with center x, and write $\tau = \tau _ { \partial B }$ . Since $E _ { x } \tau < \infty$ , we get by dominated convergence 

$$
f (x) = E _ {x} f (X _ {\tau}) - \frac {1}{2} E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \Delta f (X _ {s}) d s.
$$

Thus, $f$ is super-harmonic if the last expectation is $\leq 0$ , and the first assertion follows. 

To prove the last implication, we note that the exit time $\zeta = \tau _ { \partial D }$ is predictable, say with announcing sequence $\left( \tau _ { n } \right)$ . If $\Delta f \le 0$ , we get from (18) by optional sampling 

$$
E _ {x} \Big \{f (X _ {t \wedge \tau_ {n}}); t <   \zeta \Big \} \leq E _ {x} f (X _ {t \wedge \tau_ {n}}) \leq f (x).
$$

Hence, Fatou’s lemma yields $E _ { x } \{ f ( X _ { t } ) ; t < \zeta \} = T _ { t } f ( x )$ , and so f is excessive by Lemma 34.25. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 34.24: If f is excessive or super-harmonic, then so is $f \wedge n$ for every $n > 0$ by Lemma 34.25. The converse statement is also true, by monotone convergence, and since the lower semi-continuity is preserved by increasing limits. Thus, we may henceforth assume that f is bounded. 

Now assume (i). By Lemma 34.25 it is then lower semi-continuous, and it remains to prove that f is super-harmonic. Since the property $T _ { t } f \leq f$ is preserved as we pass to a sub-domain, we may take D to be bounded. For each $h > 0$ , we define $q _ { h } = h ^ { - 1 } ( f - T _ { h } f )$ and $f _ { h } = G ^ { D } q _ { h }$ . Since $f$ and D are bounded, we have $G ^ { D } f < \infty$ , and so $\begin{array} { r } { f _ { h } = h ^ { - 1 } \int _ { 0 } ^ { h } T _ { s } f d s } \end{array}$ f. By the strong -<sub>Markov property, we further see that for any optional time</sub> $\tau < \zeta ,$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E _ {x} f _ {h} (X _ {\tau}) = E _ {x} E _ {X _ {\tau}} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} q _ {h} (X _ {s}) d s \\ & \qquad = E _ {x} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} q _ {h} (X _ {s + \tau}) d s \\ & \qquad = E _ {x} \int_ {\tau} ^ {\infty} q _ {h} (X _ {s}) d s \leq f _ {h} (x). \end{array}
$$

In particular, $f _ { h }$ is super-harmonic for each h, and so by monotone convergence the same property holds for $f .$ 

Conversely, assume (ii). To prove (i), it sufices by Lemma 34.25 to show that $T _ { t } f \leq f$ for all t. Then fix a spherically symmetric probability density $\psi \in C ^ { \infty } ( \mathsf { R } ^ { d } )$ supported by the unit ball, and put $\psi _ { h } ( x ) = h ^ { - d } \psi ( x / h )$ for each $h > 0$ . Writing $\rho$ for the Euclidean metric in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we define $f _ { h } = \psi _ { h } * f$ on the set $D _ { h } = \{ x \in D ; ~ \rho ( x , D ^ { c } ) > h \}$ . Note that $f _ { h } \in C ^ { \infty } ( D _ { h } )$ for all h, that $f _ { h }$ is super-harmonic on $D _ { h }$ , and that $f _ { h } \uparrow f$ . By Lemma 34.26 and monotone convergence, we conclude that $f$ is excessive on each set $D _ { h }$ . Letting $\zeta _ { h }$ be the first exit time from $D _ { h }$ , we obtain 

$$
E _ {x} \left\{f (X _ {t}); t <   \zeta_ {h} \right\} \leq f (x), \quad h > 0.
$$

As $h  0$ we have $\zeta _ { h } \uparrow \zeta ,$ and hence $\{ t < \zeta _ { h } \} \ \uparrow \ \{ t < \zeta \}$ . By monotone convergence, we get $T _ { t } f ( x ) \leq f ( x )$ ✷ 

Now we prove the remarkable fact that, although an excessive function f may not be continuous, the super-martingale $f ( X )$ is a.s. continuous under $P _ { x }$ for every x. 

Theorem 34.27 (continuity, Doob) Let f be an excessive function on a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and let X be a Brownian motion, killed upon hitting ∂D. Then the process $f ( X _ { t } )$ is a.s. continuous on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ 

Our proof is based on the following invariance under time reversal, for a stationary version of Brownian motion. Though no such process exists in the usual probabilistic sense, we do have the following: 

Lemma 34.28 (time reversal, Doob) Let $P _ { x }$ be the distribution of Brownian motion X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ starting at $x ,$ , and put $\bar { P } = \mathcal { J } P _ { x }$ dx. Then for any $c > 0$ , these processes have the same distribution under $\bar { P }$ : 

$$
Y _ {t} ^ {c} = X _ {t}, \quad \tilde {Y} _ {t} ^ {c} = X _ {c - t}, \qquad t \in [ 0, c ].
$$

Proof: Introduce the processes 

$$
\begin{array}{l} B _ {t} = X _ {t} - X _ {0}, \\ \tilde {B} _ {t} = X _ {c - t} - X _ {c}, \qquad t \in [ 0, c ], \end{array}
$$

and note that $B$ and $\tilde { B }$ are Brownian motions on $[ 0 , c ]$ under each $P _ { x }$ . Fix any measurable function $f \geq 0$ on $C _ { [ 0 , c ] , \mathsf { R } ^ { d } }$ . By Fubini’s theorem and the invariance of Lebesgue measure, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \bar {E} f (\tilde {Y} ^ {c}) = \bar {E} f \Big (X _ {0} - \tilde {B} _ {c} + \tilde {B} \Big) \\ \qquad = \int E _ {x} f \Big (x - \tilde {B} _ {c} + \tilde {B} \Big) d x \\ \qquad = \int E _ {0} f \Big (x - \tilde {B} _ {c} + \tilde {B} \Big) d x \\ \qquad = E _ {0} \int f \Big (x - \tilde {B} _ {c} + \tilde {B} \Big) d x \\ \qquad = E _ {0} \int f (x + \tilde {B}) d x \\ \qquad = \int E _ {x} f (Y ^ {c}) d x \\ \qquad = \bar {E} f (Y ^ {c}). \end{array}
$$

Proof of Theorem 34.27: Since $f \wedge n$ is again excessive for each $n > 0$ by Theorem 34.24, we may assume that $f$ is bounded. As in the proof of the same theorem, we may then approximate $f$ by smooth, excessive functions $f _ { h } \uparrow f$ on suitable subdomains $D _ { h } \uparrow D$ . Since $f _ { h } ( X )$ is a continuous supermartingale, up to the exit time $\zeta _ { h }$ from $D _ { h }$ , Theorem 9.33 shows that $f ( X )$ is a.s. right-continuous on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ , under any initial distribution $\mu .$ Using the Markov property at rational times, we may extend the a.s. right-continuity to the random time set $T = \{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } \in D \}$ 

To strengthen the result to a.s. continuity on $T ,$ , we note that $f ( X )$ is right-continuous on $T , \mathrm { a . e . } \bar { P } .$ . By Lemma 34.28, it follows that $f ( X )$ is also left-continuous on $T ,$ , a.e. P<sup>¯</sup>. Thus, $f ( X )$ is continuous on $T ,$ a.s. $P _ { \mu }$ for arbitrary $\mu \ll \lambda ^ { d }$ . Since $P _ { \mu } \circ X _ { h } ^ { - 1 } \ll \lambda ^ { d }$ for any $\mu$ and $h > 0$ , we conclude that $f ( X )$ is a.s. continuous on $T \cap [ h , \infty )$ for any $h > 0$ 0. Combining with the right-continuity at 0, we obtain the asserted continuity on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ ✷ 

If $f$ is excessive, then $f ( X )$ is a super-martingale under $P _ { x }$ for every $x ,$ and hence has a Doob–Meyer decomposition $f ( X ) = M - A$ . It is remarkable that we can choose $A$ to be a continuous additive functional (CAF) of X independent of x. A similar situation was encountered in connection with Theorem 29.23. 

Theorem 34.29 (excessive functions and additive functionals, Meyer) Let f be an excessive function on a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and let $P _ { x }$ be the distribution of Brownian motion X in $D _ { \cdot }$ , killed upon hitting ∂D. Then 

$$
M = f (X) + A a. s. P _ {x}, \quad x \in D,
$$

for some a.s. unique processes $A$ and M, where 

(i) A is a CAF of X, 

(ii) M is a continuous local $P _ { x } – m a r t i n g a l e$ on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ , for every $x \in D$ 

The main dificulty of the proof is to construct a version of the process A that compensates $- f ( X )$ under every measure $P _ { \mu }$ . Here the following lemma is helpful. 

Lemma 34.30 (universal compensation) Consider an excessive function f on a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , a distribution $m \sim \lambda ^ { d }$ on $D$ , and a $P _ { m } { - } c o m p e n s a t o r$ $A$ of $- f ( X )$ on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ . Then for any distribution $\mu$ and constant $h > 0$ , the process A $\theta _ { h }$ is a $P _ { \mu }$ -compensator of $- f ( X \circ \theta _ { h } )$ on $[ 0 , \zeta \circ \theta _ { h } )$ 

In other words, the process $M _ { t } = f ( X _ { t } ) + A _ { t - h } \circ \theta _ { h }$ is a local $P _ { \mu } { \mathrm { - m a r t i n g a l e } }$ on $[ h , \zeta )$ for every $\mu$ and h. 

Proof: For any bounded $P _ { m } \mathrm { { - m a r t i n g a l e } }$ M and initial distribution $\mu \ll m$ we note that $M$ is also a $P _ { \mu }$ -martingale. To see this, write $k = d \mu / d m$ , and note that $P _ { \mu } = k ( X _ { 0 } ) \cdot P _ { m }$ . It is equivalent to show that $N _ { t } = k ( X _ { 0 } ) M _ { t }$ is a $P _ { m } \mathrm { { - m a r t i n g a l e } } .$ , which is clear since $k ( X _ { 0 } )$ is $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ -measurable with mean 1. 

Now fix any distribution $\mu$ and constant $h > 0$ . To prove the stated property of $A .$ , it is enough to show that, for any bounded $P _ { m } \mathrm { { - m a r t i n g a l e } }$ M, the process $N _ { t } = M _ { t - h } \circ \theta _ { h }$ is a $P _ { \mu }$ -martingale on $[ h , \infty )$ . Then fix any times $s < t$ and sets $F \in \mathcal { F } _ { h }$ and $G \in \mathcal { F } _ { s }$ . Using the Markov property at $h .$ , and noting that $P _ { \mu } \circ X _ { h } ^ { - 1 } \ll m$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {\mu} \Big (M _ {t} \circ \theta_ {h};   F \cap \theta_ {h} ^ {- 1} G \Big) = E _ {\mu} \Big \{E _ {X _ {h}} (M _ {t}; G); F \Big \} \\ = E _ {\mu} \Big \{E _ {X _ {h}} (M _ {s}; G); F \Big \} \\ = E _ {\mu} \Big (M _ {s} \circ \theta_ {h};   F \cap \theta_ {h} ^ {- 1} G \Big). \end{array}
$$

Hence, a monotone-class argument yields $E _ { \mu } \Big ( M _ { t } \circ \theta _ { h } \Big | \mathscr { F } _ { h + s } \Big ) = M _ { s } \circ \theta _ { h }$ a.s. ✷ 

Proof of Theorem 34.29: Let $A ^ { \mu }$ be the $P _ { \mu } { \mathrm { - c o m p e n s a t o r } }$ of $- f ( X )$ on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ and note that $A ^ { \mu }$ is a.s. continuous, e.g. by Theorem 19.11. Fix any distribution m $\sim \lambda ^ { d }$ on D, and conclude from Lemma 34.30 that $A ^ { m } \circ \theta _ { h }$ is a $P _ { \mu }$ -compensator of $- f ( X \circ \theta _ { h } )$ on $[ 0 , \zeta \circ \theta _ { h } )$ , for any $\mu$ and $h > 0$ . Since this remains true for the process $A _ { t + h } ^ { \mu } - A _ { h } ^ { \mu }$ , we get for any $\mu$ and $h > 0$ 

$$
A _ {t} ^ {\mu} = A _ {h} ^ {\mu} + A _ {t - h} ^ {m} \circ \theta_ {h}, t \geq h, \mathrm{a.s.} P _ {\mu}.\tag{19}
$$

Restricting h to the positive rationals, we define 

$$
A _ {t} = \lim _ {h \to 0} A _ {t - h} ^ {m} \circ \theta_ {h}, \quad t > 0,
$$

whenever the limit exists and is continuous and non-decreasing with $A _ { 0 } = 0 .$ , and put $A = 0$ otherwise. By (19) we have $A = A ^ { \mu }$ a.s. $P _ { \mu }$ for every $\mu ,$ , and so A is a $P _ { \mu }$ -compensator of $- f ( X )$ on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ for every $\mu .$ For each $h > 0$ , it follows by Lemma 34.30 that $A \circ \theta _ { h }$ is a $P _ { \mu }$ -compensator of $- f ( X \circ \theta _ { h } )$ on $[ 0 , \zeta \circ \theta _ { h } )$ and since this is also true for the process $A _ { t + h } - A _ { h }$ , we get $A _ { t + h } = A _ { h } + A _ { t } \circ \theta _ { h }$ a.s. $P _ { \mu }$ . Thus, A is a CAF. ✷ 

We can now establish a probabilistic version of the classical Riesz decomposition. To avoid some obscuring technicalities, we restrict our attention to locally bounded functions f. By the greatest harmonic minorant of f we mean a harmonic function $h \leq f .$ , dominating all other such functions. Recall that the potential $U _ { A }$ of a CAF A of X is given by $U _ { A } ( x ) = E _ { x } A _ { \infty }$ 

Theorem 34.31 (Riesz decomposition) Let $f \geq 0$ be a locally bounded function on a domain $D \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and let X be a Brownian motion in $D$ , killed upon hitting ∂D. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) f is excessive, 

(ii) $f = U _ { A } + h$ for a CAF A of X and a harmonic function $h \geq 0$ 

(iii) A is the compensator $o f - f ( \boldsymbol { X } )$ , 

(iv) h is the greatest harmonic minorant of $f .$ . 

A similar result for uniformly α -excessive functions of an arbitrary Feller process was obtained in Theorem 29.23. From the classical Riesz representation on Greenian domains, we know that $U _ { A }$ may also be written as the Green potential of a unique measure $\nu _ { A }$ , so that $f = G ^ { D } \nu _ { A } + h$ . In the special case where $D = \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ with $d \geq 3$ , we recall from Theorem 29.21 that $\nu _ { A } B = \bar { E } ( \mathrm { 1 } _ { B } { \cdot } A ) _ { 1 }$ A similar representation holds in the general case. 

Proof of Theorem 34.31: First let A be a CAF with $U _ { A } < \infty$ . By the additivity of A and the Markov property of X, we get for any $t > 0$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & U _ {A} (x) = E _ {x} A _ {\infty} = E _ {x} \big (A _ {t} + A _ {\infty} \circ \theta_ {t} \big) \\ & \qquad = E _ {x} A _ {t} + E _ {x} E _ {X _ {t}} A _ {\infty} \\ & \qquad = E _ {x} A _ {t} + T _ {t} U _ {A} (x). \end{array}
$$

By dominated convergence, $E _ { x } A _ { t } \downarrow 0$ as $t  0$ , and so $U _ { A }$ is excessive. Even $U _ { A } + h$ is then excessive for any harmonic function $h \geq 0$ 

Conversely, let f be excessive and locally bounded. By Theorem 34.29 there exists a CAF A, such that $M = f ( X ) + A$ is a continuous local martingale on $[ 0 , \zeta )$ . For any localizing and announcing sequence $\tau _ { n } \uparrow \zeta$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} f (x) = E _ {x} M _ {0} = E _ {x} M _ {\tau_ {n}} \\ \qquad = E _ {x} f (X _ {\tau_ {n}}) + E _ {x} A _ {\tau_ {n}} \\ \qquad \geq E _ {x} A _ {\tau_ {n}}. \end{array}
$$

As $n \to \infty$ , we obtain $U _ { A } \leq f$ by monotone convergence. 

By the additivity of A and the Markov property of X, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E _ {x} \big (A _ {\infty} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big) = A _ {t} + E _ {x} \big (A _ {\infty} \circ \theta_ {t} \big | \mathcal {F} _ {t} \big) \\ & \qquad = A _ {t} + E _ {X _ {t}} A _ {\infty} \\ & \qquad = M _ {t} - f (X _ {t}) + U _ {A} (X _ {t}). \end{array}\tag{20}
$$

Writing $h = f - U _ { A }$ , it follows that $h ( X )$ is a continuous local martingale. Since h is locally bounded, we conclude by optional sampling and dominated convergence that $h$ has the mean-value property. Thus, h is harmonic by Lemma 34.3. 

To prove the uniqueness of A, suppose that f has also a representation $U _ { B } + k$ for some CAF B and harmonic function $k \geq 0$ . Proceeding as in (20), we get 

$$
A _ {t} - B _ {t} = E _ {x} \left(A _ {\infty} - B _ {\infty} \mid \mathcal {F} _ {t}\right) + h (X _ {t}) - k (X _ {t}), \quad t \geq 0,
$$

which shows that $A - B$ is a continuous local martingale. Hence, Proposition 18.2 yields $A = B { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ 

To prove (iv), consider any harmonic minorant $k \geq 0$ . Since $f - k$ is again excessive and locally bounded, it has a representation $U _ { B } + l$ for some CAF B and harmonic function l. But then $f = U _ { B } + k + l$ , and so $A = B$ a.s. and $h = k + l \geq k$ ✷ 

For a suficiently regular measure ν on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , we may construct an associated CAF A of Brownian motion X, such that $A$ increases only when X visits the support of $\nu .$ . This clearly extends the notion of local time. For convenience we may write $G ^ { D } ( 1 _ { D } \nu ) = G ^ { D } \nu$ 

Proposition 34.32 (additive functional induced by measure) Let the measure ν on $\mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ be such that $U ( 1 _ { D } \nu )$ is bounded for every bounded domain D. Then 

(i) there exists a CAF A of Brownian motion $X _ { \cdot }$ , such that for any D 

$$
E _ {x} A _ {\zeta_ {D}} = G ^ {D} \nu (x), \quad x \in D,
$$

(ii) ν and A determine each other a.s. uniquely, 

(iii) supp $A \subset \left\{ t \geq 0 ; X _ { t } \in \operatorname { s u p p } \nu \right\} \mathrm { ~ } a . s .$ 

The proof is straightforward, given the classical Riesz decomposition, and we indicate only the main steps. 

Proof: (i) (ii) A simple calculation shows that $G ^ { D } \nu$ is excessive for any bounded domain D. Since $G ^ { D } \nu \leq U ( 1 _ { D } \nu )$ , it is also bounded. Hence, Theorem 34.31 yields a CAF $A _ { D }$ of X on $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ and a harmonic function $h _ { D } \geq 0$ , such that $G ^ { D } \nu = U _ { A _ { D } } + h _ { D }$ . In fact, $h _ { D } = 0$ by Riesz’ theorem. 

Now consider another bounded domain $D ^ { \prime } \supset D$ . We claim that $G ^ { D ^ { \prime } } \nu - G ^ { D } \nu$ is harmonic on D. This is clear from the analytic definitions, and it also follows, under a regularity condition, from Lemma 34.13. Since $A _ { D }$ and $A _ { D ^ { \prime } }$ are compensators of $- G ^ { D } \nu ( X )$ and $- G ^ { D ^ { \prime } } \nu ( X )$ , respectively, $A _ { D } - A _ { D ^ { \prime } }$ is a martingale on $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ , and so $A _ { D } = A _ { D ^ { \prime } }$ a.s. up to time $\zeta _ { D }$ . Now choose some bounded domains $D _ { n } \uparrow \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , and define $A = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { n } A _ { D _ { n } } ,$ so that $A = A _ { D } { \mathrm { ~ a . s } }$ . on $[ 0 , \zeta _ { D } )$ for all D. It is easy to see that A is a CAF of X, and that (i) holds for any bounded domain D. The uniqueness of ν is clear from the uniqueness in the classical Riesz decomposition. 

(iii) Note that $G ^ { D } \nu$ is harmonic on $D \backslash$ supp ν for every D, so that $G ^ { D } \nu ( X )$ is a local martingale on the predictable set $\left\{ t < \zeta _ { D } ; X _ { t } \notin \mathrm { s u p p } \nu \right\}$ ✷
