Chapter 35 

# Stochastic Diferential Geometry

Semi-martingales, bilinear forms, pull-back, covariation process, semimartingale integral, connection, chain rule, diferential operators and Christofel symbols, martingale criteria, induced connections, afine and convex maps, geodesics and martingale criteria, local drift and difusion rates, sub-manifolds and projection, difusions, Riemannian metric and connection, isotropic martingales, Brownian motion, harmonic maps, L´evy processes in Lie groups 

Just as diferential geometry deals with the geometric properties of smooth curves and other objects in a diferential manifold S, its stochastic counterpart involves a study of suficiently regular processes in S, which may include the development of a relevant stochastic calculus. We may think of the manifold as a smooth surface of finite dimension n, embedded in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space. Though such an embedding always exists, it is far from unique and may even allow some smooth bending and stretching. Thus, we insist that all objects on S are described intrinsically in terms of the local properties of the surface itself. Indeed, though the diferential structure of S can be described in terms of some local coordinates in a small neighborhood of an arbitrary point, the actual choice of coordinates is fairly arbitrary, and no properties are allowed to depend on any specific choice. 

When developing stochastic calculus in a Euclidean space, we may start with Brownian motion, then proceed to continuous martingales, via a stochastic integration or random time change, and eventually reach the general semimartingales via Itˆo’s formula. In a general diferential manifold S we must proceed in the opposite direction, since there is no natural way to define a Brownian motion or some more general martingales in S. Indeed, to define martingales we need to endow S with a connection , and for the notion of Brownian motion in S we need even a Riemannian metric ρ. Following such a program leads to an amazingly rich and beautiful theory, which has the further advantage of providing some deeper insight into the classical notions of martingales and stochastic calculus. 

In this chapter, we consider first the class of general semi-martingales in S, along with their covariation processes. We then introduce connections on S, and study the associated classes of martingales and geodesics. Finally, we consider a general Riemannian metric with associated canonical connection, which allow us to define a Brownian motion and related processes in S. Though no semi-martingale decomposition is possible in an abstract manifold S, owing to the lack of any additive structure, we may still define some local characteristics of a semi-martingale in $S ,$ describing the intrinsic drift and difusion rates of the process. In particular, a martingale is then a process with drift 0. 

Though the mentioned notions are all intrinsic, they can be justified by some natural embedding and projection properties. Then recall that every diferential manifold S can be embedded as a smooth sub-manifold of a suitable Euclidean space. For a Riemannian manifold S, we can even choose the embedding to preserve the Riemannian structure.<sup>1</sup> In both cases, the relevant martingale and rate properties agree with the corresponding extrinsic notions. The same thing is true for the appropriate projection properties. 

Though the reader is assumed to be at least a vaguely familiar with differential geometry, some basic notions and results are reviewed here and in Appendix 7. Write $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { S } }$ for the class of smooth functions $f , g , \ldots$ on $S _ { i }$ , and let $T _ { S }$ be the space of smooth (tangent) vector fields $u , v , . . .$ . on S. A form is a smooth function $\alpha$ on the dual space of cotangent vectors $T _ { S } ^ { * }$ , and a bilinear form is a smooth function b on the dual $( T _ { S } ^ { * } ) ^ { \otimes \bar { 2 } }$ of the product space $T _ { S } ^ { 2 }$ . Any simple or bilinear forms can be written as finite sums<sup>2</sup>

\alpha = a _ {i} d f ^ {i}, \qquad b = b _ {i j} (d f ^ {i} \otimes d g ^ {j}),

for suitable $a _ { i } , b _ { i j } , f ^ { i } , g ^ { j } \in \mathcal { S }$ , where $d f ( u ) = u f$ , and we note that in local coordinates $d f = ( \partial _ { i } f ) ( x ) d x ^ { i }$ . Further note that $( \alpha \otimes \beta ) ( u , v ) = ( \alpha u ) ( \beta v )$

Before proceeding to the intrinsic theory of martingales in a diferentiable manifold, we insert a somewhat informal discussion<sup>8</sup> of semi-martingales in a smooth sub-manifold S of a Euclidean space ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ , motivating the general results in Theorems 35.8, 35.16 35.17, and 35.20. We may then define a martingale in $S$ as an S-valued semi-martingale $X$ in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ with canonical decomposition $M + A$ , where locally for $X _ { t } = x \in S$ , the martingale increment $d M _ { t }$ is restricted to the tangent space $T _ { x } ,$ whereas the compensating part $d A _ { t }$ is perpendicular to $T _ { x }$ . The role of the drift term A is to ensure that the process X will stay in the manifold. 

Given a semi-martingale X in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ , we define the projection ${ \hat { X } } = \pi _ { S } ( X )$ onto $S$ starting at $x \in S$ as the unique strong solution to the Fisk–Stratonovich SDE 

$$
\hat {X} _ {t} ^ {i} = x ^ {i} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} P _ {j} ^ {i} (\hat {X} _ {s}) \circ d X _ {s} ^ {j}, t \geq 0, i \leq n,
$$

where $P _ { j } ^ { i } ( x )$ denotes the projection<sup>9</sup> of the j-th unit vector in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ onto the tangent space $T _ { x } \mathbf { \bar { S } }$ . Note that we must use FS rather than Itˆo integrals to ensure that the solution $\hat { X }$ will stay in the manifold. It is suggestive to use the shorthand notation 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d \hat {X} _ {t} = P _ {T} (\hat {X} _ {t}) \circ d X _ {t}} \\ & {\quad = P _ {T} (\hat {X} _ {t}) d X _ {t} - \frac {1}{2} d \Big [ Q _ {T} (\hat {X}), X \Big ] _ {t},} \end{array}
$$

where $P _ { T } ( x )$ and $Q _ { T } ( x )$ denote the complementary projections onto the tangent space $T _ { x }$ and its orthogonal complement $T _ { x } ^ { \perp }$ . Here the second expression is the Itˆo form of the same projection, which shows that if X is a local martingale in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ , then $\hat { X }$ is a martingale in S. The two covariance processes are related by 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {d [ \hat {X}, \hat {X} ] _ {t} = d \Big [ P _ {T} (\hat {X}) \cdot X, P _ {T} (\hat {X}) \cdot X \Big ] _ {t}} \\ & {\quad = P _ {T} (\hat {X} _ {t}) d [ X, X ] _ {t} P _ {T} (\hat {X} _ {t})} \\ & {\quad = P _ {T} ^ {2} (\hat {X} _ {t}) d [ X, X ] _ {t},} \end{array}
$$

which exhibits the covariance process $\hat { C } _ { t } = [ \hat { X } , \hat { X } ] _ { t }$ as the tangential projection of the process $C _ { t } = [ X , X ] _ { t }$ . It is suggestive to write the latter relation in the form $[ \hat { X } , \hat { X } ] = [ X , X ] _ { S } ,$ , or simply as $\hat { C } = C _ { S }$ 

When X is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ , we have $C _ { t } = t I$ for the identity matrix I in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ , and so 

$$
[ \hat {X}, \hat {X} ] _ {t} = P _ {T} ^ {2} (\hat {X}) I \cdot \lambda ,
$$

or simply $d { \hat { C } } _ { t } = I _ { S } d t$ , where the projection $I _ { S }$ may be regarded as the identity matrix in S. Here $\hat { X }$ is called a Brownian motion in S. More generally, if X is an isotropic local martingale in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ , so that $d [ X , X ] _ { t } = d [ X ] _ { t } I$ for a non-decreasing rate process [X] in $\mathsf { R } _ { + }$ , the projection $\hat { X }$ is again isotropic, in the sense that $d \hat { C } = d [ X ] _ { t } I _ { S }$ The latter process may clearly be time-changed into a Brownian motion, just as in the Euclidean case of Theorem 19.4. 

Our somewhat informal, extrinsic discussion is summarized below. The stated results, of some independent interest, will justify our intrinsic definitions of drift and difusion rates in Theorem 35.15. 

Lemma 35.3 (projection onto sub-manifold) Let X be a semi-martingale in ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ with projection X<sup>ˆ</sup> onto a smooth sub-manifold $S \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ . Then 

(i) $\hat { X }$ is a semi-martingale in $S _ { i }$ 

(ii) X is a local martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n } \Rightarrow \hat { X }$ is a martingale in $S ,$ 

(iii) X is an isotropic local martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n } \Rightarrow \hat { X }$ is isotropic in $S _ { i }$ , 

(iv) X is a Brownian motion in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n } \Rightarrow \hat { X }$ is a Brownian motion S. 

Returning to the intrinsic theory, we define martingales in a smooth manifold S in terms of a connection, defined as a linear map of smooth functions $f$ on S into symmetric, bilinear forms $\nabla f _ { \cdot }$ , satisfying<sup>10</sup> 

$$
\nabla f ^ {2} = 2   f   \nabla f + 2   (d f) ^ {\otimes 2}, \quad f \in \mathcal {S}.\tag{4}
$$

Given a connection $\nabla _ { : }$ we define an associated martingale in $S$ as a semimartingale X satisfying 

$$
f (X) \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} \frac {1}{2} \nabla f [ X ], \quad f \in \mathcal {S},\tag{5}
$$

where $X \stackrel { m } { = } Y$ in R means that $X - Y$ is a local martingale. 

For motivation, we state a couple of elementary results. Further justifications are given by Theorems 35.8 and 35.16 35.17 below, which show how the intrinsic martingales and projection properties agree with the corresponding extrinsic notions and results when $S$ is a smooth sub-manifold of ${ \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ 

## Lemma 35.4 (connections and martingales)

(i) A continuous local martingale X in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ satisfies $( 4 ) - ( 5 )$ with 

$$
(\nabla f) _ {i j} = \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} f, \quad i, j \leq n, f \in \mathcal {S}.
$$

(ii) For a smooth manifold S, let $\nabla$ be a linear map from $s$ to the class of symmetric, bilinear maps on S. Then for any semi-martingale X in $S$ satisfying (5), 

$$
\nabla f ^ {2} [ X ] = 2   f   \nabla f [ X ] + 2   (d f) ^ {\otimes 2} [ X ]    a. s., \quad f \in \mathcal {S}.
$$

Proof: (i) Equation (4) is obtained by repeated use of the chain rule for diferentiation, whereas (5) holds by Itˆo’s formula. 

(ii) Applying (5) to both f and $f ^ { 2 }$ and using Theorem 35.1 (i) (ii), along with Theorems 18.11 and 18.16 for real semi-martingales, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{2} \nabla f ^ {2} [ X ] \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} (f \circ X) ^ {2} \\ \qquad = 2   f (X) \cdot (f \circ X) + [ f \circ X ] \\ \qquad \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} f (X) \cdot \nabla f [ X ] + (d f) ^ {\otimes 2} [ X ] \\ \qquad = f   \nabla f [ X ] + (d f) ^ {\otimes 2} [ X ]. \end{array}
$$

Since both sides have locally finite variation and start at 0, the assertion follows by Proposition 18.2. ✷ 

The defining property (4) of connections extends to a general chain rule: 

Theorem 35.5 (chain rule) Let S be a smooth manifold with connection $\nabla$ Then for any smooth functions $f \colon S \to { \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ and ϕ: $\mathsf { R } ^ { n } \to \mathsf { R }$ 2 

$$
\nabla (\varphi \circ f) = \left(\partial_ {i} \varphi \circ f\right) \nabla f ^ {i} + \left(\partial_ {i j} ^ {2} \varphi \circ f\right) \left(d f ^ {i} \otimes d f ^ {j}\right).
$$

Proof: For any vector fields $u , v ,$ define a linear operator w on $s$ by 

$$
w f = u v f - \nabla f (u, v), \quad f \in \mathcal {S}.\tag{6}
$$

Using (4), (6), and the product rule for $u , v .$ , we get 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \frac {1}{2} w f ^ {2} & = \frac {1}{2} u v f ^ {2} - \frac {1}{2} \nabla f ^ {2} (u, v) \\ & = u (f   v f) - f   \nabla f (u, v) - (d f) ^ {\otimes 2} (u, v) \\ & = f   u v f + u f   v f - f   \nabla f (u, v) - u f   v f \\ & = f \Big (u v f - \nabla f (u, v) \Big) = f   w f, \end{array}

In local coordinates, a connection on $S$ is simply a special second order diferential operator. 

Theorem 35.6 (connections as diferential operators) For a smooth manifold S, let be a linear map of any $f \in S$ into a symmetric, bilinear form $\nabla f$ Then these conditions are equivalent:

A geodesic in (S, ) is defined as an afine mapping $\gamma \colon I  S$ , for a real interval I with the flat connection. Lemma 35.9 (geodesics) For a manifold $S$ with connection $\nabla$ and an interval $I \subset \mathsf { R }$ , consider a smooth map $\gamma \colon I  S$ . Then $\gamma$ is a geodesic, if for every $t \in I$

We may also apply (9) directly to the function $\varphi \circ f$ to get

(\varphi \circ f) (X) \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} \frac {1}{2} \nabla (\varphi \circ f) [ X ] + A (\varphi \circ f) \cdot \lambda ,
$$

and so by comparison, 

$$
A (\varphi \circ f) = (\partial_ {i} \varphi \circ f) (X) A f ^ {i} \mathrm{a.e.}
$$

Hence, Lemma A7.1 shows that A is indeed a random tangent vector. 

(ii) For any local coordinates $\varphi ^ { 1 } , \ldots , \varphi ^ { n }$ , we define 

$$
\begin{array}{c} C ^ {i j} \cdot \lambda = \Big (d \varphi^ {i} \otimes d \varphi^ {j} \Big) [ X ] \\ = [ \varphi^ {i} \circ X, \varphi^ {j} \circ X ]. \end{array}
$$

Letting b be a bilinear form with coordinate representation $b _ { i j } ( d \varphi ^ { i } \otimes d \varphi ^ { j } )$ , we obtain the duality relation 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \langle C, b \rangle \cdot \lambda = b _ {i j}   C ^ {i j} \cdot \lambda \\ = b _ {i j} \Big (d \varphi^ {i} \otimes d \varphi^ {j} \Big) [ X ] = b [ X ], \end{array}
$$

where C is the random operator $S \to T _ { S } ^ { \otimes 2 }$ with coordinate representation $\left( C ^ { i j } \right)$ Thus, C is a.e. unique and independent of any choice of local coordinates. 

(iii) Combine $( \mathrm { i } ) - ( \mathrm { i i } )$ , and use Theorem 35.5, along with the coordinate representation of A. ✷ 

We refer to the processes A and C above as the intrinsic drift and difusion rates of X. Note in particular that X is a martingale if $A = 0 ~ \mathrm { a . e }$ . Claim (i) may be surprising, since $\nabla f [ X ]$ is linear in f while $f ( X )$ is not. 

In normal coordinates around a point $x \in S$ , the random diferential operator in (iii) reduces at x to the form 

$$
{\cal L} _ {t} = \frac {1}{2} C _ {t} ^ {i j} \partial_ {i j} ^ {2} + A _ {t} ^ {i} \partial_ {i},
$$

which may be thought of as the characteristic diferential operator<sup>20</sup> of X. This suggests that we regard the pair $( A , C )$ as the random generator of X. 

Our definitions of intrinsic drift and difusion rates are justified by the following results for semi-martingales in Euclidean sub-manifolds, which formally agree with our findings in the extrinsic case.<sup>21</sup> 

Theorem 35.16 (semi-martingales in sub-manifold) Let X be an S-valued semi-martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ , where $S$ is a smooth sub-manifold with induced connection $\nabla$ . Then 

(i) the local drift of X in $S$ is the tangential projection of the drift in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ 

(ii) the local difusion rates of X in S agree with those in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ 

Proof: (i) Using the notation of Theorem 35.8, we may write condition (i) of Theorem 35.15 in the form 

$$
f (X) \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} \frac {1}{2} \nabla f [ X ] + \left\langle \operatorname{grad} \tilde {f} (X) \mid A \right\rangle \cdot \lambda .
$$

Now let $X \overset { m } { = } H \cdot \lambda + V \cdot \lambda$ , where H and $V$ denote the tangential and normal components of the Euclidean drift rate. Proceeding as in the proof of Theorem 35.8, we get 

$$
f (X) \stackrel {{m}} {{=}} \frac {1}{2} \nabla f [ X ] + \left\langle \operatorname{grad} \tilde {f} (X) \mid H \right\rangle \cdot \lambda + \left\langle \operatorname{grad} \tilde {f} (X) \mid V \right\rangle \cdot \lambda .
$$

Here the last term vanishes, since grad $\tilde { f } ( x ) \in T _ { x } \perp V$ , and so by comparison 

$$
\left\langle \operatorname{grad} \tilde {f} (X) \mid A \right\rangle \cdot \lambda = \left\langle \operatorname{grad} \tilde {f} (X) \mid H \right\rangle \cdot \lambda .
$$

Since $f$ was arbitrary, it follows that $A = H { \mathrm { ~ a . e . } }$ , as asserted. 

(ii) Writing $\varphi$ for the embedding $S \to { \mathsf { R } } ^ { n }$ , we get for any bilinear form $b = h ( d f \otimes d g )$ with $f , g , h \in S$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \varphi^ {* 2} b = (h \circ \varphi) \bigl \{(\varphi^ {*} d f) \otimes (\varphi^ {*} d g) \bigr \} \\ = (h \circ \varphi) \bigl \{d (f \circ \varphi) \otimes d (g \circ \varphi) \bigr \}, \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varphi^ {* 2} b (u, v) = (h \circ \varphi)   u (f \circ \varphi)   v (g \circ \varphi) \\ \qquad = h (u f) (v g) \\ \qquad = b (u, v), \end{array}
$$

which extends to $\varphi ^ { * 2 } b = b$ for general b. Hence, Theorem 35.1 (iii) gives 

$$
b [ \varphi \circ X ] = \varphi^ {* 2} b [ X ] = b [ X ],
$$

as desired. 

For a further justification, we show how the local characteristics of a semimartingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ are transformed by projection. This again agrees formally with the extrinsic results in Lemma 35.3. 

Corollary 35.17 (projection onto sub-manifold) Let X be a semi-martingale in $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ with projection X<sup>ˆ</sup> onto a smooth sub-manifold S with induced connection . Then 

(i) $\hat { X }$ is a semi-martingale in S, 

(ii) the local drift of $\hat { X }$ equals the tangential projection of the drift of X, 

(iii) the local difusion rates of $\hat { X }$ are tangential projections of the difusion rates of X. 

Proof: Proceed as in Lemma 35.3 and use Theorem 35.16.

In that case, the local martingale problem of Theorem 35.15 (iii) yields some more precise information about X. As before, we define a difusion in S as a continuous strong Markov process. 

Corollary 35.18 (difusions in manifold) Let X be a semi-martingale in a manifold S with connection . Then 

(i) if (10) has a unique solution X with autonomous rates $A _ { t } = a ( X _ { t } )$ and $C _ { t } = c ( X _ { t } )$ , it defines a difusion in S, 

(ii) if the functions a, c in (i) are smooth, then (10) has a locally unique solution X, defining a Feller difusion in S.

A diferentiable manifold $S$ is said to be Riemannian, if it is endowed with a positive definite, bilinear form $\rho ,$ called the metric tensor on $S .$ . For any vectors $u , v \in T _ { S } , \rho$ determines an inner product $\rho ( u , v ) = \langle u \mid v \rangle$ with associated norm $\| \cdot \|$ . For any smooth curve $\gamma \colon I  S$ , the associated length and energy are defined as integrals of $\| \dot { \gamma } _ { t } \|$ and $\frac { 1 } { 2 } \| \dot { \gamma } _ { t } \| ^ { 2 }$ , respectively. Any semi-martingale X in $S$ has the Riemannian quadratic v $\stackrel { \cdot \cdot } { a r i a t i o n } ^ { 2 3 } \rho [ X ]$ 

The Riemannian structure on $S$ induces a Riemannian metric on any submanifold $S ^ { \prime }$ , preserving the length and energy of any smooth curve, as wel as the quadratic variation of any semi-martingale. This again agrees with the situation in the extrinsic case. 

Lemma 35.20 (induced metric on sub-manifold) For a Riemannian manifold $( S , \rho _ { S } )$ , let $S ^ { \prime } \subset S$ be a smooth sub-manifold with associated embedding $\varphi :$ $S ^ { \prime } \to S$ . Then 

(i) $\rho _ { S ^ { \prime } } = \varphi ^ { * 2 } \rho _ { S }$ is a Riemannian metric on $S ^ { \prime } ,$ 

(ii) for any smooth curve $\gamma$ in $S ^ { \prime }$ , the length γ˙ and energy $\frac { 1 } { 2 } \lVert \dot { \gamma } \rVert ^ { 2 }$ agree under $\rho _ { S }$ and $\rho _ { S ^ { \prime } }$ , 

(iii) for any semi-martingale X in $S ^ { \prime }$ , the quadratic variations $\rho [ X ]$ agree under $\rho _ { S }$ and $\rho _ { S ^ { \prime } }$ 

Proof: (i) For any $u \in T _ { x } S ^ { \prime }$ , we have $( u \circ \varphi ) f = u ( f \circ \varphi ) = u f$ , and so $u \circ \varphi = u$ , which implies $\rho _ { S ^ { \prime } } ( u , v ) = \rho _ { S } ( u , v )$ 

(ii) From (i) we get $\| \dot { \gamma } _ { t } \| _ { S ^ { \prime } } = \| \dot { \gamma } _ { t } \| _ { S }$ for any curve $\gamma$ in $S .$ . 

(iii) For any semi-martingale X in $S ^ { \prime }$ , Theorem 35.1 yield 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \rho_ {S ^ {\prime}} [ X ] = \varphi^ {* 2} \rho_ {S} [ X ] \\ = \rho_ {S} [ \varphi \circ X ] = \rho_ {S} [ X ]. \end{array}
$$

We have seen how a smooth sub-manifold $S$ of $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ can be endowed in a natural way with both a connection and a Riemannian metric $\rho .$ . It is remarkable that $\nabla _ { : }$ , and hence also the associated class of martingales, depend intrinsically only on the metric $\rho ,$ regardless of the way $( S , \rho )$ is embedded<sup>24</sup> into $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ . For that reason, is often called the canonical or Riemannian connection.<sup>25</sup> 

For a precise statement, note that in local coordinates, the Riemannian metric $\rho$ on $S$ is given by a symmetric, positive definite matrix $\rho _ { i j }$ , depending smoothly on $x \in S$ . The associated inverse matrix is denoted by $\bar { \rho } ^ { i j }$ . The notions of Lie derivative $\mathcal { L } _ { u } b$ and gradient grad $f = { \hat { f } }$ are explained in Appendix 7. A coordinate neighborhood of a point $x \in S$ is said to be normal, if the local coordinates are ortho-normal at $x ,$ and every geodesic through x describes a uniform motion along a straight line. 

Theorem 35.21 (Riemannian connection) On a Riemannian manifold $( S , \rho )$ conditions (i)–(iii), (v) are equivalent and determine a unique connection $\nabla .$ : 

(i) for every $x \in S$ , we have $\Gamma _ { i j } ^ { k } ( x ) = 0$ in normal coordinates around $x ,$

(iii) in local coordinates, has Christofel symbols

$$

This holds by (v) and Theorems 35.8 and 35.20, along with the fact that any local neighborhood $U \subset S$ can be isometrically embedded into $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ for a suitable $n .$ 

(ii) To show that is a connection, we note that $\langle \hat { f } | u \rangle = d f ( u ) = u f$ , and hence for any $u \in T _ { S }$

\begin{array}{r l} \langle \operatorname{grad} f ^ {2} | u \rangle & = u f ^ {2} = 2 f (u f) \\ & = 2 f \langle \hat {f} | u \rangle \\ & = \langle 2 f (\hat {f}) | u \rangle , \end{array}

which shows that grad $f ^ { 2 } = 2 f ( { \hat { f } } )$ . Using Corollary A7.5, we get 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \nabla f ^ {2} = \frac {1}{2}   \mathcal {L} _ {\text { grad }   f ^ {2}} (\rho) \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{2}   \mathcal {L} _ {2 f (\hat {f})} (\rho) = \mathcal {L} _ {f (\hat {f})} (\rho) \\ \qquad = f   \mathcal {L} _ {\text { grad }   f} (\rho) + d f \otimes \langle \hat {f}   |   \cdot \rangle + \langle \cdot   |   \hat {f} \rangle \otimes d f \\ \qquad = 2 f   \nabla f + 2   (d f) ^ {\otimes 2}. \end{array}

(iii) Writing ${ \hat { f } } =$ grad f and $\hat { g } =$ grad g, and using Theorem A7.4 (ii) and (iv), we get from (ii) for any vector field u 

$$
\begin{array}{l} 2 \nabla f (u, \hat {g}) = (\mathcal {L} _ {\text {grad} f} \rho) (u, \hat {g}) \\ \qquad = \hat {f} \langle u | \hat {g} \rangle - \langle \mathcal {L} _ {\text {grad} f} u | \hat {g} \rangle - \langle u | \mathcal {L} _ {\text {grad} f} \hat {g} \rangle \\ \qquad = \hat {f} (u g) - (\mathcal {L} _ {\text {grad} f} u) g - \langle \mathcal {L} _ {\text {grad} f} \hat {g} | u \rangle \\ \qquad = u (\hat {f} g) - \left\langle u \big | [ \hat {f}, \hat {g} ] \right\rangle . \end{array}

Interchanging f and g and noting that $[ \hat { f } , \hat { g } ] + [ \hat { g } , \hat { f } ] = 0$ and $\hat { f } g = \hat { g } f = \langle \hat { f } | \hat { g } \rangle$ ， we obtain 

$$
\nabla f (u, \hat {g}) + \nabla g (u, \hat {f}) = u \langle \hat {f} | \hat {g} \rangle .

Choosing $u = \hat { h } =$ grad h and permuting $f , g ,$ , and h, we get 

$$
2 \nabla f (\hat {g}, \hat {h}) = \hat {g} \langle \hat {f} | \hat {h} \rangle + \hat {h} \langle \hat {f} | \hat {g} \rangle - \hat {f} \langle \hat {g} | \hat {h} \rangle .

Noting that every coordinate vector $\partial _ { i }$ in $T _ { S }$ is locally a gradient field, and inverting the mapping ${ \hat { f } } = \operatorname { g r a d } f$ into $\partial _ { i } f = \rho _ { i j } { \hat { f } } ^ { j }$ , we have by (7)

Now solve for $\Gamma _ { j k } ^ { i }$ by applying the inverse matrix $( \rho ^ { i l } )$ to both sides.

In a Riemannian manifold $( S , \rho )$ , we always choose $\nabla$ to be the canonical connection. Given a bilinear form b on $( S , \rho )$ , we define 

$$
\operatorname{tr} b = \rho^ {i j} b _ {i j} = \sum_ {i} b (e _ {i}, e _ {i}),\tag{11}

for any ortho-normal basis $( e _ { i } )$ in $T _ { x }$ . A martingale M in a Riemannian manifold $( S , \rho )$ is said to be isotropic if

(ii) $b \left[ M \right] = \operatorname { t r } b ( M ) \cdot T$ a.s. for an increasing process $T$

Since the extreme sides have locally finite variation, they agree a.s., and (13) follows by continuity, proving (i). ✷ 

A Lie group is defined as a diferential manifold endowed with a smooth group structure. On any Lie group S, we may introduce a left-invariant Riemannian metric $\rho ,$ generated by an arbitrary inner product on the basic tangent space $T _ { \iota }$ , where ι is the identity element of S. Since the group operation may not be commutative, we need to distinguish between left and right increments of a process X over an interval $[ s , t ]$ , given by $X _ { s } ^ { - 1 } X _ { t }$ or $X _ { t } X _ { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively. In the Abelian case, both versions reduce to $X _ { t } - X _ { s }$ 

As before, we define a L´evy process in S as a process with stationary, independent left increments. We proceed to characterize L´evy processes in terms of the local characteristics in Theorem 35.15. The result is a version for Lie groups of the elementary Theorem 11.5. 

Theorem 35.25 (L´evy processes in Lie groups) In a Lie group S with a leftinvariant Riemannian metric $\rho ,$ let X be a semi-martingale with local rates A and C. Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) X has stationary, independent left increments, 

(ii) $A = a ( X )$ and $C = c ( \boldsymbol { X } )$ for some smooth, left-invariant functions $a , c$ on $S _ { ☉ }$ 

Proof, (ii) (i): By Corollary 35.18 (ii), X is a Feller difusion, whose distribution is uniquely determined by a and c. If the latter are left-invariant, Theorem 11.5 shows that X has stationary, independent left increments. 

$( \mathrm { i } ) \Rightarrow ( \mathrm { i i } )$ : For any $s < t .$ , Proposition 18.17 and Theorem 35.1 show that the increment $b [ X ] _ { t } - b [ X ] _ { s }$ depends measurably on the values of X in the interval $[ s , t ]$ . By stationarity of the increments, the corresponding mapping is leftinvariant. Taking right derivatives in Theorem 2.15 and using the stationarity again, we conclude that $C _ { t }$ depends measurably on X in any right neighborhood $[ t , t + \varepsilon )$ , where the afecting map is again invariant. By the 0 1 law in Corollary 9.26, $C _ { t }$ then depends measurably on $X _ { t }$ for every $t > 0$ , and so $C _ { t } = c ( X _ { t } )$ by Lemma 1.14 for a measurable and invariant function c. 

To deal with A, we need to show that if $f ( X )$ has a semi-martingale decomposition $M + V$ , then $V _ { t } - V _ { s }$ depends measurably on X in the interval $[ s , t ]$ . The required measurability then follows by approximation with sums of conditional expectations, as in the proof in Lemma 10.7, since the conditioning σ-field $\mathcal { F } _ { s }$ may be replaced by conditioning on $X _ { s } ,$ , by independence of the increments. Since such a measurability is already known for the term ${ \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \nabla f [ X ]$ in (9), it holds for $A f$ as well. We may now proceed as before to see that $A = a ( X _ { t } )$ for some measurable and invariant function a. 

Since a is a left-invariant vector field on $S ,$ , it is automatically smooth<sup>28</sup>. A similar argument may yield the desired smoothness of the second order invariant vector field c. ✷ 

Every continuous process in $S$ with stationary, independent left increments can be shown to be a semi-martingale of the stated form. The intrinsic drift rate a clearly depends on the connection $\nabla .$ , which in turn depends on the metric $\rho ,$ via Theorem 35.21. However, $\rho$ is not unique since it can be generated by any inner product on $T _ { \iota }$ , and so there is no natural definition of Brownian motion in $S .$ . In fact, martingales and drift rates are not well-defined either, since even the canonical connection may fail to be unique<sup>29</sup>.

# Appendices

1. Measurable maps, 2. General topology, 3. Linear spaces, 4. Linear operators, 5. Function and measure spaces, 6. Classes and spaces of sets, 7. Diferential geometry 

Here we review some basic topology, functional analysis, and diferential geometry, needed at various places throughout the book. We further consider some special results from advanced measure theory, and discuss the topological properties of various spaces of functions, measures, and sets, of crucial importance for especially the weak convergence theory in Chapter 23. Proofs are included only when they are not easily accessible in the standard literature. 

## 1. Measurable maps

The basic measure theory required for the development of modern probability was surveyed in Chapters 1–3. Here we add some less elementary facts, needed for special purposes. 

If a measurable mapping is invertible, the measurability of its inverse can sometimes be inferred from the measurability of the range. 

Theorem A1.1 (range and inverse, Kuratowski) For any measurable bijection f between two Borel spaces S and T, the inverse $f ^ { - 1 } : T  S$ is again measurable. 

Proof: See Parthasarathy (1967), Section I.3. 

We turn to the basic projection and section theorems, which play important roles in some more advanced contexts. Given a measurable space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ , we define the universal completion of $\mathcal { F }$ as the σ-field $\bar { \mathcal { F } } = \cap _ { \mu } \mathcal { F } ^ { \mu }$ , where $\mathcal { F } ^ { \mu }$ denotes the completion of $\mathcal { F }$ with respect to $\mu ,$ <sub>, and the intersection extends</sub> over all probability measures $\mu$ on $\mathcal { F }$ . For any spaces Ω and S, we define the projection $\pi A$ of a set $A \subset \Omega \times S$ onto $\Omega$ as the union $\cup _ { s } A _ { s }$ , where 

$$
A _ {s} = \left\{\omega \in \Omega ; (\omega , s) \in A \right\}, \quad s \in S.
$$

Theorem A1.2 (projection and sections, Lusin, Choquet, Meyer) For any measurable space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } )$ and Borel space (S, ), consider a set $A \in { \mathcal { F } } \otimes S$ with projection πA onto Ω. Then 

$$
\pi A \in \bar {\mathcal {F}} = \bigcap_ {\mu} \mathcal {F} ^ {\mu},\tag{i}
$$

(ii) for any probability measure $P$ on ${ \mathcal { F } } _ { z }$ , there exists a random element $\xi$ in $S _ { i }$ , such that 

$$
\{\omega , \xi (\omega) \} \in A, \quad \omega \in \pi A a. s. P.
$$

Proof: See Dellacherie $\&$ Meyer (1975), Section III.44. 

We note an application to functional representations needed in Chapter 28: 

Corollary A1.3 (conditioning representation) Consider a probability space $( \Omega , { \mathcal { F } } , P )$ with sub-σ-field $\mathcal { G } \subset \mathcal { F }$ and a measurable function $f \colon T \times U  S$ , where S, T, U are Borel. Let $\xi , \eta$ be random elements in S and $U ,$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {L} (\xi \mid \mathcal {G}) \in \left\{\mathcal {L} \{f (t, \eta) \}; t \in T \right\} a. s.
$$

Then there exist a -measurable random element $\tau$ in $T$ and a random element $\tilde { \eta }$ in $U$ , such that ~ 

$$
\eta \stackrel {d} {=} \tilde {\eta} \perp \bot \tau , \qquad \xi = f (\tau , \tilde {\eta}) a. s.
$$

Proof: Fix a version of the conditional distribution ${ \mathcal { L } } ( \xi | { \mathcal { G } } )$ . Applying Theorem A1.2 (ii) to the product-measurable set 

$$
A = \Bigl \{(\omega , t) \in \Omega \times T; \mathcal {L} (\xi | \mathcal {G}) (\omega) = \mathcal {L} \{f (t, \eta) \} \Bigr \},
$$

we obtain a $\mathcal { G }$ -measurable random element $\tau$ in $T$ satisfying 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {L} (\xi   |   \mathcal {G}) = \mathcal {L} \Big \{f (t, \eta) \Big \} _ {t = \tau} \\ = \mathcal {L} (\xi   |   \tau) \text { a.s.}, \end{array}
$$

where the last equality holds by the chain rule for conditioning. Letting $\zeta \ { \overset { d } { = } } \ \eta$ in $U$ with $\zeta \perp \perp \tau$ and using Lemma 4.11, we get a.s. 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathcal {L} \bigl \{f (\tau , \zeta) \bigr | \tau \bigr \} = \mathcal {L} \bigl \{f (t, \eta) \bigr \} _ {t = \tau} \\ = \mathcal {L} (\xi | \tau), \end{array}
$$

and so $\{ f ( \tau , \zeta ) , \tau \} \stackrel { d } { = } ( \xi , \tau )$ . Then Theorem 8.17 yields a random pair $( \tilde { \eta } , \tilde { \tau } ) \stackrel { d } { = }$ $( \zeta , \tau )$ in $U \times T$ with 

$$
\left\{f (\tilde {\tau}, \tilde {\eta}), \tilde {\tau} \right\} = (\xi , \tau) \text { a.s. }
$$

In particular $\tilde { \tau } = \tau \ \mathrm { a . s . }$ ., and so $\xi = f ( \tau , \tilde { \eta } )$ a.s. Further note that $\tilde { \eta } \overset { d } { = } \zeta \overset { d } { = } \eta$ 2 and that $\tilde { \eta }$ Ⅱ $\tilde { \tau } = \tau$ since $\zeta \perp \perp \tau$ by construction. ✷ 

## 2. General topology

Elementary metric topology, including properties of open and closed sets, continuity, convergence, and compactness, are used throughout this book. For special purposes, we also need the slightly more subtle notions of separability and completeness, dense or nowhere dense sets, uniform and equi-continuity, and approximation. We assume the reader to be well familiar with most of this material. Here we summarize some basic ideas of general, non-metric topology, of special importance in Sections 5–6 below and Chapter 23. Proofs may be found in most textbooks on real analysis. 

A topology on a space S is defined as a class $\tau$ of subsets of S, called the open sets, such that is closed under finite intersections and arbitrary unions and contains S and . The complements of open sets are said to be closed. For any $A \subset S$ , the interior $A ^ { o }$ is the union of all open set contained in A. Similarly, the closure A<sup>¯</sup> is the intersection of all closed sets containing A, and the boundary $\partial A$ is the diference ${ \bar { A } } \setminus A ^ { o }$ . A set A is dense in S if ${ \bar { A } } = S .$ and nowhere dense if $( \bar { A } ) ^ { c }$ is dense in S. The space $S$ is separable if it has a countable, dense subset. It is connected if S and $\varnothing$ are the only sets that are both open and closed. For any $A \subset S$ , the relative topology on A consists of all sets $A \cap G$ with $G \in { \mathcal { T } }$ 

The family of topologies on S is partially ordered under set inclusion. The smallest topology on S has only the two sets S and , whereas the largest one, the discrete topology $2 ^ { S }$ , contains all subsets of S. For any class of subsets of $S _ { ☉ }$ , the generated topology is the smallest topology $\tau \supset \mathcal { C }$ . A topology $\tau$ is said to be metrizable, if there exists a metric $\rho$ on S, such that $\tau$ is generated by all open $\rho { \mathrm { - b a l l s } }$ . In particular, it is Polish if $\rho$ can be chosen to be separable and complete. 

An open set containing a point $x \in S$ is called a neighborhood of $x .$ A class $B _ { x }$ of neighborhoods of $x$ is called a neighborhood base at $x ,$ if every neighborhood of x contains a set in $B _ { x }$ . A base of $\tau$ is a class containing a neighborhood base at every point. Every base clearly generates the topology. The space $S$ is said to be first countable, if it has a countable neighborhood base at every point, and second countable, if it has a countable base. Every metric space is clearly first countable, and it is second countable if it is separable. A topological space S is said to be Hausdorf, if any two distinct points have disjoint neighborhoods, and normal if all singleton sets are closed, and any two disjoint closed sets are contained in disjoint open sets. In particular, all metric spaces are normal. 

A mapping f between two topological spaces $S , S ^ { \prime }$ is said to be continuous, if $f ^ { - 1 } B$ is open in $S$ for every open set $B \subset S ^ { \prime }$ . The spaces $S , S ^ { \prime }$ are homeomorphic, if there exists a bijection (1 1 correspondence) $f \colon S  S ^ { \prime }$ such that $f$ and $f ^ { - 1 }$ are both continuous. For any family $\mathcal { F }$ of functions $f _ { i }$ mapping $S$ into some topological spaces $S _ { i }$ , the generated topology on $S$ is the smallest one making all the $f _ { i }$ continuous. In particular, if $S$ is a Cartesian product of some topological spaces $S _ { i } , i \in I$ , so that the elements of $S$ are functions $x = ( x _ { i } ; i \in I )$ , then the product topology on S is generated by all coordinate projections $\pi _ { i } \colon x \mapsto x _ { i }$ . A set $A \subset S$ is said to be compact, if every cover of A by open sets contains a finite subcover, and relatively compact if its closure $\bar { A }$ is compact. By Tychonov’s theorem, any Cartesian product of compact spaces is again compact in the product topology. A topological space S is said to be locally compact, if it has a base consisting of sets with compact closure. 

A set I is said to be partially ordered under a relation , if 

$i \prec j \prec i \Rightarrow i = j ,$ 

$i \prec i$ for all $i \in I$ , 

$i \prec j \prec k \Rightarrow i \prec k .$ 

It is said to be directed if also 

• t $, j \in I \Rightarrow i \prec k$ and $j \prec k$ for some $k \in I$ 

A net in a topological space S is a mapping of a directed set I into S. In particular, sequences are nets on $I = \mathsf { N }$ with the usual order. A net $( x _ { i } )$ is said to converge to a limit $x \in S$ , written as $x _ { i } \to x ,$ , if for every neighborhood A of x there exists an $i \in I$ , such that $x _ { j } \in A$ for all $j \succ i .$ . Possible limits are unique when $S$ is Hausdorf, but not in general. We further say that $( x _ { i } )$ clusters at x, if for any neighborhood A of x and $i \in I$ , there exists a $j \succ i$ with $x _ { j } \in A$ . For sequences $( x _ { n } )$ , this means that $x _ { n } \to x$ along a sub-sequence. 

Net convergence and clustering are constantly used<sup>1</sup> throughout analysis and probability, such as in continuous time and higher dimensions, or in the definitions of total variation and Riemann integrals. They also serve to characterize the topology itself: 

Lemma A2.1 (closed sets) For sets A in a topological space S, these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) A is closed, 

(ii) for every convergent net in A, even the limit lies in A, 

(iii) for every net in A, all cluster points also lie in A. 

When S is a metric space, it sufices in (ii) (iii) to consider sequences. 

We can also use nets to characterize compactness: 

Lemma A2.2 (compact sets) For sets A in a topological space $S ,$ , these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) A is compact, 

(ii) every net in A has at least one cluster point in A. 

If the net in (ii) has exactly one cluster point x, it converges to x. When S is a metric space, it is enough in (ii) to consider sequences. 

For sequences, property (ii) above amounts to sequential compactness—the existence of a convergent sub-sequence with limit in A. For the notion of relative sequential compactness, the limit is not required to lie in A. 

Given a compact topological space X, let $C _ { X }$ be the class of continuous functions $f : X \to \mathsf { R }$ equipped with the supremum norm $\| f \| = \operatorname* { s u p } _ { x } | f ( x ) |$ An algebra $A \subset C _ { X }$ is defined as a linear subspace closed under multiplication. It is said to separate points, if for any x $\neq y$ in X there exists an $f \in { \mathcal { A } }$ with $f ( x ) \neq f ( y )$ 

Theorem A2.3 (Stone–Weierstrass) For a compact topological space X, let $A \subset C _ { X }$ be an algebra separating points and containing the constant function 1. Then ${ \bar { \mathcal { A } } } = C _ { X }$ 

Like many other results in this and subsequent sections, this statement is also true in a complex version. 

Throughout this book we are making use of spaces that are locally compact, second countable, and Hausdorf, here referred to as lcscH spaces. We record some standard facts about such spaces: 

Lemma A2.4 (lcscH spaces) Let the space S be lcscH. Then 

(i) S is Polish and σ-compact, 

(ii) S has a separable, complete metrization, such that a set is relatively compact if it is bounded, 

(iii) if S is not already compact, it can be compactified by the attachment of a single point $\Delta \neq S$ 

## 3. Linear spaces

In this and the next section, we summarize some basic ideas of functional analysis, such as Hilbert and Banach spaces, and operators between linear spaces. Aspects of this material are needed in several chapters throughout the book. Proofs may be found in textbooks on real analysis. 

A linear $s p a c e ^ { 2 }$ over R is a set X with two operations, addition $x + y$ and multiplication by scalars<sup>3</sup> cx, such that for any $x , y , z \in X$ and $a , b \in \mathsf { R }$ 

x + (y + z) = (x + y) + z, 

$x + y = y + x ,$ 

x + 0 = x for some $0 \in X$ 

x + ( x) = 0 for some x X, 

$a ( b x ) = ( a b ) x ,$ 

$( a + b ) x = a x + b x ,$ 

a(x + y) = ax + ay, 

$1 x = x .$ 

A subspace of X is a subset closed under the mentioned operations, hence a linear space in its own right. A function $\| x \| \geq 0$ on X is called a norm, if for any $x , y \in X$ and $c \in { \mathsf { R } }$ , 

$\| x \| = 0 \Leftrightarrow x = 0 ,$ 

$\| c x \| = | c | \| x \| ,$ 

$\| x + y \| \leq \| x \| + \| y \| .$ 

The norm generates a metric $\rho$ on $X$ , given by $\rho ( x , y ) = \| x - y \|$ . If $\rho$ is complete, in the sense that every Cauchy sequence converges, then X is called a Banach space. In that case, any closed subspace is again a Banach space. 

Given a linear space X, we define a linear functional on X as a function $f \colon X \to \mathsf { R }$ , such that 

$$
f (a x + b y) = a f (x) + b f (y), \quad x, y \in X, a, b \in \mathsf {R}.
$$

Similarly, a convex functional is defined as a map $p \colon X \to \mathsf { R } _ { + }$ satisfying 

$p ( c x ) = c p ( x ) , \quad x \in X , c \geq 0 ,$ 

p(x + y) p(x) + p(y), x, y X. 

Lemma A3.1 (Hahn–Banach) Let X be a linear space with subspace $Y _ { i }$ , fix a convex functional p on X, and let f be a linear functional on Y with $f \leq p$ on Y. Then f extends to a linear functional on $X ,$ , such that $f \leq p$ on $X$ 

A set M in a linear space X is said to be convex if 

$$
c x + (1 - c) y \in M, \quad x, y \in M, c \in [ 0, 1 ].
$$

A hyper-plane in X is determined by an equation $f ( x ) = a .$ , for a linear functional $f \neq 0$ and a constant a. We say that M is supported by the plane $f ( x ) = a { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } f ( x ) \leq a , { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } f ( x ) \geq a$ , for all $x \in M$ . The sets M, N are separated by the plane $f ( x ) = a \mathrm { i f } f ( x ) \leq a$ on M and $f ( x ) \geq a$ on N, or vice versa. For clarity, we state the following support and separation result for convex sets in a Euclidean space. 

Corollary A3.2 (convex sets) 

(i) For any convex set $M \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ and point $x \in \partial M$ , there exists a hyper-plane through x supporting M. 

(ii) For any disjoint convex sets $M , N \subset \mathsf { R } ^ { d }$ , there exists a hyper-plane separating M and N. 

When X is a normed linear space, we say that a linear functional f on X is bounded if $| f ( x ) | \leq c \| x \|$ for some constant $c < \infty$ . Then there is a smallest value of $c ,$ denoted by f , so that $| f ( x ) | \leq \| f \| \| x \|$ . The space of bounded linear functionals $f$ on X is again a normed linear space (in fact a Banach space), called the dual of X and denoted by $X ^ { \ast }$ . Continuing recursively, we may form the second dual $X ^ { * * } = ( X ^ { * } ) ^ { * }$ , etc. 

Theorem A3.3 (Hahn–Banach) Let X be a normed linear space with a subspace Y. Then for any $g \in Y ^ { * }$ , there exists an $f \in X ^ { * }$ with $\| f \| = \| g \|$ and $f = g \ o n \ Y$ 

Corollary A3.4 (natural embedding) For a normed linear space $X$ , we may define a linear isometry $T \colon X \to X ^ { * * }$ by 

$$
(T x) f = f (x), \quad x \in X, f \in X ^ {*}.
$$

The space X is said to be reflexive if $T ( X ) = X ^ { * * }$ , so that X and $X ^ { * * }$ are isomorphic, written as $X \cong X ^ { * * }$ . The reflexive property extends to any closed linear subspace of $X$ . Familiar examples of reflexive spaces include $l ^ { p }$ and $L ^ { p }$ for $p > 1$ (but not for $p = 1 )$ , where the duals equal $l ^ { q }$ and $L ^ { q }$ , respectively, with $p ^ { - 1 } + q ^ { - 1 } = 1$ . For $p = 2$ , we get a Hilbert space H with the unique property $H \cong H ^ { * }$ 

On a normed linear space X, we may consider not only the norm topology induced by $\lVert x \rVert$ , but also the weak topology generated by the dual $X ^ { \ast }$ . Thus, the weak topology on $X ^ { \ast }$ is generated by the second dual $X ^ { * * }$ . Even more important is the weak∗ topology on $X ^ { \ast }$ , generated by the coordinate maps $\pi _ { x }$ : $X ^ { * }  \mathsf { R }$ given by 

$$
\pi_ {x} f = f (x), \quad x \in X, f \in X ^ {*}.
$$

Lemma A3.5 (topologies on $X ^ { * } )$ For a normed linear space $X$ , write $\mathcal { T } _ { w } ^ { * }$ $\mathcal { T } _ { w } , ~ \mathcal { T } _ { n }$ for the weak∗, weak, and norm topologies on $X ^ { \ast }$ . Then 

(i) $\mathcal { T } _ { w } ^ { \ast } \subset \mathcal { T } _ { w } \subset \mathcal { T } _ { n } ,$

An inner product on a linear space $X$ is a function $\langle x , y \rangle$ on $X ^ { 2 }$ , such that for any $x , y , z \in X$ and $a , b \in \mathsf { R }$ 

$\langle x , x \rangle \geq 0 \quad$ , with equality if $x = 0$ 

$\langle x , y \rangle = \langle y , x \rangle$ 

$\langle a x + b y , z \rangle = a \langle x , z \rangle + b \langle y , z \rangle .$ 

The function $\lVert x \rVert = \langle x , x \rangle ^ { 1 / 2 }$ is then a norm on $X ,$ , satisfying the Cauchy inequality<sup>4</sup> 

$$
\bullet \quad | \langle x, y \rangle | \leq \| x \| \| y \|, \quad x, y \in X.
$$

If the associated metric is complete, then X is called a Hilbert $s p a c e ^ { 5 }$ . If $\langle x , y \rangle = 0$ , we say that x and y are orthogonal and write $x \perp y$ . For any subset $A \subset H$ , we write $x \perp A$ if $x \perp y$ for all $y \in A$ . The orthogonal complement $A ^ { \perp }$ , consisting of all $x \in H$ with $x \perp A$ , is a closed linear subspace of H. 

A linear functional f on a Hilbert space H is clearly continuous if it is bounded, in the sense that 

$$
| f (x) | \leq c \| x \|, \quad x \in H,
$$

for some constant $c \geq 0$ , in which case we define $\| f \|$ as the smallest constant c with this property. The bounded linear functionals form a linear space $H ^ { * }$ with norm $\| f \|$ , which is again a Hilbert space isomorphic to H. 

Lemma A3.6 (Riesz representation<sup>6</sup>) For functions f on a Hilbert space $H _ { \cdot }$ these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) f is a continuous linear functional on $H ,$ 

(ii) there exists a unique element $y \in H$ satisfying 

$$
f (x) = \langle x, y \rangle , \quad x \in H.
$$

In this case, $\| f \| = \| y \|$ 

An ortho-normal system (ONS) in H is a family of orthogonal elements $x _ { i } \in H$ with norm 1. It is said to be complete or to form an ortho-normal basis (ONB) if $y \perp ( x _ { i } )$ implies $y = 0$ 

Lemma A3.7 (ortho-normal bases) For any Hilbert space H, we have<sup>7</sup> 

(i) H has an ONB $( x _ { i } )$ 

(ii) the cardinality of $( x _ { i } )$ is unique, 

(iii) every $x \in H$ has a unique representation 

$$
x = \sum_ {i} b _ {i} x _ {i}, w h e r e b _ {i} = \langle x, x _ {i} \rangle ,
$$

(iv) if $\textstyle x = \sum _ { i } b _ { i } x _ { i }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { y = \sum _ { i } c _ { i } x _ { i } } \end{array}$ , then 

$$
\langle x, y \rangle = \sum_ {i} b _ {i} c _ {i}, \quad \| x \| ^ {2} = \sum_ {i} b _ {i} ^ {2}.
$$

The cardinality in (ii) is called the dimension of H. Since any finite-dimensional Hilbert space is isomorphic<sup>8</sup> to a Euclidean space $\mathsf { R } ^ { n }$ , we may henceforth assume the dimension to be infinite. The simplest infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is $l ^ { 2 }$ , consisting of all infinite sequences $\boldsymbol { x } ~ = ~ ( \boldsymbol { x } _ { n } )$ in R with $\| x \| ^ { 2 } =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { n } x _ { n } ^ { 2 } < \infty$ . Here the inner product is given by 

$$
\langle x, y \rangle = \sum_ {n \geq 1} x _ {n}   y _ {n}, \quad x = (x _ {n}), y = (y _ {n}),
$$

and we may choose an ONB consisting of the elements $( 0 , \ldots , 0 , 1 , 0 , \ldots )$ , with 1 in the n-th position. 

Another standard example is $L ^ { 2 } ( \mu )$ , for any σ-finite measure $\mu$ with infinite support on a measurable space S. Here the elements are (equivalence classes of) measurable functions f on S with $\| f \| ^ { 2 } = \mu f ^ { 2 } < \infty$ , and the inner product is given by $\langle f , g \rangle = \mu ( f g )$ . Familiar ONB’s include the Haar functions when $\mu$ equals Lebesgue measure λ on [0, 1], and suitably normalized Hermite polynomials when $\mu = N ( 0 , 1 )$ on R. 

All the basic Hilbert spaces are essentially equivalent: 

Lemma A3.8 (separable Hilbert spaces) For an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space H, these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) H is separable, 

(ii) H has countably infinite dimension, 

(iii) $H \cong l ^ { 2 } ,$ 

(iv) $H \cong L ^ { 2 } ( \mu )$ for any σ-finite measure μ with infinite support. 

Most Hilbert spaces H arising in applications are separable, and for simplicity we may often take $H = l ^ { 2 }$ , or let $H = L ^ { 2 } ( \mu )$ for a suitable measure $\mu .$ For any Hilbert spaces $H _ { 1 } , H _ { 2 }$ , we may form a new Hilbert space $H _ { 1 } \otimes H _ { 2 }$ , called the tensor product of $H _ { 1 } , H _ { 2 }$ . When $H _ { 1 } = L ^ { 2 } ( \mu _ { 1 } )$ and $H _ { 2 } = L ^ { 2 } ( \mu _ { 2 } )$ , it may be thought of as the space $L ^ { 2 } ( \mu _ { 1 } \otimes \mu _ { 2 } )$ , where $\mu _ { 1 } \otimes \mu _ { 2 }$ is the product measure of $\mu _ { 1 } , \mu _ { 2 }$ . If $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \ldots$ . and $g _ { 1 } , g _ { 2 } , \ldots .$ . are ONB’s in $H _ { 1 }$ and $H _ { 2 }$ , the functions $h _ { i j } = f _ { i } \otimes g _ { j }$ form an ONB in $H _ { 1 } \otimes H _ { 2 }$ , where $( f \otimes g ) ( x , y ) = f ( x ) g ( y )$ . Iterating the construction, we may form the n-fold tensor powers $H ^ { \otimes n } = H \otimes \cdots \otimes H$ for every $n \in \mathsf N$ 

## 4. Linear operators

A linear operator between two normed linear spaces $X , Y$ is a mapping $T$ : $X  Y$ satisfying 

$$
T (a x + b y) = a T x + b T y, \quad x, y \in X, a, b \in \mathsf {R}.
$$

It is said to be bounded<sup>9</sup> if $\| T x \| \leq c \| x \|$ for some constant $c < \infty$ , in which case there is a smallest number $\lVert \boldsymbol { T } \rVert$ with this property, so that 

$$
\| T x \| \leq \| T \| \| x \|, \quad x \in X.
$$

When $\| T \| \leq 1$ we call $T$ a contraction operator. The space of bounded linear operators $X  Y$ is denoted by $\boldsymbol { { B } _ { X , Y } }$ , and when $X = Y$ we write $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { B } _ { X , X } } = \boldsymbol { \mathcal { B } _ { X } }$ Those are again linear spaces, under the operations 

$$
\begin{array}{c} (T _ {1} + T _ {2})   x = T _ {1} x + T _ {2} x, \\ (c   T) x = c   (T x), \qquad x \in X,    c \in \mathsf {R}, \end{array}
$$

and the function $\lVert \boldsymbol { T } \rVert$ above is a norm on $\boldsymbol { { B } _ { X , Y } }$ . Furthermore, $\boldsymbol { { B } _ { X , Y } }$ is complete, hence a Banach space, whenever this is true for $Y$ . In particular, we note that $\boldsymbol { B } _ { X , \mathsf { R } }$ equals the dual space $X ^ { \ast }$ 

Theorem A4.1 (Banach–Steinhaus) Let $\mathcal { T } \subset B _ { X , Y }$ , for a Banach space X and a normed linear space $Y$ . Then 

$$
\sup _ {T \in \mathcal {T}} \| T x \| <   \infty , x \in X \Leftrightarrow \sup _ {T \in \mathcal {T}} \| T \| <   \infty .
$$

If $T \in B _ { X , Y }$ and $S \in B _ { Y , Z }$ , the product $S T \in B _ { X , Z }$ is given by $( S T ) x =$ $S ( T x )$ , and we note that $\lVert S T \rVert \leq \lVert S \rVert \lVert T \rVert$ . Two operators $S , T \in B _ { X }$ are said to commute if $S T = T S$ . The identity operator $I \in B _ { X }$ is defined by $I x = x$ for all $x \in X$ . Furthermore, $T \in B _ { X }$ is said to be idempotent if $T ^ { 2 } = T$ . For any operators $T , T _ { 1 } , T _ { 2 } , \ldots \in \mathcal { B } _ { X , Y }$ , we say that $T _ { n }$ converges strongly to $T$ if 

$$
\left\| T _ {n} x - T x \right\|\rightarrow 0 \text { in } Y, \quad x \in X.
$$

We also consider convergence in the norm topology, defined by $ T _ { n } - T   0$ in $B _ { X , Y }$ 

For any $A \in B _ { X , Y }$ , the adjoint $A ^ { * }$ of A is a linear map on $Y ^ { * }$ given by 

$$
(A ^ {*} f) (x) = f (A x), \quad x \in X, f \in Y ^ {*}.
$$

If also $B \in B _ { Y , Z }$ , we note that $( B A ) ^ { * } = A ^ { * } B ^ { * }$ . Further note that $I ^ { * } = I$ , where the latter I is given by $I f = f$ 

Lemma A4.2 (adjoint operator) For any normed linear spaces $X , Y ,$ , the map $A \to A ^ { * }$ is a linear isometry from $B _ { X , Y }$ to $B _ { Y ^ { * } , X ^ { * } }$ 

When $A \in B _ { X , Y }$ is bijective, its inverse $A ^ { - 1 } \colon Y \to X$ is again linear, though it need not be bounded. 

Theorem A4.3 (inverses and adjoints) For a Banach space X and a normed linear space Y, let $A \in B _ { X , Y }$ . Then these conditions are equivalent: 

(i) A has a bounded inverse $A ^ { - 1 } \in B _ { Y , X }$ ,

In that case, $( A ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } = ( A ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { * }$ 

For a Hilbert space H we may identify $H ^ { * }$ with H, which leads to some simplifications. Then for any $A \in B _ { H }$ there exists a unique operator $A ^ { \ast } \in B _ { H }$ satisfying 4 *

Proof: See K(17), pp. 111–117. 

On the sub-class $\mathcal { M } _ { S } ^ { b }$ of bounded measures on $S ,$ , we also consider the weak topology and associated weak convergence $\mu _ { n } \stackrel { w } {  } \mu .$ , given by (5) with $\hat { C } _ { S }$ replaced by the class $C _ { S }$ of bounded, continuous functions on $S$ . No further analysis is required, since this agrees with the vague topology and convergence, when the metric $\rho$ on $S$ is replaced by the equivalent metric $\rho \wedge 1$ , so that all sets in $S$ become bounded. 

Theorem A5.6 (vague compactness in $\mathcal { M } _ { S }$ , Prohorov, Matthes et al.) Let $A \subset { \mathcal { M } } _ { S }$ for a separable, complete metric space S. Then A is vaguely relatively compact if

We finally consider spaces of measure-valued rcll functions. Here we may characterize compactness in terms of countably many one-dimensional projections. Here we write $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { + } , S } = D _ { S }$ for simplicity. 

Theorem A5.7 (measure-valued functions) Given an lcscH space $S ,$ there exist some $f _ { 1 } , f _ { 2 } , \dots \in \hat { C } _ { S }$ , such that these conditions are equivalent, for any $A \subset D _ { { \scriptscriptstyle M } _ { S } }$

(ii) $A f _ { j } = \{ x f _ { j } ; x \in A \}$ is relatively compact in $D _ { \mathsf { R } _ { - } }$ for every $j \in \mathsf N$

In the former case, (6) yields lim su $\mathrm { p } _ { n } \left| x _ { t _ { n } } ^ { n } f _ { j } - x _ { 0 } ^ { n } f _ { j } \right| > 0$ for some $j \in \mathsf N$ , which contradicts the relative compactness of $A f _ { j }$ . Now for any $a , a ^ { \prime } , b , b ^ { \prime } \in { \mathsf { R } }$
